Biographical Notes on Office-Holders
In this and later volumes I have made use of the series Office-holders in Modern Britain, published by the Institute of Historical Research (University of London) from 1972 onwards, for dates in the notices of minor office-holders. I have treated it like Foster's Alumni Oxonienses and similar compilations: that is, I have named it when it provides the best available biographical statements about the office-holders, but not when drawing on it only for its specific information, the dates of tenure of office in notes based primarily on other materials.

Locke's Life:
Principal Dates for this Volume
This table is planned to provide dates that should be serviceable to readers of the correspondence. It is not a chronological framework for Locke's life.
The principal difficulty in its compilation is that for many incidents in his life precise dates do not exist. Thus, if the mention is accurate, Locke was acquainted with Robert Boyle on 20 May 1660; there is nothing to show how much earlier the acquaintance was made. Unsatisfactory as many of them are, the dates are the best available.
In the dates a. (for ante) is to be taken to imply shortly before. In the dates for books when a precise date accompanies the word 'published' it is to be taken as the date of the earliest notice that the book had been, was, or was about to be, published, and not necessarily as the day of publication.
                  
1694 	Spring? The second edition of Two Treatises published. 
	c. 26 May. The second edition of the Essay published. 
	c. 26 June. Locke subscribes £500 to the Bank of England. 
	23 October. Peter King admitted to the Middle Temple. Locke's affection for King emerges, and his reliance on him starts, about this time. 
	29 November. The first extant letter of the College series. 
1695 	c. 25 February. Short Observations on a Printed Paper published. 
	Late June? The third edition of Some Thoughts concerning Education published. 
	Late July? The Lords Justices consult Locke and other men about the currency. 
	12 August. The Reasonableness of Christianity advertised. 
	24 September. Somers consults Locke about Lowndes's report on the currency. 
	Autumn? The third edition of the Essay published. 
	c. October. A Vindication of the Reasonableness of Christianity published. 
	c. 15 November. Lowndes's Report is circulated to members of parliament. 
	c. 10 December. The abortive Commission for Trade and Plantations. 
	31 December. Further Considerations concerning Raising the Value of Money advertised. 
1696 	15 May. The Commission for Trade and Plantations (the Board of Trade) established; Locke appointed a commissioner. 
	25 June. First meeting of the Board. Locke attends almost all meetings until 13 November. 
1697 	13-17 February. Locke attends Board of Trade meetings. 


Letters Nos. 1702-2198
1694
January
1702. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 30 January/9 February 1694 (1684, 1741)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 113-14.
Rotterdam 9 February 1693/4
My Dear Friend
Yours of the 8/18 past from Oates, I have, and wonder to understand, that you had not heard of my marriage having wrote you, and the Baron both, of it, by mr. Sonmans from whom I have received 3 letters since his arrivall; but what I yet most of all wonder at is, that the Baron seems not to have understood that ever I received his letter by mr Charles Coke with six copies of his booke; having wrote him of the receit 3 November and sent him the Errata, which, if not remedyed, do render the book, absolutely unintelligible in some places, so that I my self could not have rectifyed it, had I not had a Dutch copy by me.†1
But however it maybe, he may have received it, and that the 4 copies you mention, as left with Joseph wright, are 4 other copies, for I received 6 by charles Coke: this I hope, because you say, he thinks his letter miscarried in the packet boat, that was taken, by the french,†2 and that in that letter he desired that the dutch copy might be transcribed by D: C.†3 and given to be printed, here, or in Amsterdam; for in his by mr Coke, by whom he sent me the 6 copyes, he mentiond nothing of having the dutch Copy transcribed, but wrote as if some in England had thoughts of translating it into Dutch, which occasiond these words in my answer,
'Is there anybody in London, that inclines to translate the book into Dutch? If so, it were wel the Translation were corrected by the Authors own dutch, and If it were so translated, seeing it is licensed in England, there are that would print it in holland, perhaps in this Town.'
The words in your letter seem to be an answer to those words of mine. The copy shalbe made ready and the appendix translated, and if any one will print it here on those conditions he shall have the
― 2 ―

copy. I should be glad in the meane time to understand that my letter with the Errata did come to hand, And if not, I would gladly make and send another over, for 'tis pitty the language should be unintelligible, when, were it so clear as possible, the matter being, in a manner, altogether new, and out of the Road of the common place makers, wilbe difficult enough to understand, and lyable to all the wrestings that such Readers are used to make use of to render what they like not, odious.
Monsieur Kolhans has this day received a letter from Dantzick that tells him that Dr. Buchius has been very dangerously sick, and was almost miraculously by a vision, when as at the point of death, restored to health again; But they think he wilbe necessitated to quit Dantsik, because the truth will not be there born, and he has many enemies there —
I doubt not, but you have read the booke through, and desire you would freely, as a friend, give me your thoughts of it, there are things boldly spoke, that will go neere to move all the Ecclesiastick gall, except they be so wise, as wholly to neglect it.
My wife, who as I told you, is a person of a large soule, and not to be mewed up within the wals of narrow spirited Catechisms, systems, and confessions, which are many times but bundles of contradictions to themselvs, has her hearty thanks returned, as well as my self, to you, for your good wishes, and to Sir Francis and my lady for their kind invitation, which we shall certainly, with all greediness embrace, if ever it pleases God to bring us together in those parts.
As for my last consorts (who yet I do not so term, as if I had relinquisht all consortship with them, no; I know not yet, where to find better, freer, and less overladen with superstition,) that narrow spirit is growing upon them apace, but no where does that Ape at any time more shew it self than where it has power to domineer, and accordingly in Pennsylvania, where they have jurisdiction, they are as stingy, as peevish, as persecuting, and arbitrary in their proceedings against their own non-conformists, as the Thing (cald church) of England to hers — witness their brutish arbitrary proceedings at the Tryals of Geo: Keith, and divers others in print:†1 which it would be a good service for one
― 3 ―

or other that understands the English Laws, and liberties to comment upon, and expose them for; if possible they might be shamed out of it, ere they go to far on in that way, and become hardened in it.
'Tis, as you say a new change of state brings new Imployment, and tho', when settled that's never like to quench the fire of my spirit, after books and learning, and so much the lesse because my dearest is also of an Inquisitive spirit, and nothing less than a Ja Suser.†a †1 Yet to this day, we are not setled and so I have hitherto had little time to enquire what is doing either here, or else where, of that nature; and when we are got into order, I have a matter of great concernment to my wife, her son and sister to bring to rights, betwixt her brother,†2 and them about their fathers Inheritance, which I purpose with all my forces to set about: that that being once helpt out of the way; I may with her, and she with me, be master of more time, in the world, if it please god to continue us health and strength: for this I will assure you, was one reason among others, that made me resolve upon seeking so meet a help: Could we have your and the Barons good company, it would be very acceptable to us, and could we find, or frame such a society, as we have sometimes spoken of, and you now again mention, we should have all the content we could wish for; in the meane while, we must be content to stumble on; as well as we can, and expect†3 what Providence will next hand forth to us; for I am fully assured that Priest-Craft will fall, and cannot stand long against that light, that has so far opend mens eyes to see through the Tiffany cover of their fulsom Authority —
Pray inform me if the Oxford Testament be out yet,†4 that was in hand when I was in London? To Camdens Britannia†5 I can ad nothing. Leers has lately printed the History of the Edict of
― 4 ―

Nantes, which I here is extant in English.†1 Remember you ow me Biddles works, an exemplar of which I sent to Monsieur Le Clerk: what book is that of one Freak about the Trinity?†2 which the house of Lords trouble their heads so much about, as to cause it to be burnt by the common hangman; I doubt not but they are full as competent Judges of those nice matters, as Calvins Cooke, that ventured his neck upon his own orthodoxy, against poore Servetus,†3 but certainly he relyed more upon the Zeale, and power of his master, to influence the Genevan Senate to burn him, than on his own abilities to manage such disputes with clearness, and perspicuity, which no man ever yet pretended to, but your Dr. Sherlok in that point; but I think South has sufficiently lasht, and exposd him for pretending easily to understand that, which all the fathers adored as an unintelligible mystery;†4 But manus de Tabula:†5 for my letter may be opend, as yours had been, ere it came to me, and they may think me a heretick to: But the best of it is I care not much what —tick men do, or may account me.
So with endeared respects from my dearest and self to Sir Fr. my Lady the Baron and your self I remain
Yours B F
my sons, and espetially your little Friend, have their service tendred to you.
― 5 ―

1704. William Popple to Locke, 3 February 1694 (1698, 1906, 1986)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 211-12.
London February 3d. 1693/94.
Sir,
The method you speak of, for curing my distemper without physick, is so charming in the general proposition of it, that you will justly wonder when I own to you that I have not yet waited upon Mr Howe†1 to enquire into the particular practice of it. But I must therefore acquaint you with the reasons of my delay. One is because I have some little remembrance of the thing, from what you have your self told me in conversation; the throwing away of his books, and using moderate exercise. The rest I remember not. But it is not out of a sleight†2 of these, that I neglect to enquire further. On the contrary: the first part I observe exactly already,
― 7 ―

and the latter I intend to do by degrees as I shall be able. But what chiefly makes me suspend my curiosity a few dayes is a composition that Dr Paul has some while promised to prepare (though I know not of what) and has yesterday begun to administer to me. He has great confidence in it; and assures me that in ten dayes time the effect will be very sensible. In this therefore I follow your general advice, whilst I give my self up intirely so long to his conduct. But if that effect chance to fail our expectations, I shall then fly speedily to you as my last anchor. I hope also in the mean while we may perhaps have a little fair weather, which may give us the opportunity of seeing you here; unless My Lady Masham's retirement, which she now threatens us withall, occasion your longer stay. But however it be that your directions come, as I am fully assured from your goodness that when needfull they will come, so I assure you that I shall meet them with all the necessary dispositions of an observant and confiding minde, which I hope will also contribute towards their more effectual operating in my cure.
Your Printer has now the last leaves of the third Book in his hands.†1 My wife salutes you alwayes most respectfully: and we both beg leave to present our humble service to Mr Van Helmont. I am
Sir,
Your most obliged and most humble servant
WILLIAM POPPLE.
Address: For Mr Locke [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmarks: FE 3; GC
Endorsed by Locke: W: Popple 3 Feb. 93/4
1705. Locke to William Stratton, 5 February 1694 (1701, 1812)
The James Marshall Osborn Collection, New Haven, Connecticut. Transcribed from photostat. Answers no. 1701.
Oates 5 Feb 93/4
Dear Cosin
Not receiveing the money according to my expectation and need of it, nor hearing any thing of it from you. Who could I demand it of or write to for it but you? When I writ to you it would be enough if you paid it in to Mr Cothrington to be returnd to Mr Clarke. It
― 8 ―

might well be understood that you needed not take a bill from him But that you should not write to give notice of it, is what I imagin you could not think I intended. It is soe constant as well as safe practise when any one has paid money to an other to give notice to him for whose account it is paid, that I could not suppose you would not write to me as soon as you had paid it. I doe not remember I ever complaind you ever faild me when you returnd me any money by your freinds. But when you spoke of a returne you hoped to finde the last terme†1 and I staid till the terme was done (as I remember) without hearing of any returne you had got I thought it a convenience to you and me too, to make use of that by Mr Cothrington which was offerd me, which I accepted of not out of any dislike of a returne by any of your freinds but because not hearing from you within the time mentiond I had reason to conclude you could then find noe return at all. I have writt to Mr Clarke this post to enquire about it and suppose as you doe that I shall suddainly hear of it, for I have noe doubt of Mr Cothrington. I am
Dear Cosin
your humble servant
J LOCKE
I suppose it goes hard with the pore at Pensford this dear Time. When you have a convenient oportunity to doe it I would desire you that twenty shillings in bread should be distributed amongst the most needy.
Address: For Mr William Stratton in Whitson Court near st James's church Bristoll
Postmark: FE 10
1706. Edward Clarke to Locke, 8 February 1694 (1690, 1716)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 83-4. Printed in Rand, pp. 385-6.
London 8º Februarii 1693/4º
Deare Sir,
Yesterday I Received yours of the 5th, and by the same Post received†a- from Mr. Codrington a Byll of forty pounds as part of the money paid in to Him by Mr. Stratton for your use, And in the
― 9 ―

same Letter Mr. Codrington desiered mee to make Good the remaining 6l. 8s. 6d. ½ to you, which for your ease I am Contented to doe;-†a What Mr. Stratton Writes Mr. Codrington's told Him touching the Returning of 90l. to mee about a fortnight since, must bee a perfect Mistake somewhere, for I know nothing at all of it, but shall bee allwayes glad of any opportunity to serve you, who am
your most affectionate Faithfull servant,
EDW: CLARKE
I have not been perfectly well ever since you went out of Town, and am now but in an ill state of health etc:
Address: These, To his worthy Freind Mr John Lock, Present:
Endorsed by Locke: E: Clarke 8º Feb 93/4
1707. James Hamilton to Locke, 8 February 1694 (1711)
B.L., MS. Locke, c. 11, ff. 132-4. The writer may be James Hamilton, c. 1661-1734; sixth earl of Abercorn (Scotland) 1701: D.N.B.He was a nephew of Anthony Hamilton. The identification is based on the statement that the future sixth earl's son James, the future seventh earl (ibid.), was born on 22 March 1685/6: Scots Peerage.
London February the 8th: 169 3/4
Sir
The universall concurrence of very competent judges of the workes of the learned, in nameing you for the Author of Some Thoughts Concerning Education,†b hath occasioned my giveing you this trouble, to which I am not only prompted by the ingenious solid and practicable notions you have layde downe, as welle for the inculcateing and cherishing Moralitye in Youthe, as the improvement of theyr understandeing, but I am further incouraged by the generous and publicke spiritte which shines throughout your booke, and is very perticularly expressed in the midle of the second paragraph of the epistle dedicatorye to that booke;†1 give me therefore leave Sir thoe unfortunately a stranger to you, to desire your assistance without any further apologye in an affaire wherein the very first mistakes are attended with such pernicious consequences, as you have judiciously expressed. I have two sons the eldest
― 10 ―

whereof wille bee eight yeares olde next monthe, and the other six in August, neither of them can yette write which I doe not looke uppon as any greate matter as to losse of tyme, thoe I woulde not have deferred the eldests learneing it thus longe, but that hee hath hitherto been of a weakely constitution and hath a tendencye to growe awrye, which made mee aprehende the consequences of a constrain'd posture, thoe nowe hee gathers strengthe I intende hee shall begin to sette pen to paper next summer, and I have not through fondnesse lette him gette a habitte of idlenesse, for as soone as hee was capable of it I had him taught to reade in his mother tounge, and imediatly after frenche, in shorte Sir he can reade and speake both languages with almost an equall facilitye, and hee hath made a faire progresse in Geographye, and hath newely begunne Chronologye, which whilst hee is learneing hee shall perfect himselfe in what he hath alreadye learnt in Geographye by pointing to such places in the Maps as there wille bee occasion to mention; hee hath alsoe newely begunne to learne the frenche grammer, for hee hath hitherto learnt noe thing but by roate, which method I am likewise followeing as to his younger brother, whose parts wille I hope in tyme exerte themselves but hee is as yette very backwarde. I thought it proper to acquaint you with thus much of my children, and likewise that I intende for the future to observe your method, before I desired the favour of you to recommende to mee a proper person to bee theyr Tutor, if you knowe any such rightly qualiffyed to forme theyr mindes as to learneing, and moralitye, and wille bee chearefully contented with twentye poundes a yeare, and a wellecome to my owne table at dinner; his due instructing and constant attendance on my children is all I expect from him, but herein hee must bee very assiduous, for my fortune wille not admitte of my further encreaseing my familye, and I shalle have fulle employement for the servants I alreadye have, soe that hee must even bee assisting to them in theyr dresseing themselves, which a discreete man wille not scruple at, thoe others more vainly punctilious maye object against this perticular, but suche persons would by noe meanes answer my endes, for besides what I have alreadye sayde I shoulde feare theyr infuseing mistaken notions in my children; I wille not trouble you with an account of the economye†aof my familye, for I take it for granted there wille bee noe difficultye in conformeing to it, especially that noe orderly
― 11 ―

person wille thinke it muche to acquaint mee or my wife when any occasion of theyr owne maye calle them abroade; I have alreadye sayde soe muche that I would adde noe thinge more to it if London were my place of residence, but my liveing in Yorcke might perhaps bee an objection if I did not solve it with an assurance of alloweing the person I shall take for a tutor to my children three poundes to beare his charges up to towne, if hee is not at any tyme satisfyed to complye further with what I have mentioned to expect from him, which as longe as hee doth hee maye depende uppon a very civill and heartye entertainement, and hee shall even bee wellecome to continue with mee at the same rate if he pleaseth even after my sons are growne up, and bee a companion to us till hee can provide better for himselfe, at least as longe as I live; neither neede hee question my using my utmost endeavours in doeing better for him when soe ever hee can putte mee in a waye, but I would not deceive any bodye, and my privatte waye of liveing wille not afforde many oppertunityes of that nature; I have indeede the presentation to a liveing, when the incumbent dyes, worthe at least 150ll: per annum in Irelande, but thoe I am my selfe of the Churche of Englande, I am loathe to have my children tutor'd by any of the Clergye, for most of them have stille a hanckering after jure divino and passive obedience principles, and are over tenacious as to indifferent ceremonyes, and very fonde of nicetyes in religion, which are matters I would have none of my children trouble theyr heades about, but barre these tenets, I have noe repugnancye to an easye well humoured man of that coate. I doupt Sir I have trespassed too farre on your patience in being thus prolix, but I <ho>pe†a your goode nature wille excuse it when you consider it proceedes <fr>om†a the tendernesse of a parent for his children, and the desire not only of theyr owne welle fare but fitting them to bee usefulle to theyr Countrye if oppertunitye offers. if you can not laye an obligation of soe high a nature uppon mee as to recommende suche a person to mee as I wante, I shall howe soe ever take it as a very greate favour if you wille please to putte mee in a waye howe to provide my selfe dureing my staye in towne which can not bee longer then a monthe; I live at present with my owne mother Madam Hamilton†1 at her
― 12 ―

house in Neweport streete neare Leyster fieldes, and I can not forbeare being further importunatte to you soe farre as to desire you to direct an answer to this letter for mee thither, which wille bee waited for with greate impatience by one who is soe greate an admirer of your usefulle goode qualityes to the publicke, that hee should bee glad if hee knewe howe otherwise then by wordes to expresse himselfe
Sir
Your very humble servant
JAMES HAMILTON
Address: For Mr: Locke at Sir Francis Maschams house At Oates in Essex
Postmarks: FE 8; IH
Endorsed by Locke: J: Hamilton 8º Feb 93/4
1708. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 9/19 February 1694 (1692, 1791)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 85-6. Answers no. 1692.
(English) Nescio, Vir Amplissime, pro qua facilitate tam amplas mihi gratias agas. Si de animo tuo, tot documentis mihi probato, vel minimum dubitassem, teque amicitiæ non legitimè cultæ insimulassem, ipse gravissime contra amicitiæ legem peccassem, et justam tui reprehensionem meritus essem. Vis ergo gratias agere homini, quia fecit quod debuit? Justius forsan ego reprehendi potui, qui te a gravioribus occupationibus avocatum familiari epistolæ scribendæ detinere volui. Sed et illam mihi importunitatem condonabis, quia tecum per literas colloqui summa mihi est voluptas, unicaque inter absentes amicitiam continuandi via est. Si duo priores libri Historiæ
― 13 ―

Inquisitionis Tibi non displicuerint, sperare ausim, nec posteriores displicituros. Quartum ego maximi facio; quia in eo mysterium illud iniquitatis maximè revelatur, et ratio procedendi coram illo tribunali explicatur, quæ omnium injustitiarum congeries est. Quæ hic illic in margine libri mei annotavi, in tui gratiam libens describam: Non sunt admodum multa, non tamen indigna quæ reliquis jungantur. Lib.III. cap.i. quando de Excommunicatione dissero mentio incidit bullæ Cœnæ Domini, quæ quotannis coram Papa legitur, quaque omnes contra Ecclesiam Romanam delinquentes, excommunicantur. Nunquam eam videram: nunc autem illam in autore, qui Inquisitionem Bisuntinam describit, reperi.†1 Utrum illa inserenda sit, hæsito. Celebris est bulla, et non ubique exstat: omniaque continet crimina ob quæ quis Romanæ Ecclesiæ excommunicationem incurrit: Sed vero admodum est prolixa, neque solam hæresem spectat, sed et alia crimina. Putarim tamen, ut lectorum curiositati satisfiat, illam inserendam. Wetstenius fasciculum librorum ad Te ante biduum aut triduum misit, directum ad bibliopolam Smith Londinensem:†2 Illi inclusum reperies volumen concionum Episcopii hactenus ineditarum, quibus ego
― 14 ―

satis prolixam vitæ ejus historiam præmisi.†1 Spero te non adeo linguæ nostræ rudem, quin, si non conciones Episcopii, saltem vitæ ejus historiam, quam stilo neutiquam inflato aut affectato, sed simplice et humili conscripsi, sis intellecturus. Varia illic leges non inutilia scitu. Videbis Ecclesiasticorum mores semper esse eosdem; et quod nunc Galli moliuntur, nullo modo a majorum vestigiis recedere. Omnia ego, paucissimis quibusdam non magni momenti circumstantiis exceptis, ex fide dignis autographis hausi, quæ adhuc a me asservantur. Cappellum hic aliquoties vidi: expertus sum virum non tantum eruditum, sed et ingenii placidissimi; quemque ob varias egregias animi dotes magni facio. Doleo itaque eum hæreseos insumulatum coram hominibus, quorum miserationes sunt crudeles. Prudenter fecit, quod colloquium cum emissariis illis (quos Inquisitionis muscis in carcere captivis insidiantibus comparo)†2 declinavit. Fuissent illi denuntiatores†3 criminis illius, et mox, juxta decretum Amstelodamense,†4 illius judices. Quicquid dixisset, in hæreseos crimen vocatum fuisset. Verum nec silentio suo se hominum illorum suspicione liberabit. Non spectant illi
― 15 ―

fratris suo judicio errantis emendationem, sed ejectionem, et vanum de eo triumphum. Quis eos sanabiles credat, quos nec exilium, nec ecclesiarum miseranda desolatio emendat? Catalogum codicum MSS. Oxonii sub prælo esse, ac brevi proditurum, gaudeo. Sed nec minus Testamenti Novi, quod illic majori forma cum omnibus variantibus lectionibus jam diu sub prælo esse audimus, editionem desidero. Vellem et Doctissimum Toinardum nobis Harmoniam suam Euangelicam impertiat. Verum ille nimium cunctari videtur. Non tamen efflagito, ut tu eam ipso vivo ac invito edas; scio id tibi integrum non esse. Hoc autem rogo, si Toinardus forte mortem oppetat, non edita suâ harmonia, ne tu eo in casu thesaurum istum publico invideas: posset enim ab hæredibus ejus, fortasse non ita curiosis, negligi ac contemni. Quod ergo ab ipso vivo impetrare non potuimus, velim a te post ejus mortem præstari. Et quoniam incertum est, uter longævior sit futurus, velim harmoniam illam a te credi homini fideli, qui eadem qua tu fide <eam>†a asservet, si te priorem mors occupet, neque eam, nisi post Toinardi mortem, edat. Ita te neutiquam fidem datam violare credo; et tandem orbis libro adeo utili non destitueretur. post obitum enim
― 16 ―

tuum in bibliotheca tuâ reperietur. Tutius ergo fidei alicujus commendari potest. Et licet ego vix sperare possim, me eam visurum; in usum tamen posteritatis illam, etiam me mortuo, prodire vellem. Hoc ego enixius peto, quia Toinardus, ut audio, jam senex est, et vivit in regione Pontificiâ, in quâ, nisi hæredes habeat valde circumspectos, facile labor hic quem Scripturæ impendit, a Jesuitis aut Monachis possit irritus reddi. Scimus quid ordines illi apud animas credulas et superstitiosas efficere possint. Tu hæc omnia maturo judicio procul dubio expendisti, et facies quod fidei datæ non adversatur. De Joanne Malela ego a te monitus antehac aliquoties conveni Wetstenium: quid actum sit ex Wetstenio resciscam: Si nondum ad Toinardum sit missus, non permitt<emus pr>imam†a quæ se offeret occasionem præterlabi. Tractatus tui de Intellectu humano alteram <nunc a>dornari†a editionem gaudeo. Doleo vero illum lingua conscriptum vestrate. Utinam eum legere possem! procul dubio multum exinde fructus perciperem; nunc tamen gaudeo illum aliis profuturum. Theologia mea Christiana jam penitus distracta est: nulla illius Wetstenio supersunt exemplaria: intra mensem alteram illius editionem, hic illic paulisper aut emendatam, aut illustratam, vel auctam, hoc vero paucissimis
― 17 ―

in locis, inchoaturi sumus.†1 Utinam doctissimas tuas haberem considerationes! plura a te monitus emendare possem. In familia Veenii nostri omnia jam pacata sunt: ipse strenue, uti antea, praxin exercet. Jubet te quam plurimum salvere: Nec non uxor mea, liberique. Salutem officiosissimam a me dices D. Cudworthiæ, nec non D. Baroni van Helmont.
Tui Amantissimus
P. A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 19 Februarii
 
(Latin) I do not know, excellent Sir, for what readiness you give me such copious thanks. If I had been at all in doubt about your affection, of which you have given me so many proofs, and if I had charged you with not rightly performing the duties of friendship, I should myself have most grievously offended against friendship's law and should have deserved your just reproof. Do you want then to thank a man for having done what he ought to have done? I could perhaps have been reproved more justly for wanting to detain you from more important occupations for the writing of a private letter. But you will pardon me even for that importunity, since talking with you by letter is my chiefest pleasure and is the only way of continuing a friendship between the absent. If the first two books of the Historia Inquisitionis have not[p. 13] displeased you neither, I venture to hope, will the later books. I most prize the fourth; for in it that mystery of iniquity is chiefly revealed and the mode of proceeding before that tribunal—a heap of all kinds of injustice—is displayed. I shall gladly transcribe for your satisfaction the things that I have recorded here and there in the margin of my copy; they are not many, yet not undeserving of being attached to the rest. In Book III, chapter 1, where I discuss Excommunication, there occurs a mention of the Bull Cœna Domini, which is read annually before the Pope and by which all offenders against the Roman Church are excommunicated. I had never seen it; now, however, I have found it in an author who describes the Besançon Inquisition.†1 I am not sure whether it ought to be inserted. The Bull is famous and is not to be found everywhere; and it contains all the offences on account of which people incur the excommunication of the Roman Church; but it is certainly very lengthy and relates not only to heresy but to other offences also. I should think, however, that it ought to be inserted to satisfy readers' desire for knowledge. Wetstein sent you a parcel of books two or three days ago, addressed to the London bookseller Smith;†2 you will find in it a volume of hitherto unpublished sermons by Episcopius, to which I have prefixed a[p. 14] fairly lengthy account of his life.†1 I hope that you are not so ignorant of our language that you will not understand, if not Episcopius's sermons, at least the account of his life, which I have written in a style in no wise inflated or affected, but simple and unpretentious. You will find in it some things that are worth knowing. You will see that the behaviour of the clergy is always the same and that what the Frenchmen are now striving for in no way departs from the footprints of their ancestors. I have drawn everything except a very few circumstances of no great moment from trustworthy manuscripts that are as yet in my keeping. I saw Cappel here several times; I found him not only a scholar but also a man of the most peaceful disposition, and one whom I prize highly for his various extraordinary mental gifts. I am sorry therefore that he has been charged with heresy before men whose mercies are cruel. He acted prudently in declining any conversation with those emissaries, whom I compare to the 'flies'†2 of the Inquisition, lying in wait to ensnare the captives in the prison. They would have been the 'denunciators'†3 of that offence and then, in accordance with the Amsterdam decree,†4 his judges. Whatever he had said would have been drawn into the offence of heresy. But neither by his silence will he free himself from the suspicion of[p. 15] those men. They aim not at the amendment of a brother who in their judgement is in error, but at his ejection and an empty triumph over him. Who would believe those to be curable whom neither exile nor the miserable desolation of churches amends? I am glad that the catalogue of the manuscript books at Oxford is in the press and shortly to appear. But I no less desire the publication of the New Testament, in larger form and with all the variant readings, which, we hear, has been in the press there this long time. Would that the most learned Toinard also would impart his Harmony of the Gospels to us! But indeed he seems to delay too much. For all that I do not demand that you should publish it while he lives and is reluctant; I know that that is not open to you. But I ask that, should Toinard happen to die leaving his Harmony unpublished, you will not in that case grudge that treasure to the public; for it could be neglected and contemned by his heirs, who perhaps might not be interested in such things. I should wish, therefore, that what we could not procure from him during his life might be presented by you after his death. And since it is uncertain which of you will be the longer lived I should wish that Harmony to be consigned by you to a trustworthy man who, if death takes you first, may keep it with the same fidelity as yourself, and not publish it except after Toinard's death. I believe that in this way you would not violate your given word; and the world would not in the end be deprived of so useful a book, for after your death it will be found[p. 16] in your library. It can therefore more safely be recommended to somebody's fidelity. And although I can scarcely hope to see it myself yet I should wish it to appear for the use of posterity even when I am dead. I request this the more earnestly because Toinard, as I hear, is now an old man and lives in a Popish country where, unless he has exceedingly wary heirs, this labour that he has expended on Scripture can easily be brought to nothing by Jesuits or monks. We know what those orders can effect with credulous and superstitious souls. You have doubtless pondered all these things with mature judgement and will do what is not opposed to your given word. With regard to Joannes Malalas: as instructed by you I have already seen Wetstein several times; I shall learn from him what has been done; if he (Malalas) has not yet been sent to Toinard we shall not let the first opportunity that presents itself slip away. I am glad that another edition of your treatise on the Human Understanding is now preparing. But I am sorry that it is written in your language. Would that I could read it! Without doubt I should obtain much profit from it; as things are, however, I am glad that it will benefit others. My Theologia Christiana is now completely sold out; no copies of it remain with Wetstein; within a month we shall start work on another edition of it, here and there somewhat amended or elucidated or enlarged, but this last only in a very few[p. 17] places.†1 Would that I might have your most learned thoughts. If I were instructed by you I could make more amendments. All is now peaceful in our friend Veen's family; he carries on his practice vigorously as before. He sends you his best respects, as also do my wife and children. Please give my best respects to Mrs. Cudworth and also to Baron van Helmont.
Your most affectionate
P. van Limborch
Amsterdam 19 February
1694

1711. James Hamilton to Locke, 15 February 1694 (1707)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 135-6.
London February the 15th: 93/4
Sir
I can not forbeare reneweing my request to you, that you would at least favour mee with a line or two, to lette mee knowe whether I am like to bee soe happye as to have a tutor for my sons of your recommendation, for if you could give mee any thoe remote hopes of it, I would leave my eldest son with my mother, in expectation of his being brought downe to mee a monthe or two hence, by one whom you shoulde judge a fitte person to take care of his, and his brothers education; my youngest son can not suffer much by soe smalle a delaye, and my eldest looses noe tyme heere in towne, for hee hath an ingenious welle bred master comes every other daye to teache him Geographye, and who can instruct him in any thinge else proper for him to learne, besides which his Grandmother is soe kinde as to keepe a frenche man purposelye to tende him, soe that I had rather staye a while if you wille please to give mee encouragement, then venture uppon any bodye commended by incompetent judges, who besides maye bee byassed in behalfe of some needye meere scholar of theyr kindred, or acquaintance, not duely considering the consequence of such a ones being entrusted with the breedeing up of a gentlemans children, whereas I knowe my selfe safe in putteing this affaire in your handes, whose mature judgement, and publicke spiritte, shines in every page of what writeings you have oblidged the worlde with. perhaps Sir you have alreadye given your selfe the trouble of answering my last letter, as I maye finde by the poste that comes in to morrowe, but unlesse you have therein fullye satisfyed my desire of helpeing mee to a tutor, I must nowe bee further thus farr importunatte as to beg the favour of your likewise takeing notice to mee of this, else I shall bee apt to renewe
― 20 ―

my aplication to you, as thinkeing my haveing stinted you to soe little tyme as a monthe, maye have hindred your being soe farre assisteing to mee as otherwise you might have beene, for I am sure your generous nature wille prompte you to oblidge even soe greate a stranger to you as Sir
Your very humble servant
JAMES HAMILTON
My letters are directed to mee at Madam Hamiltons house in Neweport streete near Leysterfieldes In London

1712. William Molyneux to Locke, 17 February 1694 (1693, 1744)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 73-6. The underlinings (here represented by italics) all appear to be by Molyneux. Answers no. 1693; answered by no. 1744.
Dublin. Febr. 17. 1693/4
Honoured Sir
I am so very sensible of the Great Caution and Deep Consideration You use before you write any thing; That I wonder at My Own Hardines when I venture to Object any thing against Your Positions. And when I read your Answers to any of such my Objections, I much more admire at my own Weaknes in making them. I have a New Instance of this in Your Last of January 18th which Came not to this Place before Yesterday. This has most abundantly satisfyd Me in the Doubt I lay under concerning the Case of a Drunken Man. which you have cleard up to me in three Words most Convincingly. So that I think you have no reason in the Least to Alter that Paragraph. unles you may think it Convenient to expres that matter a Little Plainer. Which I think
― 21 ―

indeed your Last Letter to me does better than your 22th section of that Chapter. That section runs thus.
22. But is not a Man Drunk and Sober the same Person, why else is he Punishd for the fact he Commits when Drunk, tho he be never afterwards Conscious of it? Just as Much the same Person, as a Man that Walks and does other things in his Sleep is the same Person; and is answerable for any Mischeif he shall do in it. Humane laws Punish both with a <Justice>†a Suitable to their Way of Knowledge; because in these Cases they cannot distinguish certainly what is real, what Counterfeit. and so the Ignorance in Drunkenes, or Sleep is not admitted as a Plea. etc.
Now I conceive that which makes the Expression herein not so very Clear is, Suitable to THEIR way of Knowledge. Some will be apt to Mistake the Word their to refer to the Drunken or Sleeping Man. wheras it refers to the Laws, as if you†b- had said-†b, Suitable to that way of Knowledge or Information which the Laws have establishd to proceed by.
This in your Letter is very manifest in a few words. there you say, Punishment is annexd to Personality, Personality to Consciousnes. How then can a Drunkard be punishd for what he Did whereof he is not Conscious? To this I answer, Humane Judicatures justly Punish him, because the Fact is Proved against him, but want of Consciousnes cannot be proved for him. This Sir is Most full in the Case you are there treating off. So I have nothing more to offer in that Matter.
Only Give me Leave to propose One Question more to you, tho it be forreigne to the Busines you are upon in your Chapter of Identity. How comes it to pas that Want of Consciousnes cannot be proved for a Drunkard as wel as for a Frenitick? One, my thinks, is as Manifest, as the Other. and if Drunkenes may be Counterfeit, so may a Frenzy. Wherefore to me it seems, that the Law has made a Difference in these two Cases on this account, viz, that Drunkenes is Commonly Incurd Voluntarily; and premeditately; Whereas a Frenzy is commonly without our Consent, or impossible to be prevented. but enough of this.
I should not have troubled you with this; but that according to your <Usual>†c Candour and Goodnes, you seemd to desire my farther thoughts thereon as speedily as I could
I†d- visited Captain Monk this very day on purpose to make him
― 22 ―

your Complement. He is extreamly obleidged to you for it, and returns it with all Imaginable Respect and Gratitude.
My Brother Gives you his Most Humble Service.-†d
I am
Most Worthy Sir
Your Most Obleidged Humble Servant
W: MOLYNEUX

1713. Anonymous to Locke, 19 February [1694?] (1678, 1736)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 196-7. The letter appears to be an answer to no. 1678; hence the year. No. 1736 is evidently written by the same writer.
Feb. 19
Sir
About the beginning of December last There were some papers communicated to you from an unknown hand, which you were pleased to give your self the trouble of reading over, and afterwards to return with a letter enclosed to the Authour; which was writ with soe much freedome and kindnesse that the Authour is perfectly ashamed to make his acknowledgments soe late; But I hope you will excuse the seeming neglect when I have acquainted you with the true occasion of it. which in short was this.
I was in the countrey when the papers were delivered to you, and the gentleman whose assistance I made use of in the conveyance, Received them again sealed up without any intimation of a letter enclosed, and in the same manner returned them back to me about the latter end of January when I came to town; And my stay there being short I took them Along with me into the countrey unopened, where, as soon as I had unsealed them, and discover'd what obligation I was under, I took the first opportunity of sending my thanks, and desiring that my slow returns for this favour may not deprive me of the advantage of a further correspondence. Had I been in town when your letter was writ I would certainly have
― 23 ―

waited upon you according to your desire; But since I was not, and I cannot foresee a time when I am like to enjoy the benefit of your conversation, If it was not too much for me to ask, I would make it my earnest request to you that what thoughts you had then to communicate you would be pleased to give me in writing when you have leisure for it; For tis Truth only and an impartiall Judgment of my self that I aim at, and whatever informations contribute to either of those ends will be very kindly and thankfully received. I have long thought it the most necessary and important businesse of A man's life to deliver himself from all manner of Prejudices that soe he may be able to think And act with all the Freedome he is capable of in this state, And I have endeavoured to frame all my studyes agreeable to my perswasion in this point; in which I have been very much confirmed by reading your excellent essay upon Humane understanding. t'was this Book which gave me all the knowledge I have of you; From thence I cheifly took my character, and was encouraged to send my papers to you as being wellassured of meeting with a free and impartiall Judge. could they Have been printed I had sent you a book and not loose papers, But they could not. And, If you can forgive me for telling you another story of my papers as I have done before of my self, I will acquaint you with the reasons. The occasion of my writing a discourse upon that subject was because it was the present controversy afoot, and I thought that the best time of finding the truth when there was soe much search and enquiry about it. A freind I shewed it to advised me to let it be printed, which I consented to upon promise of keeping the authour concealed. which I did, not†a much upon prospect of doing any service to the world by it, for I could not think I had any reason to hope for such successe, but what I cheifly expected from its appearing in print was a true and impartiall Judgment of my performance, and consequently of my abilityes to serve the publick in writing. to which end I Judged it absolutely necessary to conceal my name, for I am very well satisfyed mens opinions of a book are soe much influenced by the place, age, party, character and station and other circumstances of the Authour, that few men can take a true estimate of themselves or what they write if they have noe other standard to goe by but the opinion of the world especially in matters of controversy. That the discourse was not at last printed as I had designed was I believe wholly owing to the secrecy I was soe
― 24 ―

carefull of <preserving>,†a or else to the overmuch caution of the Licenser it was sent to, who might be jealous of any thing that lookt like a new way or method; or perhaps to those passages you are of opinion some may stick at. For I can Hardly perswade my self that what was alledged by Dr Royse†1 was a just exception; that it was contrary to the doctrine of the Ch. of England, if the Athanasian creed be esteemed the Highest expression of our Faith in this point. Had I been conscious of any departure from the common established notions, I would have been contented with a private rule of Faith without disturbing the Publick; the peace of which I think preferable to any speculative truth which has not a pernicious influence upon practise. If you are pleased to honour me with another letter, and a more particular account of your thoughts upon my small treatise it will come safe to me through the same hands. I do'nt subscribe my name because you will know no more of me by it than you doe already, but if you desire it, or by favouring me with a continuance of your†bcorrespondence will make it necessary to be known; I shall be very willing to discover my self to you at a distance which I had much rather doe in person If I could have an opportunity.
I am Sir
your most oblidged Humble Servant.

1715. Robert Pawling to Locke, 24 February 1694 (1699, 1720)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, f. 21.
London Feb: 24th 1693
Sir
I am troubled in that I am forced to trespass so much upon you but I hope it will not be long ere I shalbe in a capacity to repay you.
― 26 ―

I intended, had it not been very wet this afternoon, to have gon to Mr Fox and to have given you an account of what you be to pay him; but that must be deferd till my next. I waited on Mr James Hamelton†1 who I find to be very desireous of your assistance and will stay till May next in hopes you may find out a fit person to be Tutor to his sons; The eldest is not above 6 years of age; he talks french as well almost as English. I understand by him that he would allow 20 li per annum and diet and had rather he be not a Clergyman because they are generally so much for passive obedience. I fully acquainted him with what you wrot; he presents his service to you and is much obliged to you for this favour.
Mr Seager is dead but Mr Glanvill assures me he sold his place, under you, last year to one of his under dore keepers for eight score pounds and the porters place wilbe given by Mr. Guy†2 to the other dorekeeper who was his man; so I think to look no farther after that. I thank you for your advice in reference to Secretary Trenchard but I did long since get Mr Pascall†3 to mention me to him and to intreat him to encourage the design of making Greenwich an Hospitall for sick and wounded sea men which he promised to do. so that I cant do any more unless it would be proper to move him and my Lord Keeper†4 as they are privy Counsellors to mention it to their Majesties who declare on all occasions their great desire of having it don. Colonel Austen lately mentioned it to my Lord privy seal;†5 who replyed he thought because their board,†6 in his hearing, had mentioned it to the King, that they had taken it again to manage it themselvs, to which he replyed they wholy resigned it to his Lordship and Sir Thomas Millington and brought Sir John Lowther,†7 and Priestman†8 to him to confirm it, wherupon my Lord said that he would mention it to their Majesties and would go on with it. Sir Tho: went yesterday to wait on the Queen in hopes of
― 27 ―

an opportunity to revive it, but could not have an opportunity to see her. I inclose 2 letters and am
Your humble Servant
ROB PAWLING

Oates 5º Mar
Dear Sir
My Lady Masham writeing to you the last weeke by an hand that she cannot be over confident was carefull in delivering her letter in at the post, has obleiged me to propose to you in her name whether it will not be best to move the house upon what has been said of it in general than upon what has been reproachd to any one of its members. because she thinks the house may more heartily espouse the one than the other. She also desires it may be considerd whether it will not be best to complain at first against only one of these two blades without mentioning the other till that be passed, and to begin with him which will goe easiest for when an order is made to send for one of them the other can not be refused or at least will passe the easier. This she says her concerne makes her suggest to you, though she doubts not but haveing the men this comes to you by upon the place you will doe what is best and fitest.†1 She gives
― 28 ―

her service to you and Mrs Clarke and wishes you both joy of your little one.†1 Soe much from my Lady
From my self I have litle new to trouble you with, and think you too full of businesse to adde my idle and perhaps mistaken thoughts to yours concerning matters you are busy in and possibly have light from and therefor shall only mind you of my private affair with my Lord Ashley when he comes in your way. My service to Madam who I hope gets up a pace. I am
Dear Sir
your most humble and most affectionate servant
J LOCKE
My service to Sir Walter and J.F. and the rest of my freinds that come in your way
Foreseeing this letter would goe this morning by Sir Francis's man before our London letters came in I writ it yesterday not expecting to hear from you before it went. But my Lady sending yesterday to Bishop Startford for Sir Francis's letter I have yours of the 3d for which I thank you. Mr Pawling writes me word under the same date that he has deliverd the bundle he had of you for me to the Carrier which I hope I shall receive on Tuesday and then you shall have my answer to that part by the first oportunity. I thank you for soe punctually answering the bill I drew on you to Sir Francis. I am very glad the increase of your health gives you hope of a perfect recovery in a litle time. Wine watching and vexation are the three things I am sure you are to avoid for the hastening and confirming of it. The two first tis your own fault if you are not master of; for the last you must try your skill. Adieu
My Lady returns you her thanks for the favour of your letter and the concerne you expresse in it
Address: For Edward Clarke Esquire Member of Parliament in London
Endorsed by Clarke: Mr. Lock touching Sir Francis Masham etc: Received the 6th March 1693.

1719. Locke to Edward Clarke, 12 March 1694 (1717, 1722)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 63. Printed in Rand, p. 389.
Oates 12 Mar 93/4
Dear Sir
I had taken some pains to rectifie the faults yet remaining in the book you sent me, And to make the edition as good as may be: But there is noe contesting with ever lasting unalterable neglect. If I receive that other paper I sent for I shall goe on with it. If not I shall trouble my self noe more about it. Its fate is it seems to be the worst printed that ever booke was, and tis in vain for any one to labour against it.†2
I can easily guesse that ill management can spoile the best businesse in the world and some people have a facultie at it. But of this as you say when I see you. My service to Madam who I hope is now well up again. I have just time to write you this and shall in my next send you one to my dear wife in the meantime pray remember me to her. Tis soe long before my Lord Ashley comes in your way that I think it necessary to name again the two businesses to him. One is the enlargeing my security, the other £100 due to me at Christmas last whereof £50 was due last midsomer, which I had occasion for then as I have for all now. I am
Dear Sir
Your most humble and most faithfull servant
J LOCKE

1720. Robert Pawling to Locke, 15 March 1694 (1715, 1729)

Sir
I this day met with Mr: Fox who was in hopes I had brought him his money for he says he is called on for it and I find by him it may be prejudicial if it be not paid in on Monday. My papers give no light to what time the last was paid for unlesse he sees the acquittance he knows not to what time tis I tell him I paid 7 li: 10s and I remember another paid him before that, but he is not Satisfied whether they are both for the year 91. perhaps one was for the year before; if both these were not for the Yeare 91. then there is a 7 li. 10s due besides the 16 li. 5s and 20 li which I mentioned in my last he had not the book in his custody therefor was at a loss which your last acquittance must set right; in the year 91. it was 2s. in the pound in 92. 2s 2d and in the year 93. 4s. this shews you how the 2 pences come to be added.†1 I am

1721. James Tyrrell to Locke, 15 March [1694] (1665, 1800)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 126-7. Year from Locke's endorsement.
March 15.
Dear Sir
I received yours, and had answered it sooner had I any thing then fit for a letter, for tho' I knew presently after I received it of the death of our good Freind Dr: Thomas; yet not loveing to be the messenger of ill news, I declined giveing you an account of it,
― 32 ―

because I knew you would receive it but too soon from other hands: his son William was not with him when he dyed, but tells me his Father bore death with such courage, and unconcernednesse, as became both a Philosopher, and a Christian, and which I hope will prove an example to us when it comes (as it will (in a few years) to our turnes: But I am allso desired by Mr: Robert King to give you an account of his poor brothers condition, that he is now past all hopes of recovery, liveing allmost upon nothing but Asses milke, and a little bread. and is growne so weake that he is not able to walk about the room, but tho his cough is worse then ever, so that he cannot sleep without Ladanum, yet which is very strange his nocturnal sweats are allmost quite gone, which I impute to the matters being almost exhausted that supplyed them; so that in short his Doctors thinke he cannot live above a fortnight, or three weekes: but ever since this humour has fallen upon his Lungs his Frenzy hath quite left him, and his thoughts seem clear; and sedate; I give you this account that you may not beleive that there hath†a- bin any thing-†a omitted which his Doctors could doe for him, but for this fortnight or three weekes, he has not bin able to take any Physic, scarce so much as Cordials. I could wish you had bin consulted at the begining of his distemper, it might have saved longer to the world a yong man as considerable as any I know for learning and honesty. now my son is off my hands being made Capt: Leiutenant to my Lord Macclesfeild†1 I hope ere it be long to be out of your debt; in the meane time I will leave when I goe out of Towne great part (if not all) of those bookes I or my Children had of yours, with many thankes for the use of them: I am glad to hear the new Edition of your Essay etc. is so near comeing out: I ordered my bookseller to send to Mr: Pawlings the last Dialogue and the Index to the whole worke,†2 and now you may bind them all up together if you pleas<e:>†b no more but that my daughter who is with me in the same L<odg>ing†b presents her service to you, and that I am your h<umble>†b servant
J TYRRELL
― 33 ―

I shall not stay above a week or 10 days longer in Towne: this day I saw my Lord Ashley. Sir Fra: Masham, and Mr. Clarke who (understanding I would write to you) doe all present you with their service.
Address: For John Lock Esqr [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Endorsed by Locke: J. Tyrrell 15 Mar 93/4
1722. Locke to Edward Clarke, 19 March 1694 (i) (1719, 1723)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 69. Badly faded; some spellings conjectural. Printed in Rand, pp. 388-9, with incorrect date 10 March 1694. Answered by no. 1724.
Oates 19º Mar 93/4
Dear Sir
My Cosin Bonville who brings you this will with it deliver you a key sealed up which is the key of my Scrutor†1 at my Lodging, which I must desire you to open and in the second drawer of the upper row you will finde a great number of acquittances filed togeather, amongst them I must desire you to looke out the last of those that Mr Fox who is Collector for the tax gave Mr Pawling for my tax and compare it with Mr Pawlings account with me, that you may know whether it be the last mony was <pa>id†a by Mr Pawling for my tax for he sometimes forgets to give me the acquittances for money he pays for me. When you see what is the last payment you will be able to judg what remains due.
This trouble I am forced to give you. For though Mr Pawling has constantly paid this for me and I have writ to him several times about it yet as you will see by the inclosed†2 (which I received last night with your two last one of the 15th and the other of the 17th) I can get but a very lame account of it. There is another reason why I would desire you to looke into this matter and that is that I not only now but have formerly suspected there is some skill in the management of this tax in Westminster For they let it run 9 or 12 months or more without demanding and then must be paid all of a suddain. That which augments this suspition is that they require
― 34 ―

the acquittances to be shewn and doe not produce their booke of rates†1 which ought as I take it to be signed every quarter by the Commissioners and then collected and those that pay be crossed. Whereas if I mistake not once that I saw the rate the warrant to collect it was not annexed to it. Whether it be soe or noe you may observe when you pay the money, for I must desire you to pay what you finde I am in arrear, but I beleive you will think it convenient to see the rate first and then you may make what observations you think fit without takeing notice of any thing I have said to you.
I am at a losse why you hold me in suspence about my Lord Ashleys answer till I come to town. the particulars of the discourse may be perhaps too long for your time and a letter. But the result I desire you to send me that I may bethink my self what to say or doe in the case For I imagin I shall scarce be able to get to town till the Parliament rises.†2 This being to goe early to Harlow that it may come to you to night I shall not give a particular answer in it to both your letters but defer it till by and by, when I shall write another letter to you to be sent you by this days post which you will have Wednesday,†3 My humble service to Madam. I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate and most humble servant
J LOCKE
Address: For Edward Clarke Esquire at Mrs Henmans overagainst Litleturnstile in Holborn London
Endorsed by Clarke: Mr Lock  †a Answered fully 26th March 1694.
1723. Locke to Edward Clarke, 19 March 1694 (ii) (1722, 1724)
Rand, pp. 390-1. The word in square brackets is supplied by Rand. Answered by no. 1727.
Oates, 19th March, 1693-4
Dear Sir,
If the letter I sent you this morning by the Bishop Stortford coach come safe you will have received my desire, which for fear of
― 35 ―

miscarriage I hear repeat to you again to pay my tax, which I am rated in Westminster for my commission of appeals, when you are satisfied by the collector by the view of the rates and by Mr. Pawling what I am in arrear. I add to these the acquittances I have in my scriptor at Mr. Pawling's, for what has at several times been paid by him for me. I doubt not but if the letter I sent this morning came safe, but that Mr. Bonville brought you the key of my scriptor. If he did not I must desire you to send to him for it. If there be need of seeing those acquittances, you will find them filed with several others in the second of those four drawers which make the uppermost row in my scriptor, and they may be easily found from the rest, being printed. My cousin Bonville has the key of that scriptor sealed up and will bring it you if you send to him for it. But I hope this is done before the receipt of this letter, for Mr. Pawling writ me word that they pressed for the money, which they have an odd way of collecting, letting it alone nine or twelve months together and then demanding it in haste, which I understand not in the K.'s want of money. Besides I think you will do well to inspect their rate to see whether the Commissioners' hands and seals are inseparably affixed to the rate they gather by. But if you please let this be your own accidental observation.
I know not what I may do in obedience to you. But truly I am mightily discouraged from doing anything more where I meet with nothing but repeated negligence. I have other views concerning that paper that is pretended to be trod under foot and torn than you h[ave], which I believe nothing of, and therefore must desire you to press for it again, and demand the torn pieces of it. For what is pretended to be torn may be kept for other and ill uses, but say nothing of that, but let the man whose letter you sent me enclosed be forced by you to hunt it out and return it again, because without that he is not like to have any more assistance from you. And pray rub up his carelessness a little. And let him know you find, as far as you have had time to look into it, this second ten times worse than the first edition.†1
I must desire you to let me know what I am to expect of my Lord Ashley in both those points you talked of. It is very uneasy to be left under a doubt, and therefore I make account you will do me that favour though you defer the particulars passed between you till I have the happiness to see you in town.
― 36 ―

The enclosed,†1 which was writ before I received yours of the 17th, will be a sufficient answer to that kind letter of yours. I intended to have sent it by the post as it is directed, and not to trouble you with more of my affairs than necessity compels me, for I think you do not want business. But since you were so kind to concern yourself in that affair, it is fit I could only thank you to let you see what is requisite to be done in it. You may tell Mr. Freke that I intend to make an alphabetical index to the book, for I would have this edition as useful to all sorts of readers as it can, and I hope it will be of some. Whether he thinks best to speak with Dring†2 (which your letter alone has named to me), or Manship, or both, I must leave to him. Pray give him and of my friends my service, most particularly to Madam. I am,
Dear Sir,
your most affectionate and most faithful servant.†a
My Lady and all here present their service to you.
Address: For Edward Clarke, Esq., Member of Parliament, at Mrs. Henman's, over against Little Turnstile in Holborn, London.
Frank.
1724. Edward Clarke to Locke, 21 March 1694 (1723, 1726)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 76. Printed in Rand, pp. 392-3. Answers no. 1722; answered by no. 1726.
London March the 21th. 1693.
Deare Sir,
I Received your Letter, and the Key of your Scriptore Munday night late†3 by Mr. Bonvill, and went early the next morning and looked out the last Receipt that Mr. Fox gave Mr. Pawling for your Tax, and compared it with Pawlins Accompt, as you Directed; the Receipt beares Date the 14th. of Aprill 1693. and is for 7l. 10s. for the third and fourth Quarterly Payments etc: ending at Christmas 1691., and I doe find it was the last money that Mr. Pawling payd
― 37 ―

for your Tax; I went imediately after to Mr. Fox his shop, and to his House, at which places I have been severall times since to speake with Him, and left word that I had your Tax ready in my handes to pay Him when ever Hee would receive it, and lett mee see the Booke what it amounted to; And have sent Mr. Pawlin severall times in the same Message to Him, but I cannot as yett meete with Him, nor gett Him neere mee, But I will try againe to morrow, and soe on 'till your Tax bee Discharged.
As to your Affayre with my Lord Ashley, I have only time to tell you, that I had as good an opportunity as I could have desiered to speake to my Lord for the Payment of what is in Arreare to you, and did make the best use I could of it, as I shall tell you more particularly when I am soe happy as to see you next, but I have not yett received any parte of it; And as to the increase of your Security, I find it is to bee done by an Improvement to bee made on the Farme by Building, and not otherwise, but of this alsoe more at large when I see you: I am
your most affectionate Faithfull servant
EDW: CLARKE
our humble services to all the Good Company at Oates, and in that Neighbourhood etc:

1731. William Thomas to Locke, 8 April 1694 (1695, 1733)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 146-7. Answered by no. 1733.
Sarum April 8th 1694
Sir
I have been a great while in London without the good fortune of seeing you. You are not ignorant of a Mortgage of 600l upon Colingbourne farm.†1 I find the mony lent in one Mr Bonville's name, and the Interest of it sett in the Deed at 5l per Cent. However my Father declared to my Mother and Mr Powell of this place, that he had agreed with you that the Interest to be payed should be but 4l per Cent. and that otherwise he would not have taken up the mony. I have been with Mr Bonville (whom I find to be your Cosin) but he denieth the knoledge of any such aftercontract, but says that if you made any†a- such, he-†a will freely stand to it. I desire the favour of you to lett me know as soon as you conveniently can, what we are to trust to in this affair. If we must pay 5l per Cent. the mony with the Interest shall be payed in within 3 months, if but 4l per Cent. then it may remain longer in our hands. I would not have troubled you about this matter had not my Father declared, as I've said to my Mother and Mr Powell immediately after the Affair was transacted. My Mother gives her humble service to you, and at this time is tolerably well. Sir,
The Enclosd was entrusted in my hands, by a Friend, a great while ago, in order to be conveyd to You. I unluckily misplaced it, upon a Removal, and gave it over as lost; but found it agen the Other Day in One of my Books; and think my self obligd to send it to You, and to beg Your pardon for the Delay.

1733. Locke to William Thomas, [17] April 1694 (1731, 1735)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 275. Draft. Answers no. 1731. The day on which the letter was written from Thomas's answer, no. 1735.
Oates 16º Apr. 94
Sir
I was extremly troubled at the News of your fathers death and the more because I was soe unfortunately tied up here that I could not goe as I desired to Salisbury to see him, which I had certainly
― 45 ―

donne if I had been at liberty, Haveing besides the incitement of a long and steady freindship, many things to have talked to him of.
As to the businesse you write to me about in yours of the 8th instant I find there is a mistake. When your father was last year in London he asked me whether I could help him to the sum you mention which he had then need of. I answerd I thought I could, a freind of mine haveing lately spoken to me to dispose of some mony for him. If I met with an oportunity. Your father said he was unwilling to pay above 4½ per cent Interest and I told him he could scarce have it any where at that rate but at 5 per cent he might have this. To which he agreed but said if he were made to pay above 4½ he would keep it but a year but if that ½ per cent were abated he would continue it 6 or 7 years longer. to which I told him that if the interest were duely paid I doubted not but the mony would be let alone in his hands at the rate he desired as long as the owners own occasions did not call for it which I guessed would not be very speedily. with this he was satisfied nor did your father ever once propose or mention any thing lower than 4½ per cent. and what was intended and understood by him I am concerned and shall take care to have made good to you.
In a letter I writ to your father before he died you will find I mentiond to him £30 I paid to Mr Furley for his use. Lookeing over my papers here this winter a loose memorandum of it came accidentaly to hand, and upon examination I founde it was never charged to your fathers account, of which I presently writ to him. How it came to be before omitted that letter will let you see. I would desire you to looke over your fathers accounts with me and see whether it be not as I say. In the same letter I told him also of 22s more which by his order I paid for a booke which was sent to Monsieur Grævius for Mr Champnis,†1 which has likewise been omitted. I hope to be in town the next weeke and to meet a letter from you there which I therefor desire you to direct to Mr Pawlings for me.
Present my humble service to your mother for whose losse I am very sory and pray assure her that if I can any way doe her or hers any service she may command me with the same freedom that our Deceased freind ever did and that I shall be glad of all oportunitys to doe any service to those he has left behind him. I wish your brother John a good voyage. He I hope is in soe good a way and soe
― 46 ―

agreeable to his owne inclination that if he scape the danger of the sea I doubt not but he will make his fortune. I shall always interest my self in what concerns him and you or any of your family. If at any time you come to town when I am there I hope I shall see you. the uninterrupted freindship I have had many years with your father makes me concerned for his children and particularly for you which you will find upon any occasion you will afford me to shew how much I am
Sir
your
Your father had of mine the greatest part of Lightfoots peices.†1 I thinke they will not be of much present use to you and therefor I desire you would when you have a fit oportunity send them to Mr Pawlings for me.

1734. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 19/29 April 1694 (1657, 1747)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 79-80. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 70-2.
A Amsterdam le 29 d'Avril 1694.
Il y a deja quelques mois, Monsieur, que je remis au Sieur Wetstein quelques Tomes de la Bibliotheque Universelle, pour vous envoier, avec ce qui vous manquoit des Acta Eruditorum, selon que vous me l'aviez marqué. Je croi que vous l'aurez reçu à présent. C'étoit dans une bâle adressée au Sieur Samuel Smith, dont, comme je croi, je n'aurai pas sujet d'être mécontent. Je m'imagine qu'il aura paié la Lettre de change, que j'ai tirée sur lui, selon qu'il en étoit convenu, quoi que je n'en aie pas encore eu des nouvelles. Je suis occupé à l'impression de mon second volume,†2 qui auroit été commencée plûtot, sans les distractions que j'ai euës tout l'Eté passé, et que j'ai encore en partie. Cet Ouvrage est l'un de ceux, dont†a- on peut-†a dire secessus et otia quærunt,†3 et je tâche, dans l'embarras de plusieurs
― 47 ―

occupations, de me faire du loisir et de la retraite pour y travailler; ce qui consiste à demeurer presque toûjours enfermé, sans avoir d'autre plaisir, que celui de travailler sans cesse. Il ne paroit rien ici de nouveau, qui soit de quelque consequence, et je croi que plus nous irons loin,†a moins on verra ici de bons livres. Il y a quelque temps que Mr. Limbourg me lut vôtre lettre, ou vous disiez être assez avancé dans la nouvelle édition de vôtre Ouvrage.†1 J'ai de l'impatience de le voir, et sur tout le Chapitre de la Liberté,†2 qui m'avoit déja extrémement plû. Cette matiere est très-difficile, et a été de plus obscurcie par la plûpart de ceux qui en ont traité, de sorte qu'il étoit avantageux qu'elle tombât entre des mains, comme les vôtres, qui travaillent si heureusement tout ce qu'elles entreprennent. Shal we see a continuation of the Religion of a Gentleman?†3 Les versions Françoises et Flammandes, qui en ont été faites, ont eu un très-grand cours, et le Livre a été approuvé des connoisseurs. Ce seroit dommage que l'Auteur en demeurât-là. Vous connoissez, Monsieur, celui qui vous rendra cette Lettre.†4 Je lui souhaiterois un Bénéfice, en quelque part dans vôtre île, qui lui pût donner de quoi vivre honêtement dans un exil, où jusqu'à présent, il n'a rien pû trouver de fixe. Cest une misere, que de demeurer en Hollande, où il n'y a point d'esperance pour l'avenir, ni de douceur pour le présent. Il ne se passe rien de nouveau ici, qui mérite de vous être écrit, excepté la conversion d'une Demoiselle d'une bonne famille Réformée, qui se vouloit faire Juïve, et que les Ministres Cocceïens ont en vain voulu ramener, mais qui l'a été fort heureusement, par Mr. Limbourg nôtre ami.†5 La premiere fois, que vous lui écrivez, engagez le à vous en faire l'histoire. Elle est assurément remarquable. N'aiant rien ouï dire de raisonnable sur la Religion Chrétienne, elle trouvoit le Judaïsme meilleur, jusqu'a ce qu'on lui ait ouvert les yeux, par une Theologie conforme au bon
― 48 ―

sens et à l'Evangile. Cela m'a fait comprendre, mieux que jamais, la necessité qu'il y a de mettre de bons livres entre les mains du peuple et d'en multiplier le nombre, qui est si petit. Je vous souhaiterois la vie de Nestor, afin que vous le pussiez faire, car je ne connois personne, qui soit plus capable de desabuser le monde que vous, et de bannir la superstition et l'ignorance. Je prie Dieu de tout mon coeur qu'il vous conserve au moins en bonne santé le reste de vos jours, et je suis, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings in Dorset Court, in channel row Westminster
Endorsed by Locke: Le Clerc 29. Apr. 94

1736. Anonymous to Locke, 6 May [1694] (1713)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 184-5. Year from Locke's endorsement.
May 6
Sir
I am mighty glad to find that after soe many disappointments my letter has at last reacht you, and in some measure discharged those obligations your particular civility had laid upon me. Was I in town I would certainly give my self the honour of waiting upon you, though I should not expect to improve my visit into a further acquaintance. But since I am denied that happinesse I hope my not owning my self at the bottom of a letter will not lessen that favourable opinion you have been pleased to entertain of me. I confesse it is not fair conversing in a mask, but t'is more pardonable when there's no design under it, and pulling it off would be no further a discovery. Shinesse is the farthest removed from my character of any quality in the world, and I only conceal my self because I have not an opportunity of being known to you. my name you are lesse acquainted with than my person, and I cannot write any thing of my self soe distinguishing as to give you further light. The chief reason of all my secrecy is that I am not in such a station, or in possession of such a character in the world as might put me above the mean suspicions of writing, or communicating what I writ to you, upon a Private design, had I done either publickly. And therefore to secure to my self the satisfaction of acting upon higher motives I have industriously conceal'd my self, though in order to receive better information in those matters I had been looking into, I should have been mighty glad if my circumstances had permitted me to have been where I might have received the benefit of your reflexions.
I am
Sir with all respect
your most oblidged humble servant.

Postmark: MA 7
Endorsed by Locke: Anonymus 6º May 94

1737. Robert Harley, later first earl of Oxford, to Locke, 9 May 1694
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 144-5. The statesman, 1661-1724; created earl of Oxford 1711: D.N.B. About this time Locke appears to have been intimate with Harley's father, Sir Edward: no. 1792.
May 9. 1694
Sir
There is nothing I have desir'd in my whole life so much as to be master of my Time, and generally I have been unfortunate therein; but upon no occasion do I more regret my Confinement than when I hear mr Lock is in Town, and yet find my self depriv'd of the benefit of that conversation I flatter'd my self to enjoy.
That which is cal'd Business I have generally thought very Impertinent,†1 because it diverts from what is more valuable and useful; henceforward I wil give it more respect; for I shal receive a double advantage from this Pretence of Business if I succeed in my request to you, which is that you wil make me known to my Lord Privy Seal, and give me leave to wait upon you when you visit him; He is, I hear, made Lord Lieutenant of Southwales:†2 I serve for the Town of Radnor and have a smal interest in that Country, which obliges me to gratify the ambition I have long had to wait upon his Lordship, and pay him that Duty, which you have told the Learned world is owing to his Lordships merit: when ever you please to appoint I wil wait upon you, but if it be any ways uneasy to you, I shal not press it, but beg pardon for this troble from
Sir
your most faithful humble servant
RO: HARLEY

Sir
If nothing that I have said in my Essay†1 is more obnoxious to confutation than what you find in its Epistle in reference to yourselfe I shall have little cause of Apprehension concerning it. What I there affirm with the greatest justice in the name of all the learned world I must now repeat in mine own. For by your very obliging letter of the 8'th instant I am afresh convinced that Mr Lock is one of the greatest Masters of Reason seeing he is so of civility which is the height of Reason. You say so many handsome things to me that I begin to flatter myself with hopes of having a place in your esteem But not without fears that what you have been pleased to give me with so much generosity on account of the Dedication I shall be deprived of again on account of the discourse when you have leisure to consider it and so espy its defects. However I will not Despair but that your Candor being equal to your great Judgment at the same time I am instructed and corrected by your exact and learned animadversions I shall also be spared by your Goodness and kindness of which no person will be more sensible than He who Honors you in perfection, and is
Sir
Your most humble servant
RICH BURTHOGGE.
