― 53 ―

Aubrey incorporated this information in the account of Hakewell's Coit in his 'Monumenta Britannica' (no. 1714 n.; part of ff. 52-4, description and plan of the stones at Stanton Drew called the Wedding):
About a quarter of a mile from this Monument of the Wedding, is a stone called Hakewell's Coyte†a ... which is a great roundish stone, of the shape of a coyte; length†b- of it is 10 foot 16 inches. Broad 6 foot 6 inches. thick 1 foot 10 inches.-†b and lies flatt: and seemes to have been left: it is of the same sort of stone with those at the Wedding. This is not erect as they of Stoneheng etc: The common-people tell this incredible story, that Hakewell stood upon the top of Norton-hill, about halfe a mile off where the Coyte now lies, and coyted it downe to this place: for which having the Mannor of Norton given him, and thinking it too little, did give it the name of Norton-Mal-reward, which they pronounce Small-reward.
That in these parts anciently was one Hakewell a person of great estate and strength of body is manifest by the figure in his monument in Chew-church.

1741. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 19/29 May 1694 (1702, 1745)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 115.
Rotterdam 29 May 1694
Deare Friend
An order coming for a yacht to go with my lady Dursley†2 occasions the so speedy departure of this friend, that I cannot find your last letter; much less answer it, onely the main thing, which the Baron recommended me yesterday morning when he went hence to Amsterdam to get the Booke of the Divine Attributes†3 printed in Dutch, Viz, the Historicall maps of Monsieur Knor†4 I send you by the bearer Jacob Telner—who will leave them with Joseph wright for you—they are somewhat perisht, but I suppose may easily be restored. Your presents of those unitarian pieces monsieur van H. gave me,†5 and your little friend his token, for which we both return humble thanks—your friend has been calling on me severall days that he might write you a letter of thanks, but I have had no time to mind him. These maps I had got fastend to a couple of frames, and it has made me sweat to get them off. I wonder the Oxford Testament†6 comes not abroad yet, I heare that a good while since a sheet of the Apocalyps has been on this side the sea, and that its mightily approved of. Leers goes on apace with monsieur Bailes Dictionnaire critique.†7 The Baron I fancy I shal see
― 55 ―

no more, he is going to seek men that will ask him, or answer his questions, and talks of going to the Indies to seek the Brachmans, but I trust he intends no such matter, For how he will make himself be understood there, where he has no language, who can scarce meet with any that can understand him in Europe, where he has so many languages, I know not. But one to whom he told it, bad him ask him what he pleased, and he would answer him as far as he could, and where he fell short, here his answers to what he should enquire. But the discourse was very short, As is my time at present, so I must break off with Kind respects from my dearest and myself to yourself, Sir Fr: and my Lady m— and rest
Your affectionate friend
BENJAMIN FURLY

1742. Samuel Heathcote to Locke, 25 May 1694 (1743)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 182-3. Answered by no. 1743? Samuel Heathcote, 1656-1708, younger brother of Sir Gilbert (D.N.B.; p. 448); married 22 January 1691. Baltic merchant; a director of the Bank of England 1702-8: E. D. Heathcote, Account of ... Heathcote, 1899, pp. 101-6; J. M. Price, The Tobacco Adventure to Russia ... 1676-1722 (American Philosophical Soc., Trans., new ser., vol. li, pt. i, 1961), p. 107, etc.
Sir
Ever since I had the happyness to see your thoughts of Education (by the publication Whereof you have greatly obliged this Nation and perticularly myselfe) I and my Wife have practiced them in the education of our son with success even beyond our hopes; I will trouble you but with one Instance, that before he was .2. yeares old his Mother taught him to know all the letters of the Alphabet very perfectly, and never troubled him to learne them, but When the Child desired it.
This, with the great Concerne I have for the good of My Children, encourageth me to trouble you with this letter to desire you would please to resolve some difficultys I have upon me about a Tutor.
― 56 ―

but first I thinck it Needfull to acquaint you that I have three sonns, the eldest is .2. yeares and 4. Moneths old, the second one yeare and 2 months, and the third .3. weekes.
I am a Merchant Myselfe (And if it pleaseth God they and I live so long) I intend to make them so too: however I am desireous to give them an ingenuous education, supposeing that will not make them less, but more fit for such an employment, as well as any other business; And to that end I designe to have a Tutor in My house to be allwayes with them.
but one difficulty with me is, to know what age they ought to be, before they are Committed to the Care of a Tutor, (for their Mother herselfe intends to teach them to read) Another and the greatest difficulty is, What Nation the Tutor should be off: for there is scarce an English man to be found that speakes french and latine as fluently as English; And both those languages you recommend to their learning, not by the tedious way of rules, but by conversation onely, Which is Certainly the most easy and speedy way to learne any language.
An English man (I presume) can teach them all other sorts of learning assoone and as well as a forreigner, And for some sorts of learning and other considerations I should Chuse him rather then a Stranger, but without french and latine their Education will be incomplete, so that for those .2. languages a French man seems to me to be the properest Tutor. And at this time, by reason of the late persecution in France, I beleeve there are very Vertuous and learned french Divines that want employments, Who might be Willing to Accept of that of a Tutor.
And 'twill be rare to find an English man so qualified, that will undertake such a Charge. A young Man has not gravity and experience enough for it, besides they will be for Marrying, or seeking greater preferment, And then I must change their Tutor, Which you say will be very inconvenient, that a grave Batchelour or Widdower will be the Likelylest to Continue with them.
I should be Willing to give any reasonable Salary to a Tutor that is a person of great Vertue, good learning and breeding, for I would rather have my Children Vertuous then learned. And if you should Chance to meet with a person fit for my purpose that wants an employment and would Accept of mine, I beg you will recommend him to me, or direct me in my enquiry after one, Which I should esteeme a singular kindness. Pray favour me with an answere at
― 57 ―

your leasure; And let the Consideration of the care and affection I have for My Children, plead my excuse for giveing you this trouble, And if it ever lye in My Power to serve you, I shall be allways ready, and ambitious to Manifest Myselfe
Sir your obliged and affectio: friend and Servant
SAM: HEATHCOTE
St Swithings lane neare Lumbard Street the .25th. of May 1694.
Address: To Mr: John Lock att Mr: Paulings in Dorcett Court in Channell Row Westminster
Postmark: London Penny Post: B FR
Endorsed by Locke: S: Heathcote 25º May 94
1743. Locke to [Samuel Heathcote?] 26 May [1694?] (1742)
B.M., Add. MS. 17017, f. 86. By Locke's address the letter must date from between 1689 and 1694. The contents suggest that it is in answer to no. 1742.
Dorset Court 26º May
Sir
At my return last night to my lodging I received your civil letter. And should (as well as I could) have replied to all the particulars you propose in it by the way I send you this, did either my present occasions allow me time for soe long a letter, or did I think that litle assistance I am able to afford you could be soe well suited to your purpose by writeing to you, as by discourseing with you. I say not this to decline serveing of you in what you desire. Tis a duty which I think I owe every English man for my countrys sake and therefor should not refuse to a person of your reputation and character. But since you are soe much concernd for the Education of your Children as every wise and good man cannot but be; Give me leave to advise you to make my thoughts in this matter as usefull to you as you can rather by discourseing the matter than by the slow and heavy way of letters. If I come to your end of the town I shall not fail to wait upon you and if your occasions lead you this way I should be glad to see you at my Lodging. I am
Sir
your most humble servant
J LOCKE

1744. Locke to William Molyneux, 26 May 1694 (1712, 1748)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 76-8. It appears from no. 1748 that the editor omitted a passage from one of Locke's letters to Molyneux; it was probably from this letter. Answers no. 1712; answered by no. 1748.
London, 26. May. 1694.
Sir,
The slowness of the press has so long retarded my answer to your last obliging letter, that my book which is now printed and bound, and ready to be sent to you, must be an excuse for my long silence. By the obedience I have pay'd to you in the index and summaries order'd according to your desires,†1 you will see 'tis not want of deference to you, or esteem of you, that has caused this neglect. And the profit I have made, by your reflections, on several passages of my book, will, I hope, encourage you to the continuance of that freedom, to a man who can distinguish between the censures of a judicious friend, and the wrangling of a peevish critick. There is nothing more acceptable to me than the one, nor more, I think, to be slighted than the other. If therefore, as you seem to resolve, you shall throw away any more of your time in a perusal of my Essay, judge, I beseech you, as severely as you can of what you read. I know you will not forsake truth to quarrel with me; and whilst you follow her you will always oblige me, by shewing me my mistakes, or what seems to you to be so. You will find, in this second edition, that your advice at any time has not been thrown away upon me. And you will see by the errata, that though your last came a little too late, yet that could not hinder me from following what you so kindly, and with so much reason, suggested.†2
I agree with you that drunkenness being a voluntary defect, want of consciousness ought not to be presum'd in favour of the drunkard. But frenzy being involuntary, and a misfortune, not a fault, has a right to that excuse, which certainly is a just one where it is truly a frenzy. And all that lies upon humane justice is to distinguish carefully between what is real and what counterfeit in the case.
― 59 ―

My book, which I desire you to accept from me, is put into Mr. Churchill the bookseller's hand, who has told me he will send it in a bale of books, the next week, to Mr. Dobson†1 a bookseller in Castle-street, Dublin; and I have order'd him to send with it a copy of the additions and alterations which are printed by themselves, and will help to make your former book useful to any young man, as you will see (is design'd) by the conclusion of the epistle to the reader.†2 I am.
Sir,
Your most affectionate, and most humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
1745. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 26 May/5 June 1694 (1741, 1764)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 116-19.
Rotterdam 5 June 1694
Dear Friend
When I wrot you this day sennight, and sent you, by him whom I design this stil to go by, the 2 Chronological Tables, I could not, in that hurry, surprized by a sudden gust of an Easterly wind, find your letter, which you were nigh a month from the 10 march to the 8th of April, writing. And so I contented myself onely to let you know that the Baron had been here, and was gone to Amsterdam to get the book printed in Dutch which he caused to be printed in English. And then from thence, I know not whither†a to find men that will ask him questions, or answer his, which he always complains he cannot find. I hope I shall receive these tables back in
― 60 ―

print, and then shall not grudge them a place in the best chamber in my house, as I had, in the condition in which, you wil find them, already given them in my lodging chamber having been at the charge to put them into two frames.
I perceive you have received an Account of my wife, from others as wel as myself, and find the character I had given her confirmed.
She coming to me while I am writing, I shewd her your letter, and askt her what I should say on that head. She replyed, Say that you have found yourself deceived. But yet, that I have so great esteem for so worthy a Gentleman, as I understand Doctor Lock to be, that I shall always put a great value upon his friendship, and shall always be ready to shew it, upon all occasions: desiring you to accept of her humble service, and to give it to Sir Fr. and my Lady.
I see what you say of my children born out of England, And tho I have understood, that the children of marchants residing abroad, so born, are, in Law reputed natural English and capable of inheriting land, yet your Judgment in the Point, is of such weight with me, that I have, considering the Act of naturalisation did not pass this last Session, and perhaps never may, in this Parliament, resolved to sell al my land in England.†1
And have actually sold 2 parcels, one neare Colchester, having cut off the Entail. And one neare whitby, at 20 years purchase, which is a good round rate.
But the last being my wives portion,†2 (tho the division of her fathers estate betwixt the mother and 5 daughters, (whereof the eldest onely and my wife were married) was made after her being married with me) was setled upon her and her heires; and that gives me trouble, to find a way to make a title of it, because my wife, in whom it was vested, dyed without making any settlement, I presuming, that we, by will having made each other universall heires, upon paying our 2†a children certain portions therein exprest, and supposing the land would, of course go to our Eldest son Benjohan, that was sufficient.
This settlement upon my wife, which otherwise should have been upon me, (as the Eldest daughters portion is upon her husband), I beleev was by my own direction, because of the precontract of marriage by which each retaind the property in that which we brought in to the society, according to the custom of this place.
― 61 ―

The friend that has bought it of me sees this difficulty, but has such a mind to the land, that he wilbe content with what title I can give him, upon my bond for £200 or £300 that Benjohan when he comes of age shall confirm my act and deed: And that I shall secure him from all claims whatsoever, which is but reasonable.
For, if Benjohan should dye before he be naturalized, or of Age, to be invested in it, my wives 4 sisters who are all alive, and married or their heirs, wilbe heirs at law.
My request to you is, that you would be pleased to give the Deed, and bond for performance of which I send herein a copy (not to hazzard the original) to mr. Clark, mr. Freak, or some other honest man learned in the Law, to draw a conveyance, and such other Bond act or Instrument for the sayd land to Joseph Scarth master and marriner of whitby in the county of York, and to his Heires forever—
My mother in Law is dead; but my 4 sisters are living and they and their husbands being all honest, serios people, called Quakers, and I doubt not but they will sign any Instrument whatsoever that may tend to the confirmation of the sale, and surrendring all right that by that error in the first settlement might accrue to them or theirs, (if it can possibly) without putting me to the charge of naturalizing my three children, which will cost more than the land, which is but £6 per annum and is sold for £120. I beg their serious consideration of this thing. And so soone as I know what I can and must do, to make him a good Title, I shall send a letter of Attorney to Joseph Wright, to sign and seal such Instrument or Instruments in my name, upon receit of a draught of such special Letter of Attorney.
I have yet Copyhold land lying within 6 miles of Colchester, which some†a- years agoe I designed to sell and to cut off the Entaile:-†a but 'tis yet unsold.
Is there no way to be devised to secure that land (if I cannot sell it) by vesting it in my Nephew John Furly and his heirs and taking a defeasance†1 from him to pay the Rent to my children and their heires—
― 62 ―

If not, I must either send my children to England, in Parliament time, (one being about 14 year old the other about 12 and the yongest about 9½)—to be naturalized. Pray inform me what that will cost, and whether children so yong can be naturalizd or no. And inform me at what age children are capable of making wils there. A daughter may here at 12 a son at 14 year old.
I hope you will excuse me that I trouble you in this affaire, and am confident that the respect you bore to their mother, and yet do to me their father, will not make it be burthensom to you, to perform this kindness to her, and my children:
And this makes me think you mistooke when you said, that if ever you return to Holland again, you shal find one friend more than you had when you left it: For you shal find but an exchange of one friend for another.
I see your resolution to see G: Keith†1 in London, and shalbe glad to understand the Issue of your conference.
I am of your mind, and experience has taught me, that it is no easy matter to get a society so free, as you and I would gladly see, and help propagate in the world: except it should consist of a very small and select number—
For the prejudice of Education lays in mens minds such an undue reverence for some things, and persons as is not easily overcome.
The Bugbear of Authority, Tradition, and the name of Church is so sacred with them, That few people dare call in question the Doctrines which holy church has taught for so many hundred years, or which their Learned and godly ministers have all along taught since the Reformation. What! say they, within themselvs, shall we dare to call in question what so many Ages, and so many learned men have determind?
People are afraid to examin, they dare not trust their own Judgments, their own eyes, their own sence. for fear of being deceived, seduced, deluded, and what not, which is a miserable estate. And differs not from that enslaved Estate of the people under the Romish church.
But that which is yet worse, and more to be lamented is that people are afraid to examine, lest their eyes should be opened to see, and be convinced of things that may break their rest, or peace, or oblige them to profess things, that may interfere with their Interest in the world, with their reputation amongst their Priests,
― 63 ―

and neighbours; And pass them for Hereticks, Schismaticks, and what not, conceited, troublesome spirits, that wilbe wiser than their neighbours, more knowing than all the great learned, and godly men of our party.
No, No, 'tis best, say they, to be quiet, and not to trouble ourselvs to examine matters, our forefathers, our learned Teachers have examind things enough already.
These and such like snares keep men in slavery and bondage, and few men, but those that are endowed with a generous boldness, and courage, dare once examine matters.
I say not these things, dear Sir, for your sake, but for my childrens sake, who shall copy this Letter, that they may see how free their father was.
Had these considerations prevaild with Luther, Calvin, and those first reformers, who contradicted the Church, and feared not to examine the Doctrines she had establisht for so many hundreds of years, by her learned Bishops and Priests, Synods and Councils, and made no bones of Trampling all under foot, (notwithstanding the Authority of the church, that pretended not onely to learning and piety, but even to infallibility itself) which they found to be unreasonable and unscripturall
I say had such considerations of Authority, Tradition, church, learning, holyness, fear of being counted Hereticks, Schismaticks, or singular, troublesome, restless, nice heads, been able to discourage them, we had yet groaned under the Intollerable yoake of Romish slavery.
Are we escaped that, by their generous example, and shall we again bow our necks to the same pretences among their successors? Shall we put out our eyes to see with theirs? Surely no.
This makes me greedily grasp at all opportunities offered me to expose those two Words CHURCH, and HERETICK; as two of the most pernicious words that have for above 1000 years obtaind amongst mankind.
That of Church, to gain reputation to a company of Clerical Coxcombs, fooles, knaves, and slaves, who being so to their superior Ecclesiasticks would, by their lording it over Gods Heritage (or Clergy) that is the people, (which make the society of christians) make all men slaves to them, as if they alone were the church.
That of Heretick; to render odious, and run down, all honest, wel meaning, courageous, generous spirited men, that dare be so bold
― 64 ―

as to profess, and practise what they Judge to be their duty towards God, towards them selvs, and towards their neighbour,†a how contrary, and unpleasant soever it be to these church slaves and all their enslaved followers, who would make free men (if they could) bow their necks to their doctrines, decrees, orders, injunctions, and constitutions.
While I am thus writing, in come the English Letters, and among others one from G: Keith, telling me that he had spoken with thee and that in thy discourse, thou hadst proceeded upon Cartesian grounds denying all sense and life in Beasts, and in fine seemed to him to be nothing but a meer Cartesian,†1 But that afterwards one told him that thou wert no Cartesian, which makes him conclude that thou wert not in earnest—and that he dislikes— If it be so (as I cannot beleeve) you are much changd since I converst you, for you do not use to love bantering in any man, nor to practise it your self—
Now I am thus far advanced comes Colhans and desires my letter of recommendation to you in behalf of a yong Gentleman thats going to England intending to reside some time, at Cambridg or Oxford, as yourself shal best Judge for his advantage; his father is a Professor in Leipsigh, he is in great measure free, learned, and ingenuous, sees the Priestcraft sufficiently, he is sober, quiet, and of civil comportment, And as such I know will be acceptable to you, and that you wilbe ready to give him the best advice and directions you can, which I also desire of you, And so with my best respects and service to yourself and to Sir Francis and My lady I rest
Deare Friend
your most affectionate friend and servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
The yong mans name is Olearius.†2
Address: For Mr. John Locke at mr. Joseph Wrights near London Stone London per a friend
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furley 5º Jun 94

1746. Anthony Ashley Cooper, Styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 28 [May 1694] (1626, 1783)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 108-9. Printed in Rand, Shaftesbury, pp. 294-6. Month and year from postmark and Locke's endorsement.
St Giles's: the 28th
I ought to be extreamly satisfied with any thing that I have done, or any Accident happening, that should be the occasion to mee of receiving any Letter from you, more then I should have done. And I ought to be more then ordinarly satisfied with any such thing att this time: Since, as my Concerns have dispos'd of mee, I am not likely, of a long time, to receive any Pleasure or Advantage of an Acquaintance that I know so well how to Valew, except only What is of this kind. I have too little Hopes of seeing you Here, ever to Talk of them, till I have better Encouragement from You; or Fresh Ground, from my own Circumstances, to Press you upon itt. And without this; I have nothing elce to Depend upon, but the hearing from You: Since I shall hardly now be able to see you, I know not when, in Town; and far less att a Certain Place besides that I have been att, which, though not so Bigg, is worth a thousand such Towns. I wish I deserv'd the Character you Give mee; and Could willingly Flatter myself upon what You say of mee; but that I should make your Opinion of mee yet more groundless, and have no sort of worth att all, if, for as much as lay in mee, I sufferd you to continue so much Deceiv'd. And were it not that I should only look affected in what I said, and so give you occasion to Say more of a kind that I am apt to Like too well; I would honestly shew you that I was not, nor could be, of that Consideration or Worth in the world which You make mee to bee.
If, such as I am, I prove to be yet rather better then severall of our Patrician Blood; I am sorry for them, and for the Commonwealth I live in; that it should bee so bad with them. The Comparison indeed seems to give mee some advantage: but what it can amount to, I very well know, is only, not as if I should doe more Good, but a little less mischeif in the World then might be expected from one of that Number I make.
I could wish too (for I find you have sett mee a wishing) that in this absence, my Letters were able to give you that satisfaction you seek in them, and could be worth the Esteem you place upon them.
― 66 ―

For my own part, I know my self to be, in this Province of Society, (if I may use such an Expression) so very Unapt a Creature and so little able to sustain a Part, that I should be asham'd to Invite any ordinary Person, and much less You, to come into so Unfair, so Unequall a Party: nor could I be pleas'd with my self that I had designedly Engag'd you in a Commerce where there would be nothing Reciprocall, and oftenest a meer Load and Trouble sent in Exchange for an Advantage and an Entertainment. Indeed in another sort of Commerce I never apprehended so much as this. In Free Conversation, by the Advantages of being Face to Face, the Suteing and Timeing of things and a great many helps besides: One may Bee, with a little Plain Sence and a good deal of Honesty, not only of some use, but Entertaining enough in the way of Freindship. But I who am never very well satisfied with what I speak; should be verry sorry to be Oblig'd for an Agreable Present made mee, to Return so Bad a one as a Bundle of such Thought as mine, and an Essay of my own, of such a Genius, such Invention, such a Style as mine —— I Find, if I goe on, I shall Doe as bad as what I pretend to be displeas'd with. I will only say one thing more, which I am but seldome Displeas'd with Saying, and never but Pleas'd with solidly shewing, that I am
Your sincere Freind and Humble servant
A: ASHLEY
my Father returns his very Humble service to You

1747. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 29 May/8 June 1694 (1734, 1767)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 81-2. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 72-4.
A Amsterdam le 8 de Juin 1694.
Des livres que vous me marquez, Monsieur, avoir reçus, les Acta Eruditorum seuls sont de Wetstein. Mr. Limbourg y a joint la vie d'Episcopius, avec quelques uns de ses sermons, publiez de nouveau. Si vous entendez assez de Flamand, pour lire cette vie, elle vous divertira, en vous aprenant quel étoit l'esprit de l'Eglise en Hollande,
― 67 ―

au commencement de ce siecle. Pour les Tomes de la Bibliotheque, c'est moi qui les a remis à Wetstein. Il y en a encore un, savoir, la 2. Part. du XXV. qui a été imprimé depuis. Le libraire est mort en suite, et son fonds n'est pas encore vendu, de sorte que je ne sai, si l'on continuera cet ouvrage.†1 En tout cas, je vous enverrai la derniere partie. On n'imprime rien de considerable ici, que vous ne sachiez. Nous aurons bien-tôt une seconde édition in folio du Systeme de Mr. Limbourg.†2 J'en suis à la douziéme feuille de l'édition de mon Exode, et j'espere que cela ira assez vîte, dès à présent. Il y a un Libraire ici qui a sous la presse la Vie du Cardinal de Richelieu, qui méritera d'être luë, autant que j'en puis juger par ce que j'en ai vû.†3 Ce n'est ni satire, ni panegyrique, ni roman, mais une veritable histoire, où l'Auteur cite ceux de qui il a tiré ce qu'il dit, sous les pages. Je me réjouïs de voir la 2. Edition de vôtre Ouvrage, et sur tout le chapitre de la Liberté.†4 Je vous suis bien obligé, Monsieur, du soin que vous prenez de mes interêts. Nos Marchands, ennemis jurez des Lettres, m'ont accordé encore pour cette année et la suivante, la pension qu'il m'avoient donnée, pour trois ans, c'est a dire, cinq cent francs d'extraordinaire, qui avec la même somme, qui est le gage ordinaire des Ministres de la Campagne, font 1000 francs par an. J'ai eu toutes les peines du monde, d'obtenir cela de gens, qui n'estiment que l'argent; car c'est des Anciens,†5 qui sont marchands, que tout dépend. Il m'a fallu essuier des brutalitez d'un fondeur de cloches, qui est un déclamateur seditieux, qui ne sont pas concevables, pour tâcher de le gagner. Si j'avois à faire à des Cardinaux, ce ne seroit pas pis, et j'obtiendrois quelque chose pour ma vie. Vous pouvez juger par-là si j'ai suject d'être content de ces gens, quoi qu'il y en ait plusieurs à qui j'ai de l'obligation, mais leur amitié ne va pas plus loin que quelques paroles. Outres cela, quand même, après mille bassesses, <ils>†a m'accorderoient pour la vie ce qu'ils me donnent, ce seroit là
― 68 ―

le ne <plus ultra,>†a et il n'y a pas de quoi vivre ici, où tout est ex<cessi>vement†a cher. Il faut que je perde mon temps, en toute autre chose, que l'ouvrage que j'ai entrepris, pour subvenir à la dépense nécessaire de ma famille. C'est ce que je vous dis in aurem. Si vos Messieurs vouloient faire quelque chose pour moi, il faudroit que cela fût tenu secret, jusqu'à ce que l'affaire fût faite. Vous connoissez la malice, et l'envie des François, qui ne manqueroient pas de faire une députation à Mr. L'Archevêque, pour m'accuser des héresies imaginaires, dont ils font peur au peuple.†1 Comme je me conformerois volontiers à l'Eglise Anglicane, pour la Liturgie etc. je ne voudrois pas que l'on m'offrît de nouvelles signatures à faire, et je ne dirois jamais anatheme, par aucune signature particuliere, à personne qu'aux méchantes gens. Quand je saurois que tout est prêt, je pourrois faire promtement un petit voiage à Londres, mais il faudroit que je revinses pour mes livres, mes meubles etc. Autrement si cette affaire venoit à éclatter, avant que d'être faite, cent zelateurs envieux se mettroient en campagne, et ne feroient aucune difficulté d'emploier les plus noires calomnies, pour me supplanter. S'il étoit possible de prévenir adroitement ceux qui me voudroient faire du bien, contre de semblables discours, je croi que cela ne seroit pas inutile; mais en essaiant de le faire, il ne faudroit pas que je parusses m'accuser moi même. Le Dr. Kidder, Evêque de Bath, et de Wels, paroît avoir quelque estime pour mon ouvrage, dont il m'a fait demander les feuilles, même par la poste, et je m'imagine que peutêtre il me rendroit service. Je lui écrirai en lui envoiant les feuilles par Mr. Walford,†2 qui est ici. J'ai reçu depuis peu des dissertations de Mr. l'Evêque de Salisbury,†3 qu'il m'a envoiées, ce qui me donnera lieu de lui écrire. Si vous avi<ez, Monsieur>,†a occasion de parler ou à l'un, ou à l'autre, cel<a ne seroit p>eutêtre†a pas inutile; car tout se fait par recommendati<on,>†a et plus il y a de gens qui se mêlent d'une semblable chose, plus facilement elle reüssit. Je vous demande pardon de la peine, que je vous donne, et
― 69 ―

de ce que je vous amuse du détail de mes affaires. C'est une effusion de coeur, dont il est difficile de s'empêcher, quand on parle à une personne, en qui l'on a de la confiance, et une confiance fondée sur une estime aussi solide que celle que j'ai pour vous, et sur les marques de bonté pour moi que vous m'avez données plus d'une fois. Je suis, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Ma femme qui a présentement un fils de quatre mois†1 à conduire, a lû et relû vos Lettres of education,†2 avec beaucoup de plaisir et de satisfaction. Elle m'a chargé plus d'une fois de vous en remercier pour elle, lors que je v<ous>†a écrirois.

1748. William Molyneux to Locke, 2 June 1694 (1744, 1753)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed with omissions in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 78-82. Answers no. 1744; answered by no. 1753.
Dublin. June 2d. 1694.
Sir
I am highly obleidged to you for the Favour of your Last of May. 26. which I received yesterday. It brought me the Welcom News of the second Edition of Your Essay being Publishd; and that you have Favourd me with a Coppy, which I shall expect with some Impatience. and when I have perused it, I shall with all Freedom give you my Thoughts of it.
The†b- Gentleman you Directed me to speak to about the Mony†3 was a perfect Stranger to Me; however I know several of his Freinds, and I found him out, and went to Him. Upon my first
― 70 ―

Mentioning to him the busines, He readily ownd it, and took it on him as a Dett, and promised to pay it, only he desired time till the End of next Term. He desired from me Your Addres, which I gave him, so that I suppose he will write to your self about it.-†b
And now that you have cleard your Hands of Your second Edition, I hope you may have Leasure to turn your Thoughts to the Subject I have so often proposed to you; But this you will say is a Cruelty in me, that no sooner you are ridd of One Trouble, but I sett you on an other. Truly Sir were I sensible it could be a Trouble to you, I should†a- hardly presume-†a so far on your Goodnes; but I know those Things are so easy and Natural to your Mind, That they give you no Pain in the Production. And I know also, such is your Universal Love of Mankind, that you count nothing troublesom that tends to their Good in a Matter of so great Concernment as Morality.
I have formerly told you what Care I proposed to take in the Education of My Only Child. I must now beg your Pardon if I trouble you in a matter, wherein I shall be at a Losse without your Assistance; He is now five years old, of a Most towardly and promising Disposition; bred exactly, as far as his Age permitts, to the Rules you prescribe, I mean as to forming his Mind and Mastering his Passions; He reads very well, and I think it time now to putt him forward to some other Learning; In order to this I shall want a Tutor for him, and indeed this Place can hardly afford me One to my Mind. If therefore you know any Ingenious†c Man that May be proper for My Purpose, you would highly obleidge me, by procuring him for Me. I must Confes the Incouragement I can propose to such a One is but Moderate: Yet perhaps there may be some found, that may not despise it. He†d- should Eat-†d at My Own Table, and have his Lodging, Washing, Firing and Candlelight in My House, in a Good handsom apartment; and besides this I should allow him 20 pounds per An. His work for this should be only to Instruct three or four Boys in Latin and such other Learning as You recommend in your Book; I say 3 or 4 boys, because perhaps I may have a Relations Child or two; One, who is my Sisters son†1 I have always, and do intend to keep as a Companion to my Own
― 71 ―

Son; and of More I am uncertain. but if there be One or two, that will be no great Addition to his Trouble, especially considering that perhaps their Parents may recompence that by their Gratuitys. I Mention to you, of the Languages only Latin: but if I could obtain it, I should be Glad he were also Master of the French. As to his other Qualifications I shall only say in general, I could wish them such as You would desire in a Tutor to Instruct a Young Gentleman, as you propose in Your Book. I would have him indeed a Good Man and a Good Scholar, and I propose very much satisfaction to My self in the Conversation of such a One. And because a Man may be cautious of leaving his Native soil, and Coming into a strange Country, without some certainty of being acceptable to those that send for him, and of some Continuance and Settlement;†a I can say that I designe him to stay with My†b- Son to-†b his State of Manhood, whether he go into the University, or Travel, or whatever other state of life he may take to. And if perhaps on Tryal for some time, He or I may not like each other, I do promise to bear his Charges both to and from Me, so that he shall be no Looser by his Journey.
I beg your Answer to this at your Leasure, and if any such present, be pleased to let me know of him what Particulars you can, as his Parentage, Education, Qualification<s,>†c Disposition, etc, with what other particulars you please to Mention. And Accordingly I shall write to you farther about it.
In the mean time, I beseech you to pardon this Trouble given you by
Honoured Sir
Your Most Affectionate and Most obleidged Humble servant
W: MOLYNEUX
My†d- Brother gives you his Most Humble service. within two days he enters into the state of Matrimony.-†d†1

1749. Locke to Lady (Mary) Calverley, 5 June 1694 (1441, 3222)
N. Forbes Adam, Esq., Escrick. Deposited in the County Record Office, East Riding of Yorkshire, Beverley. Transcribed by Mr. N. Higson, County Archivist.
London 5º Jun 94
Madam
Had you been contriving to stay in town when you denyd yourself to me it had been an excuse I could not have refused But to make one injury the excuse for an other and to refuse me the honour of seeing you to day in order to my looseing you tomorrow and make your runing away a plea for it, is to use your friends at a rate that must make them lesse wonder at your runing away. One must yet allow that there is something extraordinary in all my Lady Cavarleys actions And when she is a litle spareing of her goodnesse to her friends she fails not to take up their minds with the admiration of her wit For she orders the matter soe that the most provoking thing she could doe to those that have the honour of her acquaintance here in town should put her out of the reach of their revenge or reproaches. How this may worke upon others I know not. I am like the man whose life was saved by takeing two poisons.†1 Had you shut me out and staid in town after it perhaps I should have complaind of you. Or had your Ladyship gon away in a lesse hurry and hast then what made you have leisure for noething but packing I possibly should have grumbled. Now I have noething to say but that I am obleiged to you for sending me word that you were got safe soe far on your journey as Okenbury.†2 I hope the remainder of it was not lesse succesfull and that you have ever since enjoyd all the satisfaction you proposd to yourself in leaveing the town. Mr. Freke was well this after noon and I am

Royal Library, Copenhagen, MS. Thott 1263-4°. Printed by C. Bastide in Revue internationale de l'enseignement, lv (January-June 1908), 392-3. The letter dates from between the end of May 1694, when Locke received no. 1682, which it answers, and probably 3 July, when he left London (he was again in London from 11 to 14 July). Answered by no. 1786.
(English) Vir Doctissime
Literæ tuæ amicissimæ 25 Decemb: datæ Ultrajecti, redditæ mihi fuerunt hic Londini Majo exeunte. Quod tam diu diverterint aliquo
― 74 ―

ex itinere non tam queror, quam gratulor mihi tandem evasisse pyratarum manus una cum comitibus libellis et ad manus meas pervenisse sinceros hosce amoris tui erga me testes. Non est ut labores an ex alienâ†a arcâ†1 an ex tuo penu depromantur quæ ad me mittis cum mihi in cujus jam dudum sum ære alieno in†b- lucro ponenda sint-†b, et omnia quæ a Te proficiscuntur non possunt non esse grata. Illud†2- tamen longe gratissimum quod me de vitâ et valetudine Toinardi nostri certiorem facis. Magnam sane hoc nuncio et diuturnam levasti animi mei ægritudinem. De eo longos jam annos solicitus et anxius vixi, ignarus quid ageret, dubius an viveret an valeret. Sæpius per alios egi cum Wetstenio ut ad illum a me transmitteret Jo: Malelam Antiochenum, quem videre uti memini olim desideravit. quid in hâc re præstitit Wetstenius nondum scio. si tardaverit, si oblitus <fuerit>,†c si nondum invenit viam, moneas rogo, excites, et impellas meo nomine ut liber iste perveniat in manus Toinardi, Dilectissimo illo et antiquæ fidei viro, nulla quæ in me, est industria, opera studium deerit unquam nec deesse poterit. Inter omnia belli hujus mala nihil gravius animo meo
― 75 ―

insedit quam interruptum cum suavissimo doctissimoque viro literarum commercium. Cupio iterum videre, cupio amplecti. <Interea>†aquod solum restat omnia illi fausta jucunda utilia animitus opto, et maxime lætor quod aliquando meminer<it>†b mei. Gratias primâ datâ occasione quæso nomine meo reddas, dicasque omnia quæ credas ab amico ad amicum†1 esse gratissima. et quotiescunque de illo quicquam tibi innotuerit fac me certiorem. Quæ jam ediderit et quæ meditatur digna sunt illius eruditione, omnia quæ molitur cupio videre sed nihil æque ac harmoniam Evangelicam tanto studio tanto diligentia et judicio elucubratam, quam omnes quotquot viderint vel fando audiverint anxie expectant, nec cur differat opus tam utile Christiano orbi, hæredibus (si ad eos delabi permittat) negligendum non satis scio. sed nolo reprehendere hominem quem <tantopere>†c diligo, quem sospitem esse lætor et tanquam e sepulchro restitutum mihi gratulor-†2
(English) In tanta meliorum scriptorum copia non est cur queraris tibi interclusum libri mei usum nostri idiomatis inscitiâ. An aliquando Latinitate donandus sit non ausim augurari, nec mihi promittere otii quod satis sit ejusmodi versioni. Nec mihi vitio vertendum
― 76 ―

credo quod animi mei sensum a vulgò receptis opinionibus satis abhorrentem nollem ea lingua erudito orbi obtrudere, cujus a multis annis intermissus usus non mihi promisit eam cogitata mea explicandi facultatem, quam argumenti novitas desiderare videbatur. (English) Grevium nostrum meo nomine quæso officiosissime salutes. Est quidam apud vos Juvenis Anglus nomine Lijde†1 an tibi notus vel discipulus nescio, quem tibi commendatum velim. Si me invenisset Londini cum hoc vere ad vos transiit literas tibi a me ad Te datas attulisset
(Latin) Learned Sir,
Your very friendly letter of 25 December from Utrecht was delivered to me here in London towards the end of May. I do not so much complain of its[p. 74] having gone astray somewhere on the way for so long a time as congratulate myself on its having escaped the pirates' hands together with the accompanying booklets, and on those sincere witnesses of your love of me having at last reached my hands. You need not be troubled as to whether the things you send me are drawn from another man's chest†1 or from your own store since for me they are to be counted a gain as coming from one in whose debt I have been so long, and all things that come from you cannot but be welcome. Yet†2- by far the most welcome thing is what you tell me about the life and health of our friend Toinard. By this news you have relieved my mind of a very great and prolonged affliction. For long years now I have been troubled and anxious about him, not knowing what he was doing and uncertain whether he was alive or well. On several occasions I have negotiated with Wetstein through other men, for him to send Toinard from me Joannes Malalas of Antioch, whom, as I remember, he formerly wanted to see. I do not yet know what Wetstein has done in this matter; if he has been slow or has forgotten or has not yet found a route, please remind, arouse, and urge him on my behalf so that that book may reach Toinard's hands. For that well-beloved man of old-fashioned uprightness no diligence that is in me, no exertion or devotion, will be wanting or ever can be wanting. Among all the[p. 75] evils of this war nothing has settled more heavily on my mind than the interruption of correspondence with that most delightful and learned man. I long to see him again, I long to embrace him. Meanwhile all that is left for me is heartily to wish him all things auspicious, delightful, and profitable, and greatly to rejoice that he remembers me sometimes. Please thank him for me at the first opportunity and say everything that you think is most pleasing from a friend to a friend,†1 and inform me whenever anything about him becomes known to you. What he has now published and what he is considering are worthy of his scholarship; I long to see everything that he attempts, but nothing as much as the Harmony of the Gospels toiled over with so much devotion, diligence, and judgement; all who have seen it or heard it spoken of eagerly await it, nor do I well know why he puts off a work so useful to the Christian world, to be neglected by his heirs if he allows it to descend to them. But I do not wish to find fault with a man whom I love so much; I rejoice that he is safe and sound, and congratulate myself that he has been as it were restored to me from the grave.-†2
(Latin) In so great an abundance of better writings there is no reason why you should complain that you are prevented from enjoying my book by ignorance of our language. I should not venture to predict whether it will ever be translated into Latin or to promise myself sufficient leisure for such a translation. Nor do I think that I am to be blamed for having been unwilling to[p. 76]obtrude on the scholarly world my views, remote as they are from commonly received opinions, in that language the use of which, after many years' interruption, did not promise me that power of expressing my thoughts which the novelty of the subject seemed to demand. Goodbye and continue to love me
Your most devoted
J LOCKE
(Latin) Please give my best wishes to our friend de Greve. There is a certain young Englishman, Lyde by name, in your city; I do not know whether he is known to you or whether he is a pupil of yours; I wish to recommend him to you. If he had found me in London when he crossed to your country this spring he would have brought you a letter from me.
Address: Monsieur Monsieur Grævius Professeur à Utrecht.
1752. William Grigg to Locke, 16 June [1694] (701, 1784)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 172-3. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Sir
I have often intended since I came to Oxford to give you this assurance of the gratefull sense I shall always retain of your many favours to me, tho I have been apt to think such an assurance needless; and you, who it may be know me better than I my self do may have done me the justice to beleive I am neither forgetfull nor unthankfull. Perhaps a Respectfull silence would have become me
― 77 ―

better, But t'is by my mother's command I now write to you: How strong soever my inclinations were I should have kept 'em within due bounds, nor should I have given you this trouble, had I not this allowable excuse at hand. By her Order I am to tell you that the stay we shall make here will be longer than either of us intended, for after a tedious expectation and waiting for a summons from the Marquiss of Worcester,†1 we have at last an account of his going very speedily into Ireland for several Months, and that I am at Liberty agen. A Liberty as undesir'd as unexpected, for having no employment, I am only free to chuse the cheapest place to live in. I am not in the least fond of this lazy life, and my health seeming more fixt now than it has been of late, I should have been glad of such a post wherein I might advantage my self and contribute†a- something to-†a the Good of Others. I shall never decline any thing merely for the trouble that attends it, and my ambition reaches no higher than a competency. In the mean time, I have spent some hours in translating the Entretiens sur la pluralité des mondes, a Diversion I remember you approv'd of as usefull and agreable, but t'other Day I accidentally met with a printed Translation of it which has put a stop to mine.†2 The Translating humour is very much in Vogue and Malebranche's search of Truth is follow'd by Mr Taylor here with great application whilst a Rival-Translation sweats under the Press at London.†3 I am afraid I have already exceeded the due bounds of a letter and therefore make hast to assure you that I am with all imaginable respect
Your most humble servant
W. GRIGG

Sir
I had sooner intimated my receipt of the favor of your kind letter but that I was willing at the same time to acknowledge my obligation to you for your excellent book. 1753. Locke to William Molyneux, 28 June 1694 (1748, 1763)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 82-4. Some part was perhaps omitted. Answers no. 1748; answered by no. 1763.
London, 28. June. 1694.
Sir,
Since the receipt of yours of the second instant, I have made what enquiry I can for a tutor for your son; the most likely, and the best recommended that I have met with, you will have an account of from himself in the inclosed, to which I need add little but these two things; 1st, That Mr. Fletcher,†1 who is a good judge, and a person whose word I can rely on, gave me a very good character of him, both as to his manners and abilities, and said he would be answerable for him: the other is, That however it comes to pass, the Scotch have now here a far greater reputation for this sort of employment, than our own countrymen. I am sorry it is so, but I have of late found it in several instances.
I hope, by this time, the second edition of my book, which I ordered for you, and a printed copy of the additions are come to your hands. I wish it were more answerable to the value you place in it, and better worth your acceptation. But, as I order the matter, methinks I make it a hard bargain to you, to pay so much time and pains as must go to the reading it over, though it were more slightly than we seem agreed, when you promise, and I expect your observations on it. There appears to me so little material, in the objections that I have seen in print against me, that I have passed them all by, but one Gentleman's, whose book not coming to my hand till those parts of mine were printed that he questions, I was fain to put my answer in the latter end of the epistle.†2
I wish the endeavours I have used to procure you a Tutor for your son, may be as successful as I desire. 'Tis a business of great concernment to both you and your son; but governours that have right thoughts concerning education are hard to be found. 'Tis happy for your son, that a good part of it is to be under your eye.
― 80 ―

I shall be very glad, if in this or any other occasion, I may be able to do you any service; for with great sincerity and respect I am,
Sir,
Your most humble servant,
J. LOCKE.

B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 129-30. The year from Locke's endorsement. The letter appears to have been written soon after no. 1753.
The writer, 1655-1716, is the Scottish republican and nationalist; it was he who killed Thomas Dare in the first days of Monmouth's rebellion; in 1698 he appears to have been an associate of the English radicals: D.N.B.; Caroline Robbins, The Eighteenth-century Commonwealthman, 1959, pp. 180-4, etc. Locke gave him a copy of the second edition of the Essay: B.L., MS. Sir
I receved yours and was foure times at your lodgings. I can say nothing for Mr Gib and he is altogedder to blame. For when he told me that his letter supposed that you had not yit writ to Mr Moleneux I told him it had been easy for him to have cleared himself of that supposition, but that his letter as to the refusal was positive. But tho he be not to be excused he is not the only man to blame for to tell you the whole story 2 or 3 years ago I did recommend him by a letter to the B. of Salisbury†1 who promised to have a care of him and send for him, but within a year denayed to my self that he had done so, I having lost the letter. Now lately upon Mr Gibs coming hier he told me had letters to the B. I said I thought he was to expect littel from them but bid him send them. His fault was that he should have maid the least steep befor he got ane answer, but he has done it because he had no hops. Now the B. at the recommendation of Mr Charteres.†2 who is trewly the wortyest man I ever knew, and from whom thes letters are, hes bid him stay at London and he will take him into his care. This is the trew story. And as he is not to be excused so I hope the only reale prejudice your friend hes receved is the delay of one post in getting a tutor for his son. For I hope since you have so bad oppinion of Mr Gib you did the veray nixt post advertise Mr Moleneux what you thought of him And indeed I can have no good oppinion of him for this, and have been veray sever to him about it. As for the conduct of the B. which has in great part been the occasion of it, you know
― 83 ―

Y.M.H.S.

1757. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 19 July 1694 (1700, 1766)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 35-8.
London July 19 1694
I thank you a 1000 times for the favour of your letter, which I did intend to have prevented (I mean by writing first) and, then to retort some of your own sayings, tho you have me not so much in rememberance as I Could wish; yet I confess my obligation to be very great to you, that where you are you Could have thought so soon of writing to me: tho I sopose something of the bussness,†a of your Letter, Might have a share in the quik dispatch, yet I well make the interpretation to my one advantage, and take it only as your kindness to me. and now to the business, I am very glad that My Lady M:†1 (to whom I give my most humble service) is enclined to Comply with her son Sam: whos desiers are I think so reasonable and as for the story you mention from Mr Pauling, I Cant imagin how it hapen'd that I did forgit when you was here to tell you of it. it falling out just at, or a day, or tow before your Coming last to town.†2 it is very true that my Cosen Sam: came one day, and told me that Pauling had sent to ther office for his sallery by severall hand's;†3 sometimes Mr Sec: ritary Johnston's Portter, and sometimes by other's: but that ther paymasster's was so angery, that <they>†b say'd possitivly they would not pay it to any; but him self, and that if it wear longer deffer'd he was told it might retard his payment, for a considerable time, so then I told him, I could not tel
― 84 ―

what to say in that Case, but if he would be suer to be a Faithfull stwart, I thought he had better receive it: it seem's he has forgott to give nottice, and from this your story Comes: you kno' I cant obtaine the favour to se Mr Pauling to have known forther, then what Cosen Sam tell's: but if Mr P: manage his Rentt's as he dos mine, for ought I kno', the money is as well Loged. but this only to your self, I have the boy now with me; and have ask't an acount of his money. he tell me, he has pay'd his governor†1 on quarter, (which is nine pound) and to his man another (which is Forty shill.) that he had some small debtts of his own toe the vallue of Forty shillings more. that the rest is all safe. as for the last article, rather then Sir Fr. should be angery with his son that upon my advice, as it may be Called he has don any thing to displeas him, I will se the Forty sh. put in to his bag; and the money that remaines, put into whos hand's My L:†2 shall advise: this is all I can say to the bussne's, only it is my opinion, that as the boy grows up; and that he proves so very sober, Sir Fr: would not doe amise to allowe him something equaly to his Companyon's;†3 for pockitt, and the rather because some ill pepolle, are still insinuating to him, what has formerly been told my Lady, with relation to the managment of his sallery; some four or five pound a year might doe, and with submission to better Judgs, in this matter; would I think be not ill bestowed. wee are in hourly expectaion of news of a battle in Flanders, if we are so happy to have good Ile keep my promis. but why was you so ill nattur'd to tell me nothing of the relicks you saw in darby shir of my ancient soveraine queen Marie of Scott's. 1758. Locke to Esther Masham, 23 July 1694 (1769)
Newberry Library, Chicago: copy of the original letter by Esther Masham in her letter-book, pp. 8-10. Printed in Fox Bourne, ii. 298; by Professor Maurice Cranston in Newberry Library Bulletin, 2nd ser., no. 4, July 1950, pp. 125-6. Transcribed from microfilm. Being at this Time in Huntington shire with my Lady Bernard formerly Mrs Wilding now married to Sir Robert Bernard.†1 I writt to Mr Locke. In Raillery he used to call me his Landabridis†2 and I cald him my John. Having heard a Rich Widdow had been visiting at Oates I pretended to be Jealous of her upon which he sent me the following Letter
Oates 23 July 1694
The greatest good the Widdow is ever like to do me, is the haveing procured me a Letter from my Landabridis and giveing me the oportunitie to let you know you possess the conquest you have made by a power that will hold it against any widdow comeing with her hundred thousands. A heart that you think worth your looking after cannot but be yours, and where gratitude joyns with inclination to make good your title you need not feare a little absence: only I wish you would shorten it as much as you could. For though I shall not fail you, yet I shall suffer for want of you, and the more faithfull I am, the less can I beare the want of your Company. Your Letter satisfies me as much as you can desire that you are not indifferent whither you loose me or no: Let your return satisfie me that tis tenderness to me more than glorying over your Rival that makes you look after me: For if she steal me not away, yet if your absence kill me, t'will be but an odd way of expressing your kindness to your Joannes, who haveing satisfied you that he is proof against Money the temptation of old men; you ought to remove his
― 86 ―

doubts that the Pride and Triumph which so usually accompany youth and beauty in a young Lady doe not make a great part of that care wherewith you hedg me in from the Widdow. If you think me to blame for this Suspition you should not have shewd me the example. If Jealousie be allowable in either it will be more excusable in my age and Experience than in your gaietie. Butt a little touch of it sometimes does well, and is sauce to affection, and I take yours kindly as you have manadgd it. I suspect my †a Daughter more than you but not your way. But she has so little ill in her that I cannot take amiss any thing she does or designs. Remember me very kindly to her if she be with you still, and give my most humble service to Sir Robert and my Lady, and all the rest of your good Company, Every body here is well and want you †b Bully and all. I am
Madam
Your most humble and most Faithfull servant
JOANNES

1760. Robert Pawling to Locke, 26 July 1694 (1729, 1772)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, f. 220.
By an act of parliament (5 and 6 W. and M., c. 21) which received the royal assent on 25 April of this year duties were imposed for four years from 28 June next on all legal documents, the amounts varying according to the importance of the transactions. The parchment or paper was to be stamped before use. In the United Provinces, where a similar tax existed, stamped paper for these documents was a government monopoly; in England parchment or paper was stamped on presentation at the Stamp Office; distributors for England and Wales were appointed.
The first commissioners and the secretary were appointed about 15 May, their salaries being backdated from Lady Day. The Receiver-General was appointed about 22 May. On 23 May Pawling was appointed Comptroller (Accomptant and Comptroller-General of the Accounts) at a salary of £150 per annum for himself and his clerks. On or shortly before 19 July he petitioned for an increase, and on 17 October was granted an additional £50 and was allowed three clerks at £40 each. In 1707 his salary was £300.
The office was kept on the west side of Searl's Court alias New Square, Lincoln's Inn. Originally there appear to have been seven commissioners, the three senior officers, at least 19 other officers, and 42 stampers. In 1710 there were five commissioners (salaries £300 per annum each), the secretary (£200), the receiver-general and the comptroller (£300 each), ten clerks
― 88 ―

(between £70 and £45), nineteen other officers (the warehouse keeper £130; the others between £60 and £20), and thirty-six stampers (£40 each): S. London July 26 1694
Sir
After much toyle and labor, I thank god, my whole family with our Goods and Chattells are safely arived in Little Lincolns Inne fields over against the Plow Inne.†1 I had little or no time to assist but my Wife and Daughters managed it so well that I think we received no damage in any of our Goods and in a day or two more will have placed every thing in our new habitation which we are all well pleased with, for the conveniencys within dores and its situation; it being in a good air and near my busines. The Chamber we design for you hath the same furniture the other had and I think wilbe altogether as convenient; if you shall like it you shalbe as heartily welcome as you was in Dorset Court
My busines increases but I go through it with great delight because it succeeds very well and the Comissioners are all so well pleased with my management that they heartily wish my Salary may be increased, in order whereto I put in my Petition which, as was desired, was referd to our Comissioners to make a report, wherein they say my Place was a Place of great care and trouble and required the attendance of severall Clerks, and that I had so well discharged my Place that they humbly presumed I might deserve their Lordships favour,†2 this Mr Stanley†3 drew and offered to put in what I thought fit to ad; I was contented; and so twas signed; but before I gave it in I advised with Mr Glanvill†4 and got Captain Dorrell,†5 one of our Stationers, who is a true friend to me, to advise
― 89 ―

with Mr Guy,†1 who by all means would have the Comissioners mention the sum and would have no less put in than £400 per annum for me and my Clerks. Mr Glanvill, seeing they were unwilling to mention the sum, because Mr Montagu†2 had consulted his Brother and he thought that not proper, advised them to mention the number of Clerks for, said he; severall may be four or fourteen, whereupo they resolved to say I could not be without 4 Clerks and I by their order had drawn up my report to be signed this morning; but before that was don Captain Dorrell came from Mr Guy to assure me it was very proper for them to mention the sum and no les than £400 per annum as he said before; this wrought upon Mr Stanley and to keep him to it, I offered to go and advise with Sir William†3 about it; which I immediately did. I should have told you that he put his kinsman our Secretary†4 to petition at the same time with me; who hastily, without consulting him or me; gave in his report without mentioning the sum; which I knew not of till I came to Sir Williams; who in answer to the advice I went for, told me that his kinsmans report was again referd to the Comissioners because they had not exprest the sum they thought he might deserve; whereupon I returned well satisfied and now I think they will not scruple to mention a sum for me notwithstanding Mr Chancellors opinion;†5 tomorrow morning they meet on purpose about it and if I can prevail with them to set £400 I dont doubt but Mr Mountague Sir William and Mr Smith†6 will readily grant it. I having been very kindly received by the 2 former and Mr Paskall†7 by the other in my behalf; to encourage our Comissioners I tell them I hope it may be one Step towards the augmentation of their own Salarys; what the issue wilbe I know not.
I am
Sir
Your very humble Servant
ROB PAWLING

Honour'd Sir
You having in so eminent a manner oblig'd the publike; tis uppon good grounds presum'd that you may be prevayl'd uppon to assist the designes of anie that looke that way: Tis therefore the humble request of Dr Bernard the undertaker, and Dr Charlet†2 the most industrious promoter, of the Worke; that you'le plese to further the purpose of the univercitie of Oxford, in printinge the manuscripts of Englande; by procuring them a catalogue of those of the Marsham familie.†3 I shal be in towne till the 8th of August, and after that mr Richard Sare stationer at Gray's Inne gate,†4 will be alwaies redie to receive and convey anie of your commands to Oxford. Deare Sir
your most affectionat, oblig'd, humble servant

1762. Edward Clarke to Locke, 28 July 1694 (1755, 1768)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 87. Printed in Rand, pp. 395-6. Answered by no. 1768.
Chipley July the 28th. 1694
Deare Sir
Your Letter of the 13th. writt in the Company of two Ladyes at Whitehall,†1 I long since thank'd you for by a Letter directed to you at Oates; But your obleigeing Letter giveing an Account of your Travells, and the Wonders you have seen, dated the 12th. came not to my handes untill the last night, tho it was sent out of London (as I find by the Post-marke on the out-side of it)†a on the 19th., But the distant date of That Letter from the Post-marke, and the long time after, it took up in its passage to mee, are not soe strange as the Wonderouse Rarityes you saw and Eate in your late Ramble; I have communicated what you Writt mee to John Barber,†2Who is verie hard of Beleife, But verie willing to know the Places where you found these Rarityes, and then I thinke Hee will hardly sleepe quiet untill Hee has seen them; But I told Him Travellers were generally too cunning to make theire Relations soe particular, as thereby to leave it in the power of a busie Inquisitour to Contradict or Detect them in any thing they say, Upon which, John hoped it might not bee all true which you had Written, Being verie Desireouse That noe Body should have Earlier or Better Fruite of all Kinds then His Masters in these Parts; I am sure Wee are obleiged to John, how Little soever you may bee in this Particular, But Hee sayes, Hee meanes honestly, And I Return you my hearty Thankes for your Letter, and rejoyce in the Pleasure you tooke in that journey, and could have heartily wish'd Chipley had layn in your Way:
I Blesse God, Madam, is something better, but farr from injoyeing perfect health, and therefore I hope shee will yett bee prevayled with to goe to Bath, and Drinke the Waters Regularly there: your Wife and all my Children here are Well, and verie much your servants, but none soe particularly as your Wife, And
Your most truly Affectionate and obleiged humble servant,
EDW: CLARKE:

1763. William Molyneux to Locke, 28 July 1694 (1753, 1781)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed with omissions in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 84-6. Apparently answers no. 1753; answered by no. 1781.
Dublin. July. 28. 1694.
My most Honour'd Freind
For so you have publickly allowd me to call you;†2 and tis a Title wherein I boast more than in Maces or Parliament-Robes. By this you may find I have received the second Edition of your Essay, which I prize as an Inestimable Treasure of Knowledge. tis but a Week since it came to me; and I have yet only lookd over those Parts which are newly added, particularly that of Liberty, the alterations wherein I take to be most Judiciously made; and now I think that whole Chapter stands so wel put together, and the Argumentation is so legitimate, that nothing can shake it. I was mightily pleased to find therein a Rational Account of what I have often wonderd at, viz, Why Men should content themselves to stay in this Life for ever, tho at the same time they will grant, that in the next Life they expect to be infinitely Happy? of this you give so clear an account in the 44th section of your 21 Chapter. Book. 2d. that my Wonder no Longer Remains. That Candid recession from your Former Hypothesis which you shew in this Chapter, where
― 93 ―

Truth required it,†1 raises in me a Greater Opinion (if possible) of your Worth than ever. This is rarely to be found amongst Men, and they seem to have something Angelical, that are so far raised above the Common Pitch.
In time I shall give you my farther Thoughts of the other Parts of your Book; where any thing Occurs to me. But at present I can only Pour out my thanks to you for the Favourable Character under which you have transmitted me to posterity pag.67. My Only Concern is that I can pretend to None of it, but that of your Freind; and this I sett up for in the highest degree. I should think my self Happy, had I but half the Title to the Rest.
I am extreamly obleidged to you for the Trouble you took on you in my last Request.†a I received your Letter with Mr Gibbs's Inclosed; to which, according†b- to your Directions,-†b I returned an Answer addresd to himself. the Import whereof was that I had some offers made to me in this Place relating to that matter, to which I thought I should hearken, at least so far as to make some tryal. that I was loath to Divert him from his Good Intentions to the Ministry, and therefore I could not Incourage him to undertake so long a Journy on such uncertaintys on both sides.etc.
Mr Hogshaw†b- does not hold touch with me so punctually as I expected; and upon your Last Letter, I have given him no farther Remembrances. But tother Day meeting him accidentally in a Booksellers Shop, he took an occasion of his own accord to speak to me about it, and told me he had writt to you, whose answer he expected in Few days, and then I should have the Result. whether this be so or Not you best know.-†b†2
I am
My Most highly esteemd Friend
Your Most Affectionate Humble servant
W: MOLYNEUX

1764. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 31 July/10 August 1694 (1745, 1789)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 120-1.
Rotterdam 10 Aug. 1694
Dear Friend
Your most acceptable letter of the 19 June I had in its due time, and kindly thank you for consulting mr. Clark, and mr. Freke about my children; whom I find to be of opinion that they are tho born here Denizons, but not naturall English†1 —to which you ad your own opinion that, as Denizons they are capable of inheriting, and that I have no more difficulty to make a good title to the Purchaser than if they had been born in England. But that you would further consult those Gentlemen upon what I propose, which I hope you have done. And I should be glad (contrary to my own opinion) to understand that you be confirmd in your opinion. And that such a conveyance may be made of that land at whitby that I have sold to Joseph Scarth, as may secure it to him and his heires for ever, from the heires of my late wife: which, if my children, as Denisons, cannot inherit as I have been informd that Denisons may purchase for a term of 99 years, but cannot inherit, nor transmit estates to their heires, but that all such lands, at expiration of 99 years go to the Crown, and that therein lyes the distinction betwixt Naturalisation, and Denization—whether my information be true or no, you will doubtless find upon further enquiry. But I say if my children be not natural English, and as Denizons cannot inherit, then my wives land goes to her heirs, that is, her 4 sisters—and their children: who, I am apt to think, are so Just, that they will sign any act or deed declaring that they have no right to the said Land.
And I intreat that such Instruments may be prepared in order to it, for if the sisters or any of them should dy, their children, Executors, or Administrators or guardians may be unwilling, and uncapable of doing any such thing—
The Historical Tables of Monsieur Knor were indeed left behind, but were sent to you at mr Joseph Wrights†a by a master of a ship
― 95 ―

that came wholly laden to me—the ships name was the Batchelors Adventure the masters John Penny I hope he has delivered it, tho, having forgot to advise mr. Wright of it, it may be otherwise.
The Baron is now, so finally gone I know not whither, that I beleeve we shall never see him more, If he fall into the Jesuits hands, they will treat him, as ill, as John Calvin treated Michiel Servetus in Geneva, roasting him alive with green wood—†1
I am told he said to some that he was going up into Germany to dy, and I fear it may be too true—
To me he writes from Amsterdam 29 July—'Having received a letter from the Prince of Sulzbach,†2 who desires me to take my Journey over Sulzbach as desiring to speak with me before I go further—I shall this evening begin my Journey over utrecht. and so takes his leave of myself, wife and children—'
It should seem by this, that he had acquainted the Duke (a Prince about 4 years yonger than himself) with his intention of going further: perhaps he may prevayl with him to end his days with him, but his son (Jesuited)†3 hates him so perfectly, that I know not what to say to it. I wish him well and pitty him. Dr. Buchius and he parted very ill friends, because he has printed his Treatise of the Divine attributes in Dutch against his will—And would not be perswaded to stop it for 2 months: till the Doctor had disposed his wives mother, who is under a Delirium, to surrender all into his hands; that she and hers might not be ruined: For this he came from Dantsick. And he feared the untimely publication of it, till that was over, might raise him such a storm from the Church men, that they would divert his mother in law from what she seemd to incline to—He promisd so soon as that was over to print it, with augmentations, and answers to objections, And a second part. But all would not help—so the Doctor protested against the printing of it so defective—And in the Gazett, to ruine this Edition, has acquainted the world that himself has begun an edition perfected, with the second part—†4
If now you have any objections to the English, favour me with
― 96 ―

them, that if it may be, he may also answer them, as he goes—This I intreat you—†1
My wife returns you her best respects, and thanks you for your good opinion of her—and would be glad to see you on this or that side the water—
which we should be thinking upon, if you can give me directions how I can make a will, with respect to my land in England. For to crosse the sea, before we have setled things, we cannot find convenient, nor indeed to defer it, till we do, but 'till I know how to doe it, I cannot settle things—
I see my Friend G.K.†2 was mistaken, people are too apt to abound in their own sence, and think their opinions infallible truths, almost self evident principles. And then they wonder that others cannot immediately yield to them. But I for my part, find so few things so plain and evident, and every opinion, or system, so clogd with difficulties, that I find it, for me, best not to be so dogmatical—
Monsieur Bailes Dictionaire Critique, is a correctory to the mistakes of all Authors with respect to the families, descent and history, or lives of certain men famous in the world—both Antient and modern, proceeding in Alphabeticall order; as under the Letter A. he has Achilles—and Arnaud—under B. Brutus and Bourignon (Anthoinette), under C. Cassius and Comenius—etc—he has some things under the denomination of reëls as, under D. Digression sur les libelles diffamatoires. under. H. Hippomanes—under J. jour— upon which word he bestows 30 pages. It wil be a book, as curious, and perhaps as exact, as we have seen—All that he undertakes is very notable, his remarks are shrewd and pleasant. It wilbe 3 folios—†3
Monsieur Kolhans salutes you, as also does the Professor Limborgh, who honourd my wife and me with a long and particular relation how he rescued a Gentlewoman of good quality in Amsterdam of 22 years old, well skild in Hebrew, from Judaism, into which she was faln from Calvinism; after having consulted some of her clergy about her doubts—And after being visited by all the preachers of Amsterdam, and most professors of the provinces, without advancing one haires breadth upon her: whereas, after 3 times discoursing her, he has perfectly restored her, and removed all her doubts to the rejoycing of her self and relations, to the belief of
― 97 ―

the christian faith. But not to any particular church, or opinion of any party, and now she is free, I beleev, shee'l keep herself so, and not put her self into any goal, or pound, under the delusive name of church.†1 <You>r†a friend†b Arent has his humble service to you I am
Sir yours
B FURLY

B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 191-2, with f. 190, the enclosure. The year from Locke's endorsement. The writer was a seceder from the Quakers: Hull, Furly, pp. 116-17. Lambourn Woodlands is in Berkshire, near the Wiltshire border.
Worthy Sir
I have made bould to Trespas on your patience to read this letter, and a scandolus book printed in Answer to my 8 queres as I had at Sir Francis's when last with the Baron of Helmont,†2 and I have sent you a True Copy of the Queres That so you may see what answer is given and what is left out in the 1th quere, And how they have abused me and the Baron, but my thoughts are They have done that which will prove of good service, peopl are in great Expectations of the reply, which I hop a friend of mine will do who can do it better then I, (I have sent one of the protended Answers to holland to go to the Baron, I have directed to a friend of myne in Amsterdam that I use to writ to, I have for the present sent out sevrall papers in print-hand to keepe up the life that is stiring in many tell some or other shall do somthing Effetialy, here followeth
― 98 ―

a Copy of it: There will be shortly printed a Reply to a Scandolus Book falsly Titled an Answer to 8 Queres of William Clarkes (Printed at Oxford) wherin theire grosse pervertions, lyes, and slanders will be made apeare, with an Illustration of the doctring of the Revolution of Human Souls: Sir I hop you will not take it amiss the Charge from Harlow will be somthing, pray pardon my bouldness, I tock care to have the Coachman payd to the Crown in harlow, my kinde love and respects To your self and to Sir Francis and his good Lady and to the young Lady:†1 my thoughts are this book might not be unwelcom to any of you, which you will see how poore the university is in true knowlidge. Sir I left them without Excuse before they had printed, when I understood they would print, I sent a letter to let them know what Bookes were in print that they might read them, that so they might not Expose themselves in print, or be Exposed by some other, these are the bookes I gave them an account of, 200 Queres, the prexistance of Souls, a letter to a gentlman, Seder Olam, the Ullger Philosephey refuted as the Paradoxe, etc:†2 Sir I Am in some hops you may make some remarkes your selfe on this booke tho you put not your nam to the publick, Sir I should be glad to have 2 or 3 lines from you whether you have received it for my satisfaction, but if you would give me 3 or 4 lines you may direct it thus, Leave this at William whits in Newbery groser for William Clarke, and a few of your thoughts on this booke, and I should be glad if you Come into our Countery to see you, tho I Cannot give such a parson entertainment,
So I Rest Your Affctionated friend, Pray forgett not to give my service: to Sir Fr: and the good ladys and I hartily thainck Them for their love and Kindness to me
WILLIAM CLARKE
Agust the first
Lamborn woodlands in berks sheir within 10 mile of Newbery
