[The enclosure:]
Some queries proposed, by an Inquiring man
after truth (that if hapily may finde it)†1
1 query†2 how shall I understand that place of Scriptur which saith the same measure you met, the same measure shall be meted or measured to you againe, whether it may not be thus understood, that a Rich man in this worlds goods, and is not kind to the poore, and his hart is set in his Riches, whether the meaning of those words of Christ may not Import thus much, that this rich man, must be Born into this world and becom poore, and misrable, and know want, and hunger, as he made or Indavered to make the poore to know, and may be born a foole into the bargain, having now the use of sence and reason and have abused it,
2 query how shall we understand that saing of John rev: 13, v. 10 he that killeth with the sword, shall be killed with the sword, he that leadeth into Captivety, shall go into Captivety, what otherwise can be understood by this, but that if thos men should dye on their beds, must not they be born againe into this world to have the same measure meted to them which they have measured to others, elce how can the Justis of god be vindicated, seeing it is said god is Just and all his ways are equal.
3 query And doth not the Justis of god the good husbandman, appere by still new grafting, and Transplanting; so that at last, they may bring forth good frut, elce to what purpos doth a gardiner grafft, and Transplant, lop, and inoculat, if it were not for to have good frut, and how much more shall the great gardinar do that planted the world.
4 query how shall we understand the apostle paul to the Romans Ch:9.v 27 where he saith tho the Children of Israll were as the sand of the sea yet but a remnant was to be saved at that tim, do he therfore Exclud them in all futer times, shurly no, read rom. 11.
― 100 ―

 

v 25.26 where mention is made that when the fullness of the gentils are come in all Israll shall be saved, see how the apostle Calls it A mistery, now it playnly appereth that the fullness of the gentils is not yet com in, And what is becom of the 10 Tribs that have beene in Captivety for it may be for above 2000 years, are not thos born of gentils, and must it not be according to the apostles words fulfilled, when the fullness of the gentils are come in all Israll shall be saved, being born of gentils. 
5th query what may be the meaning of thos words of Christ in mat: the 23.v 35 that upon you may com all the Rightou blood shed upon the Earth, from the blood of Righouts able unto the Blood of Zacharias son of barachias, whom ye slew between the tempel and the alter, do'it not playnly appeare that they were the very men that did kill Zacarias, etc, Elce what Justis were there in god, to punish them for that which their fathers had acted forty generations or nere 4000 years before, seeing god no where promised to visit the sines of the fathers beyond the 3d and 4th genration under the law
6 query what may be the meaning of the prophet Eze: Ch.16: v:55 when thy sister sodom and her daughter shall return to theier formar Estat and Simaria and her daughters shall return to theier formar Estat, then thou and thy daughters shall return To your former Estat, (that is Jerusalem and her daughters) seeing it playnly appears that they were dead and gon, how is this posable to com to pass, To return to theier format Estat without being born a new into this world.—
query 7 what is the meaning of thos words of moses in the 90 psl. thou turns man to distruction, and saith return ye Cheldren of men, were it not the same men that was turned to distruction, that was to return againe, that so they being new grafftted might bring forth better frut, and doth not Soloman say in Ecl: Ch. 1. v.4 as it is in the Original, genration goeth and genration Cometh, not one genration goeth and another cometh, (one and another is added by the translators)
תℸמו&ע םלועל ץראהו אℶ רוℸו :ℸלוה רו
8th qu What may be the meaning of thos words of peter 1: Cha: 3. v 18.19.20 for Christ also hath once suffred for sins the Just for the unjust that he might bring us to god, being put to death in the flesh, but quickned by the spirit, by which also he went and
― 101 ―
 
preached to the spirits in prison, the greek words) to the same Spirits) which were somtimes disobediant, when once the loung suffring of god waited in the days of noah, while the arke was a preparing, wherin few, that is Eight souls were saved by water, Was it not the same souls that were living in bodys of flesh againe at the tim of Christ and his apostls on Earth, that so they might have his death and resarection preached to them, elce what Benifitt could thes men have had of the dath of Christ, had they not lived and had the grace and favor of ouer Lord Jesus Christ Tendred to them—as it is writen he tasted Death for Every man: now if any man would put pen to paper To denigh the return of souls, I would put my hand to paper to prove, that man, or thos men denigh there is any god, but what they have made and Concived, writn by a seeking man aftter truth, But if any should Answer and say, it is not worth Answring, and yet say—it is damnable doctring, as I heard one say within 3 days past, Now I would aske a question, whether it be not a duty incumbant on the Teachers, to refut this doctring if they are able (that men might not be drawn into such damnable erros, as som of them Call it) but seeing this doctring hath beene printed in divers Lainguages, and in divers Cunterys, and no man as we can here of hath hetherto Writen againest it, therfore I thinck it altogether Iposable, Except that they can prove that man as to his body doth not proceed from his parents, which is altogeather Imposable for them to do 
WILLIAM CLARKE

1766. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 2 August 1694 (1757, 1834)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 39-40.
London Aug: 2 1694
I find in my selfe all the sattisfaction imaginable in your respectfull declaration. you doe the place I am in too Much honour when you think either art or good breeding spoile our understanding the use of words. you are in the right thus far that you must belive we never think when you think we indeavour to put our artificiall words on you who have time and skill Enufe to refine on them and make greater discovery's then our dexteritys. and now for the Cariage of your hart, I desire you when it makes me a vissit that it may Come in no thiner a Covert then your own person which may pass at the post office and be in noe danger of being brok up. I'll beg you to give over all thought's of your furious new invention for tho I doe not Well understand CarCass's yet to be suer they must be very fright full out of a mortar peice.†1
and now to leave raillery and say nothing of news which nither fleet's nor Armys are pleas'd to afford; I must desire you to give humble service to My L: Masham to whom I'le writ very soon but in the mean time take your own Way to let her kno' I will be suer when I se Sam. to tell him what she desier's but as to writing to Sir Francis I must ask My Lady's pardon for I am perfectly of your opinion that tis at least good breeding to let parent's alone in the disposition of ther Chilldern and besides My Lady must suspect me of very great vanity that when nither her own or your argument's Could prevail I should think I had any thing to say that would doe. tis not that I have alltered my opion that it was very much for Sir
― 103 ―
Fra: his service to have comply'd with his son the more that you kno' ther are some here very willing to take all occasions to set out Sir Fra: in that Court†1 for a hard and a Carless father to his Chelldern they are not a little asisted in this by Brisac†2 this will furnish 'em with new matter and the more that he is the only page whos frend's has not sent for home and as Sam: tells me mr Wroth's father†3 earnestly invited him to his hous which I fancy might not be so kind to Sir Fra: as it apear'd for which reason I did perswad the boy not to goe. I have sayd a great deall more then I thought to have done on this subject but I realy am a Faithfull servant to that Familly and wish it wear in my power to serve them. I cant easyly Conclude a letter to you without wishing you a speedy returne here pray let me kno' if ther be any hopes of it for I have none of seing you in the country this year but wher ever I am you must allways have a very Faithfull frend
and humble servant.
My sister†4 never writs to me but sends you her humble service. My Cosen Cutts gives her's to your self and the wholl Family. My dutty to My dear husband. I have been very Lucky for my poor Cosen Hilldsly†5 the queen has been so kind not only to promise something yearly but something to begin with
Endorsed by Locke: M. Lockhart 2º Aug 94 Answered 6.
1767. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 2/12 August 1694 (1747, 1798)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 83-4. Printed in King, pp. 318-19; Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 74-6. Answered in part in no. 1798.
A Amsterdam le 12 d'Août 1694.
Je reçus, Monsieur, la semaine passée, par la voie de Mr. Furly, les additions de vôtre Ouvrage,†6 qui m'ont infiniment plû. J'ai lû
― 104 ―
avidement l'addition du Chapitre de la Liberté, qui m'a entierement satisfait, étant convaincu depuis long-temps que la plûpart du temps les hommes ne se déterminent pas par la vuë distincte, ou confuse de ce qui peut être leur plus grand bien, ou qu'ils croient être tel, mais par le plaisir qu'il prennent à certaines choses, ausquelles ils sont habituez. On pourroit seulement demander si ce plaisir, ou cette easiness, comme vous vous exprimez plus commodément que je ne le saurois faire en François, est toûjours de telle nature que malgré cela l'esprit ne puisse se déterminer du côté opposé. Pour moi j'avouë que je ne voi pas bien comment, lors que je lis avec attention ce que vous dites; mais je ne sai si le sentiment ne nous en convainc point. Au moins il me semble qu'en mille choses je puis faire, ou non, et que je ne me détermine que parce que je le veux, sans trouver plus de plaisir d'un côté que d'un autre. Mais c'est là une matiére qui demande plus d'étenduë, qu'un billet écrit a la hâte.†1 Pour parler d'autres choses, et pour répondre à un article de vos Lettres auquel j'ai oublié de répondre trois ou quatre fois, vous disposerez comme il vous plaira de l'exemplaire relié de ma Genese, soit que vous le veuilliez garder pour vous, ou le donner à quelcun de vos Amis.†2 J'attends avec impatience le livre de Mr. l'Evêque de Bath et Wels,†3 pour voir ce qu'il dira contre moi; car les François de Londre, gens envieux et malins, s'il y en eût jamais, ont pris plaisir à semer qu'il me réfutoit en termes forts. Cela me facheroit, non à cause des raisons, ausquelles je ne ferai pas difficulté de me rendre, si elles sont bonnes, mais à cause de la consequence. Je ne sai si je me trompe, mais je m'imagines que ce sont des raisons de Theologie, in quibus magis optant viri pii quàm docent.†4 On prescrit à Dieu ce qu'il doit avoir fait, comme on le juge à propos, sans rechercher ce qui est effectivement. Quoi qu'il en soit, j'en userai avec lui, avec tout le respect qu'il pourra demander, et pour l'en convaincre, je lui ai déja envoié 18 feuilles de mon Exode, qu'il mavoit faites demander par Mr. Cappel et par Mr. Limbourg à qui il avoit écrit exprès pour cela. Il y en a à présent
― 105 ―
environ le double d'imprimées, et j'espere que nous commencerons bien tôt le Levitique. Je ne comprends pas qui avoit fait courir le bruit d'Oxfort, dont Mr. Cappel m'avoit aussi averti.†1 Il n'en est venu aucun vent à mes oreilles, que par ce que vous et lui m'avez mandé. Mylord de Salisb. pourroit beaucoup faire pour moi, s'il vouloit, mais je ne sai s'il le veut.†2 Il a un Chanoine François auprès de lui, qui feignant de m'estimer seme par tout que je me suis perdu par ce livre, parce que je n'ai pas donné dans les étranges visions qu'il a débitées sur le Messie, dans ses Reflexions sur les Livres de l'Ecriture.†3 Je tenterai néanmoins de ce côté-là, et je ne crois pas qu'il me nuise, s'il ne veut pas m'aider. Enfin il en arrivera ce qu'il pourra, et pourvu que personne de nos gens ne sache rien de ma tentative, si elle ne reüssit pas, il n'y aura rien de perdu. Mais nos boutiquiers, qui sont ici les Souverains et qui regardent les Ministres comme leurs servantes, me regarderoient de haut en bas plus que jamais, s'ils savoient que je n'eusse pas réussi. Au contraire, si je pouvois me passer d'eux et me retirer d'ici, je me mettrois peu en peine de ce qu'ils diroient. Cependant il n'est pas bon que des personnes mal-intentionnées sachent rien de mes desseins. Il ne se passe rien ici de nouveau. Je vous prie de me mander la voie par laquelle vous m'envoierez oû vous m'avez envoié le Pentateuque de Mr. L'Evêque de Bath. Je suis de tout mon coeur, Monsieur, vôtre très-humble et tres obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke in Dorset Court, in Channel row, at Mr. Pawlings Westminster
Postmark: AV 10
Endorsed by Locke: le Clerc 12º Aug. 94 Answered Oct

1768. Locke to Edward Clarke, 6 August 1694 (1762, 1776)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 73. Printed in Rand, pp. 396-7. Answers no. 1762.
Oates 6 Aug 94
Dear Sir
Yours of the 28th July brought me the good news of your health and that of our wives at least as far as they think health worth the lookeing after. I have said soe much to Madame on that account that it would I think be ill manners in me to presse her again: as if the perfect recovery of hers by drinking Bath waters were of more concernement to me than her, though I can say there is noe body that more heartily wishes her a confirmed health than I doe
I know not what you and your man John Barber think of us travellers†1 But if you continue to doubt of what I told you, you may goe to Mr Controlers at Winchington in Buckingham shire†2 and there have it verified to him that we eat there ripe Newington peaches†3 the begining of July which they there had perfect ripe and good in June. we gathering and eating the last that was left. At my Lord Ferrers's†4 we eat the ripe Oranges and at the Earle of Chesterfeilds†5 the ripe grapes where also you may see oranges planted and thriveing in the ground. If John Barber will goe to these places he will perhaps see ways of ripening fruit and haveing it early which he has not thought on. These two last houses are in Darby shire and if he will take into his walke my Lord Mountagues at Boughton in Northampton shire†6 he will there find such a garden as he never yet saw in England. I am soe much Johns Friend that I wish he had seen all these places and some others I could name that soe he might not only out doe the Gardeners of the west but most
― 107 ―
others in England, for truly I met with what I could not expect though I was prepared with stories before hand
I cannot Imagin why you refuse to be one of the Directors of the bank. I looke on it of noe small consequence to you and to England and therefor shall hope you will not persist in a refusall at least without consulting your friends who noe doubt will be ready to hear your reasons. I doe not perceive by any thing in yours of the 28th of July nor your other which I found here at my returne that you received my letter which was directed to you at Ivy church. In that you will finde a reason of what perhaps you may think a change in me. Pray remember the Chedar Cheese for Mr Bridges.†1 My humble service to Mrs Clarke and all the yonge folks espetialy my love to my wife. All here salute you. I am
Dear Sir your most affectionate and most faithfull servant
J LOCKE
Address: For Edward Clarke Esq at Chipley near Taunton
Postmark: AV 8

Brampton†2 August the 7th 1694
Your Letter has as much appeas'd my Jealousie as you can desire it to doe; if I can but satisfie you now in my turn that you have no reason to have the same suspition of me as I had of you, the business will be sett pretty right between us; hitherto what I have seen I assure you has appear'd very insipid to me, and yet I am told tis the very Cream of the Country, but I beleeve tis you have given me this distast of every thing I see, for I have yet found nothing so pleasant as being in the Garden digging with my John; if you think my absence too long tis not my fault my wishes have carried me to you severall times, but unless I had the good luck to find Fortunatus's hat, I find wishing alone will not doe it.

Your Daughter†1 desired me last week to present her humble Duty to you, and every body here present their service

1770. [William] Glanvill to Edward Clarke, 7 August 1694 (210)
Rand, p. 398. By the contents and by Greenwich as the writer's place of residence it is probable that the writer is William Glanvill of the Alienation Office: no. 1699.
Greenwich, 7th August, 1694.
Dear Son,
I am not a little proud that you, Sir Walter Young†2 and Doctor Locke call me father; the esteem I have for you all three is I am sure not less than the respect and friendship which sometimes everyone of you says he hath for me. After this prologue I suppose you begin to think what next, neither compliment or business, only be pleased to know that on Friday last†3 at a Cabinet Council, the Queen with her †b made you a commissioner of the excise, and your acquaintance Mr. Danvers,†4 one Aram†5 is turned out. Sir Walter Young, Mr. Chadwick,†6 son-in-law to the Archbishop of Canterbury,
― 109 ―
and one Mr. Clark,†1 a very knowing officer of the custom house, are made commissioners of the customs, and Sir Richard Temple,†2 Sir John Worden†3 and Mr. Booth†4 turned out. This I have from an infallible hand, and let me assure you that upon your and Sir Walter's account my joy is equal to my pride, that their Majesties have set their mark of favour on you both; for what good father is not both pleased and proud when his sons come to preferment. Could I see my dear Doctor Locke but rewarded according to his merit, which is almost impossible, my joys would be complete. Pray present my service to your Lady, and believe me you have a very affectionate friend and humble servant in
your poor father,
GLANVILL.
Endorsed: Father Glanvill's congratulatory letter received 10th of August, 1694.

1772. Robert Pawling to Locke, 9 August 1694 (1760, 1904)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 221-2.
London August 9 1694
Sir
The inclosed came from Dorset Court so late on Tuesday that I could not send it: the parcell from Hollon came safe. I sent our Porter for it who goes dayly that way, it cost 12d to Mr Wrights man who paid so much for cariage. I can give you no farther account of myne own busines here; I go chearfully on to the satisfaction of
― 111 ―
the Comissioners; but I cant convince them of a growing miscief that wilbe fatall to them, neither will they be persuaded to remedy it; telling me tis impossible or, as they are woont to say in other cases, tis impractable; tis this: severall of the Subcomissioners,†1 I am assured, sell our parchment and Paper at dearer rates than we send it them at, though tis in their charge not to do so; and the better to colour it, now send up great parcells of their own paper and Parchment to be stampt, which we very tamely submit to and return it onely putting the Stamps to their account; so then, as I have told them, they may sell their own as they please and who knows the Kings from their own? so the Subject that must pay for the Stamps shalbe imposed on in the paper and Parchment, which wilbe very hard; this I acquainted Mr Stanley with, who replyed, they had given orders to forbid them that practice; yet Mr Mountague and Mr Harris†2 yesterday when I mentioned it, said twas an abuse but could not be prevented; Mr Mountague said, if you lay by one man for that fault, the next will do it and they cant hinder any man from sending their own to be stampt and selling it as they please. I replyed that the Comissioners may put them out of their Office and may in all Corporations find men that will do it on their Terms and others wilbe weary of it; if we make them pay ready money for their stamps: and we selling the paper at a reasonable rate it will not be worth any mans while to sell it unles they can ingross our goods and mixt them with theirs and so have the whole trade of a Town to them selves. then they may set their own rates, but twill soon be complained of as a great grievance and will reflect on our Office. I do intend once more to give them my reasons and then if they will not redress it let them take their course. we are all very well pleased with our new habitation and all things are in good order; Mr Brokman†3 cald there but I was, where I now am, and where I am from 5 in the morning till 9 at night, at the Office;†4 he
― 112 ―
said you was expected here shortly, so I hope it will not be long ere I see you. no doubt but you hear of Mr Clarks being a Comissioner in the Excise Office and Sir Walter Young in the Customhouse. it seems there is an other Mr Clarke and Mr Chaddock joyned with Sir Walter. I would be glad to have my son removed either to some good place in the Custome hous or in the Excise Office. if you have occasion to write to any of those of your acquaintance I intreat you to write a line or two in his behalf. he is very industrious and does me great service; he delights in busines and the Comissioners do all observe his care and diligence and respect him for it; but yet he is but a Clark to me.†1 I am
Sir
Your humble Servant
ROB PAWLING
Address: For Mr John Lock [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Endorsed by Locke: R. Pawling 9º Aug. 94
1773. Locke to Esther Masham, 20 August 1694 (1769, 1795)
Newberry Library, Chicago: copy of the original letter by Esther Masham in her letter-book, pp. 10-12. Printed in Fox Bourne, ii. 299; by Professor Maurice Cranston in Newberry Library Bulletin, 2nd ser., no. 4, July 1950, pp. 126-7. Transcribed from microfilm. Answers no. 1769.
Oates 20 August 1694
Though I wish mightily for your Company, and I see you could be content with mine, yet I could be pleas'd you should relish the cream of the country you are in and to heighten the gusto I wish you Strawberrys to it. For those who have the goodness not to dislike me when they are with me, and to think on me when absent, I would not have uneasie when they are out of my sight. Let my Landabridis therefore be as merry as she can every day, and know that I partake in it: but now and then mix a kinde thought of her Joannes, so he does here on his side of her to preserve himself the better for her sake, since she thinks him worth the takeing care for. Pray when you return bring a little sommer with you if you intend to do any thing in the Garden with your John. For we have had
― 113 ―
nothing but winter weather since you went and I write this by the fires side whither the blustring winde and rain like December has driven me. I hope for a new Spring when you come back and to be as merry as the birds then are when they have their Mates, only I desire to be excused from Singing, that part shall be yours. Had you been at our Church yesterday there was one would have put you to it to have kept pace and tune with him, he sung the poor Clarke out of his beloved Behold and have regard and made him loose both voice and tune, Would you had been here to have stood up for the Credit of our Parish which gave up to a Stranger. Every body here is in health but want you. In the mean time you are kindly rememberd by all. I am
perfectly your most affectionate and most humble servant
JOANNES
Pray my service to Sir Robert,†1 my Lady and the rest of your good Company

1775. Dr. (later Sir) Hans Sloane to Locke 25 August 1694 (1785)
From Puttick and Simpson Sale catalogue, 28 April 1859, no. 469. Excerpt. Perhaps answered by no. 1785.
All philosophic occurrences are so well known to you that I am sure you might inform me, better than I, you ... There has been in Northamptonshire a very great whirlewind, which lasted halfe ane hour, and carried with it into the air much corn, scattering it 5 miles from the place where it lay, as good credible wittnesses relate. They are now printing an account of all the Manuscripts in England, both publicke and private, at Oxford, and one volume is already printed off, which will be of considerable use and credit to the kingdom.†1 They are likewise there finishing Dr. Morison's History of Plants,†2 and Dr. Plott is here about publishing the Natural History of Middlesex and London as well as Kent,†3 and Mr. Newton of Cambridge is about another edition of his book, which 'tis said he will make much more easy to be understood.†4 [He further continues on the subject of Books and Authors, ending,] I begg your pardon for this trouble.

1776. Locke to [Edward Clarke], 26 August 1694 (1768, 1778)
H.M.C., Rep. V, App., p. 296 (Lord Hatherton's MSS.). Perhaps answered by no. 1778.
1694, Aug. 26th, Oates.
Dear Sir,
I am glad to hear of your safe arrival in town, and when you are a little setled in your gears there I hope to receive from you now and then a litle account how the world wags. My long stay in town the last time made so lasting an impression on my lungs, that I have scarce yet got it off, tho' I find a very sensible advantage since I came hither; so that unless my own business or any service I can doe you call me to town, I shall not be very forward to come thither yet a while; I return my thanks to Madam for her kind remembrance, and shall be very glad of her recovery and health, wether from the Bath waters drank at Bath or at home, as from anything else. My service to her, my wife, and the rest of the young folks. I conclude you will now stay in town. I desire to know, intending to trouble you with a letter of attorney to receive my salary in the Excise. My service to all my friends that come in your way; particularly remember me kindly to J.F. if he be in town.
P.S.—Sir Francis, my lady, and all here give their service to you and Mrs. Clarke. I hope you found Master well.

1779. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 31 August/10 September 1694 (1725, 1824)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 59-60.
Amsterdam ce 10 Sept. 94.
Monsieur,
Il y a longtemps que je vous doibs cette lettre. mais le malheur qui nous est survenu ma tellement distrait que je nay pas mesme esté capable de mes plus pressantes occupations. le jour de lascenscion de Nostre Seigneur le 20 Mey nostre petit cadet†1 receut une fluxion sur ses gengives†2 superieures, qui non obstant toutes les precautions imaginables tourna subitement dans une gangræne si terrible quelle luy perca un grand trou dans le visage a la base de l'aisle droitte du nez. la fluxion avoit passée jusqu'a l'œil droit et le nez de sorte que nous avions crainte que la gangræne sy portast aussy, et visiblement sans la resolution que nous primes d'appliquer le cautere active et dans toucher les chairs et l'os gastées, cela seroit arrivé, mais ce remede arresta le courant tout court. depuis il a fallu attendre que los cariez, qui contenoit quatres alveoles de dents, fust tombé avant qu'on pust tendre a la reunion des bords des chairs esloignez. apres quoy nous en sommes venus a une douleureuse et cruelle operation en degagant les chairs pour les mieux faire approcher et en rafraichisant les bords et puis y passant deux aiguilles. mais comme la deperdition estoit grande, la suture dechira et ne teint pas, ce qui nous a esté une nouvelle affliction, presque autant dure que la premiere. presentement a force de se servir de sutures seiches, les levres se sont beaucoup approchees, mais pas tout a fait jointes: et il est a craindre que pour ne pas laisser une grande deformité a l'enfant, il faudra encore tenter de les resjoindres par les aiguilles. voila Monsieur l'orage dans lequel nous avons este tout cet esté et qui nous a esloigné de songer autant a nostre devoir a vostre esgard comme nous le devions.
― 118 ―
Ma femme vous remercie de l'honneur de vostre lettre, et espere trouver une autre occasion que celle qui est avortée pour se vanger de toutes les obligations quelles vous a. Monsieur Daranda se prepare a quitter ce pays pour passer le reste de ses jours dans sa patrie. je perds en luy un bon amis, cepandant jay este surpris que jamais il ne s'est voulu charger d'aucune chose pour les faire passer avec ses hardes pour Engleterre, et c'est pourquoy je nay pas osé luy demander la grace de vouloir se charger de quelque chose pour vous. c'est pourquoy il faudra que nous attendions quelque autre occasion. jaurois fort souhaitté de mettre quelque argent dans vostre banque,†1 mais vostre advis est venu trop tard, suivant le rapport que m'en fist Monsieur Daranda ou je fus dabord pour m'informer comment je feray passer mon argent. vostre argent est tousjours en repos, et c'est dommage qu'il ne faist rien depuis si long temps. il attend tousjours vostre commendement. comme je fais aussi, qui suis avec le dernier respect,
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres Obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON
Ma femme, et nostre pierot vous saluent.
Je vous remercie de l'addition de vostre traitté†2 que jay bien recu.
Endorsed by Locke: Dr. Guenellon 10 Sept. 94 Answered 17

1780. Locke to Edward Clarke, 3 September 1694 (1778, 1799)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 74. Printed in Rand, pp. 399-400. Answers no. 1778.
Oates 3 Sept 94
Sir
I thank you for the trouble you have given your self about the cheese. I doe not doubt but it was good, and I hope not unacceptable as a marke of my acknowledgment.
I am very glad to hear that the Bath waters agree soe well with Madame they are the best things I know to remove that dispiritednesse, faitnesse, and tremblings she complains of, at least the best thing I think she will be perswaded to make use of, for it lies in the
― 119 ―
want and weaknesse of the spirits, and a custome of representing to her self things on the worst side, and thereby burdening her minde and suppresseing the spirits, the proper remedie for this would be more exercise, and lesse thoughtfulnesse; if you can finde <a way>†a to compasse that, it would be of great use to her, in the mean time the best thing she can doe is to continue the waters as long as she finds them agree with her and passe well. and I know noe other medicins fit to be joynd with them. when she has given them off I will bethink my self what else may be done in that kinde as there shall be occasion. My service to her and my love to my wife and respects to the other yonge folke
I returne you my thanks for your fower kind lines the last post I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant J LOCKE
All here present their service to you
My humble service to J:F: and the rest of our friends in town.
Endorsed by Mrs. Clarke (?): Mr Lockes letter etc:
1781. Locke to William Molyneux, 3 September 1694 (1763, 1797)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 86-9. There may be some omissions, notably a passage relating to Mr. Hawkshaw. Answers no. 1763; answered by no. 1797.
Oates, 3 Sept. 1694.
Sir,
I have so much the advantage in the bargain, if friendship may be call'd one, that whatsoever satisfaction you find in your self on that account, you must allow in me, with a large over-plus. The only riches I have valued, or labour'd to acquire, has been the friendship of ingenious and worthy men, and therefore you cannot blame me if I so forwardly laid hold of the first occasion that open'd me a way to yours. That I have so well succeeded in it, I count one of my greatest happinesses, and a sufficient reward for writing my book, had I no other benefit by it. The opinion you have of it, gives me farther hopes, for it is no small reward to one who loves truth to be
― 120 ―
persuaded that he has made some discoveries of it, and any ways help'd to propagate it to others. I depend so much upon your judgment and candor, that I think my self secure in you from peevish criticism or flattery; only give me leave to suspect, that kindness and friendship do sometimes carry your expressions a little too far on the favourable side. This, however, makes me not apprehend you will silently pass by any thing you are not throughly satisfied of in it. The use I have made of the advertisements I have received from you of this kind, will satisfie you that I desire this office of friendship from you, not out of complement, but for the use of truth, and that your animadversions will not be lost upon me. Any faults you shall meet with in reasoning, in perspicuity, in expression, or of the press, I desire you to take notice of, and send me word of. Especially if you have any where any doubt; for I am persuaded, that, upon debate, you and I cannot be of two opinions; nor, I think, any two men used to think with freedom, who really prefer truth to opiniatrity, and a little foolish vain glory, of not having made a mistake.
I shall not need to justifie what I have said of you in my book: The learned world will be vouchers for me; and that in an age not very free from envy and censure. But you are very kind to me, since for my sake you allow your self to own that part which I am more particularly concern'd in, and permit me to call you my friend, whilst your modesty checks at the other part of your character. But assure your self, I am as well persuaded of the truth of it, as of any thing else in my book, it had not else been put down in it. It only wants a great deal more I had to say, had that been a place to draw your picture at large. Herein I pretend not to any peculiar obligation above others that know you. For though perhaps I may love you better than many others, yet, I conclude, I cannot think better of you than others do.
I am very glad you were provided of a tutor nearer home, and it had this particular good luck in it, that otherwise you had been disappointed if you had depended on Mr. Gibbe; as a letter I writ to you from London about it, I hope acquainted you.†1 I am,
Dear Sir,
Your most affectionate, and most humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.

1782. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, [7/17?] September 1694 (1777, 1796)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, f. 183. Toinard's dates for this letter and for the covering letter to Grævius (Royal Library, Copenhagen, MS. Thott 1266-4°), which is also dated 27 September, appear to be wrong. On 14/24 September Grævius wrote to Locke, forwarding two letters from Toinard: no. 1786. One of the two is probably no. 1777. Locke did not receive no. 1786 until 6 October or later: nos. 1787, 1791: and did not answer it until 5 November: no. 1809. On that day Locke also wrote to Toinard (no. 1808), answering no. 1777 and the present letter. There are no clear signs of loss in the tripartite correspondence between July and December 1694; it therefore is likely that the present letter is the second enclosed in no. 1786. The most appropriate date for it and for the covering letter to Grævius appears to be 7/17 September. Grævius replied to Toinard on 4 October, N.S.: B.N., MS. N.Acq. fr. 561, f. 235.

Je vous ecrivis dernierement pour vous marquer, Monsieur, combien j'ay de joie d'etre encore dans l'honneur de votre souvenir, aussi bien que l'Harmonie qui va son train; et comme je suis persuadé que les interests de l'Auteur vous sont en recommandation, je vous diray que je vous enverrai par m.Leers,†1 qui doit partir d'ici dans peu, la plus belle et la plus dificile partie de cet ouvrage, qui commence à la 21. page, et finit à la 52. Vous pourez faire voir ce receuïl aux curieux de pareilles choses, et par la les porter par la voie que vous apelez de souscription, à prendre un nombre d'exemplaires. Le tout poura être fini dans 15. ou 16. mois. Il y a deja le cart d'achevé. Je dis 15. ou 16. mois, quoique j'espere bien que cela ne tardera pas tant, mais c'est pour parler avec plus de certitude. 1783. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 8 September [1694] (1746, 1794)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 110-11. Printed in Rand, Shaftesbury, pp. 296-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.
St. Giles's Sep: the 8th:
Mr Lock
Neither my business, nor diversions, nor Studdys, which you mention, are, or can bee such as hinder mee from reflecting often, and as I ought, on the advantage I have in being Thought of, as You tell mee I am att Oates. My businesses and diversions doe not take mee up as they were us'd: nor are they follow'd by mee with that heat which with other people they generally are: nor am I any one hower so much in them, as not to have my mind much more elcewhere then upon them; having gott a Business into my head, which by nobody elce is look'd upon as a Business, but, with mee, is instead of all other Business and Diversion; that of Learning how to bee an Honest Man, and a Friend. Other people may be born to these qualityes. it is my misfortune to be Such, as that I cannot but esteem Thought Exercize and a continuall Application to be necessary in this case, for Mee.
You may Imagine that I can hardly bee, so much as I speak of, employ'd in this; and not have those People in my thoughts whome I am forc'd to Distinguish from the rest of the world whenever I think upon the subjects of Friendship, Worth, and Love of Vertue and of Mankind. as for my Studdys: since they all lye towards this Business that I speak of; all that I learn by them, or cheifly strive to learn, is, what Mankind has been heretofore, in former ages, and under former Revolutions; that I may Guess the better att what they are, and may be expected to bee, in such a Turn of an Age and Time as is this present one. The poor stock of knowledg which I pick up, is all about this single matter. Other Notions then what are of this odd kind, I have not to communicate to You, which you desire of mee, as if I could have any that were of any worth to You. and as for what My Notions are, which, in this way, I gain; I must begg your Pardon for not Communicating 'em. I might whisper them in your Ear perhaps. or I might venture to trust another person near You, with the impertinence of them: but they are not att all fitt for Writing, nor to come in the way of other people. they are either too rediculously Absurd, or too odiously True.—
― 124 ―
Wee have a Refin'd, Polite, and a Deliciouse Age. Whatever opposes what is Establishd here; is Rude, Barbarouse, Deform'd: and whatever has a contrary Tast, is contemptible. the Standard of Good Sence, of Manners, Pleasure, Vertue, everything is here.
I acquiesce—being very safe in this; that <whatsoever>†a is thought, or not thought concerning mee in this ador'd age and by the ador'd people in itt, is likely to give mee no great disturbance. which saves a man a great deal of pains; if one considers what Employment this gives to other people. I would not have you think that this which I have said so perfectly by chance, was said to place a mark of Distinction upon the Concern I show for your Friendship and Good opinion: nor to give an advantage to my way of receiving the Favours of another Person, which I pretend to know so well how to valew.
Whether I think little or think much of what is, or ever may bee said of mee in a City or a Court amongst great people or a Crowd: this I am certain of; that I think very much upon how I am, and how I may bee thought of, att Oates. and it is no small part of the Aim and Business of my Present Life, to keep and deserve that Esteem I have got there, and to Bee more and more that which I am taken for, when I am well look'd upon by Those that are there.
It is not, as You imagine, so new a thing to mee, or what I want so much to be acquainted with; how I am severall times thought of and in the Good opinion of the Lady of the House. I have Vanity enough to keep alive the remembrance of what was once made appear to mee of that kind, and to count upon itt.
I hardly need any new intimation of itt: though I can never hear of itt so often as not to receive pleasure every time. the marks I have allready had of that Esteem long since has put it out of my Power to doubt ofitt, because I am so well perswaded that whatever that Person would Seem to bee, they really are: and that any other part is unnaturall to them, as much as itt is with other people not to say, upon every occasion of that kind, much more then they think. which is one of the Cheif reasons why I so much Valew every thing in them, and receive every thing from thence with that regard. though any other body in my place would find out many more reasons that would make a greater shew then mine: and I am even satisfied that in the reall Judgment of the world, I should Undervalew my Lady Masham with my respect; if I should say
― 125 ―
fully in what manner it was grounded. Goodness and Sincerity and a great many other things of that kind would sound just as well as Good Nature and Simplicity: and I am afraid if I should speak about a valew for religion and such Thoughts about itt and about the Liberty of Mankind as I have known in my Lady Masham; I should hardly bee able to give it any turn that would make mee excusable, to this age, for Commending a Lady in that manner.
See what a hardship I am Layn under, in my Respect for one that I can never think I shew enough for, when att any time I would endeavour to shew a part!—But I have another more Just <Exclamation>†a to make: which is: how horridly Tediouse I grow! this is a Fault my Pen has, wors yet a great deal then ever I discover of my Tongue. and therefore I am forc'd to use it more slenderly. I Beg You to Excuse mee this time: and wish that of all this, You were to read no more then that I present my Hum: Service to My Lady Masham and that I am with a great deal of sincerity
your Friend and Humble Servant
A: ASHLEY
I write this post to Wheelock, who is in Town to be sure to have that ready which You spoke for.
I hope soon to be in that method that You shall never need to give your self again the trouble of speaking or writing a word on that account.
My Father is in a very good way of Recovery tho he yett keeps his Bed. My Bro:†1 presents you with his very humble service. I should be extreamly glad if you would send the Book which my Lady Masham has given mee, to Wheelock in Town; that he may send it to mee hither. for I earnestly desire itt as soon as possible.
Address: For Mr Lock [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmark: SE 10 (?)
Endorsed by Locke: L: Ashley 8º Sept. 94 Answered 27 Sep

1784. William Grigg to Locke, 9 September 1694 (1752, 1814)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 174-5.
Sir
The Additions to your Book†1 which I have received since I writt last to you were an evident token of the continuance of your Goodwill to me, but your last kind assurance of it has added very much to my satisfaction. I think my self oblig'd to give you my heartiest thanks for both: The lively sense I have of your concern for me, with the pleasure I take in expressing itt incite me to embrace all Opportunitys of paying you the Acknowledgements which are due to you for a great many undeserved Favours, to which I shall never be able to make you a suitable return. Your last, cannot be too highly valued for the clear marks it gave of your generous friendship for my Father; Time it seems has not bin able to blot out his memory, and you are pleas'd to give me leave to claim a share in your good-wishes if I improve his memory to the best advantage, by copying after so fair a pattern. Tho in this divided Age my Father have the same Fate with all deceased good men; to be made to be of all sides, yet all that knew him allow him the qualifications that make up the composition of a wise and Good man; and indeed those sermons of his which I have read†2 seem to me plainly to discover, no mean Learning, a solid judgement Moderation and a modest Temper. These are Advantages I have great reason to pursue heartily, nor do I want encouragement whilst the promise of your friendship will be a spur to my best endeavours. I am not however so vain as to flatter my self, with equal improvement; I cannot expect to make the same advances, t'will be sufficient to have done my utmost and diligently to follow him licet non passibus æquis.†3 We have no thoughts as yet of leaving this Agreable place, nor any expectation from the M. of Worcester who I hear is still in England. Notwithstanding the Good air of Oxford it has lost some of its reputation with my mother who has bin for these 3 or 4 weeks violently tormented with a cold and tooth-ach. She presents
― 127 ―
her humble service to you and we both wish you an uninterrupted health.
I am
Honoured Sir
Your very much oblig'd and very humble servant
WM GRIGG
Oxford Sept. 9th 94
Address: For Mr Lock
Endorsed by Locke: A. Grig 9º Sept 94
1785. Locke to Dr. (later Sir) Hans Sloane, 14 September 1694 (1775, 2160)
B.M., Sloane MS. 4036, f. 185. Perhaps answers no. 1775.
Oates 14 Sept 94
Sir
It is very kindly and charitably done of you to send me some news from the commonwealth of letters into a place where I seldome meet with any thing beyond the observation of a scabby sheep or a lame horse. The great spleen you found in the woman you opend seems to be oweing as you rightly judg to the polypi which sweld the sanguinary vessels since the other parts of the spleen were every way right. This is an observation very well worth recording and publishing and may give great light about tumors in the abdomen which are not always to be imputed to apostemes†1 or collections of peccant humors. Polypus's in the bloud vessels are found soe frequently that I think they would deserve to be treated of as a particular disease, If there were collections enough of their hystory and symptoms to build any theory on and lay a foundation for their cure. Pray when you doe me the favour to write to me again doe not forget to set downe the diameter of the bigest vessels you found in that spleen what part of an inch it was
The history of imperfect plants which you mention will I guesse help much towards the perfecting that part of natural history.†2
― 128 ―
The notion of equivocal generation I should quite lay aside as a groundlesse phansy if you could resolve me some instances that puzel me in that affair. One is the strange and new creatures that have been often found in the bodys of men and other animals, which could not be reduced to any species of animals in that country or else where from which they might derive their original. Another is the production of lice in any one who changes not though in a place and circumstances where there cannot be supposd to be any propogation by seed from other animals of that species. These and others that might be mentiond I think can hardly be accounted for by univocal generation†1 acc<o>rding†a to the ordinary philosophie. I hope the author in his account of submarine plants will not omitt to tell us how deep under water any of them are to be found, or whether they are any species of them are at any dept we can come at. For I am apt to suppose that the air hath something to doe with vegetation even under water, whether this will serve to discover any thing of it, or help us to guesse how far it descends in the body of the water I know not. This I conclude that there is noe thing constantly observable in nature, which will not always bring some light with it, and lead us farther into the knowledg of her ways of workeing. I returne you many thankes for these and the other parts of your communication. Though these were not what I principaly looked for when I saw your name. you know you have something of more consequence than any of these of your owne which I with all the world are in an impatient expectation of. I hoped you would have told me that your learned and curious collections were goeing to the presse and that you would not any longer delay to obleige the publique.†2 However I acknowledg my self very much indebted to you for the favour you have done me and am
Sir
your most humble and obleiged servant
JOHN LOCKE

1786. J. G. Grævius to Locke, 14/24 September 1694 (1751, 1802)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 39-40. Probably the letter enclosed in no. 1787, which was forwarded by van Limborch with his letter to Locke, no. 1791. Answers no. 1751; answered by no. 1809.
(English)
Viro singulari virtute et doctrina Joanni Lockio S.P.D.
J. G. Graevius
(English) Litteras, quas ad te dederam, mense sexto demum, postquam eas scripseram, ad te pervenisse illorum culpa est, quibus fasciculum librorum ad vos curandum commiseram.†1 Quanta voluptate perfuderim communem nostrum amicum Toinardum, ubi ex meis intellexit, quae tu de illo ad me perscripseras, ex binis his epistolis, quas eodem tempore accepi, cognosces.†2 Si quid ad illum curari velis, mihi manda, ut recte curetur mihi erit curae. Wetsteinius nullum commercium litterarum†a olim exercet cum Toinardo, de quo queritur, quod sumtus fecerit in edendis aliquot foliis harmoniae Josephi, quae postea noluerit pertexere, aut edi.†3 Hanc ob causam abrupit litterarum scriptiones. Joannem Malelam misi Toinardo per Helvetiam, qui et recte ad illum delatus est. Lingua patria te litteris prodidisse quicquid animo conceperas valde probo.
― 130 ―
Sed cum illa tam praeclara sint, ut ex gustu, quem nobis dedit Clericus, licuit intelligere,†1 doleo nullum interpretem reperiri, cujus opera istis ingenii tui deliciis alii quoque populi frui possint. Sperabam has partes suscepturum Clericum, sed videtur nunc animum applicasse ad sacras litteras illustrandas. Notas et paraphrasin in Genesin jam habemus. Sequetur brevi exodus. Itaque alii haec quercus erit excutienda.†2 Si hic nossem utriusque linguae peritum quotidiano convitio illum perpellerem, ut operi tam pulchro manus admoveret. Sed orietur, spero, qui meis multorumque aliorum desideriis satisfaciet tandem. Nos dolium nostrum volvimus.†3 Quid tu nunc agas, quid mediteris, qui otiosus esse non potes, si ex te cognoro, valde gaudebo. Cives tui mihi significarunt insignem Euripidis editionem Cantabrigiae publicatam.†4 Ad nos nondum delata est, sed expectatur brevi. Archaeologia vestri Burneti multis multum negotii facessit. Audio in Germania fuisse, qui in illius opinionibus explodendis multum operae consumserit. quo successu non ausim pronunciare, qui librum nondum vidi.†5 Sic et Simonii
― 131 ―
Criticae novi testamenti opposuisse librum Episcopum Meldensem amici narrant,†1 et patrem Societatis Jesu in Montaltii famosas epistolas strinxisse calamum, sed ab ipso Societatis ordine librum esse abolitum,†2 aeque ut Harduini de nummis Herodiadum diatriben, in qua scriptores omnes antiquos supposititios esse contendit praeter Virgilii Bucolica, Horatii sermones, Ciceronis et Plinii opera.†3 Grevius noster optime valet, qui has ad te mittet. Hanc enim fidem mihi dedit. Civem tuum, qui Lyde dicitur, nondum vidi. Simul ac videro, intelliget, quantum pondus apud me tuae litterae habeant. Vale Vir Eximie, et me ama. Trajecti D. XXIV Septembris CIↃ IↃC XCIV.
(Latin)
To John Locke, matchless in virtue and learning, J. G. Grævius sends greeting
(Latin) That the letter that I sent you reached you only some five months after I had written it is the fault of those to whom I had consigned the parcel of books to be forwarded to you.†1 How greatly I delighted our common friend Toinard, when he learnt from my letter what you had written to me about him, you will perceive from these two letters, which I received at the same time.†2 If you want anything forwarded to him entrust it to me and I shall take care that it is properly forwarded. Wetstein has this long time had no correspondence with Toinard; he complains of him that he went to some expense in the course of publishing some leaves of the Harmony of Josephus, which Toinard was later unwilling to finish or allow to be published.†3 For this reason he broke off writing letters. I sent Joannes Malalas to Toinard via Switzerland, and he was safely conveyed to him. I strongly approve of your having published in your native language whatever you have conceived[p. 130] in your mind. But since what you have conceived is so excellent, as might be learnt from the taste that Le Clerc has given us,†1 I am sorry that no interpreter has been found by whose exertion other peoples also can enjoy those delights of your genius. I hoped that Le Clerc would undertake this office, but he seems now to have applied his mind to elucidating the Holy Scriptures. We already have his notes on, and paraphrase of, Genesis. Exodus will follow shortly. And so this oak tree will have to be shaken by some other person.†2 If I knew anyone here expert in both languages I would urge him with daily clamour to set his hand to so glorious a task. But someone, I hope, will arise who will at length satisfy my and many others' desires. As for me, I roll my tub.†3 I shall be glad if I learn from you what you, who cannot be idle, are doing and what you are considering. Some of your fellow-countrymen have told me about a notable edition of Euripides published at Cambridge.†4 It has not yet been brought to us but is expected shortly. Your Burnet's Archæologia gives many people great trouble. I hear that there was someone in Germany who bestowed much labour on exploding his opinions,†5 with what success I do not venture to pronounce as I have not yet seen the[p. 131] book. So also, friends tell me, the bishop of Meaux has replied to Simon's Histoire critique of the New Testament,†1 and a father of the Society of Jesus has taken up the pen against Montalte's celebrated Lettres, but his book has been suppressed by the superiors themselves of the Society,†2 as also has Hardouin's diatribe De nummis Herodiadum, in which he contends that all the ancient writers are supposititious except Virgil's Eclogues, Horace's Satires and Epistles, and the works of Cicero and Pliny.†3 Our friend de Greve is very well; he will send you this letter, for so he promised me. I have not yet seen your fellow-countryman of the name of Lyde. As soon as I see him he will learn what weight your letter has with me. Good-bye, extraordinary Sir, and love me. Utrecht, 24 September 1694
Endorsed by Locke: Grævius 24 Sept 94 Answered 5 Nov.

M. DC. XCIV.
(Latin) Illustrious and excellent Sir
I preferred to add this very short letter to those of the illustrious Grævius[p. 131] and your friend Toinard rather than to let so good an opportunity go by. And so, to put herewith my undying affection into few but true-hearted words, having long since embraced you with my as it were naked and inmost heart, I revere you daily as if you were present. I often talk of you, incomparable Sir, with the scholarly van Limborch and the great Grævius, and I learnt with joy some years ago that the king had honoured you with an office and a salary. No king's liberality can be so great as not to be surpassed by your merits. For nobody will value sufficiently your genius, learning, and kindliness. I would say more but the man who will deliver this letter to our friend van Limborch compels me to break off. Good-bye, best of men, love your de Greve, and regard me always as a true friend. For he will sooner cease to live than to revere your virtue and scholarship who is
Yours in love, obedience, and respect,
Alb. de Greve
Utrecht 23 September

i am too well bred to desire (Even) a philosopher to leave a place which a Lady makes agreable, had i not heard so much of my Lady†a Massum's merritt i should have been tempting you sometime since, but now i must make this proposall to you, if you have any businesse in Town, i will send my Coach for you, if you have none, i will meet you att any place half way from whence we may both gett home att night. Address: For Mr Lock
Endorsed by Locke: E: Monmouth 19 Sept. 94
1789. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 21 September/1 October 1694 (1764, 1827)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 122-5.
Rotterdam primo October 1694
Dear. Sir.
Yours of the 17 August from Oates I received the 7th†b past and do return you my thanks for the pains you have taken, in informing yourself and me, of the state of my children born in these parts as to Inheriting my and their mothers lands in England. But mr. Spademan,†1 (who oft enquires after your health, as oft as he visits me and my dearest; and what you are doing, when we shal see what you gave the world a hint of in your book of education, about the flood.†2 etc)—brings a new scruple into my mind, which seems not ill
― 134 ―
founded, viz, that the marchants children residing abroad, are in Law considered as much Englishmen, as those of Ambassadors that lye abroad for the good of the Commonwealth; yet it is onely of such marchants as are free (slaves) of the Company of marchant Adventurers. Pray enquire if this be so.
I find you say nothing of getting deeds made for that land of my wives about whitby, which I have sold, as I wrote you in mine of the 5º June—I presume you have forgot, to give the copy of the deed, and bond, by which that land, was vested in my late wife, Dorothy Grainge, and is now by me sold to Joseph Scarth master and mariner of whitby, that so a sufficient Title may be given to him, who is content with my bond for £300 to save him harmless from all claims. If it be not done I do intreat you to cause it to be done, and the Instruments given to Joseph Wright, with a copy of a letter of Attorney that I must send him to passe the said deed, and signe said bond or Act of Indemnity, in my name to the use of the said Joseph Scarth.
I am in hopes to see your thoughts concerning that book of Doctor Buchius, the chiefest things are the asserting God to have been always (ab æterno) and to remaine always (in æternum) if I understand him aright, a Creator. The denying of a liberty of Indifferency in the divine being. The affirming the difference betwixt spirit and body to be onely modal, The necessity of Christs being the person of Adam revolved, in order to his being the savior of all men. And of punishing al men, for the same crimes alike. These are the most paradoxal things in the book. Which are lyable to very strong objections, that would give him, to say no more, great difficultie to clear, and fairly to resolve, in his second part. And therefore it was I desired your thoughts upon the booke. That if he can remove those objections, and establish the truth of his assertions, he may doe it. For, I long, if it maybe, to see a system, that can hold out against all objections, and make it self appear to be truth to all impartiall men that seek Truth, for Truths sake, of which number I flatter my self to be one, for I have now no Interest in the world, no attachment to any party, sect, or society of men, or their doctrines, as such. And yet I doubt not but I do in some things Impose upon my self. And therefore am willing to heare every man that can give me further light, and I would I could prevail with all men, so to be, Or could live with my children, if it be the will of God, till I have fixed this so necessary, and useful
― 135 ―
a principle in them. In the mean while, I greedily imbrace all oportunities, of leaving them the means of knowing the necessity of it, upon record.
I shall not faile, God willing of giving you an account of the additions that the doctor may make to his booke, when his edition comes forth.
I understand that matters betwixt G K†1 and his Antagonists have <be>en†a at large heard, and examind in the Generall meeting, and that it has occasioned printing, (its like) on both sides.
The Gentlewoman of Amsterdam of which I made mention,†2 was come that length, that she utterly rejected the N.T. as imposing a falshood upon mankind in asserting Christ to be the messiah of whom Moses and the Prophets prophesyed; and wresting passages of the old Testament to that purpose; as Isay. 7 v. 14. in math. 1.23. micah 5.2 in math. 2.5.†3 Hosea 11.1. in math. 2:15. etc. The ministers and Professors went all one way, and would undertake to prove even their disputes about the Trinity, out of the Old Testament, and that the Jews were bound to beleev 3 persons in the Godhead. because its said Genes.1. Breschit†b bara Elohim.†4 In the beginning Gods created. in the plural number with a verb in the singular. Ergo 3 persons, but one God. and v.26. Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. Then they fell to proving that the old Testament did prophesy of christ and was fulfilled in christ: beginning with Gen. 49. 10 The scepter shall not depart etc—till Shilo come—and so in order as they lye. But the Lady was too wel furnisht with the Jews, more naturall, and true application of those texts, (as she thought) to the people of Israel and particular persons living many 100 years before christ, than that their arguments, could make any impression upon her, And so they left her, every man of them: speaking, many of them, ill of her, as a self conceited, obstinate person, given up, for her pride, to a perverse spirit: Others, conceivd it an intrigue of love betwixt the Jew and her. And so the poore Gentlewomans reputation was exposed, and left
― 136 ―
an object of the fury of the multitude; so that she durst not go abroad, for fear of her life. Yet she remained constant in her thoughts that those scriptures were shamefully wrested, by those that applyed them to the person of our Saviour—Till Doctor Veen, the Doctor of the family coming to the house, perhaps sent for as a Doctor, told the mother (a widdow) that he wondred that she would suffer her daughter to have so much converse, with a Jew; That to ingage in dispute with a Jew, was not every mans work. That he himself durst not ingage with Orobio. That the Professor Limborgh had; and so recommended him to speak with her daughter as a man Wel Versed in those things—whereupon she intreated him to get the Professor to make her a visit, which he did. The mother intreated two things of him 1 not to let her daughter know who he was. 2 not to touch upon any thing in controversy between the Calvinist, and Arminian churches. When he began he took another course, than the others had done, viz, to prove first the Divine Truth of the N.T. This the Gentlewoman opposed with all her might—and told him she would not suffer him to begin there, telling him he must prove first that the prophesies applyed, by the writers of the N.T. to the person of christ, did speak of him, and had her bible in her hand to begin with, the Text of Shilo. A full houre dured that contest where he ought to begin. At length, being prest with this Argument, that we are bound to receive any man that can prove himself to be sent of God, altho he could not prove that any prophet ever prophesyed of him: and that that was the case of moses. That if she rejected the proofs, which he had for moses, out of the N.T. she must alledg better herself for him out of the O.T. which she would find difficult. She said that she found when they could not prove what they said of Christ, that then they put her to prove moses his mission: which was the way to bring all into doubt, but not to establish anything. He told her, that ought not to seem strange to her, for tho he doubted not of moses his being sent of God, yet the strongest evidences of it being those he found in the N.T. if she rejected them, it was but just that he required stronger of her, if she would have him beleeve mos<es>.†a And so fell to, telling her, it was now Easter munday,†1 a tim<e>†a celebrated by the Christians in commemoration of christs being
― 137 ―
raised from the dead. Which if he could prove to her, he thought she would confess him to be raisd by God. She said yes. If that story were true, God raisd him for being dead,†a he†a could not raise himself. He said then he thought it needless to prove that there was such a man that was put to death, because the Jews themselvs beleeved that. She graunted it. The being raisd to life again, he proved from the Testimony of Ey witnesses, who had known him in his life time, seen him dead, and alive, so that they could as little be mistaken as herself, of having seen her mother that day. That therefore, if false, they must have conspired to devise that Ly. But none did so but for advantage. That advantage they could not have by it appeard. 1 from the persons reporting it, who were galileans, strangers, no citizens of Jerusalem, of Interest among the people, by which they might drive on some politick design. 2 from the place where: In Jerusalem it self, where he had been so lately executed as a malefactor. 3 from the Interest of the Jews, and Pilate; church and state, who were concernd to detect the lye, and punish the spreaders of it. 4 from their doing nothing to convince the people, which had been easy to do by taking the dead body, and exposing it to publick view, which would have been a publike confutation of that pretext, and put a stop to the spreading of christianity, at once.
Asking her whether she thought that the ministers of Amsterdam, if they had induced the magistrates to hang a man as a blasphemer, would not stir up the magistrates, to seiz persons that should declare the transgresser to be the son of god whom they had murtherd, and that God had raisd him from the dead, and cause the body to be hung up in view of all men; and severely punish the inventers of such an impudent lye, to the defamation of church and state. She (ingenuously) confest the Argument to be so strong that at present she could say little against it. But would further consider of it—onely for the present these 2 things occurrd to her mind 1 that it was not without ground of suspition, that he appeard onely to those of his own sect, And not publickly to the Jews, which would (on the other hand) have been so publike a confirmation of the truth that all mouths must have been stopt. He told her, that if she considered the prejudice of that nation against him, augmented now by shedding his blood, she could not conceive that they would have been so presently convinc't upon such a view of him; seing what is recorded concerning that nation; Numbers 16.
― 138 ―
v 32 et seqq who tho <they>†a had seen that miracle of the earths opening and swallowing those 250 men, according to the prophesy of moses v.29, yet the next morning v 41. They all came and murmured against moses and Aaron, saying, ye have killed the people of the Lord—whence he concluded, that her conclusion was not so certain as she thought—She graunted it—but said her second objection was, the frequence of pretended miracles, in the Roman church, even accompanyed with publick attestations of persons on whose bodys they had been wrought, and ey and ear witnesses: of which yet himself and others, as well as she, beleeved not a word— so that there might be fraud in these things or relations as well as in those—He shewd her the vast difference between those things. In the one it was the Interest of the church and state, to incourage all men to detect the cheat, if it had been so: and a reward would have been certainly given to any body that could have done it. In the other it was the interest of church and state to cover it—and fire and faggot attended any that should attempt the discovery. He proceeded then to the sending of the holy Ghost at Pentecost— And so left her to weigh his Arguments. His sweet, meek Treatment, (not as the scribes, as one having a car<n>al†b authority or dominion over her faith and conscience) and his recommending it to her, to oppose his arguments so long as she could, and till she was per<fe>ctly†c overcome, prevaild so with her, that she conceivd (before they parted) a love for him, and desired that he would come again, but 2 houres sooner, which he did the next day, from 4 to 8 in the evening. Then they fell to the prophesyes of the old Testament and application of them to Christ in the New: from passage to passage.
First he proved that there was a time prefixed by the Prophets for the coming of the messiah, and that time was expired at the coming of christ. 2 that he should be born of a virgin. 3 that he should be born at Bethlehem, 4 that he should suffer and be cut off not for his own sins but for the sins of the people—And finally that all this was fullfilled in christ—Suffering her, and intreating her to oppose him to the utmost, even so long as she thought that there was any strength in her objections, or unclearness or weakness in his solutions: he graunted her oft what the Jews said, concerning the fulfilling of those texts many 100 years ere christ was born, but shewd her a necessity of concluding that the holy ghost designd
― 139 ―
another fulfilling, in another time, which could be in no other person, than that of christ—particularly that micah 5.2 was (as she alledged) fulfilled in measure, in the person of Zerubabel, but that it must also respect the birth of christ in Bethlehem, because Zerubabel, tho his being born in Bethlehem, added lustre to it, yet seeing David was also born there who was a greater prince than Zerubbabel, it followed that a greater than David was to be borne there, which was not Zerubbabel but christ.†1
He shewd her, by comparing the words of the Prophets that prophesied, with the words denoting the fulfilling of their prophesies, before the coming of the messiah, that divers prophesies, which she apprehended were to be fulfilled in the days of the messiah, and because she found them not to be fulfilled since christs days—were fulfilled before—which she said had taken a great burthen from off her spirit—what these prophesies, and accomplishments were, his time permitted him not to inform us.
Now when he came the second time her mother told the professor that he need not conceal himself; that her daughter had not rested till she knew who he was—
Thus in 3 discourses, the Lady profest herself so perfectly satisfyed, and all her doubts overcome, that she blest God that she had met with him, and said that she beleeved it was impossible for her, more to doubt of it—In the third discourse (ni fallor)†2 she askt him what he thought of the Priesthood of Christ, which he declined to answer, saying that he must discover a difference betwixt theirs and the publick church,†3 which being a thing that did not concern that case, that lay before them, he desired to be excused. She urging him he told her then that he would relate to her the matter of fact, wherein the 2 churches differed, without entring into any debate about it: if that would satisfy her—and so did—In the debate she forgot not to press that common objection of the Jews, that it being notorious on the one hand that the messiah was to come of the Tribe of Judah, and on the other hand, it being notorious from the Genealogies that Mary was not of the Tribe of Judah (tho Joseph) was, but of Levi, Christ, Who was maries, and not Josephs son, as you christians say, said she, cannot be the promised messiah because he was not descended from the Tribe of Judah—
― 140 ―
To which difficulty, he replyed, that there was much adoe among the learned, some of which did think they could reconcile the difference, but that he made no difficulty to confess, that he thought, that some corruption had befaln the Text in the Genealogie, since the Apostles writing. But that it was most sure, and notorious in that time that Christ sprang of Judah, because Paul writing to the Jews, speaks of it as of a thing most evident Heb. 7. v.14. which the Jews could easily have contradicted from their Genealogy, if it had been false, and would so have done. And that this need not affright her, as if all were false, or uncertain, if such a corruption could get in. For if that argument were good, it would serve as wel to invalidate the writings of moses, and the old Testament, as the writings of the N.T. shewing her evidently a corruption got in, about the Age of Abraham Gen.11. which she confessed to be convincing.†1 How much better, more ingenuous, and Christian is it, thus to confess the Truth: than impudently contrary to their consciences, and own certain knowledg, to aver to their Auditors that the providence of God has so watched over those books that not the least corruption has befaln them, nor one iota†a of them been lost. When they know that there are so many thousand various readings, which must needs all of them be variations and corruptions, voluntary, or involuntary from the first copies written by the divine writers of the old and N.T. But because many have not the capacity of understanding this; and will scarce beleeve it, when it's told them; but being thus born in hand by their ministers, whom they looke upon, as petty gods, they are apt to suspect him that tells them how it is, of having a wicked design, to invalidate the whole scripture, and being an Atheist. when they by their impudent lying, make men that discover the falshood of their assertion, think them Atheists, and all that they say to the people upon the score of Religion to be mere policy, and so to become Atheists—I say for such people, I know no shorter way to convince them of such corruptions, than by sending them to compare these places in their English, Dutch, High Dutch, french etc—Bibles— 2 Sam. 24.9.13.†b with 1 chron. 21.5.12. 2 Kings 24.8 with 2 Chron. 36.9. 2 Kings 8.26. with 2 chron. 22.2 1 Kings 7.26 with 2 chron.
― 141 ―
4.5 2 Sam. 24.24. with 1 Chron. 21.25. Nehemiah. 7.v.8†1 with Ezra 2.v.5. N.v.11 with E.v.6. N.v.13. with E.v.8. N.v.15 with E.v.10. N.v.16 with E.v.11. N.v.17 with E.v.12. N.v.18 with E.v.13. N.v.19 with E.v.14. N.v.20 with E.v.15. N.v.23. with E.v.17. N.v.22 with E.v.19 N.v.26 with E.v.21.22. N.v.37 with E.v.33. N.v.38 with E.v.35. N.v.44 with E.v.41. N.v.45 with E.v.42 and Nehemiah chap. 7 v. 62 with Ezra chapter 2 verse 60. And he shall find corruptions more than a good many, And if he wil take the pains to cast up the particulars in both, he will find neither of them to agree with the sum totall which both Nehemiah ch.7 v.66 and Ezra chap. 2 v 64 do affirm to have been 42360 For in Nehemiah they amount to no more than 31089 and in Ezra but to 29818. Excuse this digression.
The Gentlewoman being thus providentially restored to the firm belief of the N.T. and that Jesus is the Messiah and Savior of the World; it could not be conceald, but, as she her self at first, when she found her self prest with the probability, and indeed evidence of the Jews arguments shewing that those places were literally fulfilled long before Christs birth, as that of Isaia 7.v.14 in the wife and son of the Prophet Isayah him self, applyed herself to her pastor, or the minister of her quarter, for relief, So the ministers were presently acquainted with her being recovered out of that snare, And they came and visited her, enquiring how it came to pass that the professor Limborg could obtain more upon her than they all — She told the first, that he did it by first convincing her understanding of the divine authority of the N.T. which he made slight of. And said she had a great matter of that: a great nothing with a long taile. To whom she replyed that without that no arguing from the Prophesies could have helped her. The next that came, praisd the method: But asked her if she did not think that they could have usd the same arguments as he. To whom she replyed that she did not know, but they might, but she was certain that they did not, and that if they had so done, the arguments would have had the same operation upon her, from them, as from him. He replyed that if she had intimated that she had been to be helpt that way, they would have taken that course. And she, That she beleevd that she was not to be convinct at all. And did oppose with all her might that way as labour that would be lost, and time mispent — But that the issue shewd her, that it was the onely right way.
― 142 ―
However the poore Gentlewoman is to this day traduced as a proud, conceited person, that never was truly religious, nor scarce ever wilbe, And some stick not to prate as if it were a design betwixt the professor and her, to put a slur upon them, Tho the Professor was an utter stranger to the whole family. Another scandalos report he met with in the open boat from the Hague,†1 that it was an intrigue of love, that the Jew was fled with her. Which the Professor contradicting, a person of seeming quality, averd it to be true, and that he had it out of a half brothers mouth of the lady herself, and that it appeared enough because the Jew was called in by proclamation — The last said he, is true, but not for carrying away the lady, but for drawing her from the Christian Religion, to Judaism, And that he had dayly converst with her in her mothers house and therefore certainly could attest that she was never absent one day from her mothers, and so stopt that lying report —
I told him I hoped he took care to commit the whole to writing, he said he had so done, and desired the yong lady to do the same, that they might from both their memories, make a perfect narrative of it. This is the Account, so far as we can remember it, that he gave my wife and me of that affair —
I have now to request of you, if you can to cause to be sent me 3 of the additions to your booke,†2 I having bought 3 copies for my children, and would willingly have them all perfect.
so with my and my dearests service to you, and Sir F. and my Lady Masham, I rest —
Dear Friend
your affectionate friend and humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
