1790. Locke to Mrs. Honor Thomas, 22 September 1694 (1815)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 274. Draft. Answered by no. 1815.
London. 22 Sept. 94
Since†a- I came to town on Wednesday last†1 my Cosin Bonville has been with me and told me what had passed between you and him. When the money was procured which was lent your husband one consideration which made it come at that rate was that the interest should regularly be paid without any trouble That it has not been soe I finde since I came to town (which was on wednesday last) was not your fault. But my Cosin Bonville who thought it neglected when he writ and was pudderd in it by not haveing the full of it paid at the rate of fower and an half per cent when it did come was I finde vexed at it and that made him write as I perceive he did to you about the interest for the future and otherwise than he should have writ if I had been by him. But you must not think it strange if a man unexperienced in such businesse and that had his time and thoughts taken up in his trade was in the disapointment a litle quicker then otherwise he would have been. However it shall not be any prejudice to you nor you need not trouble your self about paying in the money, it shall be continued to you at the rate of 4½ per cent and now things are once set right and you understand one an other there will be noe more trouble in it for the future.-†a
Before your husband died I writ to him of £30 that I had paid for him which had never been accounted to him. your son thought it had been a thirty pounds which I lent to his hands here in town which was repaid me, but it was not but £30 which I payd to Mr Furly by his order.†b I imagind he would talke with you of it and then I should hear from him or you about it. How it came to be soe long omitted by me I signified in one of my letters, nor should I have demanded it of the Doctor had it not been soe. However I shall leave it to you and have too great a regard to the memory of my deceased friend to withdraw any of the frindship or respect I shall always have to†c those†c upon such an occasion. when ever it may lie in my way to doe you or yours any service you will always
― 144 ―
finde me ready to the utmost of my power. and I shall never omit any occasion to let you see how much concerne I have for the wife and children of a man I loved soe well
Mr Thomas†1 when he was in town seemd to me inclined to the army and was in some uncertainty whether he should not goe immediately into Flanders. I hope those thoughts are now over. For if I might interpose my opinion I should think the advances he has made in learning and particularly in physick would turne to a better account if imploid in that practise which his father had soe much successe and reputation in. Perhaps I like this because I think if I can doe him any service it will be most in this way. I am sure I advise it because I wish him extremely well and imagin it the best for him and should be glad to give him all the assistance I can. I spoke to him of some books of Dr Lightfoots which your husband had of mine which I think will be of no use to Mr Thomas and therefor I should be glad to have them, because <they>†a- will be of some to me.-†a with them I desired he would send the Corpus Juris Civilis†2 which I remember your husband had and I would borrow of you being a book too which I think your son will not use. Pray give my service to him and your daughter I am
I shall stay but a little while in town and therefor beg to hear from you by the first oportunity and pray send me word how my godson†3 does and when you heard from him
Direct your letters to me at Mr P

(English) Vir Amplissime
Ultimas tuas 13 Januar. hujus anni scriptas 14 Februarii accepi. Binas aut ternas exinde ad Te misi: nihil hactenus responsi tuli. Statui aliquoties alias addere, ut pertinax tuum expugnarem silentium: Verum, quoniam Theologiæ meæ Christianæ editio altera sub prælo erat, exspectandum duxi, donec ea prodiret: quare nec jam scripsissem, quoniam per otium prolixiores, quas Tibi destinaveram, jam scribere haud vacat. Verum quoniam Jurisconsultus Grevius has ad me misit, quibus alias D. Professoris Grævii inclusas ait, eas diutius apud me hærere nolui. Intra paucos dies alias a me exspecta prolixiores, ut sic tædiosa verbosissimarum literarum lectione nimis diuturni silentii pœnam luas. I<ntr>a†a paucos dies alteram Theologiæ meæ editionem absolutam fore spero. Paucissima quæda<m>†a emendavi; et pauca addidi. Si limatissimum tuum judicium hic coram audire licuisset, plura a Te monitus emendare potuissem. Magnam tamen mutationem in secunda editione exstare nolui, ut idem esse liber ubique appareat. Volui jam diu accuratam tibi scribere historiam colloquii mei cum puella, quæ de
― 146 ―
religionis Christianæ veritate dubia ac vacillans ad Judaismum tota inclinabat. Res est, per totam nostram patriam vulgatissima. Paucis dicam, me in eâ deprehendisse tantum ingenii acumen, judicii solertiam, argumentandi dexteritatem, et indefessam variorum librorum, tam in Theologia quam philosophia, lectionem, ut credi vix possit. Annos nata est viginti duos: sed ea judicii maturitate, ut adultos et in scholis exercitatos longe superet. Cessit illa rationibus meis, et Jesum Christum suum Servatorem ingenue professa est. Jam plura cum ipsâ colloquia instituerant tres ex præcipuis hujus civitatis ministris Ecclesiæ Contraremonstrantium, cujus ipsa membrum est: Verum sine fructu. Nec mirum, quoniam disputationem inchoarunt adstructione dogmatis de SS.Trinitate, et quidem locis e Vet. Test. depromptis; quodque magis mirere, Judæis illius credendi necessitatem in Vet. Test. fuisse impositam urgebant. Illa facile omnia ejusmodi argumenta elusit. Ego ad eam vocatus longe aliâ methodo sum usus, eâdem nimirum†a quâ Don Balthasarum†1 oppugnavi: prius nempe historiæ Novi Testamenti, ac præcipue resurrectionis dominicæ ac missionis Spiritus S. veritatem adstruxi, iis argumentis, quibus se nihil solide opponere
― 147 ―
posse, ac proinde quibus se persuasam ingenue fassa est. Exinde prophetias omnes in Vet.Test. suum in historia Novi Testamenti complementum habere probavi; quod adstructa prius Euangelii veritate mihi difficile non fuit. Jam multo quam antea in Religione Christiana confirmatior mecum quandoque de va<riis disse>rit.†a Verum finiendum mihi est: alias plura et exactiora scribam: nunc te eve<ntus tam>†a rari plane ignarum nolui. Indignantur mihi, quos maximas mihi gratias <agere decuis>set†a quasi in sui ignominiam cedat, puellam, quam ipsi suis ineptis argumentis alieniorem quotidie ab Euangelio reddebant, meis argumentis ac methodo cessisse. Alii tamen inter ipsos meliora de me loquuntur. Verum finiendum est. Vale Vir Amplissime. Saluta officiosissime meis verbis D.Cudwortham.
Tui Amantissimus
P. A LIMBORCH.
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I received your last letter, which was written on 13 January of this year, on 14 February. I have written to you two or three times since then; so far I have received no answer. I decided at various times to add another letter in order to overcome your stubborn silence; but since the second edition of my Theologia Christiana was in the press I thought it better to wait until it appeared. For this reason I should also not have written now, since there is not time for me now to write the lengthier letter which I had designed for you as leisure permitted. But since the lawyer de Greve has sent me this letter, in which he says another from Professor Grævius is enclosed, I did not want it to stick with me very long. Expect a lengthier letter from me in a few days' time, so that you may thus be punished for your all too prolonged silence by the tedious perusal of a very long-winded one. I hope that the publication of the second edition of my Theologia will be completed in a few days' time. I have amended very few things, and have added a few. If I had been allowed to hear your very refined judgement from you here in person, instructed by you I could have made more amendments. But I wanted there to be no great change in the second edition, so that it may be seen to be the same book at all points. I have for some time wanted to write for you a careful account of my conversation with a girl who was doubtful and wavering[p. 146] about the truth of the Christian religion, and altogether inclined to Judaism. The matter is widely known throughout our country. To put it shortly, I have perceived in her such acuteness of mind, shrewdness of judgement, dexterity in argument, and indefatigable reading of various books, as well in theology as in philosophy, as can scarcely be believed. She is twenty-two years old; but with such maturity of judgement that she far surpasses men of riper years and exercised in the schools. She has yielded to my reasoning and has frankly acknowledged Jesus Christ as her Saviour. Three of the leading ministers of the Contraremonstrants' church in this city, of which church she is a member, had already held several conversations with her, but without success. Nor was this surprising since they began the discussion with an affirmation of the dogma of the Holy Trinity, and indeed with passages drawn from the Old Testament; and what will surprise you more, they urged that the necessity of believing the dogma had been imposed on the Jews in the Old Testament. She easily parried all arguments of that kind. When I was summoned to her I adopted a very different procedure, in fact the same as that with which I assailed Don Balthasar:†1 that is, I first affirmed the truth of the New Testament history, and especially of the resurrection of Our Lord and the sending of the Holy Spirit, with arguments to which she frankly confessed that she could oppose nothing solid, and accordingly[p. 147] that she was persuaded by them. Next I proved that all the prophecies in the Old Testament have their fulfilment in the history of the New Testament; this, as I had previously affirmed the truth of the Gospel, was not difficult for me. Now much more confirmed than before in the Christian religion, she discusses various matters with me from time to time. But I must finish; I shall write further and more precisely some other time; I did not want you to be completely ignorant at present of a very uncommon event. Those who ought to be most grateful to me are indignant with me, as if it were a disgrace to them that a girl, whom they by their unsuitable arguments were every day making more and more averse from the Gospel, should have yielded to my arguments and procedure. Others however say better things about me among themselves. But I must finish. Good-bye, excellent Sir. Give my best wishes to Mrs. Cudworth.
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH.

Sir
Though I cannot doubt but you are assured there is noebody more your servant than I, yet I cannot but think a letter from me espetialy of the kind this will be, will somewhat surprize you. For it is noe lesse than to desire you lay by all that country businesse which you had reserved to the litle time is now between this and the parliament and to come up to town immediately.†1 Soe bold a presumption as this without farther explaining my self, will possibly appear very odd to you. Sir
your most humble and most faithfull servant

Bloxworth†1 September 25. 94.
Sir
I am desird by mr Trenchard†2 to give you a discription of his case: I thinke I need not tell you what constitution he is off, being well knowne to you: some time since he sent for me, to advise with for the indisposition he then labourd under: I found him Hecticall, but treating him with bleeding, pectoralls, and the specifick barke; the use and continuance of which method, abated that ill symptome of his consumption; but has not powre sufficient to restore him: for at present he is reduced to so great a weakness that he has hardly flesh to cover his bones: he sleeps pretty well, eates with a pritty good apitite some times, never sick after, he has no catarrh, violent cough, thrush, dropsy, colliquative swetts, or aney of those direfull symptons that attend a deplorable consumption; the worst that accompanys him, is his great spitting, which by day is a pritty laudible pus; but in the morning after sleep fetid and purulent, and in a great quantity; the true signe of the consumption of the lungs. he is allso at present a little short breathd. <he>†a is informd by Mr Amsham Churchill that you have bin in the same condition, and are now restord to health. he therefore desires you would be so kinde to communicate the methode you usd; or whose advise you had; and in so doing you will much oblidge him and
Your unknowne friend and humble servant
THO: ROSS

1794. Antony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 29 September 1694 (1783, 1816)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 112-13. Printed in King, pp. 186-9.
St: Giles's Sep: the 29th 94†a
Mr Lock
You may most certainly bee assur'd that if out of any Studdys of mine, which you mention, I could draw any thing I thought could bee anyways profitable, or other then superfluouse to you; I should not fail to Communicate itt, without any need of being press'd: since that all the End to which my Studdyes, such as they are, have any leaning, or bent, is but to learn mee this one thing in short; how to Communicate every thing freely; how to bee more Sociable and more a Friend. how is itt possible that I should bee a Niggard here, and not impart all that I were able? Itt is not with mee as with an Empirick, one that is studdying of Curiositys, raising of new Inventions that are to gain credit to the author, starting of new Notions that are to amuse the World and serve them for Divertion or for tryall of their Acuteness (which is all one
― 151 ―
as if it were some new Play, a Chess, or a Game of cards that were envented.) Itt is not in my case as with one of the men of new Systems, who are to build the credit of their own invented ones upon the ruine of the Ancienter and the discredit of those Learned Men that went before. Descartes, or Mr Hobbs, or any of their Improvers have the same reason to make a-doe, and bee Jealouse about their notions, and DISCOVERY'S, as they call them; as a practizing Apothecary or a mountebank has to bee Jealouse about the Compositions that are to goe by his name. for if itt bee not a Livelyhood is aim'd; 'tis a Reputation. and what I contend for Reputation in, I must necessarily envy another man's possession of.
But as for mee: could I make any of those admirable Discoverys, which were nothing worth but to bee commended for their Subtility; I would doe as Timon did (though out of a just contrary Principle) when he found Gold: after I had by chance dugg upon itt and found what itt was; I would put the Clod over itt again, and say nothing of itt, but forgett itt if I could.†1 for my part: I am so far from thinking that mankind need any new Discoverys, or that they lye in the dark and are unhappy for want of them; that I know not what wee could ask of God to know more then wee doe or easily may doe. the thing that I would ask of God should bee to make men live up to what they know; and that they might bee so wise as to desire to know no other things then what belong'd to 'em, and what lay plain before them; and to Know those, to PURPOSE: and that all other Affectation of Knowledg Hee would preserve us from, as from a Desease: in which sort of knowledg if wee excell'd ever so much; and were masters of all as far as wee coveted; Itt would not help us to bee one jott the Honester or Better Creatures. If there bee any one that knows not, or beleives not that all things in the Univers are done for the best, and ever will goe on so, because conducted by the same Good Cause;†2 If there bee any one who knows nothing like this of God, or can think of him constantly in this manner; and who cannot see that hee himself is a Rationall and Sociable Creature by his nature, and has an End to which he should refer his slightest actions; Such a one is indeed wanting of knowledg. But if this bee known (as what is easyer to know?) there is not, then, one Studdy or Science that
― 152 ―
signifys a rush, or that is not wors <then>†a Ignorance; which gives a Man no help in the persuance of what he has learnt to bee his Duty; Assists him not in the Government of the Irrationall and Brutall Part of himself; which neither makes him more truly satisfy'd with what God does in the World (for that is Loving God) nor more Sociable more Honest or more Just, by removing of those Passions which hee has allways to Struggle with, that he may preserve himself so. If there are any other Sciences that are worthy of Esteem; they are what must relate to the wellbeing of Mankind in Societys: and on that account a Button-maker is to bee esteem'd if hee improves his Art, and adds some Conveniency to Life. but how the Founders of Metaphysicks, of Rhetorick, of the Arts of Reasoning upon everything and never coming to an end, of the Arts that lye in words, the Turns of them, and the Division that may bee run upon them; how, I say, These Men came to bee preferr'd to the Commonest Mechanicks, I cannot well tell. Anciently, These Notable Inquisitive men, that were Curiouse in what signify'd nothing, were call'd by a name that they thought themselves highly honour'd with, and aspir'd no farther. They were calld Sophists:†1 and never expected to bee treated in the style of Philosopher or Professours of Philosophy.†2 Who were True Philosophers those Wise Men shew'd (for amongst them the Name came up) that were in early times in Greece, whome the Fancy of People that succeeded put into a certain number and call'd Seven, though the number was far greater; of whome not one but was signally remarkable for some Service to his Commonwealth; who were all united in the Strictest Friendship and by good Offices and helps one to another; and whose Studdy was that of knowing themselves, and learning how to bee serviceable to Others. When Socrates liv'd, itt was still thus. for he made the Sophists know themselves, and keep their distance. but when after his death, the Socratick Spirit sunk much; then began Philosophy and Sophistry to bee better acquainted. but it was never known till more late days that to Profess Philosophy, was not to Profess a Life: and that it might bee said of one, that Hee was a great Man in Philosophy; whilst nobody thought it to the purpose to ask how did Hee Live? what Instances of
― 153 ―
his Fortitude, Contempt of Interest, Patience etc:?—— What is Philosophy, then, if nothing of this is in the case? What Signifys itt to know (if wee could know) what Elements the Earth was made from; or how many Atomes went to make up the Round Ball wee live upon; though wee knew itt to an Atome? What signifys itt to know whether the Chaos was cast in Dr Burnet's mold or if God did itt a quite different way?†1 What if wee knew the Exact System of That and of our Frames; Should wee learn any more then this, that God did all things Wisely, and for the best? And are wee not allready satisfyd of this allready; or may bee assur'd of itt by the Thousandth part of what wee know and see? If wee should Discover anything that led us to Conceive what were Contrary to this; wee should have Learnt that which was wors then nothing. And Better then wee know allready, wee cannot Learn to know, for God cannot by any discovery, be conceiv'd to bee more wise, then perfectly so: and such itt <is>†a easy to conceive him to bee without knowing any more of the things of Nature then wee allready doe.
What I count True Learning, and all that wee can profitt by, is to know our selves; what it is that makes us Low, and Base, Stubborn against Reason, to be Corrupted and Drawn away from Vertue, of Different Tempers, Inconstant, and Inconsistent with ourselves; to know how to bee allways Friends with Providence though Death and many such Dreadfull Businesses come in the way; and to be Sociable and Good towards all men, though They turn Miscreants or are Injuriouse to us.
Whilst I can gett any thing that teaches this; Whilst I can search any Age or Language that can assist mee here; Whilst Such are Philosopers, and Such Philosophy, whence I can Learn ought from, of this kind; there is no Labour, no Studdy, no Learning that I would not undertake.
This is what I know to bee sufficiently despis'd. for who is there that can think so much to the Dishonour and <Prejudice>†b of himself as to think that he has odiouse Vices within him which only Labour and Exercize can throw out? or Who, if hee sees sometimes any such ill sights in himself, can Endure to look on that side long; but turns to that other side which his Flatterers (and Himself, the Greatest of them) allways readily present to him. To look
― 154 ―
to our Bodys, our Fortunes, is a Solid and Seriouse work, and has been, is, and will keep in good Fashion in the world. Animi autem Medicina (says one who spoke, yet, in a much better time then this) nec tam desiderata antequam inventa, nec tam culta posteaquam cognita est, nec tam multis grata et probata, pluribus etiam Suspecta et Invisa ...†1
But I must end: for I have allmost outwritt the Post time. You see what it is to Sett mee a Talking. I can add nothing now more then that I am with all Sincerity
your Intire Friend and Humble Servant
A ASHLEY
I have not yet receiv'd the book: But I have 1000 obligations to my Lady Masham.

1795. Locke to Esther Masham, 2 October 1694 (1773, 1825)
Newberry Library, Chicago: copy of the original letter by Esther Masham in her letter-book, pp. 12-14. Printed in Fox Bourne, ii. 300; by Professor Maurice Cranston in Newberry Library Bulletin, 2nd ser., no. 4, July 1950, pp. 127-8. Transcribed from microfilm. The explanatory note written by Esther.
London 2 October 1694
I take it amiss of my stars that they should order me to be out of the way when my Landabridis, whom I had so long languishd for, return'd. I will not say whither it was because you made too little hast, or your Joannes too much, but this I know it had been much more to my satisfaction and advantage if you had stole home and caught me naping, than by leaveing me forlorne so long expos'd me to a Journey that looked t'other way. This yet ought not to make you suspect that any body has stolen me, or if they have, you
― 155 ―
need not much be troubled at it whilst you have my heart with you at Oates; for without that what a purchasse they will have in such a carcasse as mine you may Judge. If you value your John so much as you say and I cannot but believe you sincere He is not such a fool to change you for the Indies. For that has nothing that can purchasse Love espetially such as yours is which can have no temptation but the great esteem and affection I have for you. You may beleeve then, that I shall make all the hast I can to even our long account of absence and compare thoughts and wishes and sighs and haveing quitted that score, begin a new one of mirth and laughing and kind words one to another with now and then a song amongst. I hope you are not much troubled that you have not your full†a foddering as you us'd to have. As to singing there be those in the Parish will tell you, you lost the perfection of that by your wandering. Had you been at home when I wishd, you had had something beyond the ordinary strain of Behold and have regard. But you must be gadding and make us sad under those heavenly strains for they were Heavenly too. To be Serious I am extreamly glad that you are safe and well returnd; exceedingly obliged to you for the favour of your Letter and shall make haste to Oates to tell you how much I am
Your Obedient
JOANNES
If you had been charitable you would have sent me some commission or other.

1797. William Molyneux to Locke, 6 October 1694 (1781, 1817)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 94-5. Answers no. 1781; answered by no. 1817.
Dublin Oct. 6. 1694.
Honoured Sir
Your favours to me increase dayly, and I find by every Letter I receive from you, that you are resolved to make them Endles. To this Excesse of Friendship in you, and not to any Desert in my self, I can easily Impute the Expressions in yours of the 3rd of September, which came not to my Hands before the 4th of this Inst. Our Pacquets of Late being long on their Way hither.
I have now gone through the second Edition of your Incomparable Work, and think verily the oftner I read it, the more I desire still to do so; and I look upon it as one of the Greatest Efforts of Humane Judgement, that ever yet appeard in the World. But I wil venture to say no more of it to your self: and shall only take this way of proving to you my Opinion of it, that I will on all Occasions Propagate it, and incourage the Reading and Studying of it. In order thereto, I have already been the Occasion of having all the Coppys, that were sent to the Booksellers of this town, bought up long since, and herein I inclose to you a small bill of Exchange for £3:6s:od: with which I desire you would purchase for me Six Coppys of your Book in sheets and direct your Bookseller to Inclose them superscribed for me in some parcel consigned to any Bookseller here; and I desire you would give me advice thereof. I am told by one Dobson a bookseller here, that he had them in sheets from his Correspondent in London at Eleven shillings a peice. I intend to bestow them upon some Poor Studious Young Batchelors in Our Colledge here.
At the same time I desire you Order the Bookseller to send me One or two supranumerary Cutts of your Effigies to Adorn mine, and My Brothers Closets.
As to any Corrections of your Work, I protest sincerely to you I have not One. and as to any Errors of the Pres, they are Inconsiderable, yet such as I have Marked I will send you by my Next; not having time Now to turn over to the Places I have marked as such being in the Margin of My Book.
Mr Hogshaw I perceive is not likely to deal wel with you. I have often left word at his Lodging that I desired to speak with him but
― 159 ―
he seems to avoid coming nigh Me. I am sure if he would spare some of his Vanitys, he may easily be just to you. but mens Folly and extravagancys ingage them sometimes to mean things, and so I fear tis with Him. However I wil not desist my Application to Him, but it shall be so tenderly, that he shall have no Reason to be offended at the solicitation.
And now, Dear Sir, seing you have done me the Honour to inlist me amongst your Freinds give me leave to Glory in the Title, and with all the Respect and Sincerity imaginable to subscribe Myself
Your Most hartily affectionate Friend
And Most Obleidged Humble servant
W: MOLYNEUX

1798. Locke to Jean Le Clerc, 9 October 1694 (1767, 1805)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 28, f. 115v. Printed in King, pp. 319-20. It is among a number of additions made by Locke for the fourth edition of the Essay, but appears not to have been used for it. Answers a passage in no. 1767.
Libertie.
As to the determination of the Will we may take it under three considerations, 1 The ordinary and successive uneasinesses which take their turnes in the common course of our lives and these are what for the most part determine the will but with a power still of suspending. 2 Violent uneasinesse which the minde cannot resist nor away with. These constantly determin the will without any maner of suspension where there is any view of a possibility of their removeal. 3 A great number of litle and very indifferent actions which mix themselves with those of greater moment and fill up as it were the litle empty spaces of our time. In these the will may be said to determin it self without the preponderancy of good or evill or the motive of uneasinesse on either side. as whether a man should put on his right or left shoe first. whether he should fold a margent or noe in the paper wherein he is goeing to write a
― 160 ―
letter to his friend, whether he should sit still or walke or scratch his head whilst he is in a deep meditation. there are a thousand such actions as these which we doe every day, which are certainly voluntary and may be ascribed to the will determining it self, but there is soe litle thought preceds them because of the litle consequence that attends them that they are but as it were appendixes to the more weighty and more voluntary actions to which the minde is determind by some sensible uneasinesse and therefor in these the minde is determind to one or tother side not by the preferable or greater good it sees in either, but by the desire and necessity of dispatch, that it may not be hinderd in the pursuit of what is judgd of more moment by a lingring suspense between equall and indifferent things and a deliberation about trifles and in these the uneasinesse of delay is sufficient to determin and give the preference to one it matters not which side.
Memorandum This writ to Mr Le Clerc. 9º Oct. 94 in answer to his 12º Aug.

Dear Sir
The agreeing of the Waters with Mrs Clarke I think of soe great use to her health, that in my opinion she ought not to impute the pain she did for some nights feele in her back on the left side (for she must observe and send me notice of some other symptoms before she or I can conclude it was in her left kidney) to the drinking them. I rather judg it was from some disorder in the humors from the cold she then had and doe wish she would continue on the use of the waters and that with more constancy than she has hitherto observed It being that cheifly which in these kinde of remedies produces such great and beneficial effects. I wish she had sent you word too how her stomach and strength is and how they improve by her drinking. for pains in particular parts of the body though they be what the patient generaly most takes notice of and soonest complains of. yet they usualy, when noe thing more is known give the least light to a physitian espetialy if they be transient and
― 161 ―
moveable pains. My service to her and my love to my wife and the rest of the yonge good company with her at Chipley. I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant

London Oct 18
Dear Sir
In the begining of last July I received a kind letter from you, for which I returne you my thankes, and should have answered it long ere this had not at first other businesse, and afterwards my absence from Okeley (where I have bin the most part of this summer hindred me) but of late, since I resolved to come up speedily to Towne, I thought better (since I had so long deferred it) to returne you an answere by word of mouth, since I know†a you†b are commonly in Towne at this time of the year before the cold weather begins to
― 162 ―
be too intense, and I am sorry I came up 2 dayes after you were gone downe,†1 for it now seems a long time since I had the happynesse of seeing you here; but since I find my self so unluckily defeated of it, I will no longer deferre paying my thankes for your kind intentions of sending me the additions to your booke, which you tell me you ordered Mr: Churchill to send me, tho' I never received them, yet it had bin easy for him to have done it, since he sent so many copyes of them, to Oxon; but the matter is not much, since I have by the expence of but 2s: made my old edition as usefull to me as a new one, by takeing the paines either to write in the margin all the shortest additions and to past in the rest in their proper places, and by stitching up those sheets that cannot be so disposed of, and puting them at the end of the book:†2 and indeed your concerne for those who had the first Edition is highly commendable, since otherwise it would not have bin half so valueable, and usefull as the new one in which you have added, and altered so many things so much for the better, as well as for the clearing of divers passages which before seemed too short, and obscure, as allso for the correcting of some things (in which (as you your self with great ingenuity acknowledge) you had not at first so well considered, especially in that great question wherein the freedome of our wills consists,†3 whereby you have as well avoyded the errours of Mr: Hobs and the old Fatalists who denyed all freedome of will, as allso of such who supposed wee might will and doe every thing wee pleased.
But as for that Chapter, which you have writ concerning the Identity, and diversity of persons,†4 tho I must confesse it contains a great many new, and very usefull notions, yet give me leave to tell you; that by your makeing that concerne, or connexion of our present thoughts with those that precede, so as to repeat the Idea, of any past Action, with the same consciousnesse they had at first, and to tye them to the like Consciousnesse of present actions, as the sole thing that constitutes a personal Identity, and makes this person to be himself to himself, and to differ from another;†5 does very much perplex me, for tho I cannot positively see where the
― 163 ―
fault lyes; yet this supposition will not onely make a mad or drunken man another person, from himself when sober; but allso will make those that quite forget, (as some have done) all that ever they did in their lives, tho' not to be different men, yet different persons from what they were an hour agone, and consequently they will be as many different persons, as they make different reflections upon themselves, or their owne actions, without any concerne of what is past, which seems very hard if not impossible to conceive, so much I thought fit to tell you as to this head, tho' there are some other things of lesser moment which seem allso exceptionable, which are too long to be mentioned here, and therefore shall reserve them till wee meet.
But I shall now make bold to acquaint you with somewhat I am now about; which is that I have bin encouraged by some of our Oxford Divines; to reduce by way of Dialogue all that hath bin written pro, and con for, and against either natural, or reveald Religion, and in particular the Christian, wherein I shall fairly represent all the considerable objections against it, with the best answeres to them that either bookes or Freinds or my owne private thoughts can furnish me with: I have allready done the two first Dialogues concerning the Being, and nature of God, wherein I have made use of all that hath bin considerably urged by Dr: Cudworth, and Dr: Moor against Atheisme; and have allso vindicated the former of those great men from some scandals that have bin cast upon his memory; I have allso done a great part of the third concerning natural Religion, and shall conclude the first volume with the fourth Dialog: concerning the reasonablenesse (if not necessity) of some divine Revelation) this first volume will be finisht this winter; if I live, and enjoy my health as I doe now thankes be to God.†1
I have no more but to assure you that as for the Manuscript†a you mention of the Course of Chymistry†2 I doe not remember I ever so much as saw it, and if it were not in the little hair trunk among your Manuscripts†b I sent and which I allways kept by themselves, I know not what is become of it: it is a thing that can doe me no good for of all studyes I have had least occasion hitherto to concerne my self in Chymistry; as for what you write about the
― 164 ―
money I owe you pray let me know whether you expect any interest for the 10l: I have had so long of your<s,>†a for if you doe the 4l: 18s: I payd for Dr: Slades funeral will goe toward that <ba>llance,†a but if not it may goe towards the principal, and then I shall be quickly in a capacity to even all accounts; especially if you can send me word what you layd out for me in Holland for bookes; for which I still owne my self your Debtor, as I must ever be for many greater obligations which you have so generously layed upon
Your most faithfull, and obedient servant
J TYRRELL.
If you doe me the favour to write to me whilst I am in Towne, which may be this fortnight or 3 weekes yet, pray direct yours to the blew perruke in Catherine street.

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
As our friend Teut†1 is leaving here for your country I could not let him go without a letter from me. There is no occasion for me to recommend further to you a young man who is highly recommended to you by his own gifts. He will stay for some time in England, whether for business or study I do not know. By my order the bookseller Samuel Smith will deliver to you a copy of[p. 165] my Theologia Christiana, of which the publication is now complete.†1 If it is true that second thoughts are always better†2 this edition also should be somewhat better than the first. In a few places I wanted to say some things more clearly, and I have added some that seemed to be lacking; but these are few as I wanted this edition not to differ greatly from the first. Would that I had been permitted to discuss some things with you in person! I have no doubt that you have now received a letter I sent you some weeks ago with a packet of Grævius's enclosed in it. I had designed a lengthier letter for you at this time, but there were several letters to be written; so now, being prevented by time, I am compelled to be briefer. My Historia Inquisitionis has been condemned at Rome in a public decree by the Congregation of Cardinals, Inquisitors General throughout Christendom, and reading it is prohibited under the penalty contained in the Index of prohibited books. At this distance I can safely observe their thunderbolts and contemn them.†3 I hear that George Bull has taken up the pen against Episcopius;†4 I have not yet seen the book. However I wonder why he particularly singles out Episcopius,[p. 166] from whom he has learnt so much, as an adversary. But far be it from me to utter anything rashly about a book that I have not yet seen; when I have got it I shall read it without passion or prejudice. Good-bye, excellent Sir; my wife and daughter send you their best respects.
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH

(Latin) First of all, most excellent Sir, I hope that you are well and happy and that all goes well with you. I have no doubt that you have received the letter which I sent to you recently, enclosing one from our common friend Toinard. Our friend de Greve undertook to forward it through the Reverend Mr. van[p. 167] Limborch. Here is another letter from Toinard which I received yesterday. I shall be very glad if you will entrust me with the answer to both of them so that I may make good my promise to Toinard. Van Limborch's system of theology has again seen the light more copiously than before. Le Clerc's commentary on the remaining four books of Moses is in the press, as is also Bayle's historical dictionary in French, a prospectus of which I think you have seen already.†1 You will also see shortly Toinard's remarks on the new French translation of the four Evangelists which Bouhours, S.J., prepared but which the Society itself suppressed when it was scarcely published, all copies being stopped; one or two of them however fell into some men's hands.†2 The same fate befell the book by Hardouin published last year which he entitled Chronologiæ ex Nummis Antiquis restitutæ Prolusio de Nummis Herodiadum,†3 and in which he proclaims with incredible audacity that all the ancient Greek and Latin writers, with very few exceptions, are supposititious. The originators of this imposture are, he says, Frenchmen who lived four centuries ago. He rails very harshly mainly against Josephus, Strabo, and Suetonius. He contends that of the Latins Cicero, Pliny, Horace's Satires and Epistles, and Virgil's Georgics, alone are genuine. Julian's works and Cyril[p. 168] against Julian will also be published soon, emended and elucidated by Ezechiel Spanheim.†1 The latter has sent me excellent and copious observations on Callimachus; these will be added to my late son's edition,†2 which you will have as soon as it emerges into the divine borders of light.†3 Goodbye, eminent Sir, and love me your most affectionate friend. Utrecht 31 October (Dionysian period)†4 1694.
Your most respectful and devoted servant
JOANNES GEORGIUS GRAEVIUS.

(Latin) Oates 26 Oct 94
Honoured Sir,
Although I cannot entirely excuse my slowness in writing, yet I should not wish you to believe that I had advanced so far in negligence as to pass you by for nine whole months without a greeting. I not unwillingly confess that my silence has been too prolonged; as neither satiety of your letters nor any lessening of my goodwill towards you caused it I hope that it will find an easy forgiveness with you. Indeed I was ashamed to write to you again before I had read your book right through and could write you my opinion of it at large, or rather my congratulations on it. I can scarcely say how much pleasure and how much light I have obtained from your careful account of the Inquisition. It is so written as an account should be written, where nothing is invented or embellished for ostentation or delight so as the more easily to deceive heedless readers, but everything is established and supported by the[p. 170] trustworthiness of authors and the evidence of documents; so much so that those who are most concerned to refute will not venture even to murmur. You have dragged that work of darkness and the hidden practices of execrable cruelty out of their dens into so clear a light that, should any vestiges of humanity remain among those henchmen of the Church, or rather of Antichrist, they would at last feel shame for so unrighteous and so fearful a tribunal, where all law, human and divine, and justice, are set at nought. If, however, these infamies — infamies that cannot be rebutted — do not move them, at least to the reformed and to those rescued from this cruellest prison may it give courage against such inhuman tyranny, under whatever semblance of religion or concord it again seeks to creep in. Such is often the vehemence of disputants, and such the acuteness and long chain of arguments, that it is not for everyone to free himself when he is entangled in quibbles and deceits, and to judge the main issue of a controversy. Indeed if any unlearned commoner should read through your account he would feel at once that religion, charity, and justice were wanting there where every rule of equity and every way of pronouncing judgement throughout the world are violated, and deeds so inhuman, so cruel, and so very far from the spirit of the Gospel are perpetrated. I therefore consider the work worthy of translation into the vernacular of every people; for you have related everything in so orderly and so exact a way, and confirmed it by such unexceptionable[p. 171] witnesses, that nothing seems to be missing for teaching the vulgar, instructing the learned, and making everyone steadfast. If, as you tell me, anything pertaining to this subject meets you by chance in books that you did not see before your Historia was published please send it to me at your leisure if it is not too troublesome, for I intend to add everything that is to the purpose in the appropriate places in the margins of your book; as recently I inserted on page 276 the following extract from an itinerary [account of a journey] to the East:
(Latin) I eagerly await the lengthier letter that you have threatened me with, and if you take vengeance on my inaction in that way how will you reward my diligence? I am glad that your Theologia is to reappear so soon; I should readily have believed that few things in it needed to be corrected; however many you have added, they will be from the same source and will increase its value for readers. I know that it is highly esteemed among Anglican theologians. I do not know what will happen hereafter, for I hear that a few are about to embrace Calvinism and (so it is agreed among them) to write openly in defence of predestination.†1 How many persons and of what kind this new and so far private fellowship of a few will bring over to their side may not yet be conjectured; all things lie hidden and are performed in secret, and if the thing may be measured by the originators, whose names a certain friend whispered secretly in my ear, I think that it will not go far unless this design arises from elsewhere and has other promoters. Time will show whether this endeavour of a few persons will produce anything more than some private conversations among themselves and then we shall judge better what they want and at what they aim.
(Latin) I earnestly congratulate you on your so successfully drawing the Judaizing young woman back to the Christian faith. I should gladly receive from you, if your leisure permits, the whole story right down to the minute circumstances.[p. 173] Some persons to whom our friendship was known have asked me by letter for this narration. I should like to obtain it from you, however, not for their sake but to satisfy my own desire, and I will not impart to others anything that you include in what you write beyond what may be allowed by you. For I believe that some want to show by this example that those are ill advised who, for the propagation of the Gospel and the conversion of the Jews, urge that first and foremost certain dogmas must be accepted which others, regarding them as not necessary, consider should be left to the judgement of anyone who has grown up in the Christian faith. Nor perhaps do those wander far from the truth who are of opinion that nothing should be imposed on the consciences of Christians except what is contained in the clear and express words of Holy Writ. I should have readily believed that it would be so were not more attention paid to the Orthodoxy of factions than to the simple truth of the Gospel.
(Latin) But enough of this. I am truly sorry that there is so great a distance between us. If I were a neighbour you would have me knocking at your door every day to consult you; there are very few men of refined judgement with whom one can freely discuss one's speculations, whatever they may be, much less matters of religion. Mutual charity is wanting, candour is wanting, and as each spreads a veil over his own ignorance he does not readily pardon that of another. Nor may one put forward any doubtful matters unless one comes[p. 174] prepared to surrender oneself completely to them and to swear allegiance,†1 or else to go away a heretic laden with censures. I do not complain of this in my own case as if I had suffered anything from the unfair judgement of friends, but all the same it is pleasant to have someone close at hand whom one may consult openly and boldly about matters great and small. The second edition of my book on the Human Understanding is selling faster than I could have believed, nor, however heterodox it may be, has that dissertation as yet found an assailant.†2 Would that it was written in that language which would allow me to avail myself of your judgement of everything contained in that work. Some are urging a translation; the bookseller is seeking a translator and hopes that one will soon be found as I have no time; thanks to my health and to business affairs that spring up daily I have scarcely been allowed to read through your Historia except slowly and at odd times, although the pleasure of reading scarcely suffered me to tear myself away when I had started it. The bookseller however begs me to consent to review the translation in order to correct it if it has anywhere wandered from my meaning, a request which I can scarcely refuse. But why do I detain you with this when you are already wearied by the tedium of a lengthy letter? Goodbye and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
(Latin) Mrs. Cudworth or rather (Lady) Masham sends you her best wishes in return.
(Latin) Please give my warmest greetings to your dear wife and to your son and daughter, and with them to the Veens and Guenellons, Le Clerc, and the rest of our friends. I wrote to our friend Le Clerc last week.

1805. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 26 October/5 November 1694 (1798, 1820)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 85-6. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 76-7.
A Amsterdam le 5 de Novembre 1694
Je ne vous suis pas moins obligé, Monsieur, du soin que vous aviez pris de m'envoier le livre de Mr. l'Evêque de Bath et de Wels,†1 quoi que celui à qui vous l'aviez remis ne se soit pas aquité de sa commission. Je l'ai reçu, depuis cinq ou six jours, par une autre voie; mais dès que j'aurai l'autre exemplaire, je ne laisserai pas d'en remercier Mr. l'Archevêque. J'ai vu qu'il me traite extrémement mal, pour avoir accordé que le Passage de Gen. xxxvi. où il est parlé des Rois d'Idumée n'est pas de Moïse,†2 quoi que ce ne soit pas un sentiment particulier, et qu'il ait visiblement tort. Comme il m'avoit fait demander les feuilles de mon Ouvrage, par diverses personnes, et qu'il en avoit écrit à Mr. Limbourg, outre que Walford me dit ici qu'il l'estimoit beaucoup, je croiois qu'il étoit de mes amis, et je lui ai envoié ces feuilles en deux fois, avec des Lettres pleines de civilité, ausquelles je n'ai pas reçu de réponse; quoi que les premieres lui aient été renduës, il y a long-temps, car pour les autres il
― 176 ―
ne les a pas encore, à cause du vent contraire. J'ai des raisons de croire que Mr. Allix, ou même Mr. le Cene,†1 qui devroient être de mes amis pour toutes sortes de raisons, lui auront mal parlé de moi, pour faire les zelez. Comme il est des amis de Mr. Limbourg, à qui il a écrit quelques lettres depuis quelques années, j'ai crû devoir tâcher de me justifier dans son esprit, en lui écrivant à lui même une Lettre respectueuse, mais forte. Peutêtre qu'elle l'adoucira; et si elle ne le fait pas, il sera dans le tort, et l'on ne pourra m'accuser de rien. Je le prie instamment de me répondre, et je†a- ne croi pas-†a qu'il le refuse. S'il ne le faisoit pas, je publierois ma Lettre, et je me défendrois avec respect, mais vigoureusement.†2 Il prétend que ce n'est qu'aux Governors of the Church qu'il devroit être permis d'écrire sur la Bible, ou au moins à ceux qui prennent leur approbation; et il voudroit faire autoriser par toute l'Eglise Anglicane ses notes, et l'engager à en répondre; pour le moins, il dit qu'elle devroit faire quelque chose de semblable, dans sa Préface. Comme je suis dans un sentiment tout contraire, et que j'ai executé mon dessein très-differemment, j'apprehende aussi que cette seule diversité ne l'ait choqué. Je voudrois bien savoir, s'il étoit possible ce que l'on dit de son livre en Angleterre, et s'il y a apparence que l'Eglise Anglicane l'autorise. Je ne sai, si je dois attribuer à quelque bienveuillance le soin, que Mr. l'Archevêque semble avoir eu de me faire avoir ce livre; ou s'il l'a fait, pour me mortifier. Le premier me paroit plus vraisemblable, mais peutêtre que je me flattes. Mr. Allix publie par tout que mon Ouvrage m'a perdu, parce que je n'ai pas donné dans les ridicules visions, qu'il a débitées dans ses Réflexions sur les Livres de Moïse.†3 Il dit même que Mr. L'Archevêque, qui avoit, dit-il, accoûtumé de prendre mon parti, est réduit par là au silence. C'est ce que m'écrit Mr. Cappel, qui est un bon homme, et d'une trèsgrande sincerité. Mr. Allix, qui est un maître Normand,†4 et ami de Mr. l'Evêque de Bath et Wels, m'aura rendu quelque mauvais
― 177 ―
office auprès de lui, comme il m'en rend par tout, quoi qu'il m'ait de l'obligation. S'il étoit possible de le faire comprendre à ce Prélat, je croi qu'il seroit fâché de m'avoir traité si indignement, dans son livre. On dit même qu'il a dit que je mériterois d'être puni, pour avoir écrit de la sorte. Mr. Allix l'a publié ainsi. J'ai de la peine à le croire. J'ai crû devoir vous avertir de ces bruits, afin que si vous aviez occasion de parler à ce Prélat, vous prissiez vos measures là dessus. Je suis fâché de vous entretenir de semblables choses, mais j'ai peur que ces impertinences ne viennent aux oreilles de Mylord Privyseal, et qu'elles ne me fassent du tort dans son esprit. Il ne se passe ici rien de nouveau. On vient d'imprimer un livre de Franc. Junius de Pictura Veterum,†1 mais je n'en ai rien lû. L'Etymologicon de Vossius augmenté par son fils paroit,†2 et l'on verra, dans quelques mois, son Ouvrage de vitiis Sermonis.†3 Ses Oeuvres se publieront ainsi in folio volume, par volume.†4 Je suis, Monsieur, de tout mon coeur, Vôtre très-humble et très obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings overagainst the plough in little Lincolns Innersfields London.

1808. Locke to Nicolas Toinard, 5 November 1694 (1796, 1818)
B.M., Add. MS. 28, 728, ff. 30-1. Printed in Ollion, pp. 123-4. Sent through Grævius: no. 1809. Answers nos. 1777 and 1782; answered by no. 1828.
(English)
5. Nov. 94
Nisi par in te esset amicitia vix cogitando concipere poteris quantum mihi fuit gaudium ex tuarum epistolarum quas ad Grævium misisti lectione. Gratulor mihi vivum valentemque amicum. nam quod sis dum vivis memor nostri ex tuo ingenio meoque
― 180 ―
simul animo facile judico. Diuturni silentii tædium non minuit dies, nec ea quæ commercium literarum interrupit necessitas. Sæpe de te cogitanti subvenit mihi beneficiorum et suavissimæ consuetudinis memoria, inde auctum desiderium et nova vota. Harmoniam tandem aliquando prodituram in lucem maxime lætor, ex folio novissimè impresso contractiùs aliquanto volumen futurum non displicet, eo facilius lectorum oculis patebit, et a legentibus tractabitur. Quot-quot unquam specimina quæ olim mihi dederas viderunt, opus laudant, mirantur, et venale in officinis cupiunt. Cum ad urbem rediero, quo rarius jam proficiscor valetudine impeditus, nec diu moror, viris doctis et harum rerum curiosis, ostendam nuper impressum folium, et subscriptiones solicitabo. de successu non ausim ego quidquam promittere. Nuper enim expertus sum in Clerici commentario et periphrasi in Genesim quam lenti sunt homines ad subscribendum ipsi, et quam negligentes in procurandis subscripsionibus etiam illi qui operam suam promiserint. ego tamen omni studio, curâ et diligentiâ enitar, ut eo numero subscriptores invenias quo desideras. Si quinquaginta apud nos non invenero, de alio methodo distrahendi exemplaria cum prodierint qua fieri possit celeritate cogitabimus. Bibliopolas ad unum fere omnes tibi adversarios expectare debes, qui quantum possint impedient libri à
― 181 ―
bibliopolâ non impressi distributionem. Sed operis utilitas et methodi novitas omnia spero superabit impedimanta. Id ego testari possum, nihil mihi tam utile fuisse in perlegendo intelligendoque evangelio, quam illud exemplar quod jam a multis annis tuo beneficio possideo, et inter libros meos maximè semper feci. Leers Bibliopola satis me novit, si per illum vel quemvis alium quicquam miseris ad Benjamin Furly Rotorodami rectè ad me curabitur. Monet Grævius se ad te misisse Joannem Malelam. scire aveo an tuo rogatu. ego enim memor tui olim desiderii quamprimum prodiit liber ille, Amstelodamum Roterodamumque et plus una vice scripsi, ut inde ad Te <quantocius>†a mitteretur, et tandem ad ipsum Grævium scribens ea de re quæsivi anxius ut illud a me acciperes munusculum, ut qua in re potuerim me tui haud oblitum testarer. Marinum nostrum data occasione quæso meo nomine officiosissime salutes. Vale et ut facis me ama Tui Studiosissimum. Video Harmoniæ authorem aliis etiam lucubrationibus vacasse, non potest non esse eximium et amicis suis gratissimum quicquid tam docta et perita manus exaraverit Iterum Iterumque vale

(Latin)
5. Nov. 94
Were not friendship equally strong in you you could scarcely conceive how much pleasure there was for me in the reading of the letter that you sent to Grævius. I congratulate myself that my friend is alive and well, for from your disposition and my affection alike I deem it beyond dispute that[p. 180] as long as you live you are mindful of me. Time did not lessen the tedium of prolonged silence, nor did that necessity which has broken off correspondence. Often when I think of you the memory of your kindnesses and of our delightful intercourse succours me; hence increased yearning and new desires. I greatly rejoice that your Harmony will now at last see the light; that, in accordance with the most recently printed leaf, it will be somewhat reduced in size is not displeasing as it will lie open more easily to the eyes of readers and will be more easily handled by them when they are reading it. As many as have seen the sheets that you gave me formerly praise and admire the work, and wish that it was on sale in the shops. When I return to town, to which, being prevented by my health, I go only seldom nowadays, and where I do not stay long, I shall show the recently printed leaf to men of learning and those interested in these things, and shall invite subscriptions. I do not venture to make any promise about the result. For I have recently found in the case of Le Clerc's commentary on, and periphrasis of, Genesis how slow men are in subscribing themselves, and how negligent in procuring subscriptions even those are who have promised their help. Nevertheless I shall strive with all my devotion, care, and diligence, in order that you may find subscribers to the number that you require. If I do not find fifty in this country we shall think of some other way of selling copies as fast as possible when they appear. You must expect to find all the booksellers almost to a man adverse to you; they will hinder as much as they can the distribution of[p. 181] a book not printed by a bookseller. But the usefulness of the book and the novelty of the method will, I hope, overcome all hindrances. I can bear witness that nothing has been so useful to me in reading and understanding the Gospel as that copy which through your kindness I have now owned for many years and which I have always valued most highly among my books. Leers the bookseller knows me well enough; if you send anything through him or anyone else to Benjamin Furly at Rotterdam it will be forwarded to me without fail. Grævius informs me that he has sent you Joannes Malalas. I want to know whether it was at your request, for, mindful of your desire of old, as soon as that book appeared I wrote to Amsterdam and Rotterdam, and that more than once, so that it might be sent to you from there as soon as possible; and at length when writing to Grævius I enquired about it, as I was anxious that you should receive it as a small gift from me in order that I might testify in what way I could that I had not forgotten you. Please remember me to our friend the Sailor when you have an opportunity. Goodbye, and continue to love me your most affectionate servant. I see that the author of the Harmony has found time for other lucubrations; whatever so learned and skilful a hand has written cannot but be excellent and most acceptable to his friends. Good-bye again and again
JL
Address: A Monsieur monsieur Toinard.
Endorsed by Toinard: 5. Nov. 94.

Vir Ornatissime
Etsi plurima a te, grata omnia et eximia acceperim, nihil tamen unquam mihi acceptius fuit quam ultimæ tuæ quæ mihi quod a te quod a Toinardo nostro optarem attulerunt. Has inclusas quandoquidem ita velis ad illum curandas tibi cum maxima gratiarum actione mitto, rogoque ut proximis tuis mihi indicare velis quomodo ad illum literæ sint inscribendæ. Pretium quod pro Joanne Malela solvisti a Furleio Roterodamensi tibi reddi curabo, et Euripidem Cantabrigiæ editam quam primum Londinum hinc concesserim ad Furleium mittam ut ad te inde transmittatur. An eam qua apud te venditatur a nostratibus laudem mereatur haud scio, ab urbe enim pene exul valetudinis causa, humaniorum literarum expers, meis quibusdam meditationibus, dicam, an otio, insenesco. Quæ commentatus sum, non ea sunt quæ linguâ Romanâ†1 volitare
― 183 ―
per orbem literarium mereantur, optarem sane eo sermone scripta fuisse ut tuum de conamine meo judicium scire possim. Hoc si aliquando acciderit tuam exposco et liberam censuram. Disputationes theologicæ nostra ferè exercent præla. quibus si addas contentiones quæ ad rem civilem spectant, nihil pene restat alicujus momenti quod apud nos hoc tempore prodit. Editus est non ita pridem dissertatio†a in qua hujus sæculi eruditio cum illa antiquorum confertur.†1 Pensum sane non cujusvis humeris sustinendum. Hujus libelli auctor Wootton appellatur Juvenis sane et non indoctus, ideoque saltem placet plurimis quia in neutram partem inclinans modeste scripserit, et æquiore animo quam Peraultus†2 judicatur. Hæc non dixissem sed liber ipse pro vel contra se coram loqueretur si eâ scriptus esset linguâ quam tu calleres. sed prodiit nostro vernaculo sermone viris eruditis ignoto. Camdeni Britania jam sub prælo est. sed nec hæc Latine. Versionis antiquæ textus religiose servabitur. sed in margine adjicientur castigationes plurimæ et additamenta, quibus Britannia hæc nostra multum illustrabitur.†3 sed
― 184 ―
quorsum hæc ad te? Livius in usum Delphini†1 qualis tibi videtur? an emendum censes? Vellem ego illius Scriptoris optimam editionem tam quoad textus puritatem quam quoad commentarium vel notas. Tu qui de auctoribus ipsis antiquis eorumque editionibus optime judicas, quorum nullæ te latent mendæ, moneas rogo. Optimum nostrum Grevium multis nominibus mihi charissimum meo nomine quæso officiosissime salutes, cujus humanissimis literis brevi responsurus interim per te gratias ago. Vale vir Doctissime et perge amare
Tui studiosissimum
J LOCKE
(Latin)
5 Nov. 94
Accomplished Sir,
Although I have received many things from you, all welcome and all notable, yet nothing was ever more acceptable to me than your last letter, which brought me what I wished for from you and from our friend Toinard. Since so you wish I send you the enclosed for you to forward to him, for which I thank you most warmly; and I beg you to inform me in your next how letters to him should be addressed. I shall see to it that the price that you paid for Joannes Malalas is returned to you by Furly of Rotterdam, and as soon as I go from here to London I shall send the Euripides that was recently published at Cambridge to Furly, to be transmitted to you from there. I do not know whether it deserves the praise with which it was recommended to you by my countrymen, for, being almost an exile from the city on account of my health, and with no part in the humanities, I grow old in some contemplations of my own, or shall I say idleness? My notions are not such as to deserve to fly about the learned world in the Roman tongue,†1 [p. 183] though certainly I might wish that they had been written in that language so that I could know your opinion of my essay. If this should some day happen I beseech you to give me your censure, your free censure. Theological discussions occupy our presses for the most part; if you add to them disputes relating to politics, there remains almost nothing of any importance that is appearing at this time in our country. Not so long ago there was published a dissertation in which the learning of this age is compared with that of the ancients.†1 A task not to be borne by everyone's shoulders. The author of this book is called Wootton, a very young man and not unlearned; at all events he pleases many because, inclining to neither side, he has written temperately, and is judged to have written more equably than Perrault.†2 I should not have mentioned this but the book itself would have spoken to you for or against itself if it had been written in a language with which you are conversant; but it has appeared in our vernacular, which is unknown to scholars. Camden's Britannia is now in the press, but this also is not in Latin. The text of the old translation will be scrupulously preserved, but very many corrections and additions will be put into the margins, by which much light will be thrown on this Britain of ours.†3 But why all this to you? What is your[p. 184] opinion of the Livy in usum Delphini?†1 Do you think it is worth buying? I should like to have the best edition of that author as regards the purity of the text and the commentary or notes. You, who judge best of the ancient authors themselves and of their editions, no faults in which escape your notice: please advise me. Please give my kindest regards to our good friend de Greve, so dear to me for many reasons; I shall shortly answer his very kind letter; meanwhile I thank him through you. Good-bye, learned Sir, and continue to love
Your most devoted
J LOCKE
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Grævius professeur á Utrecht
1810. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 9 November 1694 (1584, 1848)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 75. Printed in Rand, p. 402.
Oates 9º Nov. 94
Madam
I hope My†a answer to Mr Clarkes enquiry about your farther drinking the waters came to your hand before I received yours of the 14th of October. I was glad by that to finde that you were still in a disposition to continue them and that there wanted only my direction in the case; Mr Clarke in his last informes me of your takeing them again and the good successe of it, the assurance
― 185 ―
whereof very much rejoyces me for noe body can be more concerned for your health and the health of all your family than I am. I know not what you intend by the remainder of the waters you have by you which you intended to drink, as if you did it that those might not be lost. I measure not your drinking of them by the number of your bottles but by the good I conclude they will doe you. And being of an opinion noe thing can be better than they are for you I would have them continued without any interruption for six weeks or two months togeather, soe that what went before you left them off goes with me for noething. I am glad to hear all your litle ones are well. my service to them, and particularly my love to my dear wife whom I thank for her kind letter which I will very speedily answer. I am
Dear Madam
Your most obedient humble servant
J LOCKE
All this family present their service to you and yours

1811. Robert Liddell to Locke, 10 November 1694 (2134)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 171-2. The writer was a younger son of Sir Thomas Liddell, bart., of Ravensworth Castle, Durham, and his wife Anne, sister of Sir Henry Vane the younger and Sir Walter Vane; he married Priscilla (d. 1680), daughter of William Kiffin (no. 382): T. Wootton, The English Baronets, 1727, i. 565-6; R. Surtees, History ... of Durham, 1816-40, ii. 212-13. He was one of fifteen men chosen on 15 August of this year to prepare bye-laws for the Bank of England: Luttrell, iii. 357. Locke mentions him in his Journal for the first time on 28 September of this year.
London 10 November 1694
Sir
I was very glad before, to heare of your saftie, and health, by my Enquirie; and now, much more, to have it confirm'd, by your owne information, of the 7 Instant. Which was most acceptable to me, and needed no other introduction, than comeing from yourselfe, whom I entreate, for the future, to have somuch confidence, and
― 186 ―
good Opinion of a New acquaintance, as to be assurd, there needs no Apology, for such kind freedom, which I take as an Obligation; or any Excuse, for what I esteeme no trouble, and the advantage, of being reckon'd among your friends and acquaintance, a compleate recompense, (to say no more) for the best services, I am ever like to be capable, to do for you; so do desire, you'l with my selfe look upon, all such Debt, Over Ballancd on your part. And this, not without appearance of reason, If you were a Person, that tooke your Measures from Event; or had gon purely upon the Opinion of others, without consulting your owne Judgment, and Reason; by which, so to determin yourselfe, as not to Waver, and as it were loose all former traces, which unsteady practice, disquiets many, in most actions of their lives. For our Banke stockes, are now unacountably run up, to 62 and 63; an advance too greate to hold, so that yesterday they sunke, to the first of these rates, and seemed declining, and its likely may continue to do so, as the parliament approaches;†1 to the delay of which, the other change, may in the greatest measure be attributed. But now, our Mightie Monarch, God Bles him, is, this morning safly arriv'd, from his renown'd victoryes abroad, to a land, I pray God Bless long, with peace and quietnes, at home. You will see, by the Advertisment in the Gazette how finely they hope to Coques†2 our unsighted Country Gentlemen, with hopes, of accommodation, and low Interest, for them.†3 The more penetrateing, thinke they see thorow it; it hardly will admit of doubt, their intention, to fall warmly upon them, one may perceive men, prepar'd for the Worke; unles powerfull Court applycations, and the glut of present immergencies, overrule all other considerations.†4 Upon the whole, I cannot retract, from our former sentiments, when we discours'd; onely, could foresight have reacht so far, in spite of all chances and contingences, as to have foretold, what it's now come to: both you and I, would have thought it our Interest, to have laid hold of this advantage, tho never so foolishly given us, by Opinion and unnaturall strains, rather then from any rationall proceeding, or steady improvement. But If any
― 187 ―
good Chances, are Ever, like to favour, such prudentiall sort of reasoners, as wee are, it's not unlikely, but we may have, ere long, the Oportunitie, to Enter the list againe on such termes, as may make some, that think themselves to have the present advantage, to wish they had kept to our smaller gaine, with les hazard, and confident presumtion; when, may be the time, for you to persue your intention, of engaging againe; which, I shall readily impart to you, according to the best of my little Skill. Tho, I do oftennest Observe, in this Mad Age, the most hardy, and rash more succesfull, than others, that are not so; nor can I, for this reason, prevaile with myselfe to be so; nor were I, would, it's like, the succes turne with me.†1 You will, I hope, of thinkeing yourselfe not troublesom, and I feare, into that, of my being so, who am still sincerly
Sir
Your most kind friend and Humble servant
ROB; LIDDELL.
Banke-stock is fallen since last night to £59.
Address: For John Locke Esquire [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]

1814. William Grigg to Locke, 15 November 1694 (1784, 1876)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 176-7.
Oxford Nov: 15th†a 94
Sir
My mother having now no hopes of making me a convert to her Opinions,†1 and Mr Firmin (who has of late been very sollicitous for me) having given us reason to hope the Archbishop is willing to be kind to me, She has at last given me leave to follow my own judgement; and is content I should gratefully accept whatever favour may be conferr'd upon me and thereby ease her of a great part of the Burden which now lies very heavy on her. I must needs own I am very glad of the liberty she allows me, for the necessity of spending beyond our incom has been very irksom to us, and tho I have met with a great deal of Kindness in this place, yet some of my Schoolfellows have given me frequent occasion of applying that in the Poet,
Nil habet infælix Paupertas durius in se
Quam quod Ridiculos homines facit.†2
Pardon me Sir, if I think it both my Duty and my Interest to write to you upon this occasion, for you have given me so many assurances of your Goodwill to me, that I cannot doubt of your Kind assistance and I'm sure I ought to embrace all opportunitys of paying you the Respects which are due to you upon very many accounts. Next week (God willing) I intend to be in town, the Bishop of Ox:†3 who has been extreamly civil to my mother, and is so to me for her sake, having given me leave to wait upon him, where my chief business will be to thank my father's friends for their generous concern for me, among whom there is none to whom I am more beholden than to yourself, nor is there any among the
― 191 ―
many, whom you have oblig'd, with more sincere Respect than I am
Honoured Sir
Your very humble servant
W GRIGG

Sir
I would have answered your last long before this time, had not my Ilnes prevented me. I returne you many thanks for your kindnes in moderating the affair beetween Mr Bonville and me which was occasined through a mistake. and shall be avoided for the future. The interest shall be payed in yearly or half yearly as you shall appoint, for it is the same thing to me, having money lying ready in London — in your last you mentioned some of Dr. Lightfoots works as yours. I have look'd with care after them but cannot any exept his works entire in 2 vollumes in folio.†1 which were my husbands, his name with the prize being written with his own hand on the spare leaf before the little-page. I forbear to send the other book the Corpus Juris civilis till I have your answer to this of Dr Lightfoot. as to the thirty pounds you writ of, I have some reason to think it payed, having found a note concerning just that summ payed by my husband 3 or 4 years since. Sir I give you many thanks for all your favours to me and mine and for the assurance of your kindness you promised in your last. 1816. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, [22? November 1694] (1794, 1922)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 114-15. Printed in Rand, Shaftesbury, pp. 299-300. Date from Lock's endorsement.
London the 27th:
Mr Lock
I know not whether itt will bee possible for mee to wayt on my Lady Masham, and visit you this seson: but this I am sure of; I cannot possibly have more Desire to doe itt then I allready have. I needed nothing to convince mee, that what Good I was able to doe in the world, was better and more worthyly bestow'd in serving a Person or two, like Some that live but in a Corner of Essex, then in serving of a Croud of such People as are now making the great Doe†1 that is made in the World; and whome I am now in the midst of, as my ill Fortune has order'd itt. the greatest part of what I doe in the world is not because I hope any thing; but because I think I must be Doing. I can assure You I doe not act out of any Friendship to the Age, or to Mankind such as they are att present. were there no Principle to Engage mee to serve them, besides their own Meritt, besides their Characters, besides the opinion I had of them and the Esteem I bore them; upon my word itt would fare ill with them, for any thing I were ever likely to doe in their behalf, tho' in ever so pressing an occasion. I Fancy that I am not apt to make to my self too flattering a Picture of the world. And I beleive that whatever this Publick that You talk of, is like to have of my service; Itt will
― 193 ―
never have over much of my Respect: nor shall I bee apt to fall into any Gross Errours on that account. All I know is, that there are Some whome I have a Reall Respect for. And if I were now att liberty to doe what Respect and Inclination most led mee to; I should quickly shew my Forewardness to accept of the Invitation that is made mee.
If you beleive my sincerity in this; You will make my Excuse for mee: If otherwise; all I can say besides will signify nothing, whilst I am kept here, and can doe no more then write. But I have more Confidence in You, and in my own Character as itt stands with You, then this comes to. for if You know this it is enough (and that I cannot doubt of:) that I am very sincerely
your Reall Friend and Humble Servant
A: ASHLEY
Address: For Mr Lock [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]

1817. Locke to William Molyneux, 23 November 1694 (1797, 1829)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 89-91. Answers no. 1797, answered by no. 1829; see also no. 1838.
Oates, 23. Nov. 1694.
Sir,
You speak of my book, in such terms, that had I not convincing arguments that you are not a man of complements, I should a little suspect your civility border'd very much on them in this case. But there are so few of them to be found, that you think you cannot speak too highly of the endeavours of one who pursues truth unbyassedly, and chooses not his opinions first, and then seeks arguments to support them. Upon that account I admit of whatever you please to say; but withal give me leave to assure you, that in the performance it self, I see nothing but what any one might have done, who would have sat down to it with the same love of truth, and indifferency, that I did. However, I cannot but be pleased that you think so well of it: For whether your friendship to me bribes your judgment, or whether your good opinion of my Essay adds to your
― 194 ―
kind thoughts of the author; I find my account both ways, and should think my self well rewarded for my pains in this single purchase. But, Sir, will you not pardon so lawful a desire, in one that loves you, if I ask, Shall I never have the happiness to see you in England?
Mr. Churchill, my bookseller, sends me word by the last post, that he has sent you the six copies that you sent for, and advice of it. I sent to him a project of a new reduction of the year by Dr. Wood,†1 to be sent with the copy of my Essay to you. The author gave me it himself, and I thought it might possibly please you, if you had not seen it before. This, with the supernumerary cuts, I order'd him to send you, will with the books, I hope, come safe to your hands. The mentioning of those cuts puts me in mind again of your civility, which I see studies all manner of ways of expressing it self.
You see, by this liberty I take with you, that I am past terms of complement with you, that is, I use you as one I look on to be my friend, with a freedom of good offices, either to receive or do them, as it happens. Look upon me as such, I beseech you, and believe that I am, with the utmost sincerity,
Sir,
Your most affectionate friend, and most humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.

1819. Edward Clarke to Locke, 27 November 1694 (1813, 1821)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 92-3. Printed in Rand, pp. 403-4.
London November the 27th. 1694.
Deare Sir
I am exceedingly obleiged by your Kind Letter of the 23th, and what you therein Writt to My Daughter Betty etc: But am surprised that I heare nothing at all from you since the 15th, that I sent you by the Post a Lease to bee Executed by you, which came from Mr. Stratton to mee, Pray lett mee Know whither you have received it or not; I put it into the Post-house with my own hand and hope it went safe to you, if you Return it to mee in a few dayes, I shall bee able to send it back to Mr. Stratton by Mr. Codrington of Bristoll, who is now in Town, and goes down againe the latter end of this, or the Begining of the next weeke: I must Begg allsoe your Direction in the following Case; Mrs. Clarke Writes mee, That Little Molly†1 has had a sharpe uggly humour breakeing out all over her Face, and has Runn much, but is gone off without leaveing any scarr's or markes, other then Rednesse, and that about ten dayes since it swell'd and gathered under her Chinn, and about her Throate, and it was verie hard and much swell'd in those Parts untill it broke and began to Runn; Mrs. Clarke hopes by such a Good Dyett, and such Purgeing, or other Directions, as you shall thinke proper, the Child will doe verie well againe, Shee Beares it verie Patiently, and is willing to take any thing; my Wife has

Your most Affectionate Faithfull servant
