1820. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 27 November/7 December 1694 (1805, 1832)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 87-8. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 78-9.
A Amsterdam le 7 de Decembre 1694.
Depuis que je me suis donné l'honneur de vous écrire, Monsieur, j'ai reçu réponse de l'Evêque de Bath et Wels, à qui j'avois écrit, sur la maniere dont il a parlé de moi; et j'ai sujet d'être entierement satisfait de sa reponse, où il me fait une espece de réparation, et offre de faire ce que d'honêtes gens choisis pour arbitres jugeront à propos, si je ne suis pas content de ce qu'il me dit. Je lui récris pour le remercier, et lui dire que je suis entierement satisfait, pourvu que, dans une seconde Edition, il change les termes, dont il se sert, et qu'il ait la bonté de desabuser ceux qui lui parleroient desavantageusement de moi, croiant lui faire plaisir. En cas que vous le voiyez, en venant à Londres, et que vous en vinssiez sur cette matiere, faites moi la grace de lui témoigner que je me louë beaucoup de la maniere obligeante et génereuse, dont il en a usé envers moi, et de lui dire que je ne lui donnerai jamais de sujet de changer les bons sentimens qu'il a de moi. J'avois deviné, lors que j'avois dit que Mr. Allix m'avoit joüé un mauvais tour, puisque je vois, par la lettre de ce bon Prélat, que Mr. Allix, à qui il avoit montré sa Dissert. sur l'Auteur du Pentateuque, avoit loüé sa modération, qui assurément n'y paroit point à mon égard. Le P.Simon avoit accusé Mr. Allix d'avoir composé en partie la Diss. de l'Inspiration, qui est
― 198 ―
dans les Sentimens de quelques Theologiens de Hollande etc.†1 Cela est entierement faux, et cet écrit ne ressent point l'esprit bourru et embarrassé du Docteur. Cependant pour s'en disculper, depuis ce temps-là, il a dit le plus de mal de moi qu'il a pû. Je le lui pardonne, et je prie Dieu qu'il en fasse de même, quoi que je haïsse extrémement cette vilaine maniere d'agir. J'aurai soin de faire envoier à vôtre adresse un exemplaire de la Vie du Cardinal de Richelieu,†2 qui paroit à présent, et que le Libraire a envoiée à Londres. Elle vous divertira, car il y a une infinité de choses, qui n'avoient jamais été dites en François, et le tour en est ferme et hardi, tel que doit être le style d'un vèritable historien. Il ne s'écrit presque point de livres aujourdhui, de cette maniére. On pallie, ou l'on excuse tout dans ceux que l'on aime, et l'on exaggere excessivement les défauts de ceux que l'on hait. L'on fait un heros de celui, dont l'on écrit la vie, comme si faire un panegyrique et écrire l'histoire étoit la même chose. C'est ainsi qu'a fait l'Evêque de Nîmes, dans la vie du Cardinal Ximenès,†3 dont il fait un saint homme, malgré que l'on en ait. Un autre a écrit cette même vie,†4 après lui, mais c'est un Roman détestable. Il ne paroit rien ici, qui vaille la peine, et le froid, qui commence assez fortement, rallentira encore plus les presses. Je prie Dieu, Monsieur, qu'il vous conserve, et je suis de tout mon coeur tout à vous
J LE CLERC.
Mr. Limbourg vous répondra bien tôt, et vous dira en abregé ce qui s'est passé dans la conversion de la Demoiselle, dont vous avez ouï parler.†5

1821. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 29 November 1694 (1819, 1833)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 177-8. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's signature and the address.
Locke, Freke, and Clarke, if they had not done so already, began now to work together for political ends. Freke and Clarke constituted 'the College', the word perhaps representing the Dutch collegie; from February 1695 Clarke is generally called the Grave or occasionally the Grave Squire, or the Squire; Freke, the Bachelor; Locke at Oates is occasionally 'the Castle'. These were private names; there was no formal group; though other men, and notably Sir Walter Yonge, might join Freke and Clarke in discussion they were not admitted to the basic friendship. So far as the surviving letters provide evidence the College was vigorous politically until early in 1697; it then becomes less active, and is mentioned for the last time in 1701. In this period there are letters addressed by Locke to the College and to Clarke; and letters to Locke written by Freke and signed by him and Clarke or by him alone, and other letters to Locke written by Clarke alone; the letters from Locke, where the addresses survive, are addressed to Clarke; those to him are addressed and franked by Clarke. A few of the letters are entirely political; others are concerned with Locke's and Clarke's private affairs; but so many contain both political and private matter that the best course appears to be to bring them all into the Clarke sequence. The most recent letter from Freke is no. 1032.
The College is occasionally mentioned as if it were a building: e.g. in nos. 1907, 1911: there is, however, no reason to suppose that more is meant than the two men, Freke and Clarke.
Nov: the 29th 1694
Sir
Mr Clarke's attendance in Parliament and at his office keeps him soe continually employd that he has scarce time to eat.†1 last night he came not from the House till 7 at night and he expects to sitt as late this day and has therefore Commanded me to supply his place in writing to you to acquaint you that yesterday morning he gott an Audience of the Gentleman at the great House in Lincolns Inn Fields†2 who enquired with great concern for you and asked when you would be in Town because he has great occasion to discourse with you on matters of importance. Mr Clarke told him he knew not when you designd to be here nor whether your health would
― 200 ―

permitt you to come, at which he exprest great trouble and desired Mr Clarke to write to you to beg you to come up if possible and as soon as possible
I believe there are many things of weight wherein he desires <your>†a opinion and advice but one of them I take to be Concerning a project for raising of mony this Sessions which as near as I can state it is this
The summ to be raised is five millions for which tis proposed that twelve pence in the pound per annum shall be charged on all Land for ten years the whole product of which making (as they account it) 5 millions shall be Coind in pieces of silver (†b of a small bulk) to which shall be given severall denominations from five pounds to a hundred (or higher if thought fit) but none less than five pounds. That these pieces shall be made Current mony for ten years and that of them five hundred thousand pounds a year shall be brought in broken and destroyd till the whole be taken up again
That to prevent Counterfeiting these pieces shall be Coind in the fashion of a Starr (with such impression on them as shall be thought fit) and then broken in two and one part to remain in the Tower (as the Counterpart of a Tally do's in the Exchequer) to compare with the part given out when it shall be returnd or when ever else there shall be occasion
There are other things offerd in the project that relate to the dispersing of these pieces or Tallys but in regard they propose to have them made Current by an Act of Parliament I think those things will not deserve soe much consideration but the design it self (of which I have given you as full an account as I can) is a matter that I doe not wonder that the Gentleman desires to hear you upon who are soe well able to speak to it and I know you would lay a great obligation on him if you would give your self the trouble to come and discourse him fully about it†1
And Mr Clarke and I shall take it as noe small favour if you would bestow some thoughts on this subject and communicate them to us in which besides the service you will doe us you will likewise contribute much to the publick service and that I am
― 201 ―
confident will be a sufficient inducement to you to bestow some pains on it
I am likewise comanded by Mr Cla<rke>†a to answer your Quæré touching the Lottery†1 and for the first whose name its best f<or him>†a to take your <Transferd>†b Tickets in? I think tis absolutely indifferent: for when the <Trans>fer†a Tickets are given out who ever has the possession of them and shall at the time <of pa>yment†a bring them to the pay office is by the Act of Parliament to receive the mony there being no receit to be given for it but one half years Ticket for the benefitted and one years Ticket for the unbenefitted Tickets to be Cutt off: for the Benefits are to be paid half yearly and 32 Transfer Tickets given and the unbenefitted to be paid yearly and onely 16 Transfer Tickets given to entitle the bearer to receive them and the whole 32 for benefits to be in one paper or parchment and for the whole 16 for unbenefitted in one paper or parchment and as any payment is made one to be cutt off.†2
Now for your other Question The Price of Blanks is various but I have heard of none sold above six pounds ten shillings the Ticket and I have heard of some sold under and I my self have been offerd them at six pounds four shillings and six pence but I was unwilling to give above six pounds because I have heard they have been sold soe and under though I would not part with the Blanks I have if any body would give me eight pounds a piece
I shall add noe more but that if you can gratify your friends with your company in Town I hope you will not deny them that satisfaction and to encourage you I will promise that the Colledge shall never want a good Apple py†3 for you and that you shall not be
― 202 ―
lookt askew upon for Cutting what and how you please of it either by
Sir
Your obliged friend and humble servant
JOHN FREKE
or
EDW: CLARKE:

1822. William Stratton to Locke, 1 December 1694 (1812, 1864)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 92-3.
Bristoll the 1th: Des: 1694
Dear Cosin
I have hear Inclosed sent your Account of what was dew to you last Ladyday I gave you sum reson of my defering for I had not all Ladyday rent in my hands, and I thought it a good argument to prevaile with your tenants that wear behind that you had sent for your rent, allthough I had duned them suffisiently before, as for the two that rents Belton and Buckhill tenements they pay Well enow but it is sum others and as for your mony being thirty nine pounds fourtene shilling one peny farthing, I would Return it upp to you by a hand or two that is safe but my selfe or my Brother Chapman†1 Expects to have mony In London the latter End of this munth and It will be a kindnes to us to pay you theare I would not defer soe long if it wear not for this conveniency, you will find Joseph Barns Bills riseth hie the last year but I could not help it for the hous must bee keept dry and the well was sum Charge and the kings tax being great all ads to the charge, this years charge I hope will be mutch les, I desire you to seale the lease that our Mayor†2 Brought up, and dout not but it was delevered to mr Clarke, for I have satisfacktion that the lives are all liveing soe if you seale it and send it to mr Thomas Edwards his Chamber In Elm Court In
― 203 ―
the middle Temple he will Bring it doun at the end of the term, John Veale cumplaines of the colepits that are not filled they are dangerous and If his cattell should miscarry he will expeckt satisfacktion from you, It is Edward Taylers Duty to fill them up. but he is soe poore that I thinke he is but one step above the parishes Releife, and know not how to have it don by him, If you are content to doe it, it will be best to let it out now in the Dead of the winter to be don at agreate,†1 and if you order me I shall taske it as cheape as I can, as for the way Thorow Wills his ground I have discoursed Benjamin Smith and he saith he reaped corn in your Ground 50 years past and he conceives that you have noe way Thorow Wills his Ground but onely on suferance, and therfore conceive it best to make the way better then it is out of the hie way, I was last weake on purpose at Buck hill Indevering to bring Barns upp to the old Rent, but cannot, and uppon dew consideration thought it best to continew him for two years longer althought I abate him 20s per yeare for I find him suffisient and soe I have agreed with him and have considered what it may be for one to goe forth, and another to cum In, for others will not be content it may be with what you should consent to be don about the house as well as the grounds, for Sledg did cumplaine mutch of the outward Bounds I doe les for you then if it was my oun Sir I am your faithfull humble ser:
WILLIAM STRATTON
Address: For Mr John Locke
Endorsed by Locke: W: Stratton 1 Dec. 94 Answered 28
1823. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 2/12 December 1694 (1804, 1826)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 91-6. There is a copy by van Limborch in the Amsterdam University Library (MS. R.K. III D 16, ff. 170-7). It has some slight divergences from the letter that was sent; two of them are noted here. The part of the letter that relates to the Inquisition and the part of the postscript that relates to Tillotson are printed from the copy in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 358-62; the rest of the letter and the whole of the postscript, from the letter sent, in King, 1830, ii. 347-75. A Dutch translation, based on the Amsterdam copy, of the account of the discussion with the young woman was published by J. de Goede in 1723 (2nd ed., 1735) with a
― 204 ―
Dutch translation of van Limborch's De Veritate Religionis Christianæ (Orobio) and other matter: Barnouw, Van Limborch, p. 33 n. The letter may have taken some days to write. As no. 1824 was enclosed in it, it was probably dispatched on or a little after 3/13 December. Answers no. 1804; answered by no. 1826.
In his discussion with Orobio van Limborch was concerned to demonstrate the Messiahship of Jesus from passages in the Old Testament; the arguments in the present discussion based on the Resurrection and the Descent of the Holy Spirit are new. The passages in the De Veritate that are cited in the present account can be traced readily. For the two discussions see Barnouw, pp. 55-6, 134-5.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Magna cum voluptate tuas accepi et legi: Etsi enim affectum erga me tuum nullatenus fuisse imminutum plene persuasus essem, nihilominus post tam diuturnum silentium literas tuas videre non potuit non esse gratissimum. Historiam meam Inquisitionis calculo tuo probari, est quod mihi gratuler. Scio judicium tuum esse candidum ac limatissimum. In præconiis verò quæ addis agnosco propensissimum tuum erga me affectum, qui omnia quæ probas vero majora tibi repræsentavit. Ego veritati litare studui, et tribunal illud ita exhibere, prout ipsi Doctores Pontificii, imo Inquisitores, id nobis depingunt. Scio quidem, quando sparsim in ipsorum libris procedendi modus describitur, et fucatis coloribus palliatur, non ita patere ejus injustitiam et fœditatem, quam quando omnia simul inter se connexa nudè, sine fuco, omnium oculis exponuntur. Non crediderim quenquam, ne quidem ex acerrimis Inquisitionis
― 205 ―
patronis, me malæ fidei insimulaturum, et si quis id ausit, statim autorum, quorum nomina margini passim adscripsi, testimoniis redargui poterit. Sed quam dispari fato libri prodeunt! Tu historiam meam dignam judicas, quæ in cujusque gentis linguam vernaculam traducatur: Romæ vero xix. die mensis Maji hujus anni edicto Cardinalium, in tota Rep. Christiana Inquisitorum Generalium condemnata est, ejusque lectio severissime prohibita sub pœnis in indice librorum prohibitorum contentis. Decretum hoc, quo et alii libri condemnantur, triduo post, videl. xxii. Maji, fuit publicatum et affixum ad valvas basilicæ principis Apostolorum, palatii S. Officii, et in acie campi Floræ,†1 ac aliis locis solitis et consuetis Urbis. Sed mitiorem sententiam quis ab Inquisitione exspectet contra historiam, quæ artes ac crudelitates ipsius, quas occultas omnibusque ignotas esse cupit, e tenebris erutas palam totius mundi oculis exponit, tribunalque hoc non sanctitate venerandum, sed injustitia, crudelitate, fraudibus et imposturis execrandum exhibet? Aliter enim, si vere describatur exhiberi nequit. Quæ ego
― 206 ―
ex aliis autoribus, quos postmodum videre mihi contigit, annotavi, et quæ in posterum in aliis, qui forte mihi ostendentur, reperiam, libentissime ad te mittam. Vidi quæ ex itinerario Du Mont annotasti, quæ optime illo quem designasti loco margini historiæ meæ adscribi possunt. Sed, ut ingenue dicam, valde dubito an narratio illius vera sit. Malæ fidei ipsum neutiquam accuso: Sed fieri facile potest, ut peregrinatores non diu in regione aliquâ commorantes, incidant in homines legum et consuetudinum patriarum non admodum peritos, nonnunquam etiam mendaces, ex quorum ore quædam veritati minus consentanea sine accuratiore investigatione annotant: qualia multa in itinerariis eorum, qui patriæ nostræ mores et consuetudines describunt, observavi. Ratio dubitandi est: Quia video omnes Doctores Pontificios, nec non omnia decreta ecclesiastica sollicite admodum urgere, arcana Confessionis non esse patefacienda, imo ne hæresin quidem sub sigillo Confessionis revelatam: solummodo Sacerdotibus injungunt, ne hæresim confesso absolutionem impertiantur, sed omnibus quas potest†a rationibus hortentur, ut in judicio coram Inquisitoribus juridicè confiteatur. Scio quidem, non omnia quæ legibus præcipiuntur exacte in praxi Inquisitionis observari, et sub specioso confessionis non revelandæ
― 207 ―
prætextu simpliciores inescari posse, ut ingenue, etiam quæ Inquisitoribus ignota sunt, confiteantur, quæ a Sacerdotibus porro Inquisitoribus revelari possunt, neque a tali impostura tribunalis illius sanctitatem abhorrere credo: Attamen quia omnes ipsorum Constitutiones, Instructiones et leges, omnia illius Ecclesiæ decreta contrarium præcipiunt, non id affirmare ausim, nisi autor sit probatus, cujus nec peritia nec fides in dubium vocari possit. Quare loco, quem mihi suggessisti ex itinerario Du Mont, addi posset; si vera sit illius narratio, exinde evidenter liquere, Inquisitorum praxin sæpe adversari Inquisitionis Instructionibus et legibus; Inquisitoresque unice tantum spectare, qua ratione miseros captivos per fas et nefas decipiant, atque ita fraudibus irretitos misera morte perdant. Verum de his satis.
(English) Virginis nuper judaizantis, et ad fidem Christianam feliciter retractæ historiam, quam petis, ad minutas usque circumstantias deductam, non possem nisi multis paginis comprehendere, collationi enim isti, per quinque dies continuatæ, ultra viginti horas impendi.†1 Sed nec argumenta singula recensere opus est; multa enim paucissimis tantum verbis indicasse suffecerit. Quæ te maxime desiderare scio accurate describam: inde facile dubitationum fontes
― 208 ―
ipse deteges, et quâ methodo alii cum ipsa frustra disputaverint intelliges. Hortatu Veenii nostri, post habitas aliquot a tribus ecclesiæ publicæ†1 concionatoribus irritas collationes, a matre virginis illius, mihi antea nunquam visæ, ad illam vocatus sum. Primo congressu, qui fuit duodecimus Aprilis, seu Paschalis secundus dies,†2 dixi, intellexisse me, aliqua ipsi circa veritatem religionis Christianæ dubia esse enata. Fassa est, petiitque sibi e lege Mosis probari, mandatam fuisse Israeli fidem in Messiam. Respondi ego: Ex Lege quidem divinitatem Euangelii probari posse, esse autem alia argumenta quibus illa adstruatur: Dominum Jesum Joan. Cap. V. plura ad probandam doctrinæ suæ veritatem argumenta proferre; videl: testimonium Joannis Baptistæ, miracula sua, et tandem Mosis testimonium: Consentaneum esse, ut prius agamus de miraculis D. Jesu, et historiæ Novi Testamenti veritas, quæ miraculorum Christi narrationem continet, adstruatur; qua probata accedamus ad examen vaticiniorum de Christo, quæ in Mose et prophetis exstant. Mirabatur hoc meum responsum, credebatque me methodo non legitimâ cum ipsâ velle agere. Itaque respondit, Petrum, postquam locutus esset de gloria in monte ostensa,
― 209 ―
addere, quod habeamus sermonem propheticum, quem appellet firmiorem 2. Epist. 1. 19. Regessi ego, Petrum utraque conjungere: nos Petrum imitaturos: sed hanc esse legitimam methodum, ut primo inquiramus argumenta quibus divina Christi missio adstruatur; exinde quid Moses et prophetæ de ipso prædixerint. Cum illa urgeret: Si Israeli olim fides in Messiam venturum mandata sit, oportere ut in lege Mosis id mandatum exstet; quia omnia quæ Israeli mandata sunt lege Mosis continentur: Ego prolixe meam de fide Israelis in Messiam venturum sententiam exposui; perinde uti in Collatione mea cum Don Balthasare feci. Illa non sine admiratione hoc meum responsum sibi prorsus inexspectatum audivit: et hac occasione quorundam suorum, qui cum ipsa contulerant, rigorem incusavit, qui omnes, non tantum gentiles et Judæos, sed et discrepantes a se Christianorum cœtus orco adjudicent. Ego arrepta hac occasione prolixius sententiam meam de mutua dissentientium Christianorum tolerantia exposui: quæ valde placere videbatur. Addidi, quid sentirem de gentilibus cognitione Euangelii nunquam illustratis: tum de Judæis, quibus veritatis euangelicæ lucem affulsisse manifestum est: agnovi tamen discrimen aliquod inter Judæos Apostolorum prædicationem, virtute spiritus peractam et miraculis confirmatam, respuentes; et hodiernos, quibus Euangelium
― 210 ―
sæpe ab imperitis et inidoneis prædicatur, quibusque multa a Christianis scandala objiciuntur. Quæ etiam fusius in Collatione mea cum Orobio legi possunt. Tandem ut sermonem meum ad ipsam converterem, et ex ipsius ore elicerem, hic æternæ ipsius salutis negotium agi: dixi, esse alios qui postquam jam in Jesum Christum crediderunt rursus ab eo deficiunt: tales non posse Christum rejicere, quin simul omnia ipsius beneficia abnegent, sibique nihil cum Christo esse aperte profiteantur. Hoc cum legitime sequi agnosceret, dixi: hic est status in quo tu nunc es: tu agnovisti Christum Dominum tuum: non potes ergo ab ipso recedere, nisi abnegatis omnibus ipsius beneficiis: Si itaque religio Christiana sit vera, non potes ea deserta amplecti Judaismum, nisi amissione æternæ salutis. Quod cum legitime consequi admitteret: addidi: quoniam nunc agnosceret, quantum ipsius intersit scire utrum religio Christiana sit vera, necne, orare me, ut, quam chara ipsi esset æterna salus, mecum attente et in timore Domini expenderet argumenta, quibus religionis Christianæ divinitatem essem adstructurus. Illa denuo urgebat, initium disputationis esse faciendum ex Lege Mosis, vaticiniaque pro Messia ex illa esse petenda. Hic diu hæsimus, qua methodo procedendum sit. Ego, ut meam methodum probarem, dixi, plerisque prophetiis duplicem inesse
― 211 ―
sensum, literalem et mysticum: me ultro fateri, literalem olim suum habuisse complementum, verum in typo; mysticum in Christo esse impletum. Cum autem exinde liqueat, prophetias olim suum habuisse complementum, licet non secundum omnem literæ vim et ἐνέργειαν, ipsam facile videre, non potuisse olim Israelem mysticum illum sensum distincte cognoscere, sed illum ex eventu debuisse innotescere: Ita et nunc, seposita historiæ Novi Testamenti veritate, non posse me a priore demonstrare, quis sensus mysticus sub prophetiis illis lateat; sed necessario præcedere oportere probationem veritatis historiæ Novi Testamenti; qua adstructa, me ex eventu probaturum, vaticiniis illis sublimiorem inesse sensum mysticum, eumque in Christo secundum omnem literæ ἐνέργειαν esse impletum. Addebam obiter, hac eâdem methodo Apostolos in suis adversus Judæos disputationibus, quæ in Actorum libro exstant, esse usos. Cum illa contrariam methodum urgeret, dixi: Si evidentibus argumentis constet Jesum Christum a Deo esse missum, an non in ipsum esset credendum, etiamsi nec Moses, nec prophetæ, quicquam de ipso prædixissent? Cum hic aliquatenus hæsitaret, ostendi, ut fides alicui habeatur, nihil aliud requiri, nisi ut divina ejus missio probetur, etiamsi nulla de ipsius adventu exstent vaticinia. Id probavi exemplo
― 212 ―
Mosis, cujus adventum nusquam prædictum legimus; non tamen, quoniam missionem suam divinam evidentibus comprobavit miraculis, Judæi in eum gravantur credere. Hic illa mihi narravit, quid multi suorum concionatorum de hac materia sentirent, quæ meæ sententiæ non admodum consentanea videbantur. Rogavi ego, ut non respiceret aliorum hominum, qualescunque sint, dogmata et theses, sed solum verbum Dei, sive libros Veteris et Novi Testamenti: et manum meam sacro, qui aderat, codici imponens; dixi: hoc est purum verbum Dei, eo continetur confessio mea, extra quam aliam nullam cui sim adstrictus agnosco: Quando tibi probavero, Euangelium perinde esse a Deo ac Legem, nihil ultra a me requirere potes: Sermonemque interruptum repetens, dixi, unicam cur in Mosem credamus esse causam quod a Deo sit missus; argumentum autem missionis divinæ unicum esse ipsius miracula. Hic querebatur, aliquos sibi objecisse, unde scis Mosen a Deo esse missum? aliqua plura contra divinam Mosis missionem: addens; sic omnia possent in dubium vocari, et tandem via sterneretur ad atheismum. Hic ego tam commodam occasionem mihi elabi minime sum passus: et quia ex sermone ipsius deprehenderam, quanto in pretio ipsi esset Moses, prudenter sermonem meum esse temperandum duxi. Respondi ergo: Si relicto Christo se ad Mosen conferre
― 213 ―
vellet, non debere ipsam mirari, si Christianus ex ipsa quærat, quibus rationibus de Mosis divina missione persuasa sit? Ego, addebam, de Mosis divina missione nullatenus dubito, neque de Legis Mosaicæ divina autoritate: de ea vero, etiamsi alia mihi deëssent argumenta, satis me persuasum reddit religio Christiana: Sed quando tu relicto Christo ad Mosen transis, omnia quæ mihi suppeditat religio Christiana argumenta simul repudias. Possum itaque ut Christianus quærere, quæ tibi pro divina Mosis missione argumenta supersint? Non enim si Christum relinquas certum est amplectendum esse Mosen. Quid si enim quæram, cur non amplecteris Mahomethis Alcoranum, cur non ad gentiles abis? an non tibi argumenta proferenda sunt, quibus Legis divinitatem adstruas præ Alcorano et Gentilismo? Quid si gentilis a te petat divinitatem Legis probari, promittens se eâ probatâ Judæum futurum, an non officii tui judicares argumentis quibus ille convinci posset eam adstruere? Assensit. Itaque, ajebam, ego etiam ut Christianus a te peto, quæ argumenta, si Christum relinquas, tibi restent, quibus Mosis divinitatem†a probes: egoque in me recipio, me clare demonstraturum, eadem illa argumenta validius pro divina Christi missione, quam Mosis, concludere; ac proinde si illis argumentis de
― 214 ―
divina Mosis missione te recte persuasam credas, oportere ut per eadem illa argumenta Christum a Deo esse missum agnoscas. Sic tandem eò quò volebam deducta disputatio fuit; quod magno molimine quæsivi, quia sine hac methodo fœlicem disputationis successum non sperabam. Hic ergo collatione inter argumenta ac signa quibus Mosis, ac quibus Christi divina missio adstruitur, aliquamdiu hæsimus, in qua quicquid illa pro Mose urgebat, ego certius pro Christo esse argumentum ostendi. Cum hic diu hæserimus, ego, ut paucis absolverem, tandem dixi: Hodie est festum Paschalis, quo tota Ecclesia Christiana resurrectionis dominicæ memoriam celebrat: Si solidis argumentis tibi veritatem resurrectionis Jesu Christi ex mortuis probavero, an non agnosces ipsum a Deo esse missum? Omnino, inquiebat; mortuus enim seipsum excitare nequit: si ergo revixit, a Deo excitatum esse necesse est. Hic ego prolixe veritatem resurrectionis dominicæ adstruxi, et ad omnes objectiones et dubia quæ quandoque objiciebat, respondi. Cum omnia mea argumenta audivisset, respondet, hæc optime quidem fluere, siquidem historia prout ab Euangelistis conscripta est vera sit. Primo itaque multis historiæ Euangelicæ veritatem adstruxi; deinde probavi, libros sacrorum scriptorum incorruptos ad nos pervenisse; ac tandem, majorem multo esse certitudinem traditionis
― 215 ―
Christianæ quam Judaicæ. Cum prolixi hujus discursus finem fecissem, respondit: Non possum impræsentiarum argumentis tuis respondere, sed ea attentius considerabo. Perrexi ego: Festo pentecostes celebramus memoriam missionis Spiritus Sancti in Apostolos: si et illius historiæ veritatem tibi probavero, an non et ea tibi erit alterum argumentum, quo divina Jesus Christi missio evidenter demonstratur? Concessit. Itaque ego multis probavi, Apostolos certos fuisse, se donum illud Spiritus Sancti accepisse, neque de eo dubitare potuisse: deinde, se illud a Domino Jesu in cœlis regnante accepisse: tertio, ipsos suæ ætatis homines argumentis idoneis de doni hujus a Jesu Christo accepti veritate convicisse: tandem et nos hodie argumentis omni exceptione majoribus de illius veritate esse persuasos. Cum omnia hæc argumenta, quæ tibi satis sunt nota, et a me brevitatis causa omittuntur, fusius deduxissem, iterum respondit: Impræsentiarum nihil argumentis tuis opponere possum, sed ea attentius considerabo. Dixi, hoc mihi gratissimum fore; et quanto ea ponderaret exactius, tanto id mihi fore gratius; sed petebam, ut quascunque haberet considerationes mihi aperiret, ut et illis respondere possem. Hoc se facturam promisit; addiditque, Accusant me pervicaciæ; sed immerito: non certarunt mecum idoneis argumentis; nunc tu mihi
― 216 ―
opposuisti argumenta, nunquam mihi antea objecta, quibus me impræsentiarum respondere non posse fateor: attente ea considerabo: si quid alicujus momenti contra illa repererim, tibi indicabo: si nihil solidi contra illa reperire queam, me convictam fatebor. Ego commendavi ut serio consideraret statum suum; agi hic negotium æternæ salutis: laudavi illius prudentiam, quod non temere rationibus meis crederet, sed eas accurate ac mature meditari cuperet; neque me dubitare, quin quanto exactius eas esset consideratura, tanto evidentius illarum soliditatem esset agnitura: quibus meditationibus si addat preces ad Deum, felicem collationis hujus successum certo certius esse exspectandum. Commendavi etiam, ut eximium Hugonis Grotii de Veritate Religionis Christianæ tractatum,†1 quem sibi hactenus visum negabat, et alterum, quem ipsi dedi, ex Anglico (cui titulus est, the Gentlemans religion)†2 in linguam Belgicam versum, evolveret. Hic fuit primæ meæ collationis exitus, quam prolixius paulo descripsi, quia illis quæ tunc prolata sunt argumentis proprie convicta est: Duravit hæc collatio duabus horis.
― 217 ―
(English) Postridie reversus petii ut considerationes ad argumenta pridie a me allata, si quas haberet, mihi aperiret. Illa ingenue, præsente matre, fassa est, se attente argumenta mea considerasse, sed solidi nihil contra ea reperire potuisse: fateor, inquiebat, te mihi veritatem duorum miraculorum, resurrectionis nimirum Jesu Christi, et missionis Spiritus Sancti in Apostolos, evidenter demonstrasse: agnosco Jesum Christum a Deo esse missum. Ego gratias me agere Deo inquiebam de ingenua hac confessione: posse nos nunc reliqua collationis nostræ illi confessioni tanquam fundamento solido superædificare. Itaque, ut omnis animo ipsius scrupulus eximatur, nos jam ad Prophetarum vaticinia progressuros, meque probaturum, quicquid a Prophetis de Messia fuit prædictum, in Domino Jesu Christo suum habere complementum. Verum antequam novam hanc disquisitionem inchoavimus, repetitio argumentorum prioris diëi instituta fuit, et dubiis quibusdam, quæ Judæi contra Euangeliorum scriptores, et traditionem Christianam objicere solent, responsum, multaque prioris diëi plenius paulo fuere explicata. Etiam respondi objectioni, quod certi non simus, quo tempore singula Euangelia conscripta sint: Et, quod certius Judæi de veritate resurrectionis dominicæ potuissent convinci, si Dominus Jesus se ipsis redivivum ostendisset. Cum his aliisque ita respondissem,
― 218 ―
ut se meæ responsioni acquiescere fateretur, ad Prophetarum vaticinia transivimus.
(English) Hic ego præmonui, non esse a me exspectandas mathematicas demonstrationes, contra quas homo infidelis nihil quicquam reperire posset: quoniam non probata historiæ Novi Testamenti veritate difficile admodum sit, e Prophetarum vaticiniis ostendere, ita omnia oportuisse evenire, prout in Christo impleta sunt, quia pleraque juxta sensum literalem olim suum habuere complementum: Sed quoniam nunc historiæ Novi Testamenti veritatem agnoscebat, me probaturum, vaticiniis Prophetarum majus quid, præter id quod olim impletum fuit, contineri; eorumque complementum secundum omnem literæ ἐνέργειαν esse in Jesu Christo. Cum enim post quinque congressus penitus omnes suas dubitationes abjecerit, fundamentaque religionis Christianæ nunc distinctius cognoscat, et fide solidiore amplectatur quam antehac, omnino quicquid per ignorantiam, sive incogitantiam aut negligentiam peccatum est, æternæ tradendum est oblivioni. Fieri autem posset, ut quis pia intentione exemplum hoc allegaret, ad ostendendum legitimâ methodo plerumque non cum Judæis disputari, et excerpta ex epistola mea sibi communicata ad majorem dictorum suorum fidem scripto suo insereret: ita rei hujus memoria typis expressa nunquam obliteraretur. Video autem hic multos non tam ipsius conversione gaudere, quam dolere quod meis colloquiis ab errore suo revocata est, magisque materiam quærere errorem ejus exaggerandi, quam conversionem deprædicandi. Non enim veriti sunt passim eam tanquam præsumtuosam, procacem, pertinacem, et simul, quod mireris, instabilem, cuique nulla religio cordi sit, traducere: quidam eo usque exorbitarunt, ut et atheam vocaverint. Cum ego,
― 232 ―
quod vere testor, eam expertus sim modestam, neutiquam refractariam, sed maxime docilem, attentam ac sedulam, Deique reverentem: et, quod rarum est, ingenii admodum fælicis ac prompti, judicii peracris ac limati, supra ætatem (est enim viginti duorum tantum annorum) et sexum, ac incredibili veritatis investigandæ amore incensam, adeo ut proprio Marte sine magistro plurimos libros evolverit, et si quid minus intelligeret indefesso labore illius lectionem aliquatenus repetierit, et assidue meditata sit, nec conquieverit, donec omnia distincte intellexerit. Vix annos nata quatuordecim (ut mihi aliquoties narravit) solita fuit mane hora quarta insciis parentibus e lecto surgere, et librorum lectioni incumbere: quando autem post iteratam lectionem sensum non perciperet, aliquoties quasi desperabunda cum lachrymis librum e manibus projecit: post horam vero, ubi puellari lusu se recreasset, librum in manus resumsit, lectionem repetiit, meditata est: et hæc omnia crebro iteravit, donec tandem sensum assecuta esset. Quod sane exemplum rarissimum est in puella, quæ in otio et deliciis educata credi posset. Quare hæc ita amicis communicabis, ut nihil ex meis literis depromatur, quod ne a malevolo quidem in illius calumniam rapi possit. Verum tandem tempus est manum de tabula tollere. Ultus jam sum silentium tuum probe. Mirabor si non aliquoties prolixitatem meam sis incusaturus, epistolamque

(English) Post hasce scriptas tristis me de subita optimi Archiepiscopi Cantuariensis morte nuntius non leviter perculit.†1 Destinaveram ipsi Theologiæ meæ Christianæ exemplar; pridie autem antequam tradi potuerit mortuus est. (English) Vides hic additamenta in Historiam Inquisitionis. Liber unde aliquot loca descripsi hunc præfert titulum: Speculum Inquisitionis

Bisuntinæ ejus officiariis exhibitum a R.P.F. Joanne des Loix S.T.D. Ord. Prædicat. Convent. Audomerensis, per Bisunt. Diocesim et tot. Comitat. Burgund. Inquisitore Generali, etc. Dolæ apud Antonium Binard typographum juratum. 1628. in 8. Continet pagg. 791.†1
(English) Si per otium licet, velim quamprimum certiorem fieri literas has recte ad manus tuas pervenisse; eas enim aberrasse nollem, nec diu in incerto hærere: quia multa scripsi, et quæ in aliorum manus incidere nolim.
