(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I have received and read your letter with great pleasure; for although I was fully persuaded that your affection for me was in no wise lessened, nevertheless after so lengthy a silence the sight of your letter could not but be most welcome. That my Historia Inquisitionis has received your vote of approval is a matter on which I may congratulate myself. I know that your judgement is candid and very refined; but in the commendations that you add I recognize your very great affection for me, which has represented everything that you approve of as greater than it is in reality. I have been diligent to sacrifice to the truth and to show that tribunal just as the Pontifical doctors themselves, that is the Inquisitors, depict it for us. I know indeed that when the manner of proceeding is described in bits and pieces in their books, and is cloaked with falsified colours, its unrighteousness and foulness are not so manifest as when all things that are connected with one another are exposed together, naked and unfalsified, to the eyes of all. I should not have supposed that anyone, not even among the keenest defenders of the Inquisition, would charge me with[p. 205] bad faith, and if anyone should venture to do so it will be possible to confute him immediately by the evidence of the authors whose names I have added everywhere in the margins. But to what different fates do books proceed! You judge my Historia to be worthy of translation into the vernacular of every people, but at Rome on 19 May of this year it was condemned by an edict of the Cardinals, the Inquisitors General throughout Christendom, and the reading of it was most strictly prohibited under the penalties contained in the Index of prohibited books. Three days later, namely on 22 May, this decree, by which some other books also were condemned, was published and affixed to the doors of the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles and to those of the palace of the Holy Office, and in the corner of the Campo dei Fiori,†1 and in the other usual and customary places in the city. But who would expect from the Inquisition a more lenient sentence on an account which tears from darkness, and exposes publicly to the eyes of the whole world, its arts and cruelties, which it wishes to be hidden, and unknown to all men; and shows this tribunal as not to be venerated for its holiness but execrated for its unrighteousness, cruelty, frauds, and impostures? For it cannot be shown differently if it is truly described. I shall most willingly send you what[p. 206] I have recorded from other authors whom I have happened to see later as well as what I may find hereafter in others who will perhaps be shown to me. I have seen what you have recorded from Du Mont's itinerary, which can very well be added in the margin of my Historia in the place that you have designated for it. But, to speak frankly, I very much doubt whether his tale is true. I by no means accuse him of bad faith; but it can easily happen that travellers, not staying long in a particular region, may fall in with men not well acquainted with the laws and customs of their own country, or sometimes even mendacious, from whose mouths they record without more careful investigation some things not in agreement with the truth; I have observed many such in the itineraries of those who describe the manners and customs of my country. The reason for doubt is because I see that all the Pontifical doctors, and moreover all the Church's decrees, urge very solicitously that the secrets of confession are not to be made known, no, not even heresy that has been revealed under the seal of confession; they merely command priests not to give absolution to a person who has confessed to heresy, but to exhort him by all the reasons in their power to confess according to law in a trial before the Inquisitors. I know indeed that not all things that are enjoined by the laws are precisely observed in the practice of the Inquisition, and that under the specious pretext that confession is not to be revealed[p. 207] the simpler-minded can be enticed into frankly confessing even things that are unknown to the Inquisitors, things which can then be revealed by the priests to the Inquisitors; nor do I believe that the holiness of that tribunal is averse from such an imposture. Nevertheless, since all their Constitutions, Instructions, and laws, all the decrees of that Church, enjoin the contrary, I should not venture to affirm this unless the author is proved to be one whose experience and trustworthiness cannot be called in question. For this reason there could be added to the passage from Du Mont's itinerary that you have supplied to me: 'If his tale is true then it is fully evident that the Inquisitors' practice is often contrary to the Instructions and laws of the Inquisition; and that the Inquisitors aim only at one thing, how by fair means or foul to beguile their miserable prisoners and, when they are thus ensnared by fraud, to destroy them by a miserable death.' But enough of this.
(Latin) Except in many pages I could not recount right down to the minute circumstances the story that you ask for of the recently Judaizing young woman who has happily been drawn back to the Christian faith, for I spent more than twenty hours on that debate, which continued for five days.†1 But it is not necessary to rehearse the separate arguments, for it will suffice to indicate many of them in very few words. I shall write down carefully what[p. 208] I know you most want; then you will easily discover the sources of her doubts and you will learn with what procedure others argued with her in vain. On the advice of our friend Veen, after three preachers of the Public Church†1 had had some ineffectual debates with her, I was summoned to her by her mother, whom I had never seen before. At our first meeting, which was on 12 April, the second day of Easter,†2 I said that I had learnt that some doubts had arisen in her mind about the truth of the Christian religion. She admitted it and asked that it might be proved to her from the Law of Moses that belief in the Messiah had been enjoined upon Israel. I answered that the divineness of the Gospel can indeed be proved from the Law, but that there are other arguments by which it may be established: the Lord Jesus in John chapter 5 puts forward several arguments in order to prove the truth of his teaching: namely the testimony of John the Baptist, his own miracles, and finally the testimony of Moses; it was proper that we should first discuss the miracles of the Lord Jesus, and that the truth of the New Testament account, which contains the narration of Christ's miracles, should be established; when this was proved we should proceed to the examination of the predictions which are found in Moses and the Prophets. She was surprised by this answer of mine, and thought that I wanted to use an unrightful procedure in discussion with her. And so she answered that Peter, after he had spoken of the glory shown in the mount, adds that we have 'a word of prophecy' which[p. 209] he calls 'more sure' (2 Pet. 1: 19). I retorted that Peter joined the two things; we would imitate him; but that this is the rightful procedure, that we should first examine the arguments by which the divine mission of Christ [i.e. that he was sent by God] is established; after that, what Moses and the Prophets had foretold about him. When she urged that, if Israel had been commanded of old to believe in the coming Messiah, then, since all things that Israel was commanded to do are contained in the Law of Moses, that command ought to be found in that Law, I set forth at length my opinion concerning the belief of Israel in the coming Messiah, just as I did in my debate with Don Balthasar. It was not without surprise that she heard this wholly unexpected answer of mine; and, taking this opportunity, found fault with the rigour of some [members] of her own [church] who had debated with her, who adjudge to hell not only all heathens and Jews, but also all Christian congregations that differ from themselves. Seizing this opportunity I set out at some length my opinion concerning mutual toleration among Christians of differing views, which seemed to please her exceedingly. I added what I thought about the heathen who have never been enlightened by knowledge of the Gospel; then about the Jews, on whom it is manifest that the light of the Gospel truth has shone; nevertheless I recognized some difference between the Jews who rejected the preaching of the Apostles, performed in the might of the Spirit and confirmed by miracles; and those of to-day, to whom the Gospel[p. 210] is often preached by inexperienced and unsuitable persons and to whom many occasions of scandal are offered by Christians. This also can be read at greater length in my debate with Orobio. At length, in order to turn my discourse to herself and to elicit from her own mouth that her eternal salvation was here concerned, I said that there are others who after they have believed in Christ have forsaken him again; such persons cannot reject Christ without at the same time refusing all his benefits and openly acknowledging that they have nothing to do with him. When she recognized that this followed rightfully I said: 'This is the state in which you are now; you have recognized Christ as your Lord; you cannot therefore withdraw from him without refusing all his benefits; if, then, the Christian religion is true, you cannot abandon it and embrace Judaism except with the loss of your eternal salvation.' When she admitted that this followed rightfully I added that, since she now recognized how much it concerned her to know whether the Christian religion is true or not, I begged her by the value that she set on her eternal salvation to ponder with me attentively and in the fear of the Lord the arguments with which I was about to establish the divineness of the Christian religion. She again urged that the beginning of the discussion should be made from the Law of Moses and that predictions relating to the Messiah should be sought from it. Here we stuck for a long time over the question by what procedure we should advance. In order to make my procedure acceptable I said that in most of the prophecies there is a twofold meaning,[p. 211] the literal and the mystical; I admitted further that the literal had had its fulfilment in old time, but as a type; the mystical was fulfilled in Christ. But since it was clear from this that the prophecies had had their fulfilment in old time, although not according to the whole strength and energy of the letter, she would readily see that Israel could not in old time have distinctly perceived that mystical meaning, but that it had had to become known from the event; so too now, if the truth of the New Testament account were set aside, I could not demonstrate a priori what mystical meaning lies hidden under those prophecies; but the proof of the truth of the New Testament account must necessarily come first; when that had been established I would prove from the event that there is a more sublime mystical meaning in those predictions and that it was fulfilled in Christ according to the whole energy of the letter. I added incidentally that the Apostles in their disputations against the Jews, which are to be found in the Acts of the Apostles, had used this same procedure. When she urged a contrary procedure I said: 'If it were manifest by clear arguments that Jesus Christ was sent by God, would it not be necessary to believe in him, even if neither Moses nor the Prophets had foretold anything about him?' When she hesitated somewhat at this I showed that, in order that one may have faith in anyone, nothing else is required except that his divine mission should be proved, even if no predictions of his coming are to be found. I proved this by the example of Moses, of whose[p. 212] coming we nowhere read that it was foretold: nevertheless, since he proved by evident miracles that his mission was divine, the Jews do not hesitate to believe in him. Here she told me what many of her preachers thought about this subject, which did not seem at all to agree with my opinion. I asked her to pay no attention to the dogmas and theses of other men, of whatever sort they may be, but only to the word of God, that is, to the books of the Old and New Testaments; and laying my hand on the Holy Bible, which was by me, I said: 'This is the pure word of God, in it is contained my confession [of faith]; apart from that I recognize no other to which I am bound; when I shall have proved to you that the Gospel is of God equally with the Law you can require nothing further from me'; and, resuming my interrupted discourse, I said that the only reason why we believe in Moses is that he was sent by God; but the only argument for his divine mission is his miracles. Here she complained that some had objected to her, 'How do you know that Moses was sent by God?' and many other things against his divine mission; adding, 'In this way everything could be called in question, and in the end the way to atheism would be paved.' Here I most certainly did not suffer so advantageous an opportunity to slip by me; and as I perceived from her discourse how greatly Moses was esteemed by her, I thought that my discourse should be prudently managed. I answered therefore that, if she wished, having left Christ, to betake herself to Moses, she ought not to be surprised[p. 213] if a Christian should ask her on what grounds she was persuaded of the divine mission of Moses. 'I myself', I added, 'do not in the least doubt the divine mission of Moses or the divine authorship of the Mosaic Law; indeed, even if other arguments were wanting, the Christian religion sufficiently persuades me of that. But when you, having left Christ, go over to Moses, you at the same time repudiate all the arguments that the Christian religion supplies me with. As a Christian I can therefore ask, What arguments are left to you for the divine mission of Moses? For if you leave Christ it is not certain that Moses must be embraced. For what if I should ask, Why do you not embrace Mahomet's Koran, why do you not depart to the heathen? Are not arguments to be put forward by you by which you may establish the divineness of the Law in comparison with the Koran and heathenism? What if a heathen should ask you for proof of the divineness of the Law, promising that if it was proved he would become a Jew: would you not consider it your duty to establish it with arguments by which he could be convinced?' She assented. 'Then', I said, 'I as a Christian also ask you, if you leave Christ what arguments remain for you with which to prove the divineness of Moses; and I for my part undertake to demonstrate clearly that those same arguments make more strongly for the divine mission of Christ than for that of Moses; and therefore if you believe that you are rightly persuaded of the divine mission[p. 214] of Moses by those arguments, then it behoves you by those same arguments to recognize that Christ was sent by God.' So at last the discussion was brought to the point that I wanted; which I sought with great exertion because without this procedure I did not hope for a happy outcome from our discussion. Here therefore we stuck for some time in a comparison between the arguments and signs with which the divine missions of Moses and of Christ are established, in which I showed that whatever she urged for Moses was a surer argument for Christ. When we had stuck here for a long while at last in order to make an end in few words I said: 'To-day is the feast of Easter, on which the whole Christian Church celebrates the memory of the Lord's resurrection; if I prove to you by solid arguments the truth of the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead will you not recognize that he was sent by God?' 'By all means', she said, 'for a dead man cannot raise himself up; if, then, be lived again he needs must have been raised up by God.' On this I established at some length the truth of the Lord's resurrection and answered all the objections and doubts that she put forward from time to time. When she had heard all my arguments she answers that they indeed flowed excellently if indeed the account as it was written by the Evangelists was true. I first therefore established the truth of the Gospel account by many arguments; I next proved that the books of the sacred writers have reached us uncorrupted; and finally that the certainty of the Christian tradition is far[p. 215] greater than that of the Jewish. When I had made an end of this lengthy discourse she answered: 'I cannot at present answer your arguments but I shall consider them intently.' I proceeded: 'At the feast of Pentecost we celebrate the memory of the sending of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles; if I prove the truth of that account also to you will it not be for you another argument by which the divine mission of Jesus Christ is clearly demonstrated?' She agreed. Accordingly I proved by many arguments that the Apostles were certain that they had received the gift of the Holy Spirit and that they could not be in doubt about it; next that [they were certain that] they had received it from the Lord Jesus reigning in Heaven; thirdly that by appropriate arguments they had convinced men of their time of the truth of this gift received from Jesus Christ; and finally that we to-day are convinced of its truth by incontrovertible arguments. When I had drawn out at some length all these arguments, which are sufficiently known to you and are omitted by me for the sake of brevity, she answered again: 'I can set nothing at present against your arguments, but I shall consider them intently.' I said that that would be most pleasing to me; and that the more exactly she pondered them the more pleasing it would be to me; but I asked her to tell me whatever considerations she might have, so that I could reply to them also. She promised to do this and added: 'They accuse me of obstinacy, but undeservedly; they did not contend with me with suitable arguments; you[p. 216] have now brought against me arguments that were never set before me previously; I admit that I cannot answer them at present; I shall consider them attentively; if I find anything of any moment against them I shall inform you; if I can find nothing solid against them I shall admit that I am convinced.' I recommended her to consider her state seriously; [her] eternal salvation was here at issue; I commended her prudence in not rashly giving credence to my reasons but desiring to contemplate them carefully and maturely; nor did I doubt that the more exactly she should consider them, the more clearly would she recognize their solidity; if to these contemplations she would add prayers to God a happy outcome to this debate was to be expected with absolute certainty. I also recommended her to read the excellent treatise of Hugo Grotius De Veritatie Religionis Christianæ,†1 which she said she had not seen hitherto, and another which I gave her, translated into Dutch from English, in which it is called The Gentleman's Religion.†2 This was the end of my first debate, which I have described at some length because she was convinced especially by those arguments that were then put forward. This debate lasted two hours.
(Latin) Returning the next day I asked her to tell me about any considerations that she might have about the arguments used by me on the previous day. In her mother's presence she frankly admitted that she had attentively considered my arguments, but had not been able to find anything solid against them. 'I admit', she said, 'that you have clearly demonstrated to me the truth of the two miracles, namely the resurrection of Jesus Christ and the sending of the Holy Ghost upon the Apostles; I recognize that Jesus Christ was sent by God.' I said that I gave thanks to God for this frank confession; we could now build the remainder of our debate on that confession as a solid foundation. Accordingly, in order that every doubt should be removed from her mind, we would now proceed to the predictions of the Prophets, and I would prove that whatever was foretold by the Prophets about the Messiah has its fulfilment in the Lord Jesus Christ. But before we began this new inquiry a repetition of the previous day's arguments was undertaken and answers were made to certain doubts which Jews are wont to raise against the writers of the Gospels and the Christian tradition, and many things from the previous day were rather more fully explained. I also answered the objections that we are not sure at what time the separate Gospels were written and that the Jews could have been more surely convinced of the truth of the Lord's resurrection if the Lord Jesus had shown himself to them restored to life. When I had so answered these and other[p. 218] objections that she admitted that she was satisfied with my answers we passed on to the predictions of the Prophets.
(Latin) Here I warned her in advance that there were not to be expected from me mathematical demonstrations against which an unbelieving man could find nothing whatever [to say], since unless the truth of the New Testament account was [accepted as] proved it would be very difficult to show from the predictions of the Prophets that all things ought to have come to pass in the way in which they were fulfilled in Christ, since many of them had their fulfilment in old time according to the literal meaning; but since she now recognized the truth of the New Testament account I would prove that something greater than what was fulfilled in old time is contained in the predictions of the Prophets; and that their fulfilment according to the whole energy of the letter was in Jesus Christ. She answered that she did not require mathematical demonstrations but would be satisfied with arguments to which nothing solid can be opposed, and which suffice for anyone devoted to truth. Here, opening the Holy Bible which she had in her hand, she wanted to make a beginning of the inquiry with the celebrated passage in Gen. 3: 15. I said: 'Please allow me to put forward my arguments in the order which I shall choose. I shall not follow the order of the books of the Holy Bible, but shall take it from the subject itself. So I shall proceed in this order: First I shall show that God had previously appointed a time for the coming[p. 219] of the Messiah and that the Lord Jesus came into the world at the appointed time. Next, that the place of his birth was foretold, his lineage, and lastly that he would be born of a virgin mother; and that all these things truly so came to pass in the Lord Jesus. These things being proved, I shall prove that his offices: prophecy, priesthood, and kingship, and lastly the preaching of his doctrine throughout the whole world, were foretold and that all these things were fulfilled in the Lord Jesus. I shall put forward my separate arguments clearly and shall establish them by the predictions of the Prophets; it will be open to you to say what you think about the several arguments as they are put forward by me; it will be for me to remove all your doubts. When I have made an end of arguing you, if you have any objections to the Christian religion, will put them to me and you will not stop as long as any doubt remains with you; for it is my part to satisfy you in everything.' I first proved therefore from the celebrated passage in Gen. 49: 10 that a certain time had been previously appointed by God for the coming of the Messiah; we discussed at length the meaning of this passage and the various interpretations of it: when the sceptre was given to Judah, when it was taken away from Judah. I added another passage from Hag. 2: 7, 8, 9, 10.†1 We also discussed extensively the meaning of this passage. Taking this opportunity she asked what I thought about the temple in Ezekiel; I told her my opinion, which[p. 220] I have also stated in my debate with Orobio. This seemed to please her exceedingly. Finally I added the passage of Dan. 9: 24, 25, 26, 27. When I had explained its meaning to her I also refuted the Jews' objections to the contrary. And because I was here much concerned in assigning causes for the present dispersion of the Jews, and showed that it cannot be for any reason other than contempt of the Messiah, it was objected to me that this dispersion was foretold in Levit. 26 and Deut. 28, and that it is plain from these chapters that it befell the Jews on account of their desertion of the Law of Moses and their idolatry, and that liberation from it was still to be awaited by them. As it was now past eight o'clock in the evening I answered in a few words that these predictions referred to the Babylonian captivity, which at first was paradoxical for her. I confirmed my explanation in a few words, but since the time had now run out and this was a matter of great importance, the explanation of many predictions depending upon it, I promised to demonstrate it clearly and at length on the following day. This debate lasted four hours.
(Latin) On the third day I made a beginning of my discourse with an explanation of the chapters Levit. 26 and Deut. 28. I had put together in writing my arguments by which I proved that the threat, not of the present captivity but of the Babylonian, was contained in those chapters, extracting them from my discussion with Orobio. After I had set them all out she admitted[p. 221] that she was fully convinced by them; a little later, when she had considered them more attentively, she says: 'This is the genuine explanation of Scripture by Scripture; I now clearly perceive the meaning of many prophecies which I hitherto believed were yet to be fulfilled and which I learn have already been fulfilled; hence has arisen for me a great light for explaining the writings of the Prophets.' I gave her what I had written so that she could also in my absence re-read and ponder all the passages. Then, having first indicated its literal meaning, I proved from Mic. 5: 1†1 that the place of the Messiah's birth was to be Bethlehem and that the Lord Jesus was born in that city by the especial direction of God. As she found nothing wanting in this proof I proceeded to the lineage of the Lord Jesus. There was no need for me to prove that the Messiah would be born of the house of David as the Jews themselves admit it. All that needed to be proved was that the Lord Jesus had his extraction from David. Here we discussed at length the genealogy of the Lord Jesus and the discrepancy between Matthew and Luke, whom I so reconciled that she was satisfied with my reconciliation. Finally there remained to be proved his birth from a virgin mother, according to Isa. 7: 14, 15, etc. Here I set forth at some length the literal meaning of that prediction, and proved from the energy of Isaiah's words that there lies hidden beneath it another, a loftier and mystical meaning, which had its fulfilment in the Lord Jesus, and I showed the truth of the Lord's birth from[p. 222] a virgin. And an end was thus put to this conversation. This debate was held on Wednesday and lasted five hours.
(Latin) I returned on Friday, on which day I proved from Deut. 18: 15 and 18 Christ's prophetic office. I proved that this prediction referred to the Messiah. Here we discussed at length Christ's prophetic office, the Law and the Gospel, in what sense the Gospel can be called more perfect than the Law; the meaning of the diverse precepts of the Law and the Gospel; the promises of the Gospel and the Law, and the difference between these promises. Then I showed that the Lord Jesus did not teach or command anything contrary to the Law. This provided an opportunity for something to be said about certain dogmas of the Christians which the Jews believe to be contrary to the Law. I said that they are to be considered according as they are to be found in Scripture, not as they have later been defined by men and expressed in words and phrases not to be found in Scripture but invented by men. And we must have regard only to those things which Scripture in various places inculcates as the object of saving faith. And as for the dogmas, the proof of which must be sought not from the Old but from the New Testament, a discussion with a Jew ought not to start from them; but, as I did now, the divine authority of the books of the New Testament is first to be established against him, so that, when that has been proved from those books themselves, what is to be determined about such a dogma may be decided and he may[p. 223] then compare the statements of the two Testaments with one another. At this point she says with a smile: 'I thought that a great injustice was being done to me because you rejected the procedure which I had conceived, but I see now that you used a rightful procedure. Our preachers used a very different procedure; they produced nothing to prove the truth of the New Testament account, but made a beginning of the discussion with the dogma of the Holy Trinity, and tried to establish it by arguments drawn from the Old Testament: one of them from the name Elohim, which is a plural,†1 and from the phrase in the plural number which God used in the creation of man, "Let us make man" (the other indeed rejected the former argument but approved the latter); from the appearance of the three angels made to Abraham; and from the like. Then, the eternal pre-existence of the Son from the words of God to the serpent, "I will put enmity between thee and the seed of the woman", Gen. 3: 15, and from the words of Eve after the birth of Cain, Gen. 4: 1, "I have gotten a man Jehovah", for so [i.e. with Jehovah in the accusative] he interpreted the Hebrew text, not "from Jehovah"; and from several other [passages]. So far', said she, 'from drawing me back by their arguments, they rendered me the more obstinate in my opinion. But I see that a rightful course is followed in your procedure, for when the divine authority of the New Testament has been proved I can decide from it what is to be determined about this and other dogmas of the Christian religion, and[p. 224] compare the statements of the Prophets with the New Testament.' After this digression I resumed my former discourse and showed that the Lord Jesus had not, properly speaking, abrogated the Law of Moses, but had brought in a more perfect law which presupposes that the Law of Moses is divine, but in whose presence all the imperfections of the Mosaic Law must needs vanish. Here I set out at sufficient length my opinion about the freedom of Christians from the Law of Moses. I also showed in what sense the Law is called eternal and how the Lord Jesus in announcing a more perfect law, in whose presence the Law of Moses has vanished, taught in accordance with the oracles of the Prophets, and how God had approved this teaching of the Lord Jesus and had confirmed it by the destruction of the Temple and the overthrow of the Jewish state. I argued all these things copiously against Don Balthasar. This debate lasted five hours and she declared several times that she was greatly confirmed by it in the truth of the Gospel.
(Latin) I returned finally on the Saturday, on which day we discussed the death of Christ. I proved from Isa. 53 that the death of the Messiah, and that indeed as a sacrifice for sin, was clearly foretold in that chapter. After we had copiously discussed the meaning of this chapter she asked me to tell her my opinion concerning the priesthood of Christ. I answered that so far, having carefully avoided all matters that are in controversy between Christians, we[p. 225] had treated only the general controversy which there is between all Christians and the Jews; but if I should clearly set out to her my opinion concerning the priesthood of Christ I would leave the path so far trodden by us; for I could not do it without setting before her the opinion of the Remonstrants in so far as it recedes from the Contraremonstrants. Since she insisted, and wanted to learn my opinion, I showed that opinion about Christ's priesthood is principally threefold: that of the Contraremonstrants and that of Socinus, which I regarded as two extremes directly opposed to each other, and ours, which is midway between those two extremes. I told her what we found wanting in either extreme opinion and how ours avoids all the inconveniences of the other opinions. I added that I regard the ground of salvation as being not in Christ's priesthood alone but also in his prophetic office and his kingship. When all this had been fully enough explained I asked her whether she wished now to proceed to Christ's kingly office. She answered that there was no need for that, for she had no remaining doubt about it. I said, 'Since the Jews urge that the promised Messiah will be an earthly king shall we examine the statements of the Prophets [to see] whether they are necessarily to be accepted as referring to an earthly kingdom?' She answered, 'There is no need for that since by all that we have so far canvassed you have now removed from my mind all the doubts I had about it.' I asked[p. 226] further whether she wished it to be proved to her from the Prophets that the teaching of the Messiah must needs be proclaimed throughout all the world, and that it was fulfilled in the Lord Jesus. She answered that she had no remaining doubt about it. Finally, since I had now no arguments left to me from the Prophets' predictions I asked that, if she had any objections against the Christian religion she would put them forward, so that I could answer them. She thereupon addressed me thus: 'All the doubts that I had about the Christian religion have been more than sufficiently taken from me by those things that you have discussed. I recognize that you have proved to me the truth of the New Testament account and in particular of those two mighty miracles, the resurrection of the Lord Jesus from the dead and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles on the day of Pentecost; that you have proved to me that the prophecies of the Old Testament have their fulfilment in the Lord Jesus; and that you have shown me the connection of the New Testament with the Old. I recognize the Lord Jesus Christ as my Saviour; and this will now be for me an unshakeable truth, of which by divine grace I shall never be in doubt. I thank you for your faithful instruction and ask you not to break off our debates, but to continue them with me; for I want to build a more solid knowledge of my religion on this foundation.' I answered that the glory of this desired outcome was to be attributed to God alone; I had at most but planted or watered, but God had[p. 227] given the increase. And so, four hours having been spent in this final debate, on the sixth day from our first debate I saw by God's blessing the desired issue of my labour. Moreover, as a result of this debate an intimate friendship has sprung up between us: she reveres me as a father; I love her as a daughter.
(Latin) Here you have a lengthy account of this debate, in which I have perhaps pursued minutiae, but to gratify you I wanted to record the several parts, so that you should have the sequence of the whole story. You do not require the several arguments, nor could I rehearse them severally without writing a whole treatise. Again, what need is there to repeat what is to be found in the debate with Orobio? More than enough of what you wanted to know is, I think, included in this narrative. A report of this debate, even though I kept silent, soon spread through the whole city and just as it won me the goodwill of many, so also it provoked the anger of others against me and the envy especially of those who had assailed the young woman ineffectually. One of these approached her and asked angrily what arguments and what procedure I had used in the discussion. When she answered that I had first and foremost proved to her the truth of the New Testament account, he said with the greatest contempt that that was worthless, using these very words: 'What had you got then? A nought with a great tail.' She answered that she did not understand what he meant; she believed that she had[p. 228] profited greatly when she was persuaded of the truth of the New Testament account. He said that nothing had been effected so long as it had not been solidly proved a priori from the Prophets that all things needs must be fulfilled just as they came to pass; indeed on another day he went so far as to say without blushing that, unless everything can be proved a priori from Moses just as completely as from the Gospel, he would hold the Gospel for nothing but a fable. And indeed when she informed him that she was satisfied with my arguments he said angrily, 'Your later state is now worse than your former'; so that she and her mother gathered from his remarks that he would have preferred that she should have gone over completely to Judaism rather than that, being recalled by my arguments, she should have returned to the Christian faith. Not without anger he asked further, 'Did you say then that the Cocceians†1 had deceived you?' 'By no means,' she answered; 'but that the Cocceians are not suited to convert a Jew.' On his asking whether van Limborch can do it she retorted, 'You have an example in me.' The young woman's mother said to me afterwards, 'I had never imagined that there is so much envy in preachers. I do not know what was the occasion for your entering my house; I had never thought about you; I summoned Veen for a very different reason; you were mentioned in some connection; I believe that God sent you into my house; for from the first moment that you spoke[p. 229] to my daughter I saw that she was changed.' Still, not all the preachers have approved of this man's anger. Some of them have spoken kindly enough about me and have frankly acknowledged that I have performed what their fellow-preachers had attempted in vain. I add this so that you may recognize the fairness of some others. But it is time at last to break off this lengthy tale.
(Latin) I shall next reply briefly to the rest of your letter. I do not doubt that the second edition of my Theologia Christiana has now arrived in England. I ordered the bookseller Samuel Smith to deliver a copy of it to you. I mentioned this to you recently in another letter, the bearer of which is Marcus Teut, a young man small in bodily stature but great in mind, whom you have often seen here. Therefore if the bookseller has not yet given you a copy you can ask him for it. I do not doubt that many things in my Theologia remain to be amended. I wish that I had been able to avail myself of your advice; when you pointed them out I should have undoubtedly corrected many things which, not having been noticed by me, now go forth unamended. I have made a very few additions; you will find those that are of some importance in Bk. II. chap. i. §§ 6 and 8. chap. XXI.†1 §§ 23, 25, and 26. Bk. III. chap. iv. § 16. chap. ix. §§ 3 and 11. Bk. V. chap. xxxiii.†2 § 7. Bk. VII. chap. iv. § 7. There are some other additions in a few places, but they are shorter. Taking the opportunity of this edition I have made a few remarks about evil spirits in order to destroy[p. 230] the principal foundations of that book [that I told you of];†1 I should like to know your opinion about them. I am not surprised that some men are striving to restore Calvinism. If they are truly of that opinion they are not to be blamed for wishing others to be convinced of an opinion that in their judgement is true, but are to be confuted by solid reasons. If something else lies hidden God will judge it. Time will show where this will end. I eagerly await a Latin translation of your book on the Human Understanding; from the French abridgement of it provided for us by Mr. Le Clerc†2 I readily perceive how much light on those difficult philosophical subjects can be drawn from it. I do not doubt that to be able to read it in the language common to all scholars will be most welcome to scholars to whom the English language is unknown. The more widely it is spread abroad, the more renowned will it make the truth taught in it by you. But I shall be able to judge the several parts with greater precision when I see the book itself. Some months ago I sent you some hitherto unpublished sermons of Episcopius, to which I have prefixed an account of his life. I do not know whether you will understand everything with precision; you will read in it the various misfortunes with which he contended. The Right Reverend the bishop of Bath and Wells, to whom I sent a copy, wrote that he had commissioned someone to translate the life of Episcopius into English; so perhaps you will read it in English.[p. 231] I had almost forgotten one matter. I have written you a very long account of my debate with the recently Judaizing young woman. I do not object to its being read aloud to some friends, but let copies be given to nobody. For since after five meetings she completely cast aside all her doubts and now knows more precisely the foundations of the Christian religion and embraces it with more solid faith than heretofore, whatsoever fault she committed through ignorance, whether inadvertence or negligence, is to be consigned to eternal oblivion. But it could happen that someone, with the pious intention of showing that discussions with Jews are not generally carried on with the rightful procedure, might cite this example and might insert extracts from my letter that were communicated to him in his composition, in order to win greater authority for his own statements; and so the memory of this event, being printed, would never be blotted out. Moreover, I see that many here do not so much rejoice at her conversion as regret that she was recalled from her error by conversations with me, and seek occasion rather for exaggerating her error than for celebrating her conversion. For on all sides they have not hesitated to traduce her as presumptuous, pert, and obstinate, and at the same time, at which you may be surprised, as unstable and having no religion at heart; some have even gone so far as to call her an atheist. Whereas I, as I truly bear witness, have found her modest and by no means refractory, but most tractable, attentive, and earnest, and also God-fearing; and, what is rare, of a very happy and quick mind and a most acute and refined judgement,[p. 232] beyond her age (for she is only twenty-two) and sex; and fired with an incredible love of investigating truth: so much so that of her own accord she has read many books without a teacher, and if she did not understand something would with indefatigable labour go back to some extent to the reading of it and consider it assiduously, and would not rest until she understood everything precisely. When scarcely fourteen, as she has told me several times, she used to rise from her bed at four o'clock in the morning without her parents' knowledge, and apply herself to reading of books; moreover, when after repeated reading she did not perceive the meaning, she sometimes tearfully threw the book from her hand as if in despair; after an hour, however, when she had refreshed herself with girlish play, she took the book in hand again, went back to her reading, and considered it; and she repeated all this frequently until at last she had attained the meaning. This surely is a very rare example [of behaviour] in a girl who can be supposed to have been brought up in ease and pleasure. You will therefore communicate this to your friends on the condition that nothing is drawn from my letter that can be seized on to slander her—not even by the most malicious. But at last it is time to take my hand from the paper. I have now thoroughly taken vengeance on your silence. I shall be surprised if you do not sometimes find fault with my long-windedness and throw the letter from your hands before[p. 233] you have reached the end. Please give my best respects to Lady Masham. Veen and his wife send you their greetings, as do my wife and children. Good-bye and do not cease to love, as is your wont,
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 12 December
1694
(Latin) After I had written the above the sad news of the excellent Archbishop of Canterbury's sudden death struck me to the heart.†1 I had designed a copy of my Theologia Christiana for him, but he died the day before it could be delivered to him. I lament the state of the Protestant Church, deprived of so great a defender, so wise, so experienced, and so peace-loving a prelate. May God, who is able even from stones to raise up children unto Abraham,†2 give us another in his place, if not equal to him, which I scarcely venture to hope, at least one who treads as closely as possible in his footsteps. May He prolong your life and that of Lady Masham to a ripe old age. Again good-bye.

presentement parfaittement bien, ainsy que toute la famille.†1 nostre pierot commence a profiter dans ses estudes, je luy ay donné un precepteur refugié qui luy enseigne le latin depuis un an au logis, avec tant de succes qui parle desja assez jolliment et son francois comme un parisien. il a une facilité extreme a concevoir, designe adroittement sous Monsieur Visser,†2 et comme il avance beaucoup dans l'arithmethique, je songe a luy laisser commencer l'année prochaine la Geometrie a moins que vous trouvassiez quil fut trop jeune. en peu de jours vostre livre de l'Education paroistra traduict en francois†3 chez Schelte, qui est la boutique de feu Monsieur Wolfgangh.†4 on se console icy plus que jamais de la guerre dans l'esperance que la france sera avec le temps reduitte a laisser ses voisins en paix. je ne scay si je vous ay desja mandé que ma charge a l'hospital m'est echeue entiere par la mort de mon college dankers.†5 on ne se souvient pas davoir vu si peu de malade en cette ville comme a present, ou malgré une abondance extreme de fruicts, il ny a pas deux cents Malades dans l'hospital. ce qui marque aussy que la misere est encore tolerable icy, au lieu, a ce qu'on m'assure, quil y a actuellement pres de huict milles Malades a l'hostel dieux de Paris, ou de mon temps le nombre ne montoit pas deux milles.†6 adieu Monsieur, favorisé nous quelquefois d'un mot de lettre, que nous regardons comme un tres grande grace, puisque nous sommes tous d'un tres grand respect,

Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres Obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON.

A Little house and a little furniture must serve young beginners as you and I are Dear Landabridis. Besides my stock will not reach to much, being not furnishd with Compliment or History to fill out a large spread of paper. And you know there needs not many words to expresse a great deal of affection, respect, and esteem where it is reall as mine is, and affects not to make a Shew. I saw the Major†a to day, he told me Mr Masham†b †1 was well, and that he should not goe to the West Indies.†c This I thought would be wellcome news to you and so could not forbeare to put it into my Letter. But Leave it to his to explain to you the particulars more fully for I reproachd him for not writeing to you, and made him promisse me he would doe it this night. Madam

Librum tuum a bibliopolâ et epistolam tuam 12° datam recte accepi utramque gratissimam et quia Tuam et quia a Te. Epistolam Tuam continuò a capite ad calcem summâ cum voluptate perlegi. (English) Addenda Tua ad historiam Inquisitionis quamprimum rus rediro locis suis inseram novum amicitiæ tuæ monumentum. Recte mones de excerptis ex itinerario du Mont. Nec enim ut reliqui Tui Scriptores (qua usus es cautione) pro teste citari potest, Tum quia reformatus, tum peregrinus. Ego vero illius verba non inidonea judicabam quæ fidem facerent isti quæ ex totâ pontificiorum œconomiâ enascitur: illos sc: quicquid præ se ferant, non omissuros tantam rei suæ bene gerendæ et hæreseos extirpandæ occasionem, quæ ex confessionibus possit oriri. nec aliter confessiones tacitas esse, si quid habeant momenti, quam ut laicis et quibus non opus esset non evulgarentur. Hæc ego raptim inter urbis negotia et laborantium pulmonum anhelitus; ut scires Tua munera quibus me tam magnifice cumulasti ad me salva pervenisse. (Latin)
London 11 Dec. 94
Excellent Sir,
I have duly received your book from the bookseller and your letter dated the 12th, each of them most welcome both because it is yours and because it comes from you. I read your letter through from beginning to end continuously with very great pleasure, and I congratulate your new-made daughter on a father who is wanting in neither mind nor bowels having fallen to her lot. That the spirit of some persons thereupon was such would certainly be surprising to a Christian man if I had not for a long time been conversant with zealots of that kind, but men of the same make†1 are to be found everywhere; let others judge whether they are seeking the salvation of souls or making any gain for the Gospel; for my part I see here, there, and everywhere what I grieve for and what angers me. As soon as I find leisure I shall examine your Theologia Christiana diligently, for I think that I ought now to give my mind for the most part to such studies, and I wish so much the more that I were with you because, now that that great and candid searcher[p. 238] after truth,†1 to say nothing of his other virtues, has been taken from us, I have scarcely anyone whom I can freely consult about theological uncertainties. Others will make known sufficiently how great a man the English public weal has lost, how great a pillar the Reformed Church. I have assuredly lost, to my very great hurt and grief, a friend of many years, steadfast, candid, and sincere.
(Latin) As soon as I return to the country I shall insert in their places your additions to the Historia Inquisitionis, a fresh remembrancer of your friendship. You rightly warn me about the extracts from Du Mont's itinerary. For he cannot be quoted as a witness like the rest of your writers, with whom you have used such circumspection, because he is both a Protestant and a foreigner. I judged, however, that his words, which confirm what springs up from the Romanists' whole economy, are not unsuitable: that is, they, whatever they profess, will not neglect so great an opportunity of promoting their own interest and extirpating heresy as can arise from confessions; and confessions, if they contain anything of moment, will not be kept secret except in so far as they will not be divulged to laymen and to persons who do not require them. All this written hurriedly between town affairs and the panting of my labouring lungs; so that you may know that your gifts, with which you have so generously overwhelmed me, have reached me safely. If you take vengeance on my silence in this way it is questionable whether it was not advantageous[p. 239] to transgress; for I would have you know that what was said of Cicero's speeches can justly be said of your letters, that 'the longest is the best'.†1 I arrived in town last Friday.†2 I found at my lodging our friend Le Clerc's letter dated the 7th, which I shall shortly answer; meanwhile please give him and our friend Guenellon my best wishes. I shall myself thank them both for their letters when I have found leisure and comfort in the country, for here my lungs labour and my health will not permit a long stay in the city. Please give my regards to your dear wife and children, and likewise to our excellent friend Veen and his wife; also to de Greve of Utrecht; I owe him a letter and am ashamed of not having yet replied to his kindness. Good-bye and, as is your wont, continue to love me your most affectionate
J LOCKE
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch bij de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keÿsars Graacht t'Amsterdam.

Dear Friend
To both yours of the 2/12 Oct from London and 2/12 November from Oates I remain still debtor. The book for my son Arent,
― 240 ―
(with the Addenda, and prints) I have, and he returns you his humble thanks and service for the present to him. my late wives sisters are all in love with their sisters land, and would have, I have wrote to them to agree among themselvs, and to let me know to whom I shall cause the Deeds to be made and I shall do it.

Deare Friend

Ce mot, monsieur, n'est que vous marquer la parfaite joie que j'ay receüe à l'ouverture de votre derniere, et pour vous prier de me marquer plus distinctement l'adresse et les qualitéz de m. Benjamin Furly, et si je pouray lui envoier à droiture les feuïlles qui manquent au receuil que j'ay donné à m. Je ne m'embarasse pas de l'oposition des libraires. si le tout etoit achevé, on se passeroit bien d'eux. cependant festinatur lenté:†1 et s'il n'arive quelque diversion à l'auteur ou à l'imprimeur, vous pourez enfin voir executé, cequi seroit assez dificile sans le concours des deux ensemble. Il y a bien des choses changées, non seulement dans l'œconomie de l'ouvrage, mais encore dans les caracterismes des tems, cequi est le plus important.
comme ceque j'aurois à vous envoier n'est pas de grand volume, et que d'ailleurs il n'y a point maintenant d'autre voie que celle de la poste, il seroit bon de prevenir pour cela m. Benjamin Furly. Sir
Yours of Novembr 23d. found me Labouring under a sharp Feavour, which has held me this month past; but I am now, God be thanked, pretty wel recoverd. I am obleidged to you for the earnest desire you Expres of seing me in England; But as to that particular the Truth is thus. Last Summer I designed to make a Journy On purpose to pay my Respects to you and for no other Errand. But my Resolutions were not so fixt, as to give you any Intimations thereof; for indeed the State of My Health was so very uncertain that I was very mistrustful, whether I should be able to undertake the Journy. However, I thought to make an Essay of My Strength in Our Own Country; So that some busines calling me about threescore Miles from this Citty, the Fategue
― 243 ―
was so troublesom to me that I was quite discouraged from thinking of England that season. I have now had an other Pul-back by my Present sicknes, so that I cannot yet wel tell how to think off the other side the Water. This only I will assure you that the first Intire Health God is pleased to bestow on Me shall be imployd in a Journy towards you; there being nothing I so earnestly Covet as the Personal Acquaintance of One for whom I have so Great a Respect and Veneration; and to whom I am so highly Obleidged for many Favours.
There is a very Worthy Person, Dr StGeorge Ashe Provost of the Colledge here, lately gone from hence to London, he is a Great Admirer and zealous Promoter of your Writings in his Colledge. He desired from me a Letter of Recommendation to You, but I fear Your Being in the Country will hinder his designed happines in your Conversation. He stays in London these three or four Months to Come, in which time if your Busines call you to the Citty, you will hear of him either at your Lodging at Mr Pawlings (where perhaps he will leave the Place of his Residence) or at Mr Tuckers†1 in the Secretarys office at Whitehall, where a Penny-post Letter will find him Out.
I†a- thank you for the Care you have taken to send me the Books and Sculptures,†2 which I hope to receive in Good time, having advice thereof already from Mr Churchil.-†a I am
Worthy Sir
Your Most affectionate Humble servant

Je me suis donné l'honneur, Monsieur, de vous écrire deux fois, sans recevoir de vos nouvelles. Mr. Limbourg me fit part à la verité, il y a cinq ou six semaines, de la Lettre que vous lui écriviez,†3 par où je vis que vôtre santé étoit bonne. Depuis je n'ai reçu
― 246 ―
aucune de vos lettres, mais seulement le paquet adressé à Mr. Furly, où j'ai trouvé un exemplaire de vôtre Ouvrage,†1 de celui de l'Evêque de Bath et Wels,†2 et l'histoire de l'Eglise de Malabar.†3 Je vous en suis extrémement obligé, et je me remettrai à lire vôtre Ouvrage, dès que je serai débarrassé du mien qui est sous la presse, que le froid extrême retarde un peu, mais qui sera achevé ce printems. J'ai fait cependant un petit traité sur les 18 premiers versets de S. Jean, où je fais voir que Socin s'est entierement trompé, dans le sens qu'il donne à ces paroles.†4 Je n'entre néanmoins dans aucune idée Scholastique, et je mabstiens entierement des termes modernes. Je ne sai ce que l'on en dira, mais on verra du moins que je suis bien éloigné de fournir des mémoires à quelques Unitaires de Londres, qui ont écrit, comme Mr. l'Evêque de Salisbury me le mande, avec beaucoup d'aigreur contre quelques Prélats.†5 Il me dit encore qu'ils attribuent cet Evangile à Cerinthe,†6 et j'ai établi le contraire d'une maniere invincible. J'en envoierai quelques exemplaires par la poste, pendant que le Parlement sera assemblé.†7 Si j'osois en adresser un pour vous à Mylord Privyseal, je le ferois; mais au moins je lui en envoierai un, pour lui même, que vous pourrez voir, en attendant, que je trouve une occasion de vous en envoier un. Aliquid dandum est invidiæ,†8 et lors que l'occasion s'en présente, il faut tâcher d'étouffer ce monstre, qui a fait tant de mal au monde revêtu de l'habit d'un Theologien. La mort de feu Mr. l'Archevêque m'a délivré des doutes, où je pouvois être sur son présent. On loüe beaucoup son successeur,†9 et je souhaite qu'il soit aussi moderé que le précedent. Mr. Limbourg étoit, il y a quelques jours dans le dessein d'écrire une Lettre sur la Tolerance des Unitaires à Mr. L'Evêque de Salisbury, pour l'éclaircir de quelques doutes qu'il a sur cette matiere.†10 Il semble qu'il n'ait
― 247 ―
pas compris la doctrine des Rémontrans là dessus, et Mr. Limbourg qui la possede parfaitement, est très-capable de dissiper ses scrupules. Ce Prélat m'a témoigné assez d'amitié et d'estime dans sa Lettre, mais je comprends qu'il y a quelque envieux auprès de lui, qui me noircit horriblement, et qui feint d'avoir oui dire mille choses de moi. Il ne me parle que d'empêcher que les Deïstes et les Athées ne tirent avantage des pensées nouvelles que l'on peut avoir.†1 Je ne sai s'il y a tant de ces gens-là en Angleterre, que l'on dit, mais je sai bien que j'ai refuté diverses choses que les uns et les autres peuvent dire. Il est vrai que je ne me suis pas jetté dans le parti de superstitieux, qui regardent la Religion, comme une doctrine absurde en elle même, mais qu'il faut croire pour faire plaisir à Dieu, et comme une doctrine pleine de cet esprit de persecution et de tirannie que l'on voit dans l'Eglise Romaine. Pour le malheur du siecle, ceux qui considerent la Religion de cette sorte sont avancez, et passent pour les piliers de la Foi, pendant que ceux qui la décrivent de la maniere du monde la plus raisonnable et la plus digne de Dieu sont cruellement diffamez. Mais vous savez tout cela aussi bien que moi. Je finis en priant Dieu qu'il vous donne une bonne et une heureuse année, et je suis de tout mon cœur, Monsieur
Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings overagainst the plough in little Lincolns inne fieds London
Postmark: IA 8 (?)
Endorsed by Locke: J. le Clerc 11 Jan. 95. Answered 10
1833. John Freke to Locke, 3 January 1695 (1821, 1836)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 179. Answered by no. 1836.
January the 3d 1694/5
Sir
Mr Clarke being obliged to attend a Comittee of the House of Commons this evening†2 from whence he has noe expectations to
― 248 ―
return before 10 at night has Comanded me to give you thanks for your postscript to his Sons Letter which I very willingly undertake that I may at the same time acknowledge my own obligation for the testimony I have of your friendship by your saluting me in the same postscript
But this is not all I have to say to you. In those few lines nay in a few words of them you have said what has filld both Mr Clarkes and my head ever since we read them and to this minute we can neither of us guess your meaning and therefore I must in both our names beg you would explain your self a litle further
The words are these—[For which there is but one remedy] I am glad to find that in your opinion there is a remedy but should be gladder to know what it was that we might contribute all we could to the attaining it for I profess I think if the Case be not remediless it will soon be soe unless the onely Remedy you mention be found out and speedily applyd
Soe much for your Postscript. Now let me tell you that on the Queens death†1 the Bank Actions†2 fell from 76 to 72 but are now got up again and Lottery Tickets†3 were talkt down to six years and half for prizes and six for Blanks but none sold soe and now they are at the price they were before
The printers Bill†4 is not yet come in but designd to be soe but I believe twill not be revived let who will endeavour it
Give my service to my Lady Marsham and Mr Clark and own me as
Sir
Your friend and servant
J F

1834. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 5 January [1695] (1766, 1840)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 41-4. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London Jan: 5
There will need no excuse to you for not sooner writing nor doe I in the least question tho I have not hard from you but that I have had your pitty in the sad sceen†1 I have had my part in since I saw you. it has been indeed so fare beyond description that I must not pretend to give you any perticuliar acount at least till I have the good fortune too se you. So much in generall I cant forbear saying that the poor queen's small pox was I veryly belive of the worst sort that Could be seen and what severall of the phisitians say's in all ther practice they never meett with but on the other Side I could hartyly have wishet that Docttor Rattlif†2 had not made that fatall misstake of Calling it the Measles from Munday night till tusday night that from saying ther was noe danger it Came to the sad discovery of black spott's apearing in her face when the same Docttor Rattlife did asure uss she would be all over mortified be morning so that by this misstake some thirty hours was lost which tho the Case seemd desperate ther was so much strngth that I Cant tell if the Course was affterward's taken had been try'd in time, what effect's it might have produced the Kings greife on this occasion seem's proportiond to his loss which is the greatest man could make, and he has as deep a sence of it as can be imagin'd has thought of noe bussnes nor scarce seen any but my lord Portland†3 but the day he recev'd the adress from the parliement.†4 thus wee have all made the greatest and most unexpected experiment of the vainity of all the world calls great in the loss of this good queen who from a very perfect state of health in the prime of her age the best regulated dyat without any maner of accident ether fright or surffet droped in to this desperate deseas and with the fewest Complaint's of ether paine or sikness in five days caryed off. it has been the greatest sermon on many account's I ever meett with and what I hope I shall never forget.
her body with her poor afflicted Family was remov'd hether on
― 250 ―
Satturday night†1 by order of Counsell, where we atend as if she was alive till the Funerall sollemnity's are prepar'd. they Call it not a publick Funerall tho the body is to ly in state and as I hear the wholle parliement†2 be in long Clokes in the prosesion because they seem not willing to goe the higheth's som funerall's in our age has been. Tho it is writing at randome to give you any acount of ther procedings for tho they have sate nine days they are yet Come to noe resolution in any one perticuliar. it is like to Countinue at Least a month or six Week's longer all which time we are to waite and sit up every forth night.
how the king Will dispose of us affter this dismalle cerimoniy is over I kno' not. I find all are of opinion that the establishment Will Countinue†3 and our Lodging's as soon as I have any Ceartinty you shall be suer to kno' and youle give me leave to depend upon you for your advice as too the managment of my self in the mean time I hope I shall hear from you which Will be a great obligation too
your very Faithffull servant
M L
I beg my most humble Service to My Dear Lady Masham my husband and all the good Company at oatts. My Cosen Cutts gives you her's.
Endorsed by Locke: M: Lockhart 5 Jan 94/5 Answered 9

... I also waited upon the Bishop of Bath and Wels, and having reason to speake to him of his book, which he had done me the
― 251 ―
honor to give me, I lead him, on that occasion, insensibly into a discourse of you; whereupon he told me that he had writ to you, and made the same professions to me that he had done to you, and added that he would be very ready and glad to do you any service; and all this with such candor and frankness, that I am fully satisfied he is in good earnest very wel inclined towards you, and wil be the readier to do you any kindness, for what he had said in print. I delivered to him the acknowledgement you desired me, for his Letter to you. He told me he thought he should publish his Comment in Latin, and then in his Preface to that he would be carefull to give you satisfaction. But that yet he could not alter his opinion, wherein he differed from you. 1836. Locke to Edward Clarke, 11 January [1695] (1833, 1837)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, f. 72. Printed in part in Forster, pp. 57-8; in full in Ollion, pp. 233-4; in both as 1694; in Rand, pp. 404-5. Year from endorsement. Perhaps carried by Clarke's son: see no. 1837. Answers no. 1833; answered by no. 1837.
Oates 11 Jan
Dear Sir
I hope this aireing of your son these holydays in the country will be convenient for his health and noe prejudice to his learning, he was wellcome to every body here and particularly to me. and I am glad to finde him such a proficient in the Latin. from which I conclude that in a litle time now he will be master of that tongue. But schools I see still are schools and make school boys. I say this to make you observe whether it be not to be apprehended that the main benefit of a danceing master will be lost, though he dance constantly two or three times a weeke, if those who ought to have the constant care of him in every part doe not looke after and minde his postures cariage and motions when he is out of the danceing masters hands, for without that the steps and figures of dances I think of noe value.
The remedie which as Mr Freke tells me set you and him soe much a thinking you will finde in the begining of my letter to him.
― 252 ―
If it will have time enough now to worke I know not, but that I thought on, and can think of noe other.
I returne you my thanks for your care of my lease. Here inclosed is a Short answer to Madams kinde letter, whether she will think it <s>weet†a too I know not. Whether it be like to worke on her to the end which I propose which is her health you must be judg. If you think a longer letter and of another turne may prove more effectuall, you have but to send the inclosed back again and I shall follow your instructions though I chose the most perswasive stile I could think of. I wish you and yours a happy year and am
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate friend and humble servant
J LOCKE

Deare Sir,
The Remedy proposed in the Begining of your Letter to J: F: by my Sonn, I beleive will not bee taken whilst this Man's Mayor,†2 and I feare there is not Honesty enough left amongst us to give any Reasonable hopes of any thing like it in our Time, And therefore I dispayre of a Cure:
I cannot but Repeate my thankes to my Lady and you for your extraordinary Favours and Kindnesse to my Son whilst at Oates,
― 253 ―
And to you particularly for the Account you gave of his Profitiency in the Latin tongue, and the Hopes you thereby give mee of his being Master of that Language in a little time; And I as heartily thanke you for the Hint you give mee of his Postures, Carryage, and Motions, and the care that ought to bee taken thereof by those whose Businesse it is to minde his Behaviour in every part, for without that, I conclude with you, That the Steps and Figures of Dances signifie nothing:
Your Lease is gone safe to Mr Strattons handes, I have a Letter from Him wherein Hee owns the Receipt of it, And as soon as I can gett the Money Hee Return'd for you, it shall bee received, and I shall waite your Order how to Dispose of it, The Byll Hee sent mee gave mee some troublesome Walkes, it being ten dayes before it was Accepted, but now I beleive it will be paid in a weeke or ten dayes times at the furthest: Your verie obleigeing Letter to Mrs Clarke I allsoe particularly thanke you for, and sent it to Her by the last Post, Pray give my humble service to my Lady, and bee assured that I am

1838. William Molyneux to Locke, 15 January 1695 (1829, 1857)

Dublin. January. 15. 1694/5
Honoured Sir
I have received the six Coppys of your Book; and thank you for the Care you have taken about them. I acknowledge my self likewise Obleidged to you for your Present of Dr Woods Almonack, tho it was not new to me, having received the Favour of One from the Author himself when Accountant General here in Ireland many
― 254 ―
Years ago.†1 Tis a very pretty Project, but I beleive 'twill hardly ever be Practised; because men think what they have already sufficiently accurate for the Common Uses of Life, and are hardly Brought from what they have Used so long as they have done the Common Julian Account, unles prevaild upon by some such Potent Authority as the Church, which abrogated the Julian and Establishd the Gregorian Kalendar.
The Sculptures also I received, and thank you for them. I shall do them all the Honour that outward Ornament can give them; and I hartily wish I had more effectual Ways of Shewing my Respects, which I think I can never do sufficiently.

The abovenoted Errata are those few that I have observed in the second Edition of your Book. they are very Inconsiderable and hardly worth Notice.†b †2
I have ever thought that an Elegant Translation of your Essay into Latin would be highly acceptable to Forreiners; and of Great Use in those Countrys whose minds lye yet captivated in Verbose,
― 255 ―
Disputative Philosophy and False Reasoning. I therefore presume to Mention it to you; that tho your Own Leasure may not permit you to perform it Your self, you may think of putting Some One on it, that under your Eye may do it Correctly. and were I not perswaded that your Own Eye and Correction were absolutely requisite herein; I would venture to make a bold Proposal to have it done by some One in this Place, whom I should reward for his Labour herein. and this I do, not that I think you may not with a great deal of Ease Imploy One your self in this matter; but meerly that therein I may have an Oppertunity of doing so much good in the World. You see, Sir, what a Veneration I have for your Writings: and therefore you wil Pardon me If I desire from you sub Amicitiæ Tessera†1 the Names of what Books you have Publishd. I Remember once I proposed to you the like Request,†2 and you were silent to it. if it were, that you designedly Conceal them, I acquiesce; But perhaps it proceeded from your Cursory passing over that part of My Letter; which makes me venture again on the same Request. And now that your thoughts are at Liberty from Your Essay, You wil give me leave with all Submission to Mind you of what you once told me you would think off, viz, Of Demonstrating Morals.†3 I am sure, as no hand could perform it better, so no Age ever required it more than Ours.

Dear Sir
Your Most Obleidged Humble servant
W: MOLYNEUX

Sir
I agree the remedy you propose would probably be effectuall but I despair of procuring it for the patient has long wanted it and been advised to use it but it seems he will use noe phisick but what is to be found in his own Garden and the medicine you prescribe will not grow in that Soil, Soe that for ought I see the Consumption must goe on
Mr Clarke has already given you notice that Saterday last†1 (and not before) a Quarter of a hundred of Cacao Nutts†2 were sent to Mr Pawlins for you and that Mr Clarke†a has paid me 2li-12s-6d for them and I hope he gave you the reason why you had noe greater Quantity

1840. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 17 January [1695] (1834, 1990)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 45-6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London Jan 17
I give you many thankes for your good advice in your two last letters; which I hope shall not be lost, for when one is really sick, all remedy's that seem to ease are Wellcome: especially where they come from so good an Understanding, and from one that I know dos so much wish success; tho I must confess, by every day's experience I find, there is noe cure's of this kind easy to be made. time, and frend's, are all that I find, or can expect any relief from. I doe not remember†a- what in my last could-†a give any occasion to a very kind reprimand in your leter. in the confusion I was in when I writ I really know not how I express't my self but this I am very sure that it was never in my thought's that Mr Locke would like any body the less for not being a courtier and were your Character the Contrary ther was never any thing in my Fortune so considerable for an allteration to have any effect upon you. I hope you Will not suspect my being courtier enouf now as to think I Flater when I tell you how much reall satisfaction the title you allow me to your frendship and advice gives me which I shall allway's esteem as I ought and as I ever found in my self an enclination to deserve well

of you what ever other good quality's I may want I am sure I can never want that of being with a most perticuliar respect
Your very Faithfull and most humble Servant
M L
I writ to my Lady Masham last post. I am as yet not able to say any thing of what turn our affares are like to take I mean the queen's Family wee I hear have many frends and some enemeys, wee shall know nothing till the funerall is over till then we waite and have tables and all thing's upon the same foot it was before the day is not nam'd but it is not thought it will be sooner then the forth of March†1 the expence growes in proportion with the time which is much more then at first proposed.

1841. William Brockman to Locke, 19 January 1695 (1854)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, ff. 159-60. For the writer see p. 111. He was now promoting John Briscoe's Land Bank: Horsefield, p. 186, etc.
Dorsetcourt Westminster
19th. Jan. 94/5
Sir
I make little question but you have seen, as well as heard of a Discourse on the last Funds etc per J.B.,†2 wherein he advanceth a Proposall so solidly and, in my poor opinion, so substantiall in itself, That the more I consider it, and the more I hear it discoursed, The more I find myself invited to labour in it, if I knew well how: I am aware, and owne my Presumption in this application, But am sensible too of your Candour among the other Great and Good Qualities you are Master of, which makes me the more easily rely

Sir
Your very humble servant
WILLIAM BROCKMAN.
