1842. James Tyrrell to Locke, 28 January [1695] (1803, 1859)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 130-1. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Oxon Jan 28
Dear Sir
That morning I left London, I sent you to your Lodging by a Porter, the first Dialogue concerning God and his Attributes, and I hope you have received and read it: by this time, and markt the places you scrupled, or disliked; as haveing now the second returned me againe after the peruseall of some of my Freinds, I make bold to send it you allso by a safe hand, and desire the like favour from you, and the more because in this I have taken occasion to borrow so much from your Essay of hum: understanding, as you will find upon the peruseal; I have cited the places all along in the margin, and if I have in any place omitted it I desire you would supplye that defect; and mark what is your owne with the same characters with the rest: I hope I have made good use of such
― 260 ―
excellent notions, and that they may doe good among those (if this ever come to be printed) who perhaps otherwise might not have read them in the Original: I desire you would give me your impartial opinion of them both. either by discourse or letter as oppertunity shall permit, for by your censure I shall resolve either to proceed in this designe, or let it alone. I intend God willing to be in Towne by the end of the Terme;†1 and then hope I may be so happy as to see you at the Queens funeral,†2 or if not to hear from you, when I let you know I am in Towne: so hopeing you enjoy your health notwithstanding this excessive cold season; which has lasted the longest of any since the great Frost.†3 I remaine
your most humble servant
J TYRRELL
I delivered your message to Dr. Charlet, and he tells me, that this Epitome of Metaphics being lately printed at Oxon, (one Dr: Wills being the Author)†4 for the use of the yong men, haveing occasion to send some of them up to Mr: Churchill, he desired him to send one to you because it proceeded upon y<o>ur†a Principles; of no conate Ideas.
Address: For John Lock Esqr at Sir Francis Mashams house at Oates.
Endorsed by Locke: J: Tyrrell Jan 28. 95 Answered Feb. 8
1843. John Wynne to Locke, 31 January [1695] (1846)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 111-12. Printed in King, pp. 189-90. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answered by no. 1846.
John Wynne, c. 1665-1743; matriculated from Jesus College, Oxford, 1682; B.A. 1685; M.A. 1688; D.D. 1706; Lady Margaret professor of Divinity 1705-15; Principal of Jesus 1712-20; bishop of St. Asaph 1715; of Bath and Wells 1727: D.N.B.
Honoured Sir
After the repeated perusal of your Exellent Essay concerning Humane Understanding, (which will ever afford me most agreeable and instructive entertainment)†5 Tho I find my self deeply
― 261 ―
impress'd with motions of the greatest respect and esteem for The Author; yet I am very sensible how impertinent It would be for one of my Rank and condition to pretend to make any private acknowledgments for so publick and Universal A Benefit. But haveing some thoughts relateing to Your Book, which may be of advantage to the Publick, I make bold to offer them to you, not doubting But that your Candor will pardon my presumption, Tho your Judgment should disallow of my Proposeal. Ever since I had the happines to be acquainted with your Accurate†1 Essay, I have been perswaded that the greatest service that could be done for the Studious and Thinking part of the World, next to the composeing of It, would be to bring It into vogue and credit, and thereby into common and general use. If Men did not labour under inveterate prejudices, and obstinate prepossessions, This might easily be effected: And yet notwithstanding these, The Truths contain'd in your Book are so clear and evident, The notions so natural and agreeable to reason, That I imagine none that carefully reads, and duly considers them, can avoid being enlightend and instructed by them. I have for some Time made It my busines In my little Sphere, to recommend It to All Those, That I have any Influence over: Nor did I ever meet with Any, who after An attentive and diligent peruseal complain'd of being disappointed in their expectations; But on the contrary, They own'd themselves to have been infinitly benefitted by It. By the light which they have deriv'd from It, They so clearly perceive how useles and insignificant our Vulgar Systems are, That they have resolv'd to triffle no longer, But to ridd their hands and heads entirely of them: And In all probability It would have the same effect upon us All, If It were but read and considerd by All. Now In order to this, I am enclin'd to think, (and some others concur with me in the same opinion) That It would be very useful to publish an abridgment of the Book. If some of the Larger explications (some of which are but incidental to the general design of the work) were contracted, It might be reduc'd to the Compas of A moderate octavo. I need not represent to you the Advantages of A small over A larger Volume: But shall only tell you that It would be of excellent use to us of this place, to be put into the hands of our young men, and to be read and explaind to them instead of those Triffling and Insignificant Books, which serve only to perplex and confound,
― 262 ―
instead of enlightning and improving our Reasons. I do not see that there is Any Thing wanting In It to compleat The Third part In your Division of science.†1 I Know you mention An Epitome of this work in your preface: But 'Tis as I am inform'd In A Language not commonly understood among us, and too scarce to answer the end which I propose.†2 If upon this Intimation, you shall think what is here offer'd worthy of your regard, I would willingly contribute any assistance that I may be capeable of, to ease you of the Trouble.
I humbly crave your pardon for this bold Intrusion, and beg leave to subscribe my self what I sincerely am with all imaginable respect
Honoured Sir
Your oblig'd and very Humble Servant
JOHN WYNNE
Jan. 31. Jesus Coll: Oxon.

Dear Sir
I am to thank you for one of January the 21 directed to me and for one of the 1st Instant to my Collegue who desires your excuse that he cant doe it himself, and he has comanded me to inform you that the very day I received yours†a- in which you mention Mr Strattons Bill he got your mony which was 39li-14s-od. It is in Sir Francis Childs hand†3 at presant and will continue soe till you order otherwise
― 263 ―
Sir St: Ev:†1 has also given Mr Clarke a note for your Quarters Sallery soe that the mony matters you mention in your Letter goe well and just as you desire-†a
But alas! what shall we say that you were soe disappointed by the treatment the House of Commons gave the petitioners against the Bank? truly if noe more can be said for the house then the petitioners said for themselves I think the Commons would be unexcuseable, though as the matter was carry'd I can't blame them for my life, for when the Petitioners had affirmd they were ready to make out the allegations in their petition and had a day given them to doe it for them to appear and declare that neither they nor any other Trader could at that time say one word to Justify what they had alledged was such a trifling as in my opinion would well Justifie the dismissing the petition at least.†2
As to what you say concerning the Consequences of the Corporation†3 I know not but you may be a true prophet though at presant tis evident that thereby the publick saves a great deal since by means of it the Crown will now be supplyd on the Land Tax and first years product of the customs at 5 per Centum and all Tallys†4 on the remotest Funds are become as good if not better then ready mony but for ought I know future times may pay for this
I fear twill be impossible to doe any good on the Act of Navigation, though there seems a disposition in the House to have the Grand Comittee of Trade sit once a week which is a Comittee appointed at the beginning of every session but which I never knew sit†5
Mr Cl: thanks you for the Grafts you sent him both of us being of opinion that tis the best fruit (as you order it) that ever we met with. he has written to J Barber†b for some Grafts of the Pears

you like soe but fears the trees are soe small that you can have but few which when they come you may dispose of to what Lords or Ladys you please
Give our service to the Lady with whom you are and believe me
Your affectionate friend and humble servant
J FREKE

Mr Colledg
I thank you for makeing a poor ignorant country man understand your Parliament matters for I finde that he that now and then chops upon†2 some of the printed Votes will not be very well instructed

1846. Locke to John Wynne, 8 February 1695 (1843, 1850)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 287. Draft. Printed in King, pp. 191-2, with date 3 February. Answers no. 1843; answered by no. 1850.
Oates 8º Feb. 94/5
Sir
You cannot think it strange that I should be surprised at the receit of a letter, of soe much civility to me. from a person I had not the honour to know; and of soe great commendation of my book, from a place where I thought it litle taken notice of. And though the complements, you are pleased to bestow both on me and it, are above what belongs to either, yet I cannot but acknowledg myself sensibly obleiged by the kinde thoughts you are biased with in favour both of me and my essay. It haveing been begun by chance and continued with noe other designe but a free enquiry into that subject it would have been great vanity in me to publish it with hopes that what had been writ for the diversion of my idle hours should be made the serious businesse of studious men who knew how to imploy their time. Those who had leisure to throw away on speculations a litle out of the road I guessed might perhaps looke into it. If by the credit and recommendation of those who like you have enterteind it with a favourable opinion it be spread farther and got into the hands of men of letters and study it is more than I could expect for a treatise writ in a plain and popular stile, which haveing in it noething of the aire of learning nor soe much as the language of the schools was litle suited to the use or relish of those who as teachers or learners applyd them selves to the mysterys of scholastique knowledg. But you I see are got above Fashion and Prejudice: And you must give me leave to have noe ordinary thoughts of a man, who by those two great opposers of all new offers at improvement will not suffer your self to be hinderd from contriveing how to†a make†a the way to reall knowledg more open and easy to those beginers who have set their faces that way. I should be very glad any thing in my book could be made usefull to that purpose. I agree with you that most of the larger explications may be looked on as incidental to what you designe and soe may by one who would out of my booke make a systeme of the
― 267 ―
third part in my devision of science be wholy passed by or but lightly touched: to which let me adde that those repetitions which for reasons then†a I let it goe with may be omitted and all the parts contracted into that forme and bignesse you propose. But in my litle health and lesse leisure considering that I have been soe long a stranger to systems and am utterly ignorant what would best suit those you designe it for, it is not for me to goe about it though what you have said would incline me to beleive it would not in any case†b be wholy lost labour. Tis not for noething I hope that this thought is fallen into the minde of one who is much abler to execute it. you I see are as much master of my notions as I my self and better able to put them togeather to the purpose you intend. I say not this to decline giveing my assistance if you in civility should think I can afford you any. The abstract†c which which was publishd in French in the Bibliotheque universelle of 1688 will neither in its size or designe answer the end you propose, but if the rough draught of it, which I think I have in English some where amongst my papers†1 be of any use to you, you may command it or whatever service I can doe you in any kinde for I am with a very particular esteem and respect
Sir
Your most humble servant

1848. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 18 February [1695?] (1810, 1863)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 169. Printed in Rand, pp. 442-3. This letter and no. 1863, which is dated 22 March, are evidently closely connected with one another. Rand places both in 1696. He was probably influenced by Mrs. Clarke's and Sammy's illnesses; both were ill early in 1696, but they were ill at other times also, and the notices in these two letters do not fit closely with those in the fully dated letters for 1696. Further, in view of nos. 2043 and 2046 Locke is unlikely to have written to Mrs. Clarke on 22 March 1696. Again, young Edward Clarke was at Oates from probably a few days before 2 January 1696 until early in May; he sent his duty to his mother in Locke's letters to Mrs. Clarke of 6 January and 25 March 1696; no message from him is mentioned in the present letter or in no. 1863.
Edward was at Oates about the end of 1694, returning to London probably on 12 January 1695. This fits with the notice in the present letter which implies that he had recently visited Oates and returned from it. As 1695 and 1696 are the only known years in which Edward was at Oates in January while Mrs. Clarke was at Chipley, this letter and that for 22 March are here placed in 1695.
The present letter may be the enclosure in no. 1849 which Clarke was asked to read and forward.
Oates 18 Feb:
Madam
Whether you carve to many or but to one in my opinion it is best always to doe it with a good stomach and therefor I cannot but advise you to send for the water again and to drink and be mery, there being noe mirthe equall to that of good health. I hope by that time this is got to you the frost and snow will be gon. as soon as that is I think it will be seasonable for you to return to the use of the waters.†1
― 270 ―
When the physitian was with the child†1 and you found he had done him good you ought to have consulted him about the rickets. He was a better judg upon the place then I who am in the dark and at this distance. I hope you did and then you will not venture your childs health upon the use of a remedie grounded upon noe better light than your guesses that he is inclined to the Rickets
As to the management of your great and litle children this I think. that the biger may be made usefull to you for the governing and instructing of the lesse, if they be once set right. which I think they can never be if they be very frequently chid and for every litle fault rebukd with displeasure and made uneasy. If every litle slip brings them under such correction, and into the forfeiture of your good thoughts of them they will conclude there is noe avoiding being chid, and soe they will not be very carefull not to deserve it. The first thing you must indeavour must be to give them a tast of the pleasure it is to be in your favour and good likeing by doeing well, and when they see they are able to keep possession of it by a litle care, and every small mistake does not forfeit it. they will be unwilling to loose it, and you will have an hold upon them. If they have faults (as who has not) consider which is the greatest in each of them, and when they are guilty of that shew your displeasure more by the reservdnesse and coldnesse of your looks and cariage than by hasty or angry words, which should be but few and gentle and just enough to let them know why you are displeased, but let them finde the continuance of your displeasure in your looks and cariage till they have reconciled themselves to you by amendment of their cariage. Thus haveing masterd one you may goe on to the next. But if you indeavour to mend every fault you see in them at once by falling severely upon them as often as they commit any. you will never mend any one. Whilst they are in a state of acceptation with you by avoiding the great fault you have rebukd them for and straitly forbid them upon pein of your displeasure, any other that comes in your way worth your notice you should only in kinde words and without anger admonish them of. But I trouble you to noe purpose, you have this in print by you and need not here a hasty disorderly repetition of it.†2
Master Edward was very wellcome to every body here and to me in Particular and my Lady makes it her request to you and Mr
― 271 ―
Clarke that he may come hither whenever his schoole businesse will afford him soe much leisure. She with her service returns you her thanks for the favour of your remembrance. Pray remember me kindly to my dear wife and the rest of the yonge folks that know me. I am
Dear Madam
Your most humble servant
J LOCKE

1849. Locke to John Freke and Edward Clarke, 18 February [1695] (1847, 1853)
Rand, pp. 407-9. Year from endorsement. Answers no. 1847.
18th February.
To the College, greeting,
Let the grave Squire know that I am obliged to him for his care of my little money affair and letters; and if he pleases let him peruse the enclosed, and if he approves of it send it forward with my service, or else back to me for such amendments as he thinks convenient.
As to Bachelor John I beg his pardon for my bad memory, for either I writ the £5. 5s. od. down in my memorandums, when I received the letter where it was mentioned, and so my memory, being discharged of it took no more care of it; or else something at the time thrust it so out, that remembering the money was mentioned paid for the cocoa nut, and not that I thought Edward the grave <had>†a in his much business forgot to tell me of it. I doubted not but you had done what you had promised and return you my thanks.
My conclusion stands thus. The money in the Bank is, and I conclude always will be, managed by London merchants, whereby it will come to pass that they under under names†1 and their friends will be sooner and easier supplied for their occasions than others, whereby I am apt to think the greatest part of our trade will in a
― 272 ―
little while by secret combinations be got into a few hands, even by this monopoly of money. And I think it becomes the wisdom of the Parliament rather to consider how money might be better distributed into the country, and other ports, and trading parts of England, than to set up a corporation, and by law countenance its drawing all to London. For if you examine it I believe you will find trade in all the out ports mightily decayed: one cause whereof I looked on to be the banking trade (formerly) in London, which is now authorised by a law, and such an establishment of it as I fear will cost dear to England. And whatever good effects are boasted of now in the infancy of the corporation will not last long when they are a little grown up and know their own strength.
The Lady of the house returns her thanks and service to you both, and I am,
your most affectionate friend and humble servant,
J. LOCKE.
I desire brother Bachelor would do me the favour to look into the list of unclaimed benefited tickets mentioned in the Gazette of the 14th instant to see whether any of my numbers be there. I do not much expect it, but it is possible former list may have been misprinted.†1 'Tis good to be sure.
Address: For Edward Clarke, Esq., Member of Parliament, at Richard's Coffee House, near Temple Bar, London.
Frank.

1850. John Wynne to Locke, 20 February 1695 (1846, 1869)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 113-14. Answers no. 1846.
Honoured Sir
It cannot be so strange to you, that I, and some others of this place, should entertain so high an opinion of your Excellent Essay, as It is to me, That All who pretend to devote themselves to the pursuit of knowledg and search of Truth, should not have long since discoverd the Value of that Inestimable Treasure of Both,
― 273 ―
with which you have enrich'd The World. But whatever others may think of It, give me leave to assure you, that the expressions which I us'd in my first address to you, to signify my respect for your Person, and my opinion of your Book, are infinitely short of my real sentiments of Both: And Tho I could yeild A greater deference to your judgment on other occasions, then perhaps to any man's else, yet I cannot by Your modest thoughts of your self, and Essay be induc'd to lessen my esteem of either; nor indeed to look upon The latter any otherwise, then as The Noblest Effort, and farthest Advance towards real and usefull knowledg, that was ever made. For my own part, I shall allways own my self indebted to you, as well for that little stock of knowledg that I am allready Master of; as also for whatever accession to it I may hereafter make, by the assistance of that light, and under the conduct of those Rules which you have furnish'd me withall. In the mean Time, I cannot but acknowledg your great kindnes and condescension, in vouchafing that regard and esteem which you are pleas'd to express To One, who has so little meritt to recommend him to the notice of A Person of Your Worth, unless my frank acknowledgment of my great obligations to you may entitle me To some degree of your favour: Then which nothing can be more acceptable, or welcom to me. The more I consider On what I took the freedom lately to propose To you, The more I am perswaded of the usefulnes of It; And therefore am the more concern'd, that your health and leasure will not permitt you to go about It: For You, who have A much clearer view and comprehension of the whole, could have given us A more perfect Abridgment of It, then either I, or any one else can be suppos'd able to do. Nevertheles, since you are pleas'd to give me some encouragement to undertake It, I am very ready to contribute my endeavour; the rather, because I do not think any of my Time lost, or mispent that is employ'd in the peruseal of It. I have allready an Abstract of It By me, which I had drawn some Time since for my own private use: This I intend to enlarg by inserting some of the most considerable and necessary explications upon each head, and connecting them together. I shall not pretend to alter either your method or language, being convinc'd that neither can be done for the better. I am not so fond of our Vulgar Systems, as to think It would receive any improvement by being dress'd up In A Scholastick garb: on the contrary I hope It will soon bring them into discredit,
― 274 ―
which they do att present in some measure labour under, and att length into A Total disuse. I have communicated This design with two or three freinds, who encourage and assist me: As soon as I have finish'd It, I shall submitt It to your correction, and resign It wholly to your disposeal. I am pretty confident It will sell well, and rather promote, then hinder the sale of the Essay, If your Bookseller has any store of them unsold. Be pleas'd to let me know, how It may be convey'd safely to your hands. If you think fit to direct me in any particular relateing to this design, I shall upon your intimation, readily comply with It, and be proud of the honour of obeying your Commands, who Am
Honoured Sir
Your most oblig'd Humble Servant
JOHN WYNNE
Jes. Coll Oxon. Feb. 20. 94/5

1851. Andrew Fletcher to Locke, 22 February 1695(?) (1756, 2381)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 131-2. Fletcher used the new-style year in the dates of nos. 2381 and 2389; presumably he does so here also. MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 133-4, a series of notes by Henry Fletcher of Saltoun (no. 2901) about his wife's health, was perhaps sent with the letter (ff. 116-18, 121, and probably ff. 119-20, all relating to the health of members of the Fletcher family, date from the summer of this year).
Sir
My sister in law†1 did luckely incline rather to follow your advice than that of two other phisitians that wer sent her at the same time. Besids that I had told her that humaine understanding was the best ingredient of a phisitian, of which you must have a large share or that you had greatly imposed upon the world, for that you had writ a folio upon it. She is now much better as to her obstructions, but her sweatings contineu stil, and if they do not wear of
― 275 ―
with the good weather and more exersice it is feared they may prove fatal. But nothing she has yit taken has done her so much good, as what you did prescrive her. You whould make me almost as happy as my brother if you could perfite the cure. I have sent you her case least you should have forgot it. Sure I am never a phisitian in England but your self would have remembered it a quarter of ane houre without a fie. But you thinck to pass for Mr J. Locke and no phisitian, but I pretend it shall be other ways when you come first to toun or I to Oates, Tho I desir your answer with your first leasur. My humble service to the good Lady you may tell her that, tho we be not so, she is very happy in living in the country providing she hear no news, that I have no prejudice agenst her and theirfor writ her none. If you aske me what I am doing I shal tell you that I am tracing pristcraft from its first original in Ægipt. Wheir I find lickways many other monsters but none so abominable. I am very bussy about many other things of which I shal give you ane account at metting. I am
Sir
Your obliged humble servant
A FLETCHER
London the 22d of Feb: 95

1852. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 22 February/4 March 1695 (1830, 1961)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 129-30.
Rotterdam 4 march 1695
Dear Sir
I have now not of a long time received any from you nor wrote to you, having been extraordinarily busy, this frosty weather, if possible to get an end of differences betwixt my wife, and sister and their Brother, who would willingly possess all his fathers estate alone, in so much that we seldom stir out, and since Christmas have seldom gone to bed, my wife, self and Benjohan till 1. 2. 3 oclock in the morning. Benjohan tho but 14 year old this January, keeps my books, and posts the books of my wives father, the Journals of which I have copies of, with so much acuteness, faire and swift writing, and Judgment, that its admireable, and follows
― 276 ―
his Latine to boot, John and Arent do it also, but Arent is got afore, and keeps so, so that John cannot overtake him, they are both through the Rule of three, and almost through fractions. But what is remarkeable Arent is never satisfyed to work a thing, but he must understand wherefore; and have a reason of all things. I am purposed by the next fleet to send John to London to perfect him self there in English, and so to place him out there.
This is all but preamble, The occasion of my writing at present is this. The Professor Limborgh wrote me the 20 January last, that one in the Name of the Bishop of utrecht,†1 had been with Wetsteen†a to see the originall manuscript, but that he had told him that it was in my possession, he then desired him to enquire of the Professor of whom I had it. But he answered that he knew not the name, And precautiond me not to tell if any came to me to see it, and inquire. Because he beleevd that the design was to purchase it, and help it out of the world.†2
So this evening came a priest, reputed a Jansenist, to see it. I askt him what his intent was in desiring to see it, he said he was desired to address himself to me to that purpose, and that he beleeved that it was to be satisfyed upon his report to be really what monsieur Limborgh reports it to be.
I told him that upon condition that if he found himself convincd that it was really Authentick he would give it me under his hand, that it was so, I would let him see it. He said frankly that he made no difficulty to do that. And askt me if I had not had it from William Waller, I told him I should tell no body of whom I had it, but assured him I came honestly by it, by no other friend than my ready mony. Upon his seing it, he gave me this under his hand, just a month misdated,
Infrascriptus fidem facio me die 4ta february anno 1695 vidisse in ædibus Domini Benjamin furly Rotterdami librum antiquum manuscriptum in parquemeno inter duos asseres compactum, et
― 277 ―
continentem sententias et acta Inquisitionis Tholosanæ ab anno 1307° usque ad annum 1323° cum hac exteriori inscriptione: Liber Sententiarum. Et post exactam perquisitionem non aliter potuisse judicare, uti et modo judico, quam librum istum esse, quod præ se fert, sine ulla corruptione aut additione et plane integrum, demptis paucis foliis in quibus superior margo, et titulus currens <corrosus>†a est sine ulla offensione Textus. Incipit autem a juramento Curialium Regis, et a sententia contra Pontium Amelii relapsum. Ita testor die et loco supradictis. and was signd Carolus Bontius S. Th. Licent.†1 But he desired me not to make it publike because many might make an ill use of it.
I am now of the mind of the Professor that application wil be made to the Gentleman whom you know†2 to purchase it of him; and so help it out of the world; wherefore I now recommend to you, with all expedition to anticipate their designs, by purchasing it of him. If he will finally sell it me, for the mony I lent him upon it, if it were somewhat more I will surrender him the bond—pray lose no time in this affaire. I fancy, being post day they may have written this post. I shall long to heare what you can effect in this case, and so with my and my wives deare love to yourself and our service to Sir F:M. and my lady I rest
Dear Sir
your humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY

1853. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 28 February [1695] (1849, 1856)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 185-6. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's signature and the address. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Febr the 28th
Sir
Your Grafts came safe moonday morning and were immediately sent into the West before your Letter was received else some of them had been placed near the Town as you desire however I hope they will not receive soe much prejudice in Carryage as that none of them should grow and if any one Grow that will in a litle time afford Cuttings enough for all our friends in that Country where we most desire to propagate them
As to the printing Bill there is a new one drawn very unlike the old one and I guess twill be brought into the House in a few days but I am apt to think twill not pass this Session for those that desire an Act will not be content with what is reasonable and there are others who I believe will endeavour and be able to prevent the unreasonable designs of the Company etc:†1
Accept our Thanks for your sheet about Coynage†2 which Mr Clarke deliverd each of us 2 coppys of from you. I think you have set that matter in its due light but tis an old complaint that light is come into the world and yet men love darkness rather than light.†3 You know the House of Commons has appointed a Comittee to consider how clipping etc: may be prevented†4 but those that make most adoe about it will not be brought to understand your Treatise†5 and are still puzling themselves about methods that will rather increase than cure the evill and to say truth I believe some of them have noe other design and those who should be chiefly concernd take noe care in it soe that we are as apprehensive
― 279 ―
as you of the dreadfull consequences of the diminishing of our Coin and fear the seeming care taken by the house of Commons will but bring those consequences the sooner upon us. I know that tis come to that pass already that Guineas being sold at 1li-5s-0†1 sollicitors choose rather to give Counsellors silver and the Goldsmiths make them pay for milld mony some times 2s some times 3s in the pound exchange.†2
The House of Lords yesterday Considerd the complaint some Lords had made that the Fleet was sent into the Streights and after a long Debate came (without any Division) to a Resolution That the Counsell to send the Fleet to the Streights tended to advance the honour and Interest of the King and Kingdom.
Your Letter was sent to mrs Cl last post
Give our service to my Lady Masham and esteem us
Your faithfull friends and humble servants

I think myself very happy, that the Proposalls, I sought to be informed of, correspond with your Judgement; so far at least as you have had opportunity to consider them; And since you have thus far allowed and approv'd my Liberty I venture on to Request, That when you have weighed the Whole throughly you would please to observe to me where you find the Author short, or that he fails in obviating or answering Objections, with your owne

1855. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 5/15 March 1695 (1835, 1880)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 91-2. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 80-1.
A Londres†1 le 15 de Mars 1695.
J'ai attendu, Monsieur, depuis vôtre derniere, que les Canaux fussent ouverts, pour vous répondre, parce que j'esperois de recevoir les petits Traitez, dont vous me parliez;†2 mais comme je ne les reçois point, je m'imagines qu'ils n'ont pas encore passez la mer. Je croi que vous aurez vû cependant ma dissertation, sur le commencement de S. Jean, que j'ai envoiée par la poste à Mr. le Comte de Pembroke. Le savant homme,†3 qui est cause que je l'ai faite, ma appris ensuite que l'on avoit fait une équivoque, et que l'on avoit confondu avec moi un honête homme, nommé Clark,†4 qui étoit Unitaire et qui est mort depuis peu. Il me dit aussi que les Evêques de Worcester et de Lichfield†5 croient ma conjecture bien fondée à
― 281 ―
l'égard de Philon. Mais il voudroit qu'au lieu de Ratio, j'eusse mis Verbum, à cause de la coûtume; quoi que cela étant supposé, tout mon raisonnement ne vaille rien. L'Auteur de l'ancienne Vulgate Latine, qui n'entendoit pas trop bien le Grec est la source du mot Verbum, qui ne signifie rien ici; et l'Eglise Latine ne la suivi, que par pure ignorance. On voudroit aussi que j'eusse dit que le Λόγος est une personne, mais c'est de quoi il ne s'agissoit pas en cet endroit. D'ailleurs mon dessein n'a été, que de faire voir que je ne suis pas du sentiment des Unitaires de Londres, qui en ont usé très-indiscretement. Je vois que j'ai beaucoup perdu dans la mort de feu Mr. l'Archevêque; mais il faut se consoler de tout, et s'en remettre à la Providence. Celui qui devroit et qui pourroit me servir beaucoup, s'il vouloit, n'est pas homme à cela, comme je le vois par ses Lettres, qui sont toutes pleines de bruits et de Chimeres, assaisonnées de je ne sai quelles louänges, qui me font comprendre que c'est tout ce que j'en aurai, après les promesses qu'il m'a faites de bouche et par écrit.†1 Je suis bien obligé à Mylord Privyseal et à Vous aussi, Monsieur, et je voudrois bien trouver un moien de vous faire connoître la reconnoissance que j'ai pour toutes vos bontez. Je croi qu'on aura porté chez Churchil une vie de Richelieu,†2 au moins Mrs. Huguetan†3 me promirent d'y donner ordre. Faites moi la grace de me marquer, si cet ordre a été executé; parce que si cela n'est pas, je m'en plaindrai. Il ne paroit rien ici qui vaille la peine de le lire. Je suis, Monsieur, de tout mon cœur, Vôtre très-humble et trèsobeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings, in little Lincols inn, over against the plough London

1856. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 7 March [1695] (1853, 1858)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 187-8. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's signature and the address. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answered by no. 1858.
March the 7th
Sir
In answer to yours of the 4th I am to acquaint you that the whole College has seen and considerd the pamphlet you mention†1 and that the Bill prepared for regulating the Press is soe contrived that there is an absolute Liberty for the printing every thing that tis Lawfull to Speak†2
The Sheet of Coinage†3 I think has and will do a great deal of good in this conjuncture and we endeavour as much as we can to make it lookt into and considerd by the members of the House of Commons who now have that matter under their consideration. and we thank you for the leave you give us to take any number of coppys to disperse though I think we shall have noe great occasion to use it for the price is but small soe that none will be discouraged to buy it and people are apter to read and be influenced by what they buy then by that which is given them most men being of Davids mind not to serve the Lord with that which costs them nothing†4
We would gladly execute your Commission in making the purchase you desire of Sir W W†5 but it is not in our power for he (to avoid his Creditors) is fled the Kingdom and gone (as I hear) into Portugall however I will endeavour to find a way to send to him and buy the Book if possible though I must tell you I doubt it will not be sold for Mr Fs Bond†6 which he (I dare say) never intends to pay and would rather take twenty shillings in ready mony then have that Bond deliverd up. But pray Sir is not the Law in Holland
― 283 ―
like the Custom of London where one may attach any Goods of a Debtor and have them Condemnd and thereby the property transferrd for the Debt? If soe why may not Mr F: take that Course?
I shall take the same care of your Lottery Tickets as I doe of my own, but (it seems) we shall not have the Transferr Tickets for the Blanks till midsummer nor those for the Benefits till after our Lady day when we shall receive half a years payment and the Tickets for the future payments together. The reason of this delay is that the Treasury requires the Transfer officers to sign the Ticket for every payment vizt 32 for every Benefit and 16 for every Blank
I have here enclosed sent you the numbers of the Tickets which were not claimd by which you will see you were not concernd therein for yours began N87 M111 and soe went on successively And for the odd one I bought for you tis not likely it should have a benefit belong to it since it cost but 6li-5s and Blanks are now sold for 7li.
The House of Commons have been finding fault with one another and have appointed a comittee to examine the Books and Comittee of the East India Company and the Books and Chamberlain of the City to discover what mony was given for secret service by them when the East India Trade and orphans business were in the house†1 and Mr Brewer was accused for taking 30 Guineas for carrying on a Bill in the House†2 and there matters are further to be considerd tomorrow.
Give our service to my Lady and own us as
Your friends and servants
JO: FREKE
EDW: CLARKE

1857. Locke to William Molyneux, 8 March 1695 (1838, 1867)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 96-103. Answers nos. 1829 and 1838; answered by no. 1867.
Oates, 8 Mar. 1694/5.
Dear Sir,
You will, I fear, think me frozen up with this long winter, or else with a negligence colder than that, having two very obliging letters of yours by me, the one ever since January, the other February last, I make you no answer to either, till thus far in March. The truth is, expecting ever since I received your last letter an account from London, concerning something I had a mind to put into my letter,†1 and after writing four times about it, being yet delay'd, I can forbear no longer to return you my thanks, and to beg your pardon that I have been so slow in it. If you interpret it right, you will look upon it as the effect of a friendship got past formalities, and that has confidence enough to make bold with you, where it is without neglect of you, or prejudice to either. I was not a little rejoyced with the news you sent me in the first of your letters, of your safe recovery of a fever. Had I known it before the danger was over, that you had been ill, it would have been no small fright and pain to me. For I must assure you, that amongst all the friends your kindness or worth has procured you, there is not any one who values you more than I do, or does more interest himself in all your concerns. This makes me, that tho' I have a long time extremely desired to see you, and propose to my self an infinite satisfaction in a free conversation with you; yet what you tell me, that you were coming last summer into England, to make me a visit, makes me dread the satisfaction of my own wishes. And methinks I ought not to purchase one of the greatest happinesses I can propose to my self at so dear and dangerous a rate. I have received many and great obligations from you before, but they were such, as though I had no title to, I thought I might accept from one whom I love, and therefore was glad to find kind to me. But when I reflect on the length of the way, and the sea between us, the danger of the one, and the fatigue of both, and your no very robust constitution, as I imagine, I cannot consent you should venture so much for my sake. If any harm should happen to you in the journey, I could
― 285 ―
never forgive it my self to be the occasion of so great a loss to the world and my self. And if you should come safe, the greatness of the hazard, and an obligation out of all proportion, to what I either ought to receive, or was capable to return, would overwhelm me with shame, and hinder my enjoyment. And yet, if I may confess my secret thoughts, there is not any thing which I would not give, that some other unavoidable occasion would draw you into England. A rational free-minded man, tyed to nothing but truth, is so rare a thing, that I almost worship such a friend; but when friendship is joyn'd to it, and these are brought into a free conversation, where they meet, and can be together, what is there can have equal charms? I cannot but exceedingly wish for that happy day, when I may see a man I have so often longed to have in my embraces. But yet, though it would endear the gift to receive it from his kindness, I cannot but wish rather that fortune alone would throw him into my arms.
This cold winter has kept me so close a prisoner within doors, that, 'till yesterday, I have been abroad but once these three months, and that only a mile in a coach. And the inability I am in to breath London air in cold weather, has hinder'd me yet from the happiness of waiting on Dr. Ashe; but I hope to get to London before he leaves it, that I may, to a person whom you have an esteem for, pay some part of the respects I owe you. I had last week the honour of a visit from an ingenious gentleman, a member of your college at Dublin, lately returned from Turkey.†1 He told me he was a kinsman of yours; and though his other good qualities might have made him welcome any where, he was not, you may be sure, the less welcome to me, for being known and related to you. He seems to me to have been very diligent and curious in making observations whilst he has been abroad, and more inquisitive than most of our people that go into those parts. And by the discourse I had with him, the little time we were together, I promise my self we shall have a more exact account of those parts, in what I hope he intends to publish, than hitherto is extant. Dr. Huntington, who was formerly at Aleppo, and is my old acquaintance, and now my neighbour in this country,†2
― 286 ―
brought Mr. Smith hither with him from his house. But yet I must acknowledge the favour to you, and desire you to thank him for it when he returns to Dublin. For the friendship he knew you had for me, was, I take it, the great inducement that made him give himself the trouble of coming six or seven miles in a dirty country.
You do so attack me on every side with your kindness to my book, to me, to my shadow,†1 that I cannot but be asham'd I am not in a capacity to make you any other acknowledgement, but in a very full and deep sense of it. I return you my thanks for the corrections you have sent me, which I will take all the care of I can in the next edition, which, my bookseller tells me, he thinks will be this summer.†2 And if any other fall under your observation, I shall desire the continuance of your favour in communicating them.
I must own to you, that I have been solicited from beyond sea to put my Essay into latin, but you guess right, I have not the leisure to do it. It was once translated by a young man in Holland, into latin, but he was so little master of the english or latin tongue, that when it was shew'd me, which he did not till he had quite done it, I satisfyed him that it would be very little for his credit to publish it, and so that was laid by.†3 Since that, my bookseller was, and had been for some time, seeking for a translator, whom he would have treated with to have undertaken it, and have satisfyed for his pains. But a little before the coming of your letter, he writ me word he had been disappointed where he expected to have found one who would have done it, and was now at a loss. So that what you call a bold, is not only the kindest, but the most seasonable proposal you could have made. You understand my thoughts as well as I do my self, and can be a fit judge whether the translator has expressed them well in latin or no, and can direct him where to omit or contract any thing where you think I have been more large than needed. And though in this I know you intend, as you say, some good to the world, yet I cannot but take it as a very particular obligation to my self, and shall not be a little satisfyed to have my book go abroad into the world with stroaks of your judicious hand to it. For, as to omitting, adding, altering, transposing any thing in it, I permit it wholly to your judgment. And if there be anything in it defective, or which you think may be added with advantage
― 287 ―
to the design of the whole work, if you will let me know, I shall endeavour to supply that defect the best I can. The chapter of Identity and Diversity, which owes its birth wholly to your putting me upon it,†1 will be an encouragement to you to lay any the like commands upon me. I have had some thoughts my self, that it would not be possibly amiss to add, in lib. iv. ch. 18, something about Enthusiasm, or to make a chapter of it by it self.†2 If you are of the same mind, and that it will not be foreign to the business of my Essay, I promise you, before the translator you shall employ, shall be got so far, I will send you my thoughts on that subject, so that it may be put into the latin edition. I have also examined P. Malbranche's opinion concerning seeing all things in God, and to my own satisfaction laid open the vanity, and inconsistency, and unintelligibleness of that way of explaining humane understanding.†3 I have gone almost, but not quite, through it, and know not whether I now ever shall finish it, being fully satisfyed my self about it. You cannot think how often I regret the distance that is between us; I envy Dublin for what I every day want in London. Were you in my neighbourhood, you would every day be troubled with the proposal of some of my thoughts to you. I find mine generally so much out of the way of the books I meet with, or men led by books, that were I not conscious to my self that I impartially seek truth, I should be discouraged from letting my thoughts loose, which commonly lead me out of the beaten track. However, I want some body near me, to whom I could freely communicate them, and, without reserve, lay them open. I should find security and ease in such a friend as you, were you within distance. For your judgment would confirm and set me at rest, where it approved, and your candor would excuse what your judgment corrected, and set me right in. As to your request you now repeat to me, I desire you to believe that there is nothing in your letters which I pass over slightly, or without taking notice of it; and if I formerly said nothing to it, think it to be, that I thought it the best way of answering a friend, whom I was resolv'd to deny nothing that was in my power. There are some particular obligations that tye me up in the point, and which have drawn on me some displeasure for a time, from some of my friends, who made me a somewhat like demand.†4 But
― 288 ―
I expect to find you more reasonable, and give you this assurance, that you shall be the first that shall be satisfyed in that point. I am not forgetful of what you so kindly put me upon. I think no body ought to live only to eat and drink, and count the days he spends idly. The small remainder of a crazy life, I shall, as much as my health will permit, apply to the search of truth, and shall not neglect to propose to my self those that may be most useful. My paper is more than done, and, I suppose, you tyred, and yet I can scarce give off. I am,
Dear Sir,
Your most faithful, humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.

1859. James Tyrrell to Locke, 11 March [1695] (1842, 1885)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 132-3. Year from Locke's endorsement.
March 11
Dear Sir
I have received the papers from Mr: Pawling, as allso your letter for which I give you many thankes, as allso for your peruseal of those papers, and your letter would have bin much more acceptable if you would have bin more particular in your censure, and have told me what you dislike in them; and whether you thinke they may be usefull to the world; and how you approve of my makeing use of your words as well as sence in those places I have made bold to borrow them; but since you have now the second part of the same subject by you, I hope you will be better able to judg of the whole designe; and therefore desire that when you returne them you would doe me the favour as to let me know impartially whether you think I have performed one part of it, viz: the vindication
― 290 ―
of the reverend Dr: Cudworth, and as to that I should be very glad of the impartial Judgment of that ingenious Lady with whom you are now, if she please to doe me the honour as to peruse them; in short as you please to approve of the performance so I may be encouraged to goe on at spare times; but if not; I have a greater worke then that now under my hands and I shall lay these papers totally aside.†1
Since I came to Towne I met with pamphlet†a call'd†a a Philosophical discourse of the nature of Rational and irrational souls by one M.S.†2 the thing seems very well writ, and is to prove that the souls of brutes tho' material may have perception tho not reason, and that the difference between them and men lyes in that Brutes have onely an Animal spirit, or soul, and that men have besides that a rational soul allso: the opinion is not new, being the same with Dr: Willis de Anima Brutorum,†3 as allso many other Physitians†4 as well as some Divines; onely there are in it some new mediums whereby he†b would†b prove it, which if true, will take away the maine objections against the imperceptibility†5 of matter: but of this you will be the best Judg your self when you come to peruse it: which you shall doe the first oppertunity I meet with of sending it in the meane time with my humble service to the good Lady I remaine
your most humble servant
J TYRRELL
This day I saw our Freind Mr: Clerk at the house bids me present his service to you, and let you know that he is sorry your health will not permit you to come hither; nor the businesse of the public give him time to write to you. I allso joyn in the former, and for the latter can onely tell you that businesse or incogitancye have allso hindered me from paying my respects to you since I came
― 291 ―
up hither; next week I goe down againe: and hope the next Terme†1 to be out of your debt when I, shall come up againe.

1860. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 14 March [1695] (1858, 1862)
B.L., MSS. Locke c. 8, ff. 189-90, and b. 4, f. 77. The letter written by Freke apart from Clarke's initials and the address; the enclosure, by Freke. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answers no. 1858.
March the 14
The enclosed draught of a Bill for Regulating the Press has been approved by the Sollicitor†3 and severall other honest and able men who all agree that the Government is sufficiently secured by it and the Gentleman at the Great House†4 allows it to be a good provision, but yet the Court the Bishops and the Stationers Company take great exceptions to it for they all agree to say it is wanting as to the Securing of Property when they are asked what they mean thereby they can none of them give any good answer and if they would all speak out they (every party) mean differently. The Court means that it would be allowd the power of Granting Patents. The Stationers mean that they would have the regulation of property and disposall of it by making their Register the Standard of it and the orders of their company to Controll and Govern that Standard. The Bishops mean I know not what but they Chime in with the other two because they think property a very popular word, which Licencer is not.
But there are many other objections against this Bill as that it leaves printers at Liberty to set up in any Town in England And that there is noe care taken that new Notions in Phisick should not be publisht to prevent which the College of phisitians is very Industrious to press hard that all things relating to or concerning phisick should be brought to be perused by them before publisht
― 292 ―
lest some new Sidenham should rise up and shew they kill by the rules of Art in other distempers besides the Small Pox and Fevor
You have seen in the Votes the Resolutions of the Comittee for preventing Clipping.†1 The Grave Squire attended the Comittee till he had obtaind the Resolution That the Crowns and half Crowns hereafter to be Coynd shall be of the presant weight and fineness and then he left them to themselves knowing that when it came to be considerd in the House That Resolution would destroy all the rest†2
These Resolutions ought not to have been printed (though reported) till the House had agreed or disagreed to them but the Speaker†3 finding by the last vote past Tewsday that he was not like to be able to serve the Government any more in that Capacity was resolved to give it a cast of his office†4 at parting as a testimony of his affection but I hope in a few days an antidote may be found out for the poison, if our managers will think it worth their care
I beg your pardon I have not yet informd my self of the Charracter of Mr Wynne. I own I had forgot your Commands in it but I will doe soe noe more but inquire and with what speed I can acquaint you what I learn of him
Mr Cl: has deliverd your Letters into the office and Joins with me in subscribing
Your humble servant
J F
E: C:
Tender our dues to my Lady.

Sarum March 12th 1695/4
Sir
I received your last and doe assure you that I never received any such letter as you mention to be sent in November last,†1 otherwise I would not have failed to send you an answer to it long before this time. I sent to my Son William in London to enquire of Mr Tyrrell what books he had lent my Husband that were yours; and he writes me word that he had asked Mr Tyrrell who told him that Laurence of Marriage Morall,†2 and the History of the Royall Society,†3 and severall volumes of the Phylosophicall Transactions, were yours and lent by him to my Husband, but that the parts of Dr Lightfoot†4 which you speak of were all sent you in the boxes he sent you last from Oackly. He says also that sent to my husband a small octavo of Raymund Lully.†5 These books shall be all sent to you as soon as my Son comes home to find them out, for none of us can doe it, not knowing whereabout in the study they are, and all the books being verry†a- much confused,-†a and out of order. I hope my son will not be long out of Salisbury since his friends in London doe so little for him. I find good friends verry scarce, and am the more obliged to you for continuing your kindness to me and mine, which you are pleased to express in all your letters. I thinke the Philosophicall Transactions were sent you before my husband dyed, and the pieces†b of Lightfoot Mr Tyrrell says were all quartos bound in Vellum, none of which were ever here to the best of my remembrance. I am obliged to gett a friend to write this for me, and
― 294 ―
not knowing how to direct it to you, send it to my Son that he might gett it conveyed to you. I hope I†a have†a found a note that will discharge me of the 30 pounds you claim, which will be a great satisfaction to me at this time. I hope this will find you well in health and am
Sir your most Obliged and humble Servant
H. THOMAS.
[William Thomas:]
Sir,
I have layed aside all thoughts of studing Phisick any longer and so shall have no occasion of the bookes you were pleas'd to lend me 2 or 3 yeares since. If you please to send me a command I am ready to send them up to London to you.
I am your most humble
Servant W THOMAS.
Address: These For Mr John Locke.

1862. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 21 March 1695 (1860, 1868)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 191-2. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's initials and the address.
March the 21 1694/5
Sir
The College is obliged to you for your complement in that of the 18th and to ease your mind a litle about the words Hereticall and as it is Establisht by Law they Crave leave to inform you that by a Statute made in Queen Eliz: time†1 tis Enacted that nothing shall be adjudged Heresie but what is declared such by the Holy Scriptures or by the 4 first Generall Councills or by other Generall Councills by the express words of Scripture soe that we think the word Heresie being thus determind as to its signification by a Statute it can doe noe hurt in the printing Bill and as to the other words your self observe how the words Christian Religion influences them but let us observe to you <that>†b as the words are
― 295 ―
pend twill be incumbent on the prosecutor to shew not onely that what he prosecutes for, is contrary to the Christian Religion as he understands that Religion but that what he soe understands is Establisht by Law as he understands it. Soe that we think those words some of the best words in the Bill
We are Extremely obliged to you for your Expedients in both your Letters and shall make a right use of them in time and place if the Bill goe on which we much doubt The College being declared against by all those Confederacys I mentiond in my last for bringing in this Bill which they say is to introduce Confusion and ruin all and yet the Great House†1 seems to press us to Carry it on and to be carefall by some clause to take care of Property which is always the burthen of the Song whereas in our opinion there needs noc new care to be taken about property for tis a rule in Law that where ever there is damnum and injuria I may be recompenced in damages in an Action on the case and who ever prints my Coppy Injures me and endammages me Soe that I have the same security for this property that any one has for any other
We fear the business of Clipt mony will fall heavily and speedily upon us but cannot make those, that are chiefly Concernd, to take any care in it though good expedients have been proposed but they doe not or will not understand this affair and always decline discourse that might inform them one Gentleman that you know†2 Tossing up his nose and saying (when he was prest to Consider it) that when he thought of this matter he was like a monkey thrown into the water which always claps his paws or hands to his Eyes and sinks to the Bottom which we take to be noe unapt simile and became the poet well
Tender our service to my Lady and be assured we are
Your affectionate humble servants
J F
E: C.

1863. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 22 March [1695?] (1848, 1962)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 170. Printed in Rand, pp. 447-8. For the year see no. 1848.
Oates 22 Mar
Madam
If you enjoy a perfect health I doe not <advise>†a the waters or any other physick But if you are out of order, you know your remedie. Bath is in the same county and frost and snow are now gon
Since the Doctor had soe good successe with Sammy†1 in his late illnesse I advise you to make use of the diet drink he offerd, for he knowing what distemper he lately had and with what method he recoverd him will be the better able to judg what is fitest to be done for that which you apprehend to be the rickets, and will be at hand to help or alter his course if any thing given him should not agree well with him.
The difficulty like to arise in the Education of Children from the folly or perversnesse of Servants was what I foresaw when I writ about it, and therefor doe not wonder to finde you complain of it. I know noe other remedie but what is printed to keep them as much out of the servants company as you can espetialy the eldest of them.†2 But how far that is practicable in your family you can only judg.
Had your letter come but a day sooner. I should have said something to Betty concerning those faults you complain of, but a letter I writ to her was gon the day before. If blowing her nose be a thing which after your gravely telling her of it she neglects you must change your countenance to her make her sensible that you are displeased and keepeing her constantly with you let her finde some uneasinesse from your displeasure and restore her not to your favour till that fault be cured and then after a litle while that she has found the ease and pleasure in satisfieing you by cureing that fault advise her of the next. But still remember that the faults of Childhood that are not like to produce ill habits but that age will cure you must not trouble your self or them much about. If after
― 297 ―
being reproved for it two or three times Jack†1 persists still in holding his head on one side though it be forbiden him, if it be through obstinacy he must be soundly whipd for it; If he be willing to mend it but does it through custome or forgetfulnesse you must fasten something to his coller that may hurt him and soe mind him of it when he turns his head that way. This is all I can bethink my self of at this distance. I wish you and all your yonge family very well and am
Dear Madam
your most humble servant
J LOCKE
Pray remember me very kindly to all the litle ones. Particularly to Betty to whom I writ not long since. But pray tell her I wonder how she spends her time. For I hear she has not yet learned out her Catechise, which she went soe far in when she was here at Oates.†2 I can scarce beleive it, and should be very much ashamd if it should be true
Address: These present to Mrs Mary Clarke at Chipley
Endorsed by Mrs. Clarke: mr lockes letter etc:
