1865. Alexander Beresford to Locke, 24 March 1695 (2195)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 173-8. Letter and enclosure. The writer is probably the Alexander Beresford who was admitted to Lincoln's Inn on 8 October 1692; he was the second son of William Beresford, also of Lincoln's Inn: Lincoln's Inn Admissions, etc., 1896, i. 345.
In the enclosure I have inserted in the text the translations (in square brackets) of the Greek words.
Honoured Sir
I send, and entreat your acceptance of, two books, one concerning the Trinity,†1 t'other is th' Earth-Essay†2 I spoke of when with you. 'Twas proper to have sent them sooner; and I had so, but that I was delayed by an expectation of having Eusebius and Epiphanius to peruse: I was very desirous both to know my self,
― 299 ―
and report to you, whether or no they are as much misrepresented as Irenæus. But I still have only expectation, not possession, of them. What the Trinitarians urge about Cerinthus,†1 they build cheifly on Irenæus; and I am sure what is come down from him, though through Trinitarian hands, is, as to this Point, more against than for them: though who would ever imagine so by what Dr Williams†a writes? But 'tis plain he has with the same slightness or partialitie examin'd Irenæus, as he has severall Texts of Scripture. I had not, when at Oates, read above a quarter of his book, but have since read it through, and think I may venture to say of it in generall (passing the poor talk of Personalitie pag: 59: and other particulars) that, instead of strengthening, it really weaken's the Cause: unless that be (as I beleive it is) capable of no better Defence than has already been made for it. And if so, I hope another sort of management will be given it by some such hand as Mr Lock's. I am really in hope, Sir, that you will think it worth your while to bestow on it more than a private Consideration. You will find in the book a Paper wherein I have transcribed two or three Passages out of Irenæus, which I take to be worth your seeing: the rest are my own thoughts of the Trinity-texts of Scripture, which I send also, hoping (if you have leisure and patience to read them through) for confirmation or conviction in any thing that may be worth your taking notice of. Dr Woodward oppose's your Hypothesis about the Deluge†2 (wherein by the way I hear you are not single) only en passant in his Essay, but in another Treatise (merely on Gravity) already finish't, though not printed,†3 I hear he professedly undertake's it, and pretend's to Demonstrate that a Change of the Gravity-Center could produce, at most, but a Partiall deluge. I hope, Sir, this Peice, (though but an Abstract of what he design's to publish at large) will give some Entertainment to you, and to that Excellent Lady you converse with. I pray her Ladyship's acceptance of my most Humble Service. According as She told me, my Father is Obliged to Sir Francis for his good thoughts of him, as to the Taxes; for I find his Sir-name sett down for a Commissioner, though with his Christne'd†b name mistaken
― 300 ―

John for William;†1 so that in point of Form, I think, it is not lawfull for him, if he had a mind, to Act. The night after I left you, Sir, I enquired in Shirelane†2 for Mr Tyrrel, and was told by one of his Club, (I think the Puisne Baron of the Exchequer)†3 that he had been absent from thence severall nights, and therefore must needs be out of town. But sending next day to enquire at his lodging, how I might give him in the country notice of your expectation to hear from him, I heard he was in Town, though not within: But his man being within, I sent to him my Message: and calling on monday†4 to know whether he had deliverd it, I met with Mr Tyrrel himself, who told me he would write to you by the next Post. I give a particular account, though at this distance of time, lest Mr Tyrrel's Letter should have mention'd that he saw not your messenger till the following Monday, and so I seem less carefull than I ought to have been, and was. I write, Sir, without any expectation of an Answer, that would be a greater labour to you and Honour to me than I know how to entertain any thought of. I desire only the liberty of waiting on you, when you come to Town, or I into the Country, to know your farther Thoughts of the great Point. For truly I expect a better account of it from you, Sir, than from the whole Tribe of Levi. Some of them I beleive indeed would lay down their Lives for a Truth they are certain of; but this cannot be ascertained without close attention and diligent search, which if any of them goe's about, he must needs be disturb'd at every step with great Fear of lighting on such a Truth as the Antitrinitarian (supposing that Opinion to be true),†a it being so inconsistent with the Church-Service, that as soon as he close's with it he must immediately part from all his Splendour, if a Great one, or if one of the little Frye perhaps all his Maintenance. What a Byase must so great a Danger be, in the Enquiry after truth, even to such a Soul as, if he found it, would endure extremities for it! Searching for such a Truth is, to a Clergy-man, searching for death, which to do faithfully require's such a Generosity as few men are masters of; such a one as shine's in Mr Lock, and contribute's
― 301 ―
more Sir than even all your other excellencies to my being a very Just, in being,
Worthy Sir,
Your very Passionate Admirer
ALEXANDER BERESFORD.
Gray's-Inne 24 March 1695
Address: for Mr Lock
Endorsed by Locke: A: Beresford 24º Mar. 94/5
[Enclosure]:
Since Doctor Williams (as well as Mr Clerk)†1 insists, That the first Chapter of Saint John's Gospell was designed against the Cerinthian and Ebionite†2 Heresies And that those were, a denyall of the Trinity, and of the Incarnation; I think it proper to transcribe what has occurrd to me concerning them in
(English) Irenæus Lib:1: Cap:25 intitled Qualis est Doctrina Cerinthi.
(English) Cerinthus autem quidam in Asia non a Primo deo factum esse mundum docuit sed a Virtute quadam valde <separata>†a et distante ab ea principalitate quæ est super universa et ignorante eo (vel eum) qui est super omnia Deo (vel Deum). Jesum autem, subjecit, non ex virgine natum, (impossibile enim hoc ei visum est;) fuisse autem Joseph et Mariæ filium similiter ut reliqui omnes homines, et plus potuisse justitiâ, prudentiâ, et sapientiâ, præ omnibus. Et post baptismum descendisse in eum Christum, ab eâ principalitate quæ est super omnia, figurâ columbæ, et tunc annunciasse
― 302 ―
incognitum patrem et virtutes perfecisse: in fine autem revolâsse iterum Christum de Jesu, et Jesum passum esse, et resurrexisse: Christum autem impassibilem perseverasse, existentem spiritualem.
(English) Cap: 26: intitled Qua est Ebionitarum Doctrina. Qui autem dicuntur Ebionæi consentiunt quidem mundum à Deo factum; Ea autem quæ sunt erga Dominum, non similiter ut, Cerinthus, et Carpocrates,†1 opinantur. Solo autem eo quod est secundum Matthæum evangelio utuntur; et Apostolum Paulum recusant, apostatam eum legis dicentes†a etc:
Lib: 3: Cap 24:†2
(English) Ebionei ex Joseph generatum Jesum dicunt.
He charge's the Ebionites with a base Opinion that Joseph begat Jesus, (which might give 'em the name of anti-parthenists†3 but not of anti-trinitarians) and Cerinthus with the same indeed, but with this also that Christ had a præexistence with the first Divine Person before his appearance on earth. That the maker of the world was not the first Divine Person but an other, and if I do not mistake, that Christ was that other. If so, let a Trinitarian make his best of such an insinuation That St. John wrote against those Heresies. Truly I think he has in his 14th V. by λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο [The Word was made flesh] confuted the last Heresie, and by μονογενοῦς [only-begotten] the other, very clearly; though if clearly, yet I am not sure Designedly. For I must own I have not yet met with evidence that either those, or the Gnostick opinions were broach't when St. John wrote. Were not they (at least the Gnostick) rather formed by misinterpretation of what he wrote?
― 303 ―
As for the Gnosticks their Father is said to be Carpocrates who appeared not till the twentieth year of the second Century: whereas no body time's St. John's writing lower than the end of the first C. Nay according to a Quotation I have read out of Theophylactus it was but 32 years after Christ's death (as Luke's time was 15, Mark's 10, Mathew's 8:).†1 However in interpreting St. John, I regard not those, or any other, Opinions, or Writings, as then extant; except only the other Gospells, which tis probable he laid before him when he wrote his own, designing it for a Supplement to them. And it appearing from them (in their account of the Lord's prayer) that Jesus directed his followers to only One Object of Divine Worship, the πατὴρ [Father], without any mention of λόγος [Word], or ἅγιον πνεῦμα [Holy Spirit], I cannot be forward to make any such interpretation of St. John as will direct to 3 Objects of Such worship, or inferr the existence of 3 Divine Persons. Neither shall I readily (supposing the existence of 3 Such) make any such interpretation as will inferr that the second of Those abode in (or was united to) Jesus; since no other Evangelist mentions any such thing, (though very considerable if true) but all assert, (even John himself) that the trinitarian third did abide in and guide Jesus. John: 1. 32. Mark 1. 12. Acts 10. 38. and is not Mark 2.8 to that purpose? (though otherwise translated in our bibles) besides many other Texts. Reading the first V. of John I reflect on (what I guess few observe) the second V. of Luke, wherein mention is made of τοῦ λόγου [the Word], not the Gospel but, one that had been lookt on and waited on by Luke's informers, even the Revealer (so I translate λόγος [Word] in the new Testament as often as it stands for a Person) And (which is very considerable) those informers had themselves been beholders of the λόγου ἀπ' ἀρχῆς [the Word from the beginning] so that they were coæval with if not prior to the Λόγος
'Tis perhaps no absurd guess that John in writing his first V. had his eye upon Luke's second. However truly I take the ἀρχῆ [the beginning] and ἀρχῆς [the beginning] in the first V. of St. John's Gospell and Epistle to have been about the same time as Luke's ἀρχῆς. (Methinks the want of the article is somwhat of an objection against referring any of 'em to the Creation). And
― 304 ―
accordingly I translate those V.s in St. John's first Chapter that relate to this dispute as follows:
1 First (or in the first place Inprimis) was the Revealer; and the Revealer was with (or at) God, and was (the divine or) God's Revealer.
 
The great Change in the Frame of Religion, and the great Discoveries of God's Will concerning mankind, began in and by the Revealer, so that all might properly bear Date from him. And he was with God, not in company as his fellow, (that had been better express't by σὺν [with]) but so as a Slave, that has been at his master to receive his Orders, may be said to have been with or πρὸς δεσπότην [with (understood) the master]. He was with God, so as to be show'd by supernaturall manifestation somewhat of God's nature and Will; and thereupon became God's Revealer. I translate θεὸς [God] as if it were θεῖος or rather θεοῦ. That it should be so, I argue from the absurditie of θεὸς in this place, whether taken in the Trinitarian or Socinian sense. For the evangelist, after making mention of God, immediately to tell us of another's being God, without making distinction, (more than by leaving out the Article) seem's to me a very unsuitable way of instructing: nay had he added expressly [by Office]†a it would yet seem so. But rather worse is the Trinitarian sense, asserting that God was with God; and very lame their explanation, that the begotten Person of God was with the begetting Person, and (either they do, or, to be consistent with themselves, should, add) with the Breathed Person (though by the way I observe they generally fail of paying to πνεῦμα [Spirit] such Respect as they cannot deny is his due if he be equall with the πατὴρ [Father]). If θεὸς [God] in this place (with the best interpretation) be a word misbecoming an Inspired writer, I can more easily beleive it has been since alterd, either by Design (of such as thought it lawfull to do Evill that (what they call'd) Good might come of it) or by mistake, (even a generall mistake of all the copyists, printers and correcters, throughout Christendom) than that it was at first deliverd so by St. John. And of the same mind must I be upon occasion, as often as one peice of revelation shall appear contradictory to another, or to the Light of nature. 
― 305 ―
 
That θεὸς here is spurious, and θεὸς in Rom: 9.5. is either so, or else metaphoricall, will I suppose without much struggle be allowd, if I am right in what follow's. 
2 This person was at first with God,
3. through him was all, and without (or separately from) him was nothing of all that was.
  
All, that the other Evangelists had reported, and that this was going to add, Was or came to pass or was done Through him, that is, through his authority and assistance; and nothing was without those: 
through him that is through God: αὐτοῦ is for the order of the words no less (perhaps more) referrable to θεὸν immediately præcedent, than to λόγος or to οὗτος. Nay methinks had the Evangelist meant this of the same person as was with God, he would rather have said τούτου to answer οὗτος than ἁυτοῦ. But if grammaticall order at worst leave's it doubtfull, sure the sense may best affix it to θεὸν. 
4. In him was the Inlivener, and the Inlivener was an Inlightner of men.
  
The Inlivener, (Christ called him Ζωή [Life] John 14.6.) was, as Christ himself had affirmed John 10.38. that he was, in God (not only in him as (perhaps he is, according to Acts.17.28.) the place of all Spirits but) I guess as extraordinarily beloved of him and authorized from him in all his proceedings. All good persons are said even by others besides the Elect Canters (who continually talk of being In God and In Christ, and of getting Into God and Into Christ) to be In God in some especiall sense. 
And this inlivener was also an inlightner of mankind; he both Excited and Directed men to a nobler kind of life than they (generally) before pursued. 
5. And this Inlightner shined even to the Ignorant, but the Ignorant did not apprehend him.
9. The true Inlightner was he who coming into the world inlightned all.
 
John's light reached only a little way (among a few of his own nation); but Christ, who was The true inlightner, did and doth, 
― 306 ―
though not in person, yet by Commission, spread his light far and near through the earth.
 
I apply (as Mr. Clerk†1 dos) ἐρχόμενον [coming] to φῶς [light] rather than to ἄνθρωπον [man]. 
10. He was in the world, yea the world was For him, and yet the world did not know him.
 
Here I render διὰ [through] differently from the third V. And sure this præposition will, even with the Genitive case, be allow'd sometimes to denote the Design or Use of a Production; though indeed oftener the Instrument or the Assistant; but surely never the Efficient. This different translation of διὰ (though a word of very various significa<tion>)†a may look somewhat the harder because of ἐγίνετο [was made or became] in both places: But, what is often made very abusively, is here, I think, a pretty tolerable supposition, that the Evangelist did not expect to be handled nicely. Besides I translate ἐγίνετο in both places as expressive only of a thing's receiving Existence, not the Manner how it Received existence, whether by Creation or other kind of Action. He appeared among us, yea we are for him to præside over, and yet the most of those that he appeared to did not take notice of him. 'Tis very remarkable that God's creative Word, spoken of in Genesis and other parts of the Old Testament, is also spoken of in the New, never (that I know of) by the term λόγος [word], but (I have observed, though I remember not particularly where) at least two or three times by ῥῆμα [speech or utterance], a term that cannot stand for a Person but only the Act of a Person. Heb: 11.3. (Heb:1.3). 
11. He visited his own Country, and his Countrymen did not receive him.
 
They expelled him; according to Luke 4.29. Matth. 4.24. Mar.6.1.†2  
14. And this Revealer was Flesh and did dwell among us, so that we saw his Excellencie, an Excellencie as of God's only-begotten, full of Love and Truth.
― 307 ―
  
The Revealer was not what Cerinthus (either before or since) imagin'd, a Divine person or the Maker of the world, but was a man and really inflesh't, was as every man is, an Incarnate Spirit and had his Dwelling among us. But though, in truth, his Humane was his Only nature, yet that appeard so heavenly and excellent, as loudly spoke him to have been begotten, so as no other man had been, by God himself, who by his own (the ἅγιον) πνεῦμα [Holy Spirit] supplyd the part of a father in his generation, so that the Virgin M. did (what was deny'd by another hæresie of Cerinthus and the Ebionites) conceive, without Joseph's assistance, merely by that δύναμις ὑψίστου [power of the Highest]; for which reason the Offspring was to be called the Son of God: according to Luke 1. 35. and other places. The Trinitarians are under a necessity of acknowledging, that That thing or person, Which came out of the Virgin and had not before seen light, had his Being from God, not only in the manner other men have it from him as their Creator and preserver, but, in an extraordinary manner, had it from him as a Generating Father, insomuch that he (the man) was and ought to be called The Son of God, and God's μονογενὴς [only-begotten]. And will they now come and talk that, immediately at His birth or afterwards, another υἱὸς [Son], another μονογενὴς did joyn himself to this υἱὸς this μονογενὴς? that One Divine Person from eternity did (and consequently Doth and Will to eternity) Beget Another Divine Person, who is therefore called the first person's υἱὸς and that this Eternall υἱὸς μονογενὴς did joyn himself to the Temporary υἱὸς μονογενὴς (that was begotten by God imperante Augusto) so that there dwelt among us Two—somwhats, which were, each in his own nature the allmighty Father's μονογενὴς (a plain contradiction), and both together but One Person? 
I can find nothing of this Babel-talk in my Bible; nor dos it suit well with the honest plain-dealing of Jesus that excellent Son of God, or his beloved disciple on whom they father it. It look's more like a peice of Platonick, or that Philosophy which St. Paul advised the Colossians (Cap.2.8.) to beware of as vain and Anti-Christian. 
15. John testified of him declaring It was of him that I said one
― 308 ―
coming after me Was advance'd before me because he Was more excellent than I.
  
I think ἔμπροσθέν [before me] properly mean's before my face, (as in Matt: 10.32. and elsewhere) and relate's not to time but place, signifying here a forwarder, that is a more honourable place, which Christ did attain though he came (behind or) after the Baptist. The following word, πρῶτος [first], is equally expressive of priority in Worth, as of priority in Time; let that which make's the best ὅτι [that] for preference determine the translation. 
As to Was; we frequently in English speak so, using the præterimperfect Tense, when we repeat a former saying of a thing; even though the thing at the time of repeating be still future. 
16. Also of His fullness all We have received, even Love for Love.
 
This, without doubt, is a saying not of the Baptist's but, of the Evangelist's, who seems to be giving all along a Character of λόγος [word]; and a part of it being that He was more excellent than the Baptist,†a lest those who, (though they knew the Baptist†a to be a mere man yet) admired him, should disbeleive it, he gives the Baptist's†b own words for it. And then procede's—'Twas He that being full of noble love to God and men, form'd the like Love in us, his followers, by præcept and example. 
17. for the Law was delivered by Moses but Love and Truth (or Knowledge) came by Christ.
 
Moses delivered to the Jews their Law a Systeme of Ceremonies; but Christ taught them and us what is far more excellent, even usefull Knowledge, and Love, the Love of God and of one another. 
18. No one has ever seen God, but his only-begotten Son being (in his bosom or) admitted to his Secrets hath made him known.
If I am right in this interpretation, here is no ground for the Cerinthian Heresie, or Trinitarian Doctrine, that Christ had a præexistence with the Father and was the Maker of the world. That I am so, may be more easily beleived if I can maintain, what I think concerning the second V. to the Hebrews, that instead of
― 309 ―
proving Christ the Maker of the world (as 'tis generally thought to do) it plainly prove's he did not make the world. God, and no other, did make the world, διὰ [through] God's Son; God's Son (by whom God spoke to us, and whom God hath Appointed Distributer (κληρονόμον [distributor (of inheritance) or heir]) of all things) is not God but another; therefore God's Son did not make the world. This seems to me unanswerable, and far enough out of the reach of all the Trinitarian, or Cerinthian, Hocus-Pocus, Communicatio Idiomatum.†1 (Though supposing they could evince that Christ made the world, I should readily reply, then I not only will pay, but have all along paid Him divine worship; for if He made us, He is the person we call, and ought to call, Our Father and Our Father is constantly worship't by me: but I must confess the Father of Our (Father or) Maker is as yet unknown to me, and I have had no notice of an obligation to seek acquaintance with any Father of Our Maker, or with any third Spirit equall with our Maker and his Father).
This Text ought to determine the sense of such others as inform us the world was made διὰ [through] Christ; and they to avail no more than this, for proof that By Christ was made the world, which, in truth, was made by another and much higher Being, not ὕπο [by] but διὰ [through] Christ, viz; to be govern'd by him.
Whereas Christ asserted, John 17.22: that he and the Father were one; that Oneness cannot be an Identity of nature, because of what is added that Christ's followers and the Father were to be So one. It's plain that he, they, and God, were to be One in conformity of Will.
I suppose the 2 John.5.7.†2 is not much insisted on for proof of such a pretended Unity; it's companion the eighth V. dos too notoriously betray the forreign Extraction of both.
Nor, in my apprehension, dos Christ's command of baptizing εἰς τὸ ὄνομα [in the name] of the father, the son, and τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος [of the Holy Spirit], any better prove his and the πνεῦμα's [spirit's] equality with the father, or indeed the πνεῦμα's
― 310 ―
Personalitie. the common interpretation (of In their name or by their authority) seems to me far short of Christ's design; according to this, the Work of the Apostles was to be no more than baptizing; and the rest of the words did only make the Form of their Commission to that. And can it be thought that if the Apostles had gone and thrown water upon all men, or all under water, and then sat down, that they had accomplish't this Order of Christ's? No sure; they were directed to go and by the Ceremony of watering Engage or List all men (not ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι [in the name] but εἰς τὸ ὄνομα [into the name]) to the Acknowledgement of the father, the Son, and the ἅγιον πνεῦμα [Holy Spirit]. They were to (preach or) declare openly, and engage all men to acknowledge, the existence and true nature of One God, of God's only-begotten Son the man Jesus, and of God's (or the ἅγιον) πνεῦμα [(Holy) Spirit]. Even the πνεῦμα, (though, as I suppose, no Person, but only God's Power exercised in the world contrarily to the ordinary course of nature) was to be specially declared and acknowledged: and reason good; nay that it should have the first place in their Declaration, though twas last in their Commission. For how could they evince Christ's Veracity but by first declaring the existence of (Miracles or) Effects too Great for Humane, too Good for any Evill Power to be the Cause of? They must show Nature Contrould for Good designs by One who consequently had the Command of nature, and not only so (for so some might fancie of an eternall and very powerfull Evill δαίμων [spirit]) but also was a Good Being, so that he could not exert his Power in testimony of a Lye; the appearances therefore of this Power (and they only) were a sufficient proof of Christ's Veracity: And to prove that, was the best way of bringing people to the right acknowledgement of one God. So that what was sett last in their Commission should be even first in their Declaration and what was sett first be last: first the πνεῦμα [Spirit] be declared, then Christ about whom and in whose behalf it did appear, then the Great Father whom Christ had Revealed.
But, (as 'tis commonly objected) this πνεῦμα [Spirit] was by Christ called the Comforter of his Disciples—Very well it might, I beleive, and yet be no Person. I may give that character of money or a book, and yet not be thought to speak of a Person, or to speak improperly. I guess that God by this miraculous Power exerted after Christ's death in his disciples, did present Ideas to their minds in an extraordinary manner, give 'em remembrance and assurance
― 311 ―
of the great things Christ had told 'em, and satisfie 'em of their being themselves specially favoured by God, and consequently safe both from inward infirmities and extraneous assaults. Of some such nature I guess were the effects of this divine Power in the Disciples, and consequently 'twas their great Informer and Comforter.
Christ is said to know all things, John 16.30—I consider this was spoke not by Christ himself, but by his disciples, before they were Inspired: though even from an Inspired person this had been perhaps a very allowable Hyperbole. If it was too excessive yet Christ might very well forbear contradicting it, because they rais'd no ill but a very good Consequence from it, (and that show's they spoke it hyperbolically), they concluded not that he was God, but only one come from God.
I suppose that οὐχ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ εἶναι ἶσα θεῶ [thought it not robbery to be equal with God] (Philip: 2.6.) will not be much urged for Christ's Divinity, by any one that consider's the design of those words (being to show a pattern of humility in Christ) and the antithesis of ἀλλ' [but] in the next V. Instead of such a false, or rather no, sense as is generally raised from it, it plainly speak's a very true one, that Christ though appearing very excellent yet did not think it his Share, or Lead his disciples such a peice of Robbery as, to equall himself with God, but was very humble, so as to make the advice immediately præcedent very proper τοῦτο φρονείσθω ἐν ὑμῖν ὅ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ [Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus].
From Rom: 9.5. I conclude, in honour of the Jews that Christ was a Jew as to so much as he received of his humane nature from any of mankind, it being nevertheless implyd that the father's part in his generation was not performed by a Jew but by God's πνεῦμα [Spirit]. But for ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας [Who is over all, God blessed for ever]. I do not apprehend that, with Ἀμήν [Amen] at the end, to be a suitable sallie of zeal for the Apostle to make in that place, but rather suspect it for a peice of Comment on τὸ κατὰ σαρκὰ [that according to the flesh] written by some honest Trinitarian in imitation of 2.Cor: 11.31. and the Amen I guess another hand subscribed by way of approbation.
I have the same suspicion of Hebr:13.8. for, supposing the Trinity-doctrine to be true yet I can make no sense of this passage
― 312 ―
(with Χριστὸς in the nominative case); nor indeed of Coloss: 2:9: and part of the tenth V. And the same have I of the 7.8.9.10.11. and twelfth V.s of the first Chapt. to the Hebr:
In being thus suspicious, I am a little confirmed by what is acknowledg'd in the sixth page of Bishop Burnet's Letter,†1 in relation to Epiphanius.
As to what he (the Bishop) urges of Κύριος [Lord], I do indeed think that this Title is in some places of the new Testament emphatically given to (the Man) Jesus that great Proprietour, so as it cannot be given to any other, he alone being made by God the Head of the Church, the Distributer of all things, and having received all power in heaven and earth (as to what concern's us) though at the same time he is himself under a Lord even that God who made him Lord and Ruler over us. But I am far from thinking it ever apply'd to him in the same sense as Jehovah is to God.
Of those Texts, from which the Trinitarians argue the Præexistence of Christ, not one is, that I can perceive, to any such purpose.
What Christ said (John 8.58.) of his being before Abraham, was only to confirm his foregoing assertion, that Abraham saw his day and was glad: and therefore may very well be understood (as I think it is by the Socinian Considerer)†2 of his being in Promise and expectation. And to say so, was a sufficient Provocation to the Jews to stone him; for that was declaring himself to be the Messiah. ἐγὼ εἰμὶ [I am] cannot without great absurditie be understood of an eternall existence for want of ὁ ὢν [He who is].
As to Christ's coming from Heaven, that (supposing God was united to him yet) must needs be spoken of his Humane nature not his Divine, the Divine being not capable of Removall. Neither side can take such an expression strictly; a figure it is, and sure a much easier one to be said of a Prophet or any Messenger of God's, that he came From God and From Heaven and was Sent by God to the world, than that God came From heaven and that God in his second Person was sent by God in his first Person, (and I must add in his third Person, for sure he could not be idle in so great a business). According to such an interpretation the whole God neither came nor stayd; a peice came and two peices stayd where they were before: for truly if God subsist's in 3 Persons (mean
― 313 ―
they what they will by Persons) I do not apprehend how it is a all properer to say the λόγος [Word] is God, the πνεῦμα [Spirit] is God, or the πατὴρ [Father] is God, than to say my Understanding is a Spirit, or Light (according to the common notion of it) is the Sun; whereas this makes but a part of the solar and that but a part of the spirituall nature.
As to John 17.5. that I think argue's only that a δόξα [glory] for Christ, not that Christ himself, was with his Father from eternity. Christ here prayed to Receive something, which therefore he was not now in possession of: And to be dispossesst of what he had before the Creation, cannot agree with a Divine Person. But besides Christ had his δόξαν [glory] not σὺν [with] but πάρα θεῶ [alongside God], in God's design, not in God's company.
The beginning of St. John's first Epistle I interpret thus: What was from first, and what our Senses have assured us, concerning the Revealer of Life (Yea that Life†a was discover'd and we had sight of it and do declare to you that (Eternall) Life which was (with or) designed by our father and discoverd to us) Yea what our Senses have assured us, we declare to you, that you may have a common enjoyment with us etc:
Whereas the Trinitarian's†b object a Command of Honouring the Son as the Father, I do not remember (nor I beleive can anyone show) where that Command is. However I reflect that Christ needed, and might very well claim (of those who knew his Miracles) the same degree of one kind of Honour as was due to his Father, viz; to have his word taken in whatsoever he said beyond the reach of Reason. He appeared with his Father's authority, and therefore his Veracity was to be respected as his Father's, and slighting him had been a disrespect to his Father.
As to the Revelation ascribed to John, if the Trinitarian's†b think it worth while to prove that barbarous Greek (such as the Evangelist John did not use to write) Canonicall, and affix the Title of ὁ ὢ, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, ὁ παντοκράτωρ [He who is and was, and is to come, the all powerful] to Jesus 'twill assure us only that the same Jesus exist's now, as did exist on earth, and he is about to come again to us, and he has all power in his hands. Neither can Α and Ω, πρῶτος and ἔσχατος [Alpha and Omega, first and last] serve their Turn, or prove any thing more than Christ's Principality; because this Α, Ω, πρῶτος, ἒσχατος
― 314 ―
was once dead and is alive again; and it is not consistent with the nature of an Eternall person to dye; let 'em say He dyed As man, As what, or In what Respect best pleases the good Orthodox, still 'twas He, and I am sure He (I say not As but only If) an Eternall person could not dye.
What is commonly answerd in such cases of the Communicatio Idiomatum, is far from satisfactory to me, I take it to be no better than Jargon; or rather Juggle. Jesus is a man till their hypothesis need's a God, and then—Præsto be gone—by and by the Humane nature is needed—Pass't come here, he's a Man—What is this, but mere Hocus-Pocus? a non-sensicall Tenet obstinately maintaind by a slippery Shift of Empty words?
Arcta igitur vafro debentur Vincula Proteo,
Debetur Lockæa manus—†1
—It should,
And will be conquerd let it but, be Chaind,
Our Greatest Monster by our Greatest Hand.
If ever that's bestow'd on't, I beleive, by Tying the Words of this Protean Doctrine to a Constant signification the Cheat will be made appear, and what at present in our Church is imposed as a Necessary, no longer be allowed as a true Point of Faith.
Some of these Texts, which I have interpreted differently from Dr. Williams,†a I am pretty sure I have interpreted rightly. Some indeed I doubt of, but even as to those what I have here sett down do seem to me more suitable than any other interpretations that have yet occurrd to me. And these have occurrd from the Texts themselves, not from any Comment, Trinitarian or Anti-trinitarian.†b As to the latter I can still say, with truth, that I have never (to my knowledge) read or seen any Anti-trinitarian writing or person, except only Mr. Freke's book,†2 condemn'd by the H. of Commons, (which I laid aside without reading so much as two pages of it); unless I must Except also the Bible it self, which indeed I take to be as clear, as if it had been designed, against this Doctrine. Nay that severall Texts were so Designed, I am not forward to gainsay him, who shall argue from the great care is taken in them to apply
― 315 ―
Christ's highest Honours to him (not by his cheif name, the Son of God, but) by the name of the son of Man, lest we should mistake a Divine nature to be the Subject of those Honours, which were really spoken of, and did belong to, his Humane.
(Latin) Irenaeus Bk I, ch. 25. The nature of the doctrine of Cerinthus.
(Latin) A certain Cerinthus, living in Asia, taught that the world was not made by the First God but by a certain Power, widely separate and removed from that Governance which is over the universe and without the knowledge of (or in ignorance of) that God who is over all. As to Jesus, he suggested that he was not born of a virgin (for this seemed to him impossible) but was the son of Joseph and Mary, after the manner of all other men, and that he was superior to all in justice, prudence, and wisdom; and that after his baptism the Christ descended upon him, in the form of a dove, from that Governance which is over all things, and that he then proclaimed the unknown Father[p. 302] and performed mighty works; but that in the end the Christ flew back again from Jesus, who then suffered and rose again; but the Christ continued throughout immune from suffering, his existence being spiritual.
(Latin) Ch. 26. The doctrine of the Ebionites. Those who are called Ebionites agree, indeed, that the world was made by God; while in matters touching the Lord their opinions are unlike those of Cerinthus and Carpocrates.†1 The only Gospel they use is that according to Matthew; and they reject the Apostle Paul, saying that he was an apostate from the Law, etc.
Bk. 3, ch. 24:†2
(Latin) The Ebionites say that Jesus was begotten of Joseph.
1866. Henry Hatrell to Locke, 25 March 1695 (1914)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 146-7. For the writer see V.C.H., Staffs. viii. 7, 56 n., 65.
Sir
Your Booke concerning Humane Understanding is highly esteemed in this Country, For my owne part I have read it with much pleasure and profit. I find it of singular use to make the Perception cleare and the Judgement sound and cannot but returne my thanks to you for the benefit I have received by it and tell you I think my self exceedingly your debtor. Your free Communication of such important and usefull thoughts almost emboldens me to desire your Ideas of Baptisme and Faith or directions how to find out the simple Ideas that compose them, tho' I have nothing to give in exchange, I am afraid I shall omit some and I need not tell you the consequence of that. I doubt not but many of the first Quality are ambitious of your Conversation and Acquaintance and in such Company It is perhaps a Rudeness to trouble you thus, However 'twill be no reall Injury that some of the meanest Rank love and value you and amongst the rest tho' not worth your Notice
Sir
Your most obliged servant
H. HATRELL

1867. William Molyneux to Locke, 26 March 1695 (1857, 1887)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 104-6. Answers no. 1857; answered by no. 1887.
Dublin. March. 26. 1695.
Sir
The Concern you expres for my Welfare is extreamly obleidging, and I never prised my Health so much as since thereby I am inabled to injoy your Correspondence and Friendship. But whatever becomes of Me and My Carcas, I can hartily wish you had One more easy, healthful, and strong. for I know Mankind in General interested in you; whereas I am sure to fall unlamented to all, save a few Particular Friends.
I understand My Kinsman†1 has enjoyd that which I have earnestly longd for. He tells me by Letter the Great Obligations he bears you for the Civilitys you shewd him: and desires me to acknowledge them.
I am very Glad to find Your Essay like to suffer a third Impression. tis a Good Signe, and shews the World not so averse to truth, when fairly laid open. to have Truth Prevail the only way is calmly and meekly to publish it, and let it shift for it self; Magna res est Veritas et Prævalebit:†2 'twil make its own Party Good without Fire and Fagot, which never promoted, but I am sure has often stifled it.
This incourages me with more vigour to Promote the Translation of your Work, and to own my self infinitely obleidged to you, that you are pleased so readily to Comply with the Offer I made you in my last. Yesterday I sent for an Ingenious Young Man of the Colledge here to discourse with him about it.†3 The result was, he would make an Essay, and shew it to me, and accordingly would proceed or desist. but then he tells me, that he cannot sett himself fully to it, till towards the latter end of May; for he Designes to stand Candidate for a Fellowship in the Colledge, which by the Removal of the Provost is to be Disposed of about next Trinity Sunday,†4 and in the meantime he is to prepare himself for the Examination they undergo on that Occasion. I shall see his first
― 317 ―
Attempt the next week, and shall give you an Account. As to any alterations to be made by me, I should be very cautious of medling therein; I know the whole work has already undergone so exact a Judgement, there is no room left for amendments; However if any such offer, after your Approbation of them, I should venture to Insert them
I must freely Confes that if my Notion of Enthusiasme agrees with yours, there is no necessity of adding any thing concerning it more than by the by and in a single section in Chap. XVIII. L.IV. I conceive it to be no other than a Religious sort of Madnes and Comprises not in it any Mode of Thinking or Operation of the Mind, Differ<en>t†a from what you have treated off in your Essay. Tis true indeed, the Absurditys Men imbrace on account of Religion are most Astonishing, and if in a Chapter of Enthusiasme you indeavour to give an Account of them, 'twould be very acceptable. so that (on second thoughts) I do very well approve of what you propose therein, being very desirous of having your sentiments on any subject.
Pere Malbranche's Chapter of Seing all things in God was ever to me absolutely unintelligible; and unles you think a Polemick Discourse in your Essay (which you have hitherto avoided therein) may not be of a Peice with the Rest,†1 I am sure it highly deserves to be exposed, and is very agreable to the Busines of your Work. I would therefore humbly propose it to you to Consider of Doing something therein. Pere Malbranche has many Curious†2 Notions; and some as Erroneous and absurd; tis a Good while since I first read him, but I am now turning him over a second time. He is Mostly Platonick, and in some things almost Enthusiastical. I am
Honour'd Dear†b Sir
Your Most obleidged Humble servant
W: MOLYNEUX

1869. John Wynne to Locke, 30 March 1695 (1850, 1884)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 115-16.
Honoured Sir
I have long since return'd you my sincere acknowledgments for the favour of your obliging letter, together with my repeated assurances of the just esteem and Value I have both for your Person, and your truly excellent and judicious Composures. I did at the same time signifie to you my redines to undertake that work, which I took the freedom to propose to you, and which you could have done infinitly better. But since you thought fit to decline It, and to judge me in some measure qualified for It, I did immediately Set about It, and have almost finished It. All that I have endevour'd to do In it, was to contract it into A narrower Compass; which I have done, partly by omitting wholly the first Book, which I thought was not necessary to insert in A Treatise of this Nature (especially since the Reader may be convinc'd by what He will
― 319 ―
find in this Abridgment, that the supposition of innate Ideas and Notions is useles and unnecessary, in regard that All the knowledge he finds himself capeable of, may be attain'd without them) and partly by retrenching the larger Explications, yet so as to insert as much upon every Subject, as may serve to render it easily intelligible, and make the whole A coherent and Entire Discourse. I have not alter'd any thing In the Method, and as little as I could in the Language and Expression. Tho It will in all respects come far short of the Perfection of the Essay at large, yet I am perswaded that It will, even in this Form, far exceed, and be of much more real use, then what commonly we learn and teach, under the Name of Logick. Such as It is, I shall submit it entirely to your correction, and resign it up to your disposeal. Be pleas'd to let me know how It may be conveyed safely to you, and It shall be sent accordingly. I am in all respects
Honoured Sir
Your most Humble and Oblig'd Servant
JOHN WYNNE

1870. Dr. Andrew Broune to Locke, [c. 1 April 1695]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, ff. 167-8. Written by an amanuensis except as noted. The date is guessed from no. 1889. For the writer see nos. 1889, 1909, and the list of his publications in Wing.
Learn'd and honoured Sir
I presum'd to send you by the hands of a friend my little book
― 320 ―
the Vindicatory Schedule concerning the new cure of fevers,†1 Though the book be little, the design is great and important: The aim being a new Theory, as weel as a new practice in the cure of continuall fevers: So I humbly conceive, if I be not at first view taken for a meer boaster, It may lay claim to the Ingenious readers serious consideration and attentione, to descry if any hints therin, may amount to any thing worth the while
I must confess it came furth upon ane Emergent mention'd therin somewhat Abortive, and not so polish'd in the language and form, nor so full in the matter, as I could give it now But if the Ingenious world doe not altogether despise this my first and Ingenuus essay, It may perhaps come furth more plain and full both as to the Theory and practice in a second Editione.†2
Though the preliminaries in my book may seem at first view, from the purpose; Yea choacking, especially to Physicians; Yet I hope the same impartially considered will be found a basis both solide and pertinent to the main design; Especially considering the refractoryness in some off that profession to receive Improvements, whatever evidence they carry along with them. What then, in my humble opinione, can be more proper Then morall suasives to rouse up Physicians from such negligence and Inconsideratione And to detect vulgar errors about Physick and Physicians that are capable to stiffle or deprave the Physician's true diligence and effectuall culture
But as I am willing to submitt all to the more Judicious, whose true Characters deservedly entitules them to be Arbiters of other mens works, So more especially I humbly entreat Learned Sir your sentiments about it Whose solide and excellent Writtings bespeaks you a most competent Judge of other mens And whose candour will never suffer You to triffle in a matter of so great Import as my pretension is Which is indeed to give a Theory that lights the way to the due managment of a practice that is truely so excellent That it cures all continuall fevers more certainly and evidently then the Cortex does Intermittents. For I can sincerly affirm that these seven yeares past I have cured almost all the fevers that occured to me wher I had liberty to use it by the purging method and that compleatly and perfectly without ther translatione
― 321 ―
into other diseases as frequently falls out in other Methods, wher many, if they die not, fall unto other diseases And further within these six moneths last that fevers has been very Epidemicall here, I have cured near a hundreth patients and never any dyed that got that method. So now Sir if I be not taken for the arrogantest Impostor in the world my pretensiones cannot slip your serious consideration and early Answer. In Expectatione wherof I subscribe my self
Honoured Sir†a
Your most Humble servant
AND BROUNE

1871. William Stratton to Locke, 1 April 1695 (1864, 1890)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 94-5. Answers no. 1864.
Bristoll the 1th: Apr 1695
Dear Cosin
I Received yours of the 22th: of the last and have your Account before me that you sent me and shall answear as they are in the account
1° as for the 8d: you charge me on Sledges Acco: the coppy of my acco and the bill it selfe both mentions £8:14:10 althou your acount befor me is but £8:14:2:
2° as for the widdow Shatters chefe rent†1 the hous falling into your hand I could not gett itt and sent to you about it and the charge mite have bean more the mony would arise to and I thought you had bean satisfied
3° as for Eliza: Hopkins 11s: 6d: she answered me that she and you made up the account and would not pay it I both rode to
― 322 ―
her house and sent a letter and all would not doe although I let her know it was your mistake when you was in the countery so that I can Justly cleare my selfe
4° as for Tho: Summers and William Gullocks paying short of what the Bills amounting being 19s:3d: it was not theyr rite to pay it for it was for your perticular charge it was Received in 5 bills thou I give you account of but fowr for it was on the deth of william Sledg and at Barnes his cuming to your tenement and likewise the house was Thatched and the well mended all the perticulars arises to more then 40 Items all which Bills are put to gether and have to shew but you leaveing me to ackt for you as for my selfe I have don it and when mr: Clarke cums Into the countery I hope I shall not forget to shew him for I gets nothing by it and liwise I cannot give you soe satisfacktory an account as if I wear to speake with you

8° Inswer to the 10s: 1d: I am loath to pusell my head with accounts of 10 or 12 years standing and mad up fowr years sinc I dout not but you are fully paid for If I weare to examin ever perticular of that acco: I suppose I mite give a reson for it and it is very mutch you should not over hall the acco: sum years past,

1872. Locke to John Freke and Edward Clarke, 2 April 1695 (1868, 1874)
Rand, pp. 410-11. 'Discoloured and faded'; the words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. The postscript printed there is no. 1730 above. Answers no. 1868.
Oates, 2nd April, 1695.
Sir Edward,
I know you have so little time to spare that I scarce look for a letter from you in business, and therefore you may be sure I expect not compliments when I do you and Mrs. Clarke those little services that are in my power, and are but little more than wishes. I thank you for the care of my letters, but pray let them not be any trouble to you.
Sir John,
I thank you for the packet you sent me and the character in it of the gentleman I enquired after. I know not whether Mr. T.†1 may not have some reason about the abridgment on the bookselling account, though perhaps it may promote his business too. But whether good or ill in itself or consequence the book†2 is abroad, and his that buys it, and when he has it he may do with it as he
― 325 ―
pleases. This is sure, that Mr. W†1 writing to me very civilly about it, and as it seems to me with a good design, it was not for me to oppose it or go about to hinder him.
I told you not how much the bond was for, because I never saw it nor did Mr. Furly write me word what it was for; nor do I know whether the sum be in English or Dutch money. What is necessary for you [to write] him I beg the favour of you to demand of him in a letter, and tell him how the case stands. What you writ to me last I made all the haste I could to let him know. I am,
The College's most faithful friend and humble servant,
J. LOCKE.
Endorsed: Mr. Locke [with] letter enclosed to ..., etc. Received the 3rd of April, 1695.

Aprill the 9th 1695
Sir
Accept my thanks for yours of the 8th which I received together with Mr Ts Papers but give me leave to tell you that I hoped you would have said something to me of your opinion both of his Tract (I mean as much as you have seen of it) and of the man with respect to the Resolutions he seems by his Letters to have taken for my own part I confess I have noe great satisfaction in either.†2
As to the mony your friend has to dispose of I can but wish I knew of a security to place it on and I promise you if I hear of any I will immediately inform you of it but I can at presant tell you that none now pay above 5 per Centum Interest and much is let at a lower rate ever since the Bank has lent at 5 and having mentiond the Bank I must not forget to inform you that the Court would have had a clause in an Act that they might have had liberty to Issue Bills for as much mony (above the 1200000li which the Act that establishes them allows them to owe at one time) as they would lend the Crown on any funds Establisht this Session but the
― 327 ―
House would by noe means endure such a Clause and soe the Gentleman that offerd it withdrew it again. Had that Clause past I think The Bank must have been entirely in the power of the Court and the Nation have sufferd as much as you fear what ever it will now†1
The College is much obliged to you for the preferrence you give it and for the Bill which you ascribe to it.†2 I think I may assure you twill not pass this Session But I can tell you a pretty trick playd in the House of Lords. The Commons sent up a Bill to continue severall Acts to which their Lordships added an amendment (drawn by my Lord K)†3 that the old Act concerning printing be continued for one year and thence to the end of the next Session of Parliament.†4 but I believe the Commons will not agree to the amendment for many reasons and particularly because they allow not the Lords to begin a Bill in which there is any pecuniary penalty that being a sort of raising mony which the Commons say belongs solely to them and this clause though it be worded onely for continuance is Enacting anew a Bill in which there are many pecuniary penaltys†5
I refer you to Sir F Ms Letters for news as well of the exploits of Captain Tom†6 as of the Resolutions of the H of Commons and the examinations of the House of Lords concerning the rewards taken for service done and to be done in that House†7 and am In some haste
Your obliged humble servant

(Latin) To the distinguished Mr. John Locke Gisbertus Verrijn sends greeting. It is not so long ago, and yet no doubt it was not soon enough, that I learnt from Mijnheeren van Limborch and Le Clerc that you had been solicited by a certain London bookseller to allow a certain Englishman to make a Latin translation of your work, to be submitted to your inspection and to be corrected at your will, and that you could not altogether withstand his request. If any of it has already been done of course I desist altogether from my undertaking; if not, I beg and entreat you not to refuse to accept the first part, enlarged by your additions, to be made ready in better Latin and more carefully as soon as possible. I should long since have offered my translation, such as it is, to the public if I had not had to take account of the additions; as I now have them in readiness I impatiently desire to learn from you what is[p. 329] being done in that matter. If you will freely let me know what you have in mind, and order what you want done, you will do the greatest of favours to a most devoted reverencer of your name. Farewell.
Amsterdam, 19 April 1695.
Address: For Mr John Locke at mr Pawlings in little Lincolns-inn over against the plough.

1876. William Grigg to Locke, 13 April [1695] (1814, 1883)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 178-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London April 13th
Sir
When I had last the honour to wait upon you, you gave me leave to hope for a continuance of your kindness to me: 'tis this encourages me at present to make my Address to you who I have a great deal of reason to believe are willing to assist me. I am told the Marquiss of Tavistock†1 will travel this summer; if there be any post undispos'd of for one that understands a little french and Latin, I doubt not but your recommendation will prove succesfull, and it shall be my constant care not to make you repent the favour. This would be upon several accounts so advantagious to me that I can't believe my Wishes are at all to blame, and Your Generosity makes me willing to think, I shan't incurr the imputation of an importunate and immodest Beggar. I dare assure you that no temptation shall ever incline me to commit a base Action; If you entertain this good Opinion of me, I shall have reason to conclude my Aim will not be frustrated unless it be impracticable or the Employment improper for me. I hope you will excuse this trouble, which however impertinent it may be, perhaps it will be very much to my purpose to
― 330 ―
assure you that I will use my utmost endeavours to make myself not altogether unworthy of your patronage, and that I am, as I am many ways Oblig'd to be
Honoured Sir
Your very humble servant

1878. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 16/26 April 1695 (1826, 1901)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 97-8. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., III D 16, ff. 178-9. Printed from the copy, with some omissions, in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 365-9; Wetstein's name is replaced by 'N.N.' Answers no. 1826; answered by no. 1901.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Prolixam meam epistolam recte ad manus tuas pervenisse gaudeo. Tu, prout scripsi, historiam collationis meæ cum erudita virgine amicis quidem prælegere poteris, nulli tamen ullum, ne partis quidem epistolæ meæ apographum dabis; ne alii, qui meis colloquiis suos illi scrupulos exemtos dolent, si forte quid palam edatur, male de eâ loquendi occasionem quærant. Homines honesti et cordati non nisi benigne de ipsâ loquuntur: sed quantula illi sunt humani generis pars? Plurimos zelus inconsultus in præceps abripit. Omnia itaque quæ in calumniam a malevolis rapi possunt sollicite vitanda sunt. Ego semper hanc quam observavi methodum contra Judæos disputandi optimam esse credidi: et in sententia mea exemplum hoc me confirmatiorem reddidit. Autographum sententiarum Inquisitionis Tholosanæ Romani in manus meas incidisse mirantur,†1 quod Wetstenio Sacerdos quidam ab Episcopo Hollandiæ ad ipsum missus, ut libri possessorem ex ipso resciscat, affirmavit. Wetstenius
― 332 ―
imprudenter me eum a Furlæo accepisse respondit: verum alium esse possessorem, cujus nomen ignorabat: ajebatque librum a te olim visum Monspeliæ.†1 Ego dixi Wetstenio, librum a te in Gallia visum alium esse ab hoc. Addidit ille, sacerdotem rogasse, ut ex me nomen possessoris exquirat. Respondi ego, me nomen illius ignorare: illud semel me ex fratre ipsius Wetstenii†2 audivisse, sed penitus illius esse oblitum: et licet scirem, inconsultum esse illud sacerdoti indicare: quia hoc tam sollicite inquiri judicem, ut possessore detecto ingenti pretio exemplar hoc sibi redimant, ac Romam mittant; ut ita occasionem habeant me falsi accusandi. Idem sibi videri ajebat. Addidi ego: Optasse me Furlæi nomen non indicasset; sed quoniam vox emissa reverti nequit,†3 nihil ulterius sacerdoti esse aperiendum, sed paucis tantum respondendum, me possessoris nomen ignorare. Hoc in se suscepit; sed non recte servavit: nam ex fratre suo postea nomen hoc rescivit, et procul dubio sacerdoti indicavit; nam a me rogatus, se nescire ait an indicaverit; affirmare se non posse, nec quod indicaverit, nec quod non indicaverit. Hoc certum est, nomen sacerdoti innotuisse; quia alius postea Furlæum, ad quem hæc scripseram, accessit, et possessorem nominavit, prout tibi
― 333 ―
Furlæus scripsit. Spero librum a te jam emtum, ac Furlæum illius esse possessorem. Ita omnes illorum conatus irriti erunt. Laudo ego Furlæi prudentiam, quod a sacerdote testimonium de libri authenteiâ exegerit; et sacerdotis candorem, qui id tam luculenter dedit. Interim si forte exemplar ipsum nacti fuissent, et Romam misissent, non video qua ratione volumen quod edidi supposititium dicere possent: Adeo enim ævum illud barbarum redolet, historiasque singulares illius temporis refert, ut tale quid a quoquam nunc temporis fingi minime queat. Præstat tamen id in manibus non esse illorum, quorum interest mysteria hæc iniquitatis tegi, et coram sole non propalari. Vides hic duo adhuc additamenta ad historiam Inquisitionis epistolæ huic adscripta, quæ, si operæ pretium videtur, reliquis junges. Intellexi Oxonienses quosdam Theologiæ meæ Christianæ condemnationem molitos: addunt quidam, non tam odio mei, quam Reverendissimi Archiepiscopi defuncti, ob dedicatam illi Inquisitionis historiam; aliorum tamen prudentia ac moderatione zelum illorum igneum esse repressum.†1 Lutheranus quidam Professor Kiloniensis contra illam Exercitationes AntiLimborchianas
― 334 ―
edidit.†1 Ita Romæ, in Anglia, et Germania vapulo. Librum satis, ut audio, crassum nondum vidi; sed in Actis Lipsiensibus ejus compendium legi.†2 Verum in ejusmodi antagonistam ego calamum non stringam. Non†a- pugnant illi homines pro veritate,-†a sed pro recepta opinione, decretis humanis, et autoritate ecclesiastica. Orthodoxias illis norma est consensus cum doctrina Lutherana. Contra tales frustra disputatur. Non enim operæ pretium est, ut inquiramus quid Ecclesia Lutherana doceat; quod ex libris et decretis illius Ecclesiæ satis notum est: sed, an illius doctrina vera sit, et a scriptoribus divinis dictata. Ita papatum ubique reperimus, et sub specioso orthodoxiæ conservandæ prætextu propria dominatio stabilitur. Sic orthodoxia semper penes potentiorem erit, veritasque alia erit Romæ, alia Genevæ, alia Wittenbergæ. Hæc incommoda vitari nequeunt, si humana placita orthodoxias κριτήριον sunt. Quæ in illis Exercitationibus maxime odiosa occurrunt, Lipsienses accurate annotarunt. Observavi†b- hanc in illis, malignitatem dicam <an>†c inconsultum zelum, quod si in autoribus, quos recensent, quædam reperiantur aut convitia, aut inclementius in Remonstrantes dicta, ea sollicite indicare soleant, verbisque
― 335 ―
odiosissimis exprimere.-†b Nescio quo suo facto Remonstrantes inimicitiam eorum in se provocaverint, nisi forsan liberiore veritatis inquisitione, et dissentientium fraterna tolerantia. In ipsos enim calamum nunquam strinximus, neque ego in eos scribam, aut me a criminationibus eorum purgabo: non enim me illis purgatum dabo, nisi me aliis, quibus jam placeo, ingratum reddam.†a Sed aliud quid est quod te velim. Marcus Teuto in gratiam Reverendissimi Bathoniensis ac Wellensis in se suscepit versionem vitæ Episcopii a me conscriptæ in linguam Latinam: Varia ego citavi ex Epistolis Ecclesiasticis præstantium ac eruditorum virorum,†1 et ex Actis Remonstrantium Synodalibus;†2 quæ cum a me e Latino in Belgicum sermonem translata sint, ipse e Belgico in Latinum vertere non debet, sed prout in ipsis libris Latine leguntur exhibere. Destitutum autem se illis queritur, nec usquam se eos reperire posse. Non dubito quin in multorum Anglorum bibliothecis reperiantur. Si tua opera eos habere possit a quopiam, magnum illi non tantum faceres laboris compendium, sed et versionem efficies et meliorem et gratiorem. Ego si quid hac in parte illi prodesse queas, mihi
― 336 ―
præstitum agnoscam. Vale Vir Amplissime mihique dilectissime. Salveat plurimum Domina Masham. Salutant te Venius cum suis, uxor mea, unàque filia et filius.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 26 Aprilis

Saccus hic†b semper et ubique ex panno fieri consuevit: verum hodie decurtatus magis quam olim esset: quondam enim æque longus erat ac Monachorum scapularium, et permansit hoc modo toto tempore, quo crucibus notabatur: cum enim cruces longæ essent tres palmos, fieri non poterat, quin saccus oblongus esset: postea vero, tum quod cruces sublatæ sint, tum etiam ut saccus a Monachorum scapulario differret, in breviorem formam redactus est. In quibusdam etiam Hispaniæ tribunalibus alia vestis poenitentialis forma usu recepta est: reis enim non convictis, sed de hæresi vehementer suspectis, dimidiata vestis poenitentialis pectus tantum tegens imponitur, quæ unica tantum linea rubri coloris notatur, non duabus decussatis, ut saccus integer signari consuevit; ut ostendatur

non esse vere et formaliter hæreticum, sed de hæresi vehementer suspectum.†a
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I am glad that my lengthy letter duly reached you. As I wrote, you can certainly read aloud to friends the account of my debate with the scholarly young woman, but you will please give no one any copy of my letter, not even a part of it, lest, if by chance anything is made public, others, who regret that the difficulties that they had raised were taken away from her by my conversations, should seek an opportunity to speak ill of her. Reputable and judicious men do not speak otherwise than favourably about her; but how small a part of the human race are they! Unadvised zeal carries most away headlong. Accordingly everything that can be seized on by the malicious to slander her is to be carefully avoided. I have always believed that this procedure which I observed is the best for arguing against the Jews; and this example has made me the more confident in my opinion. The Romans are surprised that the autograph of the Sententiæ of the Toulouse Inquisition fell into my hands;†1 a certain priest, who was sent by the bishop of Holland to Wetstein to learn from him the owner of the book, assured him of this.[p. 332] Wetstein imprudently answered that I had received it from Furly, but that the owner was someone else whose name he did not know; and he said that the book had formerly been seen by you at Montpellier.†1 I told Wetstein that the book seen by you in France was not this but another. He added that the priest had asked him to inquire the owner's name from me. I answered that I did not know his name; I had heard it once from Wetstein's brother,†2 but I had completely forgotten it; and even if I knew it it would be ill advised to disclose it to the priest, since I suppose that this is being so carefully investigated in order that, when the owner is discovered, they may buy the original for themselves at an immense price and send it to Rome; so that they may thus have an opportunity of falsely accusing me. He said that it seemed the same to him. I added that I wished that he had not disclosed Furly's name, but since a word uttered cannot be recalled†3 nothing further was to be revealed to the priest; he was only to be answered in a few words that I do not know the owner's name. This he undertook; but he did not rightly keep to it; for he later learnt the name from his brother and undoubtedly disclosed it to the priest; for, when asked by me, he said that he did not know whether he had disclosed it; he could not say for certain what he had disclosed and what he had not disclosed. This is certain, that the name has become known to the priest, for another later came to Furly, to whom I had written this, and named the owner, just as Furly wrote to you. I hope that the[p. 333] book has now been bought by you and that Furly is its owner. So all their attempts will come to nothing. I commend Furly's prudence in exacting from the priest an attestation of the book's authenticity; and the priest's candour in giving it so clearly. Nevertheless, if by chance they had obtained the original itself, and had sent it to Rome, I do not see on what ground they could say that the volume that I have published is supposititious; for it is so redolent of that barbarous age, and relates histories of that time so remarkable, that anything of the kind could not be fashioned by anyone of the present time. For all that it is better that it should not be in the hands of those whose concern it is that these mysteries of iniquity should be hidden and not be published in the light of the sun. You have here in a postscript to this letter two more additions to the Historia Inquisitionis; please join them to the rest if it seems worth while. I have learnt that certain Oxonians have attempted a condemnation of my Theologia Christiana; some add that this is from hatred not so much of me as of the late Most Reverend the Archbishop on account of the Historia Inquisitionis being dedicated to him; their fiery zeal has been checked, however, by the prudence and moderation of others.†1 A certain Lutheran professor at Kiel has published Exercitationes Anti-Limborchianœ[p. 334] against the Theologia.†1 So I am being flogged at Rome, in England, and in Germany. I have not yet seen the, as I hear, rather fat volume, but I have read the summary in the Acta Lipsiensia.†2 But I shall not take up my pen against such an antagonist. Those men fight not for truth but for a received opinion, the decrees of men, and ecclesiastical authority. Their standard of orthodoxy is agreement with Lutheran doctrine. It is useless to argue against such men. For it is not worth while for us to inquire what the Lutheran Church teaches, which is well enough known from its books and decrees; but [we should inquire] whether its doctrine is true and dictated by the divine writers. Thus we find popery everywhere, and under the specious pretext of preserving orthodoxy its own supremacy is established. So orthodoxy will always be with the stronger, and truth will be one thing at Rome, another at Geneva, and another in Wittenberg. These inconveniences cannot be avoided if human ordinances are the test of orthodoxy. The Leipzigers have carefully recorded the most hateful things that occur in those Exercitationes. I have observed in them this, shall I say malignity or unadvised zeal, that if any abusive or especially harsh utterances about the Remonstrants are found in authors whom they are reviewing, they are wont to indicate them carefully[p. 335] and to express them in most hateful words. I do not know by what act the Remonstrants have provoked their hostility, unless perhaps by their more free search for truth and their brotherly toleration of those who differ from them. For we have never taken up the pen against them, nor shall I write against them or clear myself from their accusations; for I shall not clear myself from them without rendering myself disagreeable to others to whom I am at present acceptable. But there is something else that I desire of you. To please the Right Reverend the bishop of Bath and Wells Marcus Teut has undertaken a translation into Latin of the life of Episcopius that I wrote. I have quoted [in it] various passages from Praestantium ac Eruditorum Virorum Epistolœ Ecclesiasticœ†1 and from the Acta Synodalia Remonstrantium;†2 since these were translated by me from Latin into Dutch he ought not to turn them from Dutch into Latin but ought to present them just as they are read in Latin in those books. But he complains that he is without them and cannot find them anywhere. I do not doubt that they may be found in many Englishmen's libraries. If he can obtain them from someone by your means, not only would you greatly shorten his work but you will also make the translation better and more acceptable. If you can be of any service to him in[p. 336] this respect I shall recognize it as done to myself. Goodbye, excellent Sir and most dear to me. My best respects to Lady Masham. Veen and his family, and my wife with my daughter and son, send you their greetings.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 26 April 1695

Ludovicus a Paramo,†1 however, finds punishment by fire in several places in the New Testament. 'James and John deem that the Samaritans' who did not receive the Lord hospitably 'should be destroyed by fire from heaven, as St. Luke says, chapter 9. Behold the punishment of heretics, namely fire, for the Samaritans of that time were heretics. In Matthew 21 and 22, Mark 12, and Luke 20 Christ adduces three parables: the first concerning the two sons; the second concerning the vineyard let out to husbandmen; the third concerning the marriage feast already prepared for those bidden to it. By these he manifestly indicates that the kingdom is to be taken from the heretical[p. 337] Jews and that their city is to be burnt with fire. Behold the confiscation of goods and the fire with which heretics are punished.' Nor is this surprising in a man who finds the Inquisition against heretics everywhere in the Old and New Testaments, even in Paradise itself, and who strives to show by many proofs that God exercised in Paradise against Adam the office of an Inquisitor into heretical pravity: lib. 1, tit. 2. Primus qui poenam ignis.
(Latin) p. 340. line 19. after coloris rubei.
This sack [the sanbenito] has always and everywhere been customarily made of cloth; but today it is cut shorter than formerly; for it was once of equal length with the monks' scapular, and it continued in that fashion during the whole time that it was marked with crosses; for as the crosses were three palms long it could not be so marked without the sack's being oblong; later, however, because the crosses were removed and also to distinguish it from the monks' scapular, it was reduced to a shorter form. Also in certain Spanish tribunals another form of penitential garment has been adopted; for a half-length penitential garment, covering only the breast, is set on accused persons who have not been convicted but who are strongly suspected of heresy; this is marked only with a single red stripe, not with two crossed in[p. 338] saltire, as the complete sack used to be distinguished; in order that he may be shown to be not truly and formally a heretic, but strongly suspected of heresy.

1880. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 19/29 April 1695 (1855, 1912)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 93-4. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 82-3.
A Amsterdam le 29 d'Avril 1695.
J'ai reçu, Monsieur, il y a environ trois semaines, les petits livres, dont vous me parliez. Je vous en suis obligé, j'ai été bien aise de voir des livres, qui ont tant mis en colere les Druïdes,†1 et dont on me faisoit la grace de m'attribuer les materiaux.†2 Les Auteurs, ou l'Auteur ne semble pas avoir grand'peur de ce qu'ils penseront de lui; mais il auroit dû considerer bien des choses, en cette occasion, sur tout après avoir été traité plus doucement qu'à l'ordinaire, par le Grand Druïde,†3 et par un autre.†4 Il pouvoit bien traiter sa matiere, sans y mêler les traits choquans, et les raïlleries qu'il y a répanduës. Ses raisons n'en auroient pas moins eu de force, et elles auroient moins irrité les gens. Mais il est difficile de garder par tout le froid et la calme, qu'il faudroit avoir dans la Controverse. Il mèle trop de choses, qui sont sujettes à de grandes contestations, et sur lesquelles on le peut battre, ce qui tire consequence pour tout le reste. Par exemple, il soûtient qu'on peut avoir une idée complette de l'infini, ce que je ne croi pas. Sur l'affaire de l'invocation de Jesus-Christ, il ne répond point bien, et dit des choses qui semblent supposer qu'une partie d'entre eux ne l'invoquent point; ce qui est opposé à la pratique, et aux discours des Apôtres. Sur le mot d'adorer, il ne se tire pas bien d'affaire, faute de distinguer la signification de ce mot qui est équivoque. Outre cela ce qu'il dit est propre à s'attirer la haine de
― 340 ―
tout le monde, et à donner lieu à ses adversaires de le rendre plus odieux qu'il n'est. Ses doutes sur l'Evangile de S.Jean, fondez sur les raisons des Alogiens,†1 ne sont d'aucun poids, et ne peuvent que donner occasion à ses adversaires de le noircir cruellement; en disant qu'il n'y a rien d'assuré dans l'Ecriture, si l'on nie cet Evangile, et en tirant de là de très-odieuses consequences. Ceux qui ont tort dans les incidens sont bien souvent regardez comme aiant tort dans le fonds de leur procès; et il n'y a rien de plus dangereux que de donner prise contre soi, sur tout quand on a affaire à des parties puissantes. Pour moi, je suis persuadé du contraire, comme vous l'aurez vû dans ma Dissertation.†2 J'en avois envoié aux deux Archevêques,†3 et aux Evêques de Salisbury et de Bath, dans la supposition que le port ne leur coûtoit rien, quand ils étoient assemblez en Parlement, mais l'Eveque de Sal. m'a desabusé, en me disant qu'ils ne sont exempts que du port des Lettres qui viennent d'Angleterre.†4 Je suis fâché d'avoir fait cette bévuë, quoi que ce fût sur une Lettre que le même Evêque m'écrivit une fois, avant que de porter la Mitre. Aussi n'y a-t-il eu que lui, qui m'ait répondu, car les autres sont encore dans le silence. En Italie, en France et en Espagne, les plus grands Prélats font répondre par leurs secretaires, quand ils ne le peuvent pas faire eux mêmes, ou qu'ils ne le trouvent pas à propos, mais il faut que la pratique soit differente en Angleterre. Comme j'espere que vous aurez vû ma Dissertation, je vous prie de m'en dire ce que vous en pensez. Une Lettre fulminante,†5 et fondée neanmoins sur des rapports impertinens, l'a extorquée de moi, dans le milieu d'occupations beaucoup plus pressantes. Nous sommes présentement occupez à l'impression du Deuteronome, qui sera bien tôt faite. Il y a long-temps même que le Pentateuque seroit achevé, si j'avois eu tout le loisir qu'ont tant de gens, qui sont paiez pour ne rien faire. Marquez moi, s'il vous plaît, si vous avez reçu le Richelieu, la premiere fois que vous me ferez l'honneur de m'écrire. Je suis entierement, Monsieur, vôtre très-humble et très-obeissant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
