Aprill the 15th. 1695:
My Deare,
Yours, which I had not time to answare by the last post, I have since Considered as well as I can, and doe find it is more easey to me to answere the perticulars to you then to mr lock; as to sickness I thanke God I cant Complaine of any, but very often I find a Great decay of spirritts, and as you have often heard me express my selfe I want something thats Good, that is somethinge to support me, but I know not what, which is a dissease subjectt to our secx too often; but as to the matter in hand, the disorder I mentioned in my other letter, it is what I have bin trobled with for some time, but some times more, and some times less, but as to that which we women are subjectt to once a month, I have as regulerly as any body, not missing 24 howres of its time in a month, and that as well colered, and in the same proportion, as I have had thiss 20 yeares, but I observe the other Grevance is more before that tim<e>†a and after, then any other, Except it be when I hav<e>†a any Great troble upon me, and that I find increases that†b disorder very much, as for Instance the Concern I had for the queens death, increased it soe very much, and brought soe Great a weakness in my back, that I could not stoope down to have had any thinge of Ever soe much vallew, nor sitt downe nor stand up, without very Great difficulty and paine; which after a while grew som-thing better; but Sammys†1 Illness I found in Great mesure had the same Effectt on me, as to the inconvenience I could Concele, the difficulty of sturing not returning a Gen, soe that I find when any thinge doss afectt and disturbe my mind, it doss thuss refenge it selfe upon my body, beyond the common rate that it dose att other times, and by thiss meanes keeps me very leane and low sperrited, and hindred me as I beleve from Gathering that stranth by the bath waters as mr lock expectted; which by the observation I made on my selfe in the drinkeing of them Gave me a stoole or 2 in the drinking of them, According as I mannaged them, which was thuss, the warmer and quicker I dranke them the more they wraght that way, for when I dranke them Coole, and leasurely, which mr Locke advised If you remember to keepe them from fleying up in my head, then I
― 343 ―
observed they wrought alltogether by uring, but when I filled my selfe soe full as I was redy to burst, but was sure to Give off without Vomitting, then they Certainly Gave me a stoole or 2, and some times three, but that was not Common, which is all I can say as to the bath waters; and to the use of spice I beleve no body uses less, haveing bin formerly told by mr lock that it was very prejudishall to any ones health, perticulerly nutmegg in beere or otherways, nay If you remember hee would heardly alow any spice to be put in a Cake etc: whose rules I have soe Great a vally for, that I allways performe them with all exactness to the utmost of my power, and for that resen have avoided Eating Gallengen†1 and nuttmeg mixed togather, which I wase told was a very Good thinge to Carry allways about one and often to use of it, If you remember when I was in london I told mrs. blackmore†2 how apt I was to thiss disorder and she advised me to Eat Caishia in the cane†3 and accordingly I did Gett some but I found it a very troblesome sort of a sweett stuff, and very fidling to Gett out of the Cane, and noe Good by it, when I had all done, and I am apt to think such little buisnisses will doe me but very little Good, but I am Extreamly oblidged to you and mr lock for your Care and Concerne for me, and will take Care to Gett some bath waters with the first opertunity; as soone as the wether is a little milder; and will send the prescription to mr Smith for the pills soe as to have them redy a Gainst the time the water Comes, and in the meane time doe begg of you to present my humble service and thankes to mr lock and accept the same your selfe from,
Your Truley affecttionate and Faithfull wife MARY CLARKE
I hope this will Excuse my not writing to mr lock by thiss post, but I will doe it very quickley, all heare present you theyr duty and service etc:
I had noe letter from you by the last post but doe hope all is well, my humble service to mr Freak and my Blessing to ward†4 and Jenney:†5

1883. William Grigg to Locke, 20 April [1695] (1876, 3069)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 180-1. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London 20th April
Sir
Last Wensday†1 I received your Letters from Mr Churchil, when I was equally surpriz'd at the Greatness of your Kindness for me and your readiness to express it. I must own with thanks that your good Opinion of me has given me the truest pleasure I have been sensible of this long while, and though the hopes I had seem groundless, yet it is a very great satisfaction to me, that you thought they were not Unreasonable. Last Thursday I was to wait upon my Lord Ashley, but he not being within I went to Mr Fatio who, having read your letter told me I was mistaken, that my Lord was not design'd for travel this summer nor did he know when he would, that he was speedily to be married,†2 and added, that his family would be then encreast, which last particular makes me call to mind what my Lord Ashley told me when I mention'd it to him, having had the honour to be with him yesterday; That, though it be true that the Marquiss was like to have his Train encreast yet that few of the Nobility were sollicitous to have it fill'd with men of letters, in short that there were very few Mæcenasses nowadays: I don't know whither I did not exceed my commission when I hereupon offer'd my self to serve the Marquiss as his Chaplain, but I was glad to find, he only objected that I was not in Orders which gave me an Opportunity to reply that if I had the honour of this Title, I was sure I had some friends among the Bishops who would think me every way else Qualified. His Lordship generously promis'd me his Assistance, and I am particularly bound to own my Obligation to you for having been received by him as one who had a letter of recommendation from you. This morning I was again with Mr Fatio who had offer'd to deliver your letter to my Lady Russel, I could not well decline the proffer though I should have chose to have presented it my self. He told me that my Lady would write to you, and then askt me whither I could write a good hand and understood Arithmetick, so that there may be some faint hopes left, of being yet admitted into the family for which I have always had a very particular and great
― 346 ―
Respect. Sir, I am heartily asham'd that I have given you this trouble, but, when I consider how generally and how confidently it was nois'd about the town and how every body believ'd that the young Lord was design'd for Travel, I flatter my self you will give me leave to think I am not wholly inexcusable. My mother I'm sure will think herself equally oblig'd to you: for my part, I will hence-forward double my Diligence not to make you asham'd of your concern for <me>†a which is the only way I can demonstrate the just value I have for it and that I am <with the gr>eatest†a sincerity imaginable
Honoured Sir
Your most humble servant
W M GRIGG

1884. John Wynne to Locke, 20 April 1695 (1869, 1915)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 117-18.
Honoured Sir
Yours of the 8th instant came safely to my hands; but the Other you mention, I had not the happines to receive: so that I must impute it to that misfortune, that I cannot make any return to it. But your last gives me sufficient occasion to renew my professions of Esteem and Respect for you; which are not only grounded upon the perswasion that I have of your being A sincere Promoter of Truth and Knowledge; but also of your being As cordial A Freind of true Piety and Vertue, which you have upon occasion very advantagiously recommended in your Essay; and more fully in your judicious Thoughts concerning Education; which in my opinion give A better light into that important affair, than any thing I have met with upon that subject.
I have sent up the Abridgment I have made of your Essay, with orders to be left where you directed me: Some Freinds who were pleas'd to peruse it approved of the design, and gave their opinion,
― 347 ―
that it may answer the End, for which it is intended: but I submit it to your judgment, and leave it wholly to your disposal. I have enclos'd with it A letter to your self, to be prefixed, If you shall think it proper, In which I have endeavor'd to express my self with that decent reserve, as became me in an address to you; and with that caution, as might give no offence to some others whom I had in my Eye. If I had given my self the liberty to have declared my judgment freely, which I had in my thoughts to do in A Prefatory Discourse, I found It would have lead me to make some invidious Reflections, and to utter Some Truths that would be thought unseasonable, and were, as the case now stands, more advantagiously suppressed.
What you have said in answer to the quære propos'd in my last gives A satisfactory account, why you comprehend under the general Name of Intuition, the Knowledge we have of our own existence and Thoughts as well as of self-evident Truths; and dos at the same time allow, what my freind contends for, that If we come to distinguish nicely, we may conceive A difference between the Internal perception or Sensation of our own Existence, the Consciousnes of our thoughts, and the perception of Self-evident Truths, All which seem to have an equal degree of certainty and evidence, tho differing in the objects and manner of perception.
Be pleas'd when you favour me with another letter to direct it to me (Fellow of Jes: Coll:) because there is Another of both my names in the College. I am with all respect and observance
Honoured Sir
Your most humble and oblig'd Servant
JOHN <WYNNE>†a
Oxon Apr. 20th. 95.

1885. James Tyrrell to Locke, 21 April [1695] (1859, 1895)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 134-5. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Oxon: April 21
Dear Sir
I owne the receipt of a letter from you near three weekes agone, and allmost as soon as I returned hither, but have deferred the answere to it, till my occasions would permit me to goe to Okeley and search among my bookes for that you want, for tho I was allmost assured that no such book was there, yet I would not be positive till I had looked: and therefore I can now tell you. that I must still persist in what I told your self as well as Mr: Thomas, that I never had any such volume of yours in my keeping, as Lightfoot in folio:†1 those in quarto being all I ever saw among your bookes, and for that I appeal to the catalogue I sent you; in which I am sure I omitted none of the folios; nor will it doe me any good to keep it; (if I were so dishonest as to doe it) for I have long since <reduced>†a all the critical learning (that I desire to be Master of) concerning the Scriptures into a very compasse; so that if I would have kept any of your bookes; I'le assure you it shhould not have bin that: I can likewise acquit Dr: Thomas of it, for to the best of my knowledge he never had any other bookes of me then those I told you of: so that where this mistake lyes I know not, but if you will have my thoughts of it I must tell you that I thinke those that took away the catalogue of your bookes, as allso your gilt spoon, and forke might take away that too for ought I know. and you may remember that I have long since told you; that John Clerk found your study door open, before he could come to Oxford to remove your things; (I being then at London). whatsoever of yours came to my hands hath bin honestly returned you; except a small paper book without any writeing in it which†b- I made use of-†b and some other small things not worth the sending up: and I hope you have known me so long as not to distrust what I now tell you: I have directed this to London because now the weather is grown warme I fancye you are come thither: if not, Mr: Pawleing will send it you; tho I should be much more glad to find you next week newly come
― 349 ―
to Town, when I intend God Willing to be there my self, and in the mean time am ever
your most faithfull and humble servant
J TYRRELL.

1886. Locke to John Freke and Edward Clarke, 26 April [1695] (1881, 1891)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 84. Printed in Rand, pp. 412-13. Year from Clarke's endorsement. Answers no. 1881; answered by no. 1891.
Oates 26 Apr
The last post I had but just time to acknowledg the receit of their favours from the Colleg.
Sir Grave haveing now at more leisure perused Madams letter I am confirmd in the opinion of the method I have prescribd her. That decay of spirets, and want of something she knows not what is a very right discription of hir disease. I know it very well and I know noe thing soe good for that as the Bath waters and if they should noe other ways help what she last complaind of but by hindering her from being soe often and soe much disturbd with any thing that may come crosse her, yet in that they would be very usefull to her in allaying and abateing that other symptom. But besides that, I looke on them as directly helpfull for that too espetialy if she will be carefull to drink them as I have directed. to which I have at present noething more to adde of directions to be sent to hir if you have received the letter I sent you the last post and I hope we shall soon have an account of hir being better. If it should not be soe soon let it not give you any apprehensions of her life being in danger. The last ill she complaind of is sometimes obstinate and will not presently yeild to remedies, but as it often hangs on long, soe patients support them selves long under it and it very
― 350 ―
seldom proves mortall. I returne you my thanks for soe readily answering†a- my bill-†a <for>†b Sir Francis and your remembrance and care of my affair with Sir Stephen. when the quarteredg is paid. I lately found a copy of my will sealed up and writ on in a place where I lookd not for it. This made me bethink my self how it came there. After some recollection I phansie that I remember that last somer haveing some thoughts to alter something in it when I was in town I had it from you. If soe it has lain by me forgotten till now. Pray set me right in this matter in your next.†c For I finde my memory I finde is in many things too short to be relyd on. I am
Dear Sir
your most humble and faithfull servant
J L

1887. Locke to William Molyneux, 26 April 1695 (1867, 1896)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 107-12. Answers no. 1867; answered by no. 1896.
Oates, April 26. 1695.
Sir,
<You look with the eyes, and speak the language of friendship, when you make my life of so much more concern to the world, than your own. I take it, as it is, for an effect of your kindness, and so shall not accuse you of complement; the mistakes and over-valuings of good will being always sincere, even when they exceed what common truth allows. This on my side, I must beg you to believe, that my life would be much more pleasant and useful to me, if you were within my reach, that I might sometimes enjoy your conversation, and, upon twenty occasions, lay my thoughts before you, and have the advantage of your judgment. I cannot complain that I have not my share of friends of all ranks, and such, whose interest, assistance, affection, and opinions too, in fit cases, I can rely on. But methinks, for all this, there is one place vacant, that I know no body that would so well fill as your self. I want one near me to talk freely with,
― 351 ―
de quolibet ente;†1 to propose to, the extravagancies that rise in my mind; one with whom I would debate several doubts and questions, to see what was in them. Meditating by ones self is like digging in the mine; it often, perhaps, brings up maiden earth, which never came near the light before; but whether it contain any mettle in it, is never so well tryed as in conversation with a knowing judicious friend, who carries about him the true touch-stone, which is love of truth in a clear-thinking head. Men of parts and judgment the world usually gets hold of, and by a great mistake (that their abilities of mind are lost, if not employ'd in the pursuit of wealth or power) engages them in the ways of fortune and interest, which usually leave but little freedom or leisure of thought for pure disinterested truth. And such who give themselves up frankly, and in earnest, to the full latitude of real knowledge, are not every where to be met with. Wonder not, therefore, that I wish so much for you in my neighbourhood; I should be too happy in a friend of your make, were you within my reach. But yet, I cannot but wish that some business would once bring you within distance, and 'tis a pain to me to think of leaving the world, without the happiness of seeing you.
I do not wonder that a kinsman of yours†2 should magnifie civilities that scarce deserve that name; I know not wherein they consisted, but in being glad to see one that was any way related to you, and was himself a very ingenious man; either of those was a title to more than I did, or could shew him. I am sorry I have not yet had an opportunity to wait on him in London, and I fear he should be gone before I am able to get thither. This long winter, and cold spring, has hung very heavy upon my lungs, and they are not yet in a case to be ventur'd in London air, which must be my excuse for not waiting upon him and Dr. Ashe yet.
The third edition of my Essay is already, or will be speedily in the press. But what perhaps will seem stranger, and possibly please you better, an abridgment is now making (if it be not already done) by one of the university of Oxford,†3 for the use of young scholars, in the place of an ordinary system of logick. From the acquaintance I had of the temper of that place, I did not expect to have it get much footing there. But so it is, I some time since received a very civil letter from one wholly a stranger to me there, concerning such
― 352 ―
a design, and, by another from him since, I conclude it near done. He seems to be an ingenious man, and he writes sensibly about it; but I can say nothing of it till I see it, which he, of his own accord, has offer'd that I shall, wholly submitted to my opinion, and disposal of it. And thus, Sir, possibly that which you once proposed may be attained too, and I was pleased with the gentleman's design for your sake.
You are a strange man, you oblige me very much by the care you take to have it well translated, and you thank me for complying with your offer. In my last, as I remember, I told you the reason why it was so long before I writ, was an expectation of an answer from London, concerning something I had to communicate to you: It was in short this, I was willing to know what my bookseller would give for a good latin copy; he told me, at last, twenty pounds. His delay was, because he would first have known what the translator demanded. But I forced him to make his proposal, and so I send it you, to make what use of it you please. He since writ me word, that a friend of his at Oxford would, in some time, be at leisure to do it, and would undertake it. I bid him excuse himself to him, for that it was in hands I approv'd of, and some part of it now actually done. For I hope the Essay (he was to shew you the next week after you writ to me last) pleased you. Think it not a complement, that I desire you to make what alterations you think fit. One thing particularly you will oblige me and the world in, and that is, in paring off some of the superfluous repetitions, which I left in for the sake of illiterate men, and the softer sex, not used to abstract notions and reasonings. But much of this reasoning will be out of doors in a latin translation. I refer all to your judgment, and so am secure it will be done as is best.
What I shall add concerning Enthusiasm, I guess, will very much agree with your thoughts, since yours jump so right with mine, about the place where it is to come in, I having designed it for chap. 18. lib. iv. as a false principle of reasoning often made use of. But, to give an historical account of the various ravings men have embraced for religion, would, I fear, be besides my purpose, and be enough to make an huge volume.
My opinion of P. Malbranche agrees perfectly with yours. What I have writ concerning seeing all things in God, would make a little treatise of it self. But I have not quite gone through it, for fear I should by somebody or other be tempted to print it. For I love not
― 353 ―
controversies, and have a personal kindness for the author.†1 When I have the happiness to see you, we will consider it together, and you shall dispose of it.
I think I shall make some other additions to be put into your latin translation, and particularly concerning the Connexion of Ideas, which has not, that I know, been hitherto consider'd and has, I guess, a greater influence upon our minds, than is usually taken notice of.†2 Thus, you see, I make you the confident of my reveries; you would be troubled with a great many more of them, were you nearer. I am,
Honour'd Sir,
Your most affectionate, humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.

1889. Dr. John Hutton to Locke, 27 April 1695 (1035)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 253-4.
Honord Sir
I may Justly Beleave my self a Sufferer in yowr oppinion all this whyle; when yowrs came to my Hand, it put me in mind to Have Heard of the person yow mention, but the account was Lame, and from those who seemed partiall, wherefore to Inform yow and my self a Litle better, I deferred this so Long; And now I can only give but a Lame account off Dr Brown.†1 who I never saw, nor was He Heard off butt off Late, He Lived in the Contrie upon a competent paternall estate with His wiff and family, Heath bean once att London when and where He made Himself acquented with dr Sydenham; the only tyme He Heath bean out off Scotland, He administred some particular Remedies to His frinds in the contrie more from ane Inclynation, then any apearing desire off gain. A few yeares agoe att Edenbrough where He was Accedentaly, He payed a visit to my Lord Chrighton†2 who was then ill off a continued fever, and who askd Dr Brown any Remedy might Help Him out off a fever Had continued severe upon some 17 dayes; Brown without the Knowledge of my Lords physiciens gave Him a dose off purging medicinne which gave Him upwards of 20 stooles, and in a few dayes after died; Some physiciens made use off this opportunitie to Reproch both Brown and His practise; I think it was about this tyme He went to Aberdeen and took His degree off doctor†3 and then writ a small book in His own defence, as well as off His practise, publishd it with great assurrance;†4 He Heath writ some Litle papers since, non wheroff are come to my Hand as yet though they Have bean twise designed for me.†5 I am Informed He commends dr Sydenhams method in the cure off fevers beyond any other; He thinks that the cause off Heat, and frequent beating of the puls in fevers is not from the Rarifaction, Extraordinarie fermentation,
― 355 ―
nor swifness off the motion off the Blood; But from its Visciditie, Toughness, Thickness, or tendencie To a coagulation, or stagnating as He Terms it; And consequently to be ascribed to its difficult and uneasie motion, Requiering more stroaks and pulses, and more frequent contractions and delatations off the Hart, to promote and continue this Languishing, and Heavie motion, And useth the Simile off a pomp, a few Regular full stroaks off which, will put in motion a quantitie off what is fluid, when Ten times as many swift stroaks will not move and Keep in motion an equall quantitie of what is consistent: He addes that in most fevers the peristaltick motion off the arteries is but litle sensible; when the Arterie expands itself the stroak is not full, and when it contracts it self it does not subside to the Cilindricall axis of the Arterie, which frequent flaffings†1 (as He speaks) debilitates the animal spirits and Heates the patient Though the circulation moves but slowly; from this He sayes the bloud is sometimes found coagulat or stagnat in the Head and Lungs off the dead; and its not Returning from the Head causeth deliriums etc. not only from These Symtomes, but from the method off cure, He proves His conjecture: For (sayes He) the Remedies are, or ought to be such as attenuats or Rarifies the bloud, and gives it a greater freedome off circulation, or such as evacuats, whither by sweating, blooding or purging etc. He mentions yow as I am told with great Respect; the physicens att Edenbrough are Angrie with Him because He dares to prescrib for any disease, and now Heath a dale off practice; He is what we call a Banter†2 and I am told is treuly a Rugh contrie bred man, understands the Latin very well, but Heath writ is booke in a plain Scoth stile, if ever it come to my Hand yow shall be master off it, as yow Realy are, off
Honored Sir
your most affectionat fathfull servant
JO HUTTON
whyt Hall Apirl 27 1695

Oates 3º May. 95
Dear Sir Grave
By the fires side (and well I can be warme there) I returne you my thanks for yours of the 30 Apr. The inclosed from Madame giveing noe farther account of her health or any thing done in order to it does not require a present answer. That†b- which you say of my will satisfies me how litle I must relye on my memorie.-†b
What I said of the wonders might be done if there were more such colleges, or this one had more such fellows†2 I finde I have reason to repeat again upon the reading of the dozen and half. which are (contrary to custome) all Reasons,†3 would your house
― 359 ―
were stored with a number of such as drue them up. there was never more need of them, I cannot tell what to say of their plenty.
The Batchelor must give me leave to minde him again of Sir William Wallers book upon the receit of a letter lately from Mr Limborch who has some concerne in it.†1 I hope the purchase is made or at least that Sir Batchelor has writ to Ben <Furly>†a about it, as I desired, that it may be expedited
Last Tuesday I received from Churchill a catalogue of Millers Pamphlets that are now set to sale.†2 I would desire some of the College if they know any that are extraordinary good in their kinde to send a catalogue of them by the peny post to A Churchill to buy them for me. There was one I remember of the administration of the affairs of Scotland under Duke Lotherdale†3 and an other about the Scotch affairs writ about 4 or 5 years since the author was supposd Sir J.M.†4 I have forgot the titles of both of them but should be glad to have them. This though I desire yet I would not have it intrench upon any of your more serious affair, If you have an idle minuit to throw away write down a few such in a catalogue and let Churchill have it. You that live in town pray excuse such troubles from your country <fri>ends,†b if you want herbs or roots for diet drinks or plaisters pray let me <he>ar†b of you. A propos des remedes. Take†c- Juice of Selandine and honey with a litle Safron, an excellent remedie for a sore mouth and that which people call Kankers in it. Probatum est.-†c I thank you for your care and pains about my tickets and am your
Most assured Freind and humble servant
J LOCKE

1895. James Tyrrell to Locke, 6 May [1695] (1885, 2053)

May 6th:
Dear Sir
About the begining of this Terme,†1 I writ to you, in answere to yours, and directed it to Mr: Pawleings because I heard you intended to be in Towne about that time; but tho I was mistaken; yet I hope you have not missed the receipt of that letter, wherein I assured you that I could not remember any such volume of Light-foot in Folio as you mention to ever have bin among the bookes in my custody, and therefore cannot place it to Dr: Thomass account; and I am sure I have it not my self; but I have given you my thoughts how it might be lost: since I came up I have discoursed with Mr: Thomas about this book who assures me he never saw any such single volume among the bookes in his Fathers Study; but onely all Lightfoots workes together:†2 so that whence this mistake should arise I know as little as you; I should have bin very glad to have seen you whilst I continue in Towne; as well to enjoy the happynesse of your conversation, as to have had your thoughts of those

1896. William Molyneux to Locke, 7 May 1695 (1887, 1921)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 112-14. Answers no. 1887; answered by no. 1921.
Dublin. May. 7. 1695.
Sir
I am extreamly pleased to understand by yours of Apr. 26. that we are to expect an Abridgement of your Work from a Judicious Hand in Oxford; tis what I always thought might be of good Use in the Universitys, where we yet want an other sort of Language, than what has hitherto prevaild there to the great Hindrance of Science.†1
As to the Translation that is going on here; tis undertaken by One Mr William Mullart a Senior Batchelor in the Colledge.†2 He has the repute of an Ingenious and Learned young Man; and I hope he
― 363 ―
may perform it wel. I here inclose a Specimen of his performance; concerning which I desire you would give me your Thoughts before he proceed much farther. This Only may be hinted, that when he is better acquainted with the Work, and your Language; and has enterd farther into it; tis probable His translation may be better, more easy, and Natural. He proposes to finish it in half a year or 9 months at farthest; for he cannot wholy disingage himself for†a some other Studys. I perceive your Bookseller is resolved to share with me in the Good I thought to do the World by bestowing on it this Translation. and since he is so generous as to have it so, I wil by no means be the Translators hindrance in Partaking of the Booksellers Profer, and at the same time, to ingage his Diligence the more, I will increase the Reward Considerably; that I may not wholy <m>isse†b of the Good Designe I first proposed to my self. If you Incourage the Translator to go forward, you may be pleased to transmit to me the Additions you designe; as that of Enthusiasme, Connexion of Ideas, and what else you have.
And now with redoubled force I send back to you the Complaints you make for our Distance. I cannot but Hope, that Providence has yet in store for me so much Happines on this side of the Grave. and if it have not, I shall Think I have Missed the Greatest Temporal Good my Mind was ever set on. But still I say, I live in Hopes, the Accomplishment whereof would be the Greatest Satisfaction to
Your Most cordially Affectionate Humble servant
W: MOLYNEUX
Were it not too nigh approaching to Vanity I could tell you of Extraordinary Effects your Method of Education has had on my little Boy.

1897. J. G. Grævius to Locke, 8/18 May 1695 (1809, 1920)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 42-3. Grævius refers to, but scarcely answers, no. 1809. Answered by no. 1920.
(English) Vir dignitate, doctrina, et virtute Nobilissime
Novissimis tuis dudum respondissem, nisi expectassem responsum nostri Toinardi, cui binas tuas illico misi.†1 Sed nihil etiamnunc responsi recepi. Num alia via id ad te curarit, an quae alia istius diuturni silentii causa sit, equidem ignoro. Nunc vero diutius teneri non potui, cum subita et necopina se offert occasio per tres adolescentes Germanos, qui vestram beatam insulam petunt, quin ad te mitterem hanc orationem, qua parentavi incomparabilis Reginae vestrae Manibus,†2 testem ac praedam perpetui mei in te studii et amoris. Nam quamvis inter nos sit magnum mare, nunquam tamen tui suavissima imago a meis abest oculis et animo; saepe de tua probitate, virtute et multiplici doctrina loquor, saepius cogito. Nullus congressus est aut hic cum Greveo, aut Amsterodami cum Limburgio et Clerico, quin illum tanquam legitimum et suavissimum acroama condiat tui memoria, et commemoratio tuarum virtutum. Utinam possem luculenta aliqua significatione quanti te aestimo testatum facere! cognosceres sane vix inter illos esse,
― 365 ―
quorum fides longo temporis usu tibi est spectatissima, qui me tui amore antecedat. Brevi videbis mei filii Callimachum,†1 et hoc anno, ut spero, Ciceronis orationes.†2 Vester Euripides†3 nondum ad nos est perlatus, si aere meo jusseris ad me perferri illum, gratus accipiam. Sin, rejiciam. Novi hic aliquid prodiise, quod sit tui palati, non memini. Inter hos armorum strepitus hic silent Musae,†4 quae apud vos videntur <ipsis>†a lituis et tubis excitari, cum tam canorae sint hac tempestate bellica. (English) Adjeci orationi specimen harmoniae Evangelicae, et animadversiones communis amici nostri Toinardi in Bohursii novam evangeliorum versionem.†6
(Latin) Sir, most illustrious for worth, learning and virtue,
I should have answered your last letter some time ago if I had not been awaiting an answer from our friend Toinard, to whom I immediately sent your two letters.†1 But I have still received no answer. I do not know whether he has sent it to you by another way, or what other cause there is for his prolonged silence. But now, when a sudden and unexpected opportunity presents itself by three young Germans who are travelling to your happy island, I could not be held back any longer from sending you, as a witness of and surety for my perpetual regard for and love of you, this speech which I have offered to the memory of your incomparable queen.†2 For however wide the sea may be between us, yet your delightful image is never absent from my eyes and mind; I often speak and more often think of your uprightness, virtue, and manifold learning. I never meet either de Greve here or van Limborch or Le Clerc in Amsterdam without memory of you and commemoration of your virtues sweetening our meeting as if with an appropriate and most delightful harmony. Would that by some clear sign I could prove how highly I esteem you! You would then learn that, among these whose fidelity[p. 365] is most known to you by long association, there is scarcely one who surpasses me in love of you. You will shortly see my son's Callimachus,†1 and this year, I hope, Cicero's speeches.†2 Your Euripides†3 has not yet been brought to us; if you will order it to be sent to me at my expense I shall gratefully receive it; otherwise I shall reject it. I do not recollect anything new that has been published here that would be to your taste. Amid this clash of arms the Muses are silent;†4 with you they seem to be aroused by the very clarions and trumpets, so tunefully do they sing in this storm of war. But I must not write any more now as our travellers are in a hurry. Goodbye, renowned Sir, you who are worth a host of others,†5 and love me — I who love you so much. Utrecht, 18 May, 1695. To your most excellent name
the most devoted in every kind of service
J. G. GRAEVIUS
(Latin) I have added to the speech a sheet of our common friend Toinard's Harmony of the Gospels and his remarks on Bouhours's new translation of the Gospels.†6

1898. Locke to Sir William Trumbull, 9 May 1695 (1754, 1927)
Berkshire Record Office, Shire Hall, Reading: Marquess of Downshire MSS. XXIX. 37. Printed in H.M.C., Downshire MSS, I. i. 467.
Oates 9º May. 95
Sir
Though I hope to kisse your hands speedily in town, yet the great Satisfaction I have will not bear that delay; nor suffer that I who am not the least concerned in your and our good fortune should be the slowest in makeing some expression of it.†1 Occasions of Joy like this, where my particular respect and freindship findes its account in the publique advantage, come soe seldom, that you will pardon me if I am a little transported: And I may the freer give vent to the pleasure I feell in my owne minde, in that a conversation I had the honour to have with you some months since will secure me from being suspected to put on a passion only to make you a fashionable complement. All that I can say or doe (if an uncommon esteem and a personal kindenesse have not the cheif hand in it) is of soe little moment to you, that for me to congratulate a Secretary of State would be very ridiculous upon any other account. But since every one is allowed to interest him self for his country and his friend, and to professe his joy when those receive any good, give me leave to interrupt you with these few words from mine; and to assure you that though I shall always be pleased with any advancement of fortune or honour your merit shall procure you, yet I shall not for that be more than before, because upon reason and obligation I already realy am
Sir
Your most humble and most obedient servant
JOHN LOCKE

(English)
Oates 10º May 95
Vir Amplissime
Quamprimum ego novissimas tuas 26 Aprilis datas acceperam statim Londinum scripsi et quantum in me est curavi ut libri quos
― 369 ―
ad opus suum desiderat Marcus ille noster sicubi reperiri possint ei suppeditantur. Eo diutiùs responsum distuli ut quid in hoc et altero illo negotio Tholosano factum sit certiorem te facerem. Sed nec DAranda nec alter cujus curæ Librorum perquisitionem commisi hactenus quicquam rescripserunt sed ex eorum silentio nolim ego male ominari.
(English) De autographo an Furlaii jam sit rectius ex ipso quam ex me cognosces. non quod ego negligens ea in re vel otiosus fuerim procurator. sed cum per valetudinem Londinum ea tempestate <adire>†a non auderem, totum negotium amico nostrûm communi†1 commisi viro prudenti et sedulo, cui scirem rem cordi fore, et ne mora circuitu literarum per manus meas transeuntium officeret, post primum quod ab amico Londinensi accepi responsum quo intellexi illum omnem navaturum operam ut rem transigeret, monui ut recte ad Furleium scriberet ut ex illo resciret quod scitu ad rem recte perficiendam adhuc opus esset. Hoc ab eo factum nullus dubito. si quid amplius a me præstari possit omnem operam curam industriam me in eo locaturum pro certo habeas
(English) Quod de Oxoniensibus nostris dicis, quanquam nihil fando audiverim, facile crediderim: quod Kiloniensem adversarium negligis
― 370 ―
laudo, quodque ab aliis inter se dissentientibus vapulas tanti magis æstimo, veritatis enim sinceris et incorruptis authoribus sic fieri solet. Pro Theologia tua Christiana jam denuò a me tibi reddendæ sunt gratiæ non quod bibliothecam volumine sed me scientiâ auxerit. Hac enim hyeme in quo consisteret fides Christiana diligenter apud me cogitando ex ipsis scripturæ†a- S.fontibus-†a hauriendam duxi, semotis quibuscunque sectarum et systematum <opinionibus>†b et orthodoxiis. Ex intentâ et accuratâ novi testamenti lectione fœderis novi status et evangelii doctrina mihi aparuit ut mihi videbatur meridiana luce clarior, nec quid esset fides Christiana dubitari posse sincero Evangelii lectori mihi persuasissimum est. Ideoque cogitata mea in chartam conjeci ut eo melius partium inter se convenientiam et harmoniam et fundamenta quibus inniterentur sedate et per otium contemplarer.†1 Cum omnia in hoc meo symbolo sana et verbo divino ubique conformia videbantur, Theologos consulendos duxi (reformatos videlicet) ut quid illi de fide senserint viderem. Calvinum†2 adii, Touritinum†3 aliosque quos ita id argumentum
― 371 ―
tractasse fateri cogor, ut quid dicant quid velint capere nequaquam possim, adeo dissona mihi in illis omnia videntur a sensu et simplicitate evangelica, ut illorum scripta <intelligere>†a nedum cum sacro codice reconciliare non valeam. Tandem spe meliore tuam in manus cæpi Theologiam, nec sine summo gaudio legi cap. VIII. l.v.†1 ex quo intellexi aliquem reperiri Theologum cui ego non plane essem hæreticus. Ut in libro tuo legendo ultrà pergerem non dum satis vacui temporis nactus sum. Nihil mihi optatius esse possit quam te videre et te coram quæ commentatus sum legere et explicare, ut limato et incorrupto tuo judicio subjicerentur. Hæc tibi in aurem dicta sunto, nam me hoc tractasse argumentum tibi soli communicatum volo.

Illum quæso fratremque ejus meo nomine officiosissime salutes, persuasumque reddas, illius in me voluntatem et benevolentiam acceptissimam esse semperque futuram meque dolere Idioma nostrum adeo perplexum, sensumque meum phrasibus nostris ita involutum ut sæpe eum capere, nisi in lingua nostra a teneris unguiculis versatissimo difficillimum sit. (Latin)
Oates 10 May 95
Excellent Sir,
As soon as I received your last letter of 26 April I immediately wrote to London and as far as I could saw to it that the books that our friend Marcus[p. 369] requires for his work should be supplied to him if they can be found anywhere. I put off an answer for some time in order to tell you what had been done in this and in that other Toulousan affair. But neither D'Aranda nor another man to whom I entrusted the search for the books has so far sent me any reply; but I would not augur ill from their silence.
(Latin) You will learn better from Furly himself than from me whether the autograph now belongs to him. Not that I would have been negligent in that matter, or an idle agent, but since I did not venture to go to London in that season on account of my health I entrusted the whole affair to a common friend of ours,†1 a prudent and earnest man whom I knew it would please, and, lest the roundabout course of letters passing through my hands should be a hindrance, after the first answer that I received from the London friend, by which I perceived that he was acting vigorously to settle the whole matter, I instructed him to write direct to Furly so as to learn from him what he still needed to know in order to finish the matter. I do not doubt that he has done so. If I can do anything further you may be sure that I shall put all my energy, care, and industry into it.
(Latin) Although I have heard no word of what you say about our Oxonians I would readily have believed it. I commend you for disregarding your Kiel[p. 370] adversary and esteem you so much the more for being flogged by others who differ among themselves, for that is usually what happens to sincere and incorrupt promoters of the truth. I must now thank you again for your Theologia Christiana, not because it has enriched [my] library with a volume but because it has enriched me with knowledge. For this winter, considering diligently wherein the Christian faith consists, I thought that it ought to be drawn from the very fountains of Holy Writ, the opinions and orthodoxies of sects and systems, whatever they may be, being set aside. From an intent and careful reading of the New Testament the conditions of the New Covenant and the teaching of the Gospel became clearer to me, as it seemed to me, than the noontide light, and I am fully convinced that a sincere reader of the Gospel cannot be in doubt as to what the Christian faith is. I therefore set down my thoughts on paper, thereby the better to survey, tranquilly and at leisure, the agreement of the parts with one another, their harmony, and the foundations on which they rested.†1 When everything in this creed of mine seemed everywhere sound and conformable to the word of God I thought that the theologians (that is, the Reformed) ought to be consulted, so that I might see what they thought about the faith. I went to Calvin,†2 Turrettini,†3 [p. 371] and others, who, I am compelled to admit, have treated that subject in such a way that I can by no means grasp what they say or what they mean; so discordant does everything in them seem to me with the sense and simplicity of the Gospel that I am unable to understand their writings, much less to reconcile them with Holy Writ. At last with better hopes I took in hand your Theologia and not without very great joy read book V, chapter VIII,†1 from which I perceived that one theologian was to be found for whom I am not a heretic. I have not yet obtained enough free time to go further with the reading of your book. Nothing could be more desirable for me than to see you and to read and to explain to you in person what I have composed, so that it might be subjected to your refined and incorruptible judgement. All this must be for your private ear, for I want my having treated this subject to be communicated to you alone.
(Latin) I have recently received a letter from Mr. Verrijn in which he declares that he still wishes to revise his translation of my book on the understanding and so to make it ready for publication.†2 You remember what I said about this formerly, to which must now be added that a very learned man of this country has taken on himself the charge of translating it into Latin with the greatest application and splendour, and this work was commenced some time ago. I shall insert in this Latin edition some new dissertations and additions which[p. 372] do not appear in the most recent English [edition] and some of which I have conceived in my mind but have not yet committed to writing.†1 I send this enclosed letter to him, to be delivered through you, because he has not indicated the place or house where he is. Please give him and his brother my kindest regards, and assure him that his goodwill and kindliness towards me are and will always be most acceptable to me, and I am sorry that our [English] idiom is so confused, and my meaning so enwrapped in our [English] phraseology, that it is often very difficult to grasp it unless one has been thoroughly conversant with our language from childhood. Give my regards to the rest of our friends — the Veens, the Guenellons, and above all your family. Goodbye and continue to love me, your most affectionate
J LOCKE
I send my greetings to our friend Le Clerc. I wrote to him last week.
Address: Myn Heer Myn Heer Limborch bÿ de Remonstransè Kerck op de Keisars Graaft t'Amsterdam

1906. William Popple to ——, 22 May 1695 (1704, 1986)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 213-18. Not in Popple's hand. This consists of observations on Stephen Nye, A Discourse concerning Natural and Revealed Religion, followed by the letter here printed. The book was not published until 1696 (L.L., no. 2107); the observations were made on a manuscript copy, as were Locke's observations on it (B.L., MS. Locke c. 27, ff. 92-3). It is unlikely that the letter was addressed to Locke.
May 22. 1695.
Sir
I have read over the papers you gave me, concerning natural and revealed Religion, with great pleasure; and thank you heartily for the favour you have done me in it. I am perswaded, you know me to be so much of the same opinion with the Author, on this Subject, that tho' you did desire me to remark any thing in them that I thought might deserve a second Consideration, yet you hardly expect to receive any thing from me of that kind. And the truth is, that, upon the first part, all that I have observed, consists in such litle particularities, as, whether alter'd or no, change nothing in the design and scope of the whole. However I here send you them, such as they are, in the same manner that they occur'd to me as I went along; that the Author may make what use of them he thinks fit. But as I read on, and was beginning to do the same thing also on the second part; I had not proceeded far, when I perceived that all my Observations on that Subject, might be reduced to one single point: And therefore after having taken notice of it once or twice I left off.
My thoughts on that are, that the end of Jesus Christ's Coming into the world, was not to impose any new arbitrary law upon Mankind; but only to revive, explain and enforce those general Laws of nature, which God had laid upon all men from the beginning. And from thence I conclude, that no Commandment of his can properly be called new (otherwise than in respect to the Judaical
― 378 ―
Law, and by no means) in respect to the Law of Nature: because the ground of all such Laws, and our Obligation to them, lye only in the nature of things, and in the relation in which we stand towards God and towards one another. And this Opinion, if I had not my self been of it before, I could not have fail'd to draw, from the many full Expressions that the Author uses, about the extent and sufficiency of the law of nature: Which, after the proofs that he had given thereof in the beginning, appear to me as establisht Axioms, to be refer'd to upon all occasions. This being so, my general Remark upon the Subject of the second part, is only, That it does not import us so much to enquire into the Authority of what we call the Christian Religion, as into the Sutableness of it to those ends that we are led to by the Law of nature. For wherein soever we can show its tendency and aptness to promote those ends, we therein infallibly demonstrate its divine authority. But whatsoever Authority can be produced for it, in any Instances that do not tend to promote those ends, seems to be of very little significancy.
I know not whether the Author of these papers do fully agree with me in this opinion or no: But I think his words in many places, seem to authorise such an Inference. Particularly (vol. 6. p. 5.) he says that God wil never impose any services upon us, that are insignificant and frivolous: because that is contrary to his wisdom. Now by this I suppose he does not only exclude those services which have no typical signification: but also (or rather) those that have in them no advantage or usefulness. And by Usefulness I think no Body can understand anything but usefulness to mankind. The Test therefore of any pretended new precept, appears to me to be this: Do's it tend to the promoting in men's minds a greater reverence to God, and greater Good-will to our Neighbours? Those I think are the only fountains of Piety and Virtue. And Piety and Virtue, I am sure, are the only fountains of our true happiness.
Now these being with me very fundamental principles, I confess that whensoever I should go about to write any thing upon the general Subject of religion, it would always be with this view; That when I had laid the foundations of natural religion, whatsoever I added upon revealed religion, should appear, not as a separate Edifice, but as a Super-structure upon the same Ground-work. Many things indeed in the Law of Moses were otherwise. But it is from those very things, that the christian doctrin sets men free.
― 379 ―
And therefore I cannot suppose that it teaches, or authoritatively enjoyns any thing (how smal soever) that is meerly arbitrary.
But it is probable I carry this reflection further, and keep to it more strictly than this Author thinks needful. If so, I do not argue, but submit my thoughts to his better Judgment. Only I wil add, that if perhaps it be otherwise, and that he do agree with me in the ful sense of what I have endevoured here to express, then I am perswaded that (if in reading over again his own papers, he carry this thought along with him) he wil not fail to think, that many things in the second part might be contracted, and that some require to be a little alter'd. But this I say depends wholly upon our agreement in what I make my fixed principle. Without that, any further Remarks of mine would be very frivolous: and indeed not much better with it. For I am sure, that in that case, the Author would see more clearly, what I aim at, than I do my self. I therefore humbly beg his pardon for this presumption, in which you that put me upon it are also obliged to intercede for me. And I beseech God to enable him to go on daily with greater and greater vigour in edifying the Age we live in, with his useful Meditations. I am
Sir,
your most humble servant
W P
Endorsed by Locke: Mr Popples observations 95†a

1912. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 31 May/10 June 1695 (1880, 1916)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 95-6. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 83-5.
A Amsterdam le 10 de Juin 1695.
Lors que j'apprens, Monsieur, que les intemperies de l'air des païs septentrionaux, dans lesquels nous vivons, diminuent vôtre santé, je voudrois pouvoir changer le cours du soleil, et vous faire vivre dans une éternelle sérenité. Ces longs hivers, et ces Etez, qui ne valent pas les printemps des païs méridionaux, m'affligent sensiblement, quand je pense qu'ils peuvent abreger une vie, qui mérite si fort d'être conservée. Si le bon sens et le peu de liberté, qui reste dans le monde, n'étoient pas comme confinez dans ce septentrion, je serois d'avis d'aller habiter quelque meilleur climat, et d'abandonner aux rûmes et aux fluxions les païs, dans lesquels les hommes en sont si fort tirannisez. Mais puis que l'état, dans lequel se trouve le genre humain, nous a condamnez à vivre dans des païs si froids, il faut tâcher de s'y conserver de son mieux, en suppléant par l'exercice et par la diete à ce qui manque à la nature. Une personne aussi habile que vous, dans la Médecine, n'a pas besoin d'avis là dessus. Pour moi, je me porte assez bien, par la grace de Dieu, quoi que j'aie excessivement travaillé, depuis quelques années en ça. Mais j'ai un petit garçon âgé d'environ seize mois, qui n'a pas la vigueur que je voudrois qu'il eût, et qui donne beaucoup de peine à sa Mere. Quoi qu'il ait cet âge, il ne se soutient nullement; il n'a point encore aucun os tortu, mais il a le poignet un peu gros. Du reste il ne se porte pas mal, excepté qu'il dort assez peu, et qu'il sue beaucoup. Il a eu le malheur d'avoir eu une mauvaise nourrisse, qu'il n'a tettée
― 386 ―
que huit mois, et qui se trouva malade sur la fin qu'elle l'eut. Cela a fait qu'il n'a jamais été fort gras, et qu'il a encore la chair un peu molle. On l'a nourri de bouillie, jusqu'à présent, qu'on commence de lui donner de tout, parce qu'il a des dens, dont il se sert assez bien, quoi qu'il n'en ait que six, et que ce soit celles du devant de la bouche. Comme c'est une maladie commune en Angleterre,†1 aussi bien qu'ici, si vous aviez fait là dessus quelque remarque, vous m'obligeriez infiniment de me la communiquer, soit qu'elle regardât les remedes que l'on pourroit faire, soit que ce fût pour la maniere de nourrir les enfans, qui ont cette incommodité. Je vous suis bien obligé de l'offre, que vous me faites de m'envoier le livre de Mr. L'Evêque d'Ely.†2 et je l'accepterois, si Mr. Teute†3 ne me l'avoit pas acheté. Il est encore avec son fils à Bow près de Londres, mais je croi qu'il reviendra bien tôt en Hollande, quand il aura mis en train sa Teinturerie d'écarlate.†4 C'est un très-habile homme, en matiere d'inventions méchaniques, et qui a gagné bien de l'argent par là; outre que c'est un très-honête homme, pour les mœurs, et qui a plus de connoissance de la Religion que l'on n'en a parmi les Marchands. M'étant adressé à Mrs. Huguetan, pour me plaindre que leur Commis à Londres n'avoit point envoié la vie de Richelieu à l'adresse que je leur avois donnée, ils m'ont donné le billet que vous trouverez ci-joint. Il n'y a qu'à le donner au Sieur Delgas,†5 qui est leur Commis. Je ne doute pas que Mr. Churchill ne le connoisse, ou s'il ne le connoit pas, il n'y a qu'à s'en informer de quelque Libraire François, qui lui enseignera où il demeure. En lui donnant le billet, il livrera la vie de Richelieu. Je suis bien aise que vôtre ouvrage s'imprime en Latin,†6 dans un lieu où vous êtes, parce que la version en sera incomparablement meilleure, que tout ce qui se pourroit faire ailleurs. J'en ai parlé à Mr. Verreyn, et il m'a paru ne le recevoir pas mal. Je croi que vôtre lettre l'aura entierement satisfait. Il m'a dit qu'il ne souhaitoit autre chose, que de savoir, si vôtre ouvrage se traduisoit effectivement à
― 387 ―
Londres, et il ne m'a pas paru fâché, lors que je lui ai dit qu'ouï. Il ne se fait rien ici à présent, qui vaille la peine. On†a- va rimprimer les grands Critiques de Londres,†1 où l'on joindra de nouvelles annotations de Drusius,†2 mais qui sont peu de chose, quoi qu'assez étenduës. Ce bon homme n'étoit qu'un rapsode, et destitué de tout ce qu'on appelle génie. Il est rare de voir d'autres gens, en ce païs.-†a Je suis, Monsieur, de tout mon coeur entierement à vous
J LE CLERC
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings over against the plough in litle Lincolns Inne fields London.

Worthy Sir
I had once the honour and happiness of Waiting On You in your Chamber about a Yeare since by the Directions of Mr: Awnsham Churchill who not long since being at Dorchester informed me of your health, and now hopeing You will pardon my Confidence in troubling You herewith, I shall presume to acquainte You that on the 31st Marth last Dyed my Honoured Master†3 to my Great Griefe and unspeakable loss, for he was snatcht away suddenly in the Church as he was kneeling downe at the Confession, It was judged to be in An Apoplecktick fitt; so irresistable is Death, from whose so sudden approach, Good Lord Deliver us: It is not my loss only, but a Generall loss to the whole County, being a Gentleman of Great Learning and Integrity and a Lover of this Present Government: (Sic transit Gloria Mundi.) I am with my Masters Sisters who are his heires, and shall remaine here till about the next Spring
― 388 ―
Or till matters are settled; I have but few or Noe friends now Left, therefore begg of you to be my friend to Direct me what Method I shall take for a future settlement. I have heard so much of your Worth and Goodness, that I have reason to beleive You will take me into your serious Consideration and favour, Not on the account of myne Owne Deservings, but as I am fatherless and friendless, and of your Name, but whether of your bloud, I Leave your selfe to judge; I shall not further trouble You at present, but (still begging your pardon for this Presumption and Your Answer hereto) take Leave to subscribe my selfe
Sir
your most humble and Disconsolate servant

1914. Henry Hatrell to Locke, 3 June 1695 (1866)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 148-9.
Deare Sir
I take it for a great favour that you have given a kind answer to my Letter, I shall say no more of the Subject of that till tyme affords me the happiness of seeing you, An unexpected occasion hath deferr'd if not disappointed my expectation of that this terme.†2 By the help of your Booke†3 I perceive that I have reason to suspect severall Doctrines that I had taken upon trust, and finding that reall knowledge consists in perceiving the agreement or disagreement of our Ideas, I have begun that way to examine the truth of some of my Tenets, and beg leave to lay these rude thoughts before you that you may shew me my Mistakes if I have made any. I am just in the condition of a Beggar, I can only thankfully receive and
― 389 ―
pray the Father of Lights to enlarge your Discoveries, and lead you into all truth for the benefitt of yourself and others, For my part I must think that Communications of this kind are Charity in as high a degree as any, since it serves the best ends and that they cannot want inward pleasure and satisfaction nor miss of the divine acceptance and Reward. Put my debt upon the account of the great Master of the family of Heaven and Earth and hee'l pay and I shall be
Sir
Your much obliged Servant
H. HATRELL
Newcastle in Staffordshire 3d June 1695
An Enquiry touching originall Sin
Adam transgressing the Law by eating of the forbidden fruit made him self lyable to the punishment of that Law, Death. First I enquire what is meant by Death here, And since tis plaine in the new Testament that the punishment of wicked men there is called death, as well as in the old and that there is a Resurrection of the body and an Immortality of the Soul and body too after the resurrection, it seems probable that by Death is to be understood the Sufferings of Soul and Body, for I cannot think how the body should suffer and the Soul be free, that a part should be miserable and a part not, and as to the duration of this punishment as it is not defined by tyme in the first threatning but left indefinite, its thence probable it is not to be measured by it, but last for ever, or untill the debt he paid, and the new testament calls it everlasting fire: Hence I conclude that by death is meant paine and corporall death here and everlasting punishment of body and soul hereafter.
Next I enquire how far the posterity of Adam are involved in the same Guilt and punishment. Notwithstanding Mans Revolt from God I doe not see any Reason to think but that his Body was the same before and after the Fall, only subject to paine and death, nor can I tell what change befell his Soul, except probably a greater irregularity in his affections it being the naturall consequence of any action the oftener its done to make the person more ready to doe it againe but this if so is no change of the Nature or Substance of the Soul, but only a morall change of the affections of it, only an alteration of the object of its desires.
God having given Man a power to propagate his kind, Its no
― 390 ―
more absurd to me to say a Man begets a man, than that any other Animall begets another Animall of the same sort, the will of the Almighty making causes sufficient to produce effects beyond our Comprehension, And God being able out of Stones (less likely materialls) to raise Children to Abraham, Nor doth it seeme at all to derogate from the Immortality of the Soul that it should have its Originall by Generation. Adam is said to beget a son in his owne likeness after his Image and called his name Seth, and what is said of Seth may for any thing I know be said of any of the Sons of Adam, and its likely the Son partakes of the Fathers Body and Soul and I beleive Children now have the same body as Adam before the fall bating their Infancy and their lyableness to paine and death, and the Same Soul, only empty and not replenished with knowledge, I meane of the same sort and made out of the other in an unknowne way. 'Tis said in Rom: 5. That by one Mans disobedience many were made Sinners, and its there proved from the punishment because Death reigned from Adam till Moses, and that by the Offence of one Judgment came upon all men to Condemnation, here is no distinction made in the Sinners nor in the punishment therefore its probable there is no difference and that the Sin is reckoned the same in his posterity and the punishment accordingly the same, it being impossible to bring a cleane thing out of an uncleane, This supposition which carryes no absurdity that I know of seems most to cleare the Justice of God in imputing the fathers fault to the Son and to shew the Necessity the World stood in of a Redeemer to put Mankind into a Capacity of Salvation by not imputing this sin, and setting them upon a new Bottom and dealing with them according to their owne actuall wilfull sins and not according to originall transgression.
Next I enquire whether that common Phrase of having our souls and bodies our Natures and Faculties depraved by originall sin, and the bringing the habits and seeds of sin into the World be true or not, And herein the disproved Doctrine of Innate notions†1 gives me light, If the Soul have no Ideas connate but receives all from Sensation and Reflection, and if a Law cannot bind till knowne, and if Sin be a transgression of a knowne Law either in thought word or deed, and if Children before growne up to some maturity cannot understand the Law, I infer that all the thoughts and actions of
― 391 ―
Children whilst uncapable of knowing the Law are not sins. In the next place I think its plaine that Enjoyment of pleasure not referred to some Law is not sinfull in it self and I cannot think the Almighty hath made any Animall without desires to enjoy good or pleasure, and the contrary supposition would make odd work in the creation but to wave that, How should the naturall desire of pursuit and experience of pleasure be evill otherwise than as its done in instances or circumstances prohibited by some Law if Eating and drinking and the Embraces of the Bride and Groome be lawfull pleasures which I think no body questions. The Excess indeed may be reckoned a fault but that rather proves than overthroues the supposition. And I know no pleasure in the world but it may be lawfall or unlawfull in respect of the circumstances its accompanied with which shews its not evill in it self but in respect to a Law, that doth not so much forbid as regulate and limit the measures of it. But say Divines Originall Sin in the new Testament is called Flesh and Concupiscence etc. Can that be any thing els but the Inclination to pleasure that grows too strong and too unruly to be governed by the Law of God and that is not content to gratify it self in allowed ways but breakes all Rules and Bounds so that its not the thing but the manner that makes the fault, As for instance, A child loves apples. Who can say loving or eating apples with pleasure is Originall Sin or any sin, But when the Child understands that the Apples have an Owner, that the Owner will not part with them, That its Injustice to take any thing from the Owner without his consent, Then if the Child take and eat he transgresseth the Law, and the cause of his transgression is the unruliness of his Appetite, and this is sin, but I think not originall sin brought into the world with us, and if acts goe before habits, Habits cannot be brought into the world with us, acts taking their begining long after we come into the world, And how the body can be said to come defiled by sin into the world is altogether unintelligible to me and I think absurd in it self unless a Nature or Substance void of Reason can be said to be under the Government of Law which I cannot apprehend. And as to seeds of sin it may take its answer from what is said already, Metaphoricall expressions are fit to cover falshood but give me naked truth and she shall ever be welcome.
Address: For Mr John Locke
Endorsed by Locke: H. Hatrell 3º Jun. 95

1915. John Wynne to Locke, 25 June 1695 (1884, 2166)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 119-20.
Honoured Sir
I should have long before this returned you my just acknowledgments for your last obligeing letter, If some urgent occasions had not taken up my thoughts ever since. You have given me therein fresh reason to admire your great candour and Civilitie, to which alone I must impute those favourable expressions of esteem you bestow upon me, and those kind tenders of your Service you are pleas'd to make me, who am not conscious of any thing that can in the least entitle me to it, but that I profess the greatest honour and respect for you. Mr Churchill did me the favour to See me, when he was here last week, To whose care (since you were pleas'd to remit it to me) I have committed the printing of the Abridgment. He gave me to understand that he intended speedily another impression of your Essay, which he desir'd might come abroad before the Abridgment. I thought it reasonable to leave the timing of it to Him, that he might order it so as not to hinder the sale of the Essay. I have struck out that part of my Epistle, which left the disposal of it to you: And I think my self highly honoured and obliged that you are pleased to permit me to be so instrumental in the publishing of what, I hope will prove neither unacceptable nor unserviceable to the world; Tho' I could have wish'd It had fallen into A more skilful hand, that would have done less injury to the work, and more justice to the Author. I do with all thankfulnes accept of the frank offers of your Service, and may possibly hereafter take the freedom to let you know, how you may farther oblige me, who am with all respect and observance
Honoured Sir
Your most humble and oblig'd Servant
JO: WYNNE

1916. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 28 June/8 July 1695 (1912, 1933)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 97-8. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 85-7. No. 1917 was enclosed in it.
A Amsterdam le 8 de Juillet 1695
Le même jour, Monsieur, que je reçus vôtre Lettre, savoir le 5 de ce mois, je fus chez Mrs. Huguetan me plaindre de la négligence de leur Commis de Londres, qui depuis tant de mois a négligé les ordres qu'on lui a donnez trois ou quatre fois. Ils m'assurerent qu'ils lui en écriroient ce jour là même, et me dirent qu'il y avoit déja quelque temps qu'ils lui avoient envoié de nouveau des Vies de Richelieu. Je les priai donc de lui envoier un ordre précis, d'en remettre un exemplaire à Churchill pour vous, et je me persuades qu'il l'executera, parce que je me plaignis fortement de l'affront qu'ils me faisoient. Il n'est rien de plus assuré que ce qu'a dit Pline Officina nil habet ingenui.†1 Ces sortes de gens ne content pour rien les fautes, qui ne leur causent aucune perte pécuniaire; et ne s'acquittent d'aucun devoir, que dans la vuë du gain. Les gens dont il est question m'ont de l'obligation, et cependant ils en usent mal avec moi, comme avec tous les autres. J'espere néanmoins qu'ils auront tenu cette fois leur parole, et que vous n'aurez qu'à faire demander à Churchill cet exemplaire. Je suis fâché que cela ait si fort tardé, et que le livre que je vous envoiois ait perdu la grace de la nouveauté, mais une autre fois je prendrai mieux mes mesures. Je vous suis bien obligé des bons avis que vous m'avez donnez pour nôtre petit-garçon, et je prendrai la liberté de vous avertir du succès du remede. Je vous ai encore beaucoup d'obligation pour le livre de l'Evêque d'Ely, et pour le vôtre.†2 J'en ai lu une grande partie, et ma femme l'a lû tout entier avec beaucoup de plaisir, et nous n'y trouvons rien, qui ne nous plaise infiniment. Je n'aurois pas manqué de vous écrire qu'il étoit traduit en François, et par qui, si j'avois pensé que vous souhaiteriez de le savoir, puis que cet par un Etudiant en Theologie, ou, comme on dit ici, un Proposant, qui est
― 394 ―
extrémement de mes amis.†1 C'est un coup d'essai qu'il a fait, en matiere de traduction Angloise, plûtôt pour apprendre la Langue, que pour se faire connoître par là. Le livre se vend fort bien, et si l'on en fait une seconde édition, il sera bon qu'il y ajoute ce qui est dans la seconde édition Angloise. Lui aiant fait part de ce que vous me demandiez sur son sujet il m'a donné le billet qui est renfermé dans celui-ci, et si vous lui voulez répondre, il n'y aura qu'à renfermer vôtre réponse dans la premiere lettre, que vous me ferez l'honneur de m'écrire.
J'avois écrit ce que vous venez de lire lors que j'ai reçu les livres que vous m'avez fait la grace de m'envoier. Je vous en suis encore un coup très-obligé. J'espere de vous envoier bien tôt ma Physique,†2 qui s'imprime, et dont la moitié est déja faite, avec mon Comment. sur les 4 derniers livres de Moïse. J'envoierai demain sans manquer à Mr. Furly les deux livres, qui sont pour lui. C'est Grotius lui-même qui a commenté les livres de la Verité de la Rel.Chretienne.†3 J'ai dessein de faire un livre de l'Incredulité, ou je la prouverai d'une autre maniere, et où je leverai bien des doutes.†4 D'abord que mon Commentaire sera achevé, c'est à dire, en trois ou quatre semaines j'y travaillerai, et comme l'analyse en est faite, j'en viendrai bien tôt à bout. Je ne saurois trop vous remercier du soin que vous avez de mes interêts. Un certain du Veil†5 Juif converti, et Mr. Allix Chanoine de Salisbury y sont extrémement contraires, je ne sai pourquoi. Je n'ai jamais connu le premier, et le second devroit être mon ami. Mais l'envie est un monstre qui viole les devoirs les plus sacrez, et je croi qu'en cette occasion elle a étouffé dans le coeur de cet honête homme les sentimens qui y devroient être. Je suis absolument à vous, et je prie Dieu qu'il vous conserve pour le Public, et pour vos Amis
J LE CLERC.
Quand j'aurai lû les livres, je vous en dirai ce que j'en pense.

1917. Pierre Coste to Locke, 28 June/8 July 1695 (1940)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, f. 140. Printed by G. Bonno in Revue de littérature comparée, xxxiii (1959), 163. Enclosed in no. 1916.
Pierre Coste was born at Uzès near Nîmes in October 1668, the son of a cloth-merchant. He was educated for the ministry, first at the college at Anduze and then at the Académie of Geneva, where he was enrolled on 5 May 1684. He is said to have studied at the universities of Lausanne and Zürich; he was enrolled as a student at Leyden on 9 July 1688. In 1690 the Walloon Synod in Amsterdam accepted him as a proposant but he embarked almost at once on a literary career. He probably obtained work as a corrector of proofs for a bookseller. His first publication of note was his Histoire of the Grand Condé, published in 1693 nominally at Cologne. Then followed translations of Locke's Some Thoughts concerning Education (1695) and The Reasonableness of Christianity (1696). Thanks to Le Clerc's friendship he then came to England to be tutor to Francis Cudworth Masham and to translate Locke's Essay under his supervision (it was published in 1700). After Locke's death he entered Edward Clarke's household as tutor. After five unhappy years at Chipley he served as tutor probably to John West, later seventh Baron and first Earl de la Warr; then to Sir John Hobart, later first earl of Buckinghamshire; and then to Edmund Sheffield, later second duke of Buckinghamshire, to whom he dedicated the second edition (1729) of his translation of Locke's Essay. He travelled on the Continent with all three. He continued to work as a translator, publishing versions of Lady Masham's Discourse of Divine Love (1705) and Newton's Opticks (1720). He assisted the third earl of Shaftesbury in the original version—in French (1712)—of 'The Judgement of Hercules'. He also published editions of La Bruyère's Caractères (Amsterdam, 1720), Montaigne's Essais (London, 1724), and La Fontaine's Fables (Paris, 1743); the Montaigne is an especially fine achievement and ran through at least eight editions by 1801. There were also smaller translations or editions. He was elected F.R.S. in 1742. He married, probably rather late in life, Marie de Laussac, who died at Paris in 1736. He died there on 24 January 1747.
Authorities: D.N.B.; D.B.F.; Haag; letters from or to him in Esther Masham, Letter-book; Leibniz, Phil. Schriften, ed. Gerhardt, iii. 382-436; Rand, Shaftesbury (this contains incidental notices as well as letters). See also Ascoli, ii. 330; C. Dédéyan, Montaigne chez ses amis anglo-saxons, [1947], i. 20-3, ii. 3-13; etc.
Monsieur,
J'ai appris de Monsieur LeClerc que vous aviez reçû la Traduction que j'ai faite de vôtre Traité de l'Education des Enfans.†1 J'ai travaillé à cet ouvrage avec beaucoup de plaisir, et si j'en ai parlé avantageusement dans la Préface, ce n'a pas été pour prévenir
― 396 ―
l'esprit de ceux qui le liroient, mais plûtôt pour pouvoir dire ce que j'en pensois, persuadé que ceux qui auroient la curiosité de le voir, en feroient le même jugement que moy. La veritable marque qu'un Ouvrage est excellent, c'est qu'il plait géneralement à tous ceux qui peuvent l'entendre; et c'est justement ce qui est arrivé à l'égard de vôtre Traité. Il a plû en Anglois, il plait aussi en François. Il y avoit une chose à craindre, c'est qu'en le traduisant je luy fisse perdre la meilleure partie de ses agrémens, et que par ce moyen il devint entierement méconnoissable. Je n'ai rien épargné pour éviter ce malheur. J'ai consulté, ou, pour mieux dire, importuné Monsieur LeClerc pour les moindres difficultez qui se présentoient à mon esprit. Cependant la juste défiance où j'étois, que malgré tous ces soins, ma traduction ne fût très-imparfaite, m'a empêché de vous l'envoyer. Je sçavois que plus un Livre est exact et bien écrit, plus il est difficile de le bien traduire, et que rien n'est plus désagreable à un Auteur que de voir son Ouvrage entierement défiguré par une mauvaise traduction. Mais enfin puis que la Traduction de vôtre Traité est venuë entre vos mains, j'ai pris la liberté de vous écrire pour vous prier de me faire part de ce que vous y trouvez à redire. Je ne doute pas qu'il y aît bien des defauts, puis que j'y en vois moymême par rapport au Langage. Je ne sçai si vous approuverez toutes les libertés que j'ai prises. J'y ai été, ce me semble, très-réservé, et comme contraint pour me conformer au genie de nôtre Langue. Mais il est aisé de se tromper soy-même dans ces rencontres, en attribuant à la Langue ce qu'il faudroit attribuer à la petitesse de son genie. Quoy qu'il en soit, je recevrai avec plaisir toutes vos corrections pour rendre ma Traduction moins imparfaite dans une seconde Edition. Comme vous venez d'augmenter vôtre Ouvrage, le Libraire de Hollande sera bien aise d'en donner une nouvelle Edition le plus tôt qu'il pourra.†1 Je suis avec un profond respect,
Monsieur,
Vôtre très-humble, et très-obeïssant serviteur,
COSTE
à Amsterdam ce 8me. Juillet 1695.
Endorsed by Locke: Coste 8 Jul. 95 Answered 16

1918. Paul D'Aranda to Locke, 29 June 1695 (1306, 1925)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 30-1.
Oxford the 29th: June 1695.
Sir
Receiving from Holland some of the flesh most esteem'd there, I left at your lodgings for you a bundle with two Westphalia Hams and a piece of smoak'd beef, which I beg your acceptance of, hoping their taste may please. being just on my departure for the bath, saw no likelyhood of having the happynesse of your good company to eat part of them in London, nor knew how to send them to Oates, and was therefore forced to leave that trouble to Mr Pauling. My wife, who pays you her humble service, says it's needfull that they who dresse the beef be told, it must before boyling be soak'd 2 or 3 hours in water, and be put over the fire in cold water, and is to boil three hours rather a little more than lesse; you'l doubtlesse remember that the Dutch eat it cold, cut as thin as paper, on bread and butter or among sallad. pardon my rudenesse in troubling you with so many words about a present you it's Like account unwholsome. Three days before I came from London I was fill'd with pain which made me very weak. I am now freed of the former, and, if I can keep so, hope to recover some of the Lost strength: I design to be next week at the Bath and shall there observe those directions you charitably gave
Sir
Your most faithfull and most humble servant
PAUL D'ARANDA
