1919. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 29 June/9 July 1695 (1901, 2110)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 99-100. Answers no. 1901.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Jam ad me perscripsit Marcus Teuto, se libros quibus indigebat tuâ opera accepisse; itaque strenue in versione sua pergit. Maximas tibi habeo gratias. Ego ipsi indicem misi, qui omnia loca ab ipso inspicienda continet. Puto jam ipsum fœliciter omnibus quos opus habet libris usum, et versionem ferme ad finem perductam. Quæ de Oxoniensium contra Theologiam meam molitionibus scripsi, narrata mihi sunt ab amico quodam, qui se ea ex ore Episcopi mihi amici habere affirmavit: Credebat etiam illius Episcopi directione conatus illos fuisse sufflaminatos, quanquam ipse hoc plane dissimularet Episcopus, remque totam ita narraret, quasi aliorum operâ id effectum esset.†1 Video ego affectus humanos ubique dominari, et, quod pejus est, gloriæ divinæ zelum illis prætexi. Exstant multa systemata Theologiæ, quibus variantes de non paucis religionis Christianæ dogmatibus, continentur sententiæ: interim si accuratius singula ad verbi divini normam examinentur, dissensum illum minime circa capitalia versari comperiemus, sed circa ejusmodi,
― 399 ―
quibus aut non recte intellectis, aut in dubium vocatis, nihilominus salva manet fides Christiana, quam nobis ut vitam æternam obtineamus præscribit Euangelium. Laudo ego institutum tuum, quod semotis omnibus systematibus, ex sacro codice, qui unica ac perfecta fidei nostræ regula est, quid fides Christiana sit, et in quo consistat, inquisiveris. Qui Euangelium sine præjudicio legit, non diu dubius aut incertus hærebit: clare enim ibi expressa exstant, quæ a nobis credi Deus vult, ut salutem consequamur. Quæ alii de fide Christiana scripserint, legi: Verum quid sibi velint, capere nequeo. Quædam adeo sunt intricata et perplexa, ut Oedipo ad ea intelligenda opus sit; quædam adeo dissona, ut cum aliis manifeste pugnent. Ego simplicem stylum amo, qui ab euangelica phrasi non abit, neque alia credenda urget, præter ea quæ a nobis credi mandat Dominus noster, quæ et ab ipsa plebe intelligi et credi possunt. Si quid in mea Theologia reperisti, quod cum cogitatis tuis conveniat, est quod mihi gratuler: Si et in quibusdam dissentiamus considerationes tuas libens audiam. Idem, quod tu desideras, mihi maxime in votis est, te videre, et coram tecum de ejusmodi conferre, ut per amicam disquisitionem veritas nobis tanto apertior sit. Interim quæ hac de re ad me scripsisti nulli indicanda certus esto. Gaudeo eruditissimi tui tractatus versionem in linguam Latinam jam
― 400 ―
aliquamdiu esse inchoatam. Eam cum additamentis tuis videre gestio. Ex compendio Gallico, quod D.Clericus antehac in bibliotheca universali nobis exhibuit, lectionem illius maximo cum fructu a me instituendam certus sum. Verrinus non ægre fert, sibi periisse laborem suum, sed nobiscum gaudet, fœliciorem et accuratiorem versionem, te approbante adornari. Brantius noster,†1 quod summo cum dolore scribo, in gravissimam incidit melancholiam. Ante annos sexdecim eodem cum morbo graviter conflictatus est: Verum postea, uti vidisti, mente admodum secura vixit. Nunc miserrime affligitur, et se ipsum cogitationibus, quæ omne solamen respuunt, indesinenter torquet. Ego ejus sine maximo meo dolore meminisse nequeo. Quia morbus est hæreditarius, avus enim Barlæus†2 eum aliquoties expertus est, ego male ipsi metuo. Nosti ipse, quam pertinax ille sit morbus, quam ægre medicamentis cedat, quam nullis auscultet rationibus, etiamsi evidentissimis. Deum precor ut omnem sanguinis intemperiem, unde inordinatos in cerebrum spirituum animalium motus oriri credo, dispellat, ut eadem quæ antehac animi tranquillitate ac hilaritate munere suo fungi possit. Reliqui nostri amici optime valent, Tibique plurimam a me scribi salutem
― 401 ―

jubent. Salutat te uxor mea ac liberi. Salutem a me officiosissimam dices Dominæ Masham
Tui Amantissimus
P. A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 9 Julii

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
Marcus Teut has now written to me that he has received by your help the books that he required; so he is proceeding vigorously with his translation. I am most grateful to you. I have sent him a table containing all the passages that he must look into. I think that by now he has put to good use all the books that he needs and that the translation has been brought nearly to an end. What I wrote about the Oxonians' efforts against my Theologia was told me by a certain friend who declared that he had it from the mouth of a bishop, a friend of mine; he believed also that those attempts had been checked by that bishop's direction, although the bishop himself concealed that entirely and told the whole story as if it had been effected by others' exertions.†1 I see that human passions prevail everywhere and, what is worse, that zeal for God's glory is used to cloak them. There exist many systems of theology containing differing opinions about not a few dogmas of the Christian religion; nevertheless, if the single dogmas are more carefully examined by the standard of God's word, we shall find that that disagreement is concerned very little with pre-eminent matters, but is concerned rather with matters of such a kind as, whether they are not rightly understood or are called in[p. 399] question, none the less the Christian faith, which the Gospel enjoins on us in order that we may obtain eternal life, remains unimpaired. I commend your design of setting aside all systems and seeking from Holy Writ, which is the one and perfect rule for our faith, what the Christian faith is and in what it consists. He who reads the Gospel without prejudice will not remain doubtful or uncertain for long; for there is to be found, clearly expressed, what God wishes us to believe in order to win salvation. I have read what others have written about the Christian faith; but I am unable to grasp what they mean. Some of their statements are so intricate and confused that it would need an Oedipus to understand them; some so discordant that they plainly clash with others. I myself love a simple style that does not depart from the language of the Gospel and does not urge things to be believed other than those which our Lord commands us to believe and which can be understood and believed even by the common people. If you have found anything in my Theologia that agrees with your thoughts that is something on which I may congratulate myself; and if we disagree in some things I shall gladly hear your considerations. My greatest wish is the same as yours, to see you and to discuss such matters with you in person, so that by friendly inquiry the truth may be so much the clearer for us. Meanwhile you may be sure that what you have written to me about this will be disclosed to nobody. I am glad that the Latin translation of your most scholarly treatise was started[p. 400] some time ago. I long to see it with your additions. To judge from the French abridgement which Mr. Le Clerc presented to us formerly in the Bibliotheque universelle I am sure that it will be with very great profit that I shall undertake the reading of it. Verrijn does not take it ill that his labour has been wasted, but is glad like us that a more felicitous and more accurate translation is in preparation with your approval. Our friend Brandt,†1 I am very sorry to say, has fallen into the most grievous melancholia. Sixteen years ago he was grievously afflicted by the same malady; but later, as you saw, he lived with an altogether untroubled mind. He is now most wretchedly afflicted and torments himself incessantly with thoughts that reject all solace. I cannot think of him without very great grief. As the malady is hereditary, for his grandfather Barlæus†2 experienced it several times, I greatly fear for him. You yourself know how obstinate that malady is, with what difficulty it yields to remedies, and how it will listen to no reasons, although the plainest. I pray that God may dispel all the distemper of the blood, whence, I believe, disordered motions of the animal spirits rise to the brain, so that he may perform his office with the same tranquillity of mind and cheerfulness as heretofore. The rest of our friends are very well and bid me send you their best respects.[p. 401] My wife and children send you their greetings. Please give my best respects to Lady Masham.
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 9 July 1695

(Latin)
Oates 1 July 1695
Excellent and learned Sir,
Your most kind letter(s) and your frequent remembrance of me are by themselves sufficient evidence of the great goodwill with which you pursue me, and yet you do not think this is sufficient, but by adding gifts over and above you overwhelm me with your acts of kindness, seeing that, as you know, nothing can be more welcome to and valued by me than what springs at[p. 402] the same time from your heart and from your genius. I regret that I was not in London to show your Germans how much I value you. My London landlord sent to me here in the country by the post, as it is called, the letter that they brought, but kept back the parcel of your gifts for a more convenient opportunity, so that I am compelled still to wait some days for your funeral speech, which I eagerly long for. I promise myself in it a living image of our greatly lamented queen, and one worthy of so great an original. Certainly she will live and breathe in it, your monument more enduring than brass,†1 but the more we shall admire your colours in painting to the life, so much the more shall we regret that such a pattern, glory, and support of all virtues and such an ornament of our age should have been untimely torn from us by so cruel a fate.
(Latin) I gratefully accept our friend's remarks which you have added [to the speech] and the sheet of the Harmony, although when I was in London†2 I at length received some copies of the remarks and sheets of the Harmony that had been lurking for three months at a bookseller's there. You will perhaps be surprised at, indeed you will rightly blame, my slowness about Euripides unless you think of my health and at the same time of the sluggish winter that has lingered with us this year. Spring was so slow in bringing us back warm suns and pleasant days that it was only towards the end of May that [[. 403] I at last ventured to undertake the journey and to go to London. When I was there my first concern was about Euripides; as soon as I had obtained him I sent him to a London merchant, a friend of Furly,†1 through whom I am wont to send to Furly, so that, he [Euripides] being carried to Rotterdam at the first opportunity, Furly might forward him to you. I hope that this was done properly and that he has now reached your hands. I am surprised by what you say about its being at your expense; if you continue to do so I shall be angry; I scarcely forgive your having mentioned it at all. I am glad that Cicero's speeches, restored by your learned hand to their genuine splendour, will appear shortly. Allow me, however, to put forward freely one thing that I regret, namely that Manutius's notes are removed to the end of the volume. I should wish them, as all notes, always to be placed on the same page continuously with the text, so that whenever one wishes or there is need for it author and commentator may be consulted in a single view. You do not know how much distaste it brings to the reader or how much time the turning of the leaves uselessly consumes; while an explanation separated from the text is being sought time goes by ungratefully. I should therefore wish that this might be a universal practice in publishing annotations, that the commentary should always be attached to the text. Please forgive my speaking so freely. I, who have little leisure, perhaps bear too impatiently that[p. 404] any of the time that I have designed for reading should be taken from me.†1 And I am over-nice in not being content to accept the solid fruits of your scholarship and lucubrations unless they are set in order in accordance with my way of thinking. But this is an utterance not of a disdainful spirit but of one wishing you all the praises of all men, as you deserve. Goodbye, accomplished Sir, and continue to love me,
Your most devoted
J LOCKE
(Latin) Please give my regards to our friend de Greve. I wrote to him some months ago. When you write to the author of the Harmony†2 please tell him what I said above and thank him on my behalf. Shut away here in the country by the weakness of my lungs I am as it were an exile from London; if I ever make an excursion to it I return speedily, like a dog at the Nile.†3

1921. Locke to William Molyneux, 2 July 1695 (1896, 1936)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 114-20. Answers no. 1896; answered by no. 1936.
Oates, 2 July. 1695.
Dear Sir,
Did I not assure my self that our friendship were grown beyond suspition or complement, I should think I should have need to make excuses to you for my long silence; but I know you will credit me, when I tell you it has been neither forgetfulness nor negligence. The specimen of the translation you sent me, gave me some reason to apprehend, that Mr. Mullart's stile would lay too great a burthen on your kindness, by often needing the correction of your hand, to make it express my sense with that clearness and easyness which I know you desire. My bookseller therefore having before told me of one who had offer'd to undertake the translation of my Essay, I have been ever since endeavouring to get from him a specimen, that I might send it you, and have your opinion, which is like to do best; that so if this man had a talent that way, you might be eased of the trouble, which your friendship to me, and zeal to the work, I foresee, is likely to lay upon you. But, having the last post received this account from Mr. Churchill, that the gentleman proposed is in the country, and must have a book sent him down, on purpose, before we can expect to see any thing from him, and this being all to be managed by a third hand, who is not every day to be met with, I have resolved to lose no more time on that thought, but accepting of your kind offer, put that whole matter into your hands, to be ordered as you shall think best, and shall spend no more time in other enquiries, since the gentleman you propose will (as I remember you told me) be about this time at leisure to set himself in earnest to it. There is one thing I would offer, which may be of advantage to him and his work too, and that is, that he would constantly and sedulously read Tully, especially his philosophical works, which will insensibly work him into a good latin stile. I have heard it reported of Bp. Sanderson, that being asked how he came to write latin so well, as appears in the treatises he published in that tongue; he answer'd by ordering his studies so, that he read over all Tully's works every year.†1 I leave it to you, whether you will think fit to mention this to Mr. Mullart.
― 406 ―
The abridgment of my Essay is quite finish'd. It is done by a very ingenious man of Oxford, a master of arts, very considerable for his learning and virtue, who has a great many pupils. It is done with the same design you had in view, when you mention'd it. He has generally (as far as I could remember) made use of my words; he very civilly sent it me when it was done, and, upon looking it over, I guess you will approve of it, and think it well done. It is in Mr. Churchill's hands, and will be printed as soon as the third edition of my Essay, which is now in the press, is printed off.
I am extremely glad to hear that you have found any good effects of my method on your son. I should be glad to know the particulars; for though I have seen the success of it in a child of the lady, in whose house I am,†1 (whose mother has taught him latin without knowing it herself when she began) yet I would be glad to have other instances; because some men, who cannot endure any thing should be mended in the world by a new method, object, I hear, that my way of education is unpracticable. But this I can assure you, that the child above mentioned, but nine years old in June last, has learn'd to read and write very well; is now reading Quintus Curtius†2 with his mother, understands geography and chronology very well, and the Copernican system of our vortex;†3 is able to multiply well, and divide a little; and all this without ever having had one blow for his book. The third edition is now out, I have ordered Mr. Churchill to send you one of them, which I hope he has done before this.†4 I expect your opinion of the additions, which have much encreased the bulk of the book. And though I think all that I have said right, yet you are the man I depend on, for a fair and free censure, not inclined either to flatter, or quarrel. You know not of what value a knowing man, that is a sincere lover of truth, is nor how hard to be found; wonder not, therefore, if I place a great part of my happiness in your friendship, and wish every day you were my neighbour; you would then find what use I should make
― 407 ―
of it. But, not to complain of what cannot be remedied, pray let me have all the advantage I can at this distance. Read the additions, and examine them strictly, for I would not willingly mislead the world. Pray let me know whether the Doctor your brother, has any children; when he has, I count I owe him one of my books of Education.†1
With my treatise of Education, I believe you will receive another little one concerning Interest and Coinage.†2 It is one of the fatherless children, which the world lay at my door; but, whoever be the author, I shall be glad to know your opinion of it.
And now I must mightily bemoan the loss of an happiness which you designed me, and I through great misfortune missed. The impressions of the last severe winter on my weak lungs, and the slow return of warm weather this spring, confined me so long to the country, that I concluded Dr. Ashe would be gone before I should get to town, and I should lose the honour of so desired an acquaintance. However, as soon as I was got to London, I enquir'd of Mr. Churchill, who told me Dr. Ashe was lately in town; and he promised me, as I desired him, that he would enquire whether he was still there, and where he lodged. He return'd me no answer, and I (through a multitude of business) forgot to enquire again, for some few days. Upon the first thought of it again, I went to the secretary's office at Whitehall, and not finding Mr. Tucker there, I went to his house, who told me that Dr. Ashe was that very morning gone out of town. The missing of him thus unluckily, when he had been within my reach, very much vexed me, and it looked as if fortune had had a mind sensibly to cross me, in what she knew I was extremely desirous of. I enquired too for Mr. Smith,†3 but he, I heard, was gone to Flanders before I came to town. It would have been more than ordinary satisfaction to me, to have convers'd and made an acquaintance with so esteem'd a friend of yours as Dr. Ashe. I shall not be at quiet, till some business brings you into England to repair this loss, and brings me a satisfaction to the most earnest of all my desires. My decaying health does not
― 408 ―
promise me any long stay in this world, you are the only person in it, that I desire to see once, and to converse some time with, before I leave it. I wish your other occasions might draw you into England, and then let me alone to husband our time together; I have laid all that in my head already. But I talk my desires and fancies as if they were in view. I wish you all manner of happiness, and am,
Dear Sir,
Your most affectionate, and most faithful servant,
J. LOCKE.
Pray present my humble service to Dr. Ashe, and excuse my misfortunate loss to him.
When you consider the length of this, you will find my late silence was not from a sparingness of speech, or backwardness to talk with you; I have more reason now to beg your pardon for my talkativeness than silence.
The additions I intend to make,†1 shall be sent time enough for the translator.

1923. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 2/12 July 1695 (1905, 1931)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 65-6.
d'Amst. ce 12 juill. 1695
Monsieur,
Nous sommes bien affligé de ce que vostre poitrine vous donne si peu de relache. il est vray que nous avons eu un terrible hyver, dont on se seroit consolé plus facilemen<t>†a si cet esté eut esté plus doux; au moins en ce payis icy, il fait presentement un temps inconstant et orageux, avec un vend de nord perpetuel, qui a deseiché tous les fruits: en sorte quon reconnoist a peine en quelle saison on est. cepandant la famille continue a se bien porter, et vous fait la reverence. vous demandez des nouvelles de nostre pierot. il est tousjours vostre serviteur. a le genie assez bon, et assez docile. cepandant je ne scay a quelle profession il s'attachera un jour. les estudes, (comme vous scavez) sont fort ingrates en ce pays, nous aurions du penchant a le destiner au negoce, et mesme nous avions pensé de luy faire faire son aprentisage en engleterre, mais Monsieur Pecock associé de Monsieur chitty me le conseille pas, disant que les Anglois sont moins attaché au comptoir, et quon y a pas toute l'exactitude et l'application quon a icy, que la pluspart des affaires se font au cabaret, et que la jeunesse y est plus libertine. je serois bien ayse de scavoir vostre conseil. ce qui m'avoit fait songer a l'establir en engleterre, estoit pour trouver un azyle sur nos vieux jours, en cas que ces provinces eussent du malheur, comme elles en sont fort menacées, et quil y a beaucoup de changement a craindre pour l'advenir. le traducteur de vostre livre de l'Education s'appelle
― 410 ―
Monsieur Coste, c'est un jeune theologien proposant, refugié, amy de Monsieur le Clerc, qui se fera un grand honneur de vostre souvenir. quand nous aurons vostre second edition,†1 il travaillera a la traduction, et le libraire est tout prest a vouloir entreprendre une seconde edition, ayant desja vendu la plus grande partie de la premiere. on a trouvé vostre livre si bon et si utile, qu'on s'est offert au libraire de le traduire en flamend, mais il s'est pas encore determiné, preferant une traduction francoise; parce que dit il les honnestes gens en ce pays ayment mieux lire le francois que leur propre langue, et que le vulgaire qui n'entend que le flamend, n'a pour le general que fort peu d'application a la lecture des livres, qui ne sont pas de pure theologie.†2
Nos Marchands se pleignent fort icy du dechet de vostre Monnoye, ce qui a tellement alteré le change, qu'on ne scauroit remettre de l'argent icy qu'avec perte considerable. de sorte que ceux qui ont mis de l'argent a interest nont pas le revenu quils se figuroient.†3 cepandant (comme j'espere quon y mettra ordre) nous voudrions bien estre informez des occasions favorables qui pouroient survenir pour employer quelques sommes. et sil faut laisser de dela l'obligation principale ou si pour la recette des interets une copie de l'obligation suffiroit. je vous remercie par avance du livre de Monsieur Ridleys que vous avez dessin de m'envoyer,†4 ce sera une nouvelle surcharge aux obligations infinies que je vous ay, si vous vouliez bien me noter quelque livre de vostre goust qu'on imprimast icy vous me feriez un singulier playsir. ma femme tousjours vostre debitrice desespere aussi quelle se poura jamais acquitter de tout ce quelle vous doibt. elle est, comme je suis avec un profond respect,
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
GUENELLON

1925. Paul D'Aranda to Locke, 15 July 1695 (1918, 1935)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 32-3.
Bath the 15th: July 1695
Sir
I was bold to give you the trouble of a few lines from Oxford, whence ariving here the 5th: instant I the next day began to drink
― 412 ―
the waters of the Bath, and have drank them every day since, Observing your advice in beginning with half a pint, and, finding that agree well with me, increasing every day, save one, as much, so that I to day drank two quarts and half a pint, the whole to greater benifit than my best hopes before durst promise me, all I have drank not onely staying with me, but also for the most part sitting easy on my stomack, and, especially when I ride immediately after drinking or drink while in the Crosse bath; which I now therefore do every other day interchangeably, passing extraordinary well, all by Urine, and causing so good a disposition of Stomack, that as I want not appetite, so I have the advantage of well disgesting what I eat, and that so neer as it ought to be that I am as well after as before eating, almost allways wholly free from those sore pains in Stomack and back I have had so large a share of, indeed quite without any pain when I am enough master of my unruly pallat and greedy apetite to abstain from those sorts of dyet which experience has taught me will disagree with me, such as are bread and all things made of meal, fruit, herbs and roots and all liquors save these waters, warm milk at first milking and a little mum; which last I by Dr Blackmore's†1 advice made tryal of, found agree with me drinking it warm'd, and believe has contributed much toward giving me an open body, which is that way now so well that I have dayly, about 5 of the Clock afternoon, sometimes by much, sometimes with little and oftener without any straining for it, good ease on the stool. the heat in my back which I felt on and about the edge of the shoulder blade bone I now seldome feel any thing of, never but when I have in eating or drinking sinn'd against knowledge of what I ought to do, and then but gently. I have been now two whole days without the least pain any where. I feel not any more, nor have not above twice since I began to drink the water felt, the least inclination to vomit. My rest by-night is better and much more refreshing as well as somewhat longer than it used to be; and whereas I have for many past months been forced to sit well nigh upright in Bed, I have now, without any inconvenience by it, lain two nights on bed with three pillows lesse than I used to have, so that my head's no more than ordinary raised by two pillows. and I have by degrees so diminish'd the quantity of Laudanum I used to take, that, instead of 20 drops in the
― 413 ―
Evening and sometimes more, and neer as much in the mornings, as I had for some time been forced to the use of, I have now for these three last nights taken no more than 12 drops each time at or some time before going to bed. By (I suppose) much rubbing in the hottest water of the Bath I am freed quite of the numbnesse in part of my forefinger and the beginning of recovery from the same ail, in much greater degree, in the outer half of the thumb of my left hand (both which, you may perhaps remember I told you, came in my last violent fits of vomiting) is neer perfected. and though I must own my self still too weak to walk or ride much without wearynesse which I am most sensible of at going up hill but a little way, or up stairs, yet I am not to deny some increase of strength, when I find I can now mount my horse without the help of others hands or rising ground, and am not without hopes of farther growth of force, though perhaps may come but by slow degrees, if it please God the waters continue to do me as much good as they have hitherto done, from the dayly nourishment my Body receives. The main ail I have now remaining is in my thighs and legs especially the latter which, Notwithstanding my causing them to be well rub'd thrice each time I am in the Bath, continue still cold, especially my legs and feet in which is also a kind of numbnesse tho but small, but the cold's so much that I am sometimes, as but to day, glad to warm them by the fire: When I come out of the bath the upper half of my body sweats freely an hour or two after in bed, but from the middle downwards I am dry. I have not consulted any Phisician since my being here, hoping it not needfull and dreading the event of perhaps falling into hands who may mistake my ails cause. Pardon Sir this long scroul which though it do not at all concern you and may therefore well prove tedious, yet being no more than a just account of the successe of that good advice of yours to which I under God owe what I now enjoy of, at least respite if not total, freedom from intollerable pains with the hopes of farther recovery, I thought it my duty to communicate it to you as all the return I shall ever be able to make till your goodnesse extend it self somewhat farther in giving me some oportunity of proving that it's not possible to be more sincerely than I am
Sir
Your most humble and most faithfull servant
PAUL D'ARANDA
Endorsed by Locke: P: Daranda 15º Jul. 95

1930. Sir Hugh Owen, bart., to Locke, 13 August 1695
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 180-1. Forwarded by R. Griffith, 27 August: p. 430. Hugh Owen, c. 1645-99; of Orielton, Pembrokeshire; matriculated from Christ Church 7 December 1660, where he was a pupil of Locke; second baronet 1670; M.P. 1676-81, 1689-95: G.E.C., Baronetage, ii. 131; Cranston, p. 71.
Orielton Augt. 13th (95)
Sir
It was much my trouble I was absent from my Lodgeing when you oblidg'd mee with a Visitt, thereby looseing the opportunitye of renewing our ancient acquaintance which I soe much value, As alsoe of begging your Advice in a matter of neare Concerne to me, which since lefte the Towne desir'd my friend Mr Griffith to attend you in, and now doe my selfe heartilye beg your sentiments of the disposall of my second Sonn†1 a youth of about 16en years of age an Indifferent Schoole Schollar as farr as Latin and some Greeke, whom I would willingly educate towards the Law, his Apprehension tolerably quicke, and I hope his Inclinations as yet vertuous, but am to seeke what Course to take with him, best to fitt him with some Logicke and other University Learning, which might render him not Contemptible when he came to the wrangling Barre, I Confesse I am in some dread of the Carelessnesse as well as the Debaucherys of the Universitys, which doe not seeme to me to take that care of the manners and Education of Young men Committed to them (not design'd for their own Trade the Ministerye) they should doe, If they well thought that the Church will alsoe want the Countenance and Protection of a Sober and Intelligent Gentry, as well as
― 417 ―
of a Learn'd and Religious Clergye; Pray Sir give me now leave again to desire your Judgment without reserve what Course to take with him for Attainment of this end: Learned in some measure I would have him, but not debaucht, would therefore know what Corner most proper to send him to, and how to manage him there, Money I would not unnecessarily fling away on him, nor yet would be over thriftye in the well Cultivateing that Understanding God hath given him. I have alsoe but one Son more younger about 2 years, who have thoughts to remove out of the Country Schoole to some private one about London for a yeare or two, whilst can sound his Capacitye what employ most inclineable to and capable of, and there is one Mr Singleton in Hogsden†1 have a good Character of.
You see with what freedome I invade your Friendship and retirement, but it is when my Sonns greatest Secular Concerne lyes at Stake, the first forming of him for the employment he is to worke his fortunes in and with some hope that he whose father has received soe many undesered favours from you, may have the good fortune of makeing you better returns, and thinke himselfe bound in Conscience to pay his fathers Debts with his owne. I have desir'd Mr Griffith to attend you with this who will give directions how I may be directed to, when you please to favour me at your leisure with a line which will be most welcome to
Sir
Your much Oblidg'd humble Servant
H OWEN
Pardon is beg'd for this hasty imperfect scribble, which wish may prove legible.
Address: This: For my Honoured Friend John Locke Esqr. London.
Endorsed by Locke: Sir H: Owen 13 Aug. 95
1931. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 18/28 August 1695 (1923, 1973)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 67-8.
Monsieur,
Vostre agreable du 29 juillet ma bien esté rendue. mais je nay point encore receu vostre seconde Edition du traitté de l'Education.
― 418 ―
Monsieur Cyprianus a passé icy sans me voir. apparemment pressé pour retourner chez luy. Monsieur Teut†1 a donné a un amis qui a rendu en main propre a ma femme une belle medaille venant de vostre part. elle vous en remercie tres humblement et ne manquera pas a son retour de la campagne de vous en faire son compliment. je vous escris celle cy a l'occasion de Monsieur Gonston associé de Monsieur Daranda qui vient d'Italie et s'en retourne en Engleterre. jay esté bien ayse d'apprendre de luy que Monsieur Daranda se restablit et quil a pris des eaux minerales par vostre Conseil, quil luy ont fait beaucoup de bien, il me dit quil y a joint l'usage d'un extraict de kina kina, ce que J'ay peine a croire, et je crois mesme quil ny a rien qui a plus gasté la santé de Monsieur Daranda que l'usage indiscret de cette escorce, pris iterativement au premier acces de fievre sans avoir prealablement evacué un corps replet comme le sien. et quoy que je reconnoisse que cette escorce soit d'une utilité tres grande dans des cas pressants, et que j'en ay veu dans ma practique nombre de succes surprenants, je puis pourtant vous dire que j'en voy tous les jours parmis les refugiez, qui sen servent inconsiderement, de tres meschants et funestes effects; de schirres au foy, a la ratte, d'hydropisie, gravelle, asthme et semblables cachexies insurmontables. Moy mesme, il y a deux ans, qu'estant tres occupé pendant une epidemie, et estant attaqué d'une double tierce, je me tin sur pied par l'usage de cette escorce pris en substance, pour en avoir un effet plus prompt. j'en pris jusqu'a trois onces. je me remis assez bien, mais quelque mois appres j'ay esté atteint de la goutte, dont je m'estois jamais senti, et depuis je lay eue assez fortement, jay veu arriver la mesme chose a d'autre; et je doubte fort si ce nest' d'avoir detourné la Matiere febrile, qui c'est jettée en suitte sur les jointures. Quoy quil en soit, ce remede est icy tousjours fort suspect, mesme plus que jamais.
Nous avons bien de la douleur Monsieur, que vostre poitrine vous incommode tousjours, et souhaitterions y pouvoir apporter quelque remede. Toute la famille vous fait la reverence. et Je suis avec un profond respect,
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON.
d'Amst. ce 28 Aoust 1695.

1932. Nathaniel Hodges to Locke, 19 August 1695 (737, 2364)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 214-15.
Dear Sir
You are very kind in making so particular an enquiry after an old freind, especially being an old man too: since I find by dayly experience that to be so powerfull a prejudice against a man as to be able to sink his reputation not onely with little more or lesse than half the world, but with much the greater number of the other moiety. Body, which dayly strikes our eys, and youth, the result of it, having gained so powerfull an ascendent over both sexes, that the better part of us, as it is allwaies out of sight, so is it with the generality out of mind. He who by the decays of the one, or the growth of the other part of himself is once fallen into a neglect of living by the reason of†1 the world, is in little regard, for the contemptible exchange he hath made of living by the reason of god and mankind. But forgive me that I was at unawares running on as if I had been talking with you. 'Tis fit I remember That this would be chatt more proper for a fireside than a Letter: Which ought rather to be suited to the occasion of writing, than the reveries of old age. I received one of Mr. Walls a day or two before my coming from Glocester, which gave me intimation of your desire I should call at Harloe; which I had certainly done, had I come by the way of London. But my businesse at Norwich required a more speedy passage 'crosse the Country, and I had before laid all my designs in order to it. I am now I beleive set up here till towards Christmasse. And when I return for Glocester I doubt the old man will confine me to the Hacqney Coach, by which means I shalbe in no hopes of seeing you, unlesse my good Fortune will have it That you happen to be then at London. Whither I have never come, but that I have allways made a narrow search after you. To tell you the truth, what ever account you have had of it, my body is not in such a condition, as that I have the same power over
― 420 ―
it, which other men have over theirs, nor will it carry me whither I would have it, but whither it pleaseth to direct me; which is indeed, to no place of better fashion, with any decency, than either to an Inne or an Hospitall. Such as it is, together with the whole sorry composition it helps to make, it is still with the same ancient syncerity it ever was, tho with very little of its former life and vivacity
Dear Sir
Your true faithfull servant
N: HODGES
Norwich Aug: 19th. 95.
Address: For Mr John Lock at Oates in Essex
Endorsed by Locke: N: Hodges 14 Aug. 95 Answered 26. Nov:
1933. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 20/30 August 1695 (1916, 1958)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 99-100. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 87-90.
A Amsterdam le 30 d'Août 1695.
Je n'ai pas répondu d'abord, Monsieur, à vôtre Lettre du 16 de Juillet, parce que j'attendois que Mrs. Huguetan m'eussent assuré positivement, qu'ils avoient envoié de nouveau des Vies de Richelieu à leur homme, et qu'il les avoit reçuës, afin de ne vous donner pas la peine d'y envoier en vain. Ils m'ont dit, il y a déja plusieurs jours, que leur homme devoit avoir reçu un ballot où il y en avoit cinquante, de sorte qu'il n'y a qu'à y envoier à présent. Il ne manquera pas d'en donner un exemplaire; sur tout parce que Mr. Huguetan l'ainé†1 est à Londres à présent. Je suis fâché de la peine, que cette bagatelle vous a donnée, et une autre fois je prendrai une meilleure voie. Je croi vous avoir déja dit que j'avois reçu le livre de l'Evêque d'Ely, et ceux qui lui étoient joints, dont j'ai envoié à Mr. Furly ceux sur qui son nom étoit. Je vous suis extrémement obligé de tout cela, et de toutes vos autres honêtetez. A peine vous ai-je remercié pour l'une, que je trouve que je vous suis redevable, pour une autre. J'ai reçu la petite fiole dont vous me parlez, avec deux exemplaires de la 3 Ed. de l'Education, dont je ne manquerai pas de remettre un à Mr. Coste. Nôtre petit garçon a bu
― 421 ―
pendant quelque temps de la biere, où nous avions mis, dans un petit sac une dragme de Rubarbe. Nous l'avons fait jusque à trois fois, et il s'en est bien trouvé, cela lui aiant donné de l'appetit, dont il sembloit manquer. Cependant il a de temps en temps le ventre un peu gros et dur sur tout du côté gauche, ce qui me fait croire, qu'il a peut être quelque obstruction dans la rate. Il s'est néanmoins un peu fortifié cet Eté, et nous n'avons pas remarqué que ses poignets aient grossi. J'espere que l'usage du remede, que vous nous avez envoié, achevera de le mettre en bon état, et ce sera avec les autres une très-grande obligation que je vous aurai eue. Quelques personnes nous disent que la bouillie, dont il mange le plus, et qui est composée de lait et de farine, est scorbutique; cependant c'est ce qu'on donne le plus communément aux enfans, et il n'y a rien de plus commode, pour leur usage ordinaire. Le nôtre commence à manger de tout, et nous lui donnons de ce que nous mangeons, pourvu qu'il ne soit pas de trop haut goût; mais hors de nos repas il mange principalement de la bouillie. Je trouve qu'il boit trop, sur tout quand il ne dort pas bien, mais nous ne savons comment faire pour l'appaiser, lors qu'il a soif. Faites moi la grace de me mander vôtre sentiment là dessus. Pour revenir aux livres que vous m'avez envoiez, ou dont vous me parlez, il y a long-temps que j'ai†a- les Archæologiæ de M. Burnet, de l'Edit. de cette ville,†1 mais je ne les ai pas encore luës, excepté un Chapitre. C'est un homme d'esprit, mais il y a beaucoup de conjectures en son fait, et il me semble qu'il n'est pas assez Grammairien, ou Critique, pour bien juger de tout.-†a Je suis ravi de cette découverte dont vous me parlez, et la doctrine des anciens Persans pourroit être d'une grande utilité pour entendre les antiquitez orientales. Il seroit à souhaiter qu'on l'imprimât au plutôt, avec une version Latine à côté. L'ancien Persan doit approcher du Chaldéen, et si l'on en avoit une fois formé un alphabeth, on en dechiffreroit sans doute une bonne partie, par le moien du chaldéen. Il est à souhaiter que le savant homme, qui a ce MS. le publie, sans beaucoup de commentaires;†2 car s'il s'avise d'entreprendre de faire le commentateur, et d'étaler son érudition,
― 422 ―
nous attendrons long-temps, et nous y gagnerons peut-être aussi peu, qu'aux commentaires sur le Joseph.†1
Je vous remercie du Poëme Heroïque dont vous me parlez,†2 j'entends trop peu la poësie Angloise, pour la lire avec plaisir, et je suis d'ailleurs trop occupé. Il s'est vendu dernierement un Plutarque de l'Ed. de Paris,†3 assez mal conditionné, plus de 45 francs. C'est à la verité la meilleure édition, mais cela m'a paru trop cher. J'aurai soin d'y avoir l'oeuïl, à la premiére occasion, mais il ne seroit pas mal que vous me marquassiez ce que vous y voulez mettre, parce qu'il se pourroit faire, qu'il seroit à meilleur marché à Londres. Ici†a- le moins que l'on en donne est 35 francs, de l'édition de Paris, qui est plus complette que celle de Wechel,†4 que l'on a pour vint-cinq francs, ou environ.-†a Je suis bien aise que la version de Mr. Coste vous ait satisfait, elle se vend fort bien ici, et il s'en pourra bien faire une autre édition, où l'on ajoûtera ce qu'il y a de plus dans la troisiéme. Nous avions déja parlé quelquefois de traduire vôtre grand ouvrage en François, et comme il entend fort bien la Philosophie, et quil est accoûtumé à vos idées, je croi qu'il y reüssiroit fort bien. Je suis persuadé qu'une version Françoise seroit pour le moins aussi bien reçue qu'une Latine; car comment que face le traducteur, elle sera barbare et obscure, et par consequent ennuieuse à lire; au lieu qu'en François elle n'auroit pas ces défauts. Si nous étions en temps de paix, et que l'on pût envoier en France comme auparavant, cet ouvrage y seroit tres-avidement reçu. L'abregé François, qui est dans la Bibl. Universelle, en a donné une très-grande envie à tous ceux qui l'ont vû. Cependant j'en parlerai à quelques Libraires de cette ville, et je verrai ce qui se pourra faire. Mr. Coste est occupé présentement à autre chose,†5 mais comme c'est un long ouvrage, il faut s'y prendre d'avance. On imprime l'indice de mon Pentateuque, et ma Physique est achevée, excepté les figures. Dès
― 423 ―
que j'aurai l'un et l'autre je vous les envoierai. On a aussi commencé à imprimer ma version Latine de Hammond,†1 dont la moitié est faite il y a cinq, ou six ans. J'y ajoûte une Critique de quantité d'endroits de cet Auteur, qui est distinguée de ce qu'il dit, par des crochets, et par mon nom au dessous. J'y trouve bien des bévuës, et ce grand Theologien n'entendoit la Langue Greque et la Critique que bien médiocrement. Quoi que je le traite respectueusement, comme il le mérite, on verra qu'il n'est pas tout ce que l'on croit en Angleterre. Il paroitra le printemps prochain, comme je l'espere. Je ne sai, si je ne ferois pas bien de le dédier à quelque Prélat de vôtre païs; mais je ne sai à qui. Ce n'est plus le temps d'Erasme, auquel les Archevêques de ce païs-la favorisoient les étrangers, comme les autres. Nunc putant nos cismarinos esse cucurbitas.†2 Cependant les ouvrages de deux Druïdes sur l'Auteur, qu'un de vos amis a commenté,†3 sont la plus pauvre chose du monde, et s'ils sont estimez, ce'st une marque infaillible que l'ancienne discipline des Druïdes est beaucoup diminuée. O! quando erunt tempora, ubi loca, in quibus soli vero litare licebit?†4 Je m'étonne que l'on dise que je ne dis pas que S. Jean parle contre Cerinthe, car je le dis expressément p.27. Le Libraire a voulu ajoûter ce petit ouvrage à mon Pentateuque de peur qu'il ne se perdit, et je ne m'y suis pas opposé. J'y ai joint une Préface nouvelle, où je réfute en deux mots quelques objections malitieuses, que l'on a faites contre ce petit ouvrage. Vous la verrez bien tôt. Je suis, Monsieur, du fonds de mon ame Vôtre très-humble et très-obeissant serviteur
J LE CLERC

Dear Sir
When I began to read Mr Engehams letter written in your lodgings I began to be frighted. But the sequel of it and Mr Pawlings which was writ after his pretty well satisfied me with the hopes that the pain and danger is now well over. I flatterd my self when I parted with you that your distemper was at an end for that time, and would be kept off with a litle care two or three days. though I know it soe apt to returne that one is not very secure till ones health be confirmed by some days continuance, Let this be a caution to you not to be too forward in ventureing abroad or eating any thing but plain meat. and besure for this good while to keep your stomach and belly and feet very warme. I think the Doctor†1 has done exceeding well in bleeding and purgeing you upon the returne of your pains this I have great confidence will prove an effectuall cure and I see your body was soe disposed that there was noe geting it off at a cheaper rate, And notwithstanding my hopes to set you right an easier way yet had I been in town I should have been forced I conclude to come to the same discipline. Have a care of your self. I hope to hear by the next post that you have noe remains of your pain.
Pray send Mr Trent word that I doe not think that two grains will purge the child or at all make her looser But that they may continue to give it her if she be a litle loose if it does not directly purge her for if it does they must then forbeare†2 I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant

1935. Paul D'Aranda to Locke, 24 August 1695 (1925, 1969)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 34-5.
Bath the 24th. August 1695.
Sir
Pardon me if partly from fear of being too often troublesome and partly from want of expressions suited to the sense I bear of my obligations to you, I have too long deferred paying you the thanks this carrys for the continuance of your kindnesse in inquiring after me at my house; and by your letter of last month giving the greatest good could come to one in my case, needed wholesome advice, which I have observed with good successe for the most part drinking but five pints and never exceeding three quarts of water in a morning, allways remembring not to overlade my stomack which it has hitherto agreed well with, and passed well by urine, never purging by stool save twice or thrice when I was each time weaken'd by it. Tho I have not attain'd perfect recovery, being still unable to bear any malt drink or wine, or any liquor cold, or bread or other things made of meal, or herbs roots or fruit in my stomack without renewal of pain; yet I hope my self in a fair way to it, not having once cast up any thing since I came hither, and seldom feeling the
― 426 ―
usual pains in my stomack but when I, for tryal, have eaten of what I knew used to hurt me; gaining, by the good meals I make of all sorts of flesh and fish and their digesting well, aparent considerable increase of strength, and such amendment in looks that to apearance I seem neer as well as ever I was: I have not in long used any laudanum or other opiate or indeed any medicine save bath-water which I drink at meals. I am almost as constantly eas'd by stool in due course as when I was formerly in health, and generally rest well by night. Whither I am ever to get warmth in my legs again, and to eat bread etc with my meat time must shew: for drink perhaps there's no great harm in being obliged to keep to bath-water onely for yet some time; I think to try it here again next spring, and i'th'mean time to have of it sent me weekly to London, whither†a- I design-†a to return by way of Salisbury next monday come seaven night, if ere I go hence or at Salisbury I can be any way serviceable to you I beg you will please to oblige me with your commands, that I may thereby have oportunity of shewing that I am really desirous to prove my self
Sir
Your most obedient servant
P: D'ARANDA
My wife intreats you'l please to accept her humble service.

1936. William Molyneux to Locke, 24 August 1695 (1921, 1945)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 120-5. Answers no. 1921; answered by no. 1966.
Dublin. August. 24. 1695.
Sir
I deferd my Answer all this while to yours of July. 2d. (which I received some weeks ago) in Expectation of the Books you have been pleased to Order for me. but hitherto they are not arrived;
― 427 ―
and I would not omitt my Duty any Longer, least the Busines of our Parliament†1 should give me a farther Hindrance. the University has done me the Honour to Choose me as One of their Representatives; and tho I cannot pretend to do them any great service, yet it shall not be for want of Constant Attendance on their Busines, which will take up most of my time, till the Session is Ended.
I am now at a great Losse what Apology to make you for the Disappointment you are at last like to receive in the Translation of your Essay: But to a Candid and Ingenuous Man the best Excuse is a Plain Narrative of the Matter of Fact.
The Gentleman whom I formerly mentiond to you, Mr Mullart, went into the Country about the Middle of last June, and returnd about a fortnight ago. when he went away, he Assured me, he would make a Considerable Progres in the Work in a Month or six weeks time; but he was taken ill for about a fortnight, and at his return I found he had scarce done four Pages of the Book. I found also (as you rightly surmised) that his stile will hardly answer Expectation; but this Difficulty I thought might be overcome by time and Application; But what to say to his very slow performance I cannot tell; or whether it may answer your or your Booksellers Designes. But that which most off all Discourages me is, that the Young Man himself seems not very fond of the undertaking, but has fixt his thoughts on an other Pursuit. I formerly told you how he Designed for a Fellowship, had any at that time hapned vacant, as there did none. But very lately there are two Fellowships become Void, and a third like to be so before the time of sitting for them, which is next June 1696. and he tells me plainly, he must indeavour to get One of them; and that there will be at least five Competitors, if not Six,†a- Who are-†a all his Seniors; and therefore he must use his utmost Diligence, application, and study in the Intermediate time, to fitt himself for the Examination they undergo; and this, he says, will take up so much of his time, that he knows not whether he shall have any to spare for the Translation.
I cannot wel tell which way next to turn my self in this affair; I have but one Anchor more left me but it is not at hand immediately to Use, There is a Gentle Man of My Acquaintance, the Greatest master of Stile of any I have known, who I am Confident
― 428 ―
would perform this Work to your Utmost Satisfaction; but he is not at present in town; and when he comes (which I expect may be about Michaelmas next, as I have it from himself) I make some doubt, whether his other avocations will permitt him to undertake this. He is Chancellor of the Dioces of Down and Connor: and has also a Private work of his own in Latin now fitting for the Pres; which he permitts to run through my hands as he goes on with it. When he comes to town I will move him in it, if you will give me leave; and you shall know the Event.†1
I am mightily pleased that your Essay is abridged; Tho for my own Reading, I would not part with a Syllable of it. However, others may not have so much leasure as to set on a large book; and for such the Abridgement may be Usefull. Tis to me no small argument of the Curious Genii of the English Nation, that a Work so abstract as yours should now suffer three Impressions in so short a time.
I have had already so much experience of your Method of Education, that I long to see your third Edition. And since you put me upon it, (to whom I can refuse nothing in my Power) I will give you a short account of my Little Boys Progres under it.
He was six years old about the middle of Last July. when he was but just turnd five, he could read perfectly wel; and on the Globes could have traced out and pointed at all the Noted Parts Countrys and Cittys of the World both land and sea. and by five and an half could perform many of the Plainest Problems on the Globe, as the Longitude and Latitude, the Antipodes, the Time with them and other Countrys. etc. and this by the way of Play and Diversion, seldom cald to it, never chid or beaten for it. about the same age he could read any number of Figures not exceeding six places, break it as you pleased by Cyphers <or>†a zero's. By the time he was six he could manage a Compas Ruler and Pencil very prettily and perform many little Geometrical tricks, and advanced to writing and arithmetick; and has been about three Months at Latin, wherein His Tutor observes, as nigh as he can, the Method prescribed by you. He can read a Gazet, and in the Large Maps of Sanson†2 shews most
― 429 ―
of the Remarkable places as he goes along, and turn to the Proper Mapps. He has been shewn some Dogs Dissected, and can give some little account of the Grand Traces of Anatomy. And as to the Formation of his Mind, which you rightly observe to be the most Valuable part of Education, I do not beleive that any Child had ever his Passions more perfectly at Command, he is obedient and observant to the nicest Particular, and at the same time Sprightly, Playful, and Active.
But I wil say no more, this may be tiresom to others, however pleasing to my self.
I have some thoughts of seing England next spring or summer; but the Time I cannot prefix as yet, till I see how our Affairs are like to go in Parliament, and Whether we are like to have an other session, and When. Tother Day I chanced to mention your Name Accidentally to his Excellency†a my Lord Capel,†1 who thereupon expressed himself with the Utmost Respect and Esteem for you. I am
Honour'd Sir
Your Most Affectionate Humble servant
W: MOLYNEUX
Address: To Mr John Locke at Mr Robert Pawlings overagainst the Plow-Inn in Little Lincolns-Inn Feilds London
Postmark: AV 30

It might be argued that the attribution of The Reasonableness to Locke requires a longer period since its publication than is here allowed, but as Edwards could indicate the authorship other interested persons might know or guess it. 1940. Pierre Coste to Locke, 3/13 September 1695 (1917, 2107)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 141-2. Printed by G. Bonno in Revue de littérature comparée, xxxiii (1959), 164-6.
A Amsterdam. Ce 13. Septembre 1695.
Monsieur,
Il y a prés de quinze jours que j'ai reçu de Monsieur LeClerc un Exemplaire de vôtre Livre de l'Education. L'impatience où j'étois de voir les additions que vous y avez faites, m'a empêché de vous remercier plûtôt d'un si beau présent. Je souhaitois d'ailleurs de voir, avant que de vous écrire, si par hazard vous n'auriez pas satisfait à quelques legeres Objections qu'on m'avoit proposées contre certains endroits de la premiére Edition. Vous l'avez fait effectivement en certaines rencontres, comme dans l'endroit où vous prouvez par des exemples, qu'il n'y a aucun danger à laver les pieds des Enfans dans de l'eau froide.†1 Bien des gens avoient trouvé cela un peu étrange, sans sçavoir dire pourquoy. J'avois beau leur proposer les raisons sur lesquelles vous fondez cet usage, et qui me semblent tout-à-fait convainquantes; ils n'osoient les rejetter, mais ils ne laissoient pas de désapprouver la conséquence que vous en voulez tirer pour la pratique. Présentement ils seront forcez de se
― 433 ―
rendre, puis qu<e>†a vous leur montrez par des exemples incontestables que cette pratique, qui leur paroit fondée en raison, ne sçauroit être dangereuse.
Les autres Objections que j'ai ouï faire contre vôtre Ouvrage, sont à peu près de la même force, c'est pourquoy je ne vous en dirai rien; mais je prendrai la liberté de vous consulter sur un †b me paroît assez important. Il est le même <dans la troi> siéme†b Edition que dans la premiére. Lors que je †b , il m'embarrassa beaucoup; et lors que ma Traduction †b publique, presque tous ceux qui l'ont luë et qui m'ont parlé de vôtre Ouvrage, se sont trouvez dans la même peine que moy. Cet endroit est à l'article 177. p. 310.†1 où vous dites, qu'une Mére peut enseigner le Latin à son Enfant, sans le sçavoir elle-même. Je ne doute pas que <ce>la†a ne se puisse faire, puis que vous assûrez qu'on en a fait l'experience: ab esse ad posse valet consequentia,†2 cela est incontestable. Toute la difficulté roule sur la maniére dont vous racontez que cette Mére doit s'y prendre pour enseigner le Latin à son Enfant. Vous n'exigez d'elle si ce n'est qu'elle employe deux ou trois heures par jour à faire lire à son Enfant devant elle les quatre Evangiles, pour le faire passer ensuite à la lecture de quelque autre Livre Latin plus difficile. Il y a là quelque chose qui fait de la peine pour être trop merveilleux. On veut le croire, mais on ne le trouve pas assez vraisemblable. L'embarras vient sans doute de quelque circonstance supprimée, que vous supposez que le Lecteur suppléera assez de luy-même, comme que cette Mere doit avoir appris à décliner et à conjuguer, et avoir devant les yeux un Testament en langue vulgaire lors qu'elle fait lire son Enfant. Je n'y vois point d'autre denoûement. Je vous prie de m'apprendre ce qui en est. Je pourrois aussi m'être trompé dans la Traduction, et avoir détourné vos paroles de leur veritable sens.
Au reste, Monsieur, j'espere qu'on fera bientôt une seconde Edition françoise de vôtre Ouvrage,†3 car on le lit toûjours avec
― 434 ―
beaucoup d'empressement. Je travaillerai avec plaisir à l'enrichir des Additions que vous avez inserées dans cette troisiéme Edition. On n'aura pas de peine à reconnoître qu'elles n'ont pas été faites pour grossir le Volume, mais plûtôt pour l'embellir et le rendre plus parfait.
Monsieur LeClerc m'a appris que vous êtiez satisfait de mon travail. Cette approbation, au lieu de m'enorgueillir, m'engagera à prendre de nouvelles précautions, pour m'en rendre toûjours plus digne. Et c'est dans cette veûë que je prendrai la liberté de vous demander quelques éclaircissemens sur certains endroits de vôtre Ouvrage que je n'ai pû comprendre. Le premier est à la derniere ligne de la p. 19. de la 3. Edit: où l'on trouve ces mots like Larms;†1 je ne les ai point exprimez dans la Traduction, parce que je n'ai pû sçavoir la signification du mot Larms. Je l'ai cherché inutileme<nt>†a dans differens Dictionnaires. J'ai même consulté des Anglois, qui n'ont sçu me dire ce que ce pouvoit être. A la p. 188. lign. 4. j'ai passé ces mots for so plainly is the other†2 sans les traduire, parce que je n'ai pû deviner à quoy se rapportoit le mot de other. Dans les deux Editions les mots de Governour et de tutor semblent distinguez,†3 je les ai pourtant confondus dans la traduction, en quoy je pourrois m'être trompé. A la p. 279. vous parlez d'un Livre intitulé Reynard the Fox.†4 Si je sçavois ce que c'est je pourrois l'apprendre au Lecteur, ou mettre à la place quelque Livre François qui eut du rapport avec celui-là.
J'allois ajoûter un autre endroit sur lequel je me suis tourmenté en vain, mais je vois par la troisiéme Edition que c'étoit une faute de l'imprimeur. C'est à la page 371. de la 3. Edit.†5 où vous dites que les jeunes-gens qui voyagent ne se mettent nullement en peine de lier commerce avec des personnes de merite, quoy que par ce moyen ils pussent apprendre davantage en un jour qu'en roulant çà et là from one June to another, c'est ainsi qu'il y a dans la premiere Edition. J'ai rendu ces mots par ceux-ci, pendant un an, ne sçachant quel autre
― 435 ―
sens raisonnable je pourrois donner à cette expression. Je vois maintenant par la 3. Edit. qu'au lieu de June il falloit écrire Inn, ce qui fait un tout autre sens.
Je pourrois bien abuser de vôtre patience par une trop longue Lettre. Je finirai donc ici après vous avoir prié de m'apprendre si la troisiéme Edition de vôtre Essay sur l'Entendement paroîtra bientôt. Le Libraire qui a imprimé la Traduction de vôtre Livre de l'Education†1 m'a prié de vous le demander. Il souhaiteroit de faire imprimer cet Ouvrage en François. Il voudroit même me charger de la traduction, mais je crains que cette entreprise ne soit au dessus de mes forces. Je suis avec un profond respect,
Monsieur,
Vôtre très-humble et très obeïssant serviteur
COSTE
Si vous n'avez pas occasion d'écrire à Mr. leClerc et que vous veuillez me faire l'honneur de m'écrire, vous pourrez m'addresser directement vôtre Lettre de cette maniére, sur le Lawrier-gracht in de goude-appel, chez Mademoiselle Prades.†2 J'ajoûterai ici par occasion que cette Demoiselle chez qui je loge, croit vous avoir connu à Montpellier chez Mr. Verchant apoticaire.†3 En ce cas-là elle me charge de vous assûrer de ses très-humbles respects.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings in little Lincolns inne fields over against the plough London
Postmark: SE 13
Endorsed by Locke: Coste 13 Sept. 95 Answered Sept. 24.

1942. John Bonville to Edward Clarke, 8 September 1695
Rand, p. 421. The letter was probably composed by Locke: it agrees closely with no. 1943, and appears to be beyond Bonville's powers. For the dispute see no. 1937.
London, 8th September, 1695.
Sir,
I have lately seen a letter from Mr. Thomas to my Cousin Locke, wherein he writes that both Mr. Powell and Mrs. Thomas complain that she has been unfairly or unfriendly dealt with about the interest of the £600 lent to Dr. Thomas. He talks as if the Doctor were promised to have it at 4 per cent., which I never heard mentioned. Indeed, he said that if he should pay 5 per cent. he should pay in the money in a year or two, because he thought he might get it cheaper, but he said if the money might continue in
― 437 ―
his hands at 4½ he would keep it seven or eight years. That 5 per cent. was agreed it appears by the writings. Had they continued it seven or eight years as the Doctor proposed, there would have been but 4½ expected. But they pay it in so soon and without six months' notice as was agreed, it was reasonable that the interest should be paid according to the writings. I cannot believe Mr. Powell should find fault with anything which has been done, because the computation of the interest being put into his hands some days before the money was paid, I doubt not but he would have excepted against it if there had been any unreasonableness or mistake in it. However, if there be any I am ready to rectify it, counting mistakes no payment, and shall refer the whole matter to you to make what satisfaction you think fit. If I have done anything amiss in it I beg the favour of you to write to Mr. Powell about it. I rest,
your humble servant,
JN. BONVILLE.
Address: For Edward Clarke, Esq., next door to the Hen and Chicken, in Red Lyon Street.†1
Endorsed (by Clarke?): Mr. Bonville, touching Mr. Locke and Mrs. Thomas, etc. Received the 9th September, 1695. With a copy of my letter to Mr. Powell thereupon, etc.

[London. September the 10th 1695.]
Sir
Mr Bonville tells me that in a letter from Mr Thomas to Mr Locke both you and Mrs Thomas complaine that she hath been unfairly and unfreindly dealt with about the interest of the £600 Lent Dr Thomas. Mr Bonville says he cannot beleive you say any such thing because the computation of the interest being put into your hands a day or two before the mony was paid he doubts not
― 438 ―
but you would have excepted against it had there been any mistake. However if there be any he is ready to rectifye it, counting mistake to be noe payment. I desire you therefor to let me know how that matter stands and I will be answerable that if there be any thing whereof any one has reason to complain you shall have full satisfaction from him in the affair. This you are desired to communicate to Mrs Thomas. [, with my humble servise to her from
your Affectionate Faithfull servant]

1944. Locke to Cornelius Lyde, 14 September 1695 (1738, 1947)
The Pierpont Morgan Library, New York. Transcribed from Xerox print. Answered by no. 1947.
London. 14º Sept 95
Sir
By a letter that came to me this weeke from my yonge Cosin Stratton of Bristol I received the unwelcome and sad news of his fathers death. I have a very particular concerne in it both by the losse of a friend whom I had had long experience of, and in regard of the litle estate I have in your neighbourhood, which has been under his management these several years past. Death has taken away all my old friends and acquaintance there abouts, and my long absence out of the country has scarce left me soe much as the names of any body remaining in Publoe pensford or Stanton to whom I could now apply my self to desire their assistance in my little affair. you will not therefor wonder in the necessity I am if I beg the help of your hand in a businesse that I think will cost you but very litle trouble. The litle estate I have there is a great part of it in your own parish and all of it almost under your eye. The greatest part if not all of it is let already for some time by leases signed, soe that all the trouble it will give you is only to receive the rents. you cannot possibly in a businesse of noe greater bulke lay soe great an obligation upon any one. as you will upon me if you will consent to take this small affair into your care. Michaelmas is almost at hand and I know not who else to addresse my self too and if you please to doe me this favour. you may assure your self you have exceedingly
― 439 ―
obleiged one who will let slip noe occasion of acknowledging it to you. I am
Sir
your most humble servant

1945. William Molyneux to Locke, 19 September 1695 (1936, 1965)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 96-7. Carried by Burridge and forwarded by him with no. 1952. Answered by no. 1966.
Dublin Sept. 19. 1695
In my last to my Most Esteem'd Friend, I gave you some short intimations of Mr Mullarts Disappointing me in the Translation of your Essay; And at the same time I gave you to understand, that I had some thoughts of proposing that Work to another. Providence has now brought it about, that He that Delivers this to your Hands is the Person I designed for that Task; His Occasions call him into England at this Time; and he is to transact One Affair, amongst others, wherein he will beg your Assistance; and I presume to recommend him to your Notice.
He will shew you a Work which he has been upon for some time, and which perhaps will not be unpleasing to you; Tis an Historical vindication of the Late Revolutions in these Kingdoms, for the Information of Forreigners, in Elegant Latin. He will submit the whole to your Perusal, Censure, and Correction. And if you think it Deserves the Publick Light, He Hopes you may recommend it to your Printer to get it into the World. He proposes great Advantages to his Work (as he wel may) from your Opinion of it; And I have assured him, you will give it him with all the Sincerity and Candour possibly to be Expected from Mortal Man.
Whilst his Work is under the Pres (if it may receive your Incouragement to go so far) He Proposes to Translate your Essay; And if I am not much mistaken, he will do it to your Liking. You
― 440 ―
will find him a Great Master of Latin in any Stile, Philosophical, Historical. etc. His name is Ezekiel Burridge, a Master of Arts of Long Standing in the Colledge here, and Chancellor of the Dioces of Down and Connor.†1
I need say no more to you on this Occasion but Leave the Rest to your own observation of him in your Future Acquaintance. He Designes no Long stay in England, And whilst he is there I beg your Favour towards him. I am
Honour'd Sir
Your Most Affectionate Humble servant
W: MOLYNEUX
Address: To Mr John Locke at Mr Robert Pawlings over against the Plow-Inn in Little Lincolns Inn Feilds London

The Pierpont Morgan Library, New York. Transcribed from Xerox print. Answers no. 1947.
London 24º Sept 95
Sir
That which would be a very great favour at any time, my present circumstances and the state of my health does soe much increase to me at this time, that I cannot sufficiently acknowledg to you the obligation I receive by it and the franknesse wherewith you have done it. This is only to returne my thanks for the letter I received from you the last night and I doe it with a great sense of your kindenesse. I shall this weeke, god willing, goe into the country
― 442 ―
where my papers are and from thence I shall send you a particular state of my affairs at Pensford. I forbear it soe long that I may not increase your trouble by an overhasty and imperfect account from hence, and I think my concerns there will bear that delay because I doe not remember that there is any thing now to be lett.
The businesse of the mony I finde troubles every body every where and cannot be much longer without a remedie. The receit of Guineas has lately very much perplexd affairs here. The latter end of the last weeke they fell to 27s. I hear they are again to day at 29s.†1 which is the worse, those at 29s or our present bad silver mony is hard to say. and therefor I cannot blame you that you are not forward to get mony into your hands whilst it is in this pickle. I am
Sir
your most humble servant
JOHN LOCKE

1952. Ezekiel Burridge to Locke, 3 October 1695 (2475)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, ff. 205-6. With it was enclosed no. 1945.
Sir
I make bold to trouble you with a letter tho' unknown.
My worthy friend Mr Molyneux in Dublin was pleas'd to be so kind as to honour me with a letter to you, I was this day at the place where he directed it in Little Lincoln's Inn Fields. a gentlewoman there told me you wou'd be very soon in town, were it not for that I wou'd presently have waited upon you in the Countrey.
I send you, Sir, the letter inclos'd, by reading it you'l find what the contents are, if a gentleman of your worth and character wou'd give your self, the trouble of doing what Mr Molyneux proposes, 'twou'd be an obligation which I shou'd never be able to return in any service you cou'd command me.
The favour which I would beg, Sir, of you, is, that you'd be pleas'd to let me know when I may meet you at the place of your abode in the countrey. the reason why I ask this favour is because I am apprehensive your suddain Comeing to town may be a means of my missing you in the Countrey. if I may make bold to beg the favour of two lines from you. your letter to Ezekiel Burridge at Potters Coffeehouse near St James's†1 will come to my hands.
You have humanity enough to pardon this boldness from a Stranger who is very ambitious to shew himself
Sir
your Very humble and grateful servant
EZEKIEL BURRIDGE

1956. John Freke to Locke, 8 October 1695 (1955, 1971)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 199-200.
October the 8th 1695
Sir
By Comand from my Lord Keeper I am to desire you to hasten what you can the sending the Lords Justices the paper they desired of you because we now hourly expect to hear that the King is arrived the wind having been fair for bringing him above 24 hours and continues soe†1
I can't learn that any they sent to have yet given their opinions but Mr Heathcott†2 whose sense is the same with what I believe yours will be, That noe lessening the weight of your Coin nor adding Alloy to it nor change of its Denomination will hinder an ounce of Silver from being exported nor have other effect than deceiving our selves at home and lessening our trade abroad and that if you debase it by increasing the Alloy soe much more Silver must be carryd out (if our Trade or other occasions force us to
― 449 ―
export) as will pay for the refining it and separating the Alloy from it when it come abroad
However I hear Mr Lownd's Report will be printed not for sale but to be given about to such as shall be thought worthy of it†1
Last Thursday the Sales-men†2 of Smithfield (as they call the Brokers of Cattle) had a meeting and agreed to take noe Guineas the next day in the market but 3 or 4 of them broke from their Agreement and then all the rest took them but not without Grumbling and I know not what may be done this week
The Parliament was this day Prorogued to the end of this month but tis believed will be Dissolved by the end of this week
The House of Commons in Ireland have Impeacht Sir Charles Porter†3 of High Crimes and Misdemeanors and prepared Articles against him but his party here say he has friends enough there to defeat the prosecution but I doe not hear that the Lord Capell stands by him
Mr Liddell†4 gives you his service. pray present mine to Sir Fr and my Lady and be assured I am
Your affectionate friend and humble servant JO: FREKE

1957. Locke to Mrs. Elizabeth Stratton, 14 October 1695 (681, 1963)
The William Andrews Clark Memorial Library of the University of California, Los Angeles. Transcribed from photostat. Answered by no. 1963.
Oates 14 Oct. 95
Dear Cosin
I received your letter of 21º Sept with the accounts annexed, when I was in London, for which I returne you my thanks. The
― 450 ―
reason why I writ not sooner to you is that all my papers being here I could neither say any thing to it nor make that use of it I had occasion till I came hither. The account I think is perfectly right as my Cosin your husband left it. If it were not I should never trouble you about lookeing back into that part of it. For if there were any mistake remaining (as I know of none) though it would be fit to rectifie it if he were alive if it ever appeard; yet by long experience I am soe confirmd in the opinion I always have had <of>†a his great honestie, that I should not question any thing he had left under his hand now he is noe longer here to explain it. As to that part you have added your self to what your husband had stated in his life time I must beg you if you can, to explain one or two things which are necessary for me to know before I can make a particular of what my tenants owe me to send to somebody in the country that may receive it of them
1 What has been paid for taxes or any other charges but repairs out of my estate in publoe by Joseph Barns or any other since 28º Nov 1693. For without that I cannot tell what William Gullock owes me for his sixth part or Thomas Somers for his twelfth part of the taxes and charges etc:
2 I find 4s received of Corn: Abram for a years rent due at our Lady day last. I desire you to tell me for what. I guesse it is for Somers's tenement held formerly by Kent. But a lease of it being granted last year to Mary Cooke; and one Mr Deane (as I finde) haveing paid the rent for it, for some years back, and also the fine for the lease to Mary Cooke. I am not sure Corn: Abraham paid for that. Though the summ agree, and I know not why he should pay me any rent at all.
3 Another thing I beg of you is to send me a list of what writeings you have of mine in your custodie, or belonging to me. Some of them will be usefull to me in the country, and some of them it will be convenient for me to have hither, when I see what they be I shall know how to dispose of them, as my occasions shall make it most convenient.
I doe not doubt Dear Cousin but your great losse in soe good an husband sits heavy upon you. I too have my share in the losse of soe good a friend and relation. We have soe many instances dayly of death seizing all ages and conditions of men, that you cannot think it your particular case to loose soe near a relation before old
― 451 ―
age. If this common lot of all man kinde be not sufficient to allay your greif in soe sad a dispensation, religion has stronger and more powerfull arguments to doe it and those you ought to hearken to and not to sorrow as one without hope. It is the will of god and you ought to submit with patience. And though you suffer in the want of a good husband, yet the remembrance that he was a good man ought to comfort you in the surer hopes that he is removed out of this world of trouble and misery into a state of happynesse where all tears are wiped away and all trouble is at an end. I have received many good offices and acts of kindenesse from my deceased Cosin. I should be glad of any occasion to shew how ready I am to acknowledg them to his wife and children. If there be any thing in my power wherein I may be serviceable to you or them you may be sure I shall very willingly doe it and to my utmost. I wish you all comfort and am
Dear Cosin
Your most assured friend and humble servant
JOHN LOCKE
Pray remember me kindly to my Cosins your daughters and to my Cosin Peter.
