1958. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 15/25 October 1695 (1933, 1999)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 101-2. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 90-2.
A Amsterdam le 25 d'Octobre 1695
Il y a long-temps, Monsieur, que j'aurois répondu à vos dernieres Lettres, pour vous remercier de vos bons avis sur la maladie de nôtre petit garçon, et du remede que vous nous avez envoié, si je n'avois crû qu'il falloit attendre quelque temps, pour en voir l'effet. Il ne sauroit être plus heureux, puisque depuis qu'il en prend, il s'est beaucoup fortifié, est devenu plus gras, et a entierement changé de couleur; mais il ne se soûtient pas encore, et il a quelquefois le ventre assez dur. J'ai redoublé la dose du remede, sur l'avis
― 452 ―
que vous m'en avez donné dans la Lettre à Mr. Coste, et il continue à sen trouver bien. Il y a quelques jours qu'il lui est venu quatre ou cinq dents, outre six qu'il avoit déja, sans qu'on se soit apperçu qu'il ait été malade. Je ne sai néanmoins si, à cause de son ventre, qui est un peu dur, quoi qu'il ne soit pas resserré, il ne seroit point bon de mettre un peu de rhubarbe dans sa biere, comme nous avons fait ci-devant. C'est sur quoi j'attendrai vôtre avis. Je m'apperçois que les obligations, que je vous ai, augmentent tous les jours, sans que je vous en puisse marquer assez de reconnoissance; mais selon Seneque gratias habere est rependere,†1 quand on ne peut pas mieux, et j'espere que vous n'aurez pas sujet de vous plaindre de moi de ce côté-là. J'ai envoié au Sieur Sam.Smith, dans une balle de mon Pentateuque†2 un exemplaire pour vous, et un pour Mr. le Comte de Pembroke. Je les aurois fait relier, si je n'avois craint l'inégalité de la relieure, dans les volumes d'un même ouvrage. J'y aurois pû joindre ma Physique, si je n'étois obligé d'y faire un Errata, à cause des grosses fautes qui s'y sont glissées; mais il faut pour cela la lire avec application, et je n'en ai pas encore eu le temps. J'ai achevé mon petit livre de l'Incredulité, qui verra bien tôt le jour. Vous ne m'avez point fait savoir, si l'on vous avoit envoié Richelieu. Si vous l'avez, j'en suis bien-aise; sinon, je vous dirai qu'il s'en va faire incessamment une nouvelle édition, qui sera plus correcte, et qu'il vaudra mieux lire, que la précedente.†3 J'aurai soin de vous l'envoier, par une voie plus assurée, pour ne pas dépendre de la négligence et de la friponnerie des Libraires. Wetstein fait traduire en François le livre de la Reasonnablenes of Christianity etc. et il se débitera sans doute très-bien.†4 Un autre Libraire a témoigné avoir envie de faire traduire le vôtre de l'Entendement, et je croi qu'il le fera, et qu'il emploiera pour cela Mr. Coste.†5 Je l'aiderai, en toute ce que je pourrai, et je ne doute pas qu'il n'y réüssisse mieux qu'on ne pourroit faire en Latin. Mon Hammond a été arrêté pour quelques semaines, à cause de quelque autre occupation du Libraire, mais on recommencera dans peu. J'espere que cet ouvrage pourra être bien tôt fait, et que je recommencerai à travailler sur la Bible. Nos gens
― 453 ―
ne m'ont néanmoins pas encore continué les cinqs cents francs,†1 parce que le terme ne doit expirer qu'au Printemps prochain. Je ne sai <s'ils>†a le feront, car ce sont d'étranges gens; et les Hollandois sont si froids amis, qu'on ne peut guere faire compte sur eux. S'ils me refusoient la continuation de cette petite pension, il faudroit quitter cet Ouvrage, qui me rapporte trop peu pour continuer à le faire imprimer à mes frais, et que je ne pourrois pas donner pour rien. Je n'ai eu là dessus ni gratification, ni encouragement; au contraire j'ai fait assez de dépense, et divers mal honêtes gens m'ont mordu le plus qu'ils ont pu. J'ai envoié des exemplaires pour les deux Archevêques, un pour l'Evêque de Salish. et un quatriéme pour celui de Bath. Je leur ai même écrit afin du moins de les empêcher de donner trop de créance au Sieurs Du Veil, Allix et autres gens, qui se divertissent à dire du mal de ceux qu'ils ne connoissent pas. Il ne se passe rien ici de nouveau. On rimprime seulement les Critici Sacri de Londres, avec quelques additions de Drusius, et de quelques autres, mais qui ne sont rien d'exquis. Je suis de tout mon coeur, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC

1960. Locke to Cornelius Lyde, 29 October 1695 (1959, 2008)
The Pierpont Morgan Library, New York. Transcribed from Xerox print. The enclosure: B.L., MS. Locke c. 26, ff. 73-4. Copy made by Locke. Answers no. 1959.
London 29 Oct 95
Sir
I am very glad I was not out of town†1 when there was any oportunity to doe you any service there. As soon as I received yours of the 26th I immediately waited on my Lord Cheif Justice Holt†2 who told me you were not one of the three down upon the list last year and promised me you should not be put in the list this. Soe that I looke upon that businesse as donne. For my Lord Cheif Justice is soe much my freind that I make sure of this kindenesse now he has promised me and has gon soe far in it, that he with his own hand took your name and the excuses you furnished me with viz a small estate and a great family. It sometimes happens as it did last year in our County that a sherif is named by the King who is not one of the three upon the list and in that case I know not how far my Lord Cheif Justice can help you. You obleiged me soe much in soe frankly accepting the trouble of lookeing after my concernes near you, that I would not serve you by halves. I have some acquaintance and interest in some others of our great men and I shall not faile to imploy it all for you if there should be occasion. Two of the Gent upon the list are Mr Dyke and Mr Langton†3 the third I have forgot.
― 455 ―
If either of the three now in the list should as it some times falls out, endeavour to shift off the burden from themselves by endeavouring to lay it on you. I desire you (if you think fit) to furnish me with arguments more particular than saying in general that your estate is small and familie great whereby I may be able to shew reasons why either of them is fiter to serve than you. If you thinke it convenient to write any farther upon this occasion be pleased to direct your letter to me as your last was, and in my absence to Mr Clarke. with whom I will leave my request to take care of it, If my health shall force me out of town before the pricking of Sherifs.†1
Here inclosed I have sent you a particular state of my affairs with my tenants at Belton Pensford and Publoe. I have endeavourd to make it short and plain. If there be any thing in it which I have not sufficiently explaind upon any notice I shall farther make cleare to you. I hope the money†2 will now be speedily set right. In the meane time I leave it to you to doe with my tenants as you doe with your own to presse payment or to forbear as you shall think it most convenient. I am
Sir
your Faithfull friend and humble servant
J LOCKE

1961. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 7/17 November 1695 (1852, 1982)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9. ff. 131-2.
Rotterdam 17 November 1695
Dear Friend
My son Arent and I are faln into the same fault, and stand in need of the same pardon, I received yours of the 11 march, and 24 June by major Masham†1 and since the favour of those 3 books from Monsieur Le Clerq,†2 and the second Edition of your book of Education;†3 in their respective seasons, for which now I return you my hearty thanks. I pitty the poore Gentlemen that are so pesterd with those pragmatic Hereticks, that instead of explaining the Doctrine of the Trinity they do perplex and confound it so, by their various and contradictory ways of explication, that those parlous writers seem to have pleasure in so easily exposing them, as men intoxicated, each condemning his brothers system, as introducing on the one hand a Tritheism, or on the other hand destroying, what they all would seem to establish—a Trinity of persons in the Deity. Which makes me despair of ever seing it, to an impartiall mind, demonstrated to be of the number of those things, that are necessary to be beleeved in order to salvation, however it fare with the truth of the assertion: For if it be so intricate that the most learned, are so confounded in their explications of it, that they fly in one anothers faces, charging each others systems with Idolatry or Heresy—sure I am there's no possibility for the simple hearted, and unlearned people, to be ever cleare in the point. And so their securest way to passe it.
Mr. Spademan†4 askt me lately if you had sent me your new book, and I telling him you had, he was desirous to see it but when I
― 457 ―
told him it was the second Edition of your book of Education He said that that was not the book, he meant, but your book of the Christian Religion, I told him I had heard of no such thing: asking if he were certain you had publisht any such Treatise, and if your name were fixt to it, he said no: but that it was sufficiently known to be yours.†1
I doubt not but you have heard of a book, under that Title, that goes for yours, If you have not heard of it, this intimation will not be unseasonable. If you have, and you know the booke, I intreat you to direct mr. Wright where he may buy that book; whether you be the Author of it or no, for that secret I desire not to know: onely of this I am sure, common fame will never impute silly writings to you: who are too well known. But I cannot but put you in mind of your promise, in your will, to leave me a list of what writings you shall have abroad in the world at your death, that if I survive you I may discharge my promise, except you Judge some other person more fit, of collecting and causing them to be printed.†2
I have now onely to inform you that our cuntry is full of lotterys not onely all the capitall towns, that have Vote in the Assembly of States, but other Towns and villages have obtaind Octroys of the Soveraign, for relief of the poore.†3
And among others this Town has the most favourable that I have seen consisting of 62500 Lots, at 20f per lot, amounting to f1250000, among which are 15640 prizes, and consequently but (or rather scarce) 3 nuls to one prize.
One of f50000. 1 of f40000. 1 of f25000. 1 of f15000. 1 of f10000. one a f6000. 1 a f5000. 2 a f4000. 3 a f3000. 4 a f2000. 30 a f1000. 40 a f700. 50 a f500. 100 a f400. 150 a f300. 250 a f200. 500 a f100. 1200 a f80. 2500 a f70. 3200 a f60. 3600 a f50. 4000 a f40. And f1000 for them whose names shal be drawn first and last, and those immediately before and after the highest prize each f500 over and above what they may be benefited by those draughts.
I purpose for my wife, self, and children and her sister, to lay in (under the name of the English society) several f100 and have writ to divers of my friends in England, that if they pleas to have any thing added upon their account, it may go under the same title,
― 458 ―
and we shal, if any prizes be drawn, divide them proportionably amongst us. Or if they will have any layd in upon their account particularly that I shall so do.
If you think fit to be concernd let me know it, it is designd to be drawn the 1 march new stile, or sooner, if sooner full. There are divers other Lotteryes on foot, but none so favourable having, 7,8,9 10 and some 13 a 26 nuls to one prize—The advantage that the poore is designd to reap by this Towns Lottery is f100000 which those that have the prizes, must abate of their prizes, at the rate of 8 per Cent.
Inclosed comes my son Arents Apology. he is grown so expert in Arithmetick that there is no account that comes into my Comptoir, but he examines it, before it be bookt, he endorses all my letters, bills of lading, and other papers, seals and superscribes all Letters, and goes abroad, alone, and sometimes with his Brother Benjohan to fetch in mony, and is so arch at it, that he gets mony, where I can get none, having his mother, who loves him dearly, for his Instructor. I should send him now for England to his brother John but that his mother cannot part with him.
My dearest has her dearest Salutations to you and also to Sir Francis and My Lady Masham, which be pleased also to accept and tender from
Deare friend
your humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
Dr. Kohlhans who is at present here salutes you heartily

1962. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 9 November 1695 (1863, 1968)
B.L., MS. Locke. b. 8, no. 89. Printed in Rand, pp. 424-5.
London. 9º Nov 95
Madam.
I was very glad to see Mr Clarke last night returnd safe to town with other looks in his face and a lesse weight on his heart than when I last parted with him here at his goeing out of it. It was
― 459 ―
welcome news to me to receive from him an assurance that you were upon your legs again, and such an account of your health, which though yet distant from your former strength, yet I conclude there is noe more required to bring you to it again but a litle time, and a litle care in the management of your self. He tells me your legs are a litle apt to swell some times. you know I am not a man very fond of wine, and therefor I may be trusted when I advise it. I think it very necessary in your present case to drink a small glasse of good wine once or twice a day, and I think it would be best warmd. Set a litle silver cup to the fire till it be very hot, power your glasse of wine into it and power it back again presently. this will warme it, without wasting the spirits, and thus dranke, it will comfort your stomack, strengthen your spirits and hasten your recovery. For you want a restorative diet, litle and good, and oft, and if in convenient cases you use nutmeg and other spices more plentifully than you used to doe. it will not be hurtfull to you. I know that I am at a distance, and that under the care of soe good a physitian as you have,†1 my advice is needlesse. But where one has great concerne I find one cannot be wholy silent. I returne you my thanks for your kinde letter by Mrs Burges's hand.†2 I hope some time or other to convince you that your obleigeing invitations are not lost upon me. I wish you a dayly increase of your health and am
Madam
your most humble and most obleiged servant
JOHN LOCKE
Pray give me leave to present my service to Mr Burges and the little ones. Though I have not had the leisure to day yet it will not be long before I visit Mis Nany, whom her father tells me he has brought to town with him.

1963. Mrs. Elizabeth Stratton to Locke, 11 November 1695 (1957, 2010)

Bristoll Novem 11th (1695)
Deare Cousen
I beleeve you expected an answer to your kind letter before now this comes to give you my hear'ty thanks and the best account of your business as I am able, I procurd my Brother Chapman†1 to goe to Pensford to speake with your tennants but cannot find so much sattisfaction from any as I find in my deare Husbanes papers; which I have heare inclosd with a list of all the wrightings of yours now in my custodie as I have got it drawn out by a Layer a Freind of mine, the three bills of Charge (one the backside of the list), of Joseph Barns' are drawn exactly by his bills, the other you'l see is what my deare had drawn, for what use you will understand better than I doe, that 4 shillings which Corn: Abraham paid was for the House formerly Kents but now Cooks; I hope this will sattisfie the three things you mention if in any thing els I am capable to serve you or any you shall appoynt to have a sight of my Husbands books and papers tis's at your Command, but my unspeakable loss have so dimm'd my sight and clouded my head that I am unfit for business and therefore am forct to trouble my kind freind my bro Chapman with all my concerns who is exceeding kind to us and have taken home me, and my children, if you please to direct your letter to me at his house; for haveing lost the best Husband and one of the best of men and that one a sudden in the mid'st of his busine<ss>†a heare tho allways with a due sence of God, that nothing was sudden to him but the unspeakable Joys he pass'd into out of A world of trouble, I am left behind to morn as long as please God haveing lost the sweetest comfort of my life, yet not without hope of a blessed injoyment in the place of bliss and happyness to eternity. I humbly beg your pardon and remain
Deare Cousin
Your Kind freind and humble Servant
ELIZABETH STRATTON

1964. Sir John Somers, later Baron Somers, to Locke, [c. 15 November 1695] (1949, 1979)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 159-60. Printed in King, pp. 241-2. Date: The book mentioned is Lowndes's Report: p. 442, n. 2. In his entry for 16 November Luttrell reports that the book, 'newly published by the kings printers, is given to the lords of the council, etc.' The distribution of the copies probably took place on 15 or 16 November (Luttrell does not mention the Report in his entry for 14 November); Somers may have received a copy on the evening preceding the distribution; hence the date 15 or 16 November for the letter.
Lowndes gave Locke a copy of his Report during his present visit to London, and perhaps before Somers received the copy mentioned in this letter: Further Considerations, preface. L.L., no. 1816.
Sir
You will easily see by the book, which was put in my hand last night, and by the Title of a Report, which it bears, as well as by the Advertisement at the end of it, that you were in the right when you said the alteration of the Standard was the thing aimd at. The Challenge at the End, if you will allow mee to say so, is in some sort directed to you. The proposition which you and I discoursed upon yesterday is endeavourd to be represented as impracticable. The passing of money by weight is said to be ridiculous, at least in little payments. The suddain fall of Guinnies, will be an utter ruin to very great numbers. There is no encouragement proposed to invite people to bring the Clippd money into the Mint, so that will be melted down to be transported, which will be a certain profit at
― 462 ―
least till by a Law money can be Exported. And whilst this is doing nothi<n>g†a <will be>†a left to carry on Commerce, for no one will bring out his Guinnies to part with them for 20s when he paid 30s for them so lately. These, (as I remember) were the objections made use of, and I doubt not but you will without great difficulty help us with some expedients for them. I beleive it an easier task then to remove (what I see is so fixd) the Project of alteration of the Standard. I am
Your most humble servant
J. SOMMERS

1965. Locke to William Molyneux, 16 November 1695 (1945, 1966)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 125-7. Answered by no. 1984.
London, 16. Nov. 1695.
Sir,
Though there be no man in the world that I so much long to see as you, yet your last letter, of the second instant,†1 makes me afraid of your coming. Your kindness and expression, in my favour, has painted me so in your fancy, that I shall unavoidably fall many degrees in your esteem, when you find me come so much short of what you expected; paratus est mihi magnus adversarius expectatio,†2 as I remember, Tully somewhere says. One thing only I have to satisfie my self, viz. That, whatever I may want of those qualities you ascribe to me, I have one that helps mightily to cover defects, and make one acceptable, without the recommendation of great perfections, I mean friendship, true and sincere. This I can boast of to you, this I can bid you expect, and tell you you shall not be deceived. Come then, but come with this resolution, that you will be content, that shall make up to you all those fine things which you imagine before hand, in a man whom you will really find a
― 463 ―
plain, honest, well-meaning man, who unbyassedly seeks truth, though it be but a very small part of it he has yet discover'd.
I am very glad you approve the additions to the third edition of my Education;†1 you are a father, and are concerned not to be deceived, and therefore I expect you will not flatter me in this point. You speak so well of that you have, that I shall take care to have another of those treatises of Interest and Coinage sent to you.†2 The affair of our mony, which is in a lamentable state, is now under debate here, what the issue will be, I know not; I pray for a good one. I find every body almost looks on it as a mystery; to me there appears to be none at all in it. 'Tis but stripping it of the cant which all men that talk of it, involve it in, and there is nothing easier, lay by the arbitrary names of pence and shillings, and consider and speak of it as grains and ounces of silver, and 'tis as easy as telling of twenty.
I had a great deal more to say to you in answer to this, and two other obliging letters, I am indebted to you for. But I am sent for into the country by an express.†3 I am,
Sir,
Your most humble, and most affectionate servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
1966. Locke to William Molyneux, 20 November 1695 (1965, 1984)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 127-30. Answers nos. 1936 and 1945; answered by no. 1984.
Oates, 20 Nov. 1695.
Sir,
Before I left London, I gave order that the book you desired about Interest and Money, should be sent you by the first opportunity. But 'tis to you I send it, and not to any body else; you may give it to whom you please, for 'tis yours as soon as you receive it, but pray do not give it to any body in my name, or as a present from me. And however you are pleased to make me a compliment, in making me the author of a book you think well of, yet you may be sure I do not own it to be mine, till you see my name to it.†4
― 464 ―
You, I see, are troubled there about your money, as well as we are here, tho', I hope, you are not so deep in that disease as we are. A little before his Majesties return, the Lords Justices here had this matter under consideration, and, amongst others, were pleased to send to me for my thoughts about it. This is too publickly known here, to make the mentioning of it to you appear vanity in me. The paper I here inclose would seem a strange thing, did I not tell you the occasion of my writing it.†1 And, since some of my friends here persuade me, it gives some light to that, which the statesman you mention,†2 thinks so profound a mystery; I have taken the liberty to send it you, either to open that matter a little farther to you, or that you may shew me the mistakes and defects of it. But, pray, whatever use you make of it, conceal my name.
I writ to you from London, just as I was leaving the town in haste, in answer to yours of the second instant. You must pardon the faults of that to the hurry and disturbance I was then in. I am not much more at leisure, or at quiet, now; but shame will not suffer me to be silent any longer, under the obligation of two other letters I have by me of yours unanswer'd.
I cannot read yours of the 24th of August last, without finding new marks of your kindness to me, in the concern you therein express to get a good hand for the translating my Essay. I think, at last, you have got a better than I could have expected. I designed to have brought Mr. Churchill and him together, and settled that matter before I left London; but I was so unexpectedly called thence, that I left that and several other businesses undone. But I took order with Mr. Churchill, my bookseller, to go to him; he is a reasonable man, and, I doubt not, but it will be taken care of, as well as if I were there. I think the abridgment is near, if not quite printed, but I had not the time or memory to enquire, after my hasty summons into the country. I was told too, when I was in town, that some body is printing against it;†3 if it be a fair enquirer I shall be glad, if a wrangling disputant, I shall not mind him.
Mr. Burridge is the man you speak him to be, in yours of September 19. Had I stay'd in London, I think, I should have been able to have procured him some particulars, would have been of use to
― 465 ―
him in his design. Some of them I have taken care he should receive, notwithstanding my absence. But perhaps they might have been more, could I have stay'd till more of my acquaintance were come to town. I am now in an house of sorrow and business, which hinders me from that freedom I would be in, when I write to you. I am,
Sir,
your most affectionate, humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.

1968. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 22 November [1695] (1962, 1991)
Rand, pp. 425-6. Some lines 'illegible'; word in square brackets supplied by Rand. The year from Mrs. Cudworth's death.
Oates, 22nd November
Madam,
Though I could wish you had no pain at all, yet I think those which are the marks of returning health (as I look on yours to be) ought not very much to fright us, and may be borne with the more patience. The pains and swelling in your leg which returns sometimes you have a remedy for it. You have tried and cannot I think have a better than the Queen of Hungary's water. But perhaps that will be made more effectual if you first foment the part with flannel soaked in brandy made as hot as you can endure it over a chafing dish of coals, and when you have repeated the hot brandy flannels three or four times, or as often as you can bear it, then put on hot flannel soaked in the Queen of Hungary's water, and so let it lie on all night. This fomentation I would have used when you are in bed. And in the morning rub the part, if you can bear it, with a piece of dry flannel fumed with the smoke of amber powdered grossly and thrown upon some live coals.
You complain, I perceive, of another swelling in your legs increasing towards evening without pain. This I think is to be cured by diet. I would advise you to drink as little as you can, but especially to forbear much small drink. And be sure to drink every day a glass or two of good wine such as you like best, or good mum oftener, if you can get it. And for your meat, let it be fresh meat such as you like best, and let it be but of one sort at one time; eat not of varieties at the same time. But when you have a stomach again and fancy anything else, let it be got ready for you. In your case it matters not to observe hours, or set meals. Only I would not have you eat any flesh after candle lighting, for by that time I think convenient you should be in bed. Good, light, well-baked bread of the best [flour] you can take, and this I recommend to you....†a
My Lady is in great affliction for the loss of her mother.†1 She
― 467 ―
presents her service to you, and wishes the speedy return of your perfect health. I very particularly and earnestly wish you were rid of all the remains of your disease. I count a little care and time will perfect recovery. I heartily desire it, and am,
Dear Madam,
your most affectionate and most humble servant,
J. LOCKE.
Address: For Mrs. Mary Clarke, at Chipley, near Taunton.
Endorsed by Mrs. Clarke: Mr. Locke's letter concerning the swelling in my legs ...

London November the 30th 1695
Sir
Your being in Town would be of great use to your Country many ways. Your influence is needed to make the business of the Coin to be taken into consideration and to be considerd rightly and though in this you might in your absence be further serviceable than you have been already by what you have publisht by sending up your thoughts on Mr L ds Book to be made publick as I have dayly expected you would and not onely I have expected it but all your other friends great and litle, yet your writings would not doe soe much good as your writings and your discourse†1
You would alsoe serve your Country by taking care to execute your office and hear the Appeals that are made to you and that will very probably be dayly made to you for if they are not heard there will be complaints and possibly to Parliament and then tho you have a good excuse for your self the whole Comission will not and an occasion may be taken to break the Comission wholy and leave the Appeal to Westminster Hall and then the Revenue of Excise will be ruind and come to nothing which at this time I think is not a desireable thing
― 470 ―
As to your business with Mr Powell he has promised me to raze out the receit of the 6li from the Back of the Deed and then shew it me and you need not fear but it shall be done soe as there shall noe danger threaten or hurt befall you on the account of that affair
Sir F: M: as he sends you the Votes is better able to send you the Debates than any else†1 and for the Springs and tendency of things we are strangers to the first and but guessers at the last
But to your Question about the Speaker I must answer you the Court was soe wise to Join with their enemys and force their friends to comply with them by making Sir Tho Lit: be absent at the Choice†2
We hoped yesterday to have got <an>†a Address to make Clipt Mony goe by weight but the Grave Squire was deserted tho the Night before the K had Commanded the Courtiers to press that matter†3 and if possible carry it and very frankly and publickly declared that his opinion and his inclinations were right in that matter. I now hope better success the next time this thing shall be moved (which may be moonday)†4 but I'm sure if your thoughts on Mr L ds book were publick before the motion they would contribute much to the obtaining our End for really the Country Gentlemen can hardly be made understand this business
Give our service to my Lady and be assured we are
Your affectionate friends and humble servants

1972. Locke to John Freke and Edward Clarke, 2 December 1695 (1971, 1974)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 90. Printed in Rand, pp. 426-8. Answers no. 1971; answered by no. 1974.
Oates 2 Dec. 95
Sir
I am soe bad a solicitor and have acquaintance with soe few members that I imagin my presence in town would that way be very little serviceable to my Country and only wast the time I now spend in writeing what you desire,†1 which whatever may be expected from me I cannot dispatch faster than my health and leisure will permitt. The first weeke after my comeing into the country was taken up with the businesse and Bishop that was here.†2 Since that my cough and tooth ach which have†a greivously tormented me have required some allowance of time to be made to them, and yet I have not been wholy idle but cannot write post what I intend for the presse. In the meane time you have my papers on that subject†3 which you may communicate or give copys of to all those, who would be serviceable in the debate who I thinke are not many. for if any thing I can say may be usefull or of force there I think it is. And I have been the lesse forward to print on this occasion because I remember I was told when I was goeing once to print some thing on this subject, that I†b was better not, in regard of the Parliament, for that arguments that were in print were quite lost when made use of in the house and signified noething
As to the businesse of the Appeals I desired you to speake to some of my brethren to see what dispotion they were in to execute their office and hear the appeals that are before us, unlesse I know that, I may take a third journey to town and wait there to the prejudice of and danger of my health as I have done twice already to noe purpose. For I cannot hear Appeals my self and if my brethren will not I cannot help it. I had rather loose two places than one life.
― 472 ―
I thank you for your care of my businesse with Mr Powell. I looke upon it as safe in either of your hands. But when both of you joyn to consider of it I think I need not ever aske a question about it.
Thoug you are as you say, but Guessers yet pray whilst I am absent now and then communicate some of your Guesses. I had rather know them than some of the inlightend Pol's certaintys.†1
Your direct answer to my question about one person is what I suspected by the discourse of our host where we dined togeather, though how it was orderd to goe soe glibly I could not guesse till you told me.†2 Is the world stark mad? Doe you remember a question I once asked you about your Cosin P:†3 I cannot get my thoughts off from that place. Things doe not come about without some influence. and the Squires being deserted as you tell me gives me further doubt. If that point be caried all may goe well but my papers could not possibly be publique before that motion and after it I hope will come time enough for what will remain. I make what hast I can. I have a designe to dedicate it to my Lord Keeper if he will allow of it. that will give me an oportunity to say something which will not possibly come in soe well in the body of the discourse
Pray give me your thoughts of the Parliament, and tell me who is sherif for Somerset shire.
The printing act†4 I see has been taken care of to the utmost and I thank you it is lodgd and thats well. I am
Sir (which is a title belongs to either, to both, to the Colledg, as the matter directs)
your most affectionate and most humble servant
JOHN LOCKE

1973. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 3/13 December 1695 (1931, 2028)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 69-70.
Amst 13 dec. 95
Monsieur
Peu apres ma derniere, je receu de Monsieur Cyprianus le livre de Monsieur Ridley†1 que vous luy aviez donné pour moy. je vous en suis extremement obligé. et j'y trouve plusieurs bonnes remarques: quoy que pourtant on pouroit y adjouster une structure plus exacte de la dure mere et du plexus choroeide, et en mesme temps leur veritable usage. dans la peine ou nous sommes tousjours comment nous acquitter des obligations que nous vous avons, ma femme a pris la liberté de vous envoyer par la voye de Monsieur Furley (qui a bien voulu s'en charger) une robbe de chambre d'une estoffe qu'on luy avoit envoyé des Indes. elle y a joint une petite escharpe de sa facon. nous esperons que cela vous sera rendu, et que vous pardonnerez quon ose vous presenter si peu de chose. nous esperons que vostre santé sera meilleure cet hyver, que le precedent. nous avons icy presentement beaucoup de calme et de beau temps, et ma femme ne se resent presque plus de sa poitrine. je croy que la disposition de nostre demeure qui est fort exaucée†2 et aerée y contribue beaucoup. nostre pierot s'est emancipé de vous escrire une lettre francoise, et souhaitte de pouvoir le faire bien tost en latin. nostre plus petit devient fort vigoureu depuis sa maladie, et ses cicatrices sont plus supportables. toute la famille, mon beau pere, mon bonhomme de Pere qui a 92 ans,†3 mon frere ma seur et sa nombreuse famille, tous se portent bien et ma seur derechef au point d'accoucher. Ma femme et mes enfans vous presentent leurs treshumbles respects, et je suis,
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON.
il faut que je vous adjouste icy une observation de chirurgie qui est tres belle.
Monsieur Pieter Adriaensche ayant apris par une lettre de son ancien serviteur Thomas†4 que vous avez establi chez luy, que le
― 474 ―
grand pere de sa femme chirurgien a Londres avoit avec success dans l'amputation de la jambe conservé les muscles du gras de la jambe, et les faire reunir sans suppuration a la partie d'ou los est amputé. il a d'abord gousté cette experience, et la voulu imiter a la premiere occasion. il y a donc environ deux mois que devant amputer la jambe d'un petit garcon de sept ans, a qui les os du tarse et matatarse estoient fort cariez. il sy pris de cette sorte. ayant marqué l'endroit ordinaire. la largeur de la main du malade sous le genoux. et apres avoir fait ses ligatures comme on a de coustume. il passa un coutau droit joint et sous le tibia percant a l'opposite de la jambe proche et sous le peroné. puis glissa son coutau vers embas, tousjours joignant le tibia et peroné jusquau tendon du suratus et gastrocnemius, a quel endroit il coupa le tendon, et laissa pendre le lambau du gras de jambe, scia en suitte les deux os, a l'endroit ordinaire, toucha l'os pour voir sil restoit quelque esquil ou inegalité. puis replia le lambau du gras de jambe contre l'extremité des os sciés et les chairs joignantes. appliqua ensuitte ses adstringents au bords. il ne survint aucune hemorrhagie. et le lambau se trouva le troisiesme jour affermi et aglutiné a la partie superieure, couvrant exactement l'os et ne laissant quune playe recente a la partie superieure du moignon, le bout estant couvert du gras de jambe replié. le guerison fut parfaitte en moins d'un mois.†1 on luy a fait une jambe creuse dans la quelle s'emboitte son moignon sur le quel il marche a plomb sans incommodité plie le genou et le bas couvre si exactement le tout. quon s'apercoit a peine de son defaut. quand il est assis, pouvant plier l'un genou comme l'autre, il est impossible de le remarquer.
Address: For Doctor John Locke at Mr. Powlings in little lincolns inne feilds. London.
Postmark: DE 6

1974. John Freke to Locke, 5 December 1695 (1972, 1976)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 203-4. Answers no. 1972.
December the 5th 1695
Sir
You needed not have been a sollicitor had you been in Town and yet you would have been very serviceable to your Country in being here for There are very many gentlemen who would have sought to you to have been set right in their Notions what is fit to be done at this time with respect to the Coin. The Country Gentlemen come up very raw in this matter and the Monyers are soe busie buzzing hard words and unintelligible cant in their heads and then threatening them with I know not what dreadfull Consequences that not onely the Country Gentlemen but even men that have been once right in their notions are (or for some private reasons seem to be) confounded. I will onely Instance in the Gentleman whose visit you had not time to return and desired the Grave Squire in a former letter to make your excuse to for that omission.†1 You know when he and the Grave Squire met at your chamber last summer he seemed to understand the matter right but now he publickly talks otherwise and is full of fears of I know not what dangers may ensue if one could not with a clipt shilling pay a Coach man. now I dare say had you been in Town you would have cured him of all his fears and made him a usefull instrument for the obtaining what is necessary to be done speedily if it be thought necessary that this Government should subsist three months longer
However though with great difficulty The Commons in a Comittee of the whole House voted That the most effectuall way to prevent the mischiefs the Nation suffers by the Currency of Clipt mony is to recoin the same,†2 but the Lords went further and voted that an Address be made to the King to Issue a proclamation to stop the currency of Clipt mony and have this day sent it down to the Commons for their Concurrence the Consideration whereof is adjournd till to morrow though I doubt as our friends mannage the matter all of them (allways leaving the grave Squire in the lurch and never seconding him) It will be a Question whether twill come on then because by order the House is to be in a comittee concerning
― 476 ―
Trade which Sir Christopher Musgrove†1 etc: will be sure to preferr and prevail in their endeavours to doe it if none but our friend will oppose them
The Grave has not yet seen Sir William Honywood but has spoken to Major Beak and he says nothing can be done till you come to Town and I believe they†2 know not what to doe without you
You need take noe care of your business with Mr Powell all things shall be done in it to your content soe that you shall be sure to be safe
Though I have not had an oppertunity to speak with my Lord K yet I dare give you licence for him to make the dedication as you desire†3 but let me entreat you earnestly to make what haste you can in p<er>fecting†a that work which the season calls soe earnestly for and the sooner it appears <the gr>eater†a will be its grace and usefullness. In the mean time I thank you for the leave you give me to permitt coppys to be taken of what you left with me
Give our service to my Lady and tell her if anyone swore himself Freeholder that was not soe he may be indicted at the Asizes or Sessions or an Information be preferrd against him in the Crown office for the perjury though I confess I never saw it practiced nor know I of any other way of punishing him
The Printing Bill though all the objections against the last are cured raises now more Clamour then was raised on that subject last Sessions but noe matter for that the House is possest of the Bill and the young members possest with a sufficient prejudice against the old Act. I am now onely to set my hand to what I have written Mr Clarke having set his on the out side soe that this is to be subscribed from
Your obliged friend and humble servant
JOHN FREKE

1976. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 10 December 1695 (1974, 1978)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 205-6. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's initials and the address.
December the 10th
Sir
We gratefully acknowledge the obligation you have laid on us by the severall Letters we received from you of the 8th and the Grave Squire bids me assure you that there is not one Question in your Catechize that he had not asked in proper time and place and though noe one pretended to give an answer to them yet the matter was resolved as you have heard.
As to the papers though you recalld your orders for publishing them (in a postscript) yet I noe sooner had perused them but I
― 478 ―
resolved they should come abroad in the world and I was this morning confirmd in that Resolution by the Gentleman to whom you design to dedicate them and who now in person has granted leave you should. I read onely the last leaf to him and he presently took them in his hand, and said I will read them all over but presently deliverd them back and said noe let them be printed as soon as possible I will read them then which I have not leisure to doe now and I would not have them kept an hour from the Press whereupon I Carryd them to Mr Ch and bid him goe to work on them and send them to Mr P to correct and I went to Mr P and desired him to undertake to Correct them which he said he would gladly doe†1
You know there is now noe need of a Licence†2 and if there were neither of the persons you mention would doe it the matter not being within their province
You desire a list of those that are able and likely to second a friend of ours†3 in a certain Debate and I am at a loss whom to name. There are many in service that were able and I thought likely but the event has shewn me that want of will or ability has made it difficult to name one of that sort, though some of them have spoken well when it was out of season and some times been of a doubting or different opinion from our friend when else the reason he offerd had prevaild. There are two or three who are not in service who have offerd fairly but want of experience has made them speak out of time or else add what has spoild all which has soe discouraged them as to make them afterwards remain silent soe that the whole burthen has lain almost on one man
I have onely to tell you Mr Lancton†4 is Sheriff of Somerset and then I have answered all your Letters which done I have onely the News of what the House has done this day to add and soe conclude
The Severall Resolutions made in the Comittee were this day reported and all agreed to but that about the Standard bore some hours Debate and at last it was carryd to continue the old Standard on a Division of the House wherein 114 were for a New Standard and 225 for Continuing the old.
Give me leave also to inform you that these votes have already made all Clipt half crowns to be unpassable (and I believe tomorrow
― 479 ―
shillings will be soe too). The Exchange to Holland is already alterd and Bulloin abated in its price 6d an ounce†1 But the Actions in the Bank are risen from 94li (which they were last week) to 101li this evening.†2 The Goldsmiths endeavour to keep up Guineas and yesterday and this day there has been much trade in buying and selling them at 29s-9d, 29-8d, 29s-6d and 29s-4d and some tradesmen took them this day at 30s.†3
But before I end I must tell you I believe this night a Comission will be resolved on to settle a Councill of Trade in which you will be named together with 5 or 6 other persons with whom you will not be unwilling to be Joind with an appointment of 1000li per an to each Comissioner and this my Lord K bid me intimate to you that you may prepare for it in case he summon you up about it as he belives he shall next post†4
Give our service to my Lady and believe us
Sir
Your affectionate friends and humble servants

1977. Charles Mordaunt, earl of Monmouth, later third earl of Peterborough, to Locke, [12 December 1695] (1788, 2297)
B L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 119-20. Printed in King, p. 238. Date from postmark, Locke's endorsement, and contents. Monmouth was a Privy Councillor at this time.
Mr Lock.
I cannot but writt to you to give some ease to my ill humour, For Tho so acustomed to see such Follies committed, i cannot be insensible when i see them repeated espetially when The public and a Friend is concern'd. i was somedayes agoe extreamly pleased when the King was brought to so reasonable a resolution as to determine upon a Councell of Trade where some great men were to assist but where others with sallarys of a 1000 pounds a yeare were to be fixt as the constant Labourers. Mr Lock being to be of this number made me have the better opinion of the thing, and comforted me for our last disapointment upon your subject,†1 but according to our acustomed wisdome, and prudence when all things had been a good while adjusted the pattent ready for the seal and some very able and honest men provided for your compagnions, it was impossible to gett the King to signe itt, but delaying it from day to day the parlament this day fell upon itt and are going to forme such a commission to be nominated by themselves, our great managers surprised were forced to run up to some in our house, others to goe to Kensington, so that att last the Secretary informes the house at the latter end of the debate and much consultation, that the King had just Formed such a commission with all that could be said to prevent their further proceedings, but they all lookd upon it as a trick, and all they could doe was to putt it to a vote for an adjournment which in a full house after great heat they carried but by 11.†2 this is the effect of our gravity and prudence, what the event will be i Know not, but for the little i am able, i shall endeavour Mr Lock may be the choice of the house as well as the Kings, if it takes that Course, if the ill weather prevent you not
― 481 ―
it were not improper you were in Town, but above all things take care of your self, without which your friends will loose the pleasure they may have in serving you, i hope we may make the house desist and that your affaire is fix'd, but these unnecessary labours mought be spared to those that have enough to doe
Sir
your affectionate servant
MONMOUTH.
Thirday night

1978. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 14 December 1695 (1976, 1981)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 207-8. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's initials and the address.
December the 14th 1695
Sir
I imagine that nobody will for the future say that the Government do's not take all the proper methodes for the incourgement of Trade that can be invented since the House of Commons have given their approbation to the Resolutions taken by his Majesty in voting those things and onely those things necessary which his Majesty was fixt on before. For their voting and Adressing that the provisions sent to the Forces abroad should pay noe Excise nor Customs in Holland or Flanders after they were told that they were already freed from those Dutys by a Treaty†2 And their voting a Comittee or Councill of Trade to be establisht after they were assured that a Comission was passing to Establish such a Councill I
― 482 ―
look upon as an high encomium upon his Majestys Conduct in these particulars and an authentick approbation of it and in my opinion ought (and I believe will) hasten the passing the Comission Constituting the Councill of Trade of which I gave you some intimation in my last
As to the powers that the House of Commons intend to give the Councill of Trade by Act of Parliament if they are necessary for the better execution of the Trust reposed in the Councill and such as could not be given by the King alone I believe the King and People will thank them for such an Act and promote the passing it: but if the Commons would Establish that Councill on such a foundation as is inconsistent with our Constitution I believe they will hardly soe far agree amongst themselves as to make it pass their House and if they should the other two parts of the Legislature will scarce be brought to consent to make any breach in the orders of our Government†1 And beside I believe they will get noe wise men (and of such this Councill ougt to consist or else twill be useless and perhaps dangerous) to accept of it. for to Execute a power inconsistent with the Fundamentalls of our Constitution is dangerous tho an Act of Parliament should Authorise it as Empsom and Dudleys Case†2 will convince any one that considers it
The House of Commons are to be upon the consideration of this same Councill of Trade again this day what they doe you shall be informd in a post script when I come to the Tavern and receive a Report from the members. At presant I shall goe to another subject which I suppose may give you some Diversion and that is the Bill for Regulating the Press.
The Grave Squire is attacqued on all sides on account of that Bill the Bishops are Alarmd and by the AB of C†3 have treated with him that more Care might be taken of the Church and the truth on't is his Grace is soe reasonable and fair a man that he proposes litle but what will I believe be granted him and soe he will be contented though I doubt the rest of the Clergie as litle after the amendments he proposes as they are now. The Dissenters are likewise Alarmd and have Deputed one of their party to apply to the Squire and a
― 483 ―
time and place of meeting has been appointed between him and this Godly Deputy but the man of God was invited to a merry meeting together with his wife and soe faild the Squire who will therefore (I believe) be hardly brought to give him another Assignation. The Government is likewise Alarmd for fear of loosing the prerogative of granting other mens Labours and making mony by Giving a sole power to some to impose a kind of tax on others that is by enabling them to set what prices they please on books they can purchase a patent for the sole printing of. But this grieveance to the Government is not the thing it complains of but a hundred petty objections are raised against the Bill as that a printer may set up more presses than is fit and that Exeter Bristoll etc: are not places that need presses and that there is noe body in those Towns fit to Inspect them when the Bishops are at parliament. And that noe body has power to strike out or alter any thing in a Book as it is printing and a great many other such objections they make all which would vanish if it would be agreed that old Grants of the Crown should be allowd and confirmd and thereby new ones acknowledged to be good. The universitys are also Alarmd and rail at the Bill but make noe other objection but that there is noe saving of their priviledges as was in the old Act and for that I believe it will be allowd them that it shall be added in the words of the Act by a saving without words of confirmation of their priviledges. The Kings printers are likewise Alarmd and perhaps they have reason but I believe twill be hard for them to get their Grants confirmed by parliament. The Common Printers likewise complain of the Bill and take exceptions against it for matters that are not containd in the Bill and soe doe the Booksellers and Stationers and especially the Company whose great grieveance is that their property is like to be limitted to certain number of years
Temple Tavern†1

that Anthony Rowes Return†1 was not duely or Legally made and this was all their work this day and the further consideration of the Comittee of Trade is put off to Teusday

Sir
I hope the Kings nomination of you to be one of the Council of Trade, will not (in the first place) be prejudiciall to your Health in giving sometimes your attendance: If that point be secure, I am sure the Publick will have the advantage. 1981. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 17 December 1695 (1978, 1985)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 209-10. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's initials and the address.
December the 17th 1695
Dear Sir
You shall know the reason why I resolved your papers should be publisht when I see you in the mean time methinks you should have been satisfied with one reason I gave you in my last for publishing them i.e. the order of him to whom they are dedicated†2
― 486 ―
I have received the packet and Letter which you sent away the 15th and my Lord has read the Epistle and orderd me to strike out a whole line in one place and two words in another to avoid offence and with those corrections I have sent it and the rest of the papers (which I have perused and found noe need to Correct in any thing) to the press and Mr Churchill†a promises me the whole shall be printed by the end of this week†1 and I have orderd him to give a book or two more in your name then you had set down in your list†2 and now the Comission for the Councill of Trade is past†3 I think he must be orderd to give one to every one of your Brother Comissioners but I hope you will be in Town soon enough to give those orders your self, for my Lord Keeper Comanded me to write earnestly to you to be here as soon as possibly you could and said the loss of a day by your absence at this time would be of consequence
The Comission appoints the Lord Chancellor or Lord Keeper Lord President Lord Privy Seal Lord Treasurer or first Comissioner of the Treasury Lord High Admirall or first Comissioner of the Admiralty and the two principall Secretarys of State for the time being.†4 and
The Earls of Bridgewater†5 and Stampford†6 Sir Philip Meadhous†7 William Blathwait†8 John Locke John Pollixfen†9 and Samuell Clarke†10 or any 3 of them to meet in a place to be assignd them 1 To enquire into the State of the Trade of the Kingdom 2 How advanced or
― 487 ―
decayd and by what means 3 what Trades profitable what prejudiciall and by what methode advantageous Trades may be improved and hurtfull hinderd or made beneficiall 4 By what methodes Trade may be most effectually protected and secured in all its parts 5 By what means our manufactures may be improved and new and profitable ones introduced 6 How the poor may be set to work and made usefull.
They are also to Inform themselves 1° of the presant condition of the plantations 2° How they may be improved 3 What Navall stores the plantations can furnish us with 4 What the Instructions to Governors are and how they may be amended 5 What persons are fit to be Governors Deputy Governors or other officers in the plantations 6 They are to examine the Acts of the Assemblys of the plantations transmitted hither 7 <They>†a are to hear complaints of oppressions and maleadministrations 8 They are to enquire into and take all the accounts of publique mony raised in the plantations and for these purposes They are empowerd to send for persons and papers and to examine upon oath and may call to their assistance the Attorney and Sollicitor Generall
And they are from time to time to make reports of their proceedings in writing under their hands or of 5 or more of them to his Majesty or the Councill.
I shall onely add that the Bill for New Coynage is come in†1 and is as you desire or very near it and where it is not I hope it shall be amended to your content and as for the Bill about printing the severall different enemys it has will secure <u>s†b that there needs not many†c champions for the right in that case for their different interests will either hinder any Act from passing concerning printing or else make it a very good one. Give my Lady the service of
Sir
Your affectionate friends and humble servants

1982. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 20/30 December 1695 (1961, 2070)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 133-4.
Rotterdam 30 December 1695
Dear Sir
I wrote you the 17 past under covert of mr. Joseph wright, which I hope came well to your hands.
I have now a double occasion to write to you, the first in behalf of that ingenious Clergy man of Corke Mr Walter Neale, who lately wrote to me by Madam Courthop (whose husband dyed before Namur)†1 tho she came herself not over, He desired me to inform him, how he might write to you, and I answerd him under covert to mr. Jo. Wright, or at mr. Robert Pawlins over against the Plough Inn in Little Lincolns Inne fields. He is desirous, if it could be to remove out of Ireland, and to be neare the City where he may improve himself more than he can there: which is his sole motive and not out of covetousness, or to be in a higher station in the Church—
I take him to be an honest, and free man as a man under that coat, can be, and would be glad to serve him in any thing to my power— And so I hope you will—so much for that—
I have now A greater matter to intreat your assistance about, which the Engl. marchants of this town, have layd upon me to get effected if possible—And that is to be delivered a second time from the oppression of a Consul, from which 5 years ago, by my earnest sollicitation, his Maj. delivered us.†2
― 489 ―
And I am sure there are stronger reasons now than then, why we should be delivered. Because our masters are burthened very much by the Act for Tunnage,†1 from which the Dutch ships being free, they can carry goods cheaper than our English. yet that Tax going to the defraying part of the charge of the nation for the carrying on of this so just and necessary war we beare it cheerfully—
But to be taxd, and compelled by a forreign power to pay to the maintenance of an Idle man, that is noways capable of doing any service, which the meanest of ourselvs cannot do, for ourselvs and masters, is hard: And will breed ill blood betwixt him and the masters: For I know no man that will pay but under protest, and reserving their right to recover it of him in England, and to complain in Parliament.
Were the nation a farthing advantagd by it, or his majestyes revenue increasd, it were another case—
I have taken the boldness to write to my Lord Pembroke, who being abused by him, into a beleef that he could be of great advantage to our trade, assisted him, as I have been informed to get the office—
And therefore I thought it might not be amisse truly to inform his Lordship of the no service he could do us, and the great oppression he would be to our trade, to the driving English masters out of it—all men being inclined to ship their goods, at this time especially, where they can have them carryed for the lest freight.
I will not doubt, but I shall merit with my Lord (as an impartiall Englishman that understands what's advantagious and disadvantagious to trade) as much beleef as he, it being as evident that I can have no private, or separate Interest, from that of all English marchants and masters, and lovers of our nation, as it is evident that he has his own single Interest, directly contrary to ours, and therefore merits no beleef, in what he talks of his serviceableness to our commerce.
Yet I know your testimony concerning me to my Lord, to whom I cannot pretend to be so well known, as to your self, that I am a man, not to be byassed by private Interest against that of the publick, will ad great weight in the case—
I therefore beg it of you, as you are my friend, and much more as a lover of the publike good, to speak with my Lord about it not
― 490 ―
onely, but with my Lord Monmouth to, to whom, and to my Lady, give my most humble service, as also to Sir F: and my Lady. My dearest, my Benjohan, your friend Arent, with my self do kindly salute you, who am
Deare Sir
your humble Servant
BENJAMIN FURLY

1983. Locke to Esther Masham [c. 19 December 1695?] (1825, 2124)
Newberry Library, Chicago: copy of the original letter by Esther Masham in her letter-book, pp. 18-19. Printed in Fox Bourne, ii. 454; by Professor Maurice Cranston in Newberry Library Bulletin, 2nd ser., no. 4, July 1950, pp. 128-9. Transcribed from microfilm. The preliminary note is by Esther. Date: the letter belongs with Locke's appointment in either the abortive Commission of 16 December 1695 or the operative Commission of 15 May 1696. It seems more likely to belong with the former. Esther was apparently staying at Matching Hall (p. 178, n. 1). News of the appointment reached Locke at Oates probably on 17 December, and could have reached Matching Hall an hour later. He went to London on 20 December: Journal.
Upon Mr Locke's being made a Commissioner of Trade I writt him a Letter to wish him Joy, upon which he sent me the following Letter.
The Joy which you so forwardly and so kindly wrapd up in your Letter proved a fright to me when I open'd it. What could a solemn Joy be lesse to one that had before his eyes the fresh example of Mr H——†1 and when I received your Joy I knew not but Your Grandmothers Prophesie was fulfill'd and that I had been tumbled into the meal tub†2 in my Sleep without knowing it. But that which set the fright more on was that it came from my Landabridis whose business you know is to make joy and not wish it. After a little time recovering my self enough to observe some other expressions which went along with it I began to finde out the matter; and then your
― 491 ―
wishes had their effects. For Whatever I may expect from what you had in view, either satisfaction or trouble or neither, this I am sure your takeing part in what concerns me, and rejoycing in what perhaps you view but on one side extreamly pleases me. I take it as I am sure you meant it. I take it as a Sincere and great mark of your kindness to me, which the more sensibly affects me by how much I more esteem and wish well to you than to all the young Ladys I know. Would the time were come that I could return you your wish and upon a better occasion. You would then see how much your Joannes was in earnest concernd for you. I am
Your most faithfull Servant
JOANNES
Pray give my humble Service to your Grandmother†1 and the rest at Matching hall.

Dublin. Decembr. 24. 1695.
Sir
I am ashamed to say, that I have two of yours before me unanswer'd, the†a- first, being of Nov. 16. brought inclosed a Complement from Sir Francis Mashams Son to my Little Boy. tis indeed admirable for one of his Years, and such to which we cannot pretend to make a suitable return. But our Disparity in years must make some excuse for the Disparity of the Reply; and in time we hope to mend tho non Passibus æquis.-†a†2
Your†b other†b of Nov. 20th. brought me a Paper, which of all things I have ever seen on that subject, I most highly admire.†3 You
― 492 ―
have therein reveald the Whole Mystery of Mony, Exchange, Trade, etc. which have hitherto been wrap'd up in unintelligible Cant, I beleive partly out of Knavery, partly out of Ignorance. You gave me Liberty to make what Use of it I pleased; and therefore I ventur'd to give a Copy of it to His Excellency†a My Lord Deputy Capel, rather than the Book of Interest and Coynage,†1 which I thought might be too long for his present perusal in his Multitude of Busines. But I can tell you, that your Admirable Perspicuity of Writing is so clearly different from all the World, and almost peculiar to your self; that in vain you expect to be conceald in any thing that comes from you. For I assure you in some Discourse I had with his Excellency no longer ago than yesterday concerning the Busines of Mony, He asked me (without any Occasion given him from Me) whether I had ever seen Mr†b Lockes†b Book of Interest etc. for he has formerly known (as I think I have told you) that I had the Happines of Your Acquaintance, I replyd to His Lordship that I had seen such a Book, but that it did not bear your Name in it. He answerd Me, The Printer presented it to him as yours,†2 and besides (says he) All the World knows Mr Lockes Way of Writing, and if I may Gues, I believe that the Paper You gave me a few days ago came from Mr Locke; Pray did it not? I told his Excellency†c I was under some Obligation to Conceal the Author. That's enough (says he) I am sure tis his, and will put his Name to it, and lay it up amongst my Choysest Papers.
I have lately received three small Prints from London concerning the subject of Mony, they were Inclosed in a Bank Wrapper, and frank'd to me by Sir Walter Younge Baronet a Gentleman whom I never saw, and have no manner of Acquaintance with. I wonder how he comes to Confer an Obligation on me so suitable and agreable to my present thoughts. If you have any hand in this Favour to me be pleased to accept of My thanks, and to expres the same to Sir Walter. The Titles of those Papers are
 
Sir W. Pettys Quantulumcunque concerning Mony.†3

To†a- Mr John Locke-†a
[Enclosure:]†b
Corke September 6º. 1695
Dear Sir
Mr Molyneux's ingenious question of which you gave me an account at Mr Lukey's†2 yesterday has run so much in my minde ever since that I could scarce drive it out of my thoughts. to be revengd on you therefore <for>†c putting my brains in such a ferment I have resolved to be so impertinent as to send you the result of my Meditations upon the Subject
The case is this a man born perfectly blind has a globe and a cube given into his hands and instructed, as much as he is capable of, in the Notion of each of these figures and the difference between them: let us now Suppose this man suddenly to be endowed with the sense of seeing and the question is whether the globe and the Cube being placed before his Eyes, he would be able by his Sight alone and without touching them to tell which was the globe and which the Cube.
For the better understanding of what I shall say on this Question I desire you to take notice that I call every notion of any thing
― 495 ―
which a man entertains, an Idea, but that notion only, which a man entertains of a visible thing as it is visible I call an image.
This being premised I lay down these propositions.
1° A man born blind may have a true (though perhaps not a perfect) Idea of a globe and of a Cube and of some difference which is between them.
This evidently appears because he will certainly be able by his touch to distinguish them one from the Other.
2° A man who has ever bin perfectly blind and whilst he so remains can have no image in his minde either of a Cube or globe.
This in my oppinion is very evident because there is no passage (but the organs of sight of which wee Suppose him to be deprived) for such an image to enter and I take it for granted that such images are not <innate>†a in mens apprehensions.
3° Such a man as soon as he is Endowed with the sense of seeing will imediately have a different image in his minde of a globe and of a Cube as soon as they are Exposed to his Sight.
This must needs be so if his Sight and the Organs thereof be such as ours which wee suppose.
4° And if imediately upon the sight of the globe and cube there be ground enough for such a person Clearly to perceive the Agreement and the difference between his preconceived ideas and newly conceived images of those figures then may he be able to know which is the globe and which the Cube without touching them again after he has seen them.
For the agreement which he may finde between his idea and his image of a Globe and the difference of the idea of a globe from the image of a Cube (et sic vice versâ) will be a sufficient direction to him (if I say, there be Sufficient ground imediat<ely>†b to perceive the said Agreement and difference)
5° The idea which such a blind man must needs by his touch alone form of a globe will be this that it is a body which is Exactly alike on all Side<s>.†b
For lett him roll it as aften as he will between his hands and he can finde no manner of Difference between the one side and the other.
6° Part of the idea which such a man must needs by his touch conceive of a Cube will be that it is a body which is not alike in every part of its Superficies.
― 496 ―
For in one part he feels a Smooth flatt in another the Sharp point of an angle and in a third a long ridge which <reaches>†a from one Angle to another.
7 The Image which at the first Sight such a man will form of a globe must needs represent it as a body which is alike on all sides which consequently must be agreeable to the idea which he before had of i<t>†b and different from that Idea which he had of a Cube.
for turn a globe ten thousand ways and it Still Carryes the same aspect if it be all of the same collour which wee now Suppose.
8°. The Image which upon the first View such a man will frame of a Cu<be>†b must needs be this that it is a body which is not alike in all the parts of its Superficies which consequently must be agreeable to the idea which before he had of it and different from that idea which he had of a globe.
For a cube do's not carry the same aspect when it is exposed to our sight in different <positions>.†c
SINCE then the image which Such a man would have of a globe would be agreeable to the idea which before he had conceived of it and different from that idea Which before he had entertaind of a Cube (et sic vice versâ) it follows that by his sight alone he might be able to know which was the globe and which the Cube.
I have no more but to wish you a good Journey and tell you that if you call me impertinent for sending you my thoughts upon such a Speculation I will retort and tell that it was your selfe who put the Question to
Your affectionate friend and faithfull Servant
EDW: SYNGE
To†d- the Reverend Dr. Francis Quayle at his house near Mitchellstowne-†d

1986. William Popple to Locke, 2 January 1696 (1704, 1906, 2002)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 219-20. Popple was appointed secretary to the Commissioners for Trade by the commission of 16 December 1695: Luttrell, iii. 562.
London. January, the 2d. 1695/96
Sir,
I must discharge my promise of writing to you, though I know it will be don more particularly by other hands than I possibly can. But when I tell you what I know, if it be comparatively impertinent, you must blame your self, and not me, for the trouble of reading it. Yesterday, in a Committee about Coinage, Sir John Lowther†2 (Contrary to his former opinion) acknowledged himself convinced of the necessity of having clipt mony go by weight: But at the same time propounded a Method of registring the whole sum of Clipt mony, all at once, thoughout all England, in order to the stating and settling of every man's Recompence. This occasioned a long Debate, which was in the end adjourned to this day, without
― 499 ―
putting any Question. This morning the Party that have promoted the designe of a Committee of Trade in the House, being offended at the postponing of that busyness, shuffled off the Coinage without doing any thing remarkable in it, and brought on the subject of the Committee which had before been appointed. The whole day was spent in Debates; And in the end, without resolving any thing about the powers that this intended Committee should have; but agreeing that the Nature of it should be perfectly different from that intended by the King (which was mentioned and opened, not by the Court but themselves) His being onely for speculations, as they said, about the improvement of Trade in time of Peace; This for the effectual security of it in time of war; After much more of this nature than I can tell; And without agreeing upon the number of Commissioners; At seven a clock at night, the question was put, whether the Parliament or the King should name them; And carryed for the Parlaiament by one single voice: On that side being 175, and on the other side 174.
I do not know distinctly what the Lords have don about the Bill for Coinage, nor indeed any thing at all of it but what I have from those who will write it you themselves. This about the Committee I have, now late, from one that was present at the Debate. And this is all I can say. I heartily wish that your health may be re-established since your return into the Country, and indeed do not doubt but it is so. I beg the favour of you to present my humble service to the whole family where you are, and am
Sir,
Your most humble servant
WILLIAM POPPLE.

I conclude this was and is yet their dayly practice to keep some Bags of such money as could not be taken to compell men to beg of them the kindnes of paying them Guin: at that excessive rate; if it were but 6d in a Guin: tis 4d in the pound, if 12d. 8d and perhaps they might have tricks to bring in Guin: under 30s, truely twas time for you to be gon, for you have attempted the ruine of their Diana and put a stop to that craft by which such K:†4 have got their gain; but these are already what Mr Hooper†5 of Mag: College hoped he and some other like him should be in time and therefore I fear these things will mend but slowly. But Mundus vult vadere si vult vaderet etc†6
I am
Sir
Your humble servant
ROB PAWLING

1991. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 6 January 1696 (1968, 2046)
Rand, p. 432. Sent to Clarke to forward: no. 1992.
Oates, 6th January, 1695.
Dear Madam,
The marks of your concern for me will always be welcome to me. And you cannot interest yourself more in anything that you
― 504 ―
think a good fortune to me, than I shall always rejoice in the health, prosperity and happiness of you and all your family. I am sorry that you have any painful accidents that make you at all suffer in your return to health. This last I am glad is so well over that you are only concerned for the name. That which Mr. Smith gave it I think as good as any, and will serve your turn as well as a Greek or a Latin one, so you have no returns of it I desire you to observe those few easy rules I formerly sent you till you have recovered your former strength, and then if the hypocondriac wind should trouble you again I shall talk further with you about it. As a farther direction for your son Sam I have writ to Mr. Clarke to send you an yellow powder, whereof I would have you give him two grains every morning in two or three spoonfuls of black cherry water till you can get any of the herb arsmart,†1 which I would have you distil as you do roses, and then give it him in that. I wish you an happy new year. I am,
Dear Madam,
your most humble servant,
J. LOCKE.
Your son is here and well. He sends you his duty, and my Lady her service.
Endorsed: Mr. Locke's letter, etc.

1995. Robert Pawling to Locke, 7 January 1696 (i) (1987, 1996)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 27-8.
London January 7th 1695
Sir
I hoped you would have been here last night and shall expect to see you on Wednesday.†1 Our Maid took Pills according to your directions and had 23 Stools she is pretty well after it onely complains of faintness and a little weaknes in her Legs. it seems she chose rather to be blooded by her old Surgeon than my friend Mr Vernon that let my Doughter Justice Blood and saith he took away about 20℥ we are unwilling to let her take any more Pills till we hear from you.
I find the House of Commons cant agree with the Lords about the Coin and are distracted among themselvs; by their delay the confusion dayly increases insomuch that the Bankers, who influence the Blockheads, hope you wilbe put upon a necessity of taking their Paper for money and so hope to make their Marketts; the cry is, which indeed is their Cloak, that the Poor wilbe great loosers and indeed they are so as tis managed; for many poor men sell their half crowns for 18d to some cuning fellows that bring them to our office and other Offices and put them off according to his Majestys Proclamation.†2 Mr Miles†3 our Receivers Clark hath had many half crowns offered him at 2s which are much better than many that he dares not refuse at the full price that come for Stamps, how many are there that were they in his place would not make their marketts? tis said the half crowns are buying up at low rates by weight in Ireland Scotland Hollon etc and will come time enough to be paid in to the Exchequer as the Proclamation commands them to take them; where this will end I know not. This morning I was in the Commissioners Room†4 where we debated these matters. Mr Montagu†5 came in just as Mr Harris†6 and I were discoursing on that Subject. he said he was glad to see me and would know what I thought now
― 508 ―
of weighing because he knew I was for it because of my acquaintance with you. he said their house had been considering of it and found it impracticable; a word he hath often used to me in reference to Some things I have proposed relating to the Office; to confirm what he said Mr Harris replyed that he satisfied many Parliament Men yesterday that money could not be weighed; because there were not half Scales enough to be had for the purpose and how could country people recon grains, penny weights etc and beside a pair of scales would cost at lest 5s; thus learnedly did that Gentleman plead. Now I presume you never meant that every one should be at the charge of a pair of Scales or trouble of weighing their own money; I always thought that if money had, by Proclamation, gon by weight there would not onely have been an end of cliping and hanging for it, but every one would have caried in their light money as the Ladys do their old silver lace when burnt to the Goldsmith and have taken the value of it in New money which they could have Supplyed them with, when twas for their interest to part with it. I am
Sir
Your humble Servant
ROB PAWLING
