1999. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 10/20 January 1696 (1958, 2014) enclosing Hendrik Wetstein, account of his health, 5/15 January 1696 (1831, 2035)
B.L., MSS. Locke c. 13, ff. 103-4, and c. 23, f. 79. Le Clerc's letter is printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 92-3.
A Amsterdam le 20 de Janvier 1696
Il y a long-temps, Monsieur, que je me serois donné l'honneur de vous écrire, si je n'avois été fort empêché par l'édition de mon petit Ouvrage de l'Incredulité, qui est à présent achevé, outre que l'impression de Hammond m'occupe beaucoup. Pendant ce temps-là j'ai reçu une Lettre de Mr. l'Evêque de Salisbury,†1 ou il me fait beaucoup de complimens, mais où il me fait comprendre que la crainte des Jacobites, qui accusent de Socinianisme ceux qu'ils n'aiment pas l'empêche de rien faire en ma faveur. Il me demande aussi, par une Civilité toute singuliere, la permission de me faire un présent, comme s'il craignait de me choquer en le faisant. Je lui ai repondu assez simplement, en lui représentant ce que j'avois fait pour son honneur, et en sa consideration, et au contraire les remercimens que j'en avois reçus, très-opposez aux promesses <qu'il>†b m'avoit faites.†2 J'ai crû devoir en user ainsi, parce qu'il sembloit qu'il ne m'entendoit point, quoi que je lui parlasse assez clairement. Je n'en ai point encore reçu de réponse, mais je crain que je n'en reçoive de longtemps. Cependant j'ai reçu une Lettre d'un autre Prélat, qui m'a extrémement consolé, parce que je ne l'attendois point, et qu'elle est très-obligeante. C'est de Mr. l'Archevêque d'York†3 qui me remercie de ma Dissert. sur S. Jean et de mon Comment. sur le Pentateuque que je lui avois envoiez. Comme il a crû que je cherchois
― 512 ―
des Subscrybers, il m'a envoié en même temps le pris de six exemplaires, quoi qu'il n'en ait reçu qu'un. Cette maniére d'agir est obligeante pour un homme qu'on ne connoit point, et sa Lettre conçuë en des termes très-civils, a fait naître dans mon esprit quelque petite esperance. Je me persuade quelquefois que si Mylord Privy seal parloit à ce Prélat, ou à quelque autre, avec un peu de chaleur, il pourroit obtenir quelque chose. Mais d'un autre côté je n'ose pas me flatter qu'il voulût se faire une affaire de me procurer quelque avancement; et sans cela je ne vois pas qu'on puisse rien avancer. Une recommendation, qui ne vient que par occasion, et qui n'est pas soûtenue de quelque chaleur, tombe à terre, sur tout lors qu'il s'agit d'une personne absente. Je me suis donné l'honneur de lui écrire, en lui envoiant mon dernier Volume, et encore depuis, avant que de savoir qu'il l'avoit reçu, pour l'avertir que le Sieur Smith†1 étoit chargé de le lui présenter, mais je n'en ai reçu aucune nouvelle. Je sai les occupations de ces Messieurs, mais un je vous remercie ne demande pas tant de temps, et j'apprehende quelque refroidissement, dont je ne puis pas deviner la raison. Je ne laisserai pas de lui envoier mon Traité de l'Incredulité, comme je le lui ai promis dans une de mes Lettres. Je ne manquerai pas aussi de vous en envoier un exemplaire, avec ma Physique,†2 que j'ai differé de vous envoier à cause de cela. Je sai parfaitement, Monsieur, l'obligation que je vous ai, et je n'ai pas moins de reconnoissance pour vos bons offices, quand ils ne reüssiroient point, que si le bien que vous me voulez arrivoit. Je le dis sans compliment, et je vous supplie d'en être persuadé. Je suis, Monsieur, du fonds de mon ame Vôtre trèshumble et tres-obeissant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Mr. Wetstein le Libraire m'aiant ouï vanter le remede que Vous m'avez envoié pour mon petit garçon, m'a priè de vous consulter sur une incommodité qu'il a et dont voici la description ci-jointe. Comme il est aussi, Monsieur, de vôtre connoissance, j'ose vous importuner pour lui, et vous prier de lui répondre en Latin, ou en Anglois, au premier loisir. Pardonnez à ma liberté.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings, in little Lincolns Inne fields, over against the Plough London.

[Enclosure:]†a
Ce 15e. Ja<nv>ier†b 1696
J'ai 47 ans. La maladie he<re>ditaire†b de ma familie c'est le temperament melancholique et pituiteux.
Mon mal d'apresent, à mon avis, n'est autre chose que morbus hypochondriacus. en voici mes raisons:
Ayant perdu depuis dix mois ma femme,†1 qui me laissa huit enfans, dont l'ainé n'avoit pas seize ans: la tristesse que cela me causa fut extréme.
Ce que joint à l'embarras que me causoient les affaires dont je fus accablé dans mon negoce et dans ma famille et dans mon menage.
J'en perdis petit à petit le sommeil, et ensuite la memoire, ou peu s'en faut.
Surquoi succeda une furieuse attaque des hemorrhoïdes externes, qui me prit à la fin de Juin; ainsi qu'on fut obligé de les faire saigner fortement par deux fois en trois jours.
Au commencement de Juillet, je m'en fus à Swalbac,†2 y boire les eaux (:acidulas) qui me firent grand bien, puis qu'aprés leur usage le sommeil me revint et la memoire aussi.
J'en fus de retour avec la fin d'Aoust.
Mais r<ent>rant†b dans ma maison et dans mes affaires, cela empescha notablement les effets que cette cure devoit produire encore.
Insensiblement j'amassai une espece de croute (:ce sembloit) devant l'orifice de l'estomac, qui s'etendant tantot plus tantot moins par toute la poitrine me pressa plus ou moins, que je craignis quelque fois d'en etouffer.
Cette pretendue croute s'est perdue subitement, et sans que je sache comment, au commencement de decembre; ayant la respiration assez libre pour plusieurs semaines.
Au lieu de cela j'ai senti depuis au dedans de l'os sternum comme s'il y avoit une fourmiliere de fourmis qui grouilloient; quelquefois un peu plus bas une espece d'eboulition, comme si on bouilloit de l'huile à feu lent. l'un et l'autre toujours accompagné d'un redoublement de poulx, sans pourtant qu'il fut extréme, mais comme un frisson par tout le corps au commencement d'une fievre, et une commotion <ge>nerale†b en toutes mes entrailles, comme si elles se
― 514 ―
fondoient subitement, sans <po>urtant†a tomber en defaillance actuelle, bien que j'en sois, ce me semble, for<t>†a prés.
Cela m'arrive indifferemment le soir et le matin, devant et aprés midi, mais†b non pas durant mon sommeil; au moins que je sache.
Mais au lieu de cela il m'arrive que durant mon sommeil le cœur me bat d'une telle force que j'en suis eveillé, et alors je l'entens batre tresdistinctement et tresfortement quelquefois plusieurs heures.
J'ai quelquefois de ces agitations de cœur par jour, mais qui ne sont nullement comparables à celles de nuit.
Je recommence à perdre quelquefois le sommeil. J'ai beaucoup d'anxieté, d'oppressions et de serremens de cœur. Beaucoup de fois c'est comme si on me prenoit par la gorge pour m'etrangler; de nuit aussi bien que de jour.
Le plus jeune de mes enfans, qui est un garcon agé de 5. ans, fut pris de la fievre, n'ayant que deux ans et demy en septembre 1693. dans trois mois en décembre il seicha si bien, qu'il n'eut que la peau et les os; mais la <peau>†a si tanée de maigreur et avec des replis si gros, qu'il ressembloit à un sac de cuir qui auroit eté mouillé et puis seiché à la fumée. Toutes les medecines n'y firent rien. La fievre lui continua toujours, et toujours il s'afoiblissoit. On ne sauroit dire quelle sorte de fievre, puis qu'elle n'observoit ni temps, ni regle ni mesure. Mais toujours intermittente. Dans six mois en Avril 1694 cet enfant se remit peu a peu, c'est a dire que la chair lui revint, et au bout de quelque temps il recommença à marcher; mangeant cependant excessivement, et gardan<t>†a toujours sa fievre, tantot tierce, tantot double tierce; son ventre s'enflant assez fort, et qui n'est pas diminüé depuis, ni la fievre non plus, qui se chang<e>†a depuis 5 mois en septembre 1695 en quarte. Depuis ce temps là il ne mange que médiocrem<ent,>†a il a de l'embonpoint, il garde son gros ventre; mais les dents lui tombent t<ous>†a de la bouche, l'une apres l'autre, bien qu'elles soient les plus belles qu'on les saur<oit>†a peindre, et sans qu'il paroisse rien aux gencives. Ses jambes s'enflent quelquefo<is>†a mais peu: et il ne paroit plus si robuste que depuis 4 ou 5. mois.
Endorsed by Locke: Wetstein 15 Jan 96 Answered 18.

B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 14-15. Copy or draft in B.M., Add. MS. 5540, f. 66. Printed from the B.M. version in Rand, pp. 433-5. Not received by Locke until 11 April. Answered by no. 2064.

Bristoll Janu. 11th. 95
Worthy Sir
I have read your Answer to mr Loundes his Essay for the amendment of the Silver Coins†1 and I thinke the Nation obliged by the service you have done in handling a subject of that weight so fully; I know my private opinion will not adde a Mite to its valew, however I must give it this Character, that you have done it (as you doe all other things you write) with such clearnesse and strenght of Argument as if it had been the only thinge wheretoe you had bent your study; When Men undertake subjects whereof they have noe clear Notions, their bookes rather perplex the Reader then guide him to a right understanding of what they would seem to unriddle; he that desighnes to propose Methods to kepe our Mony at home must first consider what it is that causes it to be carryed abroad; in this I thinke you have hit the Marke; Its the Ballance of our Trade with Forreyn Countryes, not altering the standard of our Coin, which either encreases or lessens our Bullion at home, and then the next thinge is to consider how this Ballance may be brought of†a our side; when other Nations are brought into our depts noe room is left for fetching away our Bullion, but on the contrary they must send us theirs; and this I judge cannot better be done then by encourageing our Manufactures, which will employ our people; The Wealth of England arises cheifely from the labour of its Inhabitants, which being added to our own Product, and alsoe to the forrein Materialls we Import, encreases their valew in those Markets whither we export them, and by how much we lessen the Importation of things already manufactured, and encrease that of the Primums whereof they are made, soe much will the Ballance of our Trade alter every where in our Favour;
― 516 ―
When the Publick Good of a Nation is the desighne of a Writer it armes him with some assurance, which hath emboldend me to present you with this little Tract, or Essay on Trade,†1 the worke of some leisure houres; all I shall say concerning it is, that 'twas wrote without partiall Respect to any one Trade more then another; if you shall thinke it worth your reading twill oblidge me,
Please to give me leave to offer at somethinge in your Booke which I suppose to be an oversight, pa: 86 you propose the Halfe Crownes, Halfe Scepters, or Halfe Unites, should goe for two shillings and seven pence halfe penny each, I apprehend twas intended three shillings one penny halfe penny, else twill not agree with the exact halfe of the Crowne, Scepter, or Unite; whither I take this right I am uncertain, but the following table pa: 86 must be erroneous, where you put
    
the Halfe Crowne 	2/-½ 
3 ditto 	8/10½ 
5 ditto 	15/1½ 
7 ditto 	21/4½ 
This Table seems to be perplext, for if you desighn the Halfe Crowne (which is imperfectly printed) at 2/7d 1/2
   
then 3 ditto must be 	7/10½ 
5 ditto 	13/1½ 
7 ditto 	18/4½ 
nor will it agre with 3/1½ for the Halfe Crowne, which is according to 6/3d the Crowne; I have noe desighne in mentioning this, save that if you find it an error it may be corrected in the next Edition;†2 I shall be oblidged to you for the like Favour if you give your selfe the Trouble to read my Booke, which was seen by noe man but my selfe till it had past the Presse, therefore I cannot thinke it without oversights; I am
Sir Your most humble servant
JOHN CARY

Oates 13. Dec. 95/6
Dear Sir
My bed with other things I have used have I thank god put a stop to the increase and violence of my cough, I think it well that I am got soe far though my breath yet be very short and my cough far from being quite gon, as it was before I last came to town. But it is some comfort to be geting up the hill though it be but slowly. I wish it were soe in other places. In my last to you I inclosed one to Mrs Clarke.†1 you will finde by that, that I think it not convenient at present to trouble her with any new rules about her health, fearing that if we multiply them too much we shall have none observed, and those few I formerly sent her will I hope if kept to bring her to her former strength, and then if she feel or fear any returne of the pain she complaind of in her last to me we may give directions about it. The Ens veneris I advised for your son Sam: in that letter was not intended to thrust out the use of Mana and Syrup of Althæa directed by Dr Cole but will consist very well with it only omitting it those days that he takes either the Mana or the Syrup.
I must beg you to present my most humble service to my Lord Keeper and my thanks for his concerne for me
I doe not doubt but the Colledg is the same. I only wish that Colledg could worke upon an other college†2 not to be soe much the same as it seems to me to be.
A poor Carpenter of this Parish had a debt of £40 or 50 paid him just before the first proclamation about mony came out,†3 he tels me that he can passe away neither half crowns nor shillings though he owes mony he can get noe body to take them; and I am told that Guineas in this country goe for 1 or 2 and 30s.
― 518 ―
I see by the votes that your house dissents from the amendments of your bill about the coin made by the Lords. but what those amendments are you cheifly stick at I cannot see by the votes. nor what the amendments were. I suppose they were good for noething because your house has rejected them.†1 But is it true what I hear talkd, that false money not standard silver is to passe? I am to the whole College
Dear Sir
your most humble and affectionate servant
J LOCKE
your son is very well and presents his duty to you
My Lady and my cosin King present their service to you and to mr Freke

2002. William Popple to Locke, 16 January 1696 (1986, 2036)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 221-2.
London. January, 16th. 1695/96
Sir
Upon the receipt of your first letter, I immediatly acquainted My Lord Ashley with what you writ: And a few dayes after, he gave me the Bill that you desired, telling me at the same time that he would order his man to write about it. Tis for that reason, I thought it needless for me to trouble you on the same subject. Your†a- second letter now obliges me to tell you that I have given the Receipt, which you sent in it, to my Lord Ashley: And that I keep the Bill for you, as you desire, against your coming to town.-†a So much for busyness. I cannot forbear to ad, upon the subject of your coming to town, that however desirous I am alwayes to see you, yet I had much rather be deprived of that satisfaction, than to enjoy it at the hazard of your health. If publick service call you, I know you
― 519 ―
will take the best Measures you can to comply with what shall be a duty upon you in that occasion. (But I doubt that Call is yet remote.) If it do not, I know you can alwayes render your self no less usefull to the Publick even in your most private Retirement. Suffer me I beseech you to suggest to you some thoughts with which my own minde is at present deeply affected. The Reasonableness of Christianity (however Reasonable a Book it be) has I doubt had little Effect upon those that call themselves Deists in this Age. I dispute not how little they deserve that Title. The men I mean are such as deny all Immaterial Beings, though that dos not hinder them from talking of a God upon all occasions, but undoubtedly more for the sake of the Name than the Thing. Consequently to that, they make all Events necessary, and laugh not onely at Revealed but even Natural Religion. I say Religion: For they talk big of Virtue and Morality. But when they lay all the grounds of both Virtue and Morality onely in the good-nature of particular persons, or in the fear of the Magistrate's Rod, I fear their Superstructure will be very tottering. And what makes me fear this, is because I see plainly the Youth of this Age build all upon that Foundation. We are running from one Extream to another. Atheism, or, (if that word be too harsh), even Irreligion is a sad Sanctuary from the Mischiefs of Superstition.†1 Must we then needs lye under either the one or the other? Is there no Medium? Yes certainly there is. And these young Wits stand need†2 of one to shew it them in a pure light, without any mixture of Clerical Fard,†3 which has now utterly disgusted them. Good Sir, pardon my liberty in hinting at these things to you. I do it onely to raise the thoughts in your minde, not to direct you to the subject of a particular Treatise. For I know you are better able to judg of the best manner of benefitting the world in this kinde than I am. And when you have it in your thoughts I fear not but it will work out one way or another as may be most expedient. I pray
― 520 ―
God continue your health and strengthen it, for your own satisfaction, for the comfort of your friends, and for the service of your generation. I am
Sir,
Your most affectionate humble Servant
WILLIAM POPPLE.
I beg of you to present my most humble service to my Lady. I have no excuse to make for my not answering her last letter, but the sterility of my own Thoughts, which afforded no matter worth her perusal. But however now the time runs on too long, and I intend to write to her shortly.
Address: For Mr Locke [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]

2003. Robert Pawling to Locke, 16 January 1696 (1996, 2007)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 29-30.
London January 16 1695
Sir
I received yours. I have forgot how I worded my Letter as to what concerned Ursula. my meaning was that she had above 20 Stools in one day having taken 4 Pills, but let her excuse her self as well as <she>†a can when she sees you next, now†b- shee seems to be very well,-†b which I presume wilbe as soon as you can conveniently come; for here came an other Summons from the Treasury for your Appearing on Friday that is tomorrow; I had some busines at the Treasury yesterday morning just after the order came and I there acquainted the Clerk that signed it that you was ill and I hoped the busines was not so great but that they might dispence with your absence upon that occasion, he replyed he thought it was not very materiall; twas Mr Tilson though he forgot to put his name to it. I know not that I have don any service for my Lady Masham that may deserve so great a Present her Ladyship designed for me, Pray present my humble Service to my Lady and give her my hearty thanks for her intended kindnes and I own my self as much obliged for it as if it had come safe to my hands; perhaps those that made
― 521 ―
merry with it might drink her Ladyships health under some generall denomination in that which they and most men at lest count; better Liquor than that I do drink it in. If your Poor Carpenter†1 brings up his Coin I will assist him; and if he pleases to buy up as many very small half crowns for 12d a piece†a as may lick him whole I can help him off with them; or if he could lawfully do it, if he could with his Chizell chip off 6 penny worth of silver more from most of those he intends to bring up I can, by vertue of an order from our Board to the Receiver,†2 make him take them at 2s.6d, we have had some here that we weighed which, at 5s 3d per ounce came to but 7d½ and one braged that he bought one for 6d that we must not refuse now at 2s 6d. I presume some will leave buying hair†3 for a time and will imploy their money and time better in buying money it being the more profitable trade. I could fill this sheet with instances of abuses of this kind and the fatall consequences some mens mistakes have lead them into; but now they must not go back; they must go through if they can; if they cant let them ly there, for they are in a bog. I am
Sir
Your very humble Servant
ROB PAWLING

2004. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, [21 January 1696] (2001, 2006)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 211-12. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's initials and the address. Date from postmark and contents. Answered by no. 2006.
Dear Sir
We thank you for your Letter by Mr K†4 and rejoice in the news it brought us that your Cough yields to discipline we hope your
― 522 ―
Lungs will doe soe too and that all will be right with you again in a little time
The Grave tells me their Sallery Bill is not yet signd by the Treasury but when it is he will doe for you as well as he can in the difficult condition we are reduced to in respect to mony. And as to what you order him to pay the Batchelor that matter shall be accomodated to your Content but you must not think to slip your neck out of Coller by being bountifull your self since you are one of those that are chiefly depended on to bring in others Contribution†1
The Book you mention I am assured by a friend of the Author was left by the Author for you at Mr Pawlins before you came last to Town and before any one of them had been presented to any other person and I am likewise told that since you last went to Oats he sent another and a Letter to you by (I know not what) Coach†2
I am sorry to hear your markets are soe litle frequented ours here are full and as great plenty as ever onely things are somewhat dearer if we reckon our mony according to its Denomination which very ill agrees to it for besides that the greater part is Clipt away the most of what passes amongst us now has very litle if any silver in it yet all passes without scruple and Guineas pass amongst buyers and sellers at 30s and upwards but are sold on the Exchange under 29s
Yesterday the Lords past the Bill for Coin<a>ge†a and this day the King Came to the House and past that and the Bill for enlarging the Term for purchasing the Annuitys and the Bill to prevent Expences in Elections and the Bill for Regulating Tryalls in cases of Treason and severall private Bills. And now the Treasury begins to complain that as matters now stand they can have noe mony to carry on the war by Sea or Land for all that comes in on Loans and otherwise must be repaid out of the Land Tax etc. And when what is brought in by those Taxes is recoind there will be scarce enough to doe it and none to carry on the service. They likewise find that 1200000 li will not make good the Deficiency now base mony is to be received by the Crown as well as Clipt Soe that they say we must
― 523 ―
certainly be undone unless a larger and farther fund be given to make good the Deficiency, To which some answer that this is discoverd too late by them for the Commons can give noe more this Session on that account having voted a summ not exceeding 1200000li to be given for it
Yesterday the Commons were again on the Comittee of Trade and Voted (in a comittee of the whole House) nemine contradicente that noe member should be of it And that those that shall Act in it shall first swear they believe King William Lawfull and Rightfull King and that King James has noe right nor any other any Right during King Williams life and after his death noe one has any right but according to the Act for Settling the Crown made Anno 1mo Willelmi et Mariæ. Then they proceeded to vote severall powers which I can't repeat and the House is to be on this matter again on Thursday. This day The House of Commons voted an Impeachment against the Directors of the Scotch East India Company†1 as guilty of a misdeamour in Administring An oath in this Kingdom without being thereto Authorized by the law of this Kingdom though warranted in Scotland by an Act of Parliament there
Tender our dues to my Lady Mr Masham and Mr Clarke†2 and own us as we shall always own our selves
Your obliged friends and humble servants
J F

Oates 27º Jan 95/6
Dear Col
The concerne you expresse for my health is a very sensible obligation to me and I wish my health may enable me to doe you any service. I shall be glad of that
I desire to give the grave noe farther trouble about my Salary but to take Sir Stephens note to me for it as he used to doe, as soon as the order for payment comes from the Treasury.
― 525 ―
The Batchelor may easily conclude that he that assists with his money will not bethink†1 a few words when he meets with fit occasions. Though most of the persons I should venture to trouble on such an occasion are as well known to the Batchelor as to me. I wish he would consider with Mr Lyddel†2 How he might be made usefull and that fault which we suspect may prove an hindrance to it may be cured
I wonder Mr Pawling should faile to give me that book if it were left with him for me But I shall enquire after it
They seem to me to sadle their noses with strange spectacles who cannot see a thing soe plain and soe long before their eyes, till just the moment that it is too late†3
I thank you for the several parcels of news you sent me. But pray tell me, will an Impeachment against the Directors of the Scotch East India company for the misdemeanor they are guilty of breake that†a company and hinder it from goeing on, if soe I rejoyce at it. If it will only hinder English men from shareing in the profit and drive it into forain hands I know not what to think pray enlighten me a little. I hear some talke here of a speech my Lord Ashley made in the house. I should be glad to know a little more of the matter and forme of it, and the opinion people have of it for I am concernd for that yonge Gent as you know and shall always wish he may doe well espetialy when he appears in publique.†4
Would not the Parliament doe well to require the same oath of all other Commissioners that they have voted for those for Trade?†5 But I always finde money of more force than oathes in all countrys where clipd and counterfeit mony goes by law. I hope when that act is past the house of commons you will let me know what it is.
The Grave may know that his son is well and by me whilst I was writeing this letter he presents his duty, and thanks for the letter he received. Give me leave on this occasion to repeat what I minded you of before I left the town. viz That you would provide him masters against he returns to fill his hands with businesse that for want of it he may not fall into a santering habit or ill company
― 526 ―
both which are to be prevented as much as may be, espetialy care is to be taken at his first comeing out into the world (as I looke upon this to be) concerning these matters and therefor if you could finde him a fit and safe companion of about his age, or a little older, I think it would be usefull, and better for him than to have one of his own finding, which he will certainly doe if you doe not for tis not to be expected he should live without company. I should beg your excuse for this freedom had not your commission and long custome authorised me in it. Those here returne their dues to you respectively and I am
Your obleiged humble servant
J L†a

2007. Robert Pawling to Locke, 1 February 1696 (2003, 2013)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 31-2.
London Feb: 1º 1695
Sir
I presume my misplacing Madam and Sir was onely a mistake in directing my Letters wrong. I am glad to find you so pleasant. I hope you wilbe strong enough to breath in this thick air in a little time; I cant call to mind any Pamphlet that came hither for you;†1 this afternoon Mr Salmon enquired for you and said he had a paper to deliver to you from Mr Furley which he will bring to me next week, perhaps this may be the paper you want, he tells me tis about money.†2 And having mentioned that word and likewise being
― 527 ―
desired by you in your last to continue to write on that subject I cant forbear saying somwhat on that Subject for I have dreadfull apprehentions of what may be the fatall consequence of our late wise Act.†1 Therupon money, such as it is, comes tumbling in to our Office, I presume tis so in other Offices too, The Subcollectors send it up by Cariers dayly. one man sent up 230 li from Exon, who I beleive is an honest man, he writes word tis the same money he took and sent it sealed; when the receiver went for it, for the Carier would not bring it, he found it had been opened and charged the Carier with opening; he said perhaps the Seal might be broke but there was all the money; when he opened it he found it so much, but tis a parcell of money just of one size and seems to be all of one make, so that I dont question but that the Carier hath kept what was sent and put this in the room of it either in Exon or since he came up; this I hope our Commissioners will look into. tis†a- all in half Crowns of one size and not worth 9d a piece.†b no one can imagin that this could be taken in a retale shop for 1d 6d etc stamps-†a
severall come to the Office dayly with new cast half crowns that we are confident have not gon through many hands, they are of a base Mettle but so small that were they Sterlin would not weigh above 9d, some of them come from a Shop in the†c Strand†c that hath been suspected for a dealer in broad money†2 a long time.
One came this afternoon with a parcell of that new stuff that looked so suspicious that the Receiver would not take it. I wish he had taken his name and complained of it; but the Act obliges receivers to take such base money and as if that were not sufficient he that hath drawn and printed a breviat of the Act insteed of the word base hath put it brass†3
one hundred thousand pound may be cast in a few day for tis most of it cast and they have till 4th of May to trade that way! perhaps as they may contrive it till June 24 in which time there may
― 528 ―
be more made than the Nation can be able to make good. but tis past Nine therfore Ile conclude. I am
Sir
Your very humble Servant
ROB PAWLING
My humble service to my Lady and Mr Clark not forgetting young Master.†1

Oates 5º Feb
Dear Col:
I had by the last post made my acknowledgment for the favour of your last letter, had I not stayd to see whether the carrier yesterday (for that is his day) had brought those two books you mention whereof one was for my Lady and the other for my self, but there were none. Perhaps they may come next Tuesday for soe I am sometimes servd, if they doe I shall send you notice. I sent also to enquire of Mr Pawling for that which you were told was left with him for me, but he can say noe thing of it.
I thank the Grave for his care in geting the note from Sir St: Evans. I have known a little Boy grow a Great man, but a little man will always be soe
The Sollicitation I find was well managed. The house disagreed with the Committee and the Oath is left out†1
What ever you suppose, Sir Francis does not use to send us down the Acts as they come out and therefor my request to you about that Act I mentioned had noe mystery in it and I recommend it to you again.†2
An other Bank at this time of day†3 when such care has been taken of the credit of the Exchequer will noe doubt bring in abundance of money. But pray are the Bank, Lottery bills Annuitys etc of Christmas quarter paid and in what money? I am told that Clipd and counterfeit half crowns goe freer now even in London than before the Proclamation and Act.†4 I wonder not at it For as I understand it the Exchequer must pay it. which is like to grow rich as a trades man who buys by light weights and sels by heavie.
― 530 ―
But pray is there any milld money coind in the Mint and what becomes of it? The Gold you say the Cadiz fleet has brought†1 will help to ease us of it. But how to reduce Guineas to their true intrinsique value any otherwise than by makeing light and bad money goe for its weight in silver I doe not see.
I heare of a new Proclamation about money but cannot yet learne the Contents of it.†2 But will proclamations alter your Act? My Lady Mr Clarke and Mr Masham†3 return their thanks for your remembrances and salute you respectively as they ought. I am
your affectionate humble servant J L
Pray in your next one word in what forwardnesse our Fleet is. The great <preparations>†a the French make by sea makes a noise here.†4

Bristoll feb 5th 1695/6
Deare Cousen
according to your order I sent you the account I drew out of my deare Husbands book and an account of all the papers I have in my hands concerning your business, I hope it came safe to your hands some months since, but haveing never recivd a line from you since makes me have some doubt weither you have receiv'd them, I am desireous if you please to be dischargd of that business and indeed to even all my concerns in this world for I am often indisposd and have reason to think my time is but short, and therefore would
― 531 ―
willingly leave my poor children in as little trouble as may be whose curcumstances will be very indiferent for a maintainence when I dye, my deare Husband haveing lost a great part of his estate but I trust our good God will make it up in giveing full content with what we have, I am in hopes if I live till the spring I shall see you heare to settle your own business for I doe not heare you have order'd any one to act in it, I should have writ to you before now only I was loath to give you or my self the trouble for I take no sattisfaction in writing my deare Husbands concerns in this world I can better veiw him where he is and I hope ere long to be. my Cildren give you their humble service, my son Peter Stratton and Ann Hasell are well but know not of my writing for my bro†1 did not resolve on his Jorney one hour before he went I hope this will find you in health tho I am not, so resting deare Cousin your faithfull Freind and humble servant
ELIZABETH STRATTON
pray be pleased to give my humble service to Esq Clark and his Lady
Address: For Mr John Lock in London

2012. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 11 February [1696] (1990, 2030)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 49-50. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Feb 11
Since I write to you last, I have had so violent a Cold, as oblig'd me to keep my bed: and it has layen so in my head, and eyes, that I have not been able to hold done my head. I have in this time, had the ill news of my Eldest Brothers death;†1 this has given me some occasion, more then ordinary to my old distemper, for, tho I kno' you will not allowe it reasonable, to spend many thought's on what is not at all in ones power to help; yet it is not possible <to>†b avoide it, on some occasions. the ill luck of my poor frend Mr Johnston, is noe longer newes to you,†2 it would have been so, if you had seen me a disbanded Bedchamber woman, leading in to your hall, a disbanded secretary; which I had been very likly to have done, had not some cross accident's fall'n out. to morrow being Wedensday, I can say nothing of my business; but that like poor Pauling's expectation of greenwich, the offtener I am delay'd; the firmer I beleive it will be done. affter this apolliegy, I may tell you that I hope it will very soon answer expectation.
I must give you many thankes, for a vissit I had yesterday from the ArchBishop on your account. he in trusted me, with a packit
― 533 ―
which I sent to Mr Pauling to send you, he told me, it was a frend of his, had write something he had a mind to have your opinion of: but I did not tell him, that I had all the Curriosity imaginable, to kno whither it was on the subject of Socinianism, or Coyn. tho I belive he takes you to be a more impartiall judge of the last. I did inteind to have write to My lady, in answear to a question her son Sam: brought me; but haveing don it by word of mouth, to Sir Fr:, I shall spare her this trouble, and only give her my humble Service; and to all your good Company. I am
Your oblig'd, and most Faithfull Servant.
My Cosen Cutts, gives her service to My Lady; My Cosens and your self.

2013. Robert Pawling to Locke, 13 February 1696 (2007, 2019)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 33-4.
London Feb: 13th 1695
Sir
The inclosed Note came to me from Mr Wright the Merchants Brother in Law, I have forgotten his Name.†1
I think I mentioned in one of my last a Sum of two hundred and thirty pounds that came from Mr Robins a Stationer in Exon employed there by our Commissioners, all of an evenness, very small, and fresh, either coynd or cast. I wrot to him my self having some acquaintance with him and believing him to be an honest man. he returns me this answer and writes to the same effect to the Commissioners.
That he is very innocent in the matter and beleivs we may find by Morris's Boook in London (this Morris is the Exon Carier who hath been suspected and hath been before my Lord†2 for somwhat of this nature) how the money was received by him upon forraign Bills and sent to Mr Jefferis a Merchant of good repute in Exon. Ile give you the rest in Robins's own words.
― 534 ―
The†a only Objection is that the money is all of a size etc. It was received altogether by me de bene esse†1 If approved of above by the Commissioners upon the Act of Stampt Paper with an intent to dispose of their narrow money†2 into the Kings hands and I conceive I could not refuse the same being tendered.
I†a have great sums of money dayly tendered me on that Account and now left in my Office and I suppose complaints against me for refusing the same. So that if I may be at liberty to receive all the money tendered me on account of Stampt Paper some hundreds of pounds will speedily be received; but I will do nothing without directions from the Board.
From which I gather that the Carier deals with, if not one of those that cast this money, which he either caried from London or had it in Exon of some of those handicraft Gent: and paid it to Mr Jefferis who not knowing what to do with it. thought of this expedient; but I think if our Commissioners follow it close they may hamper the Carier.
We have every week money coming in from all quarters and have a full trade at the Office; but I understand that our money is all melted by it self at the Exchequer; and wilbe accounted in paying off our Fund for no more than it yeilds when melted; which will not be above one third of what we received it for; so that considering how much we came short the last year of what twas presumed it would amount to, together with this deduction, we shall make but a sory busines of it; but let those bear the blame that have occasioned it. Now here wilbe a tryall of Skill about keeping up or pulling down Guinneas much is said pro and con, some say they wilbe at 31 or 32 shortly because the money wilbe all gon, meaning the Silver; but at present they fall and are under 28s. I am
Sir
Your humble Servant
ROB PAWLING
― 535 ―
Address: For Sir Francis Masham a member of Parliament [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford] Frank

2014. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 13/23 February 1696 (1999, 2106)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 105-6. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 93-5.
A Amsterdam le 23 de Fevrier 1696.
Il y a déja quelques semaines, Monsieur, que j'envoiai au Sieur Furly, quatre exemplaires de mon petit livre de l'Incredulité, qu'il me promit d'envoier en Angleterre par le premier Convoi, et de vous les faire remettre. Je croi que vous les aurez reçu à présent, avec un exemplaire de ma Physique. Ce dernier avec un des quatre autres est pour vous, et je vous prie de me faire la grace d'envoier des trois autres, 1. à Mylord Privy-seal, à qui je l'ai promis il y a quelques mois: 1. à l'Archeveque d'York,†1 de qui je vous ai écrit que j'avois sujet de me louër: 1. à Mr. de Salisbury, quoi que je n'aie pas eu de lui aucune réponse qui me satisfît. Il m'a d'abord offert de me faire un présent, mais il n'est pas allé plus loin, dès que je lui ai répondu que je ne lui parlois pas de la dépense que j'avois faite dans mon ouvrage, pour m'en attirer un de lui; ce qui m'a fait comprendre que j'avois bien entendu le stile dont il se servoit quoi que nouveau, car il me demandoit permission de me faire un présent. Il m'a fait comprendre au reste que rien de ce qui dépendoit de lui ne m'accommodoit, et qu'il s'étoit fait des ennemis, en témoignant quelque amitié pour moi. Il m'a dit encore d'autres choses, qui signifient très clairement, quoi qu'enveloppées de civilitez Ecossoises, que je ne devois pas compter sur lui.†2 Cependant de peur qu'il ne devienne mon ennemi, il faut lui faire en quelque sorte la Cour. Pour l'Evêque de Bath et Wels, je ne sai ce que j'en dois penser. Je soupçonne qu'il ne soit faché que j'aie publié sa promesse; mais c'est le moins, que je pusses faire, car il n'étoit pas juste que je parusse toûjours sous la censure, en attendant une réparation, qui ne viendra peutêtre jamais.
― 536 ―
Il ne m'a point écrit depuis la lettre, qu'il mécrivit il y a plus d'un an, et il n'a pas daigné me remercier de ce que je lui ai fait présent de mon second volume,†1 quoi qu'il ait écrit deux fois à Mr. Limbourg.†2 Il est vrai qu'il le prioit de me faire ses complimens, dans l'une de ces Lettres, mais c'est avant que d'avoir reçu le Volume entier. Je vois bien que pour plaire aux Druïdes, l'amour de la verité, accompagné de toute la douceur et de toute la civilité possible, est une qualité fort inutile. Il faut crier à pleine gorge, grande est la Diane etc.†3 sans quoi il n'y a rien à faire. Je ne me sens pas d'humeur à faire rien, que ce que l'on peut exiger d'un honête homme, et je me disposerai à tout plûtôt que d'être obligé à agir autrement. Tout ce que je ferai, c'est que je ne perdrai plus mon encens, et mes civilitez. Mais laissons ces discours, qui vous importent peu, et qui ne font que me chagriner sans nécessité. On doit bien tôt rimprimer ici tous mes Ouvrages Philosophiques en 3 Tomes, et en plus grosses lettres.†4 Si vous aviez le loisir de parcourir la Physique et de me donner quelques avis, je vous serois bien obligé. C'est un ouvrage fait au milieu d'occupations fort differentes, et que je n'ai pas pû bien corriger. Comme il faut que les Etudians en Philosophie, aient un Cours imprimé, ou qu'ils le copient avec beaucoup de peine et de perte de temps; j'ai mieux aimé l'imprimer tel <qu'il>†a est, que de le retenir davantage, dans la pensée qu'une seconde édition me donneroit lieu de le corriger. On imprime à Utrecht les Ouvrages Critiques de Gathaker, et l'on m'a prié de m'informer si l'on pourroit trouver son traité of the nature and the use of lots. 2. Edition, et celui de Bivocalibus.†5 On m'a aussi chargé de savoir si l'on trouve le traité de Greave de Pede Romano,†6 et celui de Cumberland of the measures and weights.†7 J'ai le dernier, et je l'ai preté à celui qui m'a donné cette commission, mais le premier ne se trouve pas ici et je ne sâche
― 537 ―
personne qui l'ait. Si vous pouvez me donner quelque éclaircissement là dessus, vous m'obligerez. Je suis toujours avec passion, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings, in litle Lincolns inne fields, over against the Plough London.
Postmark: MR 17

2015. Locke to Cornelius Lyde, 14 February 1696 (2008, 2025)
The Pierpont Morgan Library, New York. Transcribed from Xerox print. Probably enclosed in no. 2016 for forwarding. Answers no. 2008; answered by no. 2032.
Oates 14 Feb. 95/6
Sir
I writ to you in Michaelmas terme in answer to one I received then from you wherein I gave you an account that I immediately waited on my Lord Cheif Justice Holt who promised to take care of your affair.†1 Heareing noe thing of your receit of that letter I mention it here to you again that you may not think me carelesse or negligent of any thing that you are concerned in and commit to my hands and therefor give me leave to Adde here that after I had writ to you I waited on my Lord Keeper and spoke to him on your behalf who promised me that if your name should come to be mentioned he would doe all that he could to keep you off. your soe kindely takeing upon you the trouble of lookeing after my little concernes in and about Pensford makes me glad of any occasion where in I may shew my willingnesse to serve you and therefore you may be always sure of me as far as my industry and interest can reach
I have now before me yours of the 1st instant, and returne you my thanks for takeing the pains to goe to Buckhill to see how things stand there. what is fit to be done there in Repaires of Hedges or any other or any thing of that kinde I leave wholy to you as a better judg than I not only at this distance but than I if I were upon
― 538 ―
the place: and therefor what you shall order in that or any the like case I shall certainly allow and approve of. What Joseph Barnes says about my Cosin Stratton haveing let him Buckhill for £23 per annum is as much a mistake on his side as it was on my side to set him down £25 as you will judg by what my Cosin Stratton writ me. In his of the 10th of Novemb: 1694†1 I finde these words. I have also discoursed Joseph Barnes about his continuance in Buckhill his time being out next Lady day: he will not continue if he hath not 20s abated yearly, and something done to the out bounds. I promised him I would write to you about it. what my answer was you may guesse by what my Cosin Stratton writ me in his next letter dated 1st Dec: 1694.†2 I was last weeke on purpose at Buckhill endeavouring to bring Barnes up to the old rent but cannot, and upon due consideration thought it best to continue him for two years longer although I abate him twenty shillings per year, for I find him sufficient and soe have agreed with him. This truly I had forgot and soe set him down £25- per annum as he stood in my former Rent Roll The reason of which mistake was that he has paid noe rent since this new bargain of £24- per an and soe will be in arear two years rent at our Lady day next. That consideration makes me propose it to you whether you should not call for the rents of those who are soe much in arear, and take them in any money that will be received again of you in Bristoll by any good man who will give you bills for it to be paid in London. For else great arears may prove as dangerous as the money we receive here in London. And truly to speake my opinion between you and me I doe not see when there will be an end of the bad money, but this I say only to you as my private opinion, which I would not have you mention again from me. but that you may make what use of it you shall think fit in your own affairs. I have for you a booke on the subject of our money†3 which I shall send you by the first oportunity. If the Parliament should rise without provideing some other remedie than what I yet see I fear you will finde†a milled money not very plentifull. I therefor could wish I had all my rents returned to London in good bills and that the sooner the better. I have here inclosed sent you a letter of
― 539 ―
Atturney†1 such an one as I formerly gave My Cosin Stratton. I beg your pardon for this trouble and am
Sir
your most obleiged humble servant
J LOCKE
As for the continuance of Joseph Barnes at Buckhill I must leave it to you to doe in it as you think fit, and to make what bargain with him you shall think reasonable, for his time will be out at Lady day
If you can get any returnable money from my tenants be pleased to make the bills payable to Edward Clarke Esquire, and send them to him directing your letter to him at Richards Coffee house near Temple Bar in London

Oates 14 Feb. 95
Dear Sirs
What a brave world is this. I thank you for the printed paper you sent me But whether it be for the Stoping of Cliping or for the encouragement of Clippers you must pardon us dull country folks if we are not forward to speake our opinions upon once reading, and perhaps may be more amazed after a second.†2
I am very sorry for the account you give me of the Gent I enquired after espetialy the later part of it. For as for the first it was what might easily befall a beginer though if he had taken the advice I gave him when I was last in town he had scaped that. As to the later part I know not what to say but only that I heartily wish it were not soe.
I finde by the votes (which the Gent who brings you this†3 brought hither with him) that the new Bank is to be a National Land Bank. and that this and the Royal Bank are soe opposed that
― 540 ―
noe body is to be a Sharer in both.†1 How a Land Bank shall supply the King with ready money I doe not well see. And lesse why any body is shut out unlesse you are afraid there, that subscriptions and money will come in†a to†a fast and overlay the†b Exchequer. The melting which I hear busies them there is I confesse a laborious hot worke and for ought I see may last till they are weary of it. Methinks the silver does wisely not to come into England at this time where it is like to run a perpetuall circle of torment if it stay here. Into the fire it goes at the Exchequer and is noe sooner out but is committd to the tower†2 there to goe into the furnace again to be brought to Standard and then to size and then be pressed in the mill. Assoon as it get free out of the tower it is either lockd up in some Jaylors†c chest from comeing abroad or if it peeps out tis ten to one but the thriveing company of Coiners and clippers put it again into the fire to be joynd with bad company. and then to be hammerd and cut and so conveyd to the Exchequer to run the same Gantlet again. If it be not soe pray convince me of my mistake, and ease me of the trouble I am in for a poor Lady which we bookish men find the ancients had such a respect for that they called her Regina Pecunia.†3 But this was a great while agon and the world is much alterd since. Serjeant Maynards saying was older and wiser and by an implicit faith we in the country beleive it.†4 Steadinesse and constancy goe for two marks of wisdome and to the best of my bad eyes all that I see of late seems to be of a peice. But pray how does the old Bank keep its actions since this starting of a new one?†5
― 541 ―
I am very sorry that my Lord Keeper is ill as you say and of soe painfull and stubborne a disease as a Rheumatisme and at this time.
I admire the Graves constancy and applaud him highly for it. It is a just and a noble cause and if he can carry his clause†1 he shall by my consent have a statue of better mettall than the courser alloy that now passes in the Exchequer and he will deserve it. But is there never a little man with a Lucky hand to sollicit against it?
Tis well the Abstract of the Act was sent me for Sir Fr: forgot the Act itself and left it in town though he was writ to bring it.†2
Sir Francis brought down with him tied up togeather the two books you told me were comeing by the carrier the one for my Lady and the other for me, they are very well bound and guilt and we returne our thanks where due. I am
Your most affectionate humble servant
J L
Mr Clarke†3 is very well. My Lady gives you her most humble service
Since the writeing of what you finde above I finde my self farther indebted to you for yours of the 11th
I wonder not that the Patriots you mention should carry all before them: that is but the least part of what the cure of Clipd money put into the way it is, was sure to produce. The yonge Gent you mention is if it be soe as you say in admirable good hands and will reape great advantage by it. I am very glad to hear my Lord Keeper is pretty well again. I thank you for the inclosed paper you sent to divert me If it be not banter the author seems to have had a nottable clear understanding of the matter and his reasons I think may deserve to be bound up with some of the discourses without or speeches within doors. Truly I think that subject before it has done will run us all out of our wits. Wit without money†4 was once in an old play, but I thinke the present world has settled the maxime Noe money noe wit
― 542 ―
The grave is desired if he has any occasion to write to Mr Codrington to inclose this for Mr Lyde to him that it may goe Frank, for he takeing the trouble of my affairs upon him tis best he should not be frighted with such a packet.
If you have driven the shares of the Scotch East India company out of English hands, how that will breake that company if forainers come in to supply those subscriptions I know not. I think the businesse turns upon that. And if that should happen England will loose and not gain by excludeing English men out of it

2017. Edward Clarke to Locke, 15 February 1696 (2016, 2018)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 103-4. Printed in Rand, pp. 440-1. Acknowledges no. 2016; answered by no. 2018.
London February the 15th. 1695.
Deare Sir,
If I had not been quite Worn out with an Attendance of 13. howers togather, without ever stirring out of the House on Thursday last,†1 I had then acquainted you with the Result of the Longest debate I ever yett saw in Parliament; The subject matter whereof was, the then Currant Price of Guinneas, wherein Gentlemens Reasonings were verie Different, as you may well imagine by the Length of the Debate, which lasted from about 12. at Noon, 'till 10. at night, In Which Debate a few Gentlemen forc'd the Adverse party Generally to Agree, That unlesse Gold and Silver bee brought and kept at a Parr to each other, That which Exceeds, will eate out, and carry away the other, And that unlesse Gold bee Reduced speedily to its Reall-Intrinsick-value, as well as Sylver, As it has allready Devoured a greate part of the Riches of the Nation, soe it will certainly ease us of the small Remainder of our Wooll, and Wollen, as well as other, Manufactures, and of our silver likewise, and will in a little time effectually carry away more of the Treasure and Wealth of the Kingdome, then all the Expence both of the
― 543 ―
Fleete and Army togather doth amount unto; And yett notwithstanding, The Reduceing that Exorbitant imaginary value which hath been permitted to bee sett on Gold for soe long, All at once by a Vote of Parliament, was thought to bee of such consequence, as to prevayle soe farr against the Arguments on the other syde, That by a small Majority, there was a Vote obtained in the Committee, and this Day Agreed to by the House viz: That noe Ginneas bee Allowed to Passe in any Payment above the Rate of 28s, Which 'tis expected will prevent theire Riseing higher, And I hope the true Interest of the Nation will soon Reduce them to theire Reall value,†1 All this is cheifely oweing to the Monkey†2 and some others of his Brethren, who have still strong inclynations to alter the standard, and rayse the silver to the present imaginary value of the Gold, by which you may bee satisfied They are as Wise and as honest as ever; The College have only time to thanke you for your Letter by Sir Francis,†3 which shall bee Answered the next opportunity by Him that is now quite Tyred, But my Ladys and
Your most Affectionate Faithfull servant
EDW: CLARKE:
Endorsed by Locke: E: Clarke 15 Feb. 95/6
2018. Locke to Edward Clarke, 17 February 1696 (2017, 2022)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 80. Printed in Rand, pp. 441-2. Answers no. 2017.
Oates 17 Feb 95/6
Dear Sir
I am sorry that soe plain a question should hold soe long a debate or indeed that the house should tire it self about that which ought to be noe question at all. You may as well regulate the price of wheat as gold. Silver alone is our mony. let the several species and
― 544 ―
peices of those species be of the weight and finesse the law requires and they are pretended to be and all other things gold as well as other commodities will finde their price. Gold was well before when it had none or a low price set by the law. Now you have over valued it and given 6s or 6s-6d in the pound sterling to the importer, who by this means will cary away†a instead†a of 16 ounces of silver for one ounce of gold, (which is the rate in other places) about 19 ounces of silver for one of <gold>†b . Nor can this vote or a law stop it from goeing for above 28s per guinea when any one has a minde to take it rather than the light and base money, which has been the only thing that hath raised Guineas and will raise them still till that be cured, for all the rest is pudder invain or mischeif till that be mended. which I think can have noe other cure but what you proposd. For as long as the stamp which has noe other use but to warrant the quantity of silver shall be inverted and made use of to supply the defect of silver, and soe made to warrant on the other side, never fear but people will finde ways to apply stamps to peices of mettall as long as they are of soe good value and will passe for good silver and in a large proportion. Does not our friend in the Corner†1 know the Monkey yet? you lay the matter right. Noething of these matters could ever have passed in the house without the industry and assistance of those very men. I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
My humble service to the Batchelor
My Lady gives her service to the Colledg
Your son is well and I suppose will tell you soe himself this post
Address: For Edward Clarke Esquire member of Parliament at Richards Coffee house near Temple Bar London
Frank

2019. Robert Pawling to Locke, 18 February 1696 (2013, 2037)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 35-6.
London Feb: 18 1695
Sir
I received this inclosed this day, I forgot to let you know that Mrs Lockhart sent a small parcell to be sent by the next opportunity; but I did take it for a Book which I thought might come to you time enough if I took an opportunity that might offer itself within a week or fortnight and thought there was no need of sending it by the Carier alone unles I had had somthing els to send with it, but now it shall come as you direct by the Carier on Saturday next;†1 as for your Apples; I looked on them on Candlemas day and finding some rotten I took care to secure the rest from it as you directed me at your departure; we ate them in good time and return you thanks for them.
I presume you hear what the Parliament have don about Guineas,†2 I was saying to one that now their hands are in they may <do>†a well, in regard tis likely to be a plentifull year of Corn, to vote that wheat shall not be sold for above 6s per Bush; so for Wooll Beef and Mutton etc
methinks tis a very preposterous course that they take; had they set us right in our silver; Gould would have ballanced it self by it without their care; but whither will not men wander when once out of their way and in the dark?
Twas said of Famous Dod†3 when one asked him why he did not preach against long hair and persuade his auditors to cut it shorter; he wisely replyed, if I can preach Christ into their hearts they will cut their hair of them selvs; the like was once said of an other concerning taking down Organs, saith he if I can bring them to mind the weighty matters of Religion; they will take down the Organs of them selvs. Had silver gon by weight Gold would have
― 546 ―
come down without their impertinent votes. But Ile them to do as they please and remain
Sir
Your very humble Servant
ROB PAWLING

Frank

2020. Locke to Mrs. Elizabeth Stratton, 24 February 1696 (2010, 2081)
The James Marshall Osborn Collection, New Haven, Connecticut. Transcribed from photostat. Answers nos. 1963 and 2010.
Oates 24 Feb 1695/6
Dear Cosin
I received yours of the 5th instant yesterday and had sooner returnd my answer and thanks for yours of 11th of Nov: had not severall things concurd to hinder me, Besides much businesse one part of this winter and want of health the other, I could not presently put my affairs in the country into hands there to be taken care of, But Mr Cornelius Lyde of Stanton weeke haveing done me the favour to undertake it. Some things he writ to me about made it necessary for me to have recourse to that letter of yours But I had laid it soe out of the way where I thought it had been that of a long time I could not finde it, soe that my letter of Atturney to him w<ent>†a away but the last weeke and I intended to write to you very speedily. I am sorry to finde by your last letter that melancoly sits yet soe heavy upon your minde. It must be acknowledgd you have lost a very good husband as well as I a good freind, but this ought not to take away the remaining comforts of your life. Tis a good use we make of all the dealings of providence with us to make us sit loose to this world and think of a better. And since you desire on this account to cleare your hands of those small concernes of mine you have in them I shall make all the hast I can to give you that satisfaction and
― 547 ―
to†a- set you at-†a <ease>†b in that point. Pray remember me very kindly to all my Cosins and be assured that I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant

May it please your Grace
After I had writ the inclosed†2 and was just goeing to deliver it to the person who brings it to your Grace, the letter your Grace was pleased to doe me the honour to write me togeather with the MS: sent with it, came at last to my hands. I finde thereby how unlucky the stops it hath met with by the way have been: And how ill a returne I shall thereby seem to make to the very great honour done me by your Grace and the Author, till the cause of my soe long silence be known. I can easily conclude that what has passed through your Graces hands will not need my judgment, And I should think it too great a presumption in me to interpose my opinion, were it not fit that all other considerations should give way to your Grace's commands. I shall therefor presently goe about what is expected from me and by a speedy answer let your Grace see that I shall always pay a ready obedience to all your Commands
― 548 ―
to the utmost of my power, whatever difficulty they may carry with them. I am

The Bearer hereof Mr Whately†1 a person wholy unknown to me made me yesterday a visit and brought with him some papers of his designed to extricate the nation out of the difficulties we at present lie under. He seems very well affectioned to the Government and his country. As far as appears to me upon soe little time as I have had to looke into it his project seems usefull and practicable and if soe is very seasonable. He intends to present his papers to your Grace and has desired me to procure him this admittance which your Grace will pardon me if I could not refuse him

2022. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 27 February 1696 (2018, 2024)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 213. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's initials.
Febr: the 27th 1695/6
Dear Sir
If you considerd that as long as Guineas are permitted to be currant at an imaginary vallue tis impossible to bring out whole and weighty silver as is evident by the Currency of the worst sort of Clipt mony and none else at this time tho the Kings Proclamation and an Act of Parliament prohibit it you will not think the Author of the paper I sent you soe much mistaken when he says that Guineas must (or ought to) be reduced to their true vallue by a Law (at least to continue for some time till weighty silver comes abroad).†2 And whereas you object against his saying (silver bought
― 549 ―
at 6s-2d an ounce) He do's not I think say it is or can be worth soe much of weighty mony but speaks of such shillings as make the parts of Guinea at 30s or 28s or 26s the Guinea and of such as are still current amongst us which are not worth an ounce because they weigh less than an ounce And upon the supposition of there being soe many shillings in a Guinea calculates what profit the Trader will make by Coining Guineas and with them getting our New weighty coin into his hands and melting it down and sending it abroad for Gold to be brought over and coind and this they may easily doe by buying up Tallys†1 on the late Land Tax and this with Guineas at 25s or 24s a guinea and soe be paid in the New mony as soon as it comes out of the mint to carry on the gainfull Trade. Soe that I cant agree with you that tis best to let the matter of Guineas alone
Now for what you say of setting the rate on them they were Coind at vizt 20s I should readily agree with you if men could be brought to it but tis not probable people will agree to set a Lower rate on them then they went at whilst our silver mony was good vizt 1li-1s-6d at which rate they have past these many years†2
I know not whether any thing lys heavy on the Stomach of the Gentleman you mention†3 but I believe his Rheumatism has had something in it of the nature of some Great mens Gout but by Good fortune he is now very well again and can attend the Councill and Cabinet ever since the Discovery of the Plott†4 though he do's not yet goe to the House of Lords.
Your inclosed†5 is sent forward as directed And thus much in answer to your Letter.
Now I must inform you that in the House of Commons 366 have signd the Association and 94 refused. of the Associates 30 are Lawyers; of the Recusants 9 are Lawyers and yet the Jacobites say all the Lawyers refused to sign it
The House of Lords have also Joind in an Association and in that House 84 are Associates and 14 Recusants whereof 2 are Bishops vizt Rochester and St Davids but of the 12 Lay Recusants 4 or 5 did not absolutly Refuse but desired time to Consider and the Lords Chesterfield Thanet Scarsdale Aylesbury Chandois and
― 550 ―
Jefferys were all or all but one of those that absolutely refused Anglesey Nottingham Hallifax and Ferrers considerers.†1
Give our Dues to my Lady etc: and accept it from
J F

2023. Locke to Thomas Tenison, archbishop of Canterbury, 28 February 1696 (2021, 2029)
Lambeth Palace Library, MS. 930, no. 18. Published by permission of His Grace the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury and the Trustees of Lambeth Palace Library. Printed in Fox Bourne, ii. 339-40. For the time of writing see p. 559. Answers no. 2011; answered by no. 2029.
Oates 28 Feb. 1695/6
May it please your Grace
I tooke the libertie to trouble your Grace with two letters yesterday, the one to give your Grace an account of the delay of your Graces packet in comeing hither; and the other to informe you that I had just then received it. My letters were noe sooner gon but I betook my self to the reading the M S you did me the honour to send me: and upon perusall of it, in obedience to your Grace's commands I must own to your Grace my dissent from the Author in the designe of his papers, which is as I take it to prove that the lessening of our coin would be an advantage to the Kingdom. The stresse of his argument is, if I mistake not, laid upon this supposition (viz) That though forainers will presently raise the price of their commoditys in proportion to our raiseing the denomination of our money, yet our own people will not. To make good this supposition the Author says page 3d. Instances of this may be given innumerable. For the clipping of our money had an effect equall to any publique alteration of the denomination, and yet it was a great while that
― 551 ―
was soe far from affecting our commodities that tis known the light money would have bought the heavy—and that in a Goldsmiths shop five ounces of Clipped money would have bought six ounces of plate and that purely by vertue of its denomination. I guesse these innumerable instances when examined will not amount to one. That here given I am sure is none. For if I mistake not The Clipping of our money had not an effect equall to any publique alteration. The difference was manifestly this. That though a clippd shilling had not the silver and soe not the value of a weighty one, yet there went with it a beleif that when the money should come to be rectified the publique would make good to every one the difficiency of silver in the clippd money: And soe on that presumption it was taken for as good as weighty money, since it would at last produce to every one as much silver as ought to be in weighty money, as in effect we now see care is taken it should. And according as clipd money met with more or lesse of this beleif soe it had the easier or more difficult passage. But when once a law has establishd our coin one fifth lighter; and the hopes, that ever that fifth part will be made good to the receivers of that money, are quite gon, then noe body will ever be able in a Gold smiths shop to buy six ounces of plate with five ounces of this new money by vertue of its denomination. If the author will say it will I shall grant him all the rest of his treatise to be right. If he confesses it will not, then all that he builds on it, falls with it, and is at an end. I need not apply this particularly to all this Gent's deductions drawn from this mistaken supposition; his own quicknesse, (for he is not a man of slow thoughts) will excuse me from giveing your Grace and him that trouble.†1 At least the papers haveing lain soe long by the way, I thought it my duty on once reading, to give my opinion in short by the very first oportunity, rather than adde any longer time to that delay which I feare has already much exceeded expectation. I have not with this returnd the M.S. because I thought that either the Author had an other copy; or if not, that this I have was not to be ventured by soe uncertain a way as I send this. And I have the rather kept it by me, that if any thing farther be required of me I may be able to obey your Graces commands when I am sure I may with good maners take longer time to doe it and goe over the particulars, if that or any farther thoughts of mine on this discourse be more at leisure expected from me. The Author has done me too
― 552 ―
great honour in demanding my opinion and will I doubt not forgive my complying with him soe far as to professe it though it differs from his. If your Grace please to honour me with any farther commands a letter directed to me at Oates to be left at Mr Samuel Jocelins in Bishop Startford, by the post, will find the way hither. I am
Your Graces most humble and most obedient servant
JOHN LOCKE
Address: To his Grace the Arch-Bishop of Canterbury
These humbly present

2024. Locke to Edward Clarke, 28 February 1696 (2022, 2027)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 81. Printed in Rand, pp. 444-5. Acknowledged in no. 2027?
Oates 28 Feb 95/6
Dear Sir
One would think that what is done already should satisfie It being more I think than ever was done in any country since the Creation. viz the makeing counterfeit money goe for true, light for heavy, brasse for silver by a law: But yet this is not enough some thing more yet lies behind. You writ me word sometime since, that you found an hankering yet after lessening our coin,†1 I found noe difficulty to beleive you, and have now fresh evidence that that designe is still on foot.
About three weeks since (for it was the 10th instant) the Arch-Bishop himself brought a packet to Mrs Lockhart and left it with her to be conveyd to me. It hath soe fallen out by Mr Pawlings negligence or care (for to his house it was sent) that it came not to my hands till yesterday. The designe of the paper is to shew that Raiseing the denomination of our coin would be advantageous to England, and the request that comes with it is to have my judgment upon it. After soe long a delay I thought my self obleiged to give the ArchBishop a speedy answer and therefor not goeing over the particulars not haveing time. I have only shewd that the Author grounds all upon a wrong supposition which failing all fails. This I have dispatchd away this morning. Whether the Gent will demand
― 553 ―
or I shall doe any thing more after this I know not. I have more than one reason to perswade me that this paper comes to the ArchBishop from the Monkey you formerly mentioned†1 though as I beleive dressed up by an abler hand than his who is at the bottom of all this. All this story I tell only to the colledg and desire noe part of it may goe any farther. The scene is not yet over and I beleive I shall hear farther from them. I hope in this conjuncture there will be warmth and vigor enough to settle the businesse of the money and put an end to the goeing of all clipd and base money for any more than its extrinsick value. Six pences them selves if they have not a day set beyond which they shall not be currant will leave a hole big enough to sink you were all other things settled to your minde. I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE

Your son is well and gives you his duty.
My Lady, who is this day in physick, by me presents her humble service to you and thanks for your last and the care you take of her businesse, which is the only hopes she has it will be set right and goe well

Oates 2 Mar 95/6
Sir
When I desired you in my last to receive my rents if my tenants would pay you in money passable in Bristoll for bills on responsible men here in London who would accept them, I had forgot to mention Guineas. Votes of the house of commons have brought them down
― 554 ―
to £1-6-0 a peice†1 and tis supposd they will yet be reduced lower to prevent the importation of Gold whereby the nation loses soe much. If it be with you as it is in the Country about us here Guineas are more plenty than white money. I am therefor willing to take them at the rate of £1-6-0, though they have lately gon in London lower than that and some will not take them for above one or two and twenty shillings to which rate they will certainly fall as soon as the mild money comes out and passes in payment. What Guineas you shall receive at 26 shillings or any rate under that I shall desire you to keep by you till I can finde a way to have them conveyd to me in specie without any hazard or losse to you. For what Guineas you shall receive thus for me I shall looke upon to be actualy mine in Specie to be received by me at the rate you take them whether after it they rise or fall. I therefor beg the favour of you to let me hear from you, as soon as conveniently you can that I may know what is don or like to be don in the case. that I may order my affairs accordingly. I beg your pardon for this trouble and am
Sir
your most humble servant
J LOCKE

2028. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 6/16 March 1696 (1973, 2116)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, f. 71.
d'amsterd. ce 16 Mars 1696.
Monsieur
Je vous doibs depuis long temps une responce, et j'aurois este plus exact si Monsieur pieter Adriaens ne m'avoit fait esperer d'asprester plustost quil n'a fait, la relation de sa methode pour l'amputation d'une jambe. le chirurgien de mon quartier a l'hospital de cette ville a imité la mesme operation, il y a aujourdhuy quinze jours sur un matelot alité au dit hospital avec le mesme succes. la playe cicatrise fortement et les os sont tellement couverts et les chairs si estroitement jointe quil ne paroist pas la moindre fente, et je crois que dans quinze jours la playe sera entierement consolidée. le livre de Monsieur Witsen, de la Tartarie, est imprimé, c'est un in folio, escrit en flamen; mais il ne verra le jour que l'esté prochain, il y manque encore quelque planches.†1 je m'en suis informé chez celuy qui en a la direction. ce sera sans doubte un livre curieux qui nous dira bien des choses qui n'ont pas encore esté connues dans l'histoire; comme on peut juger par la carte quil a publiée, et qui ne se trouve desja plus:†2 cepandant si vous ne l'avez pas, je scay le moyen de vous en trouver une. vous connoissez sans doubte le voyage du pere d'avril en Tartarie, escrit depuis peu [1693]†a en
― 557 ―
francois in octavo.†1 je m'en suis servi utilement pour l'intelligence de la carte de Monsieur Witsen. Nous avons eu icy une frayeur extreme pour le malheur qui vous a menacé de pres et toute l'europe par la suitte.†2 j'espere que Dieu fera avorter pour jamais des desseins si funestes, et quil nous laissera vivre et mourir en repos. Mon fils qui a concu une joye extreme de l'esperance que vous luy donnez quun jour il pourra vous aprocher pour profiter de pres de vos grandes lumieres et de vos bons conseils, s'est efforcé de vous escire cette incluse en latin. comme nostre education a trop de mollesse et d'indulgence, et q'heureusement j'ay mon neveu fils de ma seur a leyden, qui est un jeu<ne>†a homme de 24 ans; mais d'une probité exemplaire, et qui a beaucoup d'erudition, et de bonne volonté pour nous, jay cru bien faire d'esloigner mon fils d'icy, et de le confier a mon neveu qui sera tout ensemble son parent et son præcepteur. je m'en promets beaucoup. a cause quil ayme mon fils, et que l'enfant est docile et quil a de lestime pour son cousin. je fais estat quil seront deux ans ensemble, esperant qu'alors a lage de treize ans, il scaura plus de latin et d'erudition quon ne peut acquerir dans les escoles triviales;†3 outre que j'espere quil possedera les 6 premier livres d'euclide, dont il a desja quelque commencement, et tout ce quon peut aprendre dans l'arithmetique puisq<ue>†b sans peine il y est desja bien avancé. c'est sur vostre plan Monsieur quil a si bien profité, et que nous nous donnons de si belles esperances pour la suitte. vous pouvez croire par la combien nous vous devons de toutes parts. ma femme presente ses tres humble respects et moy je suis,
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON
Endorsed by Locke: Dr. Guenellon 16 Mar 96

2031. Locke to Thomas Tenison, archbishop of Canterbury, 9 March 1696 (2029, 2363)

Oates 9º Mar 1695/6
May it please your Grace
The long resting by the way of the papers which your Grace did me the honour to send me made me think it my duty to pay my obedience to your Graces commands, as soon as possible, after I received them. It was Thursday in the afternoon before I had the oportunity to looke into the ms. And though my letter bore date Friday, the day it went from hence,†3 yet I had noe more time to write it, but what was left me Thursday night, after the reading over the papers; it being to be sent away early the next morning by my servant to a coach three miles off, I was resolvd to venture it that which was the first I had of sending to avoid all farther delay of an answer, which your Grace's enquiry at Whitehall made me very sensible was sooner expected. This straitness of time not permitting me to make remarks on the whole discourse, hinderd me from unravelling the particulars: And hast confineing my remarks to a narrow compasse, I thought I should sufficiently, doe what was desired, give my sense of it, by shewing the <supposition>†a the author built on, to be wrong by one of his own instances; which I imagind made the whole mistake (as it appeard to me) soe clear,
― 560 ―
that there needed noething more to be said of my opinion in the case If I could have thought it worth the telling for any other reason but because it was demanded.
I can but owne†a my trouble that the businesse of the money continues heavy upon us, and that we are not yet at an end of it: And am sorry to find that there are thoughts of lessening our Coin, and raiseing the denomination yet remaining in any worthy member of that house.†1 I wish it could receive a perfect cure from such an alteration: But the contrary seems a Demonstration to me. I beg your Graces pardon for this Liberty. The love of my country has forced these few words from me: For I never think on the present state of our money without frightfull apprehensions, nor ever shall till clipping and all clipd money be perfectly at an end. I am very sensible of the obligation I have to the Author for his very great Civility to me And beg leave to returne my most humble acknowledgment to your Grace for the honur you have been pleased to doe me on this occasion. I shall dispose of the papers as your Grace commands in the letter you did me the honour to write me the 7th instant and am
May it please your Grace
Your Graces most humble and most obedient servant
J: LOCKE
