2033. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 10 March [1696] (2027, 2040)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 214-15. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's initials and the address. Year from Locke's endorsement and the contents.
March the 10th
Dear Sir
Yours of the 6th the Grave received this morning and I read not till this evening and was strangely surprized at the reading it for I found you see as plainly (in your retirement) the designs of a certain set of men as we that daily converse with them and receive fresh instances of their unweary'd attempts to obtain their End
― 562 ―
Guineas were reduced to 23s (on the Exchange) to be paid in Goldsmiths notes†1 and to 21s-6d paid in milld mony when the Chief Lord of the Treasurys name†2 was made use of to raise them again and all the Town Informd that he had Declared the Crown would take them at 1l-6s-od this presantly raised their price which has gradually increased ever since Fryday last soe that this day they were sold (on the Exchange) for 1li-4s-10d And This day the House of Commons was in a Committee on the Bill for incouraging the bringing out of Broad and weighty mony and there a design was manifested to have raised the Crown from 5s to 6s but after a long Debate in a Thin Committee the Designers were defeated and upon the Question lost it though but by three voices. Whether they will rest here I know not but I hope they will always be disappointed. It is brought to that pass that now every body in the Treasury disowns ever having any intention to have Guineas received in the Revenue at 26s as had been reported†3 And I have some hope that something will be done tomorrow that shall disable them from Carrying on their pernicious projects any longer. The Rheumatick Gentleman†4 is very hearty and very right in this matter but we dare not let him know what is purposed to be done tomorrow lest a certain monky whose company he delights in should play us one of his monkey Tricks, though he says the monkey will doe noe hurt for the future and has now taken his paws from his eyes and sees that his Leader was going to sink him, but we have reason to fear he still keeps his nature and will be a monkey still†5
We have Advice from Flander that the Earl of Athlone†6 has gatherd an Army of about 30000 together and amused†7 the French sometimes seeming to design to besiege Charleroy sometimes Dinant whilst Cohorn†8 went with a Force and Bombd Givet near
― 563 ―
Charlemont where the Enemy had laid up a Magazine which cost at least 150000li which is a loss they will hardly be able to repair this year.
Tomorrow 3 of the conspirators against the Kings person will be tryd and tis said Indictments will then be preferrd against 5 or 6 more of them. As yet none are prosecuted for the Intended Insurrection and Invasion though 'tis said there is great evidence of that also and we expect in a litle time to see the Scene open upon that point likewise
Give our dues to my Lady and all with you and believe us to be as we ought to be
Your faithfull friends and humble servant
J F: E: C:
I will as soon as possible inform my self and you of the person you mention
Ferguson†1 was taken yesterday. Sir William Perkins†2 was taken this night in the Temple
Address: These, For John Lock Esqr. [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford] Frank: Edw: Clarke:

2034. E. D. to Locke, 10 March 1696
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 58-9. The writer appears to be a girl or young woman; perhaps Elizabeth Duke, who was now aged sixteen: no. 867.
The four days' journey is perhaps to Exeter, about 171 miles from London by Stockbridge, Salisbury, and Shaftesbury. Hartley Row is about 38 miles from London on this route; Sutton is probably Sutton Scotney, about 24 miles further (Sutton Court, the home of the Strachey family, is about 75 miles from Hartley Row).
Don't you think I am more Constant then your frendship could hope or mine pretend to: I think it a great profe of it, amidst the fatigues of a west country journey, to give you thus an account of my insignificant self and travell's. we part'd from Hartly Row at 3 this morning through a crowd of beggars who watch your Coach
― 564 ―
for allms, and will never leave it unbles't. hence a beaux in my Company took occasion of simile, bad me observe how wakefull those wreches, wear for small Charity's; that he would doe the like in hopes of greater: and that my divine idea had so fill'd his sight, he Could not resolve to let sleep intrude for fear of shuting me out. I perceved he took pains to be thought uneasie, and I have more good maner's then to disapoint him. Mrs Mayoress of Taunton, a she neighbour in the coach, has all the low, disagreable, familiarity of people of her Rank, she entertained us all the morning with a sorry love business about her second husband, stuff so impertinent, I remember nothing of it. Beaux is very asiduous. I think none was ever so plagued with dying eyes, his are Continually in that posture, and my opposetes, that I am forced to take a good deall of pains to avoide 'em. The two other felow travellers, wear never so promoted before. and are much troubled ther journey is to last noe longer, and wish the 4 days 4 monthes, I hope every jolt will squash ther gutts out, and give 'em enough on't but they are proof against any such disaster and hugely delighted with what they are pleased to Call riding in state. affter this rediculas acount you need not doubt but I am throughly mortified: the Trout's are just brought upon the table, which are the only good thing here. they look inviting, and won't stay for Cooling Compliements. I hope time will show it none, to say I am
unallterably Yours.
E. D
Sutton. March the 10th. 1695/6.
Address: For Mr Locke to be left with Mr Pauling Seniour at his house in Little Lincolns Inn feilds. London.
2035. Hendrik Wetstein to Locke, 10/20 March 1696 (1831, 1999, 2103)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 80-1.
d'Amst: ce 20e. Mars 1696.
Monsieur
Je suis extremement sensible aux marques de la tendre amitié que me portez et que je trouve dans la Votre du 18. Janvier dernier. J'y aurois repondu d'abord. mais comme je m'eloigne des affaires
― 565 ―
autant qu'il m'est possible sans les ruiner entierement j'ai été me promener par ces provinces pendant cinq semaines ou environ, et en passant j'y ai reglé mes comptes. Je n'en suis de retour que depuis ces quatre jours. Et je n'ai pas voulu differer davantage à Vous rendre grace de tout mon cœur de la promptitude et exactitude, avec laquelle Vous avez repondu à mon memoire,†1 et de la grande affection que me continuez toujours, et dont je Vous serai eternellement obligé.
Si j'etois en etat de faire le trajet, je n'aurois pas balancé un moment à suivre vos avis et à Vous aller trouver d'abord. Mais le moindre froid me fait malade à mourir par des attaques ou de gravelle ou de colique, et je n'oserois me hazarder d'avoir froid aux pieds pour une ½ heure sans m'exposer à ces maux. Ainsi mourir pour mourir j'aime mieux à mourir chez moi, qu'en voyage. Et je ne puis croire qu'avant le mois de May je puisse m'exposer à un tel voyage. Or est la question, comme j'apprehende un peu le passage d'ici en Angleterre, si Vous ne croyez pas que nos eaux d'Aix-la-chapelle pussent faire le méme effet sur moi, que les Votres de Bath, d'autant que je les croi de méme nature, et que le voyage me seroit moins long et moins difficile. Si cela etoit je pourrois entreprendre cette cure dans le mois de May si dieu me conserve en vie jusques là. Si Vous croyez le contraire, je tacherai de prendre mes mesures pour faire le passage, et pour aller à Bath. Je croi cette saison là aussi plus propre et plus commode pour que les eaux puissent mieux faire leur effet qu'en hyver.
Ce qui m'incommode le plus ce sont le manque de sommeil (: je dors pourtant d'ordinaire 5. heures par nuit, et quelquefois 6, méme 7. mais c'est d'un sommeil si leger, que c'est plustot sommeiller que dormir) et les palpitations et battemens de coeur. Je me sers du Sal vol. C.C. et quelquefois de Safran (: crocus) il me semble que ce dernier me soulage la poitrine, mais en meme temps il m'attaque le cerveau. Si Vous saviez quelquechose de mieux, Vous m'obligeriez à m'indiquer.
Mon enfant est plus heureux. depuis qu'il a perdu toutes ses dents de devant, la fievre l'a quitté, et nous allons le purger et lui donner des Antiscorbutiques, aussitot que ce vent aigu et froid cessera qui regne presentement.
Je finis Monsieur en Vous rendant derechef mille graces de Votre bonté et affection, Vous priant de me les continuer, et d'etre
― 566 ―
persuade de la parfaite reconnoissance que j'en conserverai toute ma vie, comme etant
Monsieur
Votre tresobligé et tresobeïssant serviteur
H WETSTEIN
Address: For Mr. John Locke, at Mr Churchils Bookseller in Avemary lane near Paul Church Yard London.
Postmarks: London Penny Post: B TV; P Mor: 9

2036. William Popple to Locke, 12 March 1696 (2002, 2041)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 223-4.
London. March: 12th. 1695/96.
Sir,
I have lately told my Lady Masham of a trouble that I intended to beg of you, and at the same time of her. Tis the perusal of some papers that I have lately scribled, which I intend to send directed to you by the Carryer next Saturday, and therefore intreat you to let them be enquired after. The occasion of my writing them was really from the last letter that I received from you. It troubled me to see that you had too just grounds to decline what I thought a very necessary work: And therefore casting about in my own minde how I might contribute to give you a fit occasion to undertake it, those Thoughts have produced the Papers that I am going to send you. But in the writing of them my Minde run out further into some Arguments (as I believe it happens somtimes to any one) than I first intended; and which I doubt will appear to be beyond my Strength. I beg of you therefore, Sir, that you would please to examin the whole, impartially, with respect to the Use it may be of either one way or other to the Publick: And if in that you judg I have miss'd my End, I shall not think you less esteem the honesty of my Intention, and therefore intreat you without any scruple to condemn it absolutly. But if there be any thing in it that you judg usefull, then your trouble must needs be greater: For I shall not think it so my self, unless you please either to correct or direct me how to correct what ever is amiss in it. But besides this general
― 567 ―
Request, there is one thing that I mistrust particularly, and therefore I must name it. Tis the Quotations that I have put in the Margint, of Passages of Authors not translated in the Discourse, but which have some allusion to it. Those are things that I am delighted with my self when I meet with them any where in apposite occasions, and therefore perhaps I have run into an Excess. But if you judg either any or all of them will not have the Rellish with others that such like things have with me, I intreat you to strike them out. All that I have quoted is out of Ancient Authors, not Christians: Because I know they are suitablest to the persons to whom I write. And whereas all is in Latin, though some of the Authors writ in Greek; I did it so, partly because I wanted some of the Greek Copies, but chiefly because Latin is generally better understood by others as well as by my self: And after all, I seek not Reputation by this performance, but desire to be as little reputed the Author of it (if it should go abroad) as I would of those other Papers that are along with it. Do what you will with all.†1 I am
Sir,
Your most humble servant
WP.
I beg leave to present my humble Service to my Lady, and Sir Francis if he be in the Country; Also to Mrs Masham: And whether I name him or no, I never forget your young Philosopher.†2
Address: For Mr Locke [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmarks: MR 12; GC
Endorsed by Locke: W: Popple 12 Mar 95/6

Sir
I understand from Sir Walter Yonge that a Landwaiter†3 is very
― 568 ―
ill, therfore he advises me to apply my self; by my friends, to Mr. Chadwick,†1 who by agreement, among them selves, is to put in the next, unles the Treasury interpose as they have don lately in two cases; wherfore I intreat you to write a Letter to mr Chadwick in my Sons behalf. I have some hopes that you may prevail from the discourse he had with you at my Lord Keepers where he thanked you for recommending him to them etc

I have not been idle since Sir Walter acquainted me therewith but yesterday morning.
Mr Clarke hath promised to assist me and will recomend it to my Lord Keeper and will give him a paper which I drew up last night, and we hope he wilbe prevailed with to speak to the Lords Commissioners at the Treasury in my sons behalf; and if their Lordships please to use their authority now as they have lately don. I hope the Commissioners at the Custom hous will not take it amis when one is put in, who hath had all their approbations and they do account him a good Officer.
I beleiv <none>†a of all the sham Plots you ever heard or read of was so serviceable to the persons that forged and laid them, as this reall one so miraculously discovered will prove to this Government; it will effectually cure all the evills you feared from bad money; though through some mens folly there may <be>†a cause of complaining yet no fear of a mutiny.

2038. William Molyneux to Locke, 14 March 1696 (1984, 2050)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 139-41. Answered by no. 2059.
Dublin. March. 14. 1695/6
Sir
As nothing is more pleasing to me than a Letter from you; so my Concern is not Little when in so long a time I have wanted that Satisfaction. and More especially so, when I have reason to fear it may proceed from your Indisposition in Health. The Last Letter I had from Mr Churchil†2 intimated to me that you were not Well; and I have not yet received any Account to the Contrary; so that my Fears dayly increase upon me, and I shall be very uneasy till I receive the glad Tidings of your recovery and safety.
Mr Lowndes Book about our Coyn, and yours against him (which I understand you have sent me, and for which I most hartily thank you) are not yet arrived. When they come, you shall hear farther from me concerning them.
I have lately received a Letter from Mr Burridge, who is gone down to his Cure in the Country; He takes all Oppertunitys of thanking you for the Civil Reception you gave him: And as it was upon my Recommendation I must also thank you for my Share in
― 570 ―
the Favour. He tells me, He has read over your Essay carefully, and has just sett upon the Translation thereof. But he has not Yet sent me any specimen thereof; when he does, You shall receive it forthwith from me. I doubt not but he will perform it to your satisfaction; there is not a Man in Ireland but himself for whom I dare promise so boldly in this matter. One thing he Intimates to me, which I must needs mention to you, as being so agreable to the Apprehensions I have always had of the Excellent Author of the Essay, to whom I have sometimes presumed to propose it. Viz, that He would write a Book of Offices or Moral Philosophy. I give you Mr Burridges own Words, who goes on, The Fine Strokes which he has frequently in his Essay make me think He would perform it admirably. I wish you'd try his Inclinations; You may Assure him, I wil Cheerfully undertake the Translation of it afterwards.
Thus you see, Sir, how you are attacqued on all sides; I doubt not but you have as frequent solicitations from your Friends in England. I will at this time add nothing More to the troublesom Importunity. Only on this Occasion I will venture to tell you, that I have a Designe On Mr Burridge to get him by Degrees to translate all the Books you have written, and will give leave for.
My†a- Son gives his service to Young Mr Masham.-†a
I am
Honour'd Sir
Your Most Affectionate Humble Servant
W: MOLYNEUX

Sir

― 571 ―
should not be negligent of any businesse that concerned you. 'Twas with that designe I gave you an account of it in a second letter being apprehensive that my first had miscaried as it seems your answer did. The rate of Guineas by the parliaments reduceing them to £1-6-0 and the expectation as well as the reasonablenesse that they should be brought lower has soe sunk their value here abouts and in London that they have been at 21s-6d and 22s and most people scruple to take them for more, and therefor if my tenants have money that will be taken in Bristoll for a good bill I had rather have silver at above 22s or 23s a peice, pray doe me the favour to let me know at what rate they goe with you. I am
Sir
your most obleiged humble servant

2041. William Popple to Locke, 21 March 1696 (2036, 2503)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 225-6.
London. March 21th. 1695/96
Sir,
I am extreamly obliged to you for your last, and for the promise you make me in it of another. The subject of your next I shall highly value as a mark of your friendship to my self, and the more so for how much the more I finde in it of the severity that you mention. For what I have done in that matter was not for my self but for others: So that if any Severity can make it in any competent degree usefull to others, I shall obtain my End: Or if it be wholly useless, the greatest Severity of all will be to me the greatest Favour: I mean the throwing my Attempt into the Fire. In a word: The onely Concern I take in it is that of the Publick, and therefore I again intreat you to dispose of it intirely according to your own judgment. I beg of you to return my thanks also to my Lady M, for the trouble she is pleased to take in this busyness; and to present my service both to her and others. Yesterday I called at Mr C's shop, and found by J C that the present occasion of the stop in the work they have had so long in hand, is for want of the French Book that is cited in it.†1 For I had asked for it, because I thought I had observed some Errours in the Copy, which I knew not how to correct without the help of the Original. But now it seems they can not finde one of those Books: And therefore I am forced to desire you to let one be sent to me. I was yesterday also at the Stone-Cutters, but found him not: However I will be carefull about the Moulding, and all else that is desired in that busyness. I am
Sir
Your most obliged and most humble servant
W P.

2042. Martha Lockhart to Lady Masham, 21 March [1696]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 53-5. Year from note on letter and the contents.
March the 21rst.†a
Tho I must own myself to've been a long time a debtor to Your Ladyship, Dear Madame Yet I hope it's not too late now to give you my hearty thanks. my being still unreleas'd from my attendance on the Lords of the Treasury must Excuse that I have not yet been able to Wait on You. Ev'ry wedensday is Expected there will be a dispatch of private bussiness which as yet the more important bussiness of the publick has delay'd this has been the only hinderance of mine.†1 The plot (which is the occasion of all this delay) as it imploys the men of bussiness so all here has some share in it for tis the subject at present that all sorts of people talk on from morning to night and therfore you must not be surprised that I can't write you a letter without saying something of it all that's new to day (the rest I suppose you've heard) is that my Lord Ailsbury is Committed to the Tower for high Treason. my Lord Devonshire aquainted the house of Lords with it from the King.†2 this is publick. this perhaps may not be so but is as true that there are two Witnesses who agree in informing against him its thought more will follow and they say there will be 7 or 8 ladys to keep them company. I beleive You will find that there was never any plot so clearly made out as this is and will be. the Government has been so far from being severe in it that they've taken no manner of advantage of any of the criminalls and indeed they seem not to want it. I pray God they may make such a use of it as may better secure our peace and quiet for the future. I must ask Your leave to End this trouble to Your Ladyship by giving some to Mr Lock, that's to say if he has good nature Enufe to have any for vexing me Extreamly by neglecting my letter. however disobliging his indefference is, I can better bear that then the thought's that 'tis indisposition has hinder'd him. if he is well I've scarce Enufe to
― 575 ―
send him my humble service. I am Dear Madame with great affection and sencerity
Your most obligd humble servant
M LOCKHART.

2046. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 25 March 1696 (1991, 2119)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 95. Printed in Rand, pp. 450-1. Sent to Clarke for forwarding: no. 2047.
Oates 25º Mar 96
Dear Madam
By the last post I received an account from Mr Clarke of some indispositions that still hang upon you. This though unwellcome news did not at all surprise me. The winter with such a severity of cold hanging soe long on the close of it is noe freind to the recovery of people brought very low, nor to the use of remedies that should hasten the cure. But twill not be long now before we may be sure of a more favourable season. And then I hope the spring with the assistance of the Steel course proposd by Dr Musgrave will soe
― 578 ―
invigorate your bloud, as to make it able to concoct and master those indigested humors which now fall down into your legs and swell them. He is a learned man and has managed your last great illnesse with great skill and care, which would exempt me from saying any thing were I not very much concerned for your health. Give me leave therefor to adde to his medicines some small directions for your diet. Eat noe thing but meat of good nourishment and easy digestion, and but litle at a time, and espetialy towards bed time, and with all that you eat, take a good quantity of light and well baked bread, which is the best nourishment you can take in your present circumstances, and in it there is noe fear of excesse. For your drink let it be as little and as strong as will serve to quench your thirst. Be carefull never to sit up late, and if you lie pretty long in the morning I think it will doe you noe harme. And when you are up be as much in the open air as the season will permit, and walke or ride as much in it as your strength will allow you. I know all this might be spared to one in soe carefull hands as you are: And you might well excuse me from saying any thing, Dr Musgrave being soe near you. But I cannot excuse my self and to that you must impute it.
I am apt to thinke the powder was sent you for Samy: does the child good and therefor I think you will doe well to continue it. I wish him and you and all your family perfect health and am
Dear Madam
Your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
Pray give my service to Mrs Burges and my Love to my wife if she be with you.
My Lady Masham presents you her service and wishes you a speedy and perfect recovery of your health. And your son who is well presents his humble duty to you.
Address: These present To Mrs Mary Clarke at Chipley

Deare Sir
I have here inclosed obeyd your commands to the best of my skill, and have endeavourd to make it as effectuall as I could.†1 If there be any thing that you would have added, alterd or omitted, you are but to send it back to me and I shall doe it just as you shall think it will worke best.

I am very glad the designe of fixing a rate on Guineas espetialy at 25s was defeated.†4 The thing I looke on to be ill in its self and worse in the intention. The subscribers will not now be able to put off their Guineas at an high rate to the cost of the Government. Nor the Raisers I hope be able to compasse their soe long labourd designe of raiseing the denomination of our Coin. Did I not see soe steady a motion towards both of them espetialy the later I could scarce imagin that any English man could harbour a thought soe destructive to his country as I apprehend these to be. But what may one not beleive of English men when there are those found amongst them that would favour a French invasion?†5
My service to the Batchelor and thanks for his news. sent me 21st.
Is there noe hopes to put a totall end to Cliping and coining.
― 580 ―
Methinks the present ferment should raise some vigor and put a stop to that great and surely destructive evill?
Deare Sir
Your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE

Oates, Mar 26
Dear Co
I doe not expect my letters should be answerd only to keep touch when there is noething in them that requires it. But the reason why I enquire soe much after those two letters was Because there was several things in them that I beleive you would have thought fit to have said some thing to. For besides the copy of the paper which I here send you†1 I told you what I had answerd to an other paper which endevourd to prove that the lessening of our Coin would be an advantage to the Kingdom.†2 He built on this supposition. That though forainers would, yet our people would not raise their commoditys in proportion. As a proof thereof he said
Instances of this may be given innumerable. For the Clipping of our money had an effect equall to any publique alteration of the denomination and yet it was a great while that 'twas soe far from affecting our commodities that tis known the light money would have bought the heavy. And in a Goldsmiths shop 5 ounces of clippd money would have bought 6 ounces of plate and that purely by vertue of its denomination.
― 581 ―
To which I replyd that I guessed those innumerable instances when examind would not amount to one And that if the Author would say that five ounces of his new light money coind soe by law would buy 6 ounces of plate in a goldsmiths shop I would grant all he said to be true. If not it all fell with his false supposition
I added farther to you that if you thought it might be of any use in the debate I would revise and send my answers to the particular arguments in his paper.
I then also told you my further conjectures about these raisers of our coin and the subscribers of the Land bank†1 which tis now to noe purpose to repeat. I also desired you to send me word whether you had any news of the fleet under Sir —— Rooks command which I was in pain for and shall be till I hear they are safe in our Chanell and all our whole fleet joynd.†2
I thank you for the news and the paper you sent me in your last.†3 By soe much as I have read of it I owne your man understands the matter of our money well, and is a mettled fellow. I have been soe busy writeing ever since I received it that I have not been able to goe through it. But as soon as my letters are dispatchd I shall, and promise my self much satisfaction in it. I am
Dear Co:
Your most affectionate humble servant
J. LOCKE
Dues from all here are sent to the Colledg

2053. James Tyrrell to Locke, 31 March [1696] (1895, 2098)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 138-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.
March†a 31
Dear Sir
I confesse I ought in Kindnesse as well as good Manners to have writ to you, and congratulated your safe recovery from so dangerous a Cold as I heard you carryed out of London†1 , but since I had a great deal of businesse then (as I have still upon my hands) in makeing the Preface and introduction to my historie;†2 I chose to doe it by word of mouth to Sir Francis Mas: and hope you will beleive that no Friend you have can be more joyed at your recovery, then my self, nor wish more the continuance of your health.
you will see by these inclosed Papers the Reason of my now writeing to you: which is, to communicate this pamphlet which was yesterday publisht, and is written against your late book;†3 but so weakly, and confusedly that it hardly deserves your consideration; the Authour was pleased once at the Coffee house to discourse with me upon this subject of raiseing silver; and finding he could not satisfye me, gave me some time after these papers, being then in Manuscript,†b when he did not seem resolved to print them: whereupon I sent him these inclosed Queries, which contain my reasons why I could not be satisfyed with his notions about it; this begat another Paper from him containing his Answeres to them; to which
― 586 ―
I was allso about to replye, when seeing yesterday the first Papers in Print I thought it best to let it alone, and leave the further answere of it to you, if you please to concerne your self further in it, and if not, it were not amisse if you engaged some Freind to doe it for you upon your own Principles. I have sent you all these Papers not to teach you any thing you did not know before, but to have your opinion, whether I rightly understand this Controversie, and Whether my objections are well founded: I have allso sent you his last Paper to let you see, where his strength lyes; which is in two false suppositions first the low value of our Coign in comparison of our neighbours†a by the advantage they†b make upon us thereby both in bills of exchange as allso in buying up our Commodityes, if you will but clear this mysterie of exchange, all he hath to say on this subject falls to the ground. if you have Mun of Trade,†1 you will there see it fully discovered, where you will find he plainly makes out, that it is not the raiseing or falling of the denominations of the sorts of Coin, but the more or lesse occasions that Merchants, or others have for Money in those Countries where the Exchange runs high upon those from whence the bills were first drawn; if you have not the book, (which is now hard to be had) I doubt not but your Masterly Genius comprehends all that need to be sayed on that subject; and does not require any supplyes from others: I pray let me know what your thoughts are in this matter, and whether wee may not expect your answere by the next Terme if not sooner; and then pray returne these written papers; the begining of the last is written with Sir R. T's. owne hand, which renders it the harder to be read, but I doubt not but you will Master that as well as the rest, which I have allso mended; and interlined in some places to render it the more intelligible; I hope it may be of some service to you to let you see the utmost he can say: he has bin very earnest of late in the house of Commons to raise silver and keep up Guinyes to 25s, or 26s: but without any effect (God be thanked) for on Saturday last after a long and solemn debate, it was carryed by above 40 voices†c to reduce Guinyes to 22s: and keep the silver at the old standard:†2 the bill lyes now before the Lords, who have putt
― 587 ―
off the farther debate of it till to day and I hope it will passe as it is, with little, or no amendments: this with my humble service to my Lady I remaine
your faithfull servant
J TYRRELL
Address: For John Lock Esqr at Sir Francis Mashams House at Otes.
Endorsed by Locke: J: Tyrrell 31 Mar 95/6 Answered 6. Apr:

Deare Sir,
I have only time to tell you that your Letter with one inclosed to the Arch-Bishop came safe to hand, tho not soe soon by a day or two as it ought to have done; But yesterday I waited on His Grace with it, and stated all the matter to Him, as you had Informed mee; Hee Received your Letter with Greate Kindnesse, and desiered mee to give you his hearty service and Thankes for That, and a former Letter which Hee Received from you, and (as Hee told mee) had used to Good Advantage,†1 And that Hee had some time since Written you an Answer, and sent it to Mrs. Lockhart to bee Conveyed to you,†2 and that Hee would Write to you againe as time and opportunity would Permitt etc:
The Lords have this day Pass'd our Byll, Wherein Ginneas are Reduc'd to 22s. a peice, and Clipp'd-money rendered impassable after the 4th. of May next, the Receiver being to forfeite double the value of every peice of such money by Him Received after that time. And when the Royall-Assent is given to that Byll, I thinke wee are then safe against all further ill Attempts upon our Coyn dureing this session, where wee have often been soe neere to utter Ruine and Distruction, that I cannot but wonder at our Deliverance from that part of the Plott, as I doe at the miraculouse Discovery of the Rest etc:†3
― 588 ―
I Kept the Bishop of Gloster off from Answering Mr. Cudworth's Byll as long as I could, being sensible 'tis my Ladyes Interest that matter should not come to a verie speedy Determination; And have been forced to use all my skill in getting the Answere soe framed as to obleige Mr. Cudworth to make you and I parties before the Court make any Order or Decree in that matter, and when you and I come to Answer, 'tis more then Probable wee shall sett forth every thing more to my Ladyes Advantage, then I could possibly bring his Lordship up to; But more of this as there is occasion, in the meane time give my dues to my Lady and bee assured that I am
Affectionately yours

2055. Dr. Charles Goodall to Locke, April 1696 (1292)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, f. 29. Printed by Dr. K. Dewhurst in Review of the History of Medicine, xvii (1962), 498.
London April 1696
My old and worthy Freind
It hath pleased Allmighty God in his providence, to deprive me of an excellent wife, with a considerable estate, since I had the happinesse to see you; She after about 3 weeks or one months sickness (or rather keeping her chamber) dying of a Diabetes, which though not very much in quantity, yet so dispirited her, that no remedies which my Freinds or self prescribed would do her service, but her life and strength was carried away with her mind. thus I am once more and very unexpectedly rendered unhappy and unfortunate;†1 which the more afflicts me, because I am left without a Companion or Freind to discourse or advise with in my disconsolate condition: If therfore you would favour me with your company, when you come to town, you should have the command of the best chamber and other conveniencies which my house†2 will, or can afford; And I hope that the situation and airiness of the place with our Masters and Officers good company might contribute to your health and longer continuance in town, when you shall make
― 589 ―
us happie with your company; which is what I do desire and value more then any other, whom I know in this world.
I have another request to make, which is, that if you know a stripling about 16 or 18 years old, who hath had the small pox, can read and write, and have been bred up in any Gentlemans service, and is of a sober life; you would pleased to recommend him to my service, who shall not be back ward to give him all due encouragement.
I shall likewise be glad to heare that you have made any farther observations about the influence of the aire in reference to acute or chronical diseases, as also Endemiall or Epidemical; what you meet with in travels or other books relating to that subject, be pleased to communicate to Dear Sir
your ever obliged faithfull Freind and Servant
CHARLES GOODALL
Address: This To his Honored and worthy Freind Mr Locke at Sir Francis Massams at Oats in Essex present

2056. Locke to Cornelius Lyde, 2 April 1696 (2051, 2062)
The Pierpont Morgan Library, New York. Transcribed from Xerox print. Answered by no. 2062.
Oates 2 Apr 96
Sir
That which has of late been everybodys trouble, makes me now again trouble you with this short letter though I writ to you but very lately
The bill sent up by the house of Commons to the Lords which I mentiond to you in my last has now passed the house of Lords too. whereby Guineas are reduced to 22s after the 6th instant as I take it and clippd money prohibited to be taken after the 4th of May. This being a law (for I doubt not but the King will passe it before this gets to you)†1 that lays penalties upon those which receive either Guineas at an higher rate than the law directs, or clipd money as if it were weighty, I can not desire you to transgresse the law for my sake. It is necessary to be submitted to both to stop clipping and coining and prevent the dammage has been done the nation by the
― 590 ―
over value of Guineas. Both which togeather if not cured and that speedily will certainly ruin us. If you have received any money for me in silver I beg the favour of you to returne it to me by the first oportunity that I may gett it off before the 4th of may But as for the Guineas if you have received any pray be pleased to let me know how many that I may finde an oportunity how to dispose of them till when pray keep them by you. I hope this trouble about the sorts and value of money is now at an end soe that I shall have noe occasion to say any thing more to you here after on that subject. I am
Sir
your very humble and obleiged servant
J LOCKE

2057. Locke to Edward Clarke, 2 April 1696 (2054, 2058)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 97. Printed in Rand, pp. 455-6. Answers no. 2054.
Oates 2º April 96
Dear Sir
I beg your pardon for troubleing you with my letter to the ArchBishop. I know how little time you have to spare on triviall occasions. And am therefor the more sensibly obleiged to you for delivering that letter, a trouble I would not have given you could I have avoided it But there were some circumstances that left me not any other way.
I think the nation extremly obleiged to you for gaining the two clauses about clippd money and Guineas to stop the leake that would certainly have sunke us if we scape all other rocks. There is only in my opinion one thing wanting viz To contrive if one could that standard clippd money should goe by its weight, for as I told you in my last I mightily apprehend great disorder for want of current money if your clause about clipd money prevent its passeing after the 4th of May and if it does not we are still under the ruin of clipping and coining. I confesse there are great difficulties against touching of it again in Parliament and I know not unlesse I knew†a
― 591 ―
the temper of your house better whether I should be for that or noe. Besides that a law about it would leave I fear great room for coining still of false money. Tis I grant naturall enough for people to see that though clipd money must not goe for the value of its denomination in tale. yet that the silver in it is as good as other bullion silver and may be taken by weight as old plate. But you know how dull common people are in makeing right inferences, espetialy when they are discontented, and have by their mutual complaints warmed themselves into a clamor and there will not be wanting men ready at hand to blow the coale. I therefor propose it to the College to think of some way to spread this notion among the <people>,†a and to introduce the passeing of clipped money by weight amongst them. That the practise of it may be understood and grow a little familiar before that day that soe it may take place the easier.
In one of those letters that miscaried about three weeks agon I enquired after our Cales Squadron†1 under Sir G: Rooke and have been in pain about it ever since pray ease me in it if you can.
I have here inclosed sent you a bill on Sir Stephen Evans for £110 which I desire you to take of him in Guineas and lay by for me till I come to town. I would not have it received of him in any other money but Guineas and if he will not pay them to you at 22s a peice pray let the money alone.
My Lady returns you all manner of thanks for your care and pains in her businesse which she is the more sensible of and of the great obligation she has to you for it in the multiplicity of your businesse
My reall service to the Batchelor. Did you not receive a letter from me to the College inclosed in the same cover with that to his Grace? I am soe particularly inquisitive, not that there was any thing in it I am in†b hast†b for an answer to but because I finde my letters lie by the way and miscary of late more than they used to doe and I am jealouse of tricks. I am
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate humble service
J LOCKE
Your Son is well and gives you his duty
Excuse the trouble of the inclosed
― 592 ―

2058. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 2 April 1696 (2057, 2060)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 216-17. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's initials and the address. Answers no. 2052; answered by no. 2060.
April the 2d 1696
Dear Sir
Accept our thanks for yours of March the 30th That which came enclosed in it is sent forward by the post and that which you enclosed in a former to the Grave was deliverd to his Grace who had received two Letters you had before addrest to him.
As to the proposall you make for Clipt mony to goe by weight we doubt twill be vain to attempt any thing concerning it in Parliament tho in all Debates those that were against it at the beginning of the Session doe now acknowledge that would have been the true and proper methode of Cure and that ever since they rejected that proposition they have been out of the way but as free as they are of owning as well as acting their folly or kn....y there is too great reason to fear they would doe the same thing over again had they an oppertunity and therefore having by many turns and contrivances and strong attempts at last got into a fair way of obtaining the mastery of this iniquity by having made it penall for any one to suffer himself to be cheated in the silver coin or (much) by the Gold we think it best to stir the matter noe further in a Legislative way lest what has been done already should be spoild but if we could get the people to bring it in practice of themselves it would be of very good use but how to compass that we know not but will study all the ways we can to put them upon it and if you think of any thing that may contribute to it pray let us know it
However if we shall be able to doe nothing in this matter we hope that before the 4th of May the milld and puncht mony†1 will be soe disperst that with the help of Guineas there will be noe want found
― 593 ―
of Coin to carry on our Domestick Commerce for we are satisfyd there is a great deal of good silver mony left in the Kingdom which must come abroad now Guineas are reduced and that it might (before it became penall to receive Clipt mony) was the cause we soe earnestly prest to have the Clause pass to prohibit the currency of Guineas for more than 22s for without that clause the other that made clipt silver unpassable would after the 4th of may have reduced them but then the Stop of the Silver Coin would have been soe suddain that it was to be feard it might either have caused some Convulsion or a generall Contempt and breach of the Law. And now that both clauses are past both Houses we rest not here but endeavour to make that concerning the Gold (which is already generally complyd with and one may have Guineas for 21s-6d of milld mony) occasion the bringing out of Good Silver and to that End besides Exhorting all Tradesmen to refuse clipt mony and receive onely what is good or else Guineas at not exceeding 22s we have employd some to put the Grasiers in Smithfield on doing soe tomorrow in the Market which we hope to succeed in because Fryday last they would not take the very bad clipt mony nor Guineas at above 22s.
I have time to add noe more but our services as due and our assureance that we are
Your faithfull friends and humble servants
J F

Oates, 30. March. 1696.
Sir,
Though I have been very ill this winter, not without some apprehensions of my life, yet I am asham'd that either that or business,
― 594 ―
that has took up more of my time than my health could well allow, should keep me so long silent, to a man so kindly concern'd to hear from me. 'Twas more than once that I resolv'd on the next post, but still something or other came between; and I more readily yielded to delays, in hopes to hear something from you, concerning my answer to Mr. Lowndes. If this be a fault in me, it is such an one that I am guilty of to no body but my friends. Perhaps the running from ceremony or punctuality towards those whom I look on as my sure friends, that is, my self, may sometimes carry me a little too far to the other side. But if you disapprove of it I shall only say, it is an ill effect of a very good cause; and beg you to believe, that I shall never be tardy in writing, speaking, or doing, whenever I shall think it may be of any moment to the least interest of yours.
The business of our money has so near brought us to ruin, that, 'till the plot†1 broke out, it was every body's talk, every body's uneasiness. And because I had play'd the fool to print about it, there was scarce a post wherein somebody or other did not give me fresh trouble about it. But now the parliament has reduced guineas to two and twenty shillings a piece after the 10th instant, and prohibited the receipt of clipp'd money after the 4th. of May next. The bill has passed both houses,†2 and, I believe, will speedily receive the royal assent. Though I can never bethink†3 any pains or time of mine, in the service of my country, as far as I may be of any use, yet I must own to you, this, and the like subjects, are not those which I now relish, or that do, with most pleasure, employ my thoughts; and therefore shall not be sorry if I scape a very honourable employment, with a thousand pounds a year salary annex'd to it, to which the king was pleased to nominate me some time since.†4 May I have but quiet and leisure, and a competency of health to perfect some thoughts my mind is sometimes upon, I should desire no more for my self in this world, if one thing were added to it, viz. you in my neighbourhood. You cannot imagine how much I want such a friend within distance, with whom I could confer freely de quolibet ente,†5 and have his sense of my reveries, and his judgment to guide me.
― 595 ―
I am asham'd to receive so many thanks for having done so little for a man who came recommended to me by you. I had so little opportunity to shew the civility I would have done to Mr. Burridge, that I should not know how to excuse it to you or him, were not he himself a witness of the perpetual hurry I was in, all the time I was then in town. I doubt not at all of his performance in the translation of my book he has undertaken. He has understanding, and latin, much beyond those who usually medle with such works. And I am so well satisfyed, both of his ability, and your care, that the sending me a specimen I shall look on as more than needs. As to a treatise of morals, I must own to you, that you are not the only persons (you and Mr. Burridge I mean) who have been for putting me upon it; neither have I wholly laid by the thoughts of it. Nay, I so far incline to comply with your desires, that I ever now and then lay by some materials for it, as they occasionally occur in the rovings of my mind. But when I consider, that a book of Offices, as you call it, ought not to be slightly done, especially by me, after what I have said of that science in my Essay; and that Nonumque prematur in annum†1 is a rule more necessary to be observ'd in a subject of that consequence, than in any thing Horace speaks of; I am in doubt whether it would be prudent, in one of my age and health, not to mention other disabilities in me, to set about it. Did the world want a rule, I confess there could be no work so necessary, nor so commendable. But the Gospel contains so perfect a body of Ethicks, that reason may be excused from that enquiry, since she may find man's duty clearer and easier in revelation than in herself. Think not this the excuse of a lazy man, though it be, perhaps, of one, who having a sufficient rule for his actions, is content therewith, and thinks he may, perhaps, with more profit to himself, employ the little time and strength he has in other re-searches, wherein he finds himself more in the dark.
You put too great a value on my writings, by the design you own on Mr. Burridge, in reference to them. I am not to flatter my self, that because they have had the good luck to pass pretty well here amongst English readers, that therefore they will satisfie the learned world, and be fit to appear in the learned language. Mr. Wynne's abstract of my Essay is now published,†2 and I have sent order to Mr Churchill to send you one of them. Thus far in answer
― 596 ―
to yours of the 14th. of March. I come now to that of the 24th. of December.
My Lord Deputy and you did too great honour to the paper I sent you, and to me, upon that account. I know too well the deficiency of my stile, to think it deserves the commendations you give it. That which makes my writings tolerable, if any thing, is only this, that I never write for any thing but truth, and never publish any thing to others, which I am not fully persuaded of my self, and do not think that I understand. So that I never have need of false colours to set off the weak parts of an hypothesis, or of obscure expressions, or the assistance of artificial jargon, to cover an error of my system or party. Where I am ignorant (for what is our knowledge) I own it. And though I am not proud of my errors, yet I am always ready and glad to be convinced of any of them. I think there wants nothing but such a preference of truth to party, interest and vain glory, to make any body out-doe me in what you seem so much to admire.
Though Sir Walter Younge be an intimate friend of mine, yet I can assure you I know nothing of those three prints he franked to you, and so have no title to any part of your thanks.
I see by Mr. S's answer†1 to that which was originally your question, how hard it is, for even ingenious men to free themselves from the anticipations of sense. The first step towards knowledge is to have clear and distinct ideas; which I have just reason every day more and more, to think few men ever have, or think themselves to want; which is one great cause of that infinite jargon and nonsense which so pesters the world. You have a good subject to work on; and therefore, pray let this be your chief care to fill your son's head with clear and distinct ideas, and teach him, on all occasions, both by practice and rule, how to get them, and the necessity of it. This, together with a mind active, and set upon the attaining of reputation and truth, is the true principling of a young man. But to give him a reverence for our opinions, because we taught them, is not to make knowing men, but pratling parrots. I beg your pardon for this liberty; it is an expression of good will, and not the less so, because not within the precise forms of good breeding. I am,
Dear Sir,
Your most affectionate, humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
― 597 ―
2060. Locke to John Freke and Edward Clarke, 6 April 1696 (2058, 2061)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 98. Printed in Rand, pp. 456-8. Answers no. 2058.
Oates 6 Apr 96
Dear Sirs
I am not a little glad that about the same time you were communicateing to me your opinion concerning the clippd money my thoughts fell in with your sense and I was explaining my self a little more fully to you on that subject. You will finde then if you received a letter I sent you by a private hand on friday last†1 that we are agreed it ought not to give a new trouble to the higher powers. Tis now only to be considerd how others should second them in what they have wisely don towards our deliverance from that mischeif, which will be effected if others contribute but their parts to bring what they have enacted, into practise, and doe all they can to prepare mens mindes and remove the difficulties that may obstruct it. The care you mention to be taken with the Grasiers is one very material step. For the keeping down of Guineas now they are down is of infinite moment to the observance of the law, and reduceing clipd money. And since you aske my opinion and would have me think of ways that may contribute to it Thus I thinke: first that London in all these matters of money gives a rule to all England, what is done there the rest will follow, and that therefor it should be begun in London. Secondly that as to the makeing it take in London, a good number of substantiall citizens who understand the matter and see the danger we are in of certain ruin if clippd money be not stopd, should agree together not to take any clipd money but as bullion for its weight, and should endeavour to bring in as many as they could into this necessary obedience to the law by joyning in a preparatory lawfull practise for the benefit of every body. you know how better to spread this in the town than I who am a stranger there. I will only name one a man of weight Mr Samuell Heathcote†2 he is the yonger brother but a very sensible man and I am satisfied will be industrious in it. And what too if you should as soon as it is seasonable begin to pay clippd money by weight at Richards Coffee house, the talke and example
― 598 ―
would spread. Thirdly to this purpose I am apt to thinke that it is of moment that those who practise it should besides scales have these species of our coin by them a peny two pence three pence a groat and six pence besides bigger peices of our milled money against which to weigh the clippd. These I think much better than brasse weights, because every one knows not the value of those weights in silver and soe may suspect he has not the full allowance for his clippd money, but when he sees it weighed against money every one must presently be satisfied, and there is noe roome for scruple or debate on either side. These therefor are the materials should be got ready. Fowerthly when this is got into practise, it may not be amisse to spread the notice of it by the Post-boy†1 and such other printed papers, but in the wording of it I think that care should be taken to say that clippd money passes in London as Bullion by weight the word Bullion being put in to take off the notion that it passes as coin for that would be a violation of your law and open the flud gates again. Fifthly I think the Receits and payments of the Exchequer should be looked after and kept stanch to the law. for if I am not misinformd they pay out coin which by the law, tis supposd should stop there. If the Exchequer gives it currency 'twill he hard labour to stop it any where else. Fifthley If the Bank of England could be brought to receive and give out clipped money as Bullion by weight it would be a mighty stroake towards it. Mr Heathcote is one of them. Sixthley The Goldsmiths must be watched for I feare you will have few or none of them on your side And therefor they must be exposd and laid open by publique talke, a Kings head club†2 would doe that. and keepe them from opposeing the necessary and only means to save us. Those who acknowledg that they have been out of the way ever since they rejected this method might doe much towards the promoteing of it now, but how far these new converts are to be relied on you can better tell. This is certain this is a way to trie their sincerity if that be thought worth while. But I am not for any thing but what will help to compasse the end. You see I have readily obeyd your commands. If any thing else comes in my way you are sure to be troubled with it Not only to satisfie you that I am heartily with you, for that you know already as well as I know how little help I can
― 599 ―
adde to you; But because though my thoughts may misse the marke yet variety of suggestions though not right may be the occasion of starting thoughts that are soe
I returnd my thanks last Friday to the Grave for his care of my letters. I desire the continuance of that favour to the inclosed.†1 I am
Dear Co:
your most faithfull humble servant
J LOCKE
The Dues from our fires side to the Colledge

2063. Anonymous to Lady Masham, [c. 9 April 1696]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, f. 202. Socinianism Unmask'd is advertised in the Flying Post, 7 April, and in the London Gazette, 9 April. The letter was written probably shortly after the book was published.
Madam
This is only to inform your Ladyship that there is lately publishd a Discourse which may not be unacceptable to you, seeing your happy genius leads you to enquire into all kinds of Learning, and especially to judg of Theologicall Points, therein shewing yourself to be the True Offspring of so Learned and Judicious a Parent. The Title is, [Socinianism unmaskd. Or a Discourse shewing the unreasonablenesse of a late Writers opinion concerning the Necessity of only One Article of Christian Faith. etc.]†b †3 The Author is One that is a great Admirer and Honourer of your Ladyship, as I am informd: and who is there that bears not a high respect to that Name which carries so much Vertue and Worth in it? This was the only motive to me to give Your Ladyship notice of the foresaid
― 602 ―
book; and I request Your Ladyships pardon for this boldnesse in a Stranger, but
Your Ladyships most humble Servant.
The foresaid book is sold by Mr Robinson and Mr Wyat in St Pauls churchyard.
Address: To the Lady Masham at Oats in Essex.

2064. Locke to John Cary, 12 April 1696 (2000, 2068)
B.M., Add. MS. 5540, pp. 67-8. Printed in Rand, pp. 460-1. For transmission see pp. 603-4. Answers no. 2000; answered by no. 2068.
Oates 12 Apr. 96
Worthy Sir
Your obleigeing letter of Jan 11, with the most acceptable present of your booke which accompanied it, came not to my hands till late last night. The lingering of it soe long by the way has upon many accounts been a misfortune to me: It has deprived me of the pleasure and instructions I might have had from the perusall of your Essay: It has made me loose the oportunity of correcting a great fault, which haveing passed the presse in the first edition of my answer to Mr Lowndes, I wish your timely and very kinde admonition had come early enough to have made me set right in the second:†1 But most of all I am troubld, that it has soe long delayd my thanks to one, who by his undeserved civilitys has soe just a right to them. And I might reasonably apprehend what thoughts of me soe long a silence might raise in you, did I not perswade my self, that the good opinion, you are pleased to expresse of me in your letter, would not let you impute my silence to the worst of causes ill breeding and ingratitude, till you were satisfied, that the slownesse of my acknowledgment was oweing to noething but pure neglect in me. This stop soe unluckily put to the begining of my acquaintance with you I hope you will permitt me to repaire by my faster growth in it. Thinke not this a complement in returne to your civility, which has made the overture: This request has more weighty motives than what I have received from you, though I acknowledg your book and your letter have very much obleiged
― 603 ―
me. A worthy rational man and a disinteressed lover of his country is soe valuable a thing, that I thinke I may be allowed to be very ambitious of such acquaintance wherever I can meet with it. Give me leave then, now that you have opend the way to it, to own an impatience to be admitted into the freedom of familiarity and communication. For though I have not yet the happynesse to know your face, yet I am not wholy a stranger to your character
I shall say noething now of your booke: the few hours, I have had it, have permitted me barely to cast my eye in hast on the three or fower first pages. I shall imploy the first leisure I have to read it over with attention: and to shew that I think my self already past the terms of complement with you, I shall very frankly doe what in the close of your letter you desire of me, and whereof you have set me so friendly an example in the error you have shewd me in mine. I am
Worthy Sir
Your most humble and most obleiged servant
JOHN LOCKE
Address: For Mr John Cary merchant in Bristoll.

2066. J. B. to Locke, 12 April 1696
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 64-5. The writer is perhaps Dr. John Batteley, prebendary of Canterbury: D.N.B.
Canterbury Apr. 12. 1696.
Sir
I have with great satisfaction read over a little book (of which you are the supposed Author) intituled, The Reasonableness of Christianity as delivered†b in the Scriptures.†c I cannot in Charity have so ill an Opinion of the Age as to believe so good a Booke will not soon require another Edition. If so, I humbly submitt to your better Judgement, whether you may not think fit, towards the End of your Booke, a little to enlarge upon our Saviours Improvement of the Morals; in the Doctrin of forgiving Enemys, and doing Good for Evill.†1 It may be too as a King, in prohibiting of Polygamy, and of divorce παρεκτὸς λόγου πορνέιας.†2 And farther, among the Reasons of Gods sending the Messiah, if it may not be proper to insert; the Great Diffidence in Men who are conscious to themselves of having offended Almighty†d God.†3 How naturall†e 'tis in
― 605 ―
such case to fear that Hee will never be reconciled without some Λύτρον.†1 This seems to be the reason of Sacrifices, And God has, with wonderfull Condescension and Indulgence, so far complyed with our Fears, as to send his Son to be a Propitiation for our Sins. And to Reconcile us to Himselfe, as 'tis expressed, Romans v. 10. 2. Cor. v. 18, 19, 20. and in other places. I have had <Thoughts>†a of some other things which seem to me not improper to be intimated, but shall manum de Tabulâ,†2 being a stranger to You, but
Sir
Your humble servant
J. B.

Dear Co:
You have been soe succesfull hitherto in a point of that moment and soe heavily hung upon that I will not despair of what remains from your endeavours to compleat it. ― 606 ―

I tooke three journeys to London on purpose but neither found any more than Mr Dodington in town nor could with my utmost endeavours get three togeather. The last time my health forced me out of town in hast and there being fower there present I could not think my absence could hinder their <proc>eeding†a to judgment, and yet I should have come up had not my illnesse at that <tim>e†a kept me in bed and not permitted me that attendance without danger of <my>†a life. London April the 17th. 96
Worthy Sir
I have the favour of yours 12th Instant per Mr. John Freek, noting the receipt of mine 11th January, together with my Essay on Trade, the perusall whereof you are pleased to promise me, together with your judgment thereon; The freedome I took in laying before you the Printers Errors in your answer to Mr. Lounds you are pleased to excuse, and to take it with the same Candor I intended it; This together with those many kind expressions your Letter is filled with makes me very ambitious to be better known to you, but above all that extra: Caracter all Men give you, and your works deserve, I am sure such an acquaintance must be much my advantage; if I could serve my Country more I should be willing to do it, and this makes me to honour every Man who is able to do it better; I am apt to think Mr. Scrope to whom I enclosed the Letter I wrote you kept it by him, expecting your return from the Country, which was the reason you had it not sooner; I am
Sir
your most humble servant

2070. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 21 April/1 May 1696 (1982, 2122)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 135-6. Badly torn; some words or parts of words are lost. Locke summarized the information about the Dutch coinage contained in this letter in B.L., MS. Locke b. 3, ff. 104-5; it is printed here at the end of the letter.
Rotterdam primo May 1696
Dear Friend
I was very glad to see a letter from your self after I had from another hand, heard of your great indisposition; which I am glad to understand to be so farr restored, and hope wil go forward till you are perfectly recovered to as much strength of body, as readyness of mind to serve your cuntry.
I doubt not but you wilby this time, at lest hear that your books, are arrived in London—we having this post received advice of the fleets being safely arrived, after many months wayting then for convoy and then for a fair wi<nd.>†b
I addrest them to mr. Joseph wright f<or>†b you—by Ralph Selby. Pray what becomes of the Chronological Tables†1 wil<l>†b they be printed or no—If not returne th<em to>†b me, I may possibly get them done here.
Mr. Churchill has forgot to send me you<r>†b booke or books about our Coin, so pray put him in mind of it.†2
Upon all the Inquiry I could this day make among Polititians, Antiquaryes, Lawyers, and merchants Jews and christians so called,
― 609 ―
I could meet with no satisfactory account about the Coyn of this Cuntry—beyond this.
That 12 pennyweight is the standard of fine silver, that the Ducatons are made of silver of 11 penny 6 graines or 11¼ penny-weight —of 63 stuyvers. The 3 gilders pieces lately coynd are of the fineness of 11 penny exactly agreeing with the English standard†1 —
The Ryx dollers of 50 st.†a slighter of alloy of 10 penny 10 grains or 10½ penny weight—
But whether a Ducaton or Rix Doller ever went for less I could meet with none that could tell me. But all inclining to beleeve that here had been no alteration—
Tho, finding a Ducaton to be called in the Spanish netherlands but 60 and a Rix Doller but 48 stuyvers, I was inclined to beleeve that the one was raisd in Common payments to 63 and the other to 50 stuyvers at the beginning of their freestate, the more because in bank—bank mony they pass but for 60 and 48 stuyvers.
But I could meet with no man of my thoughts, coming home I called to mind that I had bought severall Beeldenaars as they call the books that contain the figures of their respective Coyns†2 —
And there by an Act of 21 July 1622—and another of the 4 August 1586. comparing them together I find that the Rix doller weighing 18 Ingels 28 aces†3 with the remedy†4 of 4 aces to have been worth†b and not passable, by statute for above 45 stuyvers—And the
― 610 ―
English Edward†1 and†a Elizabeth†a shilling of 3 Ingels 28 a<ces>†b with remedy of 3 aces but 10 stuyvers.
But the same pieces Anno 1627—50 Stuyvers†2 and <the>†b scotch Thistle†3 or 13 pence halfpenny 12 stuyvers at w<hich>†b rate they continue to this day.
Onely upon the Ducatons we can make half per Cent advance. And sometimes upon the Rix dollers 1 and 1½ per Cent. yea the Zealand Ri<x>†b dollers which goe here but for 50 stuyvers go curra<nt>†b in Zealand for 51 stuyvers, that is 2 per Cent advance, but then you may easily conjecture that we se<e>†b very few of them in these parts.
As to the Ducaton, tho these books pretend to give the figures of all the currant pieces of gold and silver—I find no figure: tho there be of divers stamps and figures, in the Spanish netherlands, some with single heads, some with double heads, and of divers figures here. As if it were a coyne in that time not known in the Netherlands.
I have since the above examind all the Spanish and Republike Ducatons that I have; And find, none older than 1634.
But my wives sister looking among her pot-penningen, as the Dutch call them†4 she finds of the coyn of 2 heads Albertus and Elizabeth of the years 1618 and 1619 and none older.†5 So that it should seem that that was the first appearance of that specie. But why the State takes no notice of it in their Placcaat I cannot imagine. This I further find that those 2 headed Ducatons are always among the people lookt upon as of finer silver or alloy than the rest—and therefore potted up:
The reason that was rendred me why they thought that Ducatons were never raisd, is, because they contain so much fine silver that
― 611 ―
the silversmiths find it there advantage by melting them down, and that thats the reason that there are so few to be found.
But my thinks that is an argument rather that the States may have raised them—
If I meet with any further account of this thing in Amsterdam whither I am to go in a day or two I shall give it you.
I find in the book of 1586. under the figure of <cer>tain†a small coyns The old double stuyvers does 3 stuyve<rs>.†a The old stuyver does 1½ stuyvers.
No man has any memory that ever books were kep<t>†a in holland in any other stile than that of gilders, <stuyvers,>†a penningen, nor in Zeeland and all the Spanish pro<vinces>†a other than in pounds, shillings, pence flemish. <And>†a it is all one while a pound flemish is six gilder<s>†a and a shilling 6 stuyvers and a penny half a stuyve<r>†a †1 . In the year 1586 the Ducat was f3:8 in the yeare 16...†a raisd to f4:5. And since by law to f5:- and now <by>†a way of trade they yield f5:7:—
Thus tho the silver Rix doller has since 1586. to†b 162...†a was raisd from 45 but to 50 stuyvers, the Ducat (which now is 2 Rix dollers) was raised to f4:5. from 68 stuyvers that is 17 stuyvers per ducat.†2 Mr. Neals†3 thoughts are changed, and so you are not like to hear of him, I beleeve he was girded by some superior which made him uneasy. I have seen the Reasonableness of Christianity and its defence against that Orlando furioso,†4 who yet it seems will not let the honest Gentleman rest, till he has proved him a Socinian, or himself a malicious Coxcomb. The Projet d'une Nouvelle Version†5 is finisht, I am to take 100 copies at ½ stuyver a sheete, If you could engage Mr. Churchill to take them, or most of them of me at 3
― 612 ―
farthings per sheete, you would do me a kindness: or at ½ stuyver to take them here, I desire no proffit, but to the publike: my and my wives service to Sir F. and my Lady—and to your self—
Yours.
B F—
the Baron V.H. is gone for Bohemia.†1

2071. Locke to Edward Clarke, 22 April 1696 (2069, 2073)

Oates 22 Apr 96
Sir
The ill impressions my lungs received when I was last in town are not soe wholy worne off yet that I should be forward to returne into that mischeivous air till setled warme weather hath made it a little safer for me. I am hoarse still almost every evening. this is a dayly monition to me to beware your pestilent air, which with all other circumstances of my health have made me resolve not to hazard it in London till the advance of the season shall give me some security and I should be very sorry any urgent businesse should force me thither sooner. I have discharged your commission to my Lady. She bids me tell you you very much mistake her if you think you ought to be out of countenance for haveing trusted your son some time with her which she takes for a marke of your <freindship>†b for her <and>†c confidence in her which she thinks you would not have granted every body. She says he has been very wellcome to her and shall always be soe whenever he and you shall
― 614 ―
agree to afford her his company. As for Sir Francis you must make him your complements your self for as I writ you word monday last,†1 you will see him before I shall and therefor you son and I shall expect new orders from you about his journey to town. As for my self I have been soe long accustomd to take care of your son that it is now habituall to me and I fear that may have made me some times forget that he is almost as tall as his father and therefor have been as plain with him as if he were my own son. whether it has been of any use to him I know not. I thought it would be acceptable to you. But tis time now for me to change that way of liveing with him, and converse with him as with a yonge gent of my acquaintance whom I wish well to And shall be ready to serve for his own and his fathers sake, without any marks of authority.
I thank the Batchelor for the printed letter he sent me.†2 The author I thinke makes the best use of the proceedings in parliament on that subject that could be made of them and deserves thanks for it, But unlesse the Coll: contributes some more powerfull and skilfull helps I fear his use of Exhortation will not be sufficient. Those Jobbers†3 you mention lie most in the way, and if they doe any such thing you talke of, must certainly be deceived into it.
I finde at the later end of the Flying post†4 Apr. 16 Numb. 144 A proposal of Richard Smith in Lombard street to give out milled money for Guineas at 22s a peice to be distributed in the country.†5 I see noe thing in it but good. I shall therefor desire to have twenty Guineas as soon as they can be got from Sir Stephen to be laid out in that money on purpose to get it hither to distribute as fast as I can here abouts for the benefit of commerce which is the end he proposes. And as I vent that I will send for more. As soon as I know you will have it for me I will finde some way to get it hither.
― 615 ―
In the Flying post Numb. 145 There is an Advertisement that the office of the new adventure of £61000 kept at Sadlers hall will take Guineas at 30s. Is there noe way to catch and punish them. It will be of good example, as their breach of the law with impunity will be very pernicious.†1 I am
Your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
Pray send me one of the Proclamations†2 that I may make people here abouts take notice of it and let them see the government is in earnest in the point and that every one is concerned to be soe.

2072. Locke to Cornelius Lyde, 24 April 1696 (2062, 2108)
The Pierpont Morgan Library, New York. Transcribed from Xerox print. Answers no. 2062.
Oates 24 Apr 96
Sir
I received yours of the 8th instant and returne you my thanks for the care and trouble you are at in my little concernes there. I doubt not but you have been before this time informed how the new law now stands about the regulateing of money†3 viz
1 That noe person shall after the 10th of April 1696 utter or receive any Guineas or other peices of gold coin at any higher rate or value than twenty two shillings and so in proportion
― 616 ―
 
upon the penaltie of double the value of gold soe received or paid and also twenty pounds half to the King half to the informer 
\2 That whosoever after the 4th of may 1696 shall take or receive any clipt money otherwise than what is directed by the Act of Parliament for remedying the ill state of the coin shall forfeit double the value
This must be a rule hereafter for the paying and receiveing of money and it is of soe much consequence that it should be observd for the putting an end to the currency of clipt money that if that be not now done clipt money will be increased upon us, and its continuance will unevitably ruin the nation. Sixpences I thinke that are not clipt within the ring are by law permitted to passe for the conveniency of exchange. and it would be a convenience too to take the other clipd money that is good silver as soe much bullion by weight, weighing it against milled money, soe that soe much as it weighs soe much it should be taken for, this if introduced would make what money people have passe for its value and put a stop to clipping, for noebody will clip a peice when it will goe for noe more than its weight. I wish all those who have authority and credit amongst their neighbours would promote this. The present difficultys we labour under at present in this matter needing every ones help. that the currency or passeing of clipt money by tale may be now put an end to or else we are undon
I know it is sometimes an inconvenience to tenants to pay their rent punctualy at the quarter day therefor I am always willing to allow forbearance to those who are honest and responsible men and doe not delay paying upon pretences only to delay time, according as suits their occasions and therefor I am not against consenting to John Veales request if you see noe reason to the contrary
I am and hope always shall be ready to assist according to my power my poor relations but I doe not understand my Cosin Mary Dolmans request, if it be that I should breed her son to learning I desire to be excused, when she speaks out plainly what she desires of me I shall then know what to say
I shall be very glad to see your eldest son or any one of your family to testifie my respects to them and as for my advise concerning your son in Holland I shall be very glad to serve you in it to the best of my skill. I have some acquaintance and interest in
― 617 ―
that Country, which you may be sure shall all be imploid as you shall desire if it may be of any use to your son. I am
Sir
your most faithfull humble servant
JOHN LOCKE

Oates 24 Apr. 96
Dear Col:
I see by the temper the country is in (and I doubt not but there are those who will blow the coal) that if London doe not set them good example the act will be broken through and clipping will be continued upon us. The trade I am sure goes on as brisk as ever a company was lately taken at or about Ware.†1 Some body ready as soon as the day comes to arrest a goldsmith that refused to pay money according to the law would spoile the trick espetialy if severall of them were made examples, If clipped money once get but currency in London amongst those blades but for the first weeke after the 4th of May I looke upon it as irretreiveable. but if it be stopd there the rest of the Kingdom will fall into it, espetialy if receiveing clipt money by weight can be introduced. These are at present my thoughts which I trouble those with who I know are able to make use of them if they may be of any. Duty and service respectively from all here. I am
Dear Col
Your most affectionate and faithfull servant
J LOCKE
Pray let the inclosed goe with your letters to the post
