Oates 27 Apr 96
Deare Sir
If you had said noe thing else but that I should send your son up by the first convenient oportunity as you doe order me in yours of the 25th I should certainly have sent him by the next coach which I should have thought a convenient oportunity. But you saying in yours of the 23d which came with the other that you desire your son should come up when any person from Oates or out of that Neighbourhood comes to town by coach I was not very clear what you meant by Convenient opportunity or what was best for me to doe in the case. I therefor communicated your orders to my Lady in whose house he is and at whose invitation he came hither, unwilling to doe any thing where I had not your direct order, without her consent. She presents her service to you and desires you would let him stay here till some body from hence goes to town that may accompanie him in the coache. She indeed expressed the same desire upon Sir Francis's not returning this way from Chelsmsford, but I thought this of soe little moment in respect of more weighty considerations relateing to your son that as I remember I mentiond it not to you. But since I see you have some debate in your self whether he should be venturd up in the coach alone amongst strangers I shall leave that to be agreed between you and my Lady and shall exactly follow those orders you send me. But yet shall not forbear to tell you that I think it of great concerne to your son to be in town under your eye, and under the direction of masters who may keep his hands full of businesse and this the sooner the better. The reasons whereof I discoursed to you when I was in town.
I see the College are very industrious to carry their point and save us. The opposition they finde is noe more than what I expected but if we misse the remedie at this time I fear we are lost
The printed letter of Advice concerning the currency of Clipt money which the Batchelor did me the favour to send me†1 I have disposed
― 619 ―
of and have sent to Mr Churchill for half a dozen more of them to distribute and I dispose all who come near me to obey the law by shewing them how much it is their interest to keep strictly to it. I doe what I can though that I know is but little, and would not be of great consequence as to the main were it much more For as you lead in the citty soe will the countrys follow.
One of my Brethren writ to me in January to let me know I was expected in town at the hearing which would begin the next weeke†1 this came to me when I was very ill in bed and soe in my answer I excused my self. The 15th of January there was sent me the common notice by our <Secretary>†a that they would meet the Friday following. To this Mr Pawling made answer by telling the Secretary that I was ill in the country.†2 The 24th of March Mr Tillon our Secretary sent me by their order the Association which they had signed desireing me to return it with all convenient speed, without the least mention of any thing else in his letter†3 soe that I could not but be extremly surprised when you told me the cause was not yet heard and judgd. For whatever you have been told they writt, that is all that ever I heard from them.
I Hope the Gent in the Corner will prevaile with Our Master to stay till past the 4th of may and speake to him plain English about this matter†4

2075. John Freke [and Edward Clarke] to Locke, 28 April [1696] (2074, 2076)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 218. Defective: lacks lower strip of principal leaf and whole of cover. Written by Freke. Year from contents. Answers no. 2073; answered by no. 2076.
April the 28th.
Dear Sir
We promised in our last that a third attempt should be made in the House of Commons to make Clipt mony goe by weight and we thought we might well promise it for the Gentleman in whose hands the clause concerning it was, declared to the House that he would offer it again Fryday, but though he declared this soe publickly on thursday,†1 yet when Fryday came he thought fit to forbear offering it for reasons that he has not Comunicated to us but left us to guess at, soe that now we despair seeing Clipt mony goe by weight, for unless an ounce of it or any other Quantity could procure a man as much good mony as tis worth by weight 'tis impossible the people should be brought to pass it by weight, and if you look into the Letter sent you a week since†2 pag: 10 you'll find a Clause transcribd out of an Act past last winter that makes it unlawfull to dispose of it for good mony (unless it be Cutt in pieces).†3
We agree with you that unless the Acts concerning the Coin be punctually and generally observed from the 4th of may all that has been done will prove in vain for one weeks breach in this case will be irretriveable And we know the Jobbers will doe their utmost to make the Laws insignificant but I hope all their endeavours will be ineffectuall the Common people and markets seem resolved to obey and the Bank of England begins to pay lawfull mony and will receive noe other And the two Votes which were made yesterday and you will see in the print†4 will (I Question not) have a good effect to make people doe their Duty.
<Give our dues to all at>†a Oats and accept them from
. . . . .

Oates 30 Apr 96
Dear Col
Monday†1 is neere and therefor I venture this by the penny post in answer to yours of 28th at least that part of it which conteins the objection against clipped money goeing by weight out of the clause of the Act of parliament cited in the 10 page of the printed letter you sent me. I have not that letter by me, but what you say of it at first reading†a startled me, but upon second thoughts I think that clause need not hinder at all, but may promote the passeing of clipd money by weight. For if those of the substantiall citizens who agree to receive none but lawfull mony, i.e. weighty, will also resolve to cutt all the clipd money they receive by weight before their faces whom they receive it of, and before they weigh it, that clause is not only complyd with, but people will be encouraged to bring that money to them when they see a demonstration that they can designe noe profit to them selves by it, nor any thing but an obedience to the law and the good of their country. Nor does the cutting of a clipd shilling make it more unfit to goe by weight than it was before the two peices being as fit to be weighed and worth as much as when they were in one peice
I have a thought comes into my head whilst I am writeing, but whether practicable or usefull I have not time to weigh, but suddain and raw as it is I send it you, if any use can be made of it you can judg and digest it, and that is, that the Citizens who can be brought to a resolution to keep the law should enter into some agreement and contract amongst them selves soe to doe
Sir Francis is expected home to day. If he bring me any of the money you were promised I will make the best use of it I can and
― 622 ―
if I can get but a pair of Taylors sheers I will shew the way to destroy clipt mony and yet not loose the benefit of it by weight in trade till new can be recoind. I am

your most affectionate humble servant

2078. Locke to John Freke and Edward Clarke, 1 May 1696 (2077, 2080)
Rand, pp. 470-1, from 'the abstract made by the Historical Manuscripts Commission'.
Oates, 1st May, 1696.
Dear Co.,
I sent to you yesterday by the penny post that my letter might be with you as soon as may be. If it comes to your hands, you will see how that clause of the Act of 6 and 7 Gulielmi Tertii, quoted in the printed letter, as I think may be turned to the advantage of passing clipped money by weight. If those honest citizens who resolve to receive it no otherwise will cut it in two in the sight of those they receive it from before they weigh it, which will be a demonstration to them they mean not profit to themselves by it,†a this†a will, so far as it reaches, effectually hinder clipped money from passing by tale,
― 624 ―
but not at all by weight, the two pieces of a cut half-crown being as fit to go by weight and as much worth that way as when they were whole in one piece. For in that case they will have the stamp for a mark of standard bullion as well as before. I have since my writing yesterday got some more of those printed letters, and reading the clause in it I understand it to reach no other cases, but where English money is exchanged for English money; and for that, cutting the clipped into two pieces secures the parties from the penalty of that Act, and in all other cases of giving money in exchange for commodities that clause hinders not the taking it by weight.
But I think the cutting of clipped money (whereby it would be brought to perfect market standard bullion), and passing it by weight so cut would be of great use, for the putting an end to it, if that could be brought into fashion. If Mr. Smith, the goldsmith in <Lombard>†a Street,†1 be a man that wishes well to this business, as he seemed by his proposal, and would for the advantage of the public distribute milled money for the use of the poor and commerce, let him be content to take on him the trouble of doing it this way by giving milled money for clipped weight for weight, but first cutting the clipped money in pieces. I would fain see a goldsmith of so public a spirit as this. If this be such a man I shall worship him, and by this published in the prints and done for the benefit of ordinary people but one week he will do more good than anything I can imagine. But in all such cases let him not weigh the clipped money brought him against weights, but against the new money he gives for it, that ignorant people may be satisfied they are not cheated. This I am sure would show the other goldsmiths that would not cut the clipped money, and quickly force out the hoards of milled money, and then the business is done.
The senseless country people will, I find, be very uneasy against their own interests, but to enforce the strict observance of the law and keep the majority to a compliance the two good votes made on Monday morning†2 will do well to be published in the Flying Post and those other prints, and that more than once, especially if Mr. Attorney†3 do anything therein, for then the vote and what has
― 625 ―
been done upon it may go both together and be set out to advantage. If, too, anything good be done in London Monday, that either milled money appears in payment, or clipped money pass only by weight, and that cut, pray let us have it in these prints with all advantage on Tuesday,†1 and so on. This will be of great influence in the country.
I beg your pardon for this long talk on this subject and to you that know better than I, but I count all is at stake, and in this occasion would not omit to show my concern by suggesting anything I can think of on valeat quantum valere potest.†2 This made me in mine yesterday mention some agreement or kind of association amongst those who are of the mind to observe the law, at least your city canvassers would do well to be easy to promote it: it is of more consequence than any election of sheriff or burgess.
<Tu>†a conversus confirma fratres†3 should be preached, and all hands at work to make proselytes. I should be glad to see in your next letter the name of the gentleman who failed you,†4 that I may remember him another time.
Address: For Edward Clarke, Member of Parliament, at Richard's Coffee House.
2079. Locke to John Cary, 2 May 1696 (2068, 2084)
B.M., Add. MS. 5540, ff. 70-1. Printed in Rand, pp. 472-3. Answers no. 2068; answered by no. 2084.
Oates 2 May 96
Worthy Sir
I have read over your Essay of trade you did me the favour to send me and have found that satisfaction I expected. It answers the Character I had of you and is the best discourse I ever read on that subject not only for the clearnesse of all that you deliver, and the undoubted evidence of most of it But for a reason that weighs with me more than both those and that is that sincere aime at the
― 626 ―
publick good and that disinteressed reasoning that appears to me in all your proposals; A thing that I have not been able to finde in those authors on the same argument which I have looked into. This makes me dare to owne to you that there are some few things in it wherein my opinion differs from yours, but yet I like not your booke one jot the worse, since I can promise my self from a man of your ingenuity and one who covers noe by interest of his owne under the pretence of serveing the publick that when I have the oportunity to debate them with you either I shall be brought to righter thoughts by your stronger reason, or else that you will not reject any thing I shall offer because you have been of another minde. In all debates with any one all that I desire is that between us the truth may be found. but whether I brought it thither or carry it away instead of an error, that tooke its place before, I am little concerned, only in the latter case I am sure I am the greater Gainer. One thing I have to complain of your booke, but it is the complaint of a greedy man, and that is, that it is too little, but a second Edition will give you an oportunity to enlarge it.†1 and I hope you will doe soe. He that could say soe much, can say a great deale more if he will, and you doe as good as confesse it in several parts of your Essay. You cannot employ your thoughts on a more necessary or usefull subject. The country Gent who is most concerned in a right ordering of Trade both in duty and interest is of all others the most remote from any true notions of it or sense of his stake in it. Tis high time somebody should awaken and informe him, that he may in his place looke a little after it. I know noe body soe able to doe it as you. I see noe party or interest you contend for but that of truth and your country. such a man carrys authority and evidence in what he says and those that will not take the pains to understand him throughly cannot refuse to believe him and therefor I hope the same reasons that first set you on worke will have force to make you goe on. You make apologies in yours of the 17 Apr for the freedom you tooke in shewing me a mistake in my booke and take it as a kinde of obligation that I excuse it. But I tell you I doe not excuse it: that were to suppose that it needed an excuse: Noe I assure you I thank you for it, and whether it were mine or the printers slip I take it for a great marke of your good will and freindship to me, that you advised me of it and I have given order to have it mended. Will you give me leave with the same
― 627 ―
Candor to offer two places to you to be alterd in the next Edition of your booke. the one is in the last page of your Dedication to the King, where I thinke it is more for the advantage of your argument that you should say all his dominions than Judea For he and his father David had extended their conquests as far as the Great River i.e. Euphrates and the Scripture tells us that Solomon built Tadmor, which was a great town in a pleasant and fruitfull plain a great way in Arabia deserta. The other I guesse is a slip of the printer and is of noe consequence to your argument and that is Inter Hades p 56. which I conceive should rather be In Hades or Hadou which signifies the state of the dead, and possibly you will think may be as well expressed by amongst the shades or some such other English words. I take this liberty only to shew you that I in earnest covet a familiar acquaintance with you and am without a complement
Sir
Your most humble servant
JOHN LOCKE
Address: For Mr John Cary merchant in Bristoll
Endorsed (f. 71): John Locke Esqe Oats the 2d May 96; (f. 70v): Recd: May 5th. Answ: the 9 96.
2080. Locke to Edward Clarke, 3 May 1696 (2078, 2082)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 104. Printed in Rand, pp. 474-6. Answers no. 2077.
Oates 3º May 96
Dear Sir
I thank you for the trouble you have been at with Worthy Sir St: about the Guineas But I hope the tricks of those blades are now at an end. I wish the new money had come to your hands a day sooner that I might have received some part of it by Sir Francis for the purposes I told you. I shall send order by the post to morrow to my Cosin Bonville to come to you for one half of it that it may be ready at that end of the town for any one of this neighbourhood that goes to town whom I can trust to bring it me. the remainder I must beg you to lay up for me till I can light of a way to get it hither. In the mean time for present supply I hope to borrow a little of a neighbour here by, who I am told has a summ of mild money lately paid her here. If the observation of the law take place and
― 628 ―
clipd money be not hence forwards current there will be noe need for you to take up the remaining fowerscore Guineas from Sir Stephen. I shall be able to doe it my self well enough when I come to town without giveing you that trouble and soe it may rest as it is. I hope to hear good news from you of this matter the next post and that I shall see the good effects of the Col:'s pains and labour in this point. As far as I can hear, people here abouts stand pretty right but that will all depend upon what the town does. If London stands firme the first shock all will goe easie. I writ to the Batchelor on Friday and sent it from Hongar by the penny post.†1 I should be very glad to hear that he received it, and when, that I may know how far to reley upon that conveyance, in case of necessity. I should also be glad to have the Coll's sense on the cutting the Clipt money which was the subject of that letter. I have writ†a mondays two votes at the end of the Letter about the currency of Clipt money†2 and soe given them. The summary of Queen Elizabeths reasons†3 shall now goe with them. Adde but Clipt money to base and those†b reasons contein just our case. I received them this after noon and thank you heartily for them, for I think they will be of very good use.
Pray doe me the favour to let me know whether my brethren goe not on to hear the Appeales and what they stick at, All that ever I heard from them was what I writ you word the last weeke†4 and there for could not but be surprised when I heard that none of the causes had been yet heard and cannot guesse at the reason. pray enlighten me a little in your next
I beg your pardon for mistakeing your directions about your sons comeing to town. and for my excuse must tell you what lead me into it and made me interpret your orders of comeing by the first convenient oportunity, by what you had said before, that he should come when any person from Oates or out of the neighbourhood came to town by coach. viz because you had bid me before send him up with Sir Francis when he returnd from the Sessions, which made me suspect you might have some particular reason why you would not have him come alone. However I concluded it was to
― 629 ―
erre on the safer side to keep him here till I knew your minde clearly and some few days stay longer here could not be of any great consequence one way or other. I shall give charge to Syl to make up his things safe together in one pack and he shall wait upon him to morrow morning to the Coach at Harloe and see his things put up safe. I hope you will see him safe with you in the evening. I am
Dear Sir
your most faithfull humble servant
JOHN LOCKE
Pray give my humble service to the Batchelor
My Lady has writ to you, I understand, herself.
Pray desire the Batchelor to doe me the favour to deliver the inclosed if Mr Cary be in town or else I must beg you it may goe by the post

2082. Locke to John Freke and Edward Clarke, 6 May 1696 (2080, 2083)
Rand, pp. 476-7. Answered by no. 2083.
Oates, 6th May, 1696.
Dear Sir,
I hope your son came safe and well on Monday last. I think the people hereabout are pretty rightly set as to the money matter. Only I find that the money now first coming abroad is hammered coin that has pretty well escaped the clippers. But about this, there are scruples raised about understanding the clause about punching in the fifteenth page of the Act for remedying the ill state of the coin.†1 The questions put to me were:
1. Whether a man who has punched money which had been clipped but so little that above half the letters were left on, was under the penalty of forfeiting the money if he tendered it in payment.
2. Whether by the greatest part of the letters were meant the greatest part in numbers (as it sometimes happens in that coin that in the very stamping of it without clipping it will want a great part of the letters at one end of the diameter by the misapplication of the stamp, and have them all entire at the other end of the diameter on the same flat side), or greatest part of the height of each letter, as when above half the R, half the E and half the X <is>†b left in Rex.
― 631 ―
To the first of these I thought the true answer was no. To the second above half the letters in height. But my opinion, not being of authority, I would gladly have that from you which might be so to make this matter easy to those who are willing to have the law obeyed, and yet would neither lose the benefit of broad hammered money in commerce, nor yet let it go unpunched for the benefit of clippers, nor yet be exposed to the fancy or humour of a justice of peace. I would be glad of your assistance herein to help our honest neighbours, and to hear how it goes in London. I am,
Dear College,
your most affectionate humble servant,
J. LOCKE.
Sir Francis and my Lady give you their services.
Endorsed by Clarke: Mr. Locke, with several questions touching punched money, etc. Received the 8th May, 1696. Answered the 9th per College.

2083. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 9 May 1696 (2082, 2086)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 219-20. On f. 219v there is an offset of a draft letter from Locke to J. F., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 46 (no. 2528). Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's initials and the address. Answers no. 2082; answered by no. 2086.
May the 9th 1696
Dear Sir
Tis noe wonder that people find a difficulty to understand the Clause about punching mony those that got in the words (the
― 632 ―
greatest part of the Letters) intended to Creat difficultys and doubts thereby nay they or some of them intended to encourage Clipping away near half the Letters or at least that mony soe clipt should be Current for the Carrying on a publick design they had engaged themselves in. But what ever those men meant that got the parliament to put in those words now they are in we must Construe them not according to their intentions but according to the Scope and design of the Act
Now the Act intended to hinder the Currency of Clipt mony and this Clause is to prevent the mony that has not been clipt from being clipt and the words of the clause being doubtfull and capable of a double construction ought to be understood (by those that in obedience to the Law punch the mony) soe as may best conduce to the ends aim'd at by the Act i.e. They ought not to punch any that has been unlawfully diminisht. But then on the other side when it is a Question whether a person shall be punisht for uttering a piece that has been unlawfully diminisht (and is puncht) but has the greatest part of the Letters (in number) whole or the greatest part of every one of the Letters but none of them whole I conceive the Justices in either of these Cases are not to adjudge it a forfeiture for all penall Laws are to be construed in the most favourable sense for the people, And besides the Clause in the Act makes not the forfeiture to be incurrd unless the piece be clipt after tis puncht. Soe that the Justices ought to be governd much by the Circumstances in this case viz They are to see whether the Clipping has probably been since the punching and Consider whether the person uttering the piece be of good or bad fame and therefore may or may not have been guilty of or privy to the deminishing the peice and whether it be a single piece or the whole summ or any great part of it that is soe diminisht and by these and such like prudentiall Rules they may put the Act in Execution soe as to prevent the mishief the Act intended to remedy and yet not oppress the people or make difficultys in payments and commerce
We are in great hopes that we have effectually broke the design of forcing people to take clipt sixpences. Nay we believe the very endeavours that have been used to make them the onely current mony will occasion (from the opposition that has been given to it) that noe clipt sixpence will in a litle while be taken at all by any body
― 633 ―
Give our services to Sir Fr and my Lady and Mr Masham†1 and believe we are
Your affectionate friends etc.
J F
E: C:
Address (written by Clarke): These, For John Lock Esqr. [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Frank: Edw: Clarke:
Postmarks: MA 9; GC
Endorsed by Locke: J: Freke 9º May 96 Answered 11
2084. John Cary to Locke, 9 May 1696 (2079, 2136)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 16-17. Draft or copy in B.M., Add. MS. 5540, f. 72. Printed from the B.M. version in Rand, pp. 477-9. Answers no. 2079.
London May the 9th. 96
Worthy Sir
I have yours 2d. Instant, with your Favourable opinion of my Essay on Trade, which was wrote without partiall Respect either to my selfe or anyone else; what I endeavoured was to set thinges in a true light, in opposition to those who I had observed in a former sessions to be continually perplexing the Parliament with notions fitted for their private Interests under the splendid name of the Publique Good; This was my Intention in writeing it, and your opinion that it answers this Intention is a great satisfaction to me, and though I could never be induced to valew any thinge that is my own, yet I cann doe noe lesse then thinke much better of what you esteem; That a Treatise desighned for a publique use is wrote without partiality is as great a Character as cann be given it, and this comeing from your penn makes it more weighty, I must begge your pardon if I shew my folly in being proud of it, because it makes me thinke I have hit the White I aymed at, and the more because it had the same Character from mr. Edmond Bohun, who haveing read it was pleased to write me from Ipswich to Bristoll almost in your wordes;†2 Integrity and Faithfullnesse are what I esteem above any other commendations; You thinke it toe short, and others have
― 634 ―
complayned tis toe long, those Gentlemen did not consider how difficult it is to compremise†1 soe spacious a thing as the Trade of England is in a few Lines; I am heartily sorry I shall not have the happinesse to see you in London, desighning for Bristoll on Munday next, should gladly have discoursed you on those points you differ with me, and to have owned in a second edition that they were of your Correction; There are some things I leave in the darke, as thinkeing them more proper to be spoken toe in the House of Commons then made the subject of a discourse, they might bringe me under the name of a Projector, which I carefully endeavour to avoyd, I could say much on This, but I must then find fault with our Legislators, who toe often examine thinges by the touchstone of their own Interest, and either throw them out, or coolely let them fall, as they answer that end; I wish That House were better fild with men of publique spirits then it is; our Taxes might be raysed with more Ease, our Trade better secured, and our Mony made to goe farther towards the use of the Warr, were selfe shut out, but when That is let in twill be to noe purpose for any Gentleman without dores to contend against it; when I have the honour to sit there I will endeavour to shew my desighnes are all of one peice;†2
I thanke you for the Two Alterations you propose in the close of your Letter; your Reason for the first is beyond dispute, but please to consider I had mentioned the word Dominions in the beginning of that Paragraffe, soe whither twill be proper to use it twise, or to leave it out where now it is, and put it in the place of Judea is the question, it doth not seem to runne soe well that way, but this I leave to your Judgment; As to the other, I must clear the Printer, twas my own Error, and I will mend it in the next; The Booke as it was wrote privately, soe it came abroad unexpected, being never seen till in the Booksellers shop, nor known that I was writeing till it had almost past the Presse; I was indeed then desired by a neer Relation who is a competent Judge of Words to have the peruseing it, but (besides that twas toe late) I was afraid he would have perplext the Matter by mending the Language, soe I chose to let it come abroad as it was;
Inclosed I send you the proposalls I gave to the City of Bristoll for employing and maintaining their Poor, grounded on that part
― 635 ―
of my Essay, and alsoe the Act of Parliament past this Sessions, which hath met with such approbation, that tis generally desired for a president;†1 The other is a short Reply to a paper put into the House of Lords against passing a Bill sent them by the Commons, which I thought would have been of great use to the Publique; The Managers had reprinted that part of my Essay which treated of the East India Trade, and delivered it to both Houses, wheretoe the Lynnendrapers raised Objections, to which this is a suddain Reply, made at the Request of the Manufacturers; I have fairly summed up their Arguments, though I cannot send you the Originall paper;†2 I am
Honoured Sir
Your most humble servant
JOHN CARY

2085. [Father John Sergeant] to Locke, 10 May 1696
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 134-5. The letter is attributed to Sergeant by Professor Yolton on the basis of its contents. The writer (1622-1707) was a Roman Catholic controversialist: D.N.B. Locke while at Oxford in 1682 appears to have lent him two books relating to the persecution of Protestants by Roman Catholics: Journal, p. 56. His book, The Method to Science, was published this year. L.L., no. 2627 ('ex Dono Authoris'). He gives an account of his original esteem for, and later revulsion from, Locke's Essay in his Solid Philosophy asserted, 1697, preface, p. a2. For his criticism of Locke's views see Yolton; part of this letter is printed on p. 82.
May the 10th 1696.
Much honoured Sir
After I had written and almost printed this Book I here send
― 636 ―
you, (I mean all of it but the Preface and Appendix) I was favour'd by a Friend with a sight of your Essay concerning Human Understanding; to which, till then, my circumstances had made mee a Stranger. I will not disoblige your Modesty with giving you a full account of the high Esteem I had for it. I believe that, had I had the good fortune to have perus'd it thorowly ere I began to read these Lessons to a little Academy I had last Summer of a few, but choice, Witts, I had profited by the Lights it might have given mee; and, in case I had seen no reason to depart from my own sentiments, I should have shown my respects to you by making some incidentall Reflexions on diverse passages in it. But, the hast I was in, (the Printer having almost overtaken mee) did allow mee no more leasure than onely to take a cursory view of it here and there as it light. Yet that little I saw of it (ex ungue Leonem)†1 enabled mee to make a fair Estimate of the Whole. The most substantiall Difference between us (as far as I yet observe) is about the Necessity and Usefulnes of Identicall Propositions, on which I mainly build; and to which (in my judgment) all Truths must either be reduc'd, or they will, if scann'd by Speculative and Acute Logicians, be left destitute of their Deepest and Firmest Ground. For, since you have so solidly confuted Innate Ideas, it must follow of course that Truths must be taken from the Things without us; and, consequently, must be first built on, and finally resolved into their Metaphysicall Verity or their being what they are, which is an Identicall Proposition, and can be nothing else: nor can we speak or say anything of their Natures or Essences as such (or staying there) or express them at all but by such an Identicall Speech, as upon triall you will find. Again, we must either come at last to Self-evidence, or no Dispute can ever come to an end; nor can any Propositions, but such as these, possibly lay any claim to Self-evidence, since all else can bear Explicating or the making them plainer, and clearer, which these cannot. These onely being Evident from themselves, or from the very Terms without the assistance of any other Light. I do grant, indeed, that they look at first sight, till attentive Reflexion comes to discover the Usefulnes of them, dry, Insignificant, and in a manner Foolish and Ridiculous. I grant too that there are many Principles exprest more handsomely and with a better grace, which seem to force every man, who has a good Mother-wit, to assent to them, without putting them into such an odd and nice form of words; but I must deny that
― 637 ―
there are any deserving the name of First Principles or Self-evident but because they do virtually include an Identicall; as I have exemplify'd in [A Whole is more than a Part.]†a †1 Besides, Sir, we have a Scepticall World to deal with, who will question even the verdict of our Senses and quarrell the meaning of every word, pretend it ambiguous and then distinguish it; and nothing can hamper such men but Identicalls, which put them past their Distinguishing. Add that all Truths consist in the Connexion of the Terms in the Proposition that expresses it; and the Terms of no Proposition are self-connected (to which we must either come at length or never make an end) but those of Identicall Propositions. But, I shall tire you with my insipid Speculations, and I fear my Book will weary you out of all Patience. I can onely say of it, that I am sure it goes to the bottome, and has as little of superficiall as the French have much of it. Such as it is please to accept of it, and, at the same time, the hearty respects of
Much honoured Sir
Your Reall Honourer and Humble Servant
SMITH†b
My Bookseller, as in the Title page,†2 can send your Commands to me, if you have any.
Address: For his much-honoured Friend Mr John Locke. with a Book To be left with mr Church-hill at the Black Swan in Pater-Noster Row.
Endorsed by Locke: Smith 10º May 96

2087. Locke to Edward Clarke, 12 May [1696] (2086, 2088)
Rand, pp. 480-1. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. Whatever year Locke wrote, the contents of the letter show that it should be 1696. Answered by no. 2088.
Oates, 12th May, 1695[6].
Dear Sir,
I writ some time since to my Cousin Bonville to receive of you eleven pounds of the new money you got for me of Sir Stephen
― 639 ―
Evans, that it might be lodged with him conveniently to be received by any of our neighbours who going to town lodge about that end. By your and his silence in that matter I am in doubt whether my letter came to his hands or not. Mrs. Lane, my Lady's servant who brings you this, gives me a convenience of having it hither. I have given her a letter, and desired her to call at my Cousin Bonville's for it. If she finds it there you need not trouble yourself to give it her. If it be still in your hands and not paid to my Cousin Bonville, I desire you to give her eleven pounds in milled money, which she will bring me down on Saturday. And if you have anything else to send me I beg the favour of you to send it by her. She will lodge somewhere in Holborn, and I have desired her to leave word at your lodging if she troubles you or Mr. Freke within where she lies, that you may send thither anything for me.
My Cousin King writ me word last week that he had received eight pounds of you for my account. I hope you did not pay it him out of the milled money you received of Sir Stephen Evans I desired you to keep by you till I could find a way to get it hither. For when I ordered him to receive money of you, I intended you should pay him out of what money was most convenient for you of your own, and so put it to the account between us. For I would not have given you the trouble to get new milled money of Sir Stephen Evans to pay for books, or lend anyone in London. I have done it with a prospect of putting it to a better use here.
Pray give my humble service to the Bachelor. I writ to the College in haste yesterday....†a
... If some of the judges' opinions could be got and published in the case, their authority would [be of great use to] settle the people. I am,
Dear Sir,
your most affectionate humble servant,
J. LOCKE.
Sir Francis and my Lady present their service to the College.
Address: For Edward Clarke, Esq., next door to the Hen and Chicken, in Red Lion Street in Holborn, London.

2088. Edward Clarke to Locke, 14 and 15 May 1696 (2087, 2090)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 118. Printed in Rand, pp. 481-2. Answers nos. 2086 and 2087; answered by no. 2090.
London May the 14th. 1696.
Deare Sir,
Your Letter to the College of the 11th was Received, and the Batchelor sayes Hee will Answere it in due time, But that which you propose of Procureing the Judges Opinion upon the Clause in the Act touching Punch'd-money, I am satisfied is not to bee obtained, it being a Rule with Them in noe Case to give an Extrajudiciall Opinion in a Matter that probably may come to bee Determined Judicially before Them; But if the Lords Justices, for preventing the endlesse Disputes and Controversies that doe, and will, arise amongst the People upon the Punch'd-money and hindring any further Dammage to the Nation by a New-Currency of Clipt-money in that shape, will bee prevailed upon to issue a Proclamation for quieting the minds of the People, by instructing them plainly and cleerely in the intention of the Law, as to that particular of Punch'd-money, I beleive it would bee of Infinite Good use, and therefore you may depend upon it, shall bee industriously Laboured to bee obtained;†1 The College have allready prevayled, by the methods they have taken, to procure an Order from the Lords Justices to Mr. Attorney General,†2 To Prosecute all such Persons as shall presume soe much as to Offerr or Tender any money (not allowed to Passe by Law) in any payment whatsoever, And wee shall find Mr. Attorney Evidence against some greate Offenders in that Kind verie speedily, of which care will bee taken, That you shall not fayle to have an Account in the Publique Prints;†3 And I will not Dispayre of obtaineing a usefull Proclamation touching Clipt-six-pences, that may prevent the Currency of them likewise in the Countrey,†1 Wee have Ordered the matter soe, that They are generally Refused to bee taken by any Body here, and care is taken to give Notice thereof to all the Considerable Towns in England etc:
the 15th of May.
Thus farr I had Written Thursday in the evening when Mrs Lane (my Lady's Woman) brought mee your Letter of the 12th., whereby
― 641 ―
I find that Mr Bonvill had not then given you any Account of his haveing Received the eleaven pounds in New-money as you Directed, indeed the Hurry that I am constantly in made mee forgett to acquaint you with it, But Hee Received it above a weeke since, and Mrs Lane will take it of Him and bring it to you; The eight pounds I paid Mr. King was in Punch'd-money of my own, and is placed to your Accompt, as you desire, Pray give Mr. Freke's, mine, and my sonn's humble service to Sir Francis and my Lady, and all the Good Family at Oates, and accept the like your selfe from
Your most Affectionate Faithfull servant
EDW: CLARKE:
I am told the Commission of Trade is Pass'd the Greate-seale,†1 soe that I conclude Wee shall now bee soe happy as to see you in Town verie speedily, and by that meanes I may have an opportunity to Kisse your handes before I goe into the Countrey, Which I Designe as soon as I can get Leave, of my Lords and Masters etc:†2

Dear Sir
I mentioned the Judges opinion because it being a matter of law I thought that would carry most weight with it and that if the Lords Justices or the Councill should demand their opinions in the case they would then give it. But I agree with you that a Proclamation of the Lords Justices to the purpose you mention would be of infinite use and I hope those who have done soe much in this affair will be able to obtain that too. And take care that the proclamation be soe drawn or by such an hand as may not increase the difficulties and doubts.
Some examples of the kinde you mention espetialy amongst the Lombard street blades would make the matter goe glib and raise the croke against them, and turne the pore and suffering peoples
― 643 ―
eyes upon them for there lies the great obstruction. Hold but tight as you have begun in London and we shall doe well enough. and your country will blesse the Col:
I thank you for paying the money as you did to My Cosins Bonville and King. That from my Cosin Bonville I have received and shall make the best use of it I can.
I intend to be in town as soon as the weather is but soe warme that I leave off fires. It is now with us perfect winter weather and I write this by the fires side. But warm weather cannot now be far off, But however that may happen pray give me at least a weeks warning and as much longer as is possible before the day set for your journey into the country for I must needs see you and have many things to say to you and therefor will venture my lungs a little sooner then otherwise I would in town not to misse the oportunity of kisseing your hands. Else not knowing how long I may be deteind there I would if I could have soe much warm weather as to get off the remainder of my cough before I venture into that enimie air. I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate and most humble servant

Whitehall. 19. May. 96.
Sir
Besides my particular obligations to thanke you for your kind Letter to me, I am now to call upon you in behalf of the Publick, Whose service requires your help, and consequently your attendance in Towne. The Council of Trade†1 (whereof you are most worthily appointed a Member) must go on with Effect, or the greatest inconveniencies and mischeifs will follow. I hope your Health will permitt you to come and make some stay here; And what reluctancy soever you may have to appear among us, I know your Love to your Country, and your great Zeal for our common Interests, will overcome it; So that I will trouble you no further, till I can have the happinesse of seeing you here, and assuring you by Word of Mouth, that I am unalterably
Sir

2093. Locke to Sir William Trumbull, 22 May 1696 (2091)
Berkshire Record Office, Shire Hall, Reading: Marquess of Downshire MSS. XXXI. 42. Printed in part in H.M.C., Downshire MSS. 1. ii. 665. Draft in B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 55. Answers no. 2091.
Oates 22 May 1696
Right Honourable
The commands of Sir William Trumbull my friend (pardon the liberty of the expression) would be of that authority with me, were they not sent from the Secretarys office at Whitehall, that I should make all the hast I could to obey them. Had not winter weather continueing now till almost midsomer made sensible impressions upon my yet but ill confirmed health, I had waited on you in town before this time with those thanks which upon many accounts I owe you. To that duty you have in the honour of yours
― 646 ―
of 19th: laid greater obligations upon me to hasten me thither. I know well enough how little misse there will be of soe inconsiderable a creature as I am among soe many great and able men as those are with whom it has pleased his Majestie to doe me the honour to joyn me. But that must not excuse me from attendance: And he that hath noe thing else to recommend him but willingnesse to the service must not seem wanting in the only qualification that can give him any pretence to appear amongst such a sett of men soe much every way above him. I am therefor prepareing forth with to obey your commands, and that I may the more effectualy doe it. I shall spend noe more days here than what shall be in order to my longer stay where you expect my attendance. I must beg permission to respit a larger acknowledgment of your favours till the honour of waiting on you in town will better excuse my trespasseing upon your time: I now only crave leave to assure you that I am with the utmost respect and gratitude
Right Honourable
Your most humble and obedient servant
J LOCKE
I beg permission to present my most humble service and thanks to my Lady for the honour of her remembrance
Endorsed: Mr Lock. 22. May. 96. R. 26.
2094. Locke to Sir William Honywood and the other Commissioners of Appeals, 22 May 1696 (2092, 2095)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, ff. 54-5. Draft, with many alterations. Answers no. 2092.
Oates May 22. 96
Gent
I received the honour of yours of the 19th Instant with the inclosed Queres and with the Resolutions annexed.
The Gentlemen you have consulted are of that known and allowed judgment and learning in the law that I must have some more than ordinary reason of doubt if their opinions did not determin mine though they should appear to me lesse reasonable than they doe.
Had the Spring this year brought with it soe much sun and warmth as it usd to doe I had according to my resolution waited
― 647 ―
upon you in town before this time. But the ill effects which my lungs as well as other things have felt from this late cold and winter weather have put off my journey longer than I expected. Though the same unseasonable weather still continues to make me suffer and my health be not yet well recoverd from that ill state which forced me out of town soe much against my will last winter when I was there on purpose to hear the Appeals depending before us, yet I had venturd to town in obedience to your commands to be at the hearing the first cause had they come time enough to have given me an oportunity to be there by the time it is appointed. Tis an Inconvenience I often suffer by, in the place where I am That in the ordinary course of our letters those that are sent from London Tuesday come not hither till Friday and those of Thursday and Saturday are not brought hither till the Monday following. By this means it unluckily falls out that I am now hinderd from geting a passage In the†a Coach (which goes not till Monday next)†1 soe as to be in town time enough to be at the hearing of the cause, which you have that day appointed. I should be much more troubled for this did I thinke my absence could any way hinder your proceedings or make your judgment lesse weighty or satisfactory in it than if I were there. Tis not to excuse my self from attending and bearing my part in dispatching the businesse that I say this and particularly I was soe desirous to be at the hearing of the first cause that I made three journeys to town last year on purpose and should not have faild to have been there now again had not the slow passage of letters hither hinderd me from haveing the notice you did me the favour to send me soe timely that it was possible for me to be there. However this advantage I shall make of it, that I shall not loose this oportunity of shewing how ready I am to obey your commands to the utmost of my power: Considerations <of>†b neither health nor weather shall keepe me any longer in the country now that I know the Appeals depending are like to come to a hearing. I intend god willing to wait upon you the next weeke, and doe resolve not to faille in my attendance for the dispatch of all the causes that lye before us and expect our determination
Endorsed by Locke: J. L. 22 May 96 to Sir William Honywood Mr Beke Mr Dodington and Mr Chaloner

2095. Locke to Sir William Honywood and the other Commissioners of Appeals, 23 May 1696 (2094, 2217)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 56. Draft. Answers no. 2092.
Oates 23º May 96
Gentlemen
Though neither what I writ to you yesterday, nor what I am writeing now (if my opinion were of any weight in the case) could at all influence you in the method where in you will begin the hearing of Appeals, since neither this nor my yesterdays letter will be able to reach you before the first cause which you have appointed on Monday will be over. yet I cannot forbear to acquaint you that upon a farther consideration of the matter. I am in some doubt whether we ought to Re-examin the witnesses.†a Tis not that I dispute those learned mens judgments whose opinions you did me the favour to send me. But the constant practise of former Commissioners of Appeals being (if I have not been misinformed, to judg barely upon the proceedings of the Commissioners of Excise and the evidence as it was given before them, I know not whether there be not something particular in the nature of our Commission which may give the rule herein. But this I must submit to your better judgments. I intend god willing to wait upon you the next weeke, and then doubt not but I shall receive from you full light herein. I am
Gentlemen
your most humble and most obedient servant
JOHN LOCKE
Endorsed by Locke: J L to The Commissioners of Appeals 23 may 96

2097. Locke to Mrs. Elizabeth Stratton, 30 May 1696 (2081, 2137)

London 30 May 96
Dear Cosin
I gave not Mr Lyde nor you the trouble of lookeing over my Cosin your husbands books as thinking it not necessary as long as I conceived that a letter from me to you stateing the matter as it arose was sufficient to doe it. For though I looked upon him as a mortal man that might mistake as I thinke you or I may, yet I never thought otherwise of him than <as>†a of a very honest man nor have the least suspition that I may not depend upon you for what is to be found concerning me in any papers he has left behind, And therefor I never intended to have asked any questions more concerning the accounts between us had not that unexpected answer from Joseph Barnes made it necessary for me to apply my self to you to be informed where the mistake lay. You seem to have found where it is and if you are satisfied that it was a mistake in my Cosin your husband in placeing it there as if it had been a part of the rent due and paid, for the preceding Michaelmas half year and soe you passed it by as accounted for by him before in the account I had
― 650 ―
receivd from him There†a remains noe more to be done but that you and I charge that £4-11-11 to my Cosins account since his death and soe make you Debitor†b for it. Thus I understand your letter But you haveing not spoken it clear I conclude noe thing till I hear from you again that you are fully satisfied in the point. If it be possible I will get down into those parts this long vacation that is comeing to setle my affairs there particularly with you. But what ever may happen I shall take care to spare you all the trouble that may be, and I doe not forsee any that you are like to have upon my account at all. I am sure it will be altogether against my will if you should. I hope there is noe thing in your circumstances that deserves that name you give them in your letter. I wish you and yours all manner of happynesse and am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant

Pray remember me very kindly to my Cosins your daughters, my Cosin Peter and Cosin Hazel and her husband when you see them

2098. James Tyrrell to Locke, [June 1696] (2053, 2933)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, f. 140. Date from Locke's endorsement.
Sir
yesterday I was with a woeman Relation of my wives, who among other discourse told me of a Lady an acquaintance of hers, who has an onely daughter to marry, who was allready a great fortune, and would be a greater after the death of some Relations; and asked me if I knew any person of Quality, that had an estate answereable to her Fortune, and that would be a fit match for her; It came then in my head†c to name my Lord Ashley haveing seen him so lately;†1
― 651 ―
but I sayd I did <not>†a know whether he would marry or not, but however, if she would tell me what the fortune was I would propose it to a Freind of his who should offer it to him; if I might certainly know what to propose, She told me the present fortune was 16000l: downe, besides some Jewells, 200l: per annum Inheritance, after the death of her Mother, and the blesseing of an old rich Grandmother with whom she lives, and is able to give her 5000l, or 6000l more when she dies; and it is likely she will doe it, be cause she is very fond of her: I thought fit to let you know this, that if you think my Lord hath an inclination to marry, and settle his Family, I know not where he can doe better; for the yong woeman, and her Family are not (as I am told) to be excepted against, and as for my Lord, I doe beleive they will accept of him, (if proposed) haveing the character of a civil Gentleman, not to mention his other endowments; if you think good, you may breake this to my Lord and tell me what his answere is; or if not, you may burne this paper, and let it goe no farther, but however (be assured) I am ready to serve his Lordship to the utmost of my power; who am your humble servant
J T
I will call on you in the evening or to morrow morning, and in the mean time pray doe what kindnesse you can for my freind Mr: Cook. in that affair.
Address: For John Lock Esqr. this.
Endorsed by Locke: J: Tyrrell Jun. 96

2100. William Molyneux to Locke, 6 June 1696 (2059, 2115)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed, with an omission, in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 147-52. Answers no. 2059; answered by no. 2115.
Dublin June. 6. 1696†a
Honourd Sir
Tis a Melancholy Thought to me, that since I have had the happines of your Correspondence, there has hardly hapned a Year, when both you and I have not made it an Apology for our long Silence, that we have been indisposed in our Health. Yet it has pleased God that so it has been; and so it is, on my side, at Present. About four years and an Half ago I was first seised by a Violent Cholick, Which then so weakend me, that to this time I lye so far under the Effects thereof, as upon any Cold to be very apt to relapse into the same. and so it has been with me for a while past, but now God be thanked I am again wel recoverd. I had not otherwise so long deferd my Answer to yours of March the 30th. which after a Long Silence brought me the Assurance of your Health, and therewith no small satisfaction; having before that intertaind some Painful Thoughts off your Indisposition from some Rumours I had heard. But I find. Heaven is not yet so angry with Us, as to take you from amongst Us.
And now I most hartily Congratulate you both on the Recovery of your Health, and on the Honourable preferment you have lately received from his Majesty.†1 In your Writings concerning Mony you have given such demonstrative Proofs of Your Reach even in the Busines of the World, that I should have wonderd had the King
― 653 ―
overlookd you. And I do as much Wonder, that, after what you have publishd on that subject, there should remain the least Doubt with any Man concerning that Matter. But I fancy tis only those who are prejudiced by their Interest, that seem to be Dissatisfyd, such as Bankers. etc. who made a Prey of the Peoples Ignorance in this great affair. But I think you have cleard up the Mystery, and made it so plain to all mens Capacitys, that England will never again fall into the like Inconveniencys. Till you writ, We used Mony as the Indians do their Wampompeek,†1 it serv'd us well enough for buying and selling, and we were Content and heeded it no farther; but for the Intimate Nature, Affections and propertys thereof, we no more understood them than the Indians <their>†a Shels.
I have read over Mr Wyns Abridgement of your Essay. But I must Confes to you I was never more Satisfyd with the Length of your Essay, than since I have seen this Abridgement; which, tho done justly enough, yet falls so short of that Spirit which every where shews it self in the Original, that nothing can be more Different. To One already versed in the Essay, the Abridgement serves as a Good Remembrancer; But I beleive let a Man wholy unacquainted with the former begin to read the Latter, and he will not so wel relish it. So that how desirous soever I might have formerly been of seing your Essay put into the Form of a Logick for the Schooles,†2 I am now fully satisfy'd I was in an Error; and must freely confes to you that I wish Mr Wyns Abridgement had been yet undone; That Strength of thought and Expression that every where Reignes throughout your Works makes me sometimes wish them twice as Long.
I find by some Little Peices I have lately mett with that you are the Reputed Author of the Reasonablenes of Christianity; whether it be really so or not, I will not presume to enquire, because there is no Name to the Book. this only I will venture to say on that Head, That who ever is the Author or Vindicator†3 thereof, has Gotten as Weak an Adversary in Mr Edwards to deal with as a Man could Wish; So much Unmannerly Passion, and Billings gate
― 654 ―
language I have not seen any man Use. In so much that were Mr Edwards to Defend the Best Cause in the World; should he do it in that Manner, he would Spoil it. Were an Angel of Heaven to Justify a Truth with Virulence and Heat, he would not prevail.
And now my ever Honour'd Friend, with much reluctance I am to tell you, that I cannot be so happy this summer as to see you in England. tis needles to trouble you with a Long Detale of the reasons hereof; but what between my own Private Affairs, and a Little Place I have in the Publick,†1 So it is, and I cannot help it. But as a Small Repair to my self of this Disappointment, I shall beg the Favour of You to admit a young Gentleman whom I shall send to you within a while only to Look on You, and afterwards to look on a Picture of yours which I hear is at Mr Churchils.†2 The Young Gentlemans name is Howard, a Modest and Ingenious Youth, and excellantly skild both in the Judicious and Practick part of Painting; for his advancement wherein He is now kept at London, and designes soon for Italy, He is Eldest Brother to My Brothers Wife, of a Good Fortune and Family.†3 If by his Report, I understand that that Picture of yours at Mr Churchils be an Excellent Peice and like you, He will procure it to be finely Coppyd for me and I may save you the trouble of Sitting. but if it prove otherwise and be not worth Coppying I will then make it my Request to you, that at your Leasure you would Spare me so many Hours time as to sitt for such a Hand as Mr Howard shall procure to take Your Picture. This I thought fit to Intimate to you before hand, that when he waits on you, you may be forewarnd of his Busines.
I doubt not but by this time you have heard of Our Lord Deputy Capels Death.†4 we are now under a most Unsetled Government, and Our Eyes are Fixt on England for Releif. Some here Wish for your Noble Patron my Lord Pembroke. and Go so far as to say, that he will be the Man. I am Confident we should be Happy under One that Favourd You; and if there be any thing in this Report you would highly favour me by Letting his Lordship know that Here he will find Me amongst several others that are your Admirers; for that
― 655 ―
I reckon the most Advantagious Character I can come recommended under to his Lordship.
My†a- Little Boy is exceedingly obleidged to young Mr Masham for the Honour of his Letters, to which when he is somewhat better able he shall return his due Acknowledgements. In the mean time he Desires his very Humble service may be presented to the Young Gentleman.-†a
Mr Burridge has been lately so taken up with his Eclesiastick Affairs in the Country, that (as he writes me Word) he has hitherto made but little farther progres in the Translation of the Essay; but he promises now to sett about it earnestly. I wish you would give me your free Opinion of What I have already sent You thereof.
I fear your Publick Busines will in some measure take you off from your More retired thoughts by which the World was Gainers every day. But Good Sir Let me intreat you that at your Leasure hours you would think on, and send a line to
Your Most Affectionate and humble servant
W: MOLYNEUX
Address: To John Locke Esquire at Mr Pawlings overagainst the Plow-Inn in Little Lincolns-Inn-Fields London
Postmark: IV 13
Endorsed by Locke: W: Molyneux 6 Jun. 96†b Answered Aug. 4

Sir
If when you goe to My Lord Pembrock you will see Madam Gouvernet†1 which is almost the next house, she will make you very welcome with good Tae and other good things and you can have

I returne you my thanks for the favour you have done me in letting me have a sight of that letter of the 18th instant directed to you, which had my Name to it with some others of my brethren the Commissioners of Appeales. 2105. John Jackman to Locke, 20 June 1696
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 11-12. The writer was born c. 1672; B.A., Oxford, 1689; M.A. 1692; vicar of Leek Wootton, Warwickshire, 1701; etc.: Foster.
Stoneleigh house
Jun. 20. 1696
Sir
Being unkown to you I think my-self oblig'd in the first place to beg pardon for this boldness, and in the next to give you some security, that I have no design to cavil with, or ensnare you; which I hope this declaration under my hand may pass for, viz. That I account you one of the greatest improvers of the understanding in this age, and that, whereas some are apt to suspect, or, at least, pretend to suspect, that you have ill designs in advancing some notions. I am clearly of opinion, that it is nothing so, and that you sincerely aim at truth and the good of mankind. I believe, your modesty is such, that you delight not in reading large Encomiums on yourself, and therefore I forbear them, though, in my great want of eloquence, my sense of your desert inclines and enables me to exspatiate in your praise. That which moves me to give you this trouble is a difficulty arising to my understanding from the account you give of what determines the will, in the second Edition of your Essay concerning the Hum. Underst. B.2.6.21. There you deliver it as your opinion that it is Uneasiness alone that determines the Will, and yet 4.47.†1 that the most pressing Uneasiness does not always determine it to the next action, but that the mind has a power to suspend the satisfaction of the desire accompanying the most pressing Uneasiness. Now if so, it seems plain to me, that either this Suspension must be no voluntary action, or, though it be a voluntary action, the Will must not be determin'd to it by any Uneasiness, or, it must be determin'd to it by a less Uneasiness than that, the relief whereof is suspended. Of the parts of which
― 659 ―
Disjunction, the first and last, I conceive, are too unreasonable to need any confutation to you, and the second is directly contradictory to your opinion. I am brief in stating the difficulty, because I know to whom I write. If you will be pleas'd to impart to me your thoughts concerning it, at your leisure, you will extremely gratify and oblige your real admirer and humble servant
J. JACKMAN.
If you will do me the great favour of a letter, you may direct it me Chaplain to the Right Honourable the Lord Leigh of Stoneleigh†1 near Coventry.
Address: For Mr John Locke Author of the Essay concerning Human Understanding. This to be left at Mr Churchill's Bookseller living at the Black Swan in Pater-noster-row London
Post-paid
Postmark: IV 22
Endorsed by Locke: J: Jackman 20º Jun 96
2106. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 23 June/3 July 1696 (2014, 2121)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 107-8. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, p. 95.
A Amsterdam le 3 de Juillet 1696.
Je vous suis infiniment obligé, Monsieur, des soins que vous prenez de ce qui me regarde. Je voudrois pouvoir vous en témoigner ma reconnoissance, par quelque chose de plus, que par des paroles; mais puis que c'est tout ce que je puis faire, je ne doutes pas que vous ne vous en contentiez, et que vous ne soiyez persuadé qu'elles partent du coeur. Je suis un peu embarrassés sur l'offre de My Lord Privy seal, parce que je ne croi pas que je doive refuser son honêteté, et que je ne sai comment la recevoir. Il ne seroit nullement honête de lui envoier un Marchand, avec une Lettre de ma part. Cela sentiroit trop la lettre de change. Après y avoir pensé j'ai crû que je ne pouvois mieux faire, que de vous prier de recevoir de ma part son présent, et de remettre en suite cet argent à Mr. Nicolas Tourton Marchand Banquier à Londres. Il n'y a guere de François, qui aille sur la bourse, qui ne sâche, où il demeure, et il est même assez connu parmi les Anglois. Je dis cela, parce que son frere, qui est un grand
― 660 ―
Marchand d'ici, ne sait pas lui même le nom de la ruë. Comme Mr. Tourton d'Amsterdam est un peu parent de ma femme, il me fera toucher l'argent, avec le moins de perte qu'il sera possible. Je vous demande pardon de cette commission.†1 Je me donnerai l'honneur de remercier ensuite Mylord Privyseal, mais en attendant je vous prie de luy faire mes complimens, et de lui dire que l'honneur de sa protection étoit plus que suffisant, pour me satisfaire; mais que je n'ai garde de prendre mal une marque de sa génerosité. Je suis, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeissant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Mr. Teute†2 est ici depuis quelques jours et m'a chargé de vous faire ses baisemains, aussi bien que Mr. Limborch. Je me donnerai l'honneur de vous écrire plus au long un de ces jours.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings in little Lincolns inne fields, over against the plough London.

2107. Pierre Coste to Locke, [c. 23 June/3 July 1696] (1940, 2285)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, f. 143. Printed by G. Bonno in Revue de littérature comparée, xxxiii (1959), 166-8. The date depends on that of the publication of Coste's translation of The Reasonableness of Christianity. It came out a little before 14/24 July and was selling well in August: pp. 667-8, 679, 688. Coste sent Locke a copy by Wetstein; Wetstein sent Locke some books a few days before 16/26 June, and hoped to send some more shortly: pp. 656-7. The letter perhaps accompanied no. 2106.
Monsieur,
Je viens de traduire un petit Livre Anglois intitulé the Reasonnableness of Christianity, que je prens la liberté de vous envoyer.†3 Si vous ne l'avez pas lû en Anglois, je croy que vous prendrez du plaisir à le voir en François. Le dessein de l'Auteur est digne de toute sorte de louanges, puis qu'il va à étouffer tant de disputes qui déchirent depuis si long-temps le Christianisme. On commence d'en parler
― 661 ―
beaucoup dans ces Quartiers; et comme c'est l'ordinaire, il plaît aux uns, et déplaît aux autres. Parmi ceux-là même qui entrent dans les veûës de l'Auteur, il y en a qui s'étonnent qu'il n'ait pas expliqué plus précisément qu'il n'a fait ce qu'il faut entendre par le Messie. Les deux premiéres pages du Livre font esperer quelque chose de semblable. D'autres qui n'ont jamais pensé que la foy que Jesus-Christ exige de ses Disciples, fût aussi simple que l'Auteur de cet Ouvrage prétend le démontrer, sont étonnez de n'y rien voir de la Mort de Jesus-Christ, dont il est tant parlé dans les Epîtres des Apôtres. L'idée de Sacrificateur que l'Auteur de ce Livret trouve renfermée dans l'Office du Messie, sembloit l'obliger à parler de cette Mort. A la verité pour éviter les Controverses infinies que les Théologiens ont excitées sur cet Article, il n'auroit pas dû déterminer le dégré formel de la nécessité de cette Mort par rapport à nôtre Redemption; ce qui ne paroit pas possible: mais il semble qu'il ne pouvoit éviter d'en parler historiquement, comme l'Ecriture en parle; de dire, par exemple, comme Jesus-Christ (Matth. xxvi. 28.) que son sang a été répandu pour plusieurs pour la remission des péchez. Quoy qu'il ne nous appartienne pas de définir jusqu'à quel point la Mort de Jesus-Christ a contribué à la remission des péchez, il semble qu'on ne peut s'empêcher de voir dans l'Ecriture, que cette Mort y a contribué de quelque chose. Et c'est ce qu'on auroit voulu trouver dans cet Ouvrage. Je ne sçai si l'on a raison. Mais je dirai après des personnes très-judicieuses à qui j'ai entendu parler de ce Livre, que le plan que l'Auteur s'est fait, est très-beau, et qu'il l'a rempli fort heureusement. Peut-être a-t-il laissé quelques vuides dans son Ouvrage, mais je croy qu'on peut assûrer qu'il a eû ses raisons de le faire. Dans l'état où sont les Controverses de Religion, il y a bien des choses qu'il faut taire de toute nécessité pour ne pas exciter les passions des hommes, et pour ne pas perdre le fruit des choses qu'il faut nécessairement publier.
On dit ici que le Docteur Edward†1 a refuté cet Ouvrage, et que l'Auteur a repliqué pour le défendre. Si cela est, on verra sans doute, dans cette Replique, l'éclaircissement des difficultez que je viens de proposer. Au reste, Monsieur, je ne vous envoye pas ce petit Livre, pour me decharger en quelque sorte de la reconnoissance que je vous dois pour le beau présent que vous m'avez fait en m'envoyant vôtre Ouvrage concernant l'Entendement; mais plûtôt pour en prendre occasion de vous en remercier par avance. Mr. le Clerc m'a
― 662 ―
dit il y a assez long-temps que vous luy aviez écrit, que vous croyiez que j'aurois reçu cet Ouvrage. Je ne l'ai pas encore reçû.†1 C'est un présent qui est excellent en luy-même, mais qui me sera encore plus cher par rapport à la personne de qui je le reçois. Ce n'est pas un honneur que je meritasse de recevoir de vôtre part, et c'est ce qui en rehausse d'autant plus le prix à mon égard.
Je suis déja engagé à traduire cet Ouvrage. C'est avec le même Libraire qui a imprimé en François vôtre Traité de l'Education.†2 Je n'oublierai rien pour me tirer avec honneur de cette entreprise. Je crains bien qu'elle ne soit au dessus de mes forces; mais enfin j'espere que cette crainte ne servira qu'à me rendre plus exact et plus circonspect. Dans une extreme nécessité je profiterai de la liberté que vous m'avez accordée si honnêtement, de vous consulter; mais ce ne sera qu'après avoir consulté Mr. le Clerc, ce qui vous épargnera bien des importunitez. Je vous souhaite une bonne santé, et suis avec un profond respect,
Monsieur,
Votre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
COSTE
Mademoiselle Prades vous est bien obligée de vôtre souvenir. Elle m'a chargé de vous saluer bien humblement de sa part. Lors que vous me fites l'honneur de m'écrire, elle venoit d'apprendre que Mr. Verchant étoit mort à Montpellier d'une apoplexie. Mademoiselle Verchant est encore dans ce Monde, malgré ses continuelles incommoditez. Mademoiselle sa fille est mariée depuis peu à Montpellier.†3
J'ai remis le petit Livre que je vous envoye, a Mr. Wetstein, qui l'a mis dans une balle pour Mr. Churchill à qui je l'ai addressé pour vous le rendre.
A Amsterdam ce
