2109. Mrs. Elizabeth Berkeley, later Mrs. Burnet, to Locke, 13 July 1696 (2198)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 203-4. Elizabeth, 1661-1709, daughter of Sir Richard Blake; married, first, Robert Berkeley of Spetchley, Worcs., who died in 1693; secondly, in 1700, Gilbert Burnet, the bishop of Salisbury; authoress of
― 664 ―
A Method of Devotion, 1709 (posthumous): D.N.B.; Clarke and Foxcroft, Burnet; Church Quarterly Review, cxlviii (1949), 17-51.
Sir
Having the good Fortune to read some of your excelent Books, I took in so great an opinion of the sincerity as well as great Judgment of their Author, (so far as my little knowledg made me capable of understanding them) that I was very unwilling to take as yours, some others; or if so, believe them liable to the objected defects, and errors. if I don't decieve my self I am not alltogether under the power of prejudice; and so I secure the Religion taught of God, am pretty indiferent what becomes of that which only derives from the Imagenations, and Intrests of men: further then the order peace and good government of the world is conscern'd; yet I confess, that as the Possitive or Arbitrary dutys of Christian Religion are very few and simple, so they apper to me, to be, at least a Natural, if not supernatural means of producing the effects generally imputed to them; therefore could not help being disquieted by hearing it as your Judgment, that there was no possitive obligation from scripture or Primitive practice for the use of the sacraments†1 —I hoped in Conversation for a less observable way, of speaking my thoughts: I dare not say of knowing yours, having no reasonable pretence to such a favour; but mising that satisfaction, would not venture to inquire els where, both for fear of spreading a mistake, or having your thoughts misrepresented to my self; for except this is a truth usefull to be received, I am (so sensible of the allmost irresistable force of your Authority to be) very sorry it finds so powerfull a Patron; if it is inded your Judgment (tho I havn't found cause to make it mine, yet) won't condemn what I don't understand, I know truth is too sacred to be denyed, tho want of right dispositions to receive some truths, may render them unnecessary, if not dangerous, therefore innocently detain'd; but if in this you were misunderstood: in the whole, or part; were it not a presumption allmost too great for one so condescending as Mr L— to forgive, I would desire him to be more cautious in speaking his thoughts, that his name ben't fixed to what is not his Judgment; and recolect, he has observers, proud of every shadow of his Authority to beleive as little as they can; and others, to weaken the
― 665 ―
established rules to get more liberty for their own, which perhaps in time would be as imposing, if not end in confusion;†1 I am sensible this letter requires a long apology, but that would be to make you suffer longer for my fault; the shortest and truest is, I fancy'd it might be of some use to an intrest 'tis every ones duty to serve, tho by it I exposs'd my self; I don't inded conclude Mr L — can't err, but am not at all disposed to beleive he dos, being conscious the just deference payed to your reasonings, makes it no slite inducement to doubt the truth of those opinions you reject;—the uncertainty of life made the temptation of giving you this trouble successfull, yet I am too sensible, and too glad, of your more usefull imployments, to expect, or think of any answer to it; all I ask is the concealing from others and if you could (further than it may be serviceable) forgeting your self, at least pardoning this too impertinant a liberty in
Sir
Your greatly Obliged and very Humble s<ervant>†a
E. BERKELEY
July: 13: 1696:
Address: For Mr Locke White Hall
Endorsed by Locke: E: Berkeley 13 July. 96 Answered 28
2110. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke 14/24 July 1696 (1919, 2126)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 101-2. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K. III D 16, ff. 179v-80. Printed from the copy in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 372-7. Answered by no. 2126.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Utri nostrum diuturnum ac pertinax illud silentium imputandum sit, ignoro. Importunus sim, si a Te negotiis publicis occupatissimo
― 666 ―
ad singulas meas responsum efflagitem, aut silentium tuum silentio ulciscar. Amicitia sincera rigorem illum aversatur, neque epistolarum aequali numero, sed fide ac charitate mutua constat. Interim dulcissimo consuetudinis nostræ fructu jam ultra annum carui: Ultimæ enim tuæ, quibus me respondisse memini, decimo Maji dïe anni præcedentis scriptæ sunt. Salutem mihi a Te aliquoties dixerunt DD.Clericus et Guenellonus, et literas mihi a Te brevi scribendas nuntiarunt; quas tamen hactenus frustra exspectavi: hoc autem negotiorum tuorum, quibus obrutus es, frequentiæ unice adscribendum duco. Aliquoties Tibi scribere gestii; sed veritus sum, ne importunior scriptio ab amico occupatissimo responsum minus tempestivum extorquere videretur. Nunc vero cum munus Tibi honoratissimum a Primoribus Angliæ demandatum esse constans ad nos fama pertulit,†1 silentium abrumpendum censui, ut dignitatem hanc non tam Tibi, quam Angliæ gratuler, quæ in Collegio amplissimo unà cum summis regni proceribus Te assessorem habet, cujus consilia omnia prudentiâ, fide, candore ac sinceritate diriguntur, et communi civium saluti unice destinantur. Deus vitam Tibi largiatur longævam, consiliisque tuis successum quem merentur concedat: Ego hic occupatus vivo, et tamen vix quicquam promoveo,
― 667 ―
non aliter ac si <otio>†a desidioso torperem. Arminii scripta inedita me occupatum tenent. Promisi ego bibliopolæ Germano me ea ad editionem paraturum: sed in scriptis ejus relegendis, ob characterum exilitatem et ductum neutiquam lectu commodum, tantam reperio difficultatem, ut, nisi tanti viri memoria, et non exigua quam inde ad publicum redituram video utilitas, ingrati laboris molestiam levaret, jam operæ promissæ pœnituisset. Hoc opus ubi edidero, nullis amplius posthumis aliorum operibus edendis me fatigabo. Oculorum acies sæpissime intendenda est, ut characteres exiles, et vetustate multis in locis ferme evanescentes, legantur. Ita multum temporis impendo, non tamen eo cum fructu, qui temporis diuturnitatem compensare possit. Sed quoniam alea jacta est, pergendum est. Prodibunt de novo, Prælectiones in Jonam, <et>†b in Malachiam quibus annectitur disputatio contra Judæos, in posteriorem ad Thessalonicenses, in secundum et tertium caput Apocalypseos; et disputatio contra Cardinalem Perronium;†1 quæ cum opusculis antehac editis justum conficient volumen. Præmisit D. Brantius prolixiorem vitæ Arminii historiam, quæ multa hactenus exteris ignota continebit.†2 Prodiit nuper apud nos tractatus
― 668 ―
Anglici, Quod religio Christiana qualis nobis est repræsentata in Scriptura Sacra, sit summe rationalis, Versio Gallica.†1 Illius autorem volunt esse amicum meum. Ego respondi,†a nihil mihi de eo constare; et cum autor, quisquis ille sit, latere vult, nostrum non esse conjecturis, ut plurimum fallacibus, indulgere. Ego summâ cum voluptate lectioni illius incumbo, et in præcipuo, quod toto libro de fidei Christianæ objecto tractat, argumento illi prorsus assentior. Hoc recte percepto gravissimas ac acerbissimas in Ecclesia Christianâ disputationes feliciter componi posse puto; saltem Ecclesiæ, non obstante opinionum diversitate, pacem facili negotio posse restitui. Ea enim, quæ nunc a plerisque ut unicum ferme Christianismi fundamentum urgentur, objecto fidei non comprehendi planum fiet. Quod unicum anathematismis, schismatibus, et odiis tollendis remedium est. Ego, ut videas me attente tractatum hunc legere, omniaque argumenta exacte ponderare, non possum quin tibi observationem quandam indicem, quæ licet forte non magni videri posset esse momenti, tamen argumento autoris quo utitur pondus aliquod afferre potest. Cap. IV. autor ad sententiæ suæ stabilimentum adducit locum ex 2. Epist. Joan, Vs.7. quem optime ab ipso allegatum
― 669 ―
judico: Verum Versio Gallica ita eum exhibet, ut, me judice, non exacte exprimat sensum qui in Græco exstat, quique autoris sententiam validius confirmat. Qua ratione eum Anglice expresserit autor, ignoro. Gallice autem ita legitur. Que plusieurs imposteurs†a se sont elevez dans le monde, les quels ne confessent point que Jesus, le Messie, soit venu en chair.†1 Quæ sensum hunc continere videntur, quod impostores hi non confessi sint, quod Jesus, qui est Messias, venerit in carne. Græcus autem textus ita habet. Ὃτιπολλοὶπλάνοι εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὸν κόσμον, οἱ μὴ ὁμολογοῦντες Ιἠσοῦν Χριστὸν ἐρχόμενον ἐν σαρκὶ. Quæ posteriora verba ego verto, Non, Qui non confitentur Jesum, qui est Christus seu Messias, in carne venisse: sed: Qui non confitentur Jesum Messiam qui in carne venit. Non enim est infinitivus in Græco, sed participium. Hic sensus est longe alius, et autoris hujus scopo multo accommodatior. Priore enim sensu hæc esse impostorum falsa doctrina arguitur, quod non confiteantur Jesum, qui est Messias, in carne venisse. Inde sequeretur, quod qui confitetur Jesum, de quo Joannes affirmat quod sit Messias, (vox enim Χριστὸς per appositionem hoc sensu est legenda) in carne
― 670 ―
venisse, maneat in doctrina Christi, ut est Vs.9. Atqui multi qui non credebant Jesum esse Messiam, credebant tamen Jesum, qui Messias est, in carne venisse. Si posteriore sensu vertantur, tum sensus est: Impostores non confiteri Jesum Messiam qui in carne venit: hoc est, non confiteri, quod ille Jesus, qui in carne venit, sit Messias. Confiteri enim Jesum Messiam, est, confiteri quod Jesus sit Messias, seque illius discipulum profiteri, juxta Matth. X.32. Illum autem Jesum, quem confiteri oportet, describit Joannes, quod sit ille qui in carne venit, et inter Judæos versatus est. Inde sequitur, quod ille in doctrina Christi maneat, qui confitetur, quod Jesus, qui in carne venit, sit Messias. Et hæc est sincera fidei in Christum professio. Eundem esse sensum puto 1. Joan. IV.2,3. ubi similiter non reperitur infinitivus, sed participium ἐληλυθότα. Non est quidem hæc observatio tanti in hoc negotio, facit tamen ad genuinam textus Græci intelligentiam, et autoris instituto favet. In aliis autem disputationibus, quæ cum Mennonitis nostratibus†1 instituuntur, maximi est usus. Sed tempus est ut abrumpam. Vides Tibi cum homine loquace rem esse, qui cum literis suis Te compellat calamo imperare non potest. Vale, Vir Amplissime, et feliciter age. Salveat
― 671 ―
plurimum Domina Masham. Salutant Te quam officiosissime uxor liberique, imprimis ego
Tui Observantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 24 Julii
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I do not know to which of us this long and obstinate silence is to be charged. I should be importunate if I should demand from you, who are very busy with[p. 666] public affairs, a reply to each letter of mine, or should avenge your silence by silence. Sincere friendship shuns that rigour, nor does it consist in an equal number of letters, but rather in mutual trust and love. Meanwhile for more than a year I have been without the delightful fruit of our intercourse; for your last letter, which I remember I answered, was written on the tenth of May of last year. Mr. Le Clerc and Mr. Guenellon have given me your greetings several times and have informed me that you would shortly write me a letter; so far, however, I have awaited it in vain; but I think that this should be attributed solely to the multitude of your affairs, by which you are overwhelmed. I have several times longed to write to you, but have been afraid lest a rather unseasonable letter should seem to be extorting an untimely response from a very busy friend. But now, when a sure report has informed us that a most honourable office has been intrusted to you by the chief governors of England,†1 I have judged that this silence should be broken in order to congratulate, not so much you on this dignity, as England, which now has as a councillor on a most honourable board, in company with the highest noblemen of the country, yourself, all whose counsels are guided by prudence, good faith, candour, and sincerity, and are designed solely for the general welfare of the citizens. May God bestow long life on you and grant to your counsels the success that they deserve. I myself am living a busy life here, and yet make scarcely any progress, just as if I were benumbed[p. 667] in slothful idleness. Arminius's unpublished writings keep me busy. I have promised a German bookseller to prepare them for publication; but in reading them again I find so much difficulty on account of the smallness of the characters and a manner of writing(?) by no means easy to read that, were it not that the memory of so great a man, and the no small usefulness which I see will thence return to the public, relieved the irksomeness of an unwelcome task, I should by now have regretted my promised toil. When I have published this work I shall tire myself no further by publishing other men's posthumous works. The pupils of the eyes must often be strained to read the small characters, in many places almost vanishing through age. Thus I spend much time, yet not with such profit as can compensate for the length of time spent. But since the die is cast I must go on with it. There will appear for the first time the lectures on Jonah (and) on Malachi, to which is attached a disputation against the Jews; on 2 Thessalonians (and) on the second and third chapters of the Apocalypse; and the disputation against Cardinal Du Perron;†1 which with works formerly published will make a sufficient volume. Mr. Brandt has prefixed a rather lengthy life of Arminius which will contain many things hitherto unknown to people outside our country.†2 There appeared here recently a French translation of an English treatise, 'That the[p. 668] Christian religion, as it is represented to us in Holy Scripture, is most reasonable'.†1 They will have it that the author is a friend of mine. I have answered that I know nothing for certain about it and that as the author, whoever he may be, wants to remain unknown, we ought not to indulge in conjectures, which are generally fallacious. I am reading it attentively with very great pleasure, and I assent especially to that argument which throughout the book discusses the object of Christian faith. I think that if this is rightly perceived the weightiest and bitterest disputes in the Christian Church can be happily settled; at least, notwithstanding diversity of opinions, peace can easily be restored to the Church. For it will become clear that those things which are now insisted on by the majority as almost the sole foundation of Christianity are not included in the object of faith. This is the sole remedy for abolishing anathemas, schisms, and hatreds. So that you may see that I am reading this treatise attentively, and weighing all its arguments exactly, I cannot but inform you of a certain observation which, although perhaps it can seem to be of no great moment, can yet contribute some weight to an argument that the author uses. In chapter IV, in order to support his opinion, the author adduces a passage from 2 John verse 7, which I think is very pertinently quoted by him. But the French translation shows it[p. 669] in a way that in my judgement does not exactly express the meaning which is to be found in the Greek and which more strongly confirms the author's opinion. I do not know how the author has expressed it in English, but in French it reads thus: 'Que plusieurs imposteurs se sont elevez dans le monde, les quels ne confessent point que Jesus, le Messie, soit venu en chair.'†1 This seems to contain this meaning, that these impostors did not confess that Jesus, who is the Messiah, has come in the flesh. But the Greek text has it thus, Ὅτι πολλοὶ πλάνοι εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὸν κόσμον, οἱ μὴ ὁμολογοῦντες Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐρχόμενον ἐν σαρκί, which latter words I translate, not 'Who do not confess that Jesus, who is the Christ or the Messiah, has come in the flesh', but 'Who do not confess Jesus as the Messiah who has come in the flesh'. For it is not an infinitive in the Greek, but a participle. This is a very different meaning and far more in accordance with the author's design. For by the former meaning this is declared to be the false teaching of the impostors, that they do not confess that Jesus, who is the Messiah, has come in the flesh. Thence it would follow that he who confesses that Jesus, about whom John affirms that he is the Messiah (for the word Χριστὸς by apposition is to be read with this meaning), has come in the[p. 670] flesh abides in the doctrine of Christ, as it is in verse 9. And yet many who did not believe that Jesus was the Messiah nevertheless believed that Jesus, who is the Messiah, had come in the flesh. If the words are translated with the second meaning, then the meaning is that the impostors do not confess Jesus as the Messiah who has come in the flesh; that is, they do not confess that that Jesus, who has come in the flesh, is the Messiah. For to confess Jesus as the Messiah is to confess that Jesus is the Messiah and to profess oneself his disciple, according to Matthew 10: 32. Again John describes that Jesus, whom it behoves us to confess, as he who has come in the flesh and gone about among the Jews. Thence it follows that he abides in the doctrine of Christ who confesses that Jesus, who has come in the flesh, is the Messiah. And this is the sincere profession of faith in Christ. I think that the meaning is the same in 1 John 4: 2-3 where similarly we find not an infinitive but a participle ἐληλυθότα. This observation is indeed not worth much in this matter, but it makes for the genuine understanding of the Greek text and favours the author's design. It is of the greatest use, however, in other disputations which are undertaken with the Mennonites of our country.†1 But it is time for me to break off. You see that you have to do with a talkative man who cannot control his pen when he addresses you in a letter Good-bye, excellent Sir, and prosper in all your doings. My best respects to[p. 671] Lady Masham. My wife and children send you their warmest greetings, as do I
Your most respectful
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 24 July 1696
Address: For Mr. John Locke at Mr. Pawlings overagainst the plough in Little Lincolns Inne feilds London
Endorsed by Locke: Limborch 24º July. 96 Answered 3. Sept by Mr Buckley.†1

2112. Locke to Edward Fowler, bishop of Gloucester, 22 July 1696 (2294)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, ff. 44-5. Draft.
Oates 22 July. 96
My Lord
I shall always think my self bound in duty and conscience to preserve to the utmost of my power from all unnecessary cost and all diminution of any kinde in my hands whatever is intrusted to my care or management. But I can not but wonder to finde that in your Lordships postscript to your letter of 18th instant to my Lady Masham your Lordship tells her that I know you wholy relye upon Mr Clarke and me for preventing all unnecessary cost in the sute between your Lordship and Mr Cudworth.†3 I doe not remember that ever your Lordship spoke a word to me to that purpose. This I know that if Mr Clarke and I had been advised with in the begining of that affair with Mr Cudworth (and if I misremember not my Lady Masham has told me she had made it her request to your Lordship it might be soe) I beleive we should have taken soe much care to preserve freindship between Brother and sister that there had been noe law suit at all between them: Nor any part of the estate which was intrusted to us by Mrs Cudworth to be preserved for those to whom she intended it
― 673 ―
in her will had been spent in Westminster hall. I say not this my Lord to decline any assistance your Lordship may at any time expect from me in this businesse. I wish it were ended and I thinke care ought to be taken to prevent the increase of cost and lessening the estate and to this purpose your Lordship may have my thoughts whenever you please and what upon any occasion I shall imagin may be best don in it: But I must beg your Lordship to excuse me from takeing on me the care and management of the latter end of an affaire which I have as little skil in as your Lordship and as little time for. But yet I shall not faile to wait on your Lordship about it (to consider what may be done to shorten the cost and trouble) when and as often as your Lordship shall please to command me. I am.
Endorsed by Locke: J L to Bishop of Glocester 22 Jul. 96
2113. Locke to Edward Clarke, 28 July 1696 (2096, 2114)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 106. Printed in Rand, pp. 484-5.
London 28 Jul. 96
Dear Sir
I was very glad to hear by yours of the 18th that you and your little girle†1 got soe well to Chipley and found all well there. I had sooner returned my thanks for that good news but that I have been out of town for a weeke and returned but yesterday. The want of a place to put the papers and books in belonging to our commission,†2 hindering us from haveing them and soe to goe on in our businesse gave me that liberty. which was convenient for my health and necessary for some businesse I had. I heare the last post has brought an order for the rooms soe that step farther is gaind in order to the puting us in our Geers. On Sunday about 10 in the Morning my Lord Portland arived here, and he declaring he would be glad to speake with my Lord Keeper somebody officiously went to Powis house†3 but findeing my Lord was gon to church went thither after him. This calling my Lord Keeper out of Church mightily alarmd the town and caused various reports of the businesse of his comeing which at last terminates in the opinion of most men to be for money,
― 674 ―
which they say is mightily wanted in Flanders. My humble service to Mrs Clarke. your son is well and I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE

That conduct which you admire is but a part, you would admire more if you knew more. 2115. Locke to William Molyneux, 2 July and 4 August 1696 (2100, 2129)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 152-9. Answers nos. 2050 and 2100; answered by no. 2131.
London, 2. July. 1696.
Sir,
I cannot, without great trouble, hear of any indisposition of yours; your friendship, which heaven has bestow'd on me, as one of the greatest blessings I can enjoy for the remainder of my life, is what I value at so high a rate, that I cannot consider my self within
― 676 ―
danger of losing a person every way so dear to me, without very great uneasiness of mind.
Thus far I got when I sat down to write to you about a month since, as you will see by the date at the top; business, and a little excursion into the country, has hinder'd me ever since. Were you a man I only cared to talk with out of civility, I should sooner answer your letters. But, not contenting my self with such a formal correspondence with you, I cannot find in my heart to begin writing to you, 'till I think I shall have time to talk a great deal, and pour out my mind to a man to whom I make sure I can do it with freedom; his candor and friendship allows that, and I find I know not what pleasure in doing it. I promised my self abundance of pleasure this summer in seeing you here, and the disappointment is one of the most sensible I could have met with in my private concerns; and the occasion that rob'd me of that satisfaction frights me. I have, I thank God, now as much health as my constitution will allow me to expect. But yet, if I will think like a reasonable man, the flattery of my summer vigor, ought not to make me count beyond the next winter at any time for the future. The last sat so heavy upon me, that it was with difficulty I got through it; and you will not blame me if I have a longing to see and imbrace a man I esteem and love so much, before I leave this silly earth; which, when the conveniencies of life are moderately provided for, has nothing of value in it equal to the conversation of a knowing, ingenious, and large-minded friend, who sincerely loves and seeks truth.
When I took pen in hand to continue this letter, I had yours of March and June last before me, with a design to answer them. But my pen run on, as you see, before I could get leave of my forward thoughts, to come to what was my chief business, viz. To read again, and answer those kind letters of yours.
That of March 28. brought me a sample of Mr. Burridge's translation; upon my reading of it, I began to correct it after my fashion, and intended to have gone through that, and so all the rest of the sheets, as they came to my hand; but some other more pressing occasion interrupted me, and now I am past all hopes to have any leisure at all to do any thing more to it in that kind, and must wholly leave it to his and your care. When I say your care, I do not make so ill an use of your kindness, as to expect you should look it over and correct it; but I doubt not, but you have such an interest in your college, that you can have the assistance of some
― 677 ―
able man there to do it. The subject itself, and my way of expressing my thoughts upon them, may, I doubt not, but be very different from the genius of the latin tongue, and therefore I should not think it amiss, if Mr. Burridge would take more liberty to quit the scheme†1 and phrase of my stile, and so he takes but my sense, to comply more with the turn and manner of Tully's philosophical language. For so he has but my sense, I care not how much he neglects my words; and whether he expresses my thoughts, you are as good a judge as I, for I think you as much master of them. I say this to excuse you from the trouble of sending his papers over to me as he dispatches them; for, in my present circumstances, I shall hardly have time so much as to peruse them. Pray when you see, or send to him, give him my humble service.
Though your cholick has done me no small prejudice, yet I am much more angry with it, upon the account of those inconveniencies it has made you suffer. I know you are in skilful, as well as careful hands, under the care of your brother, and it could not be adviseable in any one to draw you from them. The cholick is so general a name for pains in the lower belly, that I cannot from thence pretend to make any judgment of your case; but it can be no harm to advise you to ask him whether he does not think that the drinking of our Bath waters may be useful to you in your case. I know those waters mightily strengthen those parts.
Your congratulation to me I take as you meant, kindly, and seriously, and, it may be, it is what another would rejoyce in; but, if you will give me leave to whisper truth, without vanity, in the ear of a friend, 'tis a preferment which I shall get nothing by, and I know not whether my country will, tho' that I shall aim at with all my endeavours.
Riches may be instrumental to so many good purposes, that it is, I think, vanity, rather than religion or philosophy, to pretend to contemn them. But yet they may be purchased too dear. My age and health demand a retreat from bustle and business, and the pursuit of some enquiries I have in my thoughts, makes it more desirable than any of those rewards which publick employments tempt people with. I think the little I have enough, and do not desire to live higher, or die richer than I am. And therefore you
― 678 ―
have reason rather to pity the folly, than congratulate the fortune, that engages me in the whirlpool.
'Tis your pre-occupation, in favour of me, that makes you say what you do of Mr. Wynne's abridgment; I know not whether it be that, or any thing else, that has occasion'd it; but I was told, some time since, that my Essay began to get some credit in Cambridge, where, I think for some years after it was published, it was scarce so much as looked into. But now, I have some reason to think it is a little more favourably received there, by these two questions held there this last commencement; viz. Probabile est animam non semper cogitare: And, Idea dei non est innata.†1
What you say of the Reasonableness of Christianity, gives me occasion to ask your thoughts of that treatise, and also how it passes amongst you there; for here, at its first coming out, it was receiv'd with no indifferency, some speaking of it with great commendation, but most censuring it as a very bad book. What you say of Mr. Edwards is so visible, that I find all the world of your mind.
This is now a third sitting before I finish this letter, whereby, I fear, I shall give you an ill picture of my self. By the reading of the next paragraph of your obliging letter of June 6, I am mightily comforted to find that it is not want of health (as it run in my head, by a strong impression, I found remain'd in my mind, from the cholick mentioned in the beginning of your letter) but business that keeps me this year from the happyness of your company. This is much more tolerable to me than the other, and though I suffer by it, yet I can bear it the better, whilst there is room to hope it may be such that both you and your country may receive advantage by it. Mr. Howard, who I was resolving yesterday morning to enquire after, prevented me by a visit he made me, wherein he gave me an account he had received a letter from you since his return from Cambridge. That which you desire of me, as the chief reason of affording me his acquaintance, is what I cannot refuse, and yet it causes in me some confusion to grant. If the original could do you any service, I shall be glad; but to think my picture worthy your having, would carry too much vanity with it, to allow my consent, did not the skill of the painter often make amends for the meanness of the subject, and a good pencil frequently make the painted representation of more value than the real substance. This may
― 679 ―
probably be my case. Mr. Howard is a very pretty young gentleman, and I thank you for his acquaintance. I wish it lay in my power to do him any service whilst he is here. If the length of my letter could be excuse for the slowness of its coming, I have certainly made a very ample apology; though I satisfie my self, neither in being silent so long, nor in tiring you with talking so much now; but 'tis from an heart wholly devoted to you. I am,
4. August. 1696.
Sir,
Your most affectionate. humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
2116. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 4/14 August 1696 (2028, 2191)

Monsieur,
Je ne scaurois laisser passer l'occasion presente de vous faire la reverence. il y a long temps que nous n'avons receu de vos nouvelles que par la voye publique, qui nous a informé de l'employ dans lequel sa Majesté vous a establi pour le commerce du Royaume, nous vous en felicitons de tout nostre cœur et prions Dieu quil veuille prolonger vos jours pour le bien public. nous avons lu avec grand plaisir le livre qui a pour titre que la Religion chrestienne est tres raisonable, dont on vous dit l'Autheur. je vous puis assurer quil est fortement approuvé icy par toutes les personnes eclairées, et qui pleignent le divorce qui est parmis les chrestiens. je scay que Monsieur Hudde nostre bourgemaistre, qui est fort connu par les grandes lumieres quil a dans les Mathematiques est fort dans vostre sentiment, il ny a que quelques petits Ministres, qui n'ayment pas de voir la foy reduite a si peu de principes, mais tousjours remplis de mysteres, voudroient quon eut plus appuyé sur le merite de la mort de Jesus Christ. nous sommes assez malheureux que nos libraires ne se pourvoyent de livres anglois. on dit qu'un theologien de londres a respondu au livre susdit, et qu'on y a respliqué heureusement.†1 mais tous ces livres nous manquent, et mesme quel devoir que j'aye fait d'avoir le premier livre, je nay pu le decouvrir, mais
― 680 ―
Monsieur Pecock qui correspond avec Monsieur Daranda ma promis de me le faire venir de londres. Ma femme et toute la famille vous presente ses treshumbles respects. si a quelque heure de loisir vous pouviez nous envoyer un mot de vostre main, nous le conterions pour un grand honneur. je suis avec un tres profond respect,
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON

2117. Dr. Humphrey Prideaux to Locke, 5 August 1696
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 8-9. For the writer see no. 737. He had formerly expressed in private letters distrust and dislike of Locke: Letters, as cited in no. 185 n., etc.
Sir
You beeing one of the Committe of Trade I beg leave to offer a proposall to you which is very pertinent to your businesse and not improper for one of my profession to offer to you and will I hope be very agreable to your Charity and goodnesse to promote it. It is concerneing the Country Admiraltys and the excessive abuse and barbarity practised in wrecks on all the Sea Coasts of England more than in any other Countrey in the World. About a year since here hapned a most lamentable wreck on the Norfolk Coast of near 200 ships at one time,†1 to tell you all the barbaritys then practised by those who came to plunder would be to trespasse too much upon your good nature it may be sufficient to assure you they were greater then one that did not know them would ever be able to conceive mankind could be guilty of. And I haveing been born on the Sea Coast†2 and beeing now Archdeacon of Suffolk which lys 60 miles on the Sea I have had occasion to know and lament to many other instances of this kind, and I have heard it remarked by foreigners who have suffered in this kind on our Coasts that they
― 681 ―
would rather chuse to suffer wreck in any other Countrey in the world than in England. The station you are now in makes it very proper for you to consider this matter for I think it falls very naturally within the Compasse of your Commission for Secureing the Trade of the Nation to secure the goods and persons of Traders from that barbarous usage and rapin which they generally fall under on such occasions. That which I would humbly offer unto you is that you would be pleased to consider this matter with that thoroughnesse as you doe all things that you take in hand and when you have don soe to prepare such a bill to be offered to the next Parliament as may be sufficient to remedy this abuse.†1 in order hereto all the laws now in force about this matter must be reviewed and considerd wherein they are defective, and made soe large as to reach and prevent all the particular barbaritys which people on the Coasts out of rapin are usually guilty of on such occasions. In the former Laws I reckon <it>†a very unjust that it is determined that where neither man dog nor cat doth escape the ship must be wreck for it is possible the goods may be proved by the owner notwithstanding and its unreasonable that his misfortune should be made of the nature of a crime to forfeit them.†2 I think to make the Law just the owner ought to have his goods whenever he can prove them his within the Term by law limited and appointed reserveing to those that save them a reasonable reward. As to matters of fact I have known, that boys have industriously been removed to cause wrecks, that wicked people from land have given false signes to decoy ships in distresse into places of greatest danger, that they have stripped persons alive and thrown them into the sea for the sake of what they had, whereas otherwise they might have been recoverd and lived, that they have violently taken away from the owners their owne goods when saved by themselfes, as if persons when wrecked loose all right to what they had before, and one particular hapned in the Norfolk shipwreck which I have abovementioned very barbarous. the bodys of those who were cast up after the Storm lay along on the shore in great numbers till eaten up by dogs and ravens and other devoureing Creatures, because noe one would be at the charge to bury them, noe not as much as to dig a grave for them in
― 682 ―
the place where the carkasses lay and especially out of fear of makeing themselves liable to pay the Tax lately imposed on buryalls.†1 I think it reasonable that the Parishs where such bodys are cast up should be bound to give them buryall. but I give myselfe a needlesse trouble to mention any particulars to a person of your acurate observation if you will be pleased to take the matter in hand I am sure nothing will escape you of what is fitt to be don in it. I humbly leave it to you and am
Sir
Your most faithfull humble servant
HUMPHREY PRIDEAUX
Norwich Aug. 5th 1696.
I think it proper further to remark unto you of this matter that at the assizes to be held here this next week there will be a great many Tryalls before the Judges between Sir Henry Hobart†2 Vice Admirall for Norfolk and the Lords of Mannor of the Coast about the goods taken up in the late Wreck while the owners who have the only true right goe without them.
Address: For John Lock Esqr one of his Majestys Commissioners of the Committe of Trade
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Prideaux 5. Aug. 96 Trade Concerning wrecks

(English) Viro Illustrissimo Nobilissimo

Clarissimus Doctissimusque Dominus Petrus Guenellon, Tibi, Vir Nobilissime, mihique familiaris, inchoante hoc anno, humanissimas
― 683 ―
Tuas ad Se, 24 Dec: 95; datas, mihi exhibuit literas, in quibus inter alia, non tantum mei memineris, verum etiam de quâdam a me peractâ, et a Clariss: Domino Guenellon Tibi communicatâ, loqueris operatione; imò istius historiam ac instituendi methodum a nobis petis, Qui eam, tanquam rem utilem, et scitu necessariam, Regiæ Societatis actis inseri dignam judicabas. Magno profectò, Vir Illustrissime, me afficis honore ac dignitate, Summasque Tibi, hac de re, ago gratias: Et ut petitioni Tuæ satisfacerem, jam literas, totam Methodum, quantum id effici potuit, complectentes, ad Te transmittendas paraveram, interim varii hic viri Celebres et eruditi, quos inter etiam Amplissimus et Illustrissimus vir Nicolaus Witsen, hujus urbis Consul ac Senator, ægro viso, et ita differentiam hujus et antiquæ operandi methodi ex eventu edocti, Tecum id promulgandum maximè necessarium judicabant: Verum hac in urbe, et meo sub ductu et regimine, ne quicquam, quod ad rem pertinet, negligeretur, id fieri satius esse credebant; et hoc eò magis, quod plurimæ icones, tam instrumentorum, a nobis inventorum, quam eorum usus, ad rem illustrandam, erant adjungendæ. Hæc est ergo causa, Vir Celeberrime, quominus prædictæ literæ ad Te venerint, quod non ægre Te laturum, sed hocce ejus
― 684 ―
exemplar, quam edidi, dissertationis,†1 in veræ et sinceræ observantiæ signum, benignè accepturum spero. In hac totam methodum, quam sumus secuti (ab aliis forsan plurimum emendandam) candidè proposui: nec reticui, Thomam Davidis, olim meum famulum, ad hanc operandi rationem, quandam mihi præbuisse ansam, adjunctis a nobis ad rem requisitis: Addidi quoque alias quarundam a Magistro p:m: et nobis peractarum operationum icones, quas etiam benigne accipias, meamque hanc licentiam, vel potius audaciam æqui bonique consules quæso. Vale, Vir illustrissime, et si Sententiam tuam, hac de re, nec non si quid Scrupuli inter legendum occurrat, mihi notam facere digneris, admodum id mihi gratum foret.
(English) P:S: his literis propemodum paratis, Celeberrimus Dominus Eduardus Southwell,†2 Casu Lugduni batavorum Ægro, jam restituto, et crure arteficiali incedente, viso, me domi meæ visitare dignatus est, ille lubens, in patriam jam reversurus, ut Tibi hocce munusculum traderet, sescepit provinciam: alias aliam invenissem mittendi occasionem. Alia etiam ipsi quædam tradidi exempla, quibusdam aliis Regiæ Societatis membris, quibus maxime usui et gratum foret distribuenda, iterum vale.

(Latin) To the most illustrious and most noble Mr. John Locke, knight, etc., Pieter Adriaansch Verduin, surgeon, sends greeting.
The distinguished and learned Mr. Pieter Guenellon, your friend, most noble Sir, and mine, showed me at the beginning of this year your very kind letter to him of 24 December 1695, in which among other things you not only remember me but also speak of a certain operation performed by me and communicated to you by the distinguished Mr. Guenellon; in fact you ask us for an account of it and the method of performing it, as you considered that it merited insertion in the records of the Royal Society as being useful and needing to be known. You certainly greatly honour and compliment me, illustrious Sir, and I am most grateful to you for that; and to meet your request I had already prepared a letter to be sent to you describing the whole method, so far as that could be done; meanwhile various renowned and scholarly men here, and among them the most excellent and illustrious Nicolaas Witsen, burgomaster and councillor of this city, after seeing a patient and so being by the result apprised of the difference between this and the old method of operating, considered like you that it was most necessary that it should be published; but they thought it better that it should be done in this city under my direction and control lest anything relating to it should be neglected, and the more so because several representations, both of the instruments invented by us and of their use, were to be added to illustrate the matter. This, then, most renowned Sir, is the reason why the aforesaid letter has not come to you. I hope that you will not take it ill but that you will kindly accept as a token of my real and sincere respect the accompanying[p. 684] copy of the dissertation that I have published.†1 In it I have candidly set out in its entirety the method that we followed, which will perhaps be greatly improved by others: nor have I concealed that Thomas Davys, formerly my attendant, furnished me with a certain handle (?) for this fashion of operating, the requisites for it having been supplied (?) by me. I have also added some other representations of certain operations performed by the above-mentioned master and myself; please kindly accept them and take in good part this freedom or rather presumption of mine. Goodbye illustrious Sir, and if you will deign to let me know your opinion about this matter, as well as any doubts that may occur to you while you are reading my dissertation, that would be most acceptable to me.
(Latin) P.S. When this letter was almost ready the most renowned Edward Southwell,†2 who had by chance seen at Leyden a patient now recovered and walking on an artificial leg, deigned to visit me at my house. As he is about to return to his own country he has gladly undertaken the charge of delivering this little gift to you; otherwise I should have found some other opportunity of sending it. I have also delivered to him some further copies for distribution to some other members of the Royal Society, to whom they should be most useful and acceptable. Goodbye again.
Amsterdam, 16 August 1696.
Endorsed by Locke: Verduin Aug. 96

2119. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 13 August 1696 (2046, 2130)
Rand, p. 486.
London, 13th August, 1696.
Madam,
Though business has kept me longer from returning my thanks to your last kind letter than I intended, and so you may perhaps blame me in your thoughts, yet you have this advantage by it that you have thereby escaped an importunity I had designed for you. And I have nothing to do now but to commend you for the course you have put yourself into under Dr. Musgrave's care, instead of persuading you to do so. This was all the advice I could have given you at this distance for the swelling of the legs. To which I can only add that you should carefully follow his prescriptions. This, I think, I might have spared, because it is in itself so reasonable, but where I am so much concerned as I am for your health and
― 686 ―
perfect recovery I could not forbear saying something. I am very glad to hear your son Sam. is better. I hope the little one that Mr. Clarke took down with him†1 will find the advantage of the change of air and other things. Mr. Clarke enquires whether she should take the powder again which she did at Ditton, to which I answer yes, for I believe it will do her good. Your son is very well, and presents his humble duty to you and Mr. Clarke. I hope in the next to hear that your legs are much mended, and am,
p>Dear Madam,
your most humble and affectionate servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
Address: These present to Mrs. Mary Clarke, at Chipley.

2121. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 21/31 August 1696 (2106, 2174)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 109-10. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 96-7.
A Amsterdam le 31. d'Août 1696
Il y a long-temps, Monsieur, que je me serois donné l'honneur de vous écrire un peu plus au long, que je ne fis la derniere fois, si je n'avois crû devoir attendre que le temps de remercier Mylord Privyseal fût venu; mais comme ce temps ne vient point, je n'ai pas crû devoir tarder plus long-temps. J'avouë que je ne sai que dire de son honêteté, car encore que je ne doute nullement de sa bonne intention, je suis surpris de n'en voir aucun effect, depuis plus de six semaines, pendant lesquelles il est venu un très-grand nombre de postes. J'ai quelquefois peur d'avoir fait une faute en acceptant sa civilité; mais un homme, comme moi, feroit une espece d'affront à un Seigneur de son rang, en témoignant de ne se soucier pas de ses offres, au moins selon l'usage des autres nations. D'un autre côté, j'en recevrois un, sans l'avoir mérité; si après avoir accepté ses offres, il ne s'en souvenoit plus. Je ne puis croire qu'il eût eu dessein d'en user ainsi, ou de m'offrir afin que je refusasses. Quoi qu'il en
― 688 ―
soit, s'il l'a oublié, je vous prie de ne l'en pas faire ressouvenir. Je n'ai jamais rien demandé à personne et jespere que Dieu me fera la grace de ne demander jamais rien à qui que ce soit. S'il s'en souvient lui même, à la bonne heure, sinon je m'en passerai comme je m'en suis passé; et cela avec d'autant plus de facilité, que je n'attendois rien de semblable. Nos gens m'ont enfin accordé, pour ma vie, le gage de 1000ff. qu'ils m'avoient donné pendant cinq ans.†1 Quoi que ce soit peu ici, il faudra se contenter et faire son mieux.
Par la premiere occasion, je vous envoierai un livre de mon frere, qui est un commencement de l'histoire de la Medecine,†2 et un autre de ma façon sur les Loteries,†3 dont on parle tant en Hollande. Mon livre intitulé Ars Critica†4 est à moitié imprimé, et j'espere qu'il sera achevé dans deux mois, après quoi j'acheverai incessamment Hammond,†5 dont plus de la moitié est aussi imprimé.
La version du livre of the reasonnablenes etc. se vend fort bien. Le bruit a couru ici qu'un Docteur d'Oxford y avoit répondu, et que l'Auteur a repliqué. Si cela est, faites moi la faveur de m'envoier l'un et l'autre, et le premier en Anglois. Je vous prie aussi de m'acheter Cumberland of the measures etc.†6 et Greaves de pede Romano.†7 Il me semble que dans le même livre il traite de la mesure des Pyramides d'Egypte, et de Denario Romano. Faites moi la grace de m'en éclaircir, car c'est principalement à cause de ces traitez qu'on le souhaite. Si en échange vous avez besoin de quelque livr de Hollande, vous n'avez qu'à commander. Je prends la liberté de vous donner cette commission, afin que vous en usiez de même envers moi, s'il vous plait, et que vous soiez persuadé que je suis, sans compliment, Monsieur Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
p>J LE CLERC
Ayez la bonté de remettre ces livres, si vous les trouvez, à Mr. Teute le fils, qui aura soin de me les faire rendre, Mr. Coste a enfin
― 689 ―
reçu vôtre livre of the understanding et a commencé à y travailler. Il m'a chargé de vous remercier de sa part.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings, in little Lincolns inne fields over against the Plough London

p>Endorsed by Locke: J: le Clerc 31 Aug 96 Answered 5 Oct.
2122. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 28 August/7 September 1696 (2070, 2127)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 137-8.
Rotterdam 7 September 1696
Dear Friend
I have yours of the 21/31 past, and do observe wherein you desire to be further informed as to our mint and explication of some things in my former letters, which I shall now do as far as I can, and take time to inform myself exactly of the rest —
An Ingels is the 1/20 part of an ounce and an ace is the 1/32 part of an Ingle so that there are 640 aces in an ounce. [The Pattacon is The Rix doller]†a Our guinnyes now pass for f11:14 and the ducats f5:6—or by the ounce the Guinny is worth f43:10 and the Ducat f47—the value of the Ducat in fine gold is, as I am informed 23 carat 8 grains, and some of them 23 Carats 11 grains. But the exact weight I, as yet know not. the f0:10:8 the value of our English shilling Anno 1621—is ten styvers eight penningen, of which 16 make a styver, so that 10:8 is 10½ st. or ten stuyvers and a half —
As to the other matter about Arbitration, and the Condemnation of the Court of Justice or Hoogen Raad in Holland†1 —Herewith I send you the Translation of a Compromisse or bond of Award, at present in my hands, and under my direction, together with the Double condemnation of the said High Court.†2
― 690 ―
The first is the Condemnation upon the Bond it self, which commonly one of the parties that is most earnest for an end, obtains, sending the compromisse to his Attor<ney>†a to <de>mand†a Condemnation upon it. he speaks to one †a Attorneys, which he will, to assist in it; These two exhibit the Compromisse to the Court, by which they are authorised the one to demand,†b the other to consent to the condemnation, which they doing accordingly, the court condemns the partyes to stand to their agreement, inserting from word to word, the Compromisse in their condemnation — which being once done they cannot fly from it, but must suffer the Arbitrators to go forward to a final sentence.
The last condemnation is commonly taken out by the Arbitrators themselvs, before the parties know how the sentence lyes, by sending it to one of the Attorneys, and upon it the court condemns them in the sentence, as before they had done in the Compromisse, Bond, or Agreement. And that done there remayns no remedy, be the sentence what it will, there is no appeal, being confirmd by the highest Court in the Nation —
But if any of the Arbitrators should privately give notice to either party how things are gone, so that he can time enough get to the hague to revoke the Letter of Attorney, and seek Reduction, as they call it here, the Court will hearken to the plaintiff.
You will find in the compromiss words sublined, which are by me added to the copy I translated, because I found it defective. And am perhaps like to fall into a suit at Law for want of those or such like words, for by my marrying my wife, I am become uncapable of remayning an Arbitrator, and tho in the reason of the thing, I being civiliter mortuus,†1 my wife ought to have the same faculty of chusing one in my place, as she has in case I had dyed; yet compromesses being, as the lawyers call it, stricti juris,†2 and not binding beyond the letter — my Brother in Law, they say, needs not consent to it, and so, notwithstanding all the precaution used to prevent its being disannulled, yet, for want of adding that clause, [Or become any other way incapacitated to remain an Arbitrator]†c it may by him be disannulled.
― 691 ―
In the compromisse commonly each party states his case, as briefly as he can, that it may appeare, whereunto the Commission extends, Except where they had been at Law, and then reference (as in this Copy) is made to the declaration of the Plaintiffe and answer of the Defendant in the Registers —
I know nothing more needfull to give you a full and distinct notion of this affair; If I be mistaken, pray inform me and I shall indeavour to explain my self better if I can; For I would be glad to see so good, and serviceable a thing introduced in my native Cuntry.
Onely one caution I must give you, from experience, That the Compromisse must impower the last court of Appeal to pass this Condemnation, for if any inferiour court should do it, a superiour might give relief, to eith<er party>†a complayning —
For I once was †a in a case, wherein the Notary, whether by mistake, or order, had put in the Court (or Hof) of Holland, instead of the High Council or Hogen Raad.
When we had passed Sentence, and the Plaintiffe went about to Execute, the Lawyers found that flaw, and appeald to the Hogen Raad; But they labouring with both partyes very hard, till they brought them to submit a second time, to other Arbitrators, under their condemnation, which other Arbitrators, hearing all de Novo, confirmd our sentence and there was an end.
I hope Mr. Sonmans will bring John†1 to you, and that he will reap proffit from your good Councill, I gave it in charge to my Nephews, in his going to London to have visited you — But it would have taken up too much of their time from getting mony, and cost them a little of that too boot, and therefore, I suppose, it was not done —
My wife, and sons joyn with me in hearty salutations to you, Pray give also our humble service to Sir Francis and his Lady — heres strong talks of peace, and that the Fr. Cock yields to all conditions, but of the Truth of this I cannot assure you — I am
p>Deare friend
your humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
― 692 ―
I had not that book, it must be miscarryed
I am examining the Custom house Registers about the Consul and find in 2 years upwards of 3500 ships arrived here from all parts — which would have brought him in nigh £2000 a year. a fine salary, for an useless tool, to be squeesd out of the sweat of that part of the nation, which ought above all to be cherisht and incouraged.†1

2124. Locke to Esther Masham, 1 September 1696 (1983, 2301)
Newberry Library, Chicago: copy of the original letter by Esther Masham in her letter-book, pp. 20-1. Transcribed from microfilm. Printed in Fox Bourne, ii. 455; by Professor Maurice Cranston in Newberry Library Bulletin, 2nd ser., no. 4, July 1950, pp. 129-30.

London 1 Sept 1696
Deare Dab:†1
Your Letter the last week after so long silence looks as if you had been bottleing up kindness for your Joannes which at last you have let run to the rejoycing of his heart more than if you had overflow'd to him in Sack and Suger, or Cherry brandy. I was not a little dejected in being so long out of your thoughts as appeard to me by your no words which is a very ill sign in a prattle box of your age. But in good sooth you have now made me amends, and if what you say be but true Joannes will perk up again, and will not give place to the finest powderd Spark in the Town. I think you know my heart pretty well but you are a little mistaken about my head. Though it belongs now to a man of trade and is thwack'd with Sea coal and Fullers earth, Lamp black and hob nayles and a thousand such considerable things, yet there is a room empty and cleare kept on purposse for the Lady, and if you did but see how you sit mistris there and command all the Ambergrease and Pearles, all the fine Silks and Muslins which are in my Store house you would not complain of the overfilling of a place where you sit mistris.
I thank you for the Bible you have been at the trouble about for me, and desire it may be sent me. When I come down next I will bring it into the Country with me and you and I will be the better for it.
Pray present my humble Service to Sir Francis and my Lady, and let my Lady know that no body almost in Town paying now at sight, I hope she will not have very hard thoughts of me if I remain in her debt for a Letter I received from her yesterday, till the end of the week.
Remember me very kindly to Deare Totty and when you go to Matchinghall pray present my most humble service there. I am
p>D.D.
Your most faithfull humble servant
JOANNES.

2126. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 3 September 1696 (2110, 2209)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 257 n. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 377-9; postscript and address, in Ollion, p. 211. Answers no. 2110; answered by no. 2222.
(English)
London 3 Sept 96
Vir Amicissime
Si omnes in religione eo uterentur Candore quo tu usus es in amicitiâ, non majorem offensionem inter dissentientes parerent argumenta quam inter nos nuper peperit diuturnum nimis silentium.
― 695 ―
Si epistolarum reciprocationem <æstimem>†a an tua major taciturnitas an mea dicere non ausim, credo me ea ex parte peccasse. Ea verò utcunque se res habet, tu certe humanitate tuâ et ignoscendo prior effecisti ut culpa omnino mea sit. eoque magis probrosam mihi sentio quod tu a levissimâ quidem reprehensione abstinuisti. negotiorum excusatione quâ pro me apud te usus <es>,†b aliquid momenti erga alium habere potuisset, certe tibi me eo nomine excusatum nolim, addere etiam poteram valetudinem tota præteritâ hieme valde incommodam. sed nec hoc quidem quo minus tam fido tam charo amico scriberem impedimento esse non debuit. Vis rem ipsam ut tibi scriberem semper quæro tempus omnino vacuum, animumque ab aliis curis et cogitationibus liberum, hoc cum raro accidit ita ad voluntatem, ut non ad aliud et magis oportunum tempus rejiciam, de die in diem differendo annus elabitur, et tandem pudor culpæ superveniens tardiorem reddit. si hocignaviæ latebram dicas, non recuso, hoc certo scio imminutæ amicitiæ, vel mutatæ voluntatis non esse crimen. et forsan, ut omnia fatear, non expeditus linguæ Latinæ usus fastidium menti non bene se explicanti aggerit. Sed tua amicitia et Benevolentia vir Amplissime omnia superat. Gratulationem tuam eo quo tu scripsisti animo id est amicissimo accipio. sed quid tandem mihi senectutis et valetudinis onere succumbenti cum negotiorum publicorum tumultu. Secessus
― 696 ―
mihi jam quærendus esset, et vel annis vel studiis meis quies. Hoc si mihi credas et magis aveo, et mihi magis accomodatum credo sed nescio quo fato quod alius ambitiose et frustra quærit, alii vel inscio vel etiam detrectanti tribuitur. Viri istius magni scripta inedita tuâ operâ proditura gratulor <reipublicæ>†a Christianæ. De libro Anglicano in Linguam Gallicam verso, cujus lectioni cum ad me scripseras incubuisti idem tecum sentio, contentionum et schismatum radices evellit quantum id potest religionis Christianæ veritas et fundamentum Si id auctor recte explicuerit ut mihi videtur, cum vero totum perlegeris et tuam et aliorum de tractatu illo sententiam scire vellem. Theologis nostris tam Conformistis quam Nonconformistis displicere audio. reliqui ut fit probant <improbantve>†b prout suo vel alieno innitantur judicio. quod monuisti de loco Johannis tecum sentio. idem est in versione nostrâ quem in Gallicâ observasti error, sed ad rem facit, verum apposite magis Textus Græcus quem tu rectissime ut mihi videtur interpretaris. Vale Vir Amplissime et me ama
Tui Amantissimum
J LOCKE
― 697 ―
(English) Omnes nostros præcipue ex familia tua quæso meo nomine quam officiocissime salutes
(Latin)
London 3 Sept. 1696
Most friendly Sir,
If all men practised in religion that candour that you practise in friendship the arguments would produce no greater ill will between those who differ than our over-lengthy silence has lately produced between us. If I should[p. 695] assess the interchange of letters I would not venture to say whether your taciturnity or mine is the greater; I believe that I have offended in that respect. But, however that may be, you certainly by your kindness and as the first to forgive have caused the fault to be altogether mine; and I feel that it is the more shameful to me because you have abstained from even the very slightest reproof. As for the excuse of affairs which you have made to yourself for me, that could have some weight in relation to someone else; I certainly should not wish to be excused to you on that pretext. I could also add my health, which was very troublesome all through this last winter; but not even that should have prevented me from writing to so faithful and so dear a friend. If you want the truth, in order to write to you I always seek a completely clear time and a mind free from other cares and cogitations; since this rarely happens sufficiently in accordance with my wishes for me not to put off writing until another and more opportune time the year slips by in postponement from day to day, and at length shame for my fault, supervening, makes me slower. If you call this an idler's excuse I make no objection; this I know for certain, that it is not an offence arising from any lessening of friendship or change of affection; and perhaps, to confess everything, my unreadiness in the use of Latin brings distaste to a mind that is not expressing[p. 696] itself well. But, excellent Sir, your affection and goodwill overcome everything. I accept your congratulation in that spirit in which you wrote it, that is, the most friendly. But, when all is done, what have I, who am sinking under the burden of age and ill health, to do with the bustle of public affairs? I ought now to be seeking retirement and rest, whether for my years or for my studies. This, if you will believe me, I desire more and think more appropriate for me, but by I know not what fate what one seeks ambitiously, and seeks in vain, is bestowed on another who knows nothing of it or who even declines it. I congratulate the Christian commonwealth on the forthcoming appearance, thanks to your exertion, of the writings of that great man. I think the same as you about the English book translated into French which you were earnestly reading when you wrote to me: if the writer has set them out correctly, which I think he has, the truth and foundation of the Christian religion tear up the roots of quarrels and schisms, so far as that is possible; but when you have read through the whole I should like to know your and other persons' opinions of that treatise. I hear that it displeases our theologians, conformist as well as nonconformist; the rest, as usually happens, approve or disapprove according as they lean on their own or another's judgement. I think as you do about what you have pointed out regarding the passage in John. There is in our translation the same error as you have observed in the French, but the Greek text, which it seems to me you interpret correctly, is to the point, and indeed more pertinently. Goodbye, excellent Sir, and love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
(Latin) Please give my best wishes to all our friends and especially to the members of your family.
Address (not in Locke's hand): Aen mÿn Heer Mÿn Heer Limborch bÿ de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keÿsers Gracht tot Amsterdam

2129. Locke to William Molyneux, 12 September 1696 (2115, 2131)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 159-61. Answered by no. 2131.
London, 12 Sept. 1696.
Sir,
Could the painter have made a picture of me, capable of your conversation, I should have sat to him with more delight than ever I did any thing in my life. The honour you do me, in giving me thus a place in your house, I look upon as the effect of having a place already in your esteem and affection; and that made me more easily submit to what methought looked too much like vanity in me. Painting was design'd to represent the gods, or the great men that stood next to them. But friendship, I see, takes no measure of any thing, but by itself; and where it is great and high, will make its object so, and raise it above its level. This is that which has deceived you into my picture, and made you put so great a complement upon me; and I do not know what you will find to justifie your
― 699 ―
self to those who shall see it in your possession. You may indeed tell them, the original is as much yours as the picture; but this will be no great boast, when the man is not more considerable than his shadow. When I looked upon it, after it was done, methought it had not that countenance I ought to accost you with. I know not whether the secret displeasure I felt, whilst I was sitting, from the consideration that the going of my picture brought us no nearer together, made me look grave: But this I must own, that it was not without regret, that I remember'd that this counterfeit would be before me with the man that I so much desired to be with, and could not tell him how much I long'd to put my self into his hands, and to have him in my arms. One thing pray let it mind you of, and when you look on it at any time, pray believe, that the colours of that face on the cloath, are more fading and changeable than those thoughts which will always represent you to my mind, as the most valuable person in the world, whose face I do not know, and one whose company is so desirable to me, that I shall not be happy till I do.†1
Though I know how little service I am able to do, yet my conscience will never reproach me for not wishing well to my country, by which I mean Englishmen and their interest every where. There has been, of late years, a manufacture of linnen carried on in Ireland, if I mistake not; I would be glad to learn from you the condition it is in; and, if it thrives not, what are the rubs and hindrances that stop it.†2 I suppose you have land very proper to produce flax and hemp, why could not there be enough, especially of the latter, produced there to supply his Majesty's navy? I would be obliged by your thoughts about it, and how it might be brought about. I have heard there is a law requiring a certain quantity of hemp to be sown every year: if it be so, how comes it to be neglected? I know you have the same publick aims for the good of your country that I have, and therefore, without any apology, I take this liberty with you. I received an account of your health, and your remembrance of me, not long since, by Mr. Howard, for which I return you my thanks.
― 700 ―
I troubled you with a long letter about the beginning of the last month, and am,
Sir,
Your most affectionate, and most humble servant,
J. LOCKE.

2130. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 19 September 1696 (2119, 2133)
Rand, pp. 487-8. Answered by no. 2133.
London, 19th September, 1696.
Dear Madam.
I am very very glad you find so great an amendment in your little daughter since she came home.†1 I make no doubt but she will every day recover greater degrees of health and strength under your way of ordering her. I am of opinion with you that the rhubarb has done her a great deal of good, but I think she has taken it long enough, and that it should now be at least intermitted for some time; for I think it not convenient that anyone's, especially a child's, body should be accustomed to purging medicines constantly for any long time together. Purgings are a sort of violence to nature, and so should be used no more than necessity required and by intervals. If you find any want of it after a month or two you may give it her again. If kitchen physic will do I would never use any other, and therefore I am also for omitting the yellow powder, and would try what good ordering alone will do. When you find her recovery at a stand, and that there is a stop in the increase of her strength and vigour, you may then use the rhubarb, or the powder, or both, as there shall be occasion. For the weakness of her ankle and her treading aside as you mention, you must help this with a boot which must hinder this turning of that joint, which when kept in its due motion and straightness by this outward help will be confirmed by nature as she grows stronger.
As to your own health, I look upon you as in the safe and ready way of return to it by finding you in the Doctor's hands who has had so very good success with you all along your last illness, and to whom I look upon it under God you owe your life. I am glad
― 701 ―
to find you so much resolved (as you have reason) to follow his directions, to which I need add none but that you will often reflect upon what you say in your letter to Mr. Clarke, that you find your health as the quicksilver in the weatherglass rise and fall as your temper of mind is. It is that which I know to be so, and do tell you but that half your cure depends on the Doctor's prescriptions, the other half is in your own mind. Cheerfulness will have a greater efficacy towards your recovery than anything the apothecaries' shops can afford. And it being of all other the most pleasant remedy, you will have nothing to say to yourself and your friends if you do not use it. I am one of those, and therefore expect it of you, and am,
Dear Madam,
your most affectionate and most humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
My love to my wife and service to Mrs. Burges. Your son is well, and presents his duty to you.
Address: For Mrs. Mary Clarke, at Chipley.
2131. William Molyneux to Locke, 26 September 1696 (2129, 2170)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 162-8. Answers nos. 2115 and 2129; answered by no. 2202.
Dublin. September. 26. 1696.
Honour'd Sir
I have now before me two of Yours, One of Aug. the 4th, and t'other of the 12th Inst. I had sooner Answerd the former but that I waited to give you an Account of the Farther Progres of the Translation; which Mr Burridge faithfully promisd Me; and I lately understand from him that he has gone through the three first Chapters of the first Book. I must Confes his Avocations are Many, and therefore his Progres is not so quick, as I could desire: But I am sure he will accomplish it, and that wel too; And Mr Churchill has told him that you say Sat cito si sat bene:†1 and he is very wel Pleased that you give him time.
I do not wonder that your Essay is received in the Universitys,
― 702 ―
I should indeed have wonderd with Indignation at the Contrary. Magna est Veritas et Prævalebit.†1 We may expect a Liberty of Philosophyzing in the Schooles, But that Your Doctrine should be so soon heard out of our Pulpits is what is much more remarkable. He that, even ten years ago, should have Preachd, that Idea Dei non est Innata, Had certainly drawn on him the Character of an Atheist; Yet now we find Mr Bentley very large upon it in his Sermons at Mr Boyles Lectures, Serm. 1. p. 4. and serm. 3d. p. 5.†2 And Mr Whiston in his New-Theory of the Earth pag. 128.†3
Mentioning these books minds me to Intimate to you, that these Ingenious Authors agree also exactly with you in a Passage you have in your Thoughts of Education pag. 337. 3d Edit. Sec. 192.†4 That the Phænomenon of Gravitation cannot be Accounted for by Meer Matter and Motion, but seems an Immediate Law of the Divine Will so ordering it. And you conclude that Section thus — Reserving to a fitter Oppertunity a fuller Explication of this Hypothesis, and the Application of it to all the Parts of the Deluge, and any Difficultys can be supposed in the History of the flood. This seems to Imply that you have some thoughts of Writing on that subject; it would be a mighty satisfaction to me to know from you the certainty thereof. I should be very Glad also to hear what the Opinion of the Ingenious is concerning Mr Whistons Book.
As to the Reasonablenes of Christianity, I do not find but tis very wel approved off here amongst Candid unprejudiced Men that dare speak their thoughts; I'll tell you what a very Learned and Ingenious Prelate said to me on that Occasion. I asked him whether he had read that Book, and how he liked it; He told me, very wel; and that if My Friend Mr Locke writ it, 'twas the best book he ever labourd at; But, says he, if I should be known to think so, I should have my Lawns torn from my shoulders. But he knew my Opinion aforehand, and was therefore the freer to commit his secret thoughts in that matter to me.
― 703 ―
I am very sorry I can give you no better an Account of the Linen Manufactures of late years set up in Ireland than what follows.
About the Year 1692 (I think) One Monsieur du Pin came to Dublin from England; and here, by the King and Qs Letter, and Patents thereon, he sett up a Royal Corporation for Carrying on the Linnen Manufacture in Ireland. into this Corporation Many of the Nobility and Gentry were admitted, More for their Countenance and Favour to the Project, than for any great help could be expected either from their Purses or Heads to carry on the Work. Du Pin himself was nominated Under-Governour, and a great Bustle was Made about the Busines, Many Meetings were held, and considerable Sums advanced to forward the Work, and the Members promised themselves Prodigious Gains, and this Expectation prevaild so far (by what artifices I cannot tell) as to raise the Value of each Share to 40 or 50 pounds, tho but 5 pounds was paid by each Member at first for every Share he had. At length Artificers began to be set at Work, and some Parcels of Cloath were made, when on a sudden there hapned some Controversy between the Corporation here in Ireland, and such an other Corporation established in England, by London-undertakers, and in which Du Pin was also a Cheif Member. Much time was spent in Managing this Dispute, and the Work began in the Mean time to flag and the Price of the Shares to Lower mightily.
But some little time before this Controversy hapned, some Private Gentlemen and Merchants, on their own Stock, without the Authority of an Incorporating Patent, set up a Linnen-Manufacture at Drogheda which Promised, and thrive very wel at first; And the Corporation of Dublin†1 perceiving this began to quarrel with them also, and would never let them alone till they embodied with them; These Quarrels and Controversys (the Particulars whereof I can give you no Account of, for I was not ingaged amongst them, and I can get no one that was who can give any tollerable Account of them) I say they grew so high, and Du Pin began to play such Tricks, that all were discouraged, and withdrew as fast as they Could. So that now all is blown up; and nothing of this kind is Carried on, but by such as out of their own private purses set up Looms and bleaching Yards.†2 We have many of these in Many Parts
― 704 ―
of Ireland; and I beleive no Country in the World is better adapted for it, especially the North. I have as Good Diaper made by some of My Tenants nigh Armagh as can come to a Table, and all other Cloath for Househould Uses.
As to the Law for incouraging the Linnen Manufacture tis this. In the 17 and 18th of Char. 2. there was an Act of Parliament made Obleidging all Landlords and Tenants to sow such a Certain Proportion of their Holdings with Flax under a Great Penalty on both on failure; and impowring the Sherifs to Leavy 20 pounds in each of their Respective Countys to be Distributed at the Quarter sessions yearly to the Three persons who should bring in the Three best Webs of Linen-Cloath of such a length and breadth, 10 lbs to the first, 6 to the second, and 4 to the third. This whilst it lasted was a great incouragement to the Country <people>†a to strive to outdo each other, and it produced excellent Cloath all over the Kingdom; but then it was but Temporary, only for 20 years from passing the Act, and is now expired. But that part of the Act ordaining Landlords and Tenants to Sow Flax is Perpetual; and I can give no Reason why tis not executed; Only this I can say, that the Transgression is so Universal, and the Forfeiture thereon to the King is so severe; that if it were Inquired into I beleive all the Estates in Ireland would be forfeited to his Majesty. So that now the Multitude of Sinners is their security. This Statute you will find amongst the Irish Acts 17 and 18 Ch. 2. Chap. 9.†1
England most certainly will never let us thrive by the Wollen trade, This is their Darling Mistris, and they are jealous of any Rival. But I see not, that we interfere with them in the least by the Linnen trade, so that That is yet left open to us to grow rich by, if it were well Establishd and managed. But by What Means this should be, truly I dare not venture to give my thoughts. There is no Country has better land or Water for Flax and Hemp; and I do veryly beleive the Navy may be provided here with Sayling and Cordage Cheaper by far than in England. Our Land is Cheaper, Victuals for Workmen is Cheaper, and Labour is Cheaper, together with the other Necessarys for Artificers.
― 705 ―
I know not in What Manner to thank you for the Trouble you have been at in Sitting for your Picture on my Account; tis a favour of that Value, that I acknowledge my self extreamly obleidged to you for it; and therefore I could not think that the Expressions concerning it in your last belonged to me, did they come from One Les Sincere than Your self. Painting, tis true, was Designed to Represent the Gods, and the Great Men that stand next them; and therefore it was that I Desired Your Picture. This Sir is the Real and Sincere thought of
Your Most Obleidged Humble Servant
W: MOLYNEUX
My†a- Son gives his service to Young Mr Masham and desires the Inclosed may be presented to him; tis all Childish, but consider tis from One that was but seven year old last July.-†a
To John Locke Esquire.
Endorsed by Locke: W: Molyneux 26. Sept 96 Answered 22. Feb.

2133. Mrs. Mary Clarke to Locke, [early October? 1696] (2130, 2135)
Rand, pp. 489-90. Draft or copy, written on the back of no. 2130. The last part was 'discoloured and falling to pieces'. Words in square brackets supplied by Rand. Answers no. 2130; answered by no. 2135; hence the date.
[September, 1696.]
Dear Sir,
I humbly thank you for your last letter, notwithstanding you tell me I must often reflect on what I have formerly writ to Mr. Clarke in comparing myself to the weatherglass as I will answer it to you and the rest of my friends, which challenge I do accept as to yourself. And if I was at my own dispose, or it was more in my power, I would meet you to-morrow in the middle of Lincoln's Inn Fields at your peril. For I do assure you I pass in this country for one that has as great a temper of mind and greatness of spirit as any of my sex. I appeal to Mr. Clarke himself, who was lately an eye-witness of some of the trial I met with upon the account of his suffering in the esteem of the people by their misunderstanding of their own interest, but now I hope the generality of them at least are better satisfied. But when these sort of spirits reign among them, and they threaten to expose him and his to the rabble, can you imagine that the very noise of such a thing. should affect my quicksilver, and if I am to suppose I must not have an inward concern though I disguise it.
Pardon in that I [tell] you with this history a little to vindicate my own ill humour; and give me leave to tell you that I think
― 707 ―
poor Jenny the most mended since she came home as ever you saw. She has got a great deal of flesh and that pretty firm, and for this month has been able to run from one room to the other, and this without holding her string at all, and when she is under my charge I venture her to go to one end of the gallery by herself and I stand at the other till she comes back again. But this is a liberty I don't give anybody else leave to take with her, she having so great a weakness in one of her legs, that a small matter will throw her down, for she goes on one side of her foot almost on her ankle, but since she goes more I fancy the fault is in her knee; for the knee of that leg in her walking comes quite over to touch the other, and by that means turns her foot so upon her ankle. I have sent for a boot for her as Mr. Clarke and you directed me, but cannot yet get one here, so I have sent to borrow that Mr. Clarke mentioned of my Aunt Strachey.†1 But when it comes, if the fault prove to be in the knee, I question whether it will be proper for her. She fetches her breath much better than she did, and has always had over good stomach, so that I thought she did eat more than nature could digest, she being as I found naturally costive....
