2138. Peter Stratton to Locke, 2 November 1696 (2132, 2158)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 237-8.
Bristoll the 2d of November 1696.
Honour'd Sir
I did this day Receive a letter from Cosin Peter King†1 by which I understand you want to know where to direct a letter for me so I have under-writ where you may and I shall be sure of it—Sir I will leave what I said to you in my last at your disposall and according to your directions I will proceed. which is all but my Humble service to you. 2139. Locke to Edward Clarke, [18? November?] 1696 (2120, 2143)
Rand, pp. 491-2. Words in square brackets supplied by Rand. The letter was written at Oates, whither Locke returned on 14 November: Journal. He wrote to Clarke two days before 20 November: p. 717. This appears to be the letter; in any case its contents show that it was written about this time.
Rand prints a letter from Cary to Clarke, Bristol, 16 November 1696, relating mainly to the commons' vote on the 14th fixing the rate at which hammered money was to be received in payment of taxes: pp. 492-3.
[November] 1696.
Dear Sir,
I got hither, I thank God, very well, and [am free] already of one of my maladies that tormented me constantly every night. The cramp has spared me all but the first night since I came home.
― 713 ―
I know not what to [attribute] it to but the goodness of the air, which helping [relieve me] of those crude humors which this way rack me in town. This, I am sure, it is not lying warmer that hath eased me of those acute pains. Because the clothes that lie upon me here are thinner and cooler than those I had at little Li[ncoln's Inn Field].
The Bishop's†1 and our letter I delivered to my Lady, who is [assured] in the reasonableness of it, and neither has nor will expect of the trustees that they should in compliance with her desires do that which is not safe and reasonable for them to do. She thinks herself very much obliged to them that they will take upon them the trouble of managing her and her child's concerns entrusted to them, and does not expect or desire they should run themselves into any more expense in it. She presents her service and thanks to you and the Bishop and [will reply] concerning that matter as soon as she knows what to say to it. She and I have been served with an order from Sir John Franklin†2 to attend him on Tuesday next†3 at five of the clock to contest the account between her brother and her if we think fit. For I suppose the account about the arrears of rent due from his mother's [estate] at the time of her death which he is to take for so much †a For as much as I understand of these chancery affairs, I am apt to think it is fit somebody should appear there for us, that the account be not settled just as they please. But this I talk at random being ignorant and submit the whole matter to you. Only I think that when you speak to the Bishop you should make him sensible that going (as he says they did) into Chancery by consent, it is not reason nor conscience that my Lady's and the infant's estate should pay all the cost, and that therefore he ought to make use of his privilege†4 till Mr. Cudworth be brought to reason in that point.
Though I am eased of the cramp, yet my lungs do not recover so fast. My cough continues to shake me cruelly, though I find my lungs move better than they did in town, and I am not so
― 714 ―
much oppressed with short breathing as I was there. I wish good success to all your counsels at the College, and am,
Dear Sir,
your most affectionate humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
Pray give my humble and hearty service to the Bachelor.
Address: For Edward Clarke, Esq., Member of Parliament, at Richard's Coffee House, near Temple Bar, London.
Frank.
2140. Joseph Barnes to Locke, 18 November 1696 (2168)
The Pierpont Morgan Library, New York. Copy. The copy was made by an amanuensis for Locke, who sent it with his letter of 2 December 1696 to Cornelius Lyde (no. 2153); copy and letter are written on the same piece of paper. Transcribed from Xerox print.
The writer rented a farm at Buck Hill at an annual rental of £25; he appears to have taken it in 1693: p. 727; an earlier tenant, no. 1558.
Publoe November the 18th. 1696.
Sir
I have made bould to trouble you with these few Lines hopeing they will finde acceptance at your hands, these are to acquai<nt>†a you, that I Liveing in your Estate att Publoe. and yesterday I was by Chance inform'd that you had given your Consent for Cornelius Abram to Putt in two Lives after you in your Estate. But now his minde Changeing he is goeing to give the Priviledge unto another, and soe they are a goeing to put me out of itt att Lady day next. but if you will gra<n>t†b me that favour at your hands to give that Priveledge for to put in two Lives after you, I will take it of you Dureing <your Life>†c and give you as much as any Man shall for it Yearly; Nay I wi<ll give>†c you Tenn Shillings more for I have been at a Great Trouble late<ly.>†c I have haled out 40 Loads of soile last Winter, for Esquire Lyde told m<e>†c that I shou'd not be put out of it, which made me the more Willing to Improve it, and because in the Parish of my Nativity the more Loath to Leave it, and because I have alwaies paid my Rent to Content, which made
― 715 ―
me the more bold to trouble you: hopeing you will Consider that if he that you give the Priviledge unto will not buy it, that hee should not give it unto another without your Consent. Soe if you please to Consider and grant me that favour as to buy it after you, if you please to send your answer with all speed before any other hath bought it. Soe I rest your obliged servant
JOSEPH BARNES
Sir Direct your Letter for mee to be left with mr. Peter Straton at Mr. Samuel Bayleys Bristoll.

Sir

2147. Sylvester Brounower to Locke, 26 November 1696 (2141, 2244)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, ff. 179-80.
London November 26th: 1696
Sir
Your kinde Letter of the 23th: instant I received last night, and thanke <You>†a for Your kinde wish, shall endeavour to deserve it.
I went to Mr: Pawlings this day-noon, and delivered the Silk and Buccles to Mrs: Pawling and Mrs: Justice. I could not possibly go to Dr: Pooleys†1 to day, but shall by the very first opportunity. Upon the removing of some of my things from Mr: Pawlings, I found a Band box, and in it an old Lace Crevat, an Old Flowerd Turn-over,†2 and a Cambrick Neckcloth Laced. I forgot to
― 721 ―
deliver them to Timothy,†1 but have since carried them to Mrs: Smithby, together with a pair of Woolen Stokins.
Mr: Popple presents his humble service to you, he received a Letter from You Last night, and intends to write again on Saturday.
The Answer to the House of Commons, was signed the 24th: without any Amendment by, E:B/E:T:/Ch: of Ex/Sr: P:M/M:B:/ M:P/Mr:H/ and delivered yesterday by M.B/ who returned again and reported, that it was read; and ordered to lye upon the Table,†2 but this morning I heard Mr: Neale†3 say in our Room that it was not very well received, particularly Sir Ed: Seymour†a †4 spoke much against it, but to what purpose I cannot well tell but he named the begining of it about the Wollen Manufacture and about the Poor, which he said lay before them, and thought the Board should meddle lesse with inland and more with the Foreigne Trade.
Yesterday was also signed a Representation upon the taking of Pemaquid-Fort and the besieging of Sacoe-Fort near Piscataway, not far from Boston, by one hundred French and 600 Indians, (Sacoe is the place whence the Naval stores do cheifly come) And the Board having at the same time in consideration the want of a Governor and Vice Admiral in Massachusetts†b Bay, the want of such a Governour for that Province was represented who may likewise have the Command throughout all New England†5
The master Weavers Complaind that their people who want worke begin to be troublesome, that they endeavourd to get leave to bring a Bill in the H: of Commons, against the Importation of Indian wrought Silks, of which they said there have been brought in Engl: by the last E: India Fleet above 160000 peices, and which they say, does their Trade more damage, than all the Obstructions they meet with besides, though they do not expect relief, yet they
― 722 ―
hope by that Bill to get it printed in the Votes and so rise the hopes of the Poor weavers and so keep them quiet while they expect some help.†1 Sir I don't know, and I hope I have not transgressd in writing this news if I have I hope you will pardon me, and if you will let me know I will then forbear. If I can be serviceable to You in any thing whilst you are in the Country, or when you come to Town again, I shall thinke my self very happy if you will please to Command me it shall be faithfully perform'd by
Sir
Your most obleiged, Obedient humble servant
S BROUNOWER.
Address: To John Locke Esqre: [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmarks: NO 26; WR

Honoured Sir

― 724 ―
day, The Rule of Court, wherewith the Commissioners of Appeals were served, was, to stay all proceedings, till the court should advise, which Rule was this day discharged, whereby you are at liberty to proceed, as you think fit, but it may be on another Occasion, if not on this, You may hear from the same Gentlemen again, for the Rule was discharged, without any entry into the Merits of the Cause, whether the Commissioners of Appeals should be Obliged to Examine all witnesses vivâ voce, but only on the falsity of their suggestion, that the Notes or depositions taken by Mr Noel the Register were without legal authority, which the Court, on Noels swearing them to be taken by the <Commissioners>†a authority, and in their presence, adjudged to be by a sufficient and lawfull warrant†1 —I have Received several books from Mr Frasier†2 (the names and prices whereof are on the other side) which he bought for you at the Auction, and for which I have paid him—

2150. John Cary to Locke, 28 November 1696 (2136, 2169)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 19-20.
Bristoll Novem: 28th. 96
Sir
I have the favour of yours 20th Instant, and note you approve of my discoarse on Coin and Credit, provided I had proposed Methods to render the latter practicable, my privacy wherein you blame, please to note that not only in my dedication but alsoe pa: 33 I offer, that if the Parliament (which I made the sole Judges of what I wrote) thought the Credit I there proposed necessary I would not doupt to make it practicable, and the same I wrote both to my Lord Keper and alsoe to the Speaker of the House of Commons,†4 the Modell I have bye me, and I flatter my selfe that twill not fall short of answering all the ends I mention in my Book; I did apprehend there would be great strugglings in the House to establish the Bank of England, soe many Members being concerned therein, which I lookt on to be rotten, and altogether unable to support soe noble and solid a structure as I desighned to build,†5 which being all of a peice, and perfectly honest, and free from selfe Interest, would be lost if grafted onto that Bank, the Managers whereof have not acted hithertoe by Principles either of honesty or pollesy, and I doe not find my self mistaken, the House haveing lately voted that noe other Bank shall be setled dureing the time for continuance of That,†6
― 726 ―
which seems to me a strange Vote, as if more Regard was to be had to the Interest of a few men then to the Trade of the Kingdome, and it appeared the stranger, because the weke before they had voted that its books should not be laid open,†1 whereby it lost that little Credit which it had with the Country before, and is soe sunk in its Reputation, that all the forced Credit the parliament shall tack to it will not make it answer the end of Trade; I leave you now to judge whither I have not done as became an English Gentleman; I love my Country, and will spend my time and spirits to serve it, but to help to carry on a private desighn, where I cannot see any prospect of answering the end I aim at, I doe not think my selfe obliged, or to set forth Projects only to be made the discoarses of Coffeehouses, which are intended for soe great an Assembly, and neglected by them; The House is now resolved on the Bank of England, if they can make it serve I shall be very glad, for soe the Nation is made happy I am well pleased, perhaps I may be out in my sentiments of that Foundation, for at this time I am of opinion that the Credit of England must be setled quite another way. But if the House alters that Resolution, and doth think fit to enquire after other Moduses,†a I shall always be ready to offer my Tallent, and desire to be ever in your good Esteem, and remayne
Your most humble servant
JOHN CARY
Address: To John Locke Esqre to be left with John Freek Esqre at Richards Coffe House within Temple Barr In London
Postmark: NO 30.
Endorsed by Locke: J: Cary 28 Nov. 96 Answered 28. Dec

2153. Locke to Cornelius Lyde, 2 December 1696 (2142, 2155)
The Pierpont Morgan Library, New York. The letter is preceded, on the same sheet of paper, by a copy of no. 2140. Transcribed from Xerox print. Answers no. 2142; answered by nos. 2155(?) and 2157.
Sir
What is above written is a copy of a letter I received from Joseph Barnes since I writ to you two days since. What he writes of my haveing consented that Cornelius Abraham should buy two lives after mine in my estate at Buchill is a mistake. Cornelius Abraham never asked me nor did I ever give my Cosent to him or any body now liveing and I thinke it would not be what I should have reason to take kindely if any one should buy the reversion of my estate over my head without giveing me notice at least. I desire you would doe me the favour to enquire into it. Joseph Barnes writes me word as you see that he will give me ten shillings a yeare more than any body else will give me, if this be soe I know not why I should not continue him my tenant, unlesse you have some just exceptions to
― 729 ―
him. He writes too that he has caried out 40 load of Soyle last winter. I would be glad to know this also from you whether it be true or noe, and who it is that would be my tenant in his place and whether he has a designe to buy lives in it after mine, before you determin anything in the case and make any new bargain. For I am not soe coviteous of ten shillings a year but that I shall always prefer an honest and substantial man to one that is not soe. I shall leave Joseph Hanny to what method you shall thinke most convenient to be used with him for the recovery of my rent for three half years is too much to be in arear. I know it is hard and sometimes very prejudicial to tenants to be forced to pay their rent at or presently after quarter day, which they cannot doe often without selling their goods to losse. I have therefor always been satisfied if they paid one half year before the next half year became due. That I thinke is a fair allowance and soe much I am content to give still But to let arears run beyond that I thinke does but mak them carelesse and ill husbands and more unwilling as well as more unable to pay when the debt is increased.
<I>†a writ to you in my last about my Cosin Stratton's account. Joseph Barnes's rent for the <half y>ear†a ending at Michaelmas 1694 is not set down in the account sent me as received by <her hu>sband†a or by her since. I must have it from Joseph Barnes or her, when that is agreed <be>tween†a them, the account between her and me will be then adjusted. I beg the favour of you to informe yourself of Joseph Barnes concerning that matter and let her know how it stands. I have sent her a state of that account and acquainted her that this is the point remains to be setled for the adjusting of the account between us.
The money of mine you have in your hands I shall finde a way to dispose of when I know what it is. I desired you in my last to lay out twenty shillings for me in Bread to be given to the poor in Pensford as you shall thinke fit. Thomas Somers is my Tenant and therefor I have usualy†b always chosen to make use of him in the like occasions. I beg your pardon for this trouble and am
Sir
Your most humble and obleiged servant
JOHN LOCKE

2154. John Freke to Locke, 5 December [1696] (2151, 2156)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 221. Defective: lacks the cover and lower strip of principal leaf. Written by Freke. For him as the writer see pp. 740-1. Year from Locke's endorsement and contents.
December the 5th
Sir
You know the distress the publick†1 is in for want of mony and that the House of Comons long since gave a vote of Credit for 600000 li and that thereupon the Great officers applyd to the Common Council of this City to Borrow 200000 li all this I say you know†2 now I must tell you that by the Interest of a Certain great House†3 a good summ of it is lent and would they accept of plate (which might be coind in a weeks time) at the rate they doe clipt mony (which must also be recoind) vizt at 5s-8d an ounce the same Great House is assured and has assured others that above 100000 li's worth would be lent, but a Certain friend of his in the Treasury†4 opposes it and yet tho the Bill for making hammerd mony goe at 5s-2d the ounce past into a Law on Thursday†5 Mr Montague†a yesterday moved the House of Commons that they would consent that in the loan which the City is making milld mony might be taken at 5s-8d an ounce and Guineas at a proportionable rate and said on those Termes the whole 200000 li would be advanced but the House being ready to rise when this motion was made They would not consider it saying twas of too great weight to be moved soe late in the day and then he said he would move it again another time. Would you believe this if you saw it in the Flying post?†6 and now you are assured that its true can any thing explain it but the word†b which have been used as a key†c for us to read other things by?†7
I must likewise tell you that mr M†8 has another project for the
― 731 ―
restoring Credit (which I doe not understand) which he has opend to the House but never consulted those concernd about it. Tis to fix a Fund or Funds for paying 8 per centum for all Tallys that are out of which there are as many as amount to above 10 millions and that the Bank shall open their Books and permitt all that will to subscribe their Tallys by which he pretends great advantages will accrew to the Publick and the Bank which I meet with nobody can comprehend but himself. But the Directors and others that are concernd in the Bank and every body else that I talk with apprehend consequences to the publick and to the Bank that are quite contrary to what he professes to aim at. However he is very confident in his Scheme and tho he had never discoursed any of the Bank about it did (as I have told you) some days since open it to the House And last night he went to the Directors of the Bank to propose it to them. Whether he satisfied them and brought them to an approbation of his project either by his reasons or his Threats (for noe doubt he would threaten them as he did in the House if they would not comply) I know not for I have spoken with nobody that was at that meeting. The Grave was desired by him at the rising of the House to goe thither with him but a certain suit in Chancery that he is engaged in obliged him to be absent he being to attend a Master in Chancery at that time and this is not the first time this suit in Chancery has kept him from attending the publick service according to his Duty, which convinces me of the reasonableness of the priviledge of the members of parliament to be exempted from Lawsuits during the sessions
Endorsed by Locke: J: Freke 5 Dec. 96

2159. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 10 December [1696] (2146, 2201)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 64-5. Year from Locke's endorsement.
london Dec: 10th
I had intended with my thankes for yours by the last post to have writ you a merry letter but it happens, I am to the last degree mortified with the trajicall acount I have this day had of my poor Cosen Hambden, who to end all his missfortune's has at six aclock this morning Cut his own throat. and tho I hear the wound was very deep and long yet he affter he was drest did live and speak; my acount of the particuliars of this mellancholie accident was as this is very imperfect. it has extreemly surprised and afflicted me. when I last hard from him he was not yet dead, though it was thought impossible he could live out this night.†1
― 736 ―
this has josled all mirth and som business out of my head but however I can't longer omit my excuse to you, for the delay of my enttrest money, which is not alltogether My fault; for mr pauling has the second time made very ill use of the trust I gave him, and therty pound I had return'd me from Cornwall†1 stopt and aply'd†a to such uses as he is not willing to give me any account of, nor can I so much as get him to com at me ever since I came. this has not only made me disapoint you but has indeed put me to my shifts, for houskeeping: I did not intend to have made you this complaint till I could have talk't out the story (which I am very sure will displease you) but hearing by Mr Brownover that you are not thinking of coming up, I could noe longer delay this excuse; and at the same time beg the favour of you if it is not very in convenient to give me a little longer time. for I find the deffucultys of money as great as I left them. tho I have lying by me in my Closet 600 in stiks,†2 and paper. with sex monthes Enttrest on them: before I writ you this I went my self yesterday to the Citty, to try a 100ll Bank Notte,†3 but they that seemed to offer me favour would not discount it under 16, which I thought so extravagant†b that I brought it home and if you are not prest for Mr Bondvill I belive you will think it not unreasonable to have patience. they say that in a little time ther is better hopes, but pray let me know if it be in the least uneasy to your frend.
I give you my thankes for your concern for me, which I take reall pleasur to belive. I must desier youll make my returne of affectionat service to My lady, and all the familie and that you'le belive me as I realy am
Your most obligd and Faithfull servant
M L
the weather is so bad that I cant wish you here tho I long of all things to se you my C. C:†4 sends services to you all.

2160. Dr. (later Sir) Hans Sloane to Locke, 11 December 1696 (1785, 2219)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 118-19. Answered by no. 2219.
London Dec. 11. 1696.
Sir
I told you I had some pamphletts relating to travells, husbandry, trade or physick which I designed for you, your going out of toun was more sudden then I expected, but though you could be as little spar'd as any man I know, especially by us planters,†1 yet considering the state of your health, and that of the hard weather, with the news that I hear of Your recovery I cannot but heartily rejoice at it; especially when I hear at the same time wee may expect you again some time hence. I have ventur'd to send those Small books to Mr. Churchill to be sent you that you pick out any thing you fancy and distribute the rest for making plumm pyes, I confesse I love to look over such tracts because most of them are used to such like purposes that deserve sometimes better usage for which reason I have turn'd over many thousands within this 10. years and have bound up many volumms, which you know you will doe me a favour at any time to command what may be for Your purpose. I hope you will think of the Society†2 now you are in the Country and lay by any observations proper for them, I remember one about long nailes you halfe promis'd.†3 I wish you all health and prosperity, being most sincerely
Your most obedient and most humble servant
HANS SLOANE

2162. Locke to Cornelius Lyde, 18 December 1696 (2157, 2167)
The Pierpont Morgan Library, New York. Transcribed from Xerox print. Answers nos. 2155 and 2157; answered by no. 2167.
Oates 18 Dec 96
Sir
I am much obleiged to you for your two letters of the 5th and 8th instant and for the care that by them I finde you take of my concernes under your inspection. I was very much surprised to hear that any of my neighbours should goe about to buy my estate over my head and much more that Francis Carpenter had actualy done it without ever askeing my Consent or soe much as acquainting me with it. This I thinke is noe where accounted fair dealeing For how knows he but I had a minde to buy it my self. next year though I did not think fit to doe it this? Or must I not stay any longer than Francis Carpenter thought fit to give me leave? But be shut out of the reversion of my Estate at his pleasure? Truly Sir did you not give me an account that you had made some kinde of proposition to him of it at £30 per annum I should not be very forward to have any thing to doe with a man that hath used me soe unhandsomely without ever haveing had any thing to doe with him. But since you have talked to him of leting him have it at thirty pounds a year I consent to it on this condition that he at his own charges keep the house in repair for else he haveing the reversion I shall be every year put to charge to keep the house very neat and make it convenient and fine for him. If he likes it on these termes you may make a bargain with him for the next year. If not I shall finde a†a way†a how to make more of it For it has lain still soe long that I am sure it will now bear good corn and it shall be ploughd up and kept in tillage as long as I live for that way it will turne to most profit or I am misinformd and therefor if he takes it not I shall desire you to inquire†b out a tenant that will rent it to plough and soe pay the more rent for it at worst. Joseph Barnes writes me word that he will give twenty shillings a year rent more than it is now let for, which brings the whole within 10s of what it is offerd to Carpenter for. For the house being a very small one will not cost much to keep it tenantable, and that is the most that I shall now be willing to doe to it and that as spareingly as I can too. I allow the Exceptions you
― 740 ―
have made against Barnes and for those reasons I am not very fond of him But he has paid his rent well and he has done me noe reall injury and if he be rough it is not strange in people of his sort of breeding. But I mention him only for the present if Carpenter will not take it upon the termes proposed and you cannot for the next year get a tenant that will take it and make the best of it by ploughing it being now but a quarter of a year to our Lady day. and perhaps Joseph Barnes when you come to treat with him (for in a second letter I have received from him, of his owne accord he offers twenty seven†a shill<ings>†b a year more for <t>he†b whole estate than it <was ever>†b let for) will come up to £30 for the whole togeather; I am sorry to give you this trouble But I thinke what is offerd to Carpenter is soe reasonable that I imagine you will have little trouble in it though I trouble you with a long letter to tell you my opinion and desire, whatever may happen. I beg the favour to hear from you concerning this businesse as soon as possible. Hanny I must leave to your handleing. Now you have done me the favour to send me that extract out of my Cosin Strattons accounts I think I shall be able quickly to setle the whole account with her without any more trouble. I am exceeding obliged to you for the multiplying your favours to me in all these particulars and am
Sir
Your most humble servant
JOHN LOCKE

2164. John Freke [and Edward Clarke?] to Locke, 24 December 1696 (2163, 2175)
B.L., MS. Locke, c. 8, f. 222. Defective: the greater part of the cover is torn away, including the last lines of the text (which runs on vertically down its inner edge) and the whole of the address, etc. Written by Freke.
December the 24th 1696
Dear Sir
I must beg you to render my Lady the thanks of †a for the very fat and good Goose and Turkey with which she regaled us †a pray add our humble service of which also Mr Masham†2 and the rest of the family may also be assured
Tuesday when the Lords were to be on the Bill of Attainder of Sir John Fenwick†3 the Lord Jefferys†4 presented a petition from him to be heard by the House whereupon he was sent for and about 3 a clock came and when brought to the Barr onely prayd that his Lady†5 and her maid and the late Bishop of Norwich†6 might be admitted to have access to him but the Lord Carlisle (his Nephew)†7 desired to ask him some Questions which all amounted to This Whether some Member of that House had not given directions how he should deport himself on his Tryall (as tis calld) To which he answerd that his Lady had shown him such a paper which she had
― 742 ―
from one Mrs Lawson and she from the Dutchess of Norfolk†1 and her Grace from the Earl of Monmouth, whereupon the Ladys were sent for but none but his wife could be found that night. In the mean time they examined Sir John what he had to discover to them he insisted that his papers were true and some times said he knew noe more than was containd in them at other times that he had been promised by a Noble Duke†2 that what he Discoverd should not be made use of as evidence against him or any body else and that he should have his pardon and not be made a witness and till these things were performd that is till he were secured they should be performd he would say nothing
The Lords voted that what he should say to them should not be made use of against him in that House and sent an Address to the King by the Lord Wharton†3 that what he should say there should not be used against him as evidence in any other Court and then Calld him in and told him what they had done and that the rest of his demands were not in their power to Grant but that if he made any discovery that they should think deserved it They would intercede with the King for his pardon but he answerd he would say nothing till he knew whether the King granted their Address when the Lord Wharton returnd they calld him in and told him the King had granted their Address but he refused to say any thing till he had his other demand granted, whereupon they remanded him and it being past 11 at night they Adjourned the consideration of the Bill till next day and orderd it to be read the third time at one a clock and they orderd the Ladys that could not be found that night to attend at 5 the next day
Yesterday they spent all the day till 9 at night on the Bill and then it past by 68 against 61 the majority of Spirituall Lords 3 of Temporall 4. I know not whether any thing was done or any new day appointed for the business of the Ladys but Tis said the truth of that matter is This The Dutchess (who you know is Cousin German to the Lord Monmouth) together with one Mrs Lawson did frequently apply to my Lord Monmouth about Sir John Fenwick
― 743 ―
and ask what was fit for him to doe on this occasion and the Answers that he gave them and occasionall discourses he had with them at severall times the Dutchess put in writing in one paper and stiled it Instructions for Sir John Fenwick how to behave himself at his Tryall
Endorsed by Locke: 24 Dec 96

Honoured Sir
The experience I have allready had of your great candor and civilitie, together with those kind offers of Service you were pleas'd to make me in the last letter which I had the honour to receive from you, encourage me att this time to hope for your favourable assistance in a business wherein I have reason to think it may be very
― 744 ―
serviceable to me. Honoured Sir

2167. Cornelius Lyde to Locke, 2 January 1697 (2162, 2176)

2169. John Cary to Locke, 5 January 1697 (2150)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, f. 21. Locke's endorsement shows that Cary uses the old-style year.
London Jan.†a 5th. 96
Worthy Sir
I have the Favour of yours 28th ultimo; am very sorry you are indisposed, and that I shall be thereby hindred from seing you, yet being uncertain when I may goe hence, perhaps you may be in Town before; Inclosed I send you a Modell for a Nationall Credit,†1 which I wrote since I came up, its as short as I could comprehend a thinge of this nature in; please to kepe it private to your self, because I have not yet offerd it to the House, and am not willing to doe it till a fitter season then I have yet met with; all I shall say of it is, that there is noe Room left in it for Self Interest, which is the overthrow of all publicque affaires; I am with due Respect
Sir Your most humble servant
JOHN CARY

2170. William Molyneux to Locke, 5 January 1697 (2131, 2189)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 168-70. Answered by no. 2202.
Dublin. Januar. 5th. 1696/7
Sir
Tis now three Months since I ventur'd to trouble you with a Letter; You may see thereby, that I have a Regard to the Publick Busines you are ingaged in; but I have not been all this while without the Satisfaction of hearing that you are well; for as all my Friends know, that I have the most respectful Concern for y<o>u†b in the World; So they are no<t wa>nting†b <on>†b all Oppertunitys from tother side the Water to give me the Acceptable Tidings of your Welfare. I have lately received a Letter from Mr Howard that
― 747 ―
obleidges me to make his Acknowledgements for the Favours he has received from you; This I can hardly do without complaining off him at the same time, for not yet sending me Your Picture. but I suppose, by this time tis on the Road hither, and I forgive him, and with all gratitude Imaginable return you my Thanks on his Account.
The inclosd†a Peice of Natural History I am desired by My Brother to present to you with his most Affectionate Humble service. If upon perusing it, you think it may deserve it; You may send it by the Penny-post to the Royal Society, to fill up an empty page in the Transactions. there is nothing to recommend it, but its being exactly True, and an Account of a Non-descript Animal.†1 Formerly I had a Constant Correspondence with the Secretary of the Society, but of late it has faild; and therefore we take the Liberty of sending this through your <lb/> ands.†b †2
I have lately mett a Book here of Monsieur Le Clerks calld the Causes of Incredulity done out of French,†3 Tis the same Le Clerk that writes Ontologia, and dedicates it to you. I find thereby You are his Acquaintance and Friend; I should be very Glad you would be pleased to give me some Account of that Gentleman and his Circumstances in the World, if you know them. to me he seems an Impartial and Candid enquirer after Truth and to have the True Spirit of Christianity in that his Book. The Reason why I enquire after him is, because I suppose him One of the Refugees from France; and perhaps he may receive some Incouragement to Come into this Kingdom. I am
Sir
Your Most Affectionate servant
W: MOLYNEUX

2172. Locke to Sir John Somers, later Baron Somers, 7 January 1697 (1979, 2181)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 226. Draft. Printed in King, pp. 244-5. For transmission, etc., see pp. 751, 754. Answered by no. 2181.
7 Jan 1696/7
My Lord
Some of my brethren I understand thinke my stay in the country long and desire me to returne to beare my part and to help to dispatch the multitude of businesse that the present circumstances of Trade and the plantations fills their hands with. I cannot but say
― 749 ―
they are in the Right, and I cannot but thinke at the same time that I am in the Right to stay in the country, where all my care is little enough to preserve those small remains of health which a setled and incurable indisposition would quickly make an end of any where else. There remains therefor noe thing else to be done but that I should cease to fill up any longer a place that requires a more constant attendance than my strength will allow and to that purpose that I prevaile with your Lordship to move his Majestie that he would be pleasd to ease me of the employment he has been†a gratiously pleased to honour me with since the crazynesse of my body soe ill seconds the inclination I have to serve him in it and I finde my self every way†a uncapable of answering the ends of that commission. I am not insensible of the honour of the imployment. nor how much I am obleiged to your Lordships favourable opinion in puting me into a post which I looke upon as one of the most considerable in England. I can say that noe body has more warme wishes for the prosperity and therein for the trade of England than I have But the oportunity of shewing those good wishes in being any way serviceable to it I finde comes too late to a man whose health is inconsistent with the businesse and in whom it would be folly to hope for a returne to that vigor and strength which such a commission I see requires. Tis not without due consideration that I represent this to your Lordship and that I finde my self obleiged humbly and earnestly to request your Lordship to obtein for me a dismission out of it. I wish your Lordship many happy new years and am with the utmost acknowledgment and respect
Endorsed by Locke: J L to Sir J: Somers Lord Keeper 7 Jan 96/7

2175. John Freke and Edward Clarke to Locke, 14 January 1697 (2164, 2178)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 223. Possibly defective: the greater part of the cover is torn away, including perhaps a continuation of the postscript, which runs vertically down its inner edge, and the whole of the address, etc. Written by Freke, apart from Clarke's initials.
January the 14th 1696/7
Dear Sir
I'll warrant you think me much too blame and very unkind that I han't written to you (I think) these three weeks especially since I have received the short and the long letter by your Cousin King in the former of which you soe slyly rebuke me for my silence in excusing your self for not having answerd my Letter which you received before Christmas
Now would you know the reason I have soe long forborn writing? Why tis onely this. I had a mind to give you an account of the affair that has of late soe fully employd the House of Lords and I have all this while wayted to see the issue of it and been constantly enquiring what their examinations have discoverd but after all my enquiry and delay I am as much to seek as ever what has appeard before them what tis like to tend to or when they will be able to come to any Resolution upon it†2 and therefore I shall noe longer defer telling you that your Letter was deliverd to my Lord K†3 by the Grave the morning after we received it and his Lordship said he must speak with the Grave and me together before he could answer it. Since that tho we have both attempted it and I often and
― 752 ―
waited long to be admitted to speak with him yet this affair depending in the House of Lords has soe fully employd him as well out the House as in it early and late that it has been impossible for either of us to get access to him though he as well as we desired it, but I must take the freedom to tell you that you did ill to Come to such a Resolution without consulting your friends and after all you can't be admitted to execute your design. you may stay as long as your health requires it in the country but twould be of very ill Consequence if you should quitt your employ at this time
Give our service to my Lady Mr Masham and the rest of the good family at Oats and be assured we are
Your faithfull friends and humble servant
JOHN FREKE
E: C:
The Grave would write but cannot get time if you knew how he is hurryd with bussiness you would easily excuse him

Oates 15 Jan 96/7
Sir
By yours of the 2d instant I understand you have let my estate at Buckhill to Fr: Carpenter at £30 per annum whereby I conclude you part with Hanny too as well as Barns at our Lady day. I mention this because I imagin it may be the more necessary to get in his arear between this and that, for whilst he is a tenant the power of destraining for rent makes tenants I thinke more ready to pay than when they are quite gon off, and destraining may perhaps be the readyest way to recover this arear. 2178. John Freke [and Edward Clarke?] to Locke, 16 January 1697 (2175, 2179)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 224. Defective: apparently lacks lower strip of principal leaf, as well as whole of cover. Written by Freke.
January the 16th 1696/7
Dear Sir
Though I can't give you an account of the affair which has been soe long examining by the Lords yet I think you will expect I
― 754 ―
should acquaint you with the Resolution they came to last night (after a long Debate) with relation to the Earl of Monmouth whose friends were forced to struggle hard to obtain soe moderate a sentence other Lords pressing to have expelld him the House and laid a Judgement of Disability on him ever to sit and vote as a Peer during his life and also to have Orderd a Prosecution at Law against him soe that the House at length came to the Vote (of which I give you the substance but not the very words) with only six negatives, of whom the Bishop of London†1 was one
Resolved
That it appears to this House that Charles Earl of Monmouth has had great share in contriving three papers proved to this House in which are diverse expressions undutifull to his Sacred Majesty for which Crimes he is comitted to the Tower there to remain a prisoner during his Majestys pleasure and the pleasure of this House
After which the House orderd a Comittee to prepare an Address to his Majesty representing the Cause of their adjudging his Lordship to prison and then adjournd to Moonday morning.†2
When the Address is drawn up and presented I will endeavour to get and send you a coppy of it and in the meantime enquire as particularly as I can into the affair and the proceedings of the Lords in it and if I can get an account to satisfie my self I will write it you for your fuller information and satisfaction but hitherto I can neither make head or tail of what I have heard of this intricate business
I hope in a little time to give you my sentiments of the long Letter you sent me to peruse†3
I believe this Post will bring you a Letter from the person to whom the Grave deliverd yours though I have not yet been able to get access to him,†4 but he sent me word this morning that he would speak with me at his first leisure and in the mean time would write to you.
Endorsed by Locke: J: <Freke>†a 16 Jan 96/7 Answered 18

2180. John Wynne to Locke, 23 January 1697 (2166, 2190)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 123-4.
Oxon. Jan 23 96/7
Honoured Sir
Not long after I had received your very obliging letter, wherein you were pleas'd to signify to me that you had writt to My Lord Privy-seal on my behalf, I had another from My Lord Bishop of Bangor†2 which inform'd me of the good success of your application to his Lordship. For his Lordship was pleas'd to acquaint My Lord Bishop that he did accept of me for his Chaplain, and wish'd my Lord to give me notice of it, that I might put my self in a readines to attend his Lordship when I should be sent for; which I shall accordingly do. As I have reason to set a high value upon this Relation to A Person of his Lordship's Rank and charecter, so I shall with all diligence endeavour to do his Lordship all the Honour and service in my station that I may be capeable of. I account it no small accession to this good fortune, that it may be a means to introduce me into your conversation, in which I promise my self great satisfaction. In the mean time I cannot duly express the just sense I have of my obligations to you: For I am well assur'd that my success in this affair was wholy owing to your interposal on my behalf. This as I do with all thankfullnes acknowledge, so I shall be
― 757 ―
allwaies ready to make what other returns I may be able, and remain with great respect
Honoured Sir
Your most oblig'd and humble servant
JOHN WYNNE

2181. Sir John Somers, later Baron Somers, to Locke, 25 January [1697] (2172, 2186)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 163-4. Printed in King, p. 245, with date 26 January 1697. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answers no. 2172; answered by no. 2186.
25. Jan.
Sir
My great fatigue joynd with a very great indisposition must make my Excuse for being so slow in returning an answer for your very obliging letter. I am very sorry for your ill Health, which confines you to the Country at present, but hope you will have so much regard to yourself, your freinds, and your Country, as not to think of returning to busines till you are recovered to such a competent degree as not to run the hazard of a relapse. As to the other part of your letter which relates to your quitting the Commission, I must say you are much, in the wrong in my opinion, to entertain a thought of it, and I flatter my self so far, as to beleive I could bring you over to my Sentiment, if I had the happines of half an hours conversation with you. These being my thoughts you cannot wonder if I am not willing to enter upon the Commission you give mee of saying something to the King of your purpose. But when the new Commissioner is made,†1 and the Establishment fixed, and the Parliament up, and you have had the opinion of your Freinds here, I will submitt to act as you shall command mee. In the mean time give mee leave to say that no man alive has a greater value for you, nor is with more sincerity then my self
Sir
Your most faithfull humble servant
J. SOMMERS

2182. Locke to Edward Clarke, 26 January 1697 (2179, 2183)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 113. Discoloured. Printed in Rand, pp. 497-9.
Oates 26 Jan. 96/7
Dear Sir
The letters came soe late yesterday that when I sealed myne to the Batchelor which I writ in hast I hoped not for an oportunity to answer by this post any more of those many I received yesterday but by an accident I have now the oportunity to tell you that though your letters are always very wellcome to me, yet I did not soe much as once grumble at your silence. I know how your time is taken up, and shall always desire rather that it may be inlarged for the publick than straitend in Civility to me. When necessary businesse makes me trouble you I know I may depend on you and you will forgive me
My Lady bids me say she is exceedingly sensible of the kindnesse in yours of the 23d: and thinks it civiller, because shorter to you, to return her thanks by my hands than a letter of her own. She has seconded the Bishops†1 letter to the Debtors and explaind it soe as to make it I think more intelligible and of more force. Soe that I hope the businesse between her and her brother is now in a way to an end.
Your answer to Sir Francis about laying the Notes before the Master,†2 that it was what the Trustees were obleiged to doe and was for their security I beleive to be soe, and that which must satisfie any reasonable man, and the same too seems to me to reach the case of takeing his single bond. For I aske you whether we are not under a like obligation not to doe it, and whether with security to our selves we can? I am willing to comply as far as may be with Sir Fr:'s desires and to doe what may be for the convenience of my Lady and the child. But I must aske whether with safety to our Trust we can take this single bond, when Sir Fr: has land here which he purchasd with mony which he got by that Executorship, which, makes him liable to pay those two notes, and with which he should have paid them above a year since, with which land he may secure this debt if he pleases. Moreover I must whisper in your ear That that which makes his difficulty to pay
― 759 ―
this debt out of Sir E: Abnys†1 money when he receives it is that Sir E.A:, contrary to Sir Fr:s Expectation, tells him he will when he pays the bond (now under your reference) to him call in an hundred pounds which Sir Fr: owes him upon a bond, where in he and his son are bound. If Sir Francis will give the Trustees the same security for £100, and pay the remainder of those two notes out of Sir E.As money, he may this way too secure this debt to the Trustees beyond exception. If he has two ways to give better security than his single bond and will doe neither I aske you whether we can answer it, to consent that he should leave the Trustees and the Estate lesse secure than he can make them? And if that little time wherein the money is promised to be paid should not in a little time come Must not the Trustees either let it drill on†2 under the hazard of assets (for who has a lease of his life?) or else come to the same extremitys they decline now though Chancery†a does it now, and it will then be their voluntary act? And will not the inconvenience to my Lady and her child, if he be then forced, be the same as now? Besides if Mr Cudworth will not take his single bond, how can we be justified in doeing it? These are the objections that occur to me in the case, and would be unanswerable by Sir Fr. if I could put them. But that would bring my Lady not only into suspition but almost in view that her hand was in it and that she at the bottom hinders our accepting the single bond. For this of the £100 oweing to Sir E.A upon his and his sons bond I had from her, and the Mortgage of the new purchased land, if you mention it will also be concluded to be suggested from hence. But if you aske him as from your self, whether he hath not land, on which he can give the Trustees security I beleive he will not deny it: and by talking with Sir E.A about the affair between him and Sir Fr: you may get out the knowledg of that bond which he has (in his own or Sir Michael Henages name)†3 of Sir Fr and his son. and soe may manage this upon the obligation of our Trust. without discovering any notice you have from hence. This would be a great kindnesse to my Lady and, as I guesse, ease and security
― 760 ―
to us which I would joyn with you in were not my Lady unavoidably involved in my appearing. This appears to me the state of the whole case and I shall be glad to have your opinion in it. by which at last I doubt not but I shall be determind I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
My humble service to the Batchelor Madam and your son pardon the trouble of the <inclosed>†a
Address: For Edward Clarke Esquire member of Parliament at Richards Coffee house within Temple Bar London Frank
Postmark: IA 27
Endorsed by Clarke: Mr Lock what Methods to bee taken for getting Good Security from Sir Francis Masham for the Debt due from Mr Andrews†1 etc: Received the 27th. January 1696. Answered fully the 28th.
2183. [John Freke?] to [Locke?], 26 January 1697 (2182, 2184)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, ff. 200-2. This is an account of the examination of Monmouth's conduct in connection with Sir John Fenwick (pp. 741-2) and of his commitment to the Tower on 15 January. It appears to be the account prepared for Locke by Freke: pp. 751, 753-4, 755. There is no address, but the account is endorsed by Locke. There is nothing relating directly to Locke; the information about Monmouth is available elsewhere; the piece therefore is not printed here. The only notable passage consists of some erroneous statements about Shrewsbury.

2184. Locke to Edward Clarke, 1 February 1697 (2183, 2185)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 114 (i). Discoloured. Printed in Rand, pp. 499-500.
Oates 1 Feb. 96/7
Dear Sir
Though yours of the 28th came at the same time with the Batchelors yet I could not answer it as I did the Batchelors by Sir
― 761 ―
Francis this morning For thinkeing it likely he should say some thing to my Lady or me about the security whilst he was here I forbore writeing to you till he was gon. To me I am sure he has not said a Syllable and my Lady tells me he has said noething to her of it If it be because he is resolvd to doe what he ought, viz to give the Trustees as good security as he can it is well I am very glad of it that he is come to a resolution both becomeing him and I think for his interest. But if it be to give you farther trouble in the point, and expose the Trustees unreasonably by a mismanagement of their Trust I know not what to say to that. My Lady tells me she imagins he will be willing to give better security than his owne bond but concludes it is not the land but his and his sons bond for £100, supposeing the £100 upon their joynt bond be called in. Upon what reasons she concludes this since he has said noe thing to her I know not. But this she earnestly begs of you that you would by all gentle means endeavour to worke him from an obstinate persisting on his owne bond and soe she thinks you may be able to bring him off from it. A security for the whole £168 I find she would like best. But would I finde to avoid suspition†a and wrangleing etc be content that Sir Fr's and his sons bond should be taken for £100 and the £68 be left upon Sir Fr's single bond if Sir Fr promises to pay it out of Sir Ed. Ab:s money,†1 and that be like to be paid speedily which she says you to whom that matter is referd can best tell. But the takeing Sir Fr.s single bond for the whole she is I finde not for since if it be left in that state, she and her child shall run the greater risque, but she not live one jot the easier by it, since that debt presseing and as she supposes the Trustees not being willing to let it hang long on that single thread, it will but make a greater trouble and vexation then For if we can once take his single bond why can we not continue it. My sense of the thing you know in my former letter. If you can by the handles I there gave you gently and smoothly managed bring Sir Francis†b to doe what is fit for the Trustees to accept you will doe her a singular kindenesse. If the matter sticks before it come to that I beleive you will let me know before you come to a conclusion that I who am in lesse hurry than you may think how to remove the difficulty it sticks at. If you can get a knowledg of the Land he has morgeable,†2 from Sir Fr. himself;
― 762 ―
or from Sir Ed. Ab: the knowledg of his and his sons bond methinks the giveing of either of those securitys may be urged by you as a freind as his own interest to give them, since he thereby discharges himself of soe much personal debt of his own which cannot rest long without being troublesome to him, and lays it upon his heir who will have the estate to discharge it. But you will know how to manage this better than I can tell you. I am
Sir
Your most affectionate and most humble servant
J LOCKE
Your saying noething of Madame makes me hope she is well. Pray give her and my wife my humble service
Address: For Edward Clarke Esquire member of Parliament at Richards Coffee house within Temple Bar London

2186. Locke to Sir John Somers, later Baron Somers, 1 February 1697 (2181, 2338)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 227. Draft. Printed in King, pp. 245-6. Answers no. 2181.
My Lord
I know noe body that can with soe much Right promise himself to bring me over to his sentiments as your Lordship for I know not anyone that has such a master reason to prevaile as your Lordship nor any one to whom without attending the convictions of that†a I am soe much disposd to submitt to with an implicit faith. Your Lordship and I, I perceive from several positions take a different view of the same thing. And since your Lordship who always speaks Reason is always also ready to hear it I promise†b my self that the proposition I made would not appear to your Lordship altogeather unfit†c Had I an oportunity to offer to your Lordship all the considerations that moved and hold me to it. The obleiging promise your Lordship is pleased to make me in the honour of yours of the 25 Jan, that when I have had your Lordships opinion you will not refuse me the favour I have asked if I shall then continue my request sets me at rest for the present and a word from your Lordship that you will have the goodnesse to let me have notice time enough to lay before your Lordship what weighs with me in the case before any thing can be done either in makeing a new Commission or fixing the stablishment will ease your Lordship of any farther†d importunity from me but in the way your Lordship has proposd and then I who owe soe much to your favour shall not alone of all the subjects of England apprehend that upon a fair heareing your Lordship will not allow the equity of my case. Untoward health which complies noe more with good manners than with other obligations must be my excuse to your Lordship for this last as well as it was a great cause of my first request in this affair. If my ill lungs would permit me presently (as became me) to come to town and wait there the oportunity of discourseing your Lordship, I should not have soe much reason as I have to desire to quit the imployment. The great indulgence your Lordship expresses to my infirme constitution makes me hope it will extend it self farther and it cannot in the meane time I thinke doe lesse than make your
― 764 ―
Lordship bethink your self of a man to substitute in the place of a name and a shadow.
I cannot make an equall returne to your Lordships concerne for my health since my Countrys wellfare which is soe much interessed in your Lordships preservation mixing with my concerne for your late indisposition will not suffer my good wishes for the confirmation of your strength to be purely personal to your Lordship. though noe body can be more than I am

2188. Joseph Barnes to Locke, 2 February 1697 (2168)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, f. 157.
Publoe feb 2d 1696/7
Sir
I have made bold to troble you once more with these few Lines hopeing they will Reach your hands for I have sent two Letters unto you since that I Recevd yours but I ame afraid that they miscaryed and did not Come unto you: Wherein I somthing gave you and account that frances Cartenter as he saith hath bought the estate of yours att Buckhill and hath Come and warned mee out of the estate within these 3 weeks severall times butt I hath answared them that I will not goe out of it for there warning butt if my Landlord had warned mee out of it I would have gone out: which now the time of the year is Past Long agoe for to Remove in the Country, beside I always: Paying the Rent always: att demand, I hope that you will not put mee now being soe much to my Loss for If I will give doble the value of and estate I Cannot take it att this time of the year: as for your Rent if you Queston that altho mony is now soe scarce with us I will Pay itt three mounths before hand to whome you Plese to order mee: and I will Give you as much as any: man: envy on one hand and Interest one the other: in our Country: is very Reainging: for frances Cartender saith that you hath noething to doe with the estate and he will throw mee out of the estate att our Lady Day be order of Law: but I Refer my self whouly unto you to doe what you will: only this year I am undon if you Putt mee out of it: as for my way of Liveing in the world: and Improveing of the estate: I will not speke of myself butt I Refer my self unto mr Peter Straton or mr James Hasell or mr William Hedges: for who<m>†a you Please to order mee to pay your mony I will.
soe I Rest yours most oblige<d servant>†a to Command
JOSEPH BARONS

2189. William Molyneux to Locke, 3 February 1697 (2170, 2202)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 170-3. Answered by no. 2202.
Dublin. Febr. 3d. 1696/7.
Sir
As I had reason to rejoyce on the Nations Account, when you were first put on Publick Busines; So I find on my own Particular I had Cause to Lament. for since that time (to my Great Concern) your Letters have been les frequent, and the satisfaction I had in them abundantly diminishd. Were I assured of the Confirmd State of your Health, I could more patiently submit to this; but knowing your Sickly Disposition, a Months Silence putts me in pain for you, and I am very uneasy under the Apprehensions of any Danger that may attend you. Favour me therefore, Good Sir, tho it were but by a Line or two, in the Crowd of your Busines; for that it self would be some Contentment to me in the want of those Noble Philosophical Thoughts which sometimes you were pleased to Communicate to me.
And now Sir I shall beg a Favour of you a little out of our Common Road of Correspondence. We have here lately received the Certainty of Mr. Methwins being declared our Lord Chancellour;†1 and truly, Sir, All Moderate and Good Men I find are very wel pleased at it. I suppose by your Interest and acquaintance with my Lord Keeper of England, you have an Acquaintance likewise with Mr Methwin; and I beg the Favour of you to mention me to him as your Devoted Friend and Servant. I am sure, if he knows you rightly, I cannot be represented to him under a More advantagious Character, and I know this will give me admittance to his Graces, which I desire more as I hear he is a Good than a Great Man; And being One of the Masters in Chancery here, tis natural to Covet the Favour of Him under whom I am to Act.
I have lately mett with a Book of the Bishop of Worcesters concerning the Trinity.†2 He takes Occasion therein to reflect on
― 767 ―
some things in your Essay. But truly I think with no great Strength of Reason. However he being a Man of Great Name, I humbly propose it to you, whether you may not judge it worth your While to take notice of what he says, and give some Answer to it, which will be no difficult task. I do not intend hereby, that An Answer on Purpose for that end only should be framed by you; I think it not of that Moment. but perhaps you may find some Accidental Occasion of taking Notice thereof either in the next Edition of your Essay, or some other Discourse you may†a- Publish hereafter.-†a
I have not yet received the Satisfaction of having your Likenes before Me; and have therefore lately writ a very discontented Letter about it to Mr Howard. A Great Man here†1 told me I Something resembled you in Countenance. Could he but assure me of being like you in Mind too, 'twould have been the eternal Honour and Boast of
Your most Devoted Humble servant
and intirely Affectionate Friend
W: MOLYNEUX
My†b- Son Gives his Affectionate Respects to young Mr Masham-†b I find by a Book I lately light on of Mr Norris's That your†c- Little Gentleman and My Son-†c agree in One odd Circumstance of Life, of having both their Mothers Blind. for My Wife Lost her Sight above twelve years before she Dyed, and I find My Lady Masham is in the same Condition.†2
Address: To John Locke Esquire at mr Pawlings overagainst the Plow-Inn in Little Lincolns Inn Fields London

I give you my humble thanks for the very particular kindness you were pleas'd to do me on this occasion, which engages me to be with all gratitude and respect
Honoured Sir
your most oblig'd and humble Servant

2191. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 5/15 February 1697 (2116, 2255)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 74-5.
Monsieur
Je croy avoir respondu a vostre derniere quil vous a plu me faire l'honneur de m'escrire le 7 Octobre dernier. depuis Monsieur, jay receu le pacquet de livres que vous avez eu la bonté de m'envoyer, dont je vous suis fort obligé. connoissant vostre Pieté, vostre candeur et ce zele qui vous est si naturel pour l'avancement de l'unité et la paix du christianisme, je ne scaurois estre que fort scandalisé de la maniere malhonneste et sinistre avec la quelle Mr. Edowarts c'est dechaisné contre vous.†1 Mais Monsieur, si j'ose dire mon sentiment, ces sortes de gens qui ne preschent qu'eux mesmes et qui veulent estre admirez comme esclairez dans des mysteres sublimes, ne scauroient supporter cette simplicité de la Religion comme jesus christ et ses apostres l'ont Enseignez eux mesmes aux premiers chrestiens. mais si ces veritez n'ont pas leur aveu, elles l'ont pourtant de tout homme bien sensé et pacifique, et mesme il ne faut pas doubter que ces malheureux ne s'opposent, contre leur conscience. le petit traitté sur le mouvement des muscles†2 est fort ingenieux et pour un jeun homme de vingt ans il na pas mal pensé. il a pourtant a mon advis bien mieux refuté les autres, qu'establi son systeme, et il y manque beaucoup pour expliquer tous les phænomenes de cette surprenante machine. il ignore que dans la contraction, la totale dimension du muscle diminue, comme messieurs Swammerdam†3 et Lower†4 ont reconnu. il na pas aussi eu assez d'esgard a ce que le muscle pallit dans la contraction, et ne dit rien de ce que tout le monde scait, que le muscle de tout animal tirez d'un corps vivant se contracte par la picure, et mesme que le cœur des poissons bat longtems apres estre separé du corps et particulierement celuy de la carpe. il est difficile et presque impossible de bien resoudre ces difficultez. cepandant Monsieur ma curiosité vous a causé des frais et de la peine, je vous prie sincerement de me demander quelque livre que nous ayons icy, qui soit de vostre gout
― 770 ―
afin que je me puisse revanger aucunement de vos honnestetez. ma femme est aussi fort interdite du nouveau present que vous luy envoyez, jay nouvelle que Monsieur Daranda la delivré au fils de Monsieur Teut, et que ce Monsieur les avoit donné a un Maistre de navire qui a manqué le convoy, de sorte que Monsieur Teut a repris le pacquet pour l'apporter luy mesme ce printemps. nous avons appris avec douleur que Monsieur Cyprianus est malade a l'extremité a londres d'une fluxion sur le fondement. Nous attendons icy en bref les Plenipotentiaires que Sa Majesté a destiné pour le traitté de paix. si vous n'estiez pas si occupez et si necessaire chez vous, nous espererions que voyant le Conte de Pembroc de cette ambassade, il pouroit vous debaucher et vous faire passer la mer avec luy et nous procurer le plaisir de vous revoir, ce qui nous donneroit une joye inexprimable. vostre argent est tousjours ou vous scavez. toute la famille vous presente ses treshumble respects; mais nostre belle mere†1 est tousjours languissante. nostre escolier est a leyden,†2 qui continue a bien faire, et son cadet ne sera pas manchot avec le temps, il est de bonne volonté pour aprendre. ma femme joint ses treshumble respects et remerciements aux miens, qui suis comme je le doibs
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON
d'Amst. ce 15 feb. 1697.
Address: For Sir John Locke at Mr. Powlings in litle Lincolns inne fields London
Postmark: FE —

2192. Paul D'Aranda to Locke, 6 February 1697 (2123, 2197) with enclosure Benjamin Furly to [D'Aranda?], 22 January / 1 February 1697
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 38-9. The letter is on f. 39; the enclosure, a copy made by D'Aranda, is on f. 38. D'Aranda sent Locke another copy of the enclosure with his letter of 17 February (no. 2197). There are several variations, generally not affecting meaning; I have supplied two words and the correct name Bruxelles from this second copy. Furly's next letter to Locke is no. 2200.
― 771 ―
London the 6th. February 1696/7
Sir
The inclosed is copy of Part of a Letter from Mr Benjamin Furly who desired it might be communicated to you: I have prayd him to write what successe this new way of curing distempers continues to have; and as I learn any thing from him worth your notice you shall know it. If the Effects of that Germans Art are so great as one would on report of it from Mr. Furly, known not to be the readyest to credit things of that kind without good ground, be apt to believe they are, he would sure find much more encouragent in England than he can meet with in Holland especially at Rotterdam where you know a Phisicians fee's no more thans comonly given to our Barbers, and little mended by custom among even the genteeler sort.
Had you been in Town, when I about six weeks since received a letter from Mr Furly, in answer to one by which I let him know the miserable low Condition of poor Mr Le Cene, without prospect of any income for himself a wife and six children to subsist on. his being a noted Tolerant or Arminian etc excluding him from the charity of the greater part; and his learning and free way of using it so far exceeding the common pitch of most of the french Ministers, as to make him therefore the object of their Envy hatred and persecution as much as is in their power lies, I should have ventured to have shewn you what Mr Furly wrote me and his having named you and Mr Popple (whom want of acquaintance with has hitherto hinder'd me from speaking to of it) among others he supposed would be willing to joyn with us in allowing that good man each One Guinea a year during pleasure, as both greater real charity than much one gives and also what may render good service and advantage to the publick in raising Mr Le Cene from the pit of dejection (to the bottom of which he lately was almost sunk by the weight of present want and fears of future misery) to be in a capacity of exerting those good natural and acquired parts he has shewn himself master of in writing etc.†a without fearing to be punish'd with the worst of deaths, starving, for reasoning freely. Knowing that there are few to be found who have not within the compasse of their own acquaintance objects of charity enough to receive what they are willing to dispose of that way, I have always hitherto so strictly observ'd it as a rule to my self never to beg for others that
― 772 ―
he is the first I have ever ventured to beg of any for. But as I think I cannot do it for one more needing or better deserving relief, so I hope you will once pardon my doing it now on the likelyhood, I assure you there is, that I am not in any danger of falling into the like fault again. Might not the same charity be mention'd to Sir Francis Massam? If we could in all raise some 25 or 30 guineas per annum he and his family would make a shift to subsist, tho but poorly yet contentedly on it, and he would be in a state of freedom of mind to study etc as well as a man can without Books all his own (once large) library being sold long since for a trifle to buy bread. I have not room to add the occasion of my intending to be soon at Bath tho by others thought too early in the year: or any thing more than that I am
Sir
Your m: faithfull and obedient servant
P: D'ARANDA
Address: To John Locke Esqre. [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmark: FE 9
Endorsed by Locke: P Daranda 6 Feb 96/7 Answered 1 Mar.
[Enclosure:]†1
Rotterdam primo Feb: 1697
I am sorry to hear .... is so indisposed and full of pain: and wish him here, to participate of the wondrous cures done with us by a German, without application of any Plaisters to wounds, or internal Medicines to Distempers that hitherto have been the reproach of Phisicians. he cures the falling sicknesse and the Dropsy; Breaks the stone in the Bladder, yea in the Kidneys and draws it away in bits with matter; The Gout, Canker and Caries or Beene-vreeter, as the Dutch call it, resist not his Operations, not onely at a distance in the same Town, But even as far distant as Delft is from us he has broken the stone in the Kidneys. Aches and pains of 20 years standing, vanish before him as nothing. He makes people sweat, purge, or vomit as he pleases; And all that he does, is that the water of the Patient being sent to his lodging he treats it, as is said, with the sympathetik powder etc as he judges needfull: and preadvertises
― 773 ―
people, when he will have them dispose themselves to sweat, when to purge, and when to vomit; for the first some he orders to keep their bed or ly down, some he causes to sweat sitting in their chair, without any extraordinary fire or covering. And in spight of all our Philosophers and their declamations, and all the interest of the Phisicians and Apothecaries, the one endeavouring to prove the thing Impossible, The other to stop his practice. <he> having no Bull to beget Calves with,†1 the loud language of the Patients prevails with the magistrates to licence him to practice in their City. And the Experiments†2 refute their reasonings: They say, that the Excrements being once separate from the body have no more communication with that Body than with all other Bodys; That tho they had, the particles of Urine, are so small, that we, with the breath of our mouths, can drive them which way we will, and much more then a strong west wind, if he work in the East, and the Patient sits in the West, must needs drive them farther from the Patient; That no Body can work upon another but by contact. And that all motion is in a direct line; and consequently that if he works in the East and the Patient be in the north or south those Particles cannot move thither. And some of them threaten to expose him, and to prove that the sympathetic powder, is a fictitious powder, and they have been all cheats that have pretended to do any feats by it. But I have advised them to forbear a while till they see whether his cures do endure: for that it will be to no purpose to write against Experiments.
He has at present above 150 patients in this Town. among whom Mr. Van-der Slaart†3 is a remarkable example, who has been some months in a miserable condition, by a wound in his Thigh, which the Chirurgeons and Doctors said would never be cured, without cutting open the whole length of his Thigh, every day when they dressed it they sounded it with a long instrument, and wash'd it by spouting into it with a seringe which put him to great Torment. Having heard of this man, he sent for him; and he undertaking the Cure, the Doctor and surgeons were discharged. And now he is so well that he walks abroad without pain, his wound having been closed a week. I was just now, late, at his House (to speak with him
― 774 ―
of the second part of the Project)†1 but he was abroad. I have ask'd him how he was cured? he said this Doctor caused him to sweat every day, at first onely in his Upper parts — and that then he could not sweat beneath his girdle, but was in great pain, the next day sending for the Doctor and wondring that he sweat not where his wound was and complaining of the pain, he gave the reasons of it, and told him he should that night sweat from head to foot, and so conntinue, as he accordingly did, and in three weeks time, to the Wonder of Phisicians and surgeons, he is so restored. But the first Phisician is now turned Prophet and wagerer laying twenty five guldens that he is not cured nor shall be.†2 But that he shall be punished with more pain than ever for his over great credulity.
About 6 months ago, the first of these kind Operators, an Italian Baron appeared at Leeuwarden curing the Stone, Dropsy, falling sicknesse, Gout etc. he lately passed through this Town being sent for to <Bruxelles>†a where he <now> is. They say this young man, a student in Theology, or proponent†3 among the Lutherans, served him and got his Art. But he says that is not true, but that he found it accidentally assisting a Chimist who was labouring in that mineral, who being too lazy to go out of his laboratory to make his water, made water in a glasse in which were some fragments of the mineral which finding to ferment and himself to sweat, he fell to try upon himself and so has brought it thus far. Yet some bodyes, they say, how true I know not, he cannot move.
2193. Locke to Edward Clarke, 8 February 1697 (2185, 2211)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 115. Discoloured. Printed in Rand, pp. 501-2.
Oates 8º Feb 96/7
Dear Sir
If it were to perswade Sir Francis to doe a thing at your intreaty, which it were in your choice whether he should doe or noe, perhaps
― 775 ―
there might be more difficulty to prevaile with him than I imagine. But it being as I apprehend it, what the trustees cannot doe in pursuance of their Trust, (with which I see not how it can be reconciled to venture near a quarter of the estate upon the hazard of a single security) it seems to me a thing of necessity to be done, to give better security than his single bond. which if you stand on, I see noe roome for debate nor difficulties on the other side. If I have suggested other particulars to you it has been to shew you how easily he could doe it and to give you an handle, if you can come at it, to turne him the easier to what at last is necessary to be done and the Trust will not suffer you to recede from, whose case ever it was. And as to my Ladys concerne in it, I doe not see how she will at all be eased, but her part in the trouble will be unavoidably increased if you receede from the Obligation the Trustees are under not to venture soe considerable a part of the estate upon the uncertainty of a single life. For I know not how to answer my Lady if she should aske whether ever we can have a better oportunity to stand upon it? and whether it will ever looke lesse to be hers or the Trustees act then now, when the Decree of the Court has orderd the laying the securitys before the Master, to see which are good, and those that are not to call in the money? If this occasion be once slipd and the Trustees once content them selves with his single bond, If they after wards demand and presse for better security for ought I know he may not be in soe good a condition to give it. This at least must be presumed that there will be the same unwillingnesse, and then where shall the suspition and the quarrell light but upon my Lady? For the Trustees who were once satisfied would still be satisfied with his single bond if she pleased and if she says she has not put them upon demanding any other security. (Though it be reasonable for her to doe it) shall she not be put upon desireing the Trustees not to presse him for any other security, but let the money continue as it is upon his single bond? And what shall we have then to say but that we can not? If this be possible to be soe, I see not how takeing the single bond now will at all ease her; or any thing else but insisting on that at last (if other perswasions will not produce it) that the Trustees cannot, as you said, with safety doe it. This is as I apprehend the case. But I am not soe well skild in these matters as to depend upon my owne judgment and therefor refer it to your better skill and management.
I thank you for mindeing my businesse to Sir Stephen. Does he
― 776 ―
say noething what I may expect or when I shall have it? My humble service to the Batchelor. I am
Deare Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
JOHN LOCKE
My Lady gives her humble service to the Colledg.
Give me leave to trouble you with the inclosed
