2194. James Hodges to Locke, 8 February 1697
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 209-10. Hodges, a Scotsman, wrote pamphlets on monetary subjects, Darien, and the Union. For him see Horsefield; H.M.C., Portland MSS. iv. 104, 220, 356, 431. His present book is The Present State of England as to Coin and Publick Charges, 1697: Horsefield, no. 411. Locke received it on 9 February: Journal. L.L., no. 1467.
London Feb. 8. 1696/7
Sir
Albeit it hath happened that I differ from your opinion in relation to the Coin, yet, seeing your design and mine are one and the same, for Advancing the comon interest of the Government and people, I hope ther is nothing to hinder, why we may not be concluded to stand in no such difference one from another; But that our agriement is still greater then our opposition.
Seeing also the prospect yow have had of Raising the Value of money hath bien only General, I can very readily consent with yow that much may be said against it, in that way of considering it, as being often done with such imprudence, in the way of ordering, and at time so unseasonable, as render its effects very lyable to challenge and prejudice: As also that England, for which yow plead, hath, in its ordinary circumstances, as litle need of or use for Raising the Value of Money, as any other Nation whatsoever; seeing it neither useth to want a Vent for al its great product in way of Trade, nor money to doe al, it hath need of, either for Trade, or other occasions.
― 777 ―
But I on the other hand, not satisfying my selfe with general considerations, have endeavoured to search into the many particular sides, foldings, and various aspects of that multiform and intricat Argument; and from that inquiry have raised to my selfe a Scheme of that Subject extremly different from what useth to be practised; and therupon doe plead for it, only with respect to a seasonable opportunity, and prudent ordering, and for a certain declared and limited time, with divers other considerations, that use not to be noticed in the ordinary practise of Raising the Value of Money: and, as to England, only with Regard to the present extraordinary Circumstances.
From which it may appear, That my Particular Considerations doe no ways so contradict those of yours, which are General, whenn yow have not taken under your View what hath fallen under mine; as persons les discerning may suppose of them.
Only I must confess that, very far contrary to my inclination, who both from a natural tendency of spirit, but more especialy on the account of duety and conscience, doe use to endeavour by al means to seek for those things, and to desire to lay hold on al occasions, that may contribute for Love, Peace, and Concord; I have nevertheles found my selfe in this matter under a necessity of making many stretces,†1 and taking many advantages in Representing your opinion, which I know ther wold have bein no need of, if I had had to doe, only with persons as reasonable an' discerning, as your selfe, and as capable to judge impartialy of the weight and merit of a new consideration, tho standing somwhat cross to a former opinion, which hath been fixed, before such a consideration hath happened either to be examined or noticed.
I have found the prejudices so great against al Raising the Value of Money, grounded chiefly upon your Reasonings, that persons of considerable judgment have appeared uncapable of perceiving or admitting any thing in the contrary, tho never so fair and just; and some have declared to me ther fixed perswasion, That I should as soon convince them That twice two is not four, or that, taking two from four, ther remaineth not two, as ever I should be able to make out any fallacy in those positions, upon which you have founded your opinion against Raising the Coin. So I Behooved, as I know yow well understand, either to Bend the crooked stick as far to the opposite side, as before it Bended it selfe to the other:
― 778 ―
or then to leave my selfe no reasonable hope of ever making it straight or gaining my purpose.
This, I Assure yow Sir, is the true ground, upon which I found my selfe oblidged to charge your opinion so high on some accounts, as in ane even, modest, and frindly way of reasoning, and with persons of a judgment wholly unprejudiced, I know ther wold have been as little need for, as I otherways was inclined to doe any thing, that might siem to touch the Reputation of a person of your Character and merit.
But, as yow have secured that by the generous invitation yow have given to any to oblidge yow, by shewing, to yow, or the Publick, a mistake in any thing yow have said; so yow have before hand made my Apology for adventuring to take that charge upon me, tho I must confess very unfitt for it, considering whom I have to deal with; if your oun Encouragement had not given me hope of your easy Complyance with such evidence of Reason, and Publick concern of al in point of Interest, as seem to favour the cause, for which I plead.
I am very sensible of the disadvantage I am under by having nothing to advance my purpose, but Bare Reason, (tho I wer never so sure of that) which yow well know is, without some other Offsett, the least part of that, which useth to gain credit, or prevaile with the most part of mankind. seeing people generaly, except as to those things, which relate to ther particular employments, whereof they chiefly judge according to experience and interest, use in other things almost to give up and resign ther judgement to some one or other, who by real proofe, or comon opinion of ther extraordinary parts, have gain'd that Authority over them, that they reckon themselvs secure by thinking, as they think, without admitting any farther inquiry. So I know that one word from yow wold goe further an' doe more for setting right the wrong byass that is in the thoughts of many to ther oun prejudice, about this subject, wherof yow and I have treated, then ten from me, tho carying along with them the same strength of Reason and force of sense.
Therfor, seeing al my design is to procure a sensible and seasonble Benefite to the wholl nation and society, wheroff yow are so famous and significant a member; I must think, that I should omitt a great part both of my duety, and interest in the success of my undertaking, if I did referre al to a Rational debate with such a person as yow, without paying the deference due to your fame, by such a
― 779 ―
Respectful frindly and humble Address, as this, wherby I have paved a way, that if yow should think fitt to remitt of your own, or allow any thing to my Reasonings, yow may doe it with honour. Seeing I desire to give yow al satisfaction, that nothing, But the general Concern of the King, and comon Interest of al his people, as after a narrow search it appears to me, and more particularly that of England, on whom the weight of the publick affairs doe lye, could have forced me to enter into the list with yow after such a manner: as also to lay before yow those acknowledgments, I have made, that the opposition betwixt us is neither so great, nor so direct, as to some it may appear, nor any ways inconsistent with that general respect, which by so many is ouned and pay'd to your thoughts and judgement.
Yea I suppose that perhaps a fairer opportunity of acting suitably to your Repution hath scarcely bien offered yow, then that which I have given occasion for, if it happen to answer the design; seeing to al the Acutenes and force of reason, strength of judgement, order of thinking, and plainnes of expression, wherby your philosophical considerations of divers subjects have gain'd yow so much esteem, Yow may now add so convincing a testimony of your generous impartiality in judging of, and submitting to Reason, in whose hand soever yow find it; or whither appearing favourable or unfavourable to that, which many less discerning, then your selfe, may account it your interest to maintain. Tho, if I have happened to fall upon any considerations, that may prove sufficient to perswade you that the particular and unusual manner of Raising the Value of Money, which I have offered, may be any ways so necessary, or capable of giving Relief in the present straits and extraordinary circumstances of the Nation, until other ways can take effect, as I have supposed it may; then I hope I need not be affray'd, but you will consider that only to be your Interest, which is the common interest of al.
And if I could prevail with yow but to make a more narrow inquiry into the general pressures of the nation, the great stop that lyes upon al publick designs, the encouragement that enemyes receive, the hazard of the publick supplys proving not effectual, And particularly the sad condition of the poorer sort through the loss of credit, and great decay in al manner of Trade, and then to sett al the loss, that can be imagined by Raising the Value of money, over against those real present losses, with ther imminent dangerous
― 780 ―
consequences, which are al capable of help for a time, until other means can be provided, by multiplying money in Tale, tho in les quantity of silver; I should be very hopeful of gaining yow to my side in advancing those ways and means, which after such a diligent search into the condition of the publick and private affairs of the Nation, and with a special regard to the poor and to trade, I have been constrain'd to looke upon, as necessary to be al sett on foot together; for making helpe sure, full, and effectual.
Persons of your circumstances, who feel not the general strait so heavy and pressing on their oun particular affairs, are apt to make a more easy computation of the common difficultys, and consequently to judge that easyer means will serve for Help, then a stricter search and fuller view wold admitt to be reasonable. And I am perswaded that, if the present straits an' distempers should happen, as God forbid, to fall short of a satisfying remedy, One chief cause would be, that the want of due consideration of, and search into the greatness of the necessity, have hindered the seeking out, or embracing, when offered, such suitable help, as only can prove effectual for Relief.
The calling in of al the plate, and Raising the Value of money for a short time, as I have proposed, on which wold certainly follow the Bringing out of al the Hoarded money, the Restoring of credit, and quickening of Trade, are ways and means so large, full, and well suited to al the sides and cravings of the present necessitys publick and private, that, as they are attended with no loss nor disadvantage, but what themselvs doe abundantly recompense, as I have cleared; so nothing, but the displeasure of God, an' denying his blessing, can leave any reasonable ground to fear, that they should fail of ane effectual an' desired success.
Sir, I know no private person in a better capacity to advance this publick good, and general interest of the nation, then your selfe; as you can doe it with greater honour, and more universal applause, then your concern doth afford yow a present occasion for
I have with this sent yow one of my Books, which, with what I have here lay'd before yow, I leave to your generous consideration, judgment, and censure. And shall give yow no farther trouble, save to Assure yow, that, tho after perusal of my thoughts, which, by the shortnes of the time, could not be gathered together without much hast, and perhaps some precipitation, our opinions should stand at a greater distance, then I promise my selfe they will,
― 781 ―
Yet yow may firmly Believ, that I am, and will still remain with al due estiem an' deference
Worthy sir
Your most humble real servant
J HODGES
Sir,
If, after reading my Book, yow shall think fitt to allow this any favourable Return, yow may direct it to be left at Andrew Bell†1 Bookseller his shope at the Bible and Cross Keys in Cornhill near Stocks Mercat; which with this Letter, and your permission, I will publish for general satisfaction, and promoting the comon interest. If this come a day or two later, than the respect I owe yow did require it should, my hearing yow wer in the countrey, and the want of your address, will I hope excuse it.
Address: For Master John Lock
Endorsed by Locke: J: Hodges 8º Feb. 96/7
2195. Alexander Beresford to Locke, 12 February 1697 (1865, 2216)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 179-80. Locke's movements at this time are uncertain. He was at Oates on 9 February: Journal; and attended the meeting of the Board of Trade on the 13th: its minutes.
12 February 1696/7:
Honoured Sir
Yesterday, after I saw you, the Lady Clinton, a relation of Mrs Johnson's,†2 sent me with an unexpected letter of commendation to her. Mr Johnson himself happening to be present, declared a great regard to my Lady Clinton and readiness to gratify her in my affair, but yet ask't whether, (the Judgement of men being more weighty than the best women's,) I could tell him of any man that knew me. Hitherto Sir I had been silent of you, but having now so fair an opportunity answer'd, that Mr. Locke had
― 782 ―
for above two years given me the honour of admittance to see him, and is too discerning a person not to know what I am; that I dare not flatter my self I have his good opinion unless he say so, but that whatever his thoughts are of me, I beleive'd he would be ready to declare them: and I said farther, Sir, you had given me a little hope of your own application to Mr. Johnson in my behalf if you have opportunity before you go out of town. He seemd to receive this as if I could not have named a more agreeable man than Mr. Locke, and said he should have opportunity of talking with you this day at the Committee.†1 The way thus prepared, Sir, be pleased to make what steps you think fit. Having told you plainly my circumstances, and been too importunate allready, I will not be more so, but referr all to your generous inclination; though I could with more ease be modest in a request for my life, than for the means of being helpfull to my father, for this really is of much more concern than life itself to,
Sir,
your most distressed humble servant
ALEX: BERESFORD:
Address: For the honoured Mr Locke
Endorsed by Locke: A: Beresford 12 Feb 96/7

2197. Paul D'Aranda to Locke, 17 February 1697 (2192, 2204)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 40-1. The letter is on f. 41; the enclosure on f. 40. For the latter see p. 770 n.
Charlecomb neer Bath the 17th. february 1696/7.
Sir
This importunes you as soon as I hear of your being in London to pay you thanks for remembring the good man recommended to your charity—and to pray you'l please to consider if on Mr Furly's order to communicate to you to Mr Le Cene and to the Royal Society the account he gave me of the wonderworking German sympathetick Doctor I ought to give the Secretaty of that Society copy of his letter (or neer it's words in the sence of it) as I did to you—I wrote him I would, and intended it when I drew th'inclosed copy in haste, but afterwards thought 'twould be better waiting till should hear from him how the new way of Curing continues etc and took it with me hither; because giving the Society a paper without a name would be no service to them or the publick, and I doubted whither I should do well to put his name to it as 'tis or not. You'l please to do me the favour to judge and, if you think it proper, to give or send it to the Secretary, otherwise let it ly by you.
I have no reason to complain of loosing my labour in coming hither for tho I suffer'd great pain the two first days of my drinking the water, yet I felt little the third day and have ever since been much better than I was before I came. this small vilage I prefer'd to Bath it self for lodging, partly to have the more of the open Air,
― 784 ―
but chiefly to be forced to ride (tho but little) every day, because I find riding does me good. Pardon my being too apt to talk to you as my Phisician, which I shall scarce be able to forbear doing till I can forget the best advice I have had was from you to whom I can give no other returne than entire command of me as
Sir
Your most obedient servant
PAUL D'ARANDA

2198. Mrs. Elizabeth Berkeley, later Burnet, to Locke, [c. 18 February 1697] (2109, 2273)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 205-6. Locke was in London on 19 February: Journal. The date in his endorsement here is probably that of receipt; as Mrs. Berkeley appears to have been in London the letter is likely to have been written on the 18th or 19th.
Sir
Recolecting the answer you made to what I read out of the Bishop of Worcester's letter†1 maks me fear my ill reading gave it a sense he was far from designing; I have often heard him speak of you with great esteem and respect, and should think my self very unfortunate, to give the least suspession of the contrary, I am sure it was quit beside my intention and what my Lord might justly condem me for, therefore beleeve you will be so charitable to me and just to my Lord as not to remember my fault in misreading his letter to his Lordships disadvantage; I have a great deall to beg pardon for on my own account, but my ill health, and confussion I had from the consideration of the trouble I had given you, will I hope help to excuse the impertenances of
Sir
Your Obliged servent
E. BERKELEY

Appendix
Documents relating to the termination of the Licensing Act, 1695
No. 1. B.L., MS. Locke b. 4, ff. 75-6; Locke's criticism of the act of 1662: p. 248, n. 4. In Locke's hand. Printed in King, pp. 202-8. Date: On 30 November 1694 the commons appointed a committee to examine recently expired and expiring laws. On 9 January 1695 it recommended that the Licensing Act should be continued. On 11 February the house rejected the recommendation and ordered a new bill to be prepared: C. J. The paper therefore probably belongs about January. For the termination of the act see R. Astbury, 'The Renewal of the Licensing Act in 1693 and its Lapse in 1695', in The Library, 5th series, xxxiii (1978), 296-322.
Anno 14° Car: 2di Cap. XXXIII
An Act for preventing abuses in Printing Seditious Treasonable and unlicensed books and pamphlets and for regulateing printing and printing presses.
§. 2 Heretical Seditious, Schismatical or offensive books, wherein any thing contrary to Christian†a Faith, or the doctrine or discipline of the Church of England is asserted, or which may tend to the Scandal of Religion or the Church or the Government or Governors of the Church State or of any Corporation or particular person are prohibited to be printed†b imported published or sold.
Some of these termes are soe general and comprehensive or at least soe submitted to the sense and interpretation of the†c Governors of Church or state for†d- the time being-†d that it is impossible any book should passe but just what suits their humors. And who knows but that the motion of the Earth may be found to be Heretical, etc,†e as asserting Antipodes once was?
I know not why a man should not have liberty to print what ever he would speake. and to be answerable for the one just as he is for the other if he transgresses the law in either. But gaging a man for
― 786 ―
fear he should talk heresie or sedition has noe other ground then such as will make gives necessary for fear a man should use violence if his hands were free and must at last end in the imprisonment of all whom you will suspect may be guilty of Treason., or misdemeanour.
To prevent mens being undiscoverd for what they print you†a may†a Prohibit any book to be printed published or Sold without the printers or booksellers name under great penalties whatever be in it. And then let the printer or bookseller whose†a name is to it be answerable for whatever is against law in it as if he were the author unlesse he can produce the person†b- he had it from-†b which is all the restraint ought to be upon printing
§. 3. All books prohibited to be printed that are not first Enterd in the Register of the company of Stationers and licensed.
Whereby it comes to passe that sometimes†c when a booke is brought to be entred in the register of the Company of Stationers, if they think it may turne to account, they entre†c it there as theirs, whereby the other person is hinderd from printing and publishing it an Example whereof can be given by Mr Awnsham Churchill.
§ 6 Noe books to be printed†a or†a imported, which any person or persons by force or vertue of any letters patents have the right priviledg authority or allowance solely to print, upon pein of forfeiture, and being proceeded against as an offender against this present act and upon the further penalty and forfeiture of six shillings eightpence for every such book or books or part of such book or books imported bound stiched or put to sale. a moiety to the K— and a moiety to the owner.
By this clause the Company of Stationers have a Monopoly†d of all the Clasick Authers and scholers cannot but†e- at excessive rates-†e have the fair and correct editions of these books and†e- the comments on them-†e printed beyond seas. For the company of stationers have obteind from the crown a patent to print all†c or at least the greatest part of the clasick authers, upon pretence, as I hear,†f that they should be well and truly printed where as they are by them scandalously ill printed both for letter paper and correctnesse and scarse one†g tolerable edition made by them of any one of them: whenever any†h of†h these books of better editions are imported from beyond seas,
― 787 ―
the company seize them and make the importer pay 6s 8d for each booke soe imported or else they confiscate them. unlesse they are soe bountifull as†a to let the importer compound with them at a lower rate.†b There are dayly examples of this I shall mention one which I had from the sufferers owne mouth. Mr Sam Smith two or three years since imported from Holland Tullis†c works of a very fine edition with new corrections made by Gronovius who had taken the pains to compare†d that which was thought the best edition before, with several ancient MSS and to correct his by them. These†e Tullis works upon pretence of their patent for their alone printing Tullis works or any part thereof and by virtue of this clause†a of this act the†f- company of Stationers-†f seized and kept a good while in their custody demanding 6s. 8d per book, how at last he compounded with them I know not. But by this act Scholers are subjected to the†g power of these dull wretches who doe not soe much as understand Latin whether they shall have any true or good copys of the best†h ancient Latin authers, unlesse they will pay them 6s. 8d a book for that leave.
Another thing observable†i is that what ever mony by vertue of this clause they have levied upon the subject either as forfeiture or composition I am apt to beleive not one farthing of it has ever been accounted for to the K or brought into the exchequer, though this clause reserve a moiety to the King, and tis probable considerable sums†j have been raised.
Upon occasion of this instance of the Clasick authers I demand whether if an other act for printing should be made it be not reasonable that noebody should have any peculiar right in any book which has been in print fifty years, but any one as well as an other might have the liberty to print†k it†k for by such titles as these which lie dormant and hinder others many good books come quite to be lost. But be that determined as it will†l in regard of those Authors†a who now write†m and†m sell their copys to booksellers. This certein is very absurd at first sight that any person or company should now have a title to the printing of the†n- works of-†n Tullie Cæsars or Livys who†o- lived soe many ages since-†o exclusive of any other, nor can
― 788 ―
there be any reason in†a nature†a why I might not print them as well as the Company of Stationers if I thought fit. This liberty to any one of printing them†b is certainly the way to have them the cheaper and the better and tis this which in Holland has produced soe many fair and excellent editions of them whilst the printers†c all strive to out doe one an other which has also brought in great sums to the trade of Holland. Whilst our Company of Stationers haveing the monopoly here†a by this act and their patents slubber them over as they can cheapest, soe that there is not a book of them vended beyond seas both for their badnesse and dearnesse nor will the Schollers†d beyond seas look upon a book of them now†a printed at London soe ill and false are they besides†e- it would be hard to finde how a restraint of printing the Classick Authors does any way prevent printing Seditious and Treasonable pamphlets which is the Title and pretence of this Act-†e
§. 9. Noe English book may be imprinted or imported from beyond the sea. Noe foreigner or†f- other unlesse stationer of London-†f may import or sel any books of any language whatever.
This clause serves only to confirme and enlarge the Stationers Monopoly.
§ 10. In this†g § besides a great many other clauses to secure the Stationers monopoly of printing which are very hard upon the subject†h the stationers interest is soe far preferd to all others that a Landlord who lets an house forfeits five pounds if he know that his tenant has a printing presse in it and does not give notice of it to the master and wardens of the Stationers company. Nor must a Joyner, Carpenter or Smith etc: worke about a printing presse without giveing the like notice under the like penaltie.
Which is greater caution than I think is used about the presses for coynage to secure the people from false money.
By†i § 11†i the number of Master printers were reduced from a greater number to twenty and the number of Master founders of letters reduced to fower, and upon vacancy the number to be filled by the ArchBishop of Canterbury and Bishop of London and to give security not to print any unlicensed books.
This hinders a man who has served out his time the benefit of seting up his trade which whether it be not against the right of the
― 789 ―
subject as well as contrary to common equity deserves to be considerd
§ 12 The number of presses that every one of the twenty master printers shall have are reduced to two only those who have been Masters or upper wardens of the company may have three and as many more as the ArchBishop of Canterbury or Bishop of London will allow.
§ 13 Everyone who hath been master or upper warden of the company may have three. Every one of the Livery two, and every master printer of the yeomanry but one Apprentice at a time
By which restraint of presses and takeing of apprentices and the†a prohibition in†b § 14†b of takeing or useing any journey men except English men and freemen of the Trade is the reason why our printing is soe very bad and yet soe very dear in England. they who are hereby priviledgd to the exclusion of others workeing and seting the price as they please. where by any advantage that might be made to the realme by this manifacture is wholy lost to England and thrown into the hands of our neighbours. The sole manifacture of printing bringing into the low Countrys great sums every year. But our ecclesiastical laws seldom favour trade. and he that reads this act with attention will finde it upse Ecclesiastical. The nation looses by this act for our books are soe dear and ill printed that they have very litle vent amongst forainers unlesse now and then by truck for theirs which yet shews how much those who buy here†c books printed here are imposed on. Since a book printed at London may be bought cheaper at Amsterdam than in Pauls churchyard notwithstanding all the charge and hazard of transportation. For their printing being free and unrestraind they†d sell their books at soe much a cheaper rate than our†e booksellers†e doe ours. that in truck valueing ours proportionably to their own, or their own equaly to ours which is the same thing, they can afford books received from London upon such exchanges cheaper in Holland than our Stationers sell them in England. By this Act England looses in General Schollers in particular are ground and noe body gets but a lazy ignorant company of Stationers to say noe worse of them. But any thing rather than let mother Church be disturbd in her opinions or impositions, by any bold enquirer from the presse.
― 790 ―
§ 15 One or more of the Messengers of his majesties chamber. by warrant under his Majesties signe manual, or under the hand of one of his Majesties principal secretarys of State, or the master and wardens of the company of Stationers takeing with him a constable and such assistance as they shall think needfull†a has an unlimited power to search all houses and to seise upon all books which they shall but think fit to suspect
How the gent much more how the Peers of England came thus to prostitute their houses to the visitation and inspection of any body much lesse a messenger upon†b- pretence of searching for books-†b I cannot imagin. Indeed†c- the houses of Peers and others not of the trades mentiond in this act are pretended to be exempted from this search § 18 where tis provided they shall not be searchd but by special warrant under the Ks signe manual or under the hands of one of the secretarys of state. But this is but the shadow of an exemption for they are still subject to be searchd every corner and coffer in them under pretence of unlicensed books, a mark of Slavery which I think their ancestors would never have submitted to. Thus to lay their houses which are their castles open not to the pursuit of the law against a malefactor convicted of Misdemeanor or accused upon oath, but to the suspition of haveing unlicensed books, which is whenever it is thought fit to search his house and see what is in it-†c
§ 16 All printers offending any way against this act incapacitated to exercise their trade for 3 years. And for the second offence perpetual incapacity with any other punishment not reaching to life or Limb.
And thus a man is to be undone and starve for printing†d Dr Burys case or the history of Tom Thumb unlicensed
§ 17 Three copys of every book printed†e are†e to be reservd†f whereof two to be sent to the two universitys by the master of the Stationers company
This clause upon examination I suppose will be found to be mightily if not wholy neglected, as all things that are good in this act, the company†g of Stationers mindeing noe thing in it but what makes for their monopoly. I beleive that if the publique Librarys of both universities be looked into (which†h this will give a fit occasion to doe) there will not be found in them half perhaps not one in ten
― 791 ―
of the copys of books printed since this act. vid 17° Car. 2. Cap 4
§ last. This act though made in a time when every one strove to be forwardest to make court to the church and Court by giveing whatever was asked. yet this was soe manifest an invasion on the trade liberty and propertie of the subject that it was made to be in force only for two years. From which 14th†a Car: 2. it has by the joynt endeavour of Church and Court been from time to time†b revived and soe continued to this day. Every one being answerable for books†c he publishes prints or sels conteining any thing†d seditious or against law makes this or any other act for the restraint of printing very needlesse in that part and soe it may be left free in that part as it was before 14° Car. 2. That any†e person or company should have patents for the†f sole printing of Ancient authors is very unreasonable and injurious to learning. And for those who purchase copies from Authors that now live and write it may be reasonable to limit their property to a certein number of years after the death of the Author†g or the first printing of the book as suppose 50 or 70 years. This I am sure tis very absurd and ridiculous that any one now liveing†h should pretend to have a propriety in or a power to dispose of the proprietie of any copys or writeings of authors who lived before printing was known and used in Europe.
Endorsed by Locke: Printing 94
No. 2. B.L., MS. Locke b. 4, f. 77: The Licensing Bill, 1695. In John Freke's hand. Presumably the draft sent with no. 1860 (pp. 291-2).
For preventing the mischiefs that may happen in church or State for want of a due Regulation of Printing and Printing Presses Be it Enacted etc. That from and after the day of Noe Printing Press shall be erected used or kept within the City of London or Suburbs thereof untill notice hath been given in writing to the Lord Chancellor or Lord Keeper of the Great Seal of England for the time being or to one of the Principall Secretarys of State for the time being or to one of their Secretarys to be Registred in their office or to the Lord chief Justice of the Court of Kings Bench for
― 792 ―
the time being of the name of the person who is to use such printing press and the place where the same is or shall be erected or kept and that noe printing press shall be erected used or kept in either of the universitys untill like notice hath been given to the respective Chancellor or vicechancellor for the time being of the said Universitys and that noe printing press shall be erected used or kept in any other City or Town untill like notice hath been given to the chief Magistrate of the same City or Town for the Time being and that noe printing Press shall be erected used or kept in any part of England except within the City of London or Suburbs thereof or within either of the universities or within some other City or Town Corporate. And every Printing press erected used or kept after the said day of whereof noe such notice is or shall be given or in any other place than is allowd by this Act shall be and are hereby declared and adjudged forfeited together with all Letters and utinsills thereto belonging or therewith used and shall or may be seized to the use of his Majestys his heirs and Successors And whosoever shall erect use or keep such printing press shall be disabled to use or Exercise the art trade or mistery of a printer for the space of and shall forfeit the summ of the one moiety thereof to the use of his Majesty his heirs and successors the other to such person as will inform and sue for the same
And be it further Enacted that upon such notice as abovesaid given to the Lord Chancellor or Lord Keeper of the Great Seal of England for the time being or to either of the Secretarys of State or their Secretarys respectively or to the said Lord Chief Justice Chancellor vicechancellor or chief magistrate they shall respectively without Fee or reward give a certificate in writing of the receit of Such notice
And be it further Enacted That from and after the day of Every person who shall print any book pamphlet pourtraicture or paper which was never before printed in England with Licence as soon as any Sheet or paper thereof shall be printed if the matter in such Book pamphlet pourtraicture or paper concern or relate to Divinity shall carry or send and cause to be deliverd one printed Coppy thereof to the ArchBishop of Canterbury or the Bishop of the Diocess in wich the same is printed or to the vice-chancellor of the university where the same is printed and if the matter containd in such Book Pamphlet pourtraicture or Paper
― 793 ―
concern or relate to the Laws of England then shall carry or send a printed coppy thereof and cause the same to be deliverd to the Lord Chancellor or Lord Keeper of the Great Seal of England for the time being or to one of the Judges Justices or Barons of one of the Courts of Record at Westminster for the time being and if the matter of Such Book Pamphlet Pourtraicture or paper concern or relate to affairs of State or the history of this Realm then shall carry or send and cause to be deliverd one printed coppy thereof unto one of the Secretarys of State or one of their Secretarys in their respective office under the penalty of forfeiting for every omission the Summ of
And be it further Enacted that noe person shall Print any thing Contrary to the Laws of this Realm or Contrary to the Christian Religion as it is Establisht by Law in this Realm under the penalty of being disabled from using the Art Trade or Mistery of a Printer for the space of from the time of Conviction of any such offence And the Printing press Letters and Utinsills employd in printing the same are hereby declared and adjudged forfeited and shall or may be seized to the use of his Majesty his heirs and successors
And be it further Enacted That every person who shall hereafter Print any pamphlet pourtraicture or paper Shall thereunto or thereon Print or set the christian and sirname and place of aboad of the master printer and of the publisher of the same under the penalty of and forfeiture of the same and of the printing Press Letters and utinsills imployd in the printing thereof and being further answerable for any matter or thing contrary to Law or to the Christian Religion as Establisht by Law that shall be therein containd
And be it further Enacted That whosoever shall order his name to be printed to any matter or thing shall be answerable to the Law as if he were the Author of the same nevertheless the Author to be also answerable and punishable for any thing illegall containd therein if such author can be discoverd
And be it further Enacted that noe person shall sell or publish any Book pamphlet pourtraicture or paper hereafter printed in England whereon the printer and publishers name is not printed under the penalty of forfeiting for every offence
And be it further Enacted that noe person shall print the name of any person as publisher of any book pamphlet pourtraicture or
― 794 ―
paper without authority given in writing for soe doing under the penalty of forfeiting the sum of to the party whose name shall be soe printed as Author or publisher and the further sum of one moiety thereof to his Majestys his heirs and Successors and the other moiety to such person as shall sue for the same and also under the penalty of being disabled from exercising the Art trade or mistery of a printer for the space of after conviction of such offence
And be it further enacted that every Printer shall reserve 3 coppys of the largest paper of every new book and Book reprinted with additions and shall before any publick vending of such book carry or send and cause to be deliverd one coppy thereof bound to the Keeper of his Majestys Library the other two to the vicechancellors of the two universities respectively for the use of the publick Librarys of the said Universitys
And be it further enacted that either of the Secretarys of State or either of the Chief Justices of the Courts of Kings Bench Common Pleas or chief Baron of the Exchequer the Chancellor or vicechancellor of either university and the chief Magistrate of any City or Town where any printing press is or may be erected or kept Shall or may by virtue of this Act within their respective Jurisdiction by their respective warrants empower any person or persons from time to time and at all times to enter into and search any printing house or place where any printing press is kept and the rooms Warehouses and Cellars thereunto belonging or which are employd by any printer or any other place where they shall be informd upon oath that there is any private printing press and to Seize and take away all or any Coppys or prints of any Treasonable Seditious Atheisticall or hereticall Book pamphlet or paper and also such private printing press and the Letters and utinsills thereunto belonging and to apprehend and bring to Justice every person using such private printing press or concernd in printing such Treasonable Seditious Atheisticall or hereticall Book pamphlet or paper
And be it further enacted that all the penaltys of this Act for which noe particular methode is herein prescribed for the recovering and Leavying of the same shall or may be recoverd by Bill plaint Information Endictment or Action of Debt in which noe Essoin protection priviledge or wager of Law or more then one Imparlance shall be allowd
Provided always and be it further enacted That noe person shall

be prosecuted for any offence committed against this Act unless such prosecution shall be commenced within after the offence comitted
Provided also that this Act shall continue and be in force for years and to the end of the next Session of Parliament and noe longer

Index of Correspondents in this Volume
This index is by the numbers of the letters, italics being used as in the text to indicate letters not by Locke. A bracketed number is either for a letter between persons other than Locke, in which case it appears under the names of both writer (or writers) and person addressed, or for an item other than a letter. If there is correspondence in earlier or later volumes between Locke and a person in this index it is indicated by the citation of the next volume or volumes in which any of it occurs.
The citation immediately following a name is that of a biographical note on the person. For persons concerned with only one or two letters the citation is omitted sometimes if the biographical note occurs in the headnote and is insignificant.

Recurrent Designations Other Than Proper Names
This list is intended to enable readers to identify persons mentioned in the letters in this volume by dignities, initials, nicknames, and similar designations. These designations are variable; a person may be indicated in several ways.
Archbishop of Canterbury: Dr. John Tillotson until 23 November 1694; then Dr. Thomas Tenison
Baron, the: Baron Franciscus Mercurius van Helmont
Bath and Wells, bishop of: Dr. Richard Kidder
Capitaine de Marine, le: Raymond Formentin
F., J.: John Freke
Gloucester, bishop of: Dr. Edward Fowler
K., the: the King
Keeper, Lord: Sir John Somers, later Baron Somers
Privy Seal, Lord: Thomas Herbert, earl of Pembroke
Salisbury, bishop of: Dr. Gilbert Burnet
Stephen, Sir: Sir Stephen Evance
Triumvirat, le: R. Formentin, F. Gendron (deceased), and N. Toinard
Walter, Sir, or Sir W. Y.: Sir Walter Yonge
The Masham household at Oates: Sir Francis Masham (Sir Fr., Sir F. M.); his second wife Lady Masham (my Lady, etc.; Mrs. Cudworth in van Limborch's letters until p. 147); his children by his first wife, Esther (Mrs. Masham; Mrs. Lockhart's Cousin Tetty; Locke's Landabridis) and Samuel (Mrs. Lockhart's Cousin Sam); his son by his second wife Francis Cudworth Masham (Mr. Masham; Totty; Little Frank; he and Mrs. Lockhart call one another husband and wife); and Lady Masham's mother Mrs. (Ralph) Cudworth. Sir Francis's mother, Mrs. (William) Masham, lived nearby at Matching Hall.
The Clarke family: Edward Clarke; his wife Mary (Madam); their children: Edward ('your son' without further distinction; Mr. Clarke); Elizabeth (Betty; Locke's 'wife'); and others.
The College (p. 199 n.): Edward Clarke (the Grave, the Squire, etc.) and John Freke (the Bachelor). The Castle in the College letters is Locke.
The Bank: the Bank of England unless further distinguished.

†1 George Keith, c. 1639-1716, the 'Christian Quaker', was personally acquainted with Furly. He settled at Philadelphia in 1689. Influenced by van Helmont and others he diverged from Quaker orthodoxy, and was tried by special courts meeting on 20 June and 9, 10, and 12 December 1692. Accounts of the dispute, etc., were
― 3 ―

published in 1692-4: L.L., nos. 1617-24, 2414, 2421; further, The Tryals of Peter Boss, George Keith ..., 1693 (Wing, T 2254). In 1700 Keith took Anglican orders: D.N.B.; Hull, Furly, pp. 45-8, 112-14, etc.

†2 William Freke (1662-1744; D.N.B.) published early in December 1693 A Dialogue, by way of question and answer, concerning the Deity; and a Brief, but Clear, Confutation of the Doctrine of the Trinity, and sent copies of it to members of both houses of parliament. On 11 December the commons ordered it to be burnt by the public hangman; the lords, on 3 January: C.J.; L.J.
†3 Michael Servetus, 1511-53; physician and anti-Trinitarian writer; burnt as a heretic at Calvin's instigation at Geneva: N.B.G.Calvin's cook is derived from S. Castellion (no. 1646), Contra Libellum Calvini in quo ostendere conatur hæreticos jure gladii coercendos esse, 1612; Dutch translation in Castellion, Opera, Haarlem, 1613. For the passage see Buisson, Castellion, ii. 53 (Buisson remarks that 'cook' is an exaggeration; the man was Calvin's famulus or secretary); for the book, ibid. ii. 29-55, 365, 376-8. L.L., no. 620.
In support of the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes Roman Catholic controversialists cited the execution of Servetus to show that Protestants held the same views as themselves on the use of force to extirpate heresy: J. Jacquot in Autour de Michel Servet, etc., pp. 116-29. Van Limborch intended to treat it at length in his projected 'Reformatorum de poena haereticorum sententia' (no. 2596 n.)

†2 The marginal summaries and index, 'with a great number of short additions, amendments, and alterations are advantages of this Edition, which the Bookseller hopes will make it sell. For as to the larger additions and alterations, I have obliged him, and he has promised me to print them by themselves, so that the former Edition may not be wholly lost to those who have it, but by the inserting in their proper places the passages that will be reprinted alone, to that purpose, the former Book may be made as little defective as possible.'
The additions and alterations were printed on folio leaves; on both sides for the longer passages (e.g. the new II. xxvii); on one side only for the shorter; the sheets containing the latter were to be cut into slips to be inserted at the places indicated. This emerges from some leaves inserted in Tyrrell's copy of the Essay: nos. 1800 n., 3263 n. Very small alterations could be entered in writing.

The principal books for the early history of the Bank are Sir John Clapham, The Bank of England, 1944; J. E. Thorold Rogers, The First Nine Years of the Bank of England, 1887 (this quotes weekly prices of Bank stock from 1694 to 1703; the dates are those of the issues of Houghton's Collections, from which Rogers took the prices; the dates of the quotations were usually three days earlier: Horsefield, pp. 254-5); W. †4 A tally was 'a stick or rod of wood, usually squared, marked on one side with transverse notches representing the amount of a debt or payment. The rod being cleft lengthwise across the notches, the debtor and creditor each retained one of the halves, the agreement or tallying of which constituted legal proof of the debt, etc.'; such a cloven rod was given by the Exchequer as 'the official receipt ... for a tax ... paid, or in acknowledgement of a loan to the sovereign': O.E.D. Tallies were given at this time to persons making advances to the king in anticipation of revenue: Feavearyear, p. 110, etc.

Doctor Brown was graduat at Aberdeen, he was never out of this Country except once at London, wher he had occasion to converse with Dr Sydnham, of whose opinions he is very fond, especialy of the method of purging in feavers, which he carrys a greater length then it seems it was designed by that Author, for he uses it universaly in all feavers. and has published a book concerning it called Schedula Vindicatoria which, tho it have some good things in it, yet the style is so harsh and the connection so bad that one knows not what to make of the most part of it. This gave occasion to some Physitians to write a little Pamphlet against him wherin ther was more of bantre than serious, to which the Looking-glass was ane answer. [Probably A Survey of the Vindicatory Schedule and In speculo Teipsum: p. 354 nn.] His reputation for knowledg and learning is but very smal, he has never been well founded, and tho some of his thoughts taken singly are good, yet when he endeavours to put them together in a system they do not frame and look like a disjoynted peece of work. as for his success in the cure of feavers, he having seldom the occasion to consult with other Physitians, it must depend upon his own testimony both as to the certainty of the thing and as to the circumstances the sick were in, but it is certain that no body talks so much of it as he does himself. As for the opinion of Physitians here concerning the method of curing feavers by purging, some are for it, and some against it, but none that I know of are for it in all sorts of feavers except Dr Brown.

†1 At this time, prior to the publication of Toland's Christianity not Mysterious, Deism was regarded by the orthodox as nearly identical with atheism: quotations from R. †8 Montagu. The government had at this time outstanding tallies for about £5,000,000 secured on tax funds which had proved deficient. Montagu proposed that there should be an unlimited subscription for new Bank stock, payable four-fifths
― 731 ―
in tallies and one-fifth in the Bank's own bills or notes. The government was to pay 8 per cent interest on the tallies until they were paid off and on the tallies already held by the Bank. The proposal was put into operation by an act, 8 and 9 Wm. III, c. 20, which received the royal assent on 1 April 1697.
Tallies and the Bank's own bills and notes were to be taken at par although both classes of instruments were depreciated to such an extent that for about £65 worth of tallies and bills or notes a subscriber was credited with £100 stock. Altogether £1,001,171 10s. was subscribed. This development was known as the ingrafting of tallies. The new subscription was not added to the Bank's capital of £1,200,000, but was repaid to subscribers between 1698 and 1707: Dickson, pp. 353-5; Clapham, i. 47-52; Horsefield, pp. 134-5; no. 3185.
